sum: Combine completed instruction count, cycles per instruction and clock period in one fixed-frequency measurement.
x: Two processors can run at the same clock frequency and complete the same task in different times. Clock speed alone does not specify how much useful work a processor completes. To reason about CPU performance you need one equation. Computer architects call it the iron law of processor performance, and every other lesson in this module is about improving one of its three terms. The equation For one thread’s measured CPU execution interval at a fixed clock frequency, using matching instruction and cycle counts, run time is the product of three ratios: instructions per program, cycles per instruction and seconds per cycle. What each term really means: IC (instruction count) is the dynamic count of architecturally completed instructions in the measured scope, not how many lines it has. A loop of 3 instructions that runs a million times contributes 3 million. CPI (cycles per instruction) is total counted cycles divided by completed instructions. It is not the average latency of individual overlapping instructions. The clock period is the length of one cycle, the reciprocal of the clock frequency. The clock period follows directly from the frequency. For a 3 GHz clock: With variable frequency, use compatible cycle/time accounting or sum over fixed-frequency intervals. Waiting off-CPU and concurrent threads need separate accounting; CPU time is not automatically wall-clock response time. The units cancel neatly: instructions × cycles per instruction × seconds per cycle leaves seconds. That is a good check whenever you do one of these calculations. A first calculation A program executes 2 × 10⁹ instructions with an average CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz CPU. First count the cycles, then divide by how many cycles happen each second: Key takeaways Use matching instruction, cycle and time scopes at a fixed clock frequency. CPI is a measured average; overlapping instruction latency is a different quantity. Account separately for off-CPU waiting and variable frequency. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining Linux perf tutorial MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics

t: IPC and the three performance knobs
sum: Read IPC and understand how algorithms, compilers, instruction sets and circuits affect the performance equation.
x: The previous unit combined instruction count, CPI and clock frequency to obtain CPU execution time. This unit reads the same counts as IPC and asks which design decisions change them. All comparisons still need matching measurement scopes. IPC: the same idea, inverted Modern processors can finish several instructions in one cycle, which makes CPI less than 1. People then usually quote its reciprocal, IPC (instructions per cycle): A CPI of 0.5 is an IPC of 2. Both describe the same measured instruction/cycle totals; IPC is just more natural when the number is above 1. Linux's perf stat can report IPC when compatible counters are available and permitted. This is an illustrative, trimmed transcript, not a measurement performed for this lesson: (Actual tool output and available events depend on the system.) Here 6,000,000,000 instructions divided by 3,000,000,000 cycles gives the 2.00 shown, which is a CPI of 0.5. Who controls which term? The three terms are not independent knobs. Each is influenced by different people, and improving one often hurts another. Term Mainly set by Example --------- IC Algorithm, compiler, ISA Different sorting algorithms CPI Microarchitecture, compiler Pipelining, caches Clock period Circuit design, process Logic depth, voltage The algorithm can substantially change the work required. Hardware instructions, accelerators and compiler transformations can also reduce architectural IC. The best improvement depends on the measured bottleneck. The compiler changes IC (removing redundant work, vectorising four additions into one instruction) and CPI (ordering instructions so they don't wait on each other). The instruction set (ISA) matters too. x86's rep movsb encodes a repeated byte copy using one instruction encoding. Implementation work and performance-event counting of repeated instructions need inspection; one compact encoding is not a count of the operations performed. Instruction count is not a fair standalone comparison across ISAs; counts also depend on vectorization and other instructions. The microarchitecture (how the chip implements the ISA) drives CPI: pipelining, branch prediction, out-of-order execution and caches all aim to lower it. The circuit and process technology set how short a cycle can be. Key takeaways IPC and CPI are reciprocals for the same counted instructions and cycles. Instruction count is dynamic, so source lines and executable size do not determine it. Changing an algorithm, compiler or implementation can affect more than one performance term. Further reading Linux perf tutorial MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics

t: Compute CPI from an instruction mix
sum: Use a hypothetical additive cost model to find which instruction class contributes most to average CPI.
x: A program mixes arithmetic, memory and control-flow instructions. This unit uses an explicitly additive teaching model: the listed cycle costs do not overlap. Real superscalar measurements need consistent cycle attribution rather than the sum of instruction latencies. CPI is an average over an instruction mix For a simple non-overlapping cost model, assign a cycle cost to each instruction class. The overall CPI is then its instruction-frequency-weighted average. On an overlapping superscalar processor, adding individual instruction latencies would double-count shared cycles; a measured CPI breakdown needs a consistent attribution method. The following numbers are hypothetical additive costs: Here is the calculation in Python for a hypothetical mix: The same working by hand: Notice that loads are only 20% of instructions but contribute 1.0 of the 2.2 cycles, almost half. This is how architects decide what to optimise: find the term that dominates the weighted sum. Halving the load cost (5 cycles to 2.5) saves 0.2 × 2.5 = 0.5 cycles per instruction and brings CPI to 1.7; halving the ALU cost (1 cycle to 0.5) saves only 0.25 and brings it to 1.95. Key takeaways Weight each class cost by its share of executed instructions. Do not add overlapping instruction latencies as if execution were serial. Compare weighted savings before choosing which class to optimise. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics

sum: Calculate total time or cycles when clock rate, instruction count and CPI change together.
x: Use the fixed-frequency iron law from the earlier units. Each example below changes one or more terms, so a headline clock rate or instruction count cannot settle the comparison. Comparing machines correctly The iron law stops you being fooled by any one number. Faster clock, slower machine Same program, same instruction count (10⁹). Machine A runs at 2 GHz with CPI 1.2; machine B runs at 3 GHz with CPI 2.0. Apply the iron law to each: A is about 1.11× faster despite a clock 33% slower. More instructions, less time The same trap catches compilers. Compiler X emits 1.0 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.1; compiler Y emits 0.8 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5. On the same clock, compare total cycles: When you compare, compute total cycles (IC × CPI) on the same clock, or total time on different clocks. Never compare one term in isolation. Speedup Performance is the reciprocal of time, so "A is S times faster than B" means: Be careful with phrases like "50% faster": it means a speedup of 1.5, not that time fell by 50% (which would be a speedup of 2, twice as fast). Key takeaways On one fixed clock, compare total cycles; on different clocks, compare execution time. A reduction in instruction count can lose if CPI rises enough. Speedup divides old time by new time; halving time doubles speed. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics

sum: Distinguish task completion time from the MIPS rating, clock frequency and peak throughput scores.
x: Earlier units established CPU execution time, IPC and weighted CPI. This unit tests performance headlines against those definitions. The examples remain hypothetical fixed-frequency measurements unless explicitly identified otherwise. Misleading metrics The megahertz myth A shorter clock period can be offset by a larger CPI, for example if a deeper design incurs more recovery cycles on mispredicted branches. Exact historical processor stage counts and cross-product performance comparisons are omitted here: they need a specific primary hardware description and benchmark, rather than a general clock-speed anecdote. The MIPS rating The MIPS rating (millions of instructions per second; nothing to do with the MIPS instruction set) counts how many millions of instructions a machine completes each second: As a throughput score it does not account for how many instructions the task requires, so it rewards a machine or compiler that runs lots of cheap instructions. For example, on a 1 GHz CPU, compiler P emits 1.2 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.0, and compiler Q emits 0.6 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5: A MIPS rating can describe instruction throughput, but it predicts task completion time only when the relevant dynamic instruction counts are fixed. The same binary can still execute different counts on different inputs or execution paths. Peak numbers Vendors quote peak IPC or peak FLOPS: what the chip can do if every functional unit is busy every cycle. Real code waits on memory and mispredicted branches. Realized IPC depends on instruction mix, dependency chains, front-end delivery, memory behaviour and prediction. No universal IPC value or dominant bottleneck is asserted for databases or web servers. Measure, don't guess perf stat gives you cycles, instructions and IPC for a real run. Low IPC alone does not identify the cause: serial arithmetic dependencies, execution-unit pressure, front-end limits, branch recovery and memory stalls can all contribute. Use architecture-specific counters and profiles before choosing a fix. How the performance techniques fit Every technique in the following lessons attacks one term of the iron law, and usually costs something in another: Pipelining overlaps instructions so CPI approaches 1 and the clock can be shorter. Cost: hazards. Forwarding and branch prediction claw back the CPI lost to hazards. Superscalar and out-of-order execution push CPI below 1 (IPC above 1). Cost: area, power and complexity. Power and thermal limits constrained frequency scaling and encouraged multicore designs. Frequency did not stop increasing altogether. Multiple cores can improve throughput and can reduce the time of a parallelizable single job. Key takeaways The MIPS rating measures instruction throughput and predicts time only when the relevant dynamic count is fixed. Peak IPC or FLOPS needs a workload and a stated counting convention. Low IPC suggests investigation, not a unique bottleneck diagnosis. Further reading Linux perf tutorial MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining Intel: top-down analysis MIT: processor-performance equation and pipeline mechanics

sum: Trace a load and see why overlapping instructions improves throughput.
x: Imagine doing laundry. Each load needs washing (30 minutes), drying (30) and folding (30). Doing four loads one after another takes 6 hours. But the moment the first load moves to the dryer, the washer is free. Start the second load then, and four loads finish in 3 hours. No individual load got faster: each still takes 90 minutes. What improved is throughput, the rate at which loads come out the end. That is pipelining, and it is a fundamental technique in CPU design. Executing one instruction A simplified processor can organize instructions into a common sequence of stages. The classic RISC design, from the MIPS processors of the 1980s and the Patterson and Hennessy textbooks, splits it into five stages: Stage Name Does --------- IF Fetch Read instruction at PC ID Decode Decode, read registers EX Execute ALU op or address MEM Memory Load or store data WB Write back Write result register Follow a load, lw x1, 8(x2) (RISC-V: load a 32-bit word using x2 plus an eight-byte offset; on RV64I, sign-extend it into x1): IF: read the instruction from the instruction cache at the address in the program counter (PC); compute the sequential next PC by adding four bytes for the uncompressed base instruction used here. ID: decode the opcode; read register x2; sign-extend the immediate 8. EX: the ALU adds the eight-byte offset to x2 to form the byte address. MEM: read the data cache at that address. WB: write the loaded value into x1. Other instructions use a subset. An add x3, x4, x5 does its addition in EX and has nothing to do in MEM. A store sw writes memory in MEM and has nothing to write back. A branch compares registers and decides the next PC. With a pipeline Pipelining puts the next instruction into IF as soon as the current one moves on to ID. Once the pipeline is full, all five stages are busy, each with a different instruction: Read it column by column. In cycle 5, i1 is writing back, i2 is in MEM, i3 in EX, i4 in ID, and (if there were one) i5 in IF. From cycle 5 on, one instruction completes every cycle: an ideal CPI of 1. Here is a small Python function that draws the diagram: Key takeaways IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB describe the five-stage teaching pipeline. Several instructions occupy different stages simultaneously. The ideal scalar pipeline completes one instruction per cycle after filling. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification BOOM implementation: pipeline

t: Pipeline registers set the clock budget
sum: Compare a single-cycle clock with the slowest pipelined stage and explain why interstage registers are necessary.
x: Continue with the five-stage load/store teaching pipeline: IF fetches, ID decodes and reads registers, EX operates, MEM accesses data, and WB writes a result. The stage delays below are hypothetical. They illustrate timing budgets, not a particular fabricated processor. Without a pipeline A simple single-cycle processor does all five steps in one long clock cycle. The cycle must be long enough for the slowest instruction. Using these hypothetical combinational stage delays, with single-cycle boundary overhead ignored: A load uses all five steps, so the single cycle must cover their sum: So the clock period is 800 ps (1.25 GHz), and each instruction takes one cycle. Most of the hardware sits idle most of the time: while the ALU is working, the fetch unit has nothing to do. Pipeline registers Between each pair of stages sits a pipeline register (named IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB). At every clock edge, each stage's output is latched into the next register. This holds everything the instruction still needs: its operand values, destination register number and control signals (is it a load? does it write a register?). Without these registers, the next instruction would overwrite the values the previous one is still using. The clock period The clock now only needs to cover the slowest pipeline stage, not the whole instruction. In reality a pipeline register adds its own delay, setup time and clock skew, which must be budgeted: Here the slowest stages are IF, EX and MEM at 200 ps. With no overhead the period is 200 ps. Assuming 20 ps of combined per-cycle boundary overhead gives 200 + 20 = 220 ps; this is a teaching assumption, not a measured device value. Key takeaways The single-cycle period covers the longest whole instruction path in this model. The pipeline period covers the slowest stage plus boundary overhead. Interstage registers keep one instruction’s operands and controls aligned. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining BOOM implementation: pipeline

sum: Count a finite burst and distinguish instruction latency from long-run throughput.
x: Use a scalar five-stage pipeline with one-cycle stages and no hazards. The earlier timing unit used an 800 ps single-cycle period and a 200 ps pipelined period before register overhead; IF, EX and MEM each took 200 ps, while ID and WB took 100 ps. Keep these assumptions explicit in the calculations. How much faster? Take a run of instructions on an initially empty, single-issue pipeline with no stalls. The first instruction needs one cycle per stage to come out, and each later one comes out 1 cycle after the one before: For 1,000 instructions, compare the single-cycle design with the pipelined one: The ideal long-run speedup approaches the number of stages, here five: that requires perfectly balanced stages, so each stage takes one fifth of the single-cycle period, and no register overhead. We got about 4 for two reasons: Unbalanced stages. ID and WB need only 100 ps but get a full 200 ps slot. The pipeline runs at the pace of its slowest stage. Fill and drain. The first four cycles have at least one empty stage in this five-stage model. With 1,000 instructions this barely matters (4 cycles); with 5 it would matter a lot. For a long run, the instruction count is so large that the fill cycles become negligible and the speedup settles at the ratio of the two clock periods: Throughput and latency differ With a 200 ps cycle, a single load now takes five cycles of 200 ps, 1,000 ps in all, to pass through, compared with 800 ps unpipelined. In this comparison, pipelining raises throughput while increasing instruction latency. Balanced stages with no register overhead could preserve latency; real overhead and imbalance often increase it. Enough independent work allows the improved throughput to outweigh fill/drain overhead; billions of instructions are not required. Key takeaways An initially empty unstalled scalar run needs the stage count plus one cycle for each additional instruction. Fill/drain overhead matters more for a short burst. Stage imbalance and register overhead reduce long-run gains; latency need not improve. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining

sum: Explain which ISA properties simplify pipelining and why splitting one stage changes the bottleneck.
x: The previous units showed that the slowest stage sets the pipeline period. This unit asks what makes fetching and decoding manageable, and what changes when a designer adds stages. These are implementation choices; the ISA alone does not prescribe one pipeline. Why RISC was designed for this Regular encodings and load/store operations, as in the base RISC teaching model here, simplify pipeline design: Fixed-length base instructions (32 bits in the model; compressed forms such as RISC-V C differ) let IF fetch one per cycle and let ID start decoding before it knows what the instruction is. Register specifiers in regular positions across formats, allow register selection alongside opcode decoding. Load/store data operations: ordinary arithmetic in this model uses registers; separate loads and stores transfer data. Instruction fetch and specialised atomic operations are outside that simplification. Naturally aligned scalar accesses avoid line splits when their power-of-two size does not exceed the line size and divides it. Real ISAs can also allow unaligned accesses, with additional handling. x86, with variable-length instructions from 1 to 15 bytes and memory operands on arithmetic, needs additional instruction-boundary and operand handling relative to this simplified fixed-width, load/store teaching design. Many Intel and AMD implementations translate x86 instructions into simple, RISC-like micro-operations (µops), and pipeline those. Real pipelines The five-stage design is a teaching model. Real implementations divide work differently, and “pipeline depth” may refer to different instruction paths or recovery events. A cross-product table of stage counts is omitted because comparable primary documentation was not established for every entry. Splitting a critical stage can shorten the clock period, while adding register overhead and potentially delaying particular result or branch-resolution paths. Not every hazard penalty necessarily increases: that depends on where stages are added and which bypass paths exist. Where it goes wrong The ideal "one instruction per cycle" assumes every instruction can enter the pipeline the cycle after the previous one. Three things break that: Structural hazards: two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle. Data hazards: an instruction needs a result the previous one hasn't produced yet. Control hazards: after a branch, the CPU doesn't know which instruction to fetch next. The following hazard units cover each kind and the tricks, chiefly forwarding, that keep this pipeline flowing. Key takeaways Regular register fields and load/store data operations simplify the teaching pipeline. RISC-V compressed instructions and real unaligned accesses need extra handling. Splitting one stage helps only until another path or overhead sets the period. Further reading RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining BOOM implementation: pipeline Intel implementation and optimisation manuals

sum: Recognise structural hazards and distinguish true register data flow from register-name reuse.
x: Use IF, ID, EX, MEM and WB from the preceding pipeline units. Keep the model assumptions below: the exact stall counts follow from the stated stage timing, not from the RISC-V instruction set itself. This lesson uses a single-issue, in-order five-stage teaching pipeline with one-cycle stages, cache hits, register writes before reads in the same cycle, and the stated bypass paths. Numerical stalls below belong to this model, not every real CPU. The earlier overlap unit's pipeline diagram assumed every instruction could start the cycle after the previous one. Real programs break that assumption constantly. The very next instruction often needs the result the current one is still computing. A situation that prevents the next instruction from starting in its slot is a hazard. There are three kinds, and the hardware has a different trick for each. Whatever is left over shows up as extra CPI. Structural hazards A structural hazard happens when two instructions need the same piece of hardware in the same cycle. The classic example is memory. In cycle 4, instruction i1 is in MEM reading data while i4 is in IF fetching an instruction. With one single-ported memory, one of them must wait. Possible fixes include stalling, adding ports or separating resources. Many CPUs use separate L1 instruction and data caches (a "modified Harvard" design), and register files often have multiple read and write ports. The ideal five-stage design assumes sufficient independent resources to avoid these structural hazards; in wider, real processors they appear as contention for ports and functional units. Data hazards Consider: sub reads its registers in ID, in cycle 3. But add only writes x1 in WB, in cycle 5. If nothing intervenes, sub reads the old x1. This is a read-after-write (RAW) hazard, also called a true dependence. Option 1: stall The simplest fix is for the hardware to detect the dependence in ID and hold sub there, inserting bubbles (do-nothing slots, effectively nops) into EX until add has written x1. A common trick helps: the register file is written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second half. So sub can read x1 in the same cycle that add writes it back (cycle 5). That still means sub waits in ID for cycles 3 and 4: two stall cycles for every back-to-back dependency. Since dependent instructions are extremely common, this would be ruinous for CPI. WAR and WAW There are two other orderings of register access: Write after read (WAR): a later instruction writes a register an earlier one still needs to read. Write after write (WAW): two instructions write the same register, and the final value must come from the later one. These are name dependences: they exist only because two instructions happen to reuse a register name, not because data flows between them. In the in-order 5-stage pipeline they cannot cause trouble, since every instruction reads in ID and writes in WB in program order. They become real problems in out-of-order processors, where register renaming removes them (the later register-renaming unit). Key takeaways A shared single memory port can conflict between instruction fetch and data access. RAW carries a produced value; WAR and WAW arise from reuse of register names. The stated register timing permits same-cycle write then read, leaving two stalls without bypasses. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification BOOM implementation: rename stage

t: Forward values and handle load-use stalls
sum: Choose the newest available result, exclude the zero register and explain the remaining one-cycle load-use gap.
x: This unit uses the scalar five-stage pipeline with one-cycle cache-hit stages and operand bypasses into EX. A dependent instruction needs its input at the start of EX; an ALU result appears at the end of EX, while loaded data appears at the end of MEM. Exclude the zero register RISC-V x0 always reads zero and discards writes. A forwarding comparison must reject destination x0: otherwise an attempted write could be incorrectly supplied to a later reader. For example, add x0, x1, x2 must not affect the x0 operand of add x3, x0, x4. Option 2: forwarding The key observation: the value sub needs exists at the end of add's EX stage, in cycle 3. It just hasn't reached the register file yet. Forwarding (also called bypassing) adds wires and multiplexers that route results from the pipeline registers straight back to the ALU inputs. There are two main paths: EX/MEM to EX: the result of the instruction directly ahead (one instruction back). MEM/WB to EX: the result of the instruction two ahead. A forwarding unit compares the source register numbers of the instruction entering EX with the destination register numbers in EX/MEM and MEM/WB. If they match (and the earlier instruction really writes a register, and the register isn't x0), it selects the forwarded value instead of the stale one from ID/EX. If both match, the most recent producer takes priority, but its value must actually be available: a load in EX/MEM does not yet provide its loaded data. Stalling must prevent accidentally forwarding that load’s address or an older superseded value. With forwarding, add followed by sub runs with zero stalls. The load-use hazard Forwarding cannot fix everything. A load's data only arrives at the end of MEM: add needs x1 at the start of its EX. If add ran in cycle 4, it would need a value that lw only produces at the end of cycle 4. Time cannot run backwards, so the hardware must stall for one cycle, then forward from MEM/WB. This is the load-use hazard, and a hazard detection unit in ID spots it: "the instruction in EX is a load, and its destination is one of my sources". Key takeaways EX/MEM and MEM/WB bypasses can supply a result before register write-back. A newer producer wins, but an unavailable load result must stall rather than forward its address. A next-instruction EX consumer of a load needs one stall in this teaching model. Further reading RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining

t: Schedule independent work around a load
sum: Reorder a straight-line sequence without changing its values or observable memory behaviour.
x: Continue with a five-stage, single-issue, cache-hit teaching pipeline. ALU-to-ALU forwarding needs no stall; a load immediately followed by an EX consumer needs one. Scheduling fills that gap with useful independent work rather than changing the hardware. The two listings below compute the same two independent expressions only under their stated memory assumptions. Option 3: let the compiler schedule around it Since the load-use stall is predictable, the compiler can reorder independent instructions to fill the gap. For ordinary valid, nonvolatile memory accesses with independent values and no aliasing or observable-order constraints, take a = b + c; d = e + f. The listings below are schematic (symbolic addresses rather than literal RISC-V load/store syntax;! marks a load-use stall and is not an instruction): The naive order has two load-use stalls (marked!). In the scheduled order every load has an independent instruction between it and its first dependent operation, so there are none. Counting cycles for the 8 instructions from first fetch to last write-back: Compilers do this routinely (instruction scheduling), and it matters most on simple in-order cores when the target implements the assumed instruction timing. Key takeaways Move only independent operations across the load-use gap. Memory faults, aliasing, volatile accesses and observable order can forbid a reorder. Count one additional cycle for each remaining bubble in this finite-run model. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification

t: Trace stalls with a dependency model
sum: Use a small readiness-slot simulation and recognise the hardware behaviour it intentionally omits.
x: The previous unit compared two schedules for eight instructions. This unit turns the same assumptions into a small executable model: in-order issue, one-cycle stages, and all operands needed by EX. With forwarding, the earlier naive schedule had two stalls and its reordered version had none; without forwarding, same-cycle WB then ID determines when a consumer may continue. Counting stalls in code This function counts stall cycles for a straight-line program on the 5-stage pipeline. It records the earliest logical issue slot compatible with each dependency. With forwarding this is not the cycle when the register file itself contains the new value. Program entries are (op, dst, srcs) with integer register IDs 0–31, dst=None for no register result, and register 0 hard-wired to zero. All forwarded sources, including store data, are required by EX in this simplified model; it does not model a separate late store-data bypass, branches, cache misses or multicycle units: On the naive sequence above it returns 2 with forwarding and 8 without; on the scheduled one, 0 and 4. For this sequence and model, forwarding removes more stalls than scheduling alone; combining them removes all modelled stalls. Key takeaways Readiness slots represent when a dependent operation may start, not register-file update time. Loads and ordinary ALU results have different forwarding latencies. This model omits branches, cache misses, multicycle units and a late store-data bypass. Further reading MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification

sum: Compare branch-resolution choices and combine nonoverlapping hazard penalties.
x: Use the same scalar IF–ID–EX–MEM–WB teaching design. The earlier data-hazard units established forwarding and one-cycle load-use stalls; this unit adds branch control flow. All branch penalties below specify their resolution stage and prediction rule, so they are model-specific. Control hazards After fetching a branch in cycle 1, what should IF fetch in cycle 2? The branch hasn't even been decoded, let alone compared its registers. This is a control hazard. Suppose the branch outcome is known at the end of EX (cycle 3). Options: Stall until the branch resolves: 2 lost cycles on every branch. Predict not taken: keep fetching sequentially. If the branch isn't taken, no cost. If it is, flush the two wrongly fetched instructions (turn them into bubbles) and fetch from the target: a 2-cycle penalty. Resolve earlier: add a comparator and target adder in ID so the branch is decided in cycle 2. The penalty falls to 1 cycle, but now the branch may need forwarding into ID and can stall on an instruction ahead of it. Branch delay slot: classic MIPS normal delay slots execute on both paths; some branch-likely forms have annulment rules. The compiler fills the slot with useful work when it can (or a nop). It provides one architecturally executed slot; that does not necessarily hide the entire branch penalty of a particular implementation, but became a burden when pipelines got deeper and wider. RISC-V and ARM64 do not have delay slots. Real processors use dynamic branch prediction, covered in the following prediction units. Putting numbers on it For a long run in this scalar model, ignoring fill/drain and avoiding double-counting overlapping penalties, hazards add stall cycles to the ideal CPI of 1. Each hazard type contributes how often it can occur, times how often it actually bites, times what it costs: A worked example: 25% of instructions are loads, and 40% of those are immediately followed by a dependent instruction (1-cycle stall each). 15% are branches; with predict-not-taken, 60% of them are taken, costing 2 cycles. Assume these penalties are additive, and the stated dependencies need operands in EX: Notice branches cost more than loads here. That is why branch prediction gets an entire lesson, and why it matters even more in deeper pipelines, where recovery penalties may be larger. Exact real-core cycle counts require a specified core and measurement. Keep the earlier zero-register rule The data-hazard units also excluded writes to RISC-V x0 from forwarding. Control-hazard accounting does not relax that correctness requirement. Key takeaways Resolving a branch later leaves more sequential fetches to discard in the stated model. Earlier resolution can trade fewer flushes for operand waits or a slower clock. Add hazard contributions only when their costs do not overlap. Further reading MIPS architecture manual: branches and delay slots RISC-V unprivileged ISA specification BOOM implementation: branch prediction

t: Cost branch misses and apply static rules
sum: Estimate additive branch CPI and distinguish fixed prediction rules from learned behaviour.
x: A processor can fetch and execute instructions beyond a branch before its direction and target are known. If its prediction is wrong, it must discard younger wrong-path work and redirect execution. How much work is lost depends on the processor and when the branch resolves. Evidence limits Universal branch frequencies, prediction accuracies, pipeline depths and product-specific predictor details are omitted: they need a named workload and reliable documentation or measurements. The numerical examples below are explicit teaching models. What a misprediction costs In an additive model with a fixed average recovery penalty and no overlap with other counted stalls, mispredictions add this many cycles to every instruction on average: Why 95% isn't good enough Assume unchanged retired instruction count and clock frequency, with additive penalties. 20% of instructions are branches, the predictor is 95% accurate, and the penalty is 15 cycles. The core is 4-wide, with an ideal CPI of 0.25 when every prediction is right: The program runs 1.6× slower than with perfect prediction. Getting to 98% accuracy, with the other assumptions unchanged, brings the extra branch contribution down to 0.06 cycles per instruction. The wrong-prediction fraction is now 2% rather than 5%. Lower base CPI makes a given additional CPI more significant. Width and pipeline organisation can affect recovery, but neither alone determines a universal penalty or area cost. Static prediction The simplest predictors use fixed rules with no history: Always not taken: just keep fetching sequentially. Simple; it misses each taken iteration of a loop-back branch. Backward taken, forward not taken (BTFN): a branch that jumps backwards is probably a loop, so predict taken; a forward branch is probably an if, so predict not taken. This is a heuristic, not a guarantee about source-level control flow. Compilers help by laying out code so the likely path falls through. GCC and Clang's __builtin_expect, C++20's [[likely]] and [[unlikely]], and profile-guided optimisation can inform these layout and optimisation decisions; they do not guarantee a particular hardware predictor action. Key takeaways Branch fraction, miss rate and recovery cycles determine the additive miss contribution. A small additional CPI is a larger slowdown when base CPI is already low. BTFN is a direction heuristic; compiler hints guide optimisation without guaranteeing hardware action. Further reading McFarling: Combining Branch Predictors (original report) GCC: branch expectation built-in BOOM implementation: branch prediction

sum: Trace one-bit and two-bit predictor state, warm-up, loop exits and predictor aliasing.
x: This unit predicts taken versus not-taken for each observed branch. Taken jumps to a target; not-taken continues sequentially. The counters are teaching models updated after each known Boolean outcome, with no speculative updates or recovery. Dynamic prediction: learning from history The branch history table In this simple bimodal model, a branch history table (BHT, also called a pattern history table here) is an array indexed by selected bits of the branch’s address (PC). Each counter remembers the outcomes mapped to it. Other predictors index history tables differently, and shared entries need not belong to just one branch. A 1-bit entry stores the last outcome and predicts it will happen again. It has a flaw with loops. Consider a loop branch that is taken 9 times and then falls through, with the loop itself run repeatedly: The exit mispredicts, then flips the bit to N, so the first iteration of the next run mispredicts too: 2 misses per 10, or 80% accuracy. The 2-bit saturating counter A 2-bit saturating counter adds hysteresis: a strongly biased state needs two consecutive opposite outcomes to reverse its prediction. From a weak state, one opposite outcome is enough: Taken increments the counter (stopping at 3), not taken decrements it (stopping at 0), and the top bit is the prediction: A single loop exit moves "strongly taken" to "weakly taken", which still predicts taken next time. Now there is only 1 miss per 10. One-bit: 200 misses in 1,000 (80%). Two-bit: 101 (about 90%; the extra 1 is the first warm-up miss). Predictor aliasing The table is indexed by only some PC bits, so two different branches can share an entry and corrupt each other's counters. This is predictor aliasing. More capacity can reduce interference. Tags help distinguish entries, but finite capacity and partial tags do not eliminate every collision or replacement effect. Key takeaways One-bit predictors reverse their guess after one contrary outcome. A two-bit counter needs two opposite outcomes to move from a strong prediction to the opposite prediction. Initial state and interference matter; the loop accuracy figures state their trace and assumptions. Further reading McFarling: Combining Branch Predictors (original report) BOOM implementation: branch prediction

sum: Mix branch address bits with recent outcomes to distinguish correlated contexts.
x: The preceding unit’s two-bit counter uses one state to predict one branch. Here, recent history selects among counters. The executable model observes outcomes in order; it is an algorithm demonstration, not a cycle-accurate predictor in a current commercial CPU. Correlation: using global history A dedicated two-bit counter without a history-based index learns only from the outcomes sent to that counter. But branches are often correlated with each other: The following is source-level pseudocode; assume x and y stay unchanged. Compiler lowering may introduce, remove or invert machine branches. The third condition is determined by the first two conditions. When corresponding machine branches and relevant history are available, this provides a learnable correlation. A predictor that knows the last few outcomes of all branches can learn this. A global history register (GHR) is a shift register holding the outcomes of the most recent branches (1 = taken). The gshare predictor (McFarling, 1993) XORs the GHR with the branch's PC to index a table of 2-bit counters: In the example, a branch whose low PC bits are 1011 sees history 0110 and uses counter 13. The same branch now gets a different counter for each recent history, so it can learn patterns. For the following single-branch model, pass Boolean outcomes and an integer PC; it uses the low PC bits directly, without modelling instruction alignment or speculative history recovery. A pattern that defeats a plain 2-bit saturating counter is strictly alternating outcomes, T N T N: Starting weakly not-taken, a lone 2-bit saturating counter mispredicts all 1,000 of these (it bounces between the two weak states). gshare, after a 3-miss warm-up, gets every one right, because "last outcome was T" and "last outcome was N" select different counters. The same gshare with only 4 bits of history produces 108 misses in the 1,000-outcome nine-taken-then-exit loop from the preceding counter unit (10.8%): it can't see far enough back to count to 9. That is the motivation for long histories. Key takeaways Global history carries context from recent branch outcomes. Gshare mixes that history with a branch address to select a counter. The trace model uses raw low PC bits and omits alignment and speculative history repair. Further reading McFarling: Combining Branch Predictors (original report) BOOM implementation: branch prediction

t: Predict targets and compare predictor families
sum: Separate direction, target and return prediction and understand what newer history structures add.
x: Earlier units taught one-bit/two-bit counters, predictor aliasing and gshare’s global history. This unit keeps that direction-prediction context and adds target selection: knowing that a branch is taken does not by itself tell fetch which address to read next. Modern predictors Tournament predictors combine different predictors, such as local and global history, with a chooser trained to select between them. TAGE (Seznec and Michaud, 2006) combines a base predictor with tagged tables using geometrically increasing history lengths. Long histories can distinguish contexts that short histories merge. Matching and alternate-prediction policies vary with the TAGE design. Perceptron predictors (Jiménez and Lin, 2001) predict using a learned weighted sum of signed history bits and a bias. A single perceptron has a linear-separability limitation; it cannot represent every Boolean history pattern. These are predictor families, not a verified inventory of any current commercial CPU. Product-specific implementation claims are omitted because sufficiently reliable documentation was not established here. Predicting the target, not just the direction Direction alone does not supply the next fetch address. An early target prediction can redirect fetch before decoding and executing the branch; exact stages and latencies depend on the design. The branch target buffer (BTB) is a cache, indexed by PC, of "there is a branch at this address, and last time it went to that address". In the teaching design, IF looks up the BTB in parallel with the instruction cache; real organisations can differ. The return address stack (RAS) predicts ret instructions. Conceptually, recognised calls push return addresses and returns pop them. Real structures have finite capacity and may lose synchronisation; prediction is not guaranteed correct. A last-target BTB does not track nested caller context at the same return instruction; a return stack supplies that context. Indirect branch predictors handle jumps through registers (virtual method calls, switch jump tables, interpreter dispatch) by combining the PC with history to pick among several targets. Predictors are shared state On affected processors, predictor state can allow one security context to influence indirect-branch speculation in another. Spectre variant 2 exploits such mistraining, together with a disclosure mechanism. Sharing and isolation depend on the processor, firmware, operating system and enabled mitigations; this is not a claim that every CPU exposes all predictor state across domains. Key takeaways TAGE, tournament and perceptron predictors are families rather than a product inventory. A taken direction also needs a target for early redirection. Return prediction uses call context; predictor isolation depends on the processor and mitigations. Further reading Seznec and Michaud: TAGE (original paper) Jiménez and Lin: perceptron prediction (original paper) BOOM implementation: branch prediction Spectre: original research paper

sum: Explain sorted-data behaviour and evaluate branchless source without assuming a speedup.
x: A predictor learns machine-level branches, while a compiler can transform source control flow. The following C fragments are illustrative loop bodies with explicit types and valid-array assumptions. Their numerical results can be checked, but they establish no timing advantage for any particular phone or processor. Writing code that predicts well Data-dependent branches Illustrative C loop body: assume data is a valid array of uint8_t, n is its length (size_t), and sum is uint64_t initially zero. Include <stdint.h> and <stddef.h>. Unsigned accumulation is defined modulo 2^64: If byte values are independently uniform over 0–255 and unpredictable from available history, the condition is a fair coin flip. If a machine branch remains, history prediction has expected accuracy 50%. Sorting the same values produces long runs of false then true conditions, which simple predictors learn. This can reduce misprediction cost, but supplies no guaranteed speedup: inspect the generated code and exclude or amortise sorting cost. The compiler may remove the branch in both versions. Branchless code For an unpredictable branch, consider a branchless implementation and measure it. A conditional move (x86 cmov, ARM csel) selects a value without a jump: A compiler can use a conditional move, arithmetic selection or vectorisation; it may also retain a branch. The source form does not promise a particular lowering, which is why naive benchmarks of this effect are often misleading. Branchless is not always faster Branchless selection can introduce data dependencies or work on both alternatives, whereas a predicted branch permits speculative execution. Either source form may compile to the same machine code. Compare generated code and measure the actual workload; on supported Linux systems, perf stat -e branches,branch-misses provides useful counters, subject to hardware availability and permissions. Other habits Keep hot loops simple, with predictable trip counts. In interpreters, "threaded" dispatch (a separate indirect jump per opcode handler) can give a PC-indexed indirect predictor more context than one central switch, if the compiler preserves separate dispatch sites. This does not guarantee a speedup. Sort or partition data by the condition you'll branch on, if changing order preserves semantics and repeated processing amortises the rearrangement cost. Key takeaways A source condition can become a branch, conditional select or vector code. Sorting may improve a remaining branch’s predictability but has its own cost and semantic constraints. Inspect generated code and measure the actual workload before claiming a speedup. Further reading GCC: branch expectation built-in Linux perf tutorial Spectre: original research paper

t: Find independent work beyond a stall
sum: Distinguish superscalar width from out-of-order scheduling and preserve the architectural execution contract.
x: A scalar pipeline, however well forwarded and predicted, peaks at one instruction per cycle. In this instruction-level model, sustaining CPI below 1 requires starting more than one instruction per cycle on average. That is superscalar execution. In-order superscalar execution can improve throughput, but a blocked instruction can prevent younger independent work from issuing. Out-of-order execution finds ready work further ahead while preserving the architectural rules. The 200-cycle load used below is hypothetical, not a universal DRAM latency. In-order retirement does not imply sequentially consistent interthread memory ordering. The following units separate scheduling, register versions and recovery. Instruction-level parallelism Instruction-level parallelism (ILP) is the number of instructions in a stretch of code that could, in principle, run at the same time. Assume b, c, e and f are already available input values. This Python fragment illustrates the data-flow edges; it does not print a result. The first two can run together; the third must wait. True (RAW) dependences limit the independent operations available in a trace. Branches, fetch limits and memory behaviour also constrain how much parallelism a core can discover and exploit. In-order superscalar A simple in-order superscalar design can issue two instructions per cycle when pairing rules, operands and execution resources allow. Multiple issue does not itself require out-of-order scheduling. The weakness of in-order issue: when one instruction stalls, everything behind it stalls too, even independent work. An out-of-order core runs mul and sub while the load is outstanding. The out-of-order pipeline A common out-of-order (OoO) teaching design has three parts. Real designs differ in µop grouping, scheduler organisation and retirement bookkeeping: Front end, in order: fetch (guided by the branch predictor), decode into µops, rename registers, and allocate tracking space in the reorder buffer (ROB) and in a scheduler. Execution, out of order: each µop waits in the scheduler until its source operands are ready and a suitable unit is free, then becomes eligible to issue. The scheduler chooses among ready operations; result delivery wakes dependent µops. Retirement, in order: the ROB commits results to the architectural state strictly in program order, so exceptions and mispredictions can be handled precisely. Key takeaways Multiple issue and out-of-order scheduling are separate choices. A true dependence chain limits throughput even on a wide core. A common design fetches/renames in order, executes ready work out of order, then retires in order. Further reading BOOM implementation: pipeline BOOM implementation: rename stage BOOM implementation: reorder buffer

sum: Trace physical mappings and remove WAR/WAW without removing true dependences.
x: The preceding unit separated in-order front-end work, ready-instruction execution and in-order retirement. Register renaming supports that design by giving simultaneously live register versions distinct storage. RAW means read-after-write data flow; WAR and WAW are name dependences from reusing an architectural register. Register renaming Out-of-order execution exposes the name dependences from the earlier hazard units: i3 and i4 have nothing to do with i1 and i2; they just reuse the name x1. But if i3 ran before i1 finished, it could have its x1 overwritten by the slow mul (WAW), or i2 could read i3's x1 instead of i1's (WAR). Register renaming assigns distinct storage to simultaneously live register versions. A physical-register implementation maintains more result storage than the architectural register set. Exact counts depend on the core and ISA extensions; they are omitted without a specified implementation. A register alias table (RAT) maps each architectural register to the physical register holding its newest value. This teaching renamer handles a finite straight-line sequence of ordinary register-producing operations. It has no retirement, branches, zero-register semantics or free-list reclamation; names beginning with x are generic, not a complete RISC-V implementation. Output lists each new destination followed by its already-renamed sources: The two x1s are now p32 and p34. Only true register dependences remain in this arithmetic trace (p32 → p33, p34 → p35), so i3 and i4 can execute while the mul is still running. Sources are renamed before the destination, so add x1, x1, x2 correctly reads the old x1. In a simple design without shared physical mappings or other retained references, the free list is refilled at retirement: when an instruction that overwrites x1 commits, the physical register that held the previous x1 can no longer be needed and is freed. Key takeaways Read source mappings before allocating a fresh destination version. Renaming removes register-name WAR and WAW, leaving the real data-flow edges. Retirement may free the previous physical register only once all required references are finished. Further reading BOOM implementation: rename stage

sum: Follow reservation-station values, waiting tags and result broadcasts through a worked snapshot.
x: The previous renaming unit used a separate physical register file. Tomasulo’s original design instead tracks producers with tags in reservation stations and the register status table. Both distinguish versions, but the data structures and recovery mechanisms are different. Tomasulo's algorithm Robert Tomasulo devised the original scheme for the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91 (1967). Its tag-based scheduling and renaming ideas are foundational; modern implementations need not use the original structure. Three structures: Reservation stations (RS) sit in front of each functional unit. Each holds one waiting instruction and, for each operand, either its value (V) or the producer tag (Q) of the reservation station that will produce it. A register status table records, for each register, which RS tag will write it next (blank if the register file value is current). A common data bus (CDB) broadcasts every result as a (tag, value) pair to all reservation stations and the register file at once. Each instruction goes through: Issue: take the next instruction in order, if a matching RS is free. For each source, copy the value from the register file if it is current, or else copy the producing tag. Then set the destination register's status to this RS's tag. Execute: when both operands are values, start executing. Independent instructions overtake stalled ones here. Write result: broadcast (tag, value) on the CDB. Every RS waiting on that tag grabs the value. The register file is updated only if its status still names this tag. Tags distinguish producer versions, providing renaming without requiring the separate physical register file used in the preceding example. A reservation station is not literally a physical register. A worked snapshot Assume enough reservation stations, ready initial registers and sufficiently long operation latencies for all four to issue before any result broadcasts. This is a schematic floating-point instruction trace, not literal IBM instruction syntax: RS Op Operand j Operand k ------------ Load1 L.D addr R2+0 Mult1 MUL Q = Load1 V = F4 Add1 ADD V = F8 V = F2 Add2 SUB Q = Add1 V = F4 Register status: F0 ← Mult1, F2 ← Add2, F6 ← Add1. What happens next: Add1 can start immediately. It copied F8 and F2 at issue, so it waits for neither the load nor the multiply. When Load1 broadcasts, Mult1 captures the value. But F6's status says Add1, not Load1, so the register file is not updated. The load's F6 is now an orphan that only Mult1 needed. That is the WAW hazard with instruction 3, resolved. When Add1 broadcasts, Add2 (the SUB) captures it, and F6 in the register file is updated. SUB overwrites F2, which ADD read. That WAR is harmless: ADD copied F2's value into its RS at issue. Mult1 can finish last despite issuing second; exact completion order depends on latencies and resource availability. What the original lacked The Model 91 wrote results to registers as soon as they were computed, out of order, so a fault in an earlier, slower instruction left a state where later instructions had already taken effect. It could produce imprecise floating-point exceptions. The original tag-and-broadcast algorithm described here lacks the modern speculative branch-recovery machinery. Key takeaways Reservation stations hold copied values or tags naming unfinished producers. A broadcast wakes matching operands and updates a register only if its status still names that producer. Original Tomasulo scheduling is distinct from modern precise retirement and branch recovery. Further reading University of Edinburgh: executable HASE Tomasulo model Smith and Pleszkun: precise interrupts (original paper) BOOM implementation: rename stage Tomasulo: original 1967 paper

t: Retire precisely and recover memory ordering
sum: Explain reorder-buffer commitment, branch squashing, store visibility and speculative loads.
x: The earlier out-of-order units used ready-instruction scheduling and register versions. This unit adds recovery: completed speculative results are not yet an irrevocable architectural update. The circular reorder-buffer and squash behaviour below is a teaching organisation; real cores choose their entry granularity and recovery details. The reorder buffer A reorder buffer, discussed by Smith and Pleszkun in their work on precise interrupts, is one solution. In this teaching model it is a circular queue with one entry per in-flight instruction, in program order. Real entry granularity can differ. Checkpointing and other bookkeeping are also needed for speculative recovery. Instructions execute out of order and write results into their ROB entry (or a physical register), not the architectural state. The head of the ROB retires (commits) only when it has completed. Retirement is in order, up to the supported retirement width per cycle. If the head instruction faulted, the core discards it and every younger entry, and the exception appears exactly at that instruction: precise exceptions. If a branch turns out mispredicted, the core performs a pipeline flush, discarding every younger entry. The rename table is restored to the state it had at the branch, and fetch restarts on the right path. This is what makes speculative execution safe, architecturally: wrong-path instructions execute, but never commit. But "never commits" is not the same as "leaves no trace": some microarchitectural effects, such as cache state, may persist, and recovery of predictor history is implementation-dependent. The Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities exploited exactly such leftover traces. Memory ordering Loads and stores need extra care, because whether two of them conflict depends on addresses that aren't known until they execute. Ordinary cacheable stores retain speculative data in a store queue or buffer until it is safe to commit. Squashing a store must not make its data architecturally visible; related address translation or ownership requests can still affect microarchitectural state. A load may forward bytes from the youngest matching older store when address, data and coverage requirements permit. Partial overlaps or unavailable data can require stalling or replay. A core may let a load pass older stores with unknown addresses (memory disambiguation). If required ordering was violated, recovery re-executes affected work; a pipeline squash starting from the load is one implementation, not a universal mechanism. Key takeaways In-order retirement supports precise architectural exceptions while execution remains out of order. Wrong-path results must not commit, although microarchitectural traces can remain. Loads passing unknown older stores require checking for conflicts and replaying affected work. Further reading BOOM implementation: reorder buffer BOOM implementation: load/store unit Smith and Pleszkun: precise interrupts (original paper) Spectre: original research paper

t: Size the window and account for complexity
sum: Estimate allocation capacity during a blocked retirement interval and recognise the limits of wider execution.
x: In the preceding recovery unit, the reorder buffer retired oldest first. If its oldest instruction waits, younger completed instructions still occupy entries. This unit sizes a hypothetical allocation window and considers other bottlenecks. The numbers are teaching assumptions, not measured commercial ROB sizes. How big is the window? Product data omitted Exact commercial decode widths and ROB sizes are omitted because sufficiently reliable, consistently defined primary-source figures were not established here. Instruction counts, µop counts and ROB entries are not interchangeable. While a load at the head of the reorder buffer waits for memory, nothing behind it can retire, but the CPU front end keeps allocating new entries. How many entries would it take to keep allocating for the whole wait? Convert the miss time to cycles, then multiply by the allocation rate. For a hypothetical 80 ns miss at 4 GHz: So maintaining allocation at four entries per cycle while retirement is blocked would require space for roughly 1,280 entries. This estimates how many entries would be occupied, assuming sufficient independent work and no earlier resource limit. It does not prove all real misses stall for a fixed duration. A larger window may discover independent memory accesses whose latencies overlap (memory-level parallelism); bandwidth and other queues still limit progress. Why not let the compiler do it? VLIW (very long instruction word) designs expose operation grouping to the compiler, shifting much scheduling work from hardware to software. Variable memory latency makes static scheduling harder. Intel Itanium used EPIC, an explicitly parallel design with bundles, instruction groups, predication and speculation; it should not be reduced to a simple VLIW machine with no means to tolerate uncertain execution. A single-cause explanation of its commercial outcome is omitted because this lesson has not established evidence for one. The costs Area and power. Rename tables, schedulers that compare every result tag with every waiting operand each cycle (wakeup and select), and large multi-ported register files are expensive. Scheduler logic scales badly with width. Diminishing returns. Dependence chains, branch recovery, fetch limits and memory behaviour can leave issue capacity unused; achievable IPC is workload- and core-dependent. Mispredictions cost more. More speculative capacity can allow more wrong-path work, but does not by itself fix the recovery latency or amount discarded. These costs are part of why performance per core stopped growing fast enough, helping motivate the multicore and power-budget units that follow. Key takeaways Convert latency to cycles before multiplying by an entry-allocation rate. Free entries alone do not guarantee independent work, memory bandwidth or available queue space. Static and dynamic scheduling trade hardware complexity against information available at run time. Further reading BOOM implementation: pipeline BOOM implementation: reorder buffer BOOM implementation: rename stage BOOM implementation: load/store unit Fisher: original VLIW paper Intel Itanium architecture manual: predication and speculation

sum: Separate voltage, frequency and activity effects without confusing switching power with total energy.
x: Clock increases and microarchitectural improvements contributed to rapid single-thread performance growth before the mid-2000s. Power and thermal constraints made continuing that trend harder and encouraged multicore designs. Clock rates and single-core performance did not stop improving, and there is no universal 3–4 GHz ceiling. Evidence limits Universal cooling wattages, voltage floors, current limits on clock rate and specific cancelled-product explanations are omitted because they need product- and process-specific evidence. The power examples below are models, not operating advice or measured processor specifications. Dynamic power CMOS circuits use energy charging and discharging capacitances. A common approximation for average capacitive switching power is: At fixed activity and capacitance, power is linear in frequency and quadratic in voltage. Higher frequencies may require higher voltage, but voltage is not universally proportional to clock frequency. A cubic frequency rule follows only if voltage also scales proportionally over the modelled range. Total chip power includes leakage, other switching effects and other components. What 15% less frequency buys Drop voltage and frequency by 15% each, keeping activity and capacitance unchanged. Because the voltage is squared, the power ratio is: With unchanged activity and capacitance, capacitive switching power falls about 39%. Performance falls 15% only if throughput is proportional to frequency; total energy and total system power need separate accounting. There is also static (leakage) power: current that trickles through transistors even when they are not switching. It depends on voltage, temperature and transistor design, and cannot be inferred from transistor dimensions alone. Key takeaways Capacitive switching power depends on activity, capacitance, voltage squared and frequency. A cubic frequency rule requires an additional proportional voltage change. Leakage and execution duration prevent a switching-power ratio from determining total system energy. Further reading Texas Instruments: CMOS power consumption Dennard et al.: constant-field scaling (original 1974 paper) Intel processor technology definitions

sum: Combine constant-field scaling factors and identify why its assumptions matter.
x: The previous unit modelled capacitive switching power using activity, capacitance, voltage squared and clock frequency. Dennard scaling combines assumptions about all of these as transistor dimensions shrink. Its factors below are ideal scaling relationships, not a guarantee about a current process node. Dennard scaling and its end In 1974 Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM observed how MOSFETs scale. In the ideal constant-field model, shrink dimensions and voltage by the same factor, 0.7 in the example. In the table and following card, k denotes that dimensionless factor, strictly between zero and one: Quantity Scales by ------ Capacitance per transistor k Voltage k Frequency 1 / k Power per transistor k² Transistors per area 1 / k² Power per area 1 (constant) Multiply the scale factors from the table to see why power density stays constant: With a scaling factor of 0.7, power per transistor falls to 0.49 of its old value while about 2.04 times as many transistors fit in each square millimetre. So power density stays constant: each generation gives more transistors, each faster, at the same watts per square millimetre. Together with Moore's law, this is what drove decades of rising clock speeds. Maintaining performance while reducing supply voltage puts pressure on threshold voltage and leakage. Real devices did not continue the ideal scaling relationships indefinitely. Once voltage and other properties no longer scale together, constant power density no longer follows. Power delivery and heat removal then constrain feasible operating points: the power wall is an engineering constraint, not a universal frequency or wattage limit. Key takeaways Ideal dimension and voltage scaling can keep power density constant at fixed activity. Power per transistor and power per area are different quantities. The power wall is an operating constraint, not a universal frequency ceiling. Further reading Dennard et al.: constant-field scaling (original 1974 paper) Esmaeilzadeh et al.: dark silicon (original 2011 paper) Texas Instruments: CMOS power consumption

t: Compare two slower cores with one faster core
sum: Estimate relative throughput and switching power under explicit parallel-work assumptions.
x: The earlier switching-power unit squared voltage and multiplied by clock frequency. Here the same relationship compares alternative core organisations. The workload is CPU-bound and perfectly parallel in the example; a serial thread would receive only one core’s throughput. Nothing here sets a safe voltage for real hardware. Why more cores instead? For a hypothetical CPU-bound workload, hold per-core activity, capacitance, IPC and work per instruction fixed; ignore shared-system power, communication and leakage. Take one core as the reference operating point. Now build two otherwise identical cores, each at 85% of that core’s frequency and voltage: If the work splits across both cores perfectly, you get 1.7× the throughput for 1.23× the power. If a single-core 1.7× clock increase also required 1.7× voltage, this model would predict about 4.9× switching power. That hypothetical scaling is not a claim that such an operating point is feasible or universally impossible to cool. Multicore can improve aggregate throughput per watt when work can run concurrently, including independent jobs. It does not automatically accelerate one serial task; algorithmic and single-core improvements still matter. Key takeaways Two cores help a single job only if suitable work can run concurrently. Multiply per-core switching power by core count; do not count one slowed core as the total. Frequency/voltage extrapolations are hypothetical ratios rather than feasible operating points. Further reading Texas Instruments: CMOS power consumption Esmaeilzadeh et al.: dark silicon (original 2011 paper) Dennard et al.: constant-field scaling (original 1974 paper)

sum: Keep the serial part of a fixed job when dividing its parallel time across equal cores.
x: Multicore can improve throughput for independent jobs. For one fixed-size job, the serial fraction changes the answer: even perfectly balanced parallel work leaves serial work behind. Assume equal core speeds, unchanged time for the one-core component and zero added parallel overhead for every calculation in this unit. Amdahl's law The catch is that most programs are not perfectly parallel. Split a fixed-size job's single-core run time into a serial part, which still runs on one core, and a parallel part, which divides evenly over the cores. Assume unchanged serial time and no communication, scheduling, contention or other parallel overhead: For example, with 90% parallel code on 8 cores: The same calculation in Python, for several core counts: Even with 90% parallel code, 8 cores give only 4.7×, and no number of cores gets past 10×. The serial 10% dominates. This shows why serial performance still matters for this workload. Other workloads can justify many smaller cores; the model does not prescribe one chip organisation. (Gustafson's law gives a more hopeful view when the problem size grows with the machine; that is covered in the parallel hardware module.) Key takeaways The parallel fraction measures original single-core execution time, not lines of code. More equal cores divide only the parallel component in this ideal fixed-work model. A nonzero serial fraction sets a finite ceiling; parallel overhead can lower realised gains. Further reading MIT: fixed-work parallel speedup MIT Computation Structures: performance and pipelining Esmaeilzadeh et al.: dark silicon (original 2011 paper)

t: Manage power budgets and specialise work
sum: Distinguish DVFS, boost, idle, clock/power gating, heterogeneous placement and dark silicon.
x: The earlier units modelled switching power, ideal scaling and parallel speedup. Real systems also choose supported operating points and where work runs. These mechanisms cooperate under platform-specific power and thermal limits; no universal idle-power figure or accelerator efficiency multiplier follows. Living within a power budget Performance per watt is one important CPU design objective, alongside latency, throughput, cost and other constraints. The main techniques: Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) DVFS changes operating frequency and voltage at runtime within supported operating points. Lowering voltage can substantially reduce switching power; frequency changes alone are not governed by a universal cubic law. The best setting depends on workload demands and total energy, including how long execution lasts. Turbo boost Supported processors can raise frequency above a specified base level when power, current, thermal and other limits allow. The available boost depends on the processor and active-core configuration; boost can involve multiple or all active cores, and idle cores need not all be power-gated. Maximum advertised boost is not a guarantee for every workload. Race to idle Sometimes it is better to run fast and then enter a lower-power idle state, because completing work can permit more components to become idle. Whether racing or pacing wins depends on how much static power the rest of the system burns while the work is running. Power gating and clock gating Clock gating suppresses clock transitions and associated switching activity; it does not remove leakage or necessarily prevent every data-driven transition. Power gating disconnects selected supply domains to reduce leakage, with transition costs and possible state-retention requirements. Neither implies that the whole system consumes zero power. Heterogeneous cores Heterogeneous processors combine cores with different performance and energy characteristics. An energy-aware scheduler can use workload demand and an energy model to choose placement, subject to affinity, ISA compatibility, policy and available capacity. A background task is not guaranteed to consume less energy on any core simply labelled “efficient”; evaluate the actual workload and system. Dark silicon Dark silicon describes a power-constrained inability to use all available circuitry simultaneously at full performance. The 2011 study by Esmaeilzadeh and colleagues modelled such limits; its projections are not measurements of every current chip or proof that a fixed fraction must be physically powered off at every instant. Specialised units can perform supported workloads with less instruction-processing overhead or more suitable data paths than general-purpose cores. Benefits depend on utilisation, data movement, programmability and implementation. Idle units may be gated; no universal efficiency multiplier or idle-power figure is established here. The bigger picture Clock frequency, IPC, parallel execution and specialised hardware all contribute to performance. Their importance varies by workload. More cores or an accelerator help only when software and data movement can use them effectively. Power is a software problem too Busy-waiting, polling loops and unnecessary wake-ups keep cores out of their low-power states. On battery-powered devices and in data centres (where electricity and cooling are a large part of running costs), efficient code is measured in watts as well as seconds. Key takeaways Power, energy and performance need workload-specific measurement. Clock gating reduces clock switching; power gating targets supply-domain leakage with transition costs. Dark silicon concerns power-constrained utilisation, and accelerators help only suitable workloads. Further reading Linux implementation: Energy Aware Scheduling Intel processor technology definitions Esmaeilzadeh et al.: dark silicon (original 2011 paper) Texas Instruments: CMOS power consumption

sum: Small nearby memories trade capacity for access cost.
x: Many high-performance CPU cores overlap several instructions. A dependent load missing all caches can stall work while DRAM responds; independent requests may overlap. Actual latency depends on the chip, workload and memory configuration. Computers use a hierarchy to balance capacity, cost and latency: small memories close to execution units backed by larger levels. Locality, reuse of the same or nearby data, makes this arrangement effective. Why small memories can be fast Three design costs motivate the hierarchy: Distance. Signals take time to cross a chip. A small memory sitting right next to the execution units can be read in a few cycles; a large one is physically further away and has longer wires. Technology. Many CPU caches are built from SRAM: each bit is a little latch of about six transistors. It is fast and needs no refresh, but it is big and expensive per bit. Main memory is DRAM: one transistor and one capacitor per bit. It is dense and cheap but slow, and it leaks (it must be refreshed, see the DRAM lesson). Search cost. Finding an item in a bigger structure takes more decoding and comparing, so even the same technology gets slower as it grows. The hierarchy in numbers A common general-purpose hierarchy is shown below. Exact capacities and latencies require a named processor and measurement conditions; not every machine has every level. Register operands are not zero-time physical accesses, even when they add no separate cache-load instruction. Level Role ------ Registers Small operand storage near execution units L1 Small, low-latency instruction/data caches L2 More capacity with a different latency trade-off L3 / last-level cache Often shared across cores DRAM Main volatile storage SSD Persistent storage reached through I/O Generic latency, cache-hit-rate and size ranges are omitted because no representative processor/workload measurements were verified for the earlier figures. Use specifications and measurements for the target machine. Where the OS fits in The operating system can cache file contents in DRAM (the page cache). Virtual memory and TLBs support address translation for memory accesses. Those are covered in the Operating Systems subject; here we focus on the CPU caches and DRAM. Locality: why a small cache works Imagine a program that used every byte of its memory equally and at random. Assume independent uniformly distributed byte accesses, a full cache, equal-sized cache lines and no overhead counted as data. The chance of a hit then follows the fraction of addressable data held: This independent uniform-access model is a poor-locality case that many real programs do not resemble. Adversarial conflict patterns can have even fewer hits; it is not a universal worst-case bound. Programs with useful locality can do much better. Two common forms of locality explain why. Temporal locality If you used something recently, you will probably use it again soon. Loop counters, the top of the stack, a hot function's instructions, the root of a B-tree, an accumulating total: all are touched over and over. A cache exploits temporal locality by keeping recently used data and evicting data that has not been used for a while. Key takeaways Small nearby memories trade capacity for access cost. Temporal locality is reuse soon; uniform random accesses lose that advantage.
