sum: A line fill supplies adjacent bytes, with the useful count depending on alignment and element size.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on spatial locality and cache-line traffic. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Spatial locality If you used something, you will probably use its neighbours soon. Instructions run one after another. Arrays are walked element by element. Fields of a struct are read together. A cache exploits spatial locality by moving data in fixed-size blocks called cache lines, not single bytes. This module normally assumes 64-byte lines and 4-byte ints; real line sizes vary, including 128-byte examples. A fill supplies other ints in the same line, not necessarily the next 15: that depends on the accessed int's position. Later accesses still have lookup costs. How many values one line holds is the line size divided by the size of each value: Summing an array shows how much this saves. Summing 1,000,000 4-byte ints walks 4 MB in order. Take a line-aligned array (it starts exactly on a line boundary) and a cold cache that starts empty, fetches only on demand, and suffers no interfering evictions. Every line then misses exactly once, on its first int: This is a model, not a measurement. An unaligned start can add a line. Prefetching and interference change demand miss counts. Key takeaways A line fill supplies adjacent bytes, with the useful count depending on alignment and element size. Cold sequential miss counts require explicit allocation and interference assumptions. sum: A fitting working set enables reuse without guaranteeing hits.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on working sets and access order. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Hits, misses and the working set Some vocabulary used throughout this module: Cache hit (hit): the data is in this level. Cache miss (miss): it is not, and the request goes to the next level down. Hit rate and miss rate: the fractions of accesses that hit and miss (formulas below). Miss penalty: the extra time a miss costs (the time to get the line from below). Working set: the data a program touches over a short window of time. Fitting in a level makes reuse possible, but set conflicts, other activity, coherence and replacement policy can still evict data. Exceeding capacity can increase misses. Every access either hits or misses, so the two rates always add up to 1: For example, 950 hits out of 1,000 accesses is a hit rate of 0.95 (95 %) and a miss rate of 0.05 (5 %). These are rates for one level: an L2 miss rate here counts only the accesses that reached L2 (the AMAT lesson calls this the local miss rate, and also defines a global one). The working set is why performance graphs often show performance cliffs. A carefully controlled repeated-access benchmark may show transitions near cache capacities. Streaming bandwidth, prefetching and access dependencies can make the curve quite different. The staircase below is schematic: its size labels are hypothetical boundaries, not measurements or a processor specification. Seeing locality in code The same amount of work can have very different locality. Both functions below add up the same list of numbers; only the order differs. In CPython, a list contains references to objects. Sequentially reading the reference array has spatial locality; shuffled indices scatter those accesses and can increase cache misses. Object allocation, shared objects, interpreter work, the extra array of indices and cache size affect the result. Run a controlled benchmark rather than assuming a fixed slowdown. A universal 5–10× slowdown and interpreter nanoseconds-per-iteration figure are omitted because no matching runtime, machine and benchmark were verified. Real-world consequences Arrays can improve traversal locality compared with scattered linked lists, even at the same big-O complexity. A dependent next pointer limits when the next demand address becomes known; whether it misses depends on placement, residency and prefetch capabilities. B-trees can reduce serial node accesses compared with binary trees for large indexes. A B-tree node is sized to hold many keys in a few cache lines (or one disk page), so each visited node can provide several nearby keys. A node may span several lines; cache misses depend on residency and search layout. Hot loops should be small. Instructions are cached too (in a separate L1 instruction cache). Huge unrolled or inlined code can overflow it. Data size matters. Using int32 instead of int64 fits twice as many integers per line; packing one-byte booleans into bits fits eight times as many flags, excluding layout overhead. Pitfalls Assuming the big-O tells the whole story. Two O(n) algorithms (time growing in proportion to n, the number of elements) can differ by 10× because one streams memory and the other jumps around. Benchmarking with tiny inputs. If the test data fits in L1, you are measuring the fast path. Production data that overflows into DRAM behaves differently. Assuming 64-byte lines everywhere. Line sizes vary by processor and cache level. Query the target (sysctl hw.cachelinesize on macOS, getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE on Linux) rather than hard-coding it in portable code. Key takeaways A fitting working set enables reuse without guaranteeing hits. Sequential reference-array access and dependent pointer chains have different locality and overlap opportunities. sum: Divide data capacity by line size and ways to count sets.
x: A cache holds copies of memory lines. The lookup must determine whether the requested bytes are present. The conventional organisations below use address-derived indexing and tag comparison to locate possible entries efficiently. Exact lookup pipelines and latency vary. Lines, sets and ways Three numbers describe a cache: Capacity C: total bytes of data (e.g. 32 KiB). Line size B: bytes per line (e.g. 64). Cache associativity E: how many places (cache ways) a given line may go. The cache is a grid of equal-sized lines, so dividing the capacity by the line size counts the lines. Those lines are then dealt out into sets of E ways each, so dividing the line count by E counts the sets. You need the set count every time you size an index field or predict which addresses collide: Doubling the ways at the same capacity halves the sets; doubling the capacity at the same ways doubles them. The formula counts bytes of data only: the tags and status bits live in extra storage on top (see the later cache-metadata unit). A memory line maps to exactly one set, but may sit in any way within that set. Organisation Ways per set Sets --------- Direct-mapped One One per cache line Set-associative Several Lines divided by ways Fully associative All lines One Splitting the address For this conventional byte-addressed, modulo-indexed model, the address is split into three fields. Mappings that hash or scramble the address need different indexing rules. For the drawing below, the address width is m bits, with t tag bits, s index bits and b offset bits; the next formula card defines how to calculate those widths: Offset: which byte within the line. Index: which set to look in. Cache tag (tag): the remaining high bits, stored alongside each line and compared to tell apart the many memory lines that share a set. How wide is each field? Each extra bit doubles the number of values a field can hold (1 bit gives 2 values, 2 bits give 4, 6 bits give 64), so the offset needs just enough bits to number every byte of a line, and the index just enough to number every set. "Just enough bits" is what log base 2 gives you: For 64-byte lines and 64 sets, offset and index each need 6 bits, leaving 36 tag bits in a 48-bit address. A base-two logarithm gives a whole-number field width only for a power-of-two count. The line size and set count must be powers of two for this simple bit-field split. Capacity and way count need not be: 48 KiB with 12 ways and 64-byte lines still has 64 sets. A lookup then goes: Use the index to select one set. Compare the address's tag against the stored tag of every way in that set, in parallel. A way hits if its tag matches and its valid bit is set. On a hit, use the offset to pick the bytes out of the line. Key takeaways Divide data capacity by line size and ways to count sets. The conventional power-of-two model divides an address into tag, index and byte offset. sum: Work out the geometry before interpreting an address.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on decode a direct-mapped address. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Worked example 1: a small direct-mapped cache A 1 KiB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte lines and 32-bit addresses. First calculate the geometry, repeating the earlier definitions so this example stands alone: Now break down address 0x00001A2C by writing it in binary and cutting it into fields from the right: So byte 12 of the line in set 34, with tag 0x6. A quicker way, without binary, uses whole-number division. Cutting off the low bits of a number is the same as dividing by a power of two and keeping the whole part: This arithmetic version works for any address and agrees with the bit-cutting version whenever line size and set count are powers of two. Key takeaways Work out the geometry before interpreting an address. Whole-number division and remainders reproduce the tag/index/offset split. sum: Physical address width determines the physical tag.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on physical tags and vipt indexing. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Worked example 2: an L1-style model Assume 32 KiB, 8 ways, 64-byte lines and 48-bit physical addresses. The tag calculation uses physical addresses; a 48-bit virtual address is not generally its physical tag. Address 0x7FFE12345678. The low 12 bits are 0x678 = 0110 0111 1000. Cut that into a 6-bit index and a 6-bit offset; the tag is the address with those 12 bits removed: Hex shortcut When the combined offset and index width is a multiple of 4 bits, read the fields straight off the hex digits. Here the combined width is 12 bits, the last three hexadecimal digits (678), so the tag is everything before them: 0x7FFE12345. Notice that the combined index and offset width is exactly 12 bits, the size of a 4 KiB page offset. That is not a coincidence. It lets the L1 pick the set using address bits that are the same in the virtual and physical address, so the set lookup can start while the TLB translates the rest (a virtually indexed, physically tagged or VIPT cache; translation itself is covered in the OS subject). It is one reason a design might grow L1 by adding ways: 48 KiB with 12 ways also gives 64 sets. Other geometries can use other alias-management techniques. Key takeaways Physical address width determines the physical tag. Indexing within the unchanged page offset enables lookup alongside translation in the stated model. sum: Two lines sharing one direct-mapped slot can evict each other while other slots are empty.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on trace conflicts and associativity. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Direct-mapped: simple but fragile Each line has exactly one home. Lookup needs one candidate tag comparison in this model, reducing comparison hardware. The weakness is conflict: two hot lines whose addresses share an index keep evicting each other, even if the rest of the cache is empty. Take a tiny 128-byte cache with 16-byte lines (8 lines) and this trace, with an initially empty cache, demand-only reads and no interference: Direct-mapped, 8 sets: offset 4 bits, index 3 bits. 0x00 and 0x80 both have index 0 (tags 0 and 1); 0x10 and 0x90 both have index 1. Addr Set Tag Result ------------ 0x00 0 0 miss 0x04 0 0 hit 0x80 0 1 miss (evicts 0) 0x00 0 0 miss (evicts 1) 0x84 0 1 miss 0x10 1 0 miss 0x90 1 1 miss 0x10 1 0 miss 1 hit in 8, with six of the eight lines sitting empty the whole time. Set-associative: the usual compromise Make the same 128 bytes 2-way: 4 sets of 2 ways. Now the index is 2 bits; the tag occupies the address width minus 6 bits (2 tag bits if addresses are 8 bits). 0x00 (tag 0) and 0x80 (tag 2) both go to set 0, but there are two ways, so they coexist. With LRU replacement: Addr Set Tag Result ------------ 0x00 0 0 miss 0x04 0 0 hit 0x80 0 2 miss 0x00 0 0 hit 0x84 0 2 hit 0x10 1 0 miss 0x90 1 2 miss 0x10 1 0 hit 4 hits in 8. The remaining misses are all first-time (compulsory) misses. Making it fully associative would not help this trace any further. The price of associativity is hardware: one tag comparator per way, all working in parallel, a multiplexer to choose the hitting way, and replacement state. More ways usually means slightly higher hit time and power. Exact associativities depend on the named cache. A generic L1/L2/L3 associativity table is omitted because the earlier ranges were not verified against a representative set of specified processors. Key takeaways Two lines sharing one direct-mapped slot can evict each other while other slots are empty. More ways allow several such lines to coexist, at a hardware cost. sum: Use first touch and a same-capacity fully associative LRU reference to distinguish the three Cs.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on classify misses and choose victims. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. The three Cs of misses Classifying misses tells you what would fix them: Compulsory miss (cold miss): the first access to a line. Prefetching can turn a first demand access into a hit; changing line size or avoiding accesses also changes the count. Capacity miss: the working set is bigger than the cache. In the conventional three-C classification, a previously seen line also misses in a fully associative LRU reference cache of the same capacity and line size. Fix with a bigger cache or better locality (loop blocking). Conflict miss: a previously seen line misses here but hits in that fully associative reference cache, often because competing lines share a set. Fix with more associativity, or by changing addresses (padding). Multicore systems add a fourth C, coherence misses, when another core invalidated your copy (see the coherence lesson). Replacement: choosing a victim In a set-associative cache, allocating a new line into a full set requires a victim; a bypassed or no-write-allocate access need not allocate. LRU: evict the least recently used way. Exact LRU for 8 ways needs to track an ordering of 8 items per set, which is costly. Pseudo-LRU (tree-PLRU): for a power-of-two number of ways, a binary tree with one bit fewer than the number of ways in each set (7 bits for 8 ways) points roughly away from recent accesses. It uses less state than a full ordering, but can choose a different victim from true LRU. RRIP-style policies: give each line a small "re-reference prediction" counter to distinguish likely distant reuse from likely near reuse. A streaming line can receive a less favourable prediction than a reused line; those predictions do not guarantee a particular victim order on every trace. Such policies can resist scans; a particular processor’s policy requires implementation documentation. Random replacement (pseudo-random): choose a victim using a random or pseudo-random mechanism. This can avoid maintaining a recency order; effectiveness is trace-dependent. Key takeaways Use first touch and a same-capacity fully associative LRU reference to distinguish the three Cs. Replacement approximations and RRIP-style predictions are policies, not universal processor guarantees. sum: Tags and status bits add storage beyond the advertised data capacity.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on cache metadata and indexing pitfalls. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Storage overhead The data array is not the whole cache. Each line also stores its tag, a valid bit and (for a write-back cache) a dirty bit, plus replacement bits per set. To size that metadata, add up the bits one line needs and multiply by the number of lines. For the 32 KiB 8-way example from worked example 2: That figure is a floor: replacement state, coherence state and error-checking bits add more, and a wider physical address increases tag width; fewer sets also widen the tag when the remaining geometry is held fixed. Pitfalls Power-of-two strides. In the 64-set, 64-byte-line model, 64 sets × 64 bytes = 4,096 bytes, so strides divisible by 4,096 bytes retain the same set index. An 8-way set holds only eight such lines. Padding can spread rows across sets, but whether it prevents thrashing depends on the new stride and working set. (The friendly-code lesson works through this.) Forgetting the tag bits shrink as the cache grows. Doubling the number of sets moves one bit from tag to index. Mixing up KB and KiB. KiB denotes a binary unit: 32 KiB = 32,768 bytes; KB denotes 1,000 bytes when used in the SI sense. Key takeaways Tags and status bits add storage beyond the advertised data capacity. Simple modulo indexing can make a power-of-two stride repeatedly select one set. sum: Write-through and write-back decide when modified bytes travel downstream.
x: Reads are the easy half of caching: if the line is present, return it; if not, fetch it. Writes raise harder questions. When a store hits in L1, does memory get updated now or later? When a store misses, do we bother fetching the line at all? The answers change how much traffic flows between levels, and that changes performance. Later short lessons combine these policies with the average memory access time (AMAT) model and then the cost in cycles per instruction. On a write hit: write-through or write-back Write-through Every store updates the cached copy and must be propagated to the next level. A write buffer can defer or merge those updates, so the next level need not reflect a pending store immediately. A clean write-through line does not need a dirty eviction write-back; pending buffered writes still must complete correctly. Without write merging, one million issued stores send one million writes downstream. Merging can reduce that traffic. A full write buffer can stall further stores. Write-back A store updates the cache line and marks it dirty (it sets the line's dirty bit). Modified data is propagated when required, for example on dirty eviction, explicit write-back, or a coherence request; eviction is not the only trigger. Repeated local writes can avoid repeated downstream data writes while the core retains ownership. They still consume execution/cache resources. In the simple allocate-on-miss model, replacing a dirty victim requires preserving its data and fetching the incoming line. A lower cache or DRAM may hold stale data, so coherent agents must obtain the current copy through the coherence mechanism. Non-coherent DMA requires the platform's cache-maintenance rules. The following traffic example assumes no write merging, no intervening coherence requests, and one final eviction. The assignment trace writes one cached variable, x; arrows show downstream propagation: Write-back is common for ordinary cacheable memory, but policies depend on the processor, cache level, memory type, and instruction. A processor-by-processor policy catalogue is absent here because those specific configurations have not been reliably verified. On a write miss: allocate or not Write-allocate: allocate a cache line on a store miss, then update it. A partial-line store commonly fetches the old line; hardware may avoid that fetch for a complete overwrite. Good if you will read or write nearby data soon. No-write-allocate (write-around): send the write to the next level and leave the cache alone. Good for data you will not touch again. The natural pairings are write-back + write-allocate (the usual choice) and write-through + no-write-allocate. In a coherent fetch-on-write model, a store miss requests exclusive permission, often through a read for ownership (RFO) coherence transaction that also obtains the line. Data may come from another cache rather than DRAM. A full-line overwrite may permit an implementation to omit the old-data fetch. Modelled traffic for overwriting 64 MiB Assume aligned 64-byte lines initially absent from all caches, no useful old data, no write-fetch elimination, and eventual write-back of every dirty line. Ordinary fetch-on-write stores read 64 MiB and write 64 MiB: 128 MiB of DRAM data traffic. In an ideal full-line streaming-store path that avoids allocation/old-data reads, the corresponding data traffic is 64 MiB. Real non-temporal instructions and library thresholds are implementation-specific; this is a traffic model, not a guarantee for every memset call. Inclusion between levels These properties apply to the particular pair or collection of cache levels being discussed: Inclusive hierarchy: presence in an included upper level implies presence in the lower level. The lower copy need not contain the newest bytes when an upper copy is dirty. Evicting the lower entry requires invalidating the included upper entries. Inclusion can help filter snoops, at the cost of duplicated capacity. Exclusive hierarchy: a line is resident in only one of the specified levels. Their nominal capacities can therefore add without duplication between those levels; other caches and metadata remain separate concerns. Neither inclusive nor exclusive (NINE): neither presence nor absence in one level guarantees the corresponding state in another. “Non-inclusive” alone does not necessarily rule out an exclusive design. Specific processor-generation inclusion policies are not catalogued here because the necessary configuration-specific verification is unavailable in this lesson. Key takeaways Write-through and write-back decide when modified bytes travel downstream. Allocation and hierarchy inclusion are separate policy choices with different traffic and residency consequences. sum: The initial lookup is paid on every access in the serial blocking model.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on average one blocking-cache access. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Average memory access time How fast is "the memory" when some accesses hit in a fast cache and some go much further? A single average answers that. For the serial, blocking lookup model used here (look in the cache, and only after a miss go to the next level, with the core waiting the whole time), AMAT is the expected service time of one memory access: The formula comes from averaging: hits pay the lookup alone; misses pay the lookup plus the extra penalty. Weighting those costs by their hit and miss fractions simplifies to the card’s expression. It holds only while accesses are served one at a time and every miss is fully exposed to the core. The hit time is paid on every access, and the miss penalty is the extra time when you miss. Worked example 1: one level L1 hit time 4 cycles, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 100 cycles. The extra miss penalty contributes 5 cycles per access, versus 4 cycles for the lookup paid on every access. In the alternative weighted form below, only hit events contribute 3.8 cycles. Two conventions, same answer Some books weight hits and misses separately, and count the whole time of a miss, including its initial lookup: Same result. Mixing the conventions by treating the 100-cycle extra penalty as the entire miss time gives 8.8 cycles, which undercounts the initial lookup on misses. Always check whether a quoted penalty includes the hit time. Key takeaways The initial lookup is paid on every access in the serial blocking model. Use either incremental miss penalty or total miss time consistently. t: Nested AMAT and local miss rates
sum: Use the average cost of the lower levels as the upper miss penalty.

Worked example 2: two levels With two caches, the L1 miss penalty is no longer a fixed number: an L1 miss goes to L2, which itself may hit or miss. So the L1 miss penalty is the AMAT of everything below L1, and the formula nests. In this serial model, the miss penalty of L1 is the incremental time spent accessing L2 and any lower level. The table uses incremental lookup times, not end-to-end latencies that already include earlier lookups. Level Hit time Local miss rate --------- L1 4 cycles 5% L2 12 cycles 20% DRAM 200 cycles - Adding a level does not change the formula; it only replaces a fixed miss penalty with the AMAT of the level below. Local vs global miss rate The miss rate of a lower cache can be measured against two different counts, and the two give very different numbers. This unit’s L2 figure of 20% is a local miss rate: of the 5% of accesses that reach L2, 20% miss, so its global miss rate is 1%. These products describe the same stream of demand accesses filtered through successive levels, ignoring additional prefetch, write-back, and coherence traffic. Use local rates in the nested formula. A quoted L2 miss rate of "20%" sounds terrible but, here, only 1 access in 100 goes to DRAM. Key takeaways Use the average cost of the lower levels as the upper miss penalty. A lower level’s local and global miss rates use different denominators. t: Convert miss costs to processor stalls
sum: Add exposed miss stalls to a base CPI that already includes hits.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on convert miss costs to processor stalls. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. From AMAT to CPI AMAT tells you the cost of one access; what you usually care about is total run time. The "iron law" of processor performance splits run time into three factors: Memory stalls make each instruction take more cycles, so for a simple in-order core that blocks on misses they add directly to CPI: Assume base CPI already includes cache-hit execution cost and that miss penalties cannot overlap. With base CPI 1.0, 0.4 data references per instruction, L1d (level-1 data cache) miss rate 5%, and an L1 miss penalty of 52 cycles (the L2 AMAT above): About half of all cycles (1.04 of 2.04) are spent waiting for memory. Instruction fetches add a stall term of their own, using one reference per instruction and the L1i (level-1 instruction cache) miss rate, if the L1i misses. The model breaks down once misses overlap: see the first pitfall below. Trade-offs and pitfalls AMAT is a model for blocking caches. Out-of-order cores keep running independent instructions during a miss and can have many misses outstanding at once (memory-level parallelism). Ten overlapped 100-cycle misses do not cost 1,000 cycles. AMAT alone cannot reliably rank such designs or predict total stall time: dependency chains, overlap, bandwidth, and queueing can change the result. Average hides the tail. A loop with 99% hits can still be dominated by the 1% if those are DRAM misses. Evaluate hit time and miss rate together. In this model L1 lookup time is paid on every access; lower-level costs are weighted by how often accesses reach them. Which change matters most depends on the workload and trade-off. Write-allocate can double traffic for streaming writes; use streaming stores or library routines that do. Key takeaways Add exposed miss stalls to a base CPI that already includes hits. Out-of-order overlap, queueing and bandwidth limit what a blocking AMAT model predicts. sum: Rectangular C-order rows are contiguous; F-order columns are contiguous.
x: The previous lessons explained how caches work. This one is about using that knowledge. The rules boil down to two: Use every byte of every line you fetch (spatial locality). Reuse data while it is still in the cache (temporal locality). Most cache-friendly techniques are one of these two ideas applied to a loop or a data structure. The examples are in C, because C makes memory layout explicit; the same ideas apply to NumPy, Java arrays, Rust and Go. Row-major layout and loop order Built-in rectangular arrays in C/C++, Rust and the Go programming language have contiguous rows. Nested pointers, vectors or slices need not form one contiguous matrix. NumPy's default dense allocation is row-major (order='C'), but views can have other strides. Conventional dense arrays in Fortran, MATLAB, Julia and R use column-major order. Where exactly does an element live? In a row-major array, all of row 0 comes first, then all of row 1, and so on, so to reach a[i][j] you skip i whole rows and then j elements: So a[2][1] in the 3 × 4 array above sits 72 bytes after a[0][0]. Incrementing j steps one 8-byte double; incrementing i steps one complete row. The formula assumes a genuine rectangular block of memory; an array of pointers to separately allocated rows does not follow it. Reordering a floating-point sum can change its rounding and final value. Layout optimisation must preserve the accuracy and dependency requirements of the application. Take a model: a 1024 × 1024 array of 8-byte doubles, aligned 64-byte lines, an initially empty 32 KiB fully associative LRU cache, no prefetching or other accesses. The row walk misses once per line, because the other 7 doubles in each line are used straight after: The column walk misses every time because it comes back to a line only after touching 1,023 intervening lines (a cycle of 1,024 lines, or 64 KiB), more than this 32 KiB cache holds, so the line has already been evicted. These are simulated cache misses, not a promised 8× run-time difference. Representative hardware slowdown figures are absent because no matching workload/processor measurements have been verified. In NumPy np.zeros((n, n)) defaults to C order. Its row slices are contiguous and its column slices are strided. Reduction performance also depends on NumPy's implementation and shape; sum(axis=1) is not universally fastest. np.asfortranarray supplies F-contiguous storage, copying when necessary. For a 2D array, a.T exchanges shape/strides in a view; it does not physically rearrange the elements. Key takeaways Rectangular C-order rows are contiguous; F-order columns are contiguous. Inspect actual strides and preserve floating-point accuracy when changing traversal order. t: Count misses for matrix loop orders
sum: Fixed, contiguous and row-stride accesses have different costs under the stated simplified model.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on count misses for matrix loop orders. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Counting misses per iteration Use the following simplified steady-state model: 64-byte lines, aligned 8-byte doubles, demand allocation on reads/writes, no prefetching or conflict/interference misses, and no row/column retained between sweeps. A current line survives long enough to use its adjacent elements. Ignore first-touch overhead for a fixed element, which can be kept in a register. A stride-1 walk (consecutive elements) misses only on the first element of each line, so its cost per iteration is one miss shared among all the elements a line holds: A stride of a whole row (larger than a line) lands in a new line every time, so it costs 1 miss per iteration. Under those assumptions: Access pattern Misses / iteration ------ Fixed (same element) 0 Stride 1 (8-byte elements) 1/8 = 0.125 Stride of a row 1 Matrix multiply: loop order matters The loops below compute the matrix product of A and B and add it into C; initialise C to zero to obtain just the product. Assume disjoint square arrays of doubles; n is the number of rows and columns, and i, j and k are zero-based loop indices. Whichever order the three loops nest in, the work is the same: The six loop orders all perform these updates, but their locality differs. Floating-point transformations, fused operations and reassociation can affect rounding. Inner loop over k: A[i][k] is stride 1, B[k][j] walks down a column, C[i][j] is fixed. Add up each array's misses per iteration from the table: Inner loop over j: A[i][k] is fixed (0 misses per iteration), B[k][j] is stride 1 (0.125) and C[i][j] is stride 1 (0.125). Total: 0 + 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.25 misses per iteration. Order Inner loop Misses / iter --------- ijk, jik k 1.125 ikj, kij j 0.25 jki, kji i 2.0 The jki order walks both A and C down columns: two misses per iteration, 8 times worse than ikj. Changing loop order can improve performance when memory access is the bottleneck. (In practice the row of C in ikj often stays cached across k, so it can do even better than 0.25.) Key takeaways Fixed, contiguous and row-stride accesses have different costs under the stated simplified model. The six multiplication loop orders do the same scalar updates with different access patterns. sum: Blocking exposes reuse by revisiting small tiles before moving on.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on keep matrix tiles together. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Loop blocking (tiling) The unblocked ikj order revisits input matrix B for each row of input matrix A; C is the output accumulator. In this unit, n denotes the common square matrix edge. For 1024 × 1024 matrices of 8-byte doubles, B occupies 8 MiB; whether it survives between sweeps depends on the cache hierarchy. There is still reuse within each fetched line, and lower caches may retain data. The preceding simplified no-between-sweep-reuse model multiplies the work by the misses per iteration: That is a model of line fills, not universal DRAM traffic. Loop blocking splits the matrices into small tiles that fit in cache together, and does all the work on those tiles before moving on. In the drawing, a and b are input tiles, c is the accumulating output tile, and T is the tile edge in elements. Here n is the matrix edge in elements; i, j and k are element indices, ii, jj and kk are tile origins, and T is the tile edge. This fragment assumes disjoint allocated arrays, valid dimensions and n divisible by T; a complete implementation also handles allocation failures and edge tiles. Choosing the tile edge: a first capacity check is the useful bytes in three equal square tiles (one each from A, B and C), which should not exceed the cache you are targeting (with additional headroom needed in practice). For a 32 KiB target and 8-byte doubles: (1,365 is 32,768 / 24 rounded down; the square root of 1,365 is about 36.9, and T must be a whole number.) A tile edge of 32 gives 24 KiB of useful tile data, but that does not guarantee residency. Row fragments occupy whole lines, other data competes for space, and an 8 KiB row stride can cause set conflicts even when useful bytes fit. Packing tiles contiguously or padding rows can help. In an ideal model where the three tiles remain resident, many input values are reused T times; actual traffic and speed depend on the implementation. Optimised matrix libraries combine blocking with techniques such as packing, register reuse and vectorisation. For a separate ideal traffic model, assume packed aligned tiles, sufficient associativity, no interference and no retained data between tile steps. With 32-element tile edges in a 1,024-element matrix, there are 32 tile positions along each of three dimensions. Each step loads three cold tiles once and performs every update in their cubic subproblem. This deliberately pessimistic reset-between-steps model is separate from actual code that can retain data across tile steps. The focused question works through its line counts. Key takeaways Blocking exposes reuse by revisiting small tiles before moving on. Useful-byte capacity is a first check; line coverage, set conflicts and competing data still matter. sum: A stride equal to the set count times the line size retains the same modulo index.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on break cache-set stride conflicts. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. The power-of-two stride trap Under simple modulo indexing, certain strides repeatedly select the same set. Take a model 32 KiB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines. Its number of sets, and the set an address falls in, are: Six bits can count from 0 to 63, so bits 0–5 pick the byte within a 64-byte line and the next six bits, 6–11, pick one of the 64 sets. If you step by exactly 4,096 bytes (64 sets × 64 bytes), or any multiple of it, bits 6–11 never change: every access lands in one set, and only 8 lines fit. Take a 256 × 1024 array of doubles: each row is 8,192 bytes. Walk it column by column. Each column touches 256 lines, only 16 KiB, which should fit easily in 32 KiB. For an aligned array, initially empty cache, LRU replacement, demand allocation, no prefetching and no other accesses, simulating this cache gives 16,384 misses out of 16,384 accesses for the first 64 columns without padding, and 2,048 (12.5%, the same as walking by rows) with one line of padding per row. This motivates padding or packing in FFT and image-processing implementations when their access patterns suffer such measured conflicts. Key takeaways A stride equal to the set count times the line size retains the same modulo index. One line of row padding distributes this example across sets and changes its simulated misses. t: Choose AoS, SoA and compact fields
sum: Store frequently scanned fields densely to avoid fetching unused record fields.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on choose aos, soa and compact fields. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Array of structs vs struct of arrays How you group fields decides how many useful bytes each line brings in. Assume 4-byte floats, a 32-byte Particle, aligned cold 64-byte lines, and each needed line fetched once. Consider a pass that only does x += vx dt. The following counts cover data brought into the cache, excluding later dirty write-backs and extra hardware traffic: AoS: each particle's 32 bytes come in together, but only 8 (x and vx) are used. 75% of every line is wasted. For 1,000,000 particles, the loop drags 1,000,000 × 32 bytes = 32 MB through the cache. SoA: x[] and vx[] are dense arrays, so every byte fetched is used: 8 MB read. Contiguous values can also support vectorisation; for example, a 256-bit AVX vector holds eight 32-bit floats when that instruction set is available. AoS can be useful when accessing most fields of one record together; SoA can still win for some vectorised whole-record workloads. Columnar storage, including the Parquet file format, applies the related idea of grouping values by column, but a file format is not itself an in-memory C SoA structure. A middle path is hot/cold splitting: keep the frequently used fields in a compact struct, and move rarely used ones (names, debug info) behind a pointer or into a parallel array. Other habits that help Consider contiguous numeric storage. C++ std::vector (apart from specialised representations such as vector<bool>), Rust Vec, conventional HotSpot Java primitive arrays and contiguous NumPy arrays keep element storage together. NumPy views need not be contiguous. Reference containers such as CPython lists and Java ArrayList<Integer> add indirection; elements can share objects. Inspect struct alignment and padding. On an ABI with 8-byte doubles and 8-byte double alignment, a char followed by a double can require 7 padding bytes. Reordering can help, but may merely move padding to the end; compare sizeof and offsets rather than assuming sorting by size shrinks every record. Fuse loops that walk the same arrays so data is reused while hot, instead of streaming the arrays twice. Shrink the data. float instead of double, int32 indices instead of pointers, bitsets instead of bool arrays. Measure. perf stat -e cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses on Linux, or Instruments on macOS, tells you whether a change actually reduced misses. Python’s array.array('d') is another dense numeric representation: it stores C doubles rather than object references. Check its itemsize for the platform; NumPy float64 specifically uses eight bytes. Conventional HotSpot primitive arrays contain values inline, while ArrayList<Integer> contains references to boxed objects. A managed language’s abstract array semantics do not by themselves specify every runtime’s physical placement. Pitfalls Optimising cold code. Restructuring data only matters in loops that dominate run time; profile first. Loop blocking for the wrong level or size. A tile that fits L1 on one machine may not on another; libraries tune or detect sizes. Trusting the compiler to fix loop order. Compilers can interchange simple loops, but aliasing (a pair of pointers that might overlap) often stops them. Key takeaways Store frequently scanned fields densely to avoid fetching unused record fields. Compare actual layout, alignment, indirection and hot-loop measurements before choosing a representation. sum: Coherence orders writes per location without making language data races valid.
x: Many multicore CPUs have private per-core caches, though which levels are private or shared depends on the design. If two cores both cache the line holding variable x, and one of them writes x, the other now holds a stale copy. Without a fix, two threads could see different values for the same address forever. Within a hardware-coherent domain, cache coherence makes participating caches agree on a per-location write order. This does not make unsynchronised C/C++ data races valid, order accesses to different locations, or guarantee coherence with every device or memory type. Software still needs the language's atomics/synchronisation and any required device cache maintenance. The invariant Coherence protocols maintain one rule per cache line: Single writer, multiple readers In a stable state, a line can have one cache with exclusive write permission (which can also read), or multiple read-only cached copies. It must not have a writable copy alongside independently usable shared copies. In the write-invalidate protocol studied here, a writer must obtain exclusive permission and invalidate other usable copies. Write-update protocols instead distribute new data; their traffic trade-offs differ. Note that coherence is about one location. The ordering rules across different locations are the memory consistency model (x86-TSO, Arm's weaker model), covered in the Parallel Hardware module. MESI The classic simplified protocol assigns each participating cache-line entry one of four stable states: State Valid Dirty Other copies? ------------ Modified yes yes none Exclusive yes no none Shared yes no maybe Invalid no - - M: this cache has the only copy and it has been written; the backing level may be stale. A request by another cache must obtain the current data through the protocol, potentially causing a write-back or ownership handover. E: the only copy, clean. The core can write it silently (E → M) without telling anyone. S: clean, and other caches may have it too. A write first requires invalidating them. I: not usable; any access is a miss. Key takeaways Coherence orders writes per location without making language data races valid. MESI distinguishes private clean, private dirty, clean shared and invalid line entries. sum: Textbook serialised requests model reads, ownership acquisition and upgrades.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on trace ownership transitions. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Recall MESI’s stable states: Modified is the sole writable dirty copy; Exclusive is the sole clean copy; Shared is clean and may have peer copies; Invalid cannot serve an access. This unit traces those permissions for one line. Transitions For this textbook snooping model, coherence transactions are serialised and observed by the other participating caches. The table omits transient states, retries and simultaneous-request races: BusRd: "I want to read this line." BusRdX: "I want to write this line; everyone else invalidate" (a read-for-ownership). BusUpgr: "I already have it in S; everyone else invalidate." Now Event Action Next ------------ I local read BusRd E (no sharers) or S I local write BusRdX M S local write BusUpgr M E local write none M M snoop BusRd supply data S M snoop BusRdX supply data I E snoop BusRd - S E/S snoop BusRdX/Upgr - I In this textbook MESI model, M → S also updates the backing level so shared copies are clean relative to it. That backing level can be another cache; a real coherence transaction need not reach DRAM. Worked trace Two cores, line X not cached anywhere. Core 0 reads: nobody else has it, so E. Core 1 reads: core 0 sees the BusRd and drops to S; both S. Core 0 writes: it must invalidate core 1 (BusUpgr). Core 0 M, core 1 I. Core 1 reads: miss. Core 0 snoops, supplies the dirty data (and updates the backing level in this model), and both end in S. Core 1 writes: invalidates core 0; core 1 M. When a different core acquires write permission, coherence communication is required; data need not always be transferred directly from the previous writer. That is the cost to keep in mind. Why E exists Without E (the simpler MSI protocol), a single-threaded program that reads then writes private data would pay two requests: BusRd to get it in S, then BusUpgr to write. E recognises "nobody else has this" and avoids a separate ownership-upgrade coherence transaction for that write. The store still has local execution cost; how often this helps is workload-dependent. Key takeaways Textbook serialised requests model reads, ownership acquisition and upgrades. Exclusive permits a private clean-to-dirty transition without a separate coherence request. t: Route coherence and share dirty data
sum: Owned can defer a backing-level write-back; Forward designates a clean responder.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on route coherence and share dirty data. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Recall the preceding textbook MESI model: Modified means one writable dirty owner, Shared means clean read-only copies, and Exclusive means a sole clean copy. The variants below change how clean or dirty shared data is supplied. Variants used in real chips MOESI, used in some processor coherence designs: adds an Owned (O) state: dirty but shared. A core in M that is snooped by a reader moves to O and keeps supplying the data, while retaining responsibility for the dirty data. This can defer a backing-level write-back for read-shared dirty data. MESIF, used in some processor coherence designs: adds a Forward (F) state: a clean copy can be designated to supply later sharing requests. This avoids requiring every clean sharer to respond; exact routing, including service when no Forward copy remains, is implementation-specific. Arm's AMBA CHI interconnects use their own state names with equivalent ideas (unique/shared, clean/dirty). Snooping vs directories How does a write find all the copies it must invalidate? Snooping: every request is broadcast and every cache checks its tags. Simple and fast with a few cores on a shared bus, but broadcast traffic grows with core count. Directory: a structure (often alongside the L3 or memory controller) tracks actual or possible sharers of a line. A write can target those candidates instead of broadcasting to every cache. Scales to many cores and CPU sockets. Modern many-core chips mix the two: snoop filters (Intel) and directory caches track which cores might hold a line, so most requests avoid broadcasting. An inclusive L3 can act as a natural snoop filter: if a line is absent from that inclusive L3, it cannot be resident in the upper caches covered by the inclusion guarantee. What coherence costs A coherence miss is a miss caused by a coherence invalidation of a previously cached line. A first-ever access can also obtain dirty data from another core, but that fact alone does not make it an invalidation-caused miss. Remote ownership/data transfers can be much slower than a local L1 hit. A representative nanosecond range is absent because processor topology, load, placement and measurement method have not been reliably specified here. Measure the target system rather than treating a universal range as a guarantee. Read-only shared lines can produce local hits after warming and while resident; initial fills, evictions and replication still consume resources. Repeated writes by different cores are a particularly costly pattern because they require ownership changes. Key takeaways Owned can defer a backing-level write-back; Forward designates a clean responder. Directories and snoop filters narrow candidate sharers, while read-only resident hits need no ownership change. t: Avoid false sharing and write contention
sum: Independent variables can compete for one coherence line.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on avoid false sharing and write contention. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. False sharing This unit assumes the coherence granule is a cache line; real protocols can have implementation-specific granularity. Coherence tracks that granule rather than the individual language variables within it. If two threads write two different variables that happen to sit in the same line, the hardware requires ownership of the shared line, much as it does for contended writes to one variable: the line ping-pongs between their caches in M state. volatile requires observable accesses according to the C implementation; it is not an atomic or thread-synchronisation mechanism. This example has one writer per distinct scalar object; read the final counts only after joining both threads. A shared counter written by both threads would need atomics or a lock. Each store requires ownership, but a core may execute many increments before ownership changes. The following is one possible interleaving, not one transfer guaranteed per increment: False sharing can make the two-core run slower; the size of the effect requires measurement. Under this 64-byte-line model, separate the independently written variables: Padding in practice C++17: std::hardware_destructive_interference_size (where the library provides it) provides an implementation-defined separation hint, not a runtime measurement of every machine on which the binary may run. Linux kernel: ____cacheline_aligned_in_smp. Java: @Contended (internal; user code needs -XX:-RestrictContended). LongAdder uses striped cells to reduce update contention; its sum() is not an atomic snapshot, and performance depends on contention and usage. Rust: crossbeam_utils::CachePadded documents a conservative 128-byte padding choice on x86-64, including concern about adjacent-line prefetching on some processors. This library heuristic is not proof that every x86 CPU requires 128 bytes or every other platform has the same line size. Go: golang.org/x/sys/cpu.CacheLinePad. Better than padding: don't share writes Padding fixes false sharing. True sharing (many threads updating one counter) still ping-pongs. The real fix is structural: Give each thread a private accumulator and combine at the end. Use sharded/striped counters (like LongAdder) when approximate concurrent aggregation is acceptable; cells are not necessarily one per thread, and a concurrent sum need not be a single-time snapshot. Batch updates, e.g. publish every 1,000 local events, accepting delayed visibility and flushing remaining events before a final total. Finding it False sharing does not show up in source code review easily. Tools: perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines with heavy cross-core "HITM" traffic (loads that hit a modified line in another core) and the offsets within the line being touched. A tell-tale sign: performance gets worse as you add threads, while CPU utilisation stays high. Spinlocks and coherence A naive spinlock repeatedly performs an atomic exchange. Under contention, competing read-modify-write requests can repeatedly transfer exclusive ownership. An exchange by a core that already owns the line need not cause a fresh transfer. Test-and-test-and-set first spins on an atomic relaxed load, then tries an acquire exchange when the lock appears free; unlocking uses a release store. An ordinary non-atomic C/C++ load racing with a write is invalid, even on coherent hardware. Read polling can hit locally while the line remains shared, but it still reacts to invalidations. Queue locks such as MCS let each waiter poll its own node; laying out nodes to avoid false sharing preserves that advantage. This is a protocol overview, not a complete lock implementation. Key takeaways Independent variables can compete for one coherence line. Use target-appropriate separation, private accumulation and valid atomic lock polling, then measure the effect. t: From DRAM cells to banks and ranks
sum: Sense amplifiers restore disturbed charge and refresh maintains retention.
x: Earlier examples used assumed DRAM latencies to explain cache arithmetic. Below the last-level cache is a memory system with controllers, channels, ranks, banks and rows. Access latency depends on its state, traffic and placement. Streaming throughput benefits from overlapping requests, including useful prefetches; it is not guaranteed to reach peak bandwidth. The numerical examples below are explicit models. Representative end-to-end latency and speedup figures are absent where the necessary processor, memory configuration and benchmark have not been reliably verified. The DRAM cell and why it is slow A conventional DRAM cell uses one transistor and one capacitor. Information is represented by charge state; the mapping of charged/discharged to logical 1/0 can depend on cell organisation. That makes DRAM dense and cheap, but it has three consequences: Reads are destructive. Activation shares the cell's small charge with a bit line. A sense amplifier resolves the voltage difference and restores the cell while the row is active. This disturbs the stored charge; it is not simply a complete drain followed by restoration during precharge. Cells leak. Charge drains away in milliseconds, so every row must be refreshed (read and rewritten) periodically, whether or not anyone uses it. Access is row-at-a-time. The chip cannot read one bit cheaply. It opens a whole row (thousands of bits) into the sense amplifiers, called the DRAM row buffer, and then reads columns from it. Inside a DIMM: channels, ranks, banks, rows The following is an illustrative DDR4-style topology, excluding ECC bits; actual widths, ranks, bank counts and address mapping vary. A memory channel is an independent bus with its own controller logic. More channels means more bandwidth in parallel. A DRAM rank groups DRAM devices operated together. In the illustrated 64-data-bit DDR4 channel, eight ×8 (8-bit-wide) devices supply the data width; ECC may add bits. DDR5 DIMMs divide their data interface into sub-channels. Each chip has several DRAM banks, with counts depending on device width and generation; DDR5 configurations can have up to 32. Each bank has its own DRAM row buffer, so different banks can work on different rows at the same time. A DRAM row (sometimes called a page) is distinct from an operating-system page. Its aggregate byte size depends on device geometry and rank width; no universal row size is assumed here. The memory controller maps, and may hash, physical address bits to choose channel, rank, bank, row and column. Controllers can interleave consecutive cache lines across channels and banks; the exact mapping determines whether a stream uses those resources in parallel. Key takeaways Sense amplifiers restore disturbed charge and refresh maintains retention. Channels, ranks, banks and rows are different levels of organisation. t: Row hits, conflicts and clock timings
sum: A simplified command path distinguishes an open-row hit, an empty bank and a conflicting row.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on row hits, conflicts and clock timings. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. The three cases of an access Each bank's DRAM row buffer retains an activated row. The table gives simplified command-to-first-data minima, assuming precharge is already legal, the command bus is available, and all other timing constraints are satisfied. Queueing, transfer completion and earlier operations can add delay: Case Commands Cost --------- Row hit READ CL Row empty ACT, READ tRCD + CL Row conflict PRE, ACT, READ tRP + tRCD + CL CL (CAS latency): column read from an open row to first data. tRCD: minimum delay from row activation (ACT) to a column command such as READ, while sensing and restoration proceed. tRP: precharge time to close the row and prepare/equalise the bit lines for another activation. Cell restoration occurs while the row is active. Timings are quoted in clock cycles, as in "DDR4-3200 CL22-22-22". To convert to nanoseconds you need the clock. DDR means double data rate: two transfers per clock. So DDR4-3200 runs 3,200 mega-transfers per second (MT/s) on a 1,600 MHz clock, and one clock is 0.625 ns. To turn a timing quoted in clock cycles into nanoseconds, divide the cycles by the clock frequency. The clock is half the data-transfer rate, which is where the 2,000 comes from: The rule holds for any DDR generation, because all of them make two transfers per clock. It converts the quoted minimum only; real loads add queueing and other delays. Worked example: hit, empty, conflict Assume a DDR4-3200 timing configuration with CL, tRCD and tRP all equal to 22 clocks, so each is 13.75 ns. Add up the steps each case needs, from the table above: In this simplified example, the command-to-first-data interval for a conflict is three times the hit interval. That is why controllers reorder queued requests to group hits to the same open row (FR-FCFS scheduling), and why two streams repeatedly accessing different rows of the same bank are slow. These are simplified DRAM command intervals. A measured core load also includes cache lookups, interconnect traversal, controller scheduling and possible contention; its latency cannot be inferred from CL alone. Faster MT/s is not always lower latency DDR4-3200 CL16 and DDR4-3600 CL18 both work out to 10 ns of CAS latency (calculation below). A higher CL number at a higher data-transfer rate can be the same latency, with more bandwidth. Key takeaways A simplified command path distinguishes an open-row hit, an empty bank and a conflicting row. DDR clock-cycle timings convert to time using half the data-transfer rate. sum: Peak data bandwidth is transfers per second times bytes per transfer.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on compute ddr channel bandwidth. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. DDR means two data transfers per memory clock. Here bandwidth counts data bytes, excluding ECC overhead, and uses decimal gigabytes. Command scheduling and transfer rate are separate from end-to-end core-load latency. Bandwidth maths The most data a channel can ever move is one bus-width of bytes per transfer, times the number of transfers each second: This is a ceiling: refresh, row-buffer conflicts, bus turnarounds and too few requests in flight keep real programs below it. A 64-byte line is one DRAM burst of 8 transfers of 8 bytes (BL8). Two transfers happen per clock, so that is 4 clocks of 0.625 ns, or 2.5 ns of bus time on DDR4-3200. A conventional DDR5 DIMM splits its 64-bit data interface into two independent 32-bit sub-channels, excluding additional ECC bits, each using bursts of 16 (BL16 × 4 B = 64 B, still one line). Two narrower channels give the controller more parallelism. The same peak-bandwidth formula applies, counting both sub-channels together as 8 bytes per transfer: DDR5 devices add on-die ECC, while conventional DDR5 DIMMs include on-module power management; bank counts depend on device geometry. On-die ECC protects internal storage and does not replace end-to-end memory-system ECC. For an example DDR5-4800 CL40 timing, CAS latency is about 16.7 ns, versus the example DDR4-3200 CL22 timing’s 13.75 ns. The preceding timing unit defines the conversion; the extra worked card below repeats it locally. These two configurations do not establish a universal latency ordering between generations. Key takeaways Peak data bandwidth is transfers per second times bytes per transfer. DDR5 sub-channels improve scheduling opportunities without making peak bandwidth a measured result. t: Keep enough memory requests in flight
sum: Little’s law relates steady-state request residency to throughput and bytes in flight.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on keep enough memory requests in flight. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Little's law: requests in flight Peak bandwidth is only reached if enough requests are in flight at once. Little's law, from queueing theory, says that in a steady state the number of items inside a system equals the rate they flow through it times how long each stays. Rearranged for memory: It applies to averages over a steady period, not to single requests. As an illustrative demand-request limit, assume 12 outstanding 64-byte transfers with a steady-state average residency of 80 ns: Turned round, the law says how many requests a target bandwidth needs: So at 51.2 GB/s and an 80 ns average request residency you need 64 lines in flight. The hypothetical 12-request limit cannot sustain that rate by itself. Actual limits and prefetch queues are implementation-specific. One strictly dependent cold pointer chain can expose only one next demand address at a time: with the assumed 80 ns per line, it moves one 64-byte line per 80 ns, which is 0.8 GB/s of line traffic. Useful pointer-byte throughput is lower, and other chains or hardware speculation can create additional requests. Key takeaways Little’s law relates steady-state request residency to throughput and bytes in flight. One dependent cold chain exposes fewer independent demand requests than a concurrent stream. sum: Refresh timing and affected resources depend on the device and operating mode.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on refresh availability and disturbance. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Refresh DRAM retention requires periodic refresh; the interval, blocking time, temperature rules and supported modes are part-specific. For an illustrative all-bank refresh model, assume one operation every 7,812.5 ns, blocking the rank for 350 ns. The share of time lost is the blocked time divided by the interval: If that interval halves while the blocking duration stays fixed, the fraction doubles to 8.96%. A product-specific density/temperature timing table is absent because those exact operating modes have not been reliably verified here. DDR5 same-bank refresh targets one selected bank in each bank group, allowing other banks to remain available subject to timing constraints. It is not a refresh of only one bank in the entire device. A demand request can still be delayed by refresh. Row hammer Activating one row very rapidly can disturb the charge in neighbouring rows and flip their bits, faster than refresh restores them. Researchers have used this to escalate privileges from unprivileged code. Mitigations include target row refresh (TRR) in the DRAM, DDR5's refresh management, and ECC, but none is perfect. Key takeaways Refresh timing and affected resources depend on the device and operating mode. The illustrative unavailable-time fraction divides blocking duration by interval. t: Place fresh pages near their users
sum: NUMA nodes and CPU sockets need not correspond one-to-one.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on place fresh pages near their users. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. NUMA: not all DRAM is equally far In a multi-socket server, each CPU socket has its own memory controllers and DRAM. A core can reach the other CPU socket's memory, but only over the inter-socket link (Intel UPI, AMD Infinity Fabric). This is non-uniform memory access. Remote access can add interconnect delay and encounter link-bandwidth limits. A universal local/remote latency ratio is absent because a specific measured topology is not established here. numactl --hardware reports node memory and relative distance values; these are not nanoseconds. A CPU socket can expose multiple NUMA nodes, and a NUMA node need not correspond one-to-one with a CPU socket. Worked example: average latency For a hypothetical workload with local 90 ns, remote 140 ns, and a quarter of accesses remote: The average is a weighted mix: each latency counts in proportion to how often it happens. If every access were remote, the average would be 140 ns, about 1.56 times the all-local figure, or about 56% higher latency. The model assumes fixed latencies; in reality remote latency rises when the inter-socket link is busy. First touch Under Linux's default local allocation policy, a newly faulted writable anonymous page is normally allocated near the CPU taking the fault, subject to allowed nodes, free memory and fallback. malloc may return already backed reused storage, so calling or writing through it does not necessarily cause a new allocation. Placement can also change through migration or automatic NUMA balancing. For the following example, assume fresh untouched pages, a pinned initialising thread, sufficient local memory, and no policy override or migration: Under those assumptions, initial page faults place the pages on the main thread's node. Workers on another node then reach remote memory when accesses miss the cache hierarchy; hits in a core's own caches are not remote DRAM accesses. Fixes: Parallel first touch: initialise newly allocated, unbacked slices with the workers that will later process them, pinned appropriately. Re-zeroing already placed pages does not by itself relocate them. Pin threads and memory: numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0./app, or taskset plus mbind/set_mempolicy from libnuma. Interleave: numactl --interleave=all spreads pages round-robin. This can balance placement for large shared structures, but does not guarantee equal access latency or eliminate bandwidth hotspots. Automatic NUMA balancing (kernel.numa_balancing) migrates pages towards the threads that use them, at the cost of page faults to sample accesses. Some database and managed-runtime configurations expose NUMA options. Collector/version-specific JVM behaviour is not detailed here because the necessary configuration-specific verification is unavailable. Key takeaways NUMA nodes and CPU sockets need not correspond one-to-one. First-touch placement requires fresh unbacked pages, suitable policy, allowed nodes and sufficient memory. t: Prefetch safely and choose a lead distance
sum: Hardware pattern capabilities and page crossing are engine-specific.
x: This unit builds on the earlier cache lessons and focuses on prefetch safely and choose a lead distance. Keep each example’s stated hardware geometry and model assumptions when applying its result. Prefetching: hiding demand latency A prefetch fetches a line before the demand load asks for it. A timely, retained prefetch can turn a later demand miss into an L1 or L2 hit; it does not eliminate the earlier transfer cost. Hardware prefetchers Depending on the processor, engines may detect adjacent lines, sequential streams or constant strides associated with a load instruction. Their triggering, how far ahead they run, target cache and page-crossing behaviour vary. Conventional stream/stride predictors struggle with irregular indirection. However, it is false that all hardware prefetchers are unable to use indirect data: Intel documents a data-dependent prefetcher that can use loaded values to predict addresses in supported patterns. That feature is not an unrestricted recursive pointer-chasing engine. Likewise, a universal “all prefetchers stop at 4 KiB boundaries” rule is incorrect; translation and boundary handling are engine-specific. Software prefetching For irregular but computable addresses, you can issue the prefetch yourself. GCC and Clang provide __builtin_prefetch: Assume every index used here is in bounds for table, idx contains at least n entries, and sum arithmetic is valid. A prefetch hint may be ignored, but evaluating its address must still be valid. The prefetch must be issued early enough that the data arrives by the time the loop reaches it. With a constant cost per iteration, an initial prefetch-distance estimate is: With assumed 100 ns latency and 5 ns per iteration, a lead of 20 iterations is a starting estimate. Actual latency, issue overhead, resource limits and evictions determine whether it hides the miss. Too small and the data arrives late; too large and it may be evicted before use, or waste fill buffers. When prefetching hurts Cache pollution: prefetched lines that are never used evict useful ones. Bandwidth waste: on a memory-bound multi-threaded workload, useless prefetches steal bandwidth from demand misses. Some firmware configuration interfaces expose controls for individual prefetchers; whether disabling one helps depends on the measured workload. Overhead: software prefetches are instructions too; in a loop that is already compute-bound they only cost. Putting it together Some practical consequences: A sufficiently concurrent streaming loop can become bandwidth-limited. Too few outstanding requests or substantial computation can prevent this. Measure achieved GB/s. A strictly dependent, cache-missing pointer chain is often latency-limited: one next demand address at a time. Restructure the data (arrays, B-trees), or interleave several independent chases so their misses overlap. On multi-socket machines, check numastat and placement before blaming the code. Bandwidth is shared. Several cores streaming at once can saturate the channels before exhausting arithmetic resources; adding threads to a memory-bound loop stops helping once DRAM is full. Key takeaways Hardware pattern capabilities and page crossing are engine-specific. Software hints need valid address evaluation and a useful lead distance without excessive pollution or overhead. t: Classifying parallel instruction and data streams
sum: Flynn classifies instruction and data streams; one machine can combine classes.
x: Clock scaling and microarchitectural improvements contributed to single-thread performance growth. Power and thermal constraints made rapid clock increases harder in the mid-2000s; clock rates and single-core performance did not stop improving. Designers also pursued more cores, vector execution and specialised accelerators. Parallel hardware only helps if the work can be split. These units give you two tools. Flynn's taxonomy is a vocabulary for how hardware is parallel. Amdahl's law and Gustafson's law tell you how much that parallelism can buy. Flynn's taxonomy Flynn’s taxonomy classifies computers by two questions. How many instruction streams run at once? And how many data streams does each one act on? Class Instr. Data Example ------------ SISD 1 1 Classic single core SIMD 1 Many AVX, NEON, vector units MISD Many 1 Abstract multiple-instruction/single-data class MIMD Many Many Multicore CPUs, clusters SISD (single instruction, single data): one instruction operates on one piece of data at a time. This is the mental model of a simple CPU, even though real cores pipeline and overlap work internally. SIMD (single instruction, multiple data): one instruction applies the same operation to many data elements. The 256-bit YMM form of AVX vaddps adds eight pairs of float32 values; narrower and wider forms differ. MISD (multiple instruction, single data): several different operations on the same data. Its classification depends on the instruction and data streams being modelled. Redundant voting systems are not automatically MISD: identical replicated instruction streams do not establish multiple different instruction streams. MIMD (multiple instruction, multiple data): processors with independent instruction streams operating on multiple data streams. They may execute the same program and share data; ordinary multicore CPUs can provide MIMD execution. Modern refinements Flynn's four boxes are coarse. Real machines mix them, and some extra terms are common: SPMD (single program, multiple data) is a programming style in which participants run the same program on different data, potentially taking different branches. It can be used on MIMD CPUs or SIMT GPUs; MPI also supports other programming styles. SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) is NVIDIA's term for GPUs. You write scalar code for one thread; the hardware groups 32 threads into a GPU warp and issues instructions to active threads within it. Divergence and independent thread scheduling mean software must never assume implicit lockstep synchronisation. The later warp lessons examine that execution model. A CPU can combine MIMD across cores with SIMD within cores. A hypothetical 16-core design sustaining one 512-bit float32 add per core per cycle would produce 256 additions per cycle (16 cores with 16 lanes each). ISA width alone does not specify instruction throughput. Key takeaways Flynn classifies instruction and data streams; one machine can combine classes. SPMD describes a program organisation; SIMT describes NVIDIA thread execution. sum: Speedup compares the same job; efficiency divides speedup by processor count.
x: Speedup and efficiency Before the laws, two definitions. Both compare the time the same job takes on one processor with the time it takes on several. Speedup says how many times faster the parallel run is; parallel efficiency says how much of that speedup each processor contributes. For example, a job taking 100 seconds on one core and 20 seconds on eight cores has a speedup of five and efficiency of 62.5%. These numbers describe completion time; they do not mean every core was busy for exactly that fraction of every second. Linear speedup means the speedup equals the number of processors, so efficiency is 1 (100%). Efficiency may fall as processors are added because of serial work, communication, load imbalance or shared resources. It need not decrease monotonically. Amdahl's law: the serial part wins Gene Amdahl's 1967 argument is simple. Split a program's single-core run time into a parallel fraction that can be spread across processors and a serial fraction that cannot (start-up, reading input, a final merge, anything inherently sequential). For a fixed amount of work, assume equally fast processors, unchanged serial time, perfect division of the parallel work and no new overhead. Then only the parallel part shrinks, and dividing the old time by the new time gives the speedup: Add processors and the parallel contribution shrinks towards zero, but the serial contribution never does. That sets a ceiling: The ceiling exists only while some work is serial. If the parallel fraction were one, this ideal model would give linear speedup with no finite ceiling. Here is the same formula as code: With 90% of the work parallel, the ceiling is 10×. Going from 64 to 1,024 cores, sixteen times the hardware, takes you from 8.8× to 9.9×. Example: where the time goes. Take a job that is 90% parallel and takes 100 s on one core, and run it on 8 cores: The 10 s serial part is now nearly half the run. As the parallel portion shrinks, the serial portion can become more important. Profile again and compare achievable total-time reductions, including new overhead and implementation cost. Key takeaways Speedup compares the same job; efficiency divides speedup by processor count. A fixed serial duration limits ideal fixed-work speedup. Further reading Flynn’s original stream classification Amdahl’s original argument Gustafson’s scaled-speedup paper Karp and Flatt’s measurement paper

t: Accelerating only part of a program
sum: A local improvement must be weighted by its fraction of the original total time.
x: Amdahl beyond cores Amdahl’s law applies to any optimisation that speeds up only part of the work, not just to adding cores. Replace “divided across processors” with “made a specified number of times faster”: The actual benefit must also cover transfer and setup costs; even a smaller offloaded fraction can be worthwhile if its saving justifies those costs. Comparing two investments Suppose a batch job spends 30 seconds reading from storage and 70 seconds computing. Those intervals do not overlap. A faster storage device cuts the reading part to three seconds, so the complete run still takes 73 seconds. A code change that halves computation instead leaves 30 seconds of reading plus 35 seconds of computation: 65 seconds total. The second proposal wins even though its local improvement is much smaller. The comparison depends on the measured fractions. If storage time overlaps computation, adding the original durations double-counts elapsed time. If a change adds allocation, conversion or transfer work, include it in the new total. Profile the complete workload again after the change; the old fraction is a description of the baseline, not a permanent property of the program. For GPU offloading, also decide which result matters: the GPU kernel time, the complete request time or sustained throughput across many requests. A faster GPU kernel can still make a single request slower if moving the data dominates. A pipeline that overlaps copies and computation needs a dependency-aware timing model rather than simply adding all component durations. Key takeaways A local improvement must be weighted by its fraction of the original total time. Include transfers and setup when evaluating an offload. Further reading Flynn’s original stream classification Amdahl’s original argument Gustafson’s scaled-speedup paper Karp and Flatt’s measurement paper

t: Gustafson: using more hardware for more work
sum: Gustafson measures the serial fraction on the parallel run.
x: Gustafson's law: grow the problem Amdahl assumes a fixed problem size (strong scaling). In 1988 John Gustafson, working on a 1,024-processor machine at Sandia, described workloads that use larger machines to solve bigger problems in approximately the same time: finer weather grids, larger simulations, more training data. Gustafson measures fractions on the parallel run instead: the serial fraction of the parallel run. Assume the serial duration is unchanged, all processors have equal speed and the measured parallel interval contains perfectly divided useful work rather than added overhead. Now ask how long one processor would need for that same, larger job. The serial part takes the same time, but the parallel part, which kept n processors busy, would take n times as long: This is the scaled speedup. It is linear in n when the parallel-run serial fraction s is held fixed. For example, with 10% serial time on 64 processors: Are they contradictory? No. They answer different questions.
