First, for small inputs, nothing matters much. On 10 items, even exponential subset search needs only 1,024 steps. This is why a naive algorithm often works fine in testing. Second, for large n, the growth rate is everything. Suppose a machine does about 10^8 simple operations per second (an illustrative assumed rate, not a general hardware benchmark). Turning an operation count into a time is a division: The same division for the other growth rates gives these illustrative times for a million items: Growth Operations Time --------- Linear 1,000,000 0.01 s Linear times log 20,000,000 0.2 s Quadratic 1,000,000,000,000 about 2.8 hours The quadratic algorithm is not "a bit slower". It is the difference between instant and unusable. The production surprise A team writes the pairwise has_dup check for a feature that validates uploaded CSV files. In testing, files have 200 rows: 19,900 comparisons, unnoticeable. A customer uploads 2 million rows: about 2 x 10^12 comparisons. The request times out, retries, and takes the worker pool with it. Nothing was "wrong" with the code except its growth rate. Key takeaways Repeated halving produces logarithmic growth. Large inputs separate linear, linearithmic, quadratic and exponential work. The example timings use an illustrative operation rate; actual runtime requires measurement. Further reading Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia Time complexity — Wikipedia

sum: Translate a hardware speedup into the input size each growth rate can handle.
x: Keep the time budget fixed and ask how much larger the input can become. The growth rate decides how much value a faster machine provides. Faster hardware does not save you It is tempting to think faster hardware fixes a slow algorithm. Here N is the old input limit and N_new the new one, with the same time budget. The table compares growth shapes for a 10-times-faster machine. Growth Original limit New limit --------- Linear original ten times original Quadratic original about 3.16 times original Cubic original about 2.15 times original Exponential original about 3.3 extra items Where do these numbers come from? Set the work the new machine can do in the same time equal to 10 times the old work, and solve for the new input size: For a cubic algorithm the same steps give the cube root of 10, about 2.15. Better algorithms routinely give improvements of thousands or millions of times; hardware gives you a constant factor. Key takeaways A hardware speedup changes a constant factor in runtime. For quadratic work, the input gain follows the square root of the speed gain. Exponential search gains only a few extra items from a large constant speedup. Further reading Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: Choose the right input measure and simplify a cost without forgetting its limits.
x: What "input size" means n should measure whatever drives the work. Usually it is obvious, but not always: For a list or string, n is its length. For a graph, cost may depend on both vertices V and edges E; state both, as in O(V + E). For big-number arithmetic, count digits or bits rather than the value. Testing every divisor up to a number’s value is linear in that value but exponential in its bit length. For matrices, distinguish side length from entry count. A 1,000-by-1,000 matrix has a million entries. The number-size point is easy to get wrong, so here it is as a formula: When you describe an algorithm's cost, always say what n is. Why we ignore the small stuff Precise pair counting quickly becomes tedious and depends on what counts as one operation. The card expands that count to show which term eventually dominates. Keep only the fastest-growing term. The quadratic part dominates the linear correction: at 1,000 items their contributions are 500,000 and 500. Drop constant factors. Half the square and three times the square have the same doubling behaviour. Their constants depend on the machine and counting model; their growth shape does not. The result is a coarse but robust label: "this algorithm is quadratic". The following asymptotic-notation lessons make this precise with Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta. Constants are not irrelevant in practice Dropping constants compares growth; it does not mean constants never matter. The card’s linear alternative loses to the quadratic one below 100 items, including its 50-item example. The later practice lessons explain when constants and hardware decide the winner. Key takeaways For integers, input size usually counts bits or digits rather than the represented value. State separate dimensions when several quantities drive the work. Dominant terms predict growth; constants can still decide the winner for small inputs. Further reading Analysis of algorithms — Wikipedia Time complexity — Wikipedia

sum: Use fixed constants to prove or disprove a Big-O claim.
x: The last lesson said we keep the fastest-growing term and drop constants. Asymptotic notation is the precise language for doing that. It describes how a function behaves as n, the input size, grows towards infinity, which is why it is called asymptotic. There are three main symbols. Think of them as comparisons between growth rates, where f and g are two functions of n: Notation Read as Pointwise analogy --------- Big-O upper growth bound no greater than Big-Omega lower growth bound no smaller than Big-Theta tight growth bound equality O is the capital letter O ("Big-O"), Ω is Greek capital omega and Θ is Greek capital theta. Here f is the exact operation-count function and g a simpler comparison function, often quadratic. These labels compare eventual growth, rather than literal pointwise inequalities. Big-O: an upper bound Definition. Big-O says f is eventually no bigger than a fixed multiple of g: The two constants are what let us ignore details. c absorbs constant factors (a faster machine, a different way of counting). n_0 lets us ignore small inputs, where odd things can happen. Proving a Big-O bound To prove a Big-O claim, find fixed constants that make its definition true. The example below bounds a quadratic polynomial by replacing its smaller terms with quadratic terms, which only increases the right-hand side. These constants work. Any larger multiplier or starting threshold also works; one pair suffices. A quick table confirms it: Items Exact count Upper limit --------- 1 10 10 2 24 40 10 352 1,000 100 30,502 100,000 The ratio of the polynomial to the square settles towards 3. The card evaluates it at 100 items, giving about 3.05. A multiplier of 10 is loose, but loose is fine for Big-O. Disproving one To disprove a Big-O claim, show that no fixed constants can work. A quadratic function is not O(n), where n is the input size. Suppose that bound were possible: But n keeps growing and c is fixed, so this fails as soon as n is bigger than c. Contradiction. A ratio tending to infinity disproves an upper bound for an eventually positive comparison function. It is sufficient, not necessary: ratios can oscillate. The card’s final condition gives the general negation. Key takeaways An upper bound eventually holds with one fixed multiplier. Proving a bound means choosing constants that work for every sufficiently large input. A valid upper bound may be looser than useful. Further reading Big O notation — Wikipedia Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: Distinguish lower bounds, tight bounds and input cases.
x: Here n is the input size. A lower bound and a tight bound add information that an upper bound alone cannot provide. Big-Omega: a lower bound Definition. Big-Omega is the mirror image: f is eventually at least a fixed positive multiple of g. The quadratic polynomial from the upper-bound example also has a quadratic lower bound: its remaining terms are nonnegative. The example follows the definition below. Omega is used to say "at least this much work is unavoidable". A famous example you will meet later: any sorting algorithm that only compares elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, where n is the number of items being sorted. Big-Theta: a tight bound Definition. Big-Theta says f is squeezed between two multiples of g, so it is both O(g) and Ω(g): The same polynomial is squeezed between the two quadratic multiples below. This makes Theta the most informative statement: it pins growth down up to constants. Industry "Big-O" usually means Theta Strictly, O is only an upper bound. Binary search on n items is O(log n), but it is also O(n) and O(n^2), because those are bigger. All true, the last two useless. When engineers say "this is O(n)", they almost always mean "this is Θ(n)": the bound is tight. In interviews and code reviews, give the tightest bound you can. Not every function has a tidy Theta Consider a function doing one step on odd input sizes and as many steps as the input size on even sizes. It is O(n) and Ω(1), where n is the input size, but neither Θ(n) nor Θ(1). A tight bound still exists: every function has its own growth rate as a tight bound, or use that same piecewise cost as the comparison. It simply does not match a familiar monotone growth class. Big-O is not "worst case" A very common confusion. O, Ω and Θ describe functions. Best, average and worst case describe which input you are talking about. They are independent. For insertion sort on n items: Its worst-case time is Θ(n^2). Its best-case time (already-sorted input) is Θ(n). So its running time overall is O(n^2) and Ω(n). You can put a Θ on the worst case, an O on the average case, and so on. The code-analysis lessons cover cases in detail. Key takeaways A tight bound combines an upper and lower bound for the same cost function. Best, average and worst cases describe inputs; asymptotic notation describes the resulting functions. An irregular function need not fit a familiar monotone growth class. Further reading Big O notation — Wikipedia Asymptotic analysis — Wikipedia

sum: Drop dominated terms while preserving distinctions between exponential bases.
x: Here n is the input size. These rules simplify a cost after the meaning of upper, lower and tight bounds is clear. Simplification rules These all follow from the definitions. In each, n is the input size: Constants vanish. Fixed multipliers go into the bound’s constant. Sums take the maximum. Eventually the fastest-growing term dwarfs the others. Log bases do not matter. Any two logarithms differ by a fixed factor, so O(log n) ignores their bases. Exponent bases do matter. Cubic-base and quartic-base exponentials outgrow a base-two exponential. Polynomials beat logs, exponentials beat polynomials. The examples below hold eventually even when small inputs suggest the reverse. Products multiply. Θ(n) iterations each costing Θ(log n) give Θ(n log n) overall. Here n is the input size. Why log bases don't matter: the change-of-base rule turns a log in one base into a log in another by dividing by a constant. Why exponent bases do matter: dividing one exponential by another leaves an exponential, not a constant. The "=" is one-way A growth class is a set of functions. Saying a function has an upper bound means membership in that set, rather than ordinary equality. Reversing that statement treats a class as a value. Two functions in the same class need not equal one another. An expression that incorrectly treats the class as a number is: Key takeaways Constants and lower-order terms disappear when comparing eventual growth. Changing a logarithm base changes a constant factor. Changing an exponential base can change the growth class. Further reading Big O notation — Wikipedia Asymptotic analysis — Wikipedia

sum: Use ratios and the growth ladder to compare unfamiliar cost functions.
x: Here n is the input size; logarithms use base 2 unless a different base is stated. Use the simplification rules and ratio limits together. The limit test A quick way to compare two functions is to look at what their ratio does as n grows without limit: Ratio limit Conclusion ------ Zero upper bound, no lower bound Finite positive constant tight bound Infinity lower bound, no upper bound For example, compare the linear and quadratic functions in the following substitution: The linear function therefore has a quadratic upper bound but no quadratic tight bound. A zero ratio limit is also called little-o: strictly slower growth. The limit test only works when a limit exists; for oscillating functions, return to the definitions. The ladder of common classes From slowest to fastest, these classes use n for input size. Logarithms are base two, a square root means the nonnegative root, and factorial is the product of all positive integers up to the item count. Most example algorithms are studied later. Class Name Example --------- O(1) constant array index O(log n) logarithmic binary search O(√n) square root divisors up to the square root O(n) linear scan a list O(n log n) linearithmic merge sort O(n^2) quadratic all pairs O(n^3) cubic naive matrix multiply O(2^n) exponential all subsets O(n!) factorial all orderings A few points worth knowing: O(1) means bounded by a constant, not "one step". Reading 1,000 fixed fields is still O(1). O(log n) is what you get by repeatedly halving the problem. The base-2 log of a billion is about 30, because 2^30 ≈ 1.07 billion. Factorial grows faster than any exponential with a fixed base. Stirling’s approximation gives its size; taking its logarithm gives the comparison-sorting lower bound: Multiple variables are fine and often necessary. A graph algorithm might be O(V + E), where V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges; joining two lists of lengths n and m might be O(n + m). Do not collapse them into one n unless you know how they relate. Key takeaways A ratio limit compares growth when that limit exists. Polynomial, exponential and factorial functions can be ordered by their eventual growth. The logarithm of a factorial grows like the item count times its logarithm. Further reading Big O notation — Wikipedia Stirling's approximation — Wikipedia

sum: Add sequential work and count the true length of dependent inner loops.
x: You now have the notation. This lesson is about using it: looking at a piece of code and working out its time complexity quickly and correctly. Most code reduces to a handful of patterns, plus a few traps that catch even experienced engineers. Throughout, n is the input size (for example the length of the list), and m is the size of a second input when there is one. O(...) is Big-O, an upper bound on growth; Θ(...) is Big-Theta, a tight bound; and logarithms use base two, roughly how many times you can halve n before reaching 1. The basic rules Cost model. Treat fixed-size arithmetic, comparison and indexing as O(1). Python arbitrary-precision integers, long strings, user-defined comparisons and output can cost more; the counts below abstract those costs unless stated otherwise. Sequential blocks add. A linear block followed by a quadratic block has quadratic overall growth, because the quadratic term dominates. Nested independent loops multiply. O(n) iterations, each doing O(m) work, give O(nm), where n and m are the separate input sizes. Branches take the worse side. For the worst case, choose the more expensive branch. Function calls cost whatever the function costs. A one-line call to sorted() is O(n log n), where n is the list length. Those cover simple code. The interesting cases are loops whose bounds change. Dependent nested loops When the inner loop depends on the outer variable, you have to sum rather than multiply. The inner loop lengths rise from zero to one less than the outer bound. Add those lengths: Halving the work does not change the class. Three nested loops over i < j < k do one step per triple of different positions: A quick sanity check For nested loops, ask "roughly how many times does the innermost line run, as a fraction of the full box?" If it's a constant fraction (a half, a sixth), the class is the same as the full product. Key takeaways Sequential blocks add; independent nested counts multiply. When the inner bound depends on the outer variable, sum the actual counts. A function call contributes the work of its body, rather than a single free step. Further reading TimeComplexity — Python wiki Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: Recognise logarithmic loops and sum a geometric series of inner-loop lengths.
x: Here n is the positive input size. Do not multiply the largest possible inner count by every outer pass without checking how the inner length changes. Logarithmic loops A loop whose variable is multiplied or divided by a constant each step runs a logarithmic number of times. i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8,..., stopping once it reaches n. Count the steps: For a bound of 16, the loop has four passes through 1, 2, 4 and 8; a bound of 17 requires a fifth pass. The same logarithmic growth holds for halving (n //= 2) or another fixed factor. Tripling uses a base-three logarithm, but fixed log bases differ only by a constant factor. Here n is the positive input bound. This is the shape behind binary search and balanced trees. A loop that stops at a square root is different again: This loop stops when the square of its variable passes the bound, so its iteration count follows the square root. A bound of a million gives about a thousand iterations. Here is that count, followed by the independent-loop product: Mixed loops and two classic traps A linear outer loop around an independently restarted logarithmic inner loop has Θ(n log n) work, where n is its bound: Now the trap. What about an outer loop that doubles with an inner loop that runs i times? Multiplying the logarithmic outer count by the maximum inner length would overestimate it. The actual inner lengths double from one through the last power of two below the bound. Adding them gives a geometric series, dominated by its last term: So the whole thing is Θ(n). Always sum the actual counts. Key takeaways Multiplying a loop variable by a fixed factor gives logarithmic iteration counts. Resetting an inner loop makes each outer pass pay its cost again. Growing inner lengths can form a geometric series whose largest term dominates. Further reading Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: Sum the shrinking inner counts in a harmonic loop.
x: Here n is the positive input size. This example varies the step of the inner range instead of varying its endpoint. A harmonic loop The second trap is the harmonic loop: The inner range starts at zero, stops before the bound and jumps by the outer variable’s value. Its count is the input bound divided by that step, rounded up. Sum those actual counts: So this is Θ(n log n), where n is the input bound, rather than quadratic. Similar sums appear in sieves; the Sieve of Eratosthenes has the tighter Θ(n log log n) bound, where the second logarithm is applied to the first. They also occur in graph and number-theory problems. Pattern Approximate count ------ Inner bound grows with outer half the square Doubling variable logarithmic Squared variable within bound square root Doubling outer, inner to outer less than twice the bound Inner step equals outer bound times natural log Key takeaways A range step can change the inner length even when the stop stays fixed. The harmonic loop adds many shrinking contributions rather than equally sized passes. Summing actual counts can reveal a tighter bound than multiplying maximum bounds. Further reading Harmonic series — Wikipedia) Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: Count recursive calls and uncover work hidden inside ordinary Python operations.
x: Here n is the input size or recursive argument. A small amount of source code can describe a large amount of executed work. Recursion For recursive code, count how many calls happen and how much work each does outside the recursive calls. Linear recursion makes one call per level: Θ(n) calls and multiplications in the unit-cost model, where n is the recursive argument. Actual Python multiplication gets more expensive as the factorial grows; factorial means the product of all positive integers up to the argument. Branching recursion is where things explode. Naive Fibonacci makes two calls per level: Draw the recursion tree: (Here f5 means fib(5).) fib(5) makes 15 calls. In general: fib(30) makes about 2.7 million calls; fib(50) would make about 4 × 10^10. The waste is visible in the tree: fib(3) is computed twice, fib(2) three times. Caching results (memoisation, covered with dynamic programming later) reduces this to n distinct calls: Θ(n). Divide-and-conquer recursion (halving the problem) needs the tools in the recurrence lessons, but a rough guide: One call on half the input, O(1) extra work: Θ(log n) (binary search). Two calls on halves, O(n) extra work: Θ(n log n) (merge sort). Hidden costs Many "one-line" operations aren't O(1). In this CPython table, n is the list length: Operation Cost ------ x in some_list O(n) x in some_set O(1) average lst.append(x) O(1) amortised lst.insert(0, x) O(n) lst.pop(0) O(n) lst[a:b] O(b - a) copy sorted(lst) O(n log n) len(lst) O(1) This turns innocent-looking code quadratic: The membership test scans seen, so the function is Θ(n^2) when most items are distinct. Changing seen to a set makes it Θ(n) on average. The algorithm didn't change; the data structure did. Slicing in recursion binary_search(arr[mid:], target) looks logarithmic, but each slice copies the chosen half. The shrinking halves add to just under the original length, so a search on n items is O(n) rather than O(log n). Pass indices (lo, hi) instead. Key takeaways Count all recursive calls and the work performed outside those calls. Naive Fibonacci repeats subproblems; memoisation stores their answers. Membership tests and slices can turn a short-looking Python function into expensive work. Further reading TimeComplexity — Python wiki Memoization — Wikipedia Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: State which inputs or random choices a performance claim describes.
x: Here n is the number of input items. Case analysis describes which inputs or random choices are being counted. Best, average and worst case The same algorithm can take very different time on different inputs of the same size. Linear search shows this: Best case: target is first. 1 comparison, Θ(1). Worst case: target is last or absent. n comparisons, Θ(n). Average case: if the target is present and equally likely to be at any position, average the comparison counts over all n positions: For a list of 1,001 items that is 501 comparisons on average. Which one should you report? Worst case is the default. It's a guarantee, it's usually easiest to analyse, and adversarial inputs exist (users and attackers will find your slow path). Average case describes typical behaviour, but it depends on an assumption about the input distribution, which may be wrong for your data. Best case is rarely useful on its own. Any algorithm can be given a fast best case by checking for one special input. A related term is expected time for randomised algorithms. For distinct keys with uniformly random pivots, randomised quicksort is expected Θ(n log n) on every fixed input, because the randomness is in the algorithm, not the input. For distinct keys, quicksort with a first- or last-element pivot is average Θ(n log n) over uniformly random permutations but Θ(n²) on sorted input, which real data often is. Early exits An early return can improve best or average time. Whether it changes the worst case depends on whether any inputs still force the original expensive path. Ask which inputs attain the maximum after adding the check. Key takeaways Different inputs of the same size can follow different paths. An average-case claim needs an input distribution. Expected time for a randomised algorithm averages its random choices under a stated input model. Further reading Best, worst and average case — Wikipedia Algorithms by Jeff Erickson (free textbook)

sum: Distinguish extra storage, output memory and lazy value generation.
x: Space counts memory rather than elapsed work. The examples below use the usual one-word model unless they explicitly discuss integer bit lengths. Time is not the only resource an algorithm consumes. Space complexity measures how much memory an algorithm needs as a function of the input size n. It uses exactly the same notation (O for an upper bound, Ω for a lower bound, Θ for a tight bound) and the same habits (drop constants, keep the dominant term). Memory often matters more than people expect. A job allocating a dense n-by-n table (n rows of n cells) needs a lot of cells very quickly: Its memory budget may be exhausted before runtime becomes the main concern. Phones, serverless functions and containers usually have hard memory limits, and exceeding them kills the process outright. What counts There are two common conventions, and you should say which you mean: Total space: everything, including the input itself. Auxiliary space: only the extra memory the algorithm uses beyond its input. Auxiliary space is usually the more useful figure, because every algorithm that reads an n-item list has Ω(n) total space just from the input. When people say "merge sort uses O(n) space" or "this is O(1) space", they mean auxiliary. Output is sometimes counted separately too. A function that returns all n squares of its input needs O(n) memory for the result, but it couldn't do better, so some authors exclude it. Like time analysis, space analysis assumes each number, pointer or character takes one "word" of memory: O(1). That breaks down for unbounded integers, whose size grows with their value: Treating each number as one word is still the normal assumption. Examples total only ever holds one running sum, however long the list. reversed_copy builds a new list of n items. table builds n rows of n entries. In a model that reads or writes only O(1) cells per step, an O(T)-time computation can touch only O(T) auxiliary cells. This excludes the pre-existing input and does not bound untouched virtual memory reserved by an allocator. Low space does not imply low time: an n-bit counter can enumerate 2ⁿ values while reusing O(n) bits. Producing values one at a time The reverse also happens: when memory is tight, you can recompute values instead of storing them, or process data as a stream. Key takeaways Say whether the space count includes the input and output. Measure the largest amount of extra memory held at once. A generator can supply values one at a time instead of storing the whole intermediate list. Further reading Space complexity — Wikipedia

sum: Count live stack frames and understand why caching does not remove the first recursive descent.
x: Here n is the input length or recursive argument. Memoisation remembers returned answers, but the first uncached chain still has to reach its base case. A bottom-up loop avoids that chain. The recursion stack This is where most space mistakes happen. Every call that hasn't returned yet holds a stack frame with its local variables, arguments and return address. Recursive code uses space proportional to the maximum depth of the recursion, even if it never creates a list. When fact(5) reaches its base case, five frames are alive at once: Counting frames and treating values as atomic, fact has Θ(n) auxiliary space, where n is its argument; an iterative version keeps a constant number of values. Python integers are not fixed-size: a factorial alone needs Θ(n log n) bits. Its bit length follows the logarithm of its value, and the logarithm of a factorial has that growth rate. Note that it's depth, not the total number of calls, that matters. Naive fib(n) makes an exponential number of calls, but at any moment only one path from the root to a leaf is active: In the table below, n is the input (the argument, or the list length) and logarithmic means base-two logarithmic growth: Function Calls Maximum live depth --------- Factorial linear linear Naive Fibonacci exponential linear Binary search logarithmic logarithmic Merge sort about twice the item count logarithmic Merge sort’s stack has Θ(log n) depth, where n is the list length, because each call halves its range. The merge buffer needs O(n) space, so total auxiliary space is O(n). Python stops at 1,000 CPython's default recursion limit is 1,000 frames (sys.getrecursionlimit()). fact(5000) raises RecursionError. You can raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit, but very deep recursion stays fragile: every frame costs memory, and recursion that passes through C code can still overflow the real thread stack and crash the interpreter. Python doesn't do tail-call optimisation, so even tail-recursive functions use one frame per call. For deep linear recursion, rewrite it as a loop. Other languages vary. Scheme guarantees proper tail calls. Some C and C++ compilers eliminate tail calls when optimising, but the language standards don't require it. Stack limits depend on the operating system, thread configuration and build, so measure the actual limits and frame costs before relying on a recursion depth. Memoisation and stack depth Memoisation. Caching fib results turns Θ(φ^n) time into Θ(n) time, at the cost of Θ(n) space for the cache. A loop keeping just the last two values gets Θ(n) time and O(1) space. Key takeaways Stack space follows the deepest chain of pending calls. Many calls over time do not imply that all their frames coexist. Caching completed answers avoids repeated work; a cold recursive descent can still reach the recursion limit. Further reading Call stack — Wikipedia sys.setrecursionlimit — Python docs Tail call — Wikipedia

sum: Mutate an existing list and bound quicksort stack depth by recursing on the smaller side.
x: Here n is the number of input items. In-place transformations save memory by reusing the input itself. In-place algorithms An algorithm is in-place if it transforms its input using only O(1) auxiliary space, a constant amount however big the input of n items is (some definitions allow O(log n), to cover a recursion stack). Reversing a list with two pointers is the classic example: Compare xs[::-1], which is simpler but allocates a whole new list. In-place algorithms save memory and often run faster (less allocation, better cache use). The costs: They destroy the input. If the caller still needs the original, it has to copy it first, and the saving vanishes. They can be harder to get right. Swapping elements around inside one array is fiddlier than building a new one. They don't play well with sharing. Mutating a list that other code (or another thread) holds a reference to causes surprising bugs. Sorting is the familiar case. Heapsort sorts in place with O(1) auxiliary space. Quicksort partitions in place, but its recursion needs a stack: O(log n) expected depth, O(n) in the worst case. A standard trick bounds it at O(log n) even in the worst case: recurse into the smaller partition and loop on the larger one, because the smaller side is at most half the size. Python's list.sort() mutates its input, but is not in-place in the strict O(1)-auxiliary-space sense; it may allocate a temporary buffer of up to half the list (half the items) while merging. Why does recursing into the smaller side bound the depth? Each recursive call at least halves the size of the part it works on: For a million items that is at most 20 frames including the initial call, instead of up to a million. Key takeaways Strict in-place analysis permits only a constant amount of extra storage. Mutating the input can affect other references to the same list. Recursing on the smaller quicksort partition bounds stack depth even when partition balance is poor. Further reading In-place algorithm — Wikipedia Call stack — Wikipedia

sum: Choose a representation and balance extra memory against speed.
x: Here n is the input size. The earlier lessons established how to count extra storage; now use that count to choose an algorithm and representation. Time-space trade-offs Here n is the input item count. Many speed-ups work by spending memory: Hashing for lookups. Checking for duplicates with a set takes expected O(n) time and O(n) space. Sorting in place, then scanning neighbours, takes O(n log n) time with little extra space. Precomputation. A prefix-sum array (n extra numbers) answers "sum of xs[a:b]" in O(1) instead of O(b − a), the length of the range (formula below). Lookup tables. Counting set bits in a byte with a 256-entry table instead of looping over bits. The prefix-sum trick stores running totals once, then answers any range sum with one subtraction: For input [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], the running totals are [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. The card’s substitution adds the middle three values, giving 6: Constants matter for memory Asymptotic notation hides constant factors, but with memory, those constants decide whether something fits. For a typical 64-bit CPython build (check sys.getsizeof on the actual build): A small int object is 28 bytes (sys.getsizeof(1)). A list stores an 8-byte pointer per element, plus the objects themselves. So a list of 10 million distinct small integers costs: That is roughly 80 MB of pointers plus about 280 MB of int objects. A NumPy int64 array or the standard array module stores the same numbers as raw 8-byte values: about 80 MB. Both are "O(n)", but the packed data fits below a 256 MB budget, while the list does not. Runtime overhead and temporary conversion buffers still need headroom. An interview-style check "Find whether any two numbers in this list of n numbers sum to a target." Hash set: expected O(n) time, O(n) space. Sort then two pointers: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra if you may sort in place. Neither is "better"; it depends on whether memory or time is the constraint, and whether you may modify the input. Key takeaways Hashing and precomputation can save time by storing additional data. Recomputation, streaming and in-place algorithms can reduce extra memory. Object overhead and representation decide whether real data fits a memory limit. Further reading Space complexity — Wikipedia

t: Dynamic arrays and total append cost
sum: Bound the total writes and copies over a sequence of dynamic-array appends.
x: Some operations are usually cheap but occasionally very expensive. Appending to a Python list is the standard example: almost every append writes one slot, but now and then the list runs out of room and copies every element to a bigger block of memory. Here n is the number of elements in the list (or the number of operations in a sequence). If you judged each operation by its worst case, you'd call append O(n), and a loop of n appends O(n^2), with quadratic growth. O(n²) is a valid but unnecessarily loose upper bound; the tight bound (Θ, Big-Theta) for n appends from an empty list is Θ(n). Amortised analysis gives the right answer by bounding the total cost of a sequence of operations, then dividing by the length of the sequence. Amortised is not average-case Average-case analysis assumes a probability distribution over inputs. Amortised analysis uses no probability at all. It says: for any sequence of n operations, even one chosen by an adversary, the total cost is at most n times the amortised cost. It's a worst-case guarantee about sequences. The dynamic array A dynamic array keeps its elements in a fixed-size block of memory with some spare capacity. Append writes into the next free slot. When the block is full, it allocates a new block of double the capacity, copies everything across, and frees the old one. Count the cost of appending nine items, starting from capacity 1, as one unit per element written or copied: Append # Copies Write Capacity after ------------ 1 0 1 1 2 1 1 2 3 2 1 4 4 0 1 4 5 4 1 8 6-8 0 3 8 9 8 1 16 Total copies: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Total writes: 9. Total cost 24 for 9 appends, 24 / 9 ≈ 2.67 per append, under 3. This lesson uses aggregate analysis to prove that this always holds; the following lessons give accounting and potential proofs. All three prove the same kind of statement. The amortised cost per operation is the total cost of a sequence divided by its length: Method 1: aggregate analysis Bound the total cost of n operations directly, then divide. Writes: exactly n. Copies: the array resizes when its size hits 1, 2, 4,..., up to the largest power of two below n. The copy costs are a geometric series (each term double the one before), whose sum is just under twice its last term: Check against the nine-append table: four copy rounds total 15 copies, plus nine writes. The aggregate card confirms that the 24-unit total stays below the 27-unit bound. Thus the amortised cost is at most three units: O(1), independent of sequence length. Aggregate analysis is the simplest method, but it gives every operation the same amortised cost. When a data structure supports several operations with different costs, the next two methods are more flexible. Key takeaways Amortised analysis bounds whole operation sequences without assuming probabilities. A doubling array performs a geometric series of copies. Bounding total sequence cost can give constant amortised append cost despite an expensive individual resize. Further reading Amortized analysis — Wikipedia Dynamic array — Wikipedia Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Use the accounting method to save credit during cheap operations.
x: The aggregate proof bounded all appends together. The accounting method instead assigns credit to elements so that each future copy has already been paid for. Method 2: the accounting method Charge each operation a fixed amortised cost, which may be more than it really costs. The overcharge is stored on elements of the structure as amortised credit, and expensive operations pay for themselves out of saved credit. The rule: credit must never go negative. For the dynamic array, charge 3 units per append: 1 unit pays for writing the new element now. 1 unit is stored on the new element, to pay for copying it at the next resize. 1 unit is stored on an element from the older half of the array, which already spent its credit in the previous resize. Why it works: consider the append that doubles capacity, plus the subsequent appends filling the new block. Together they number the old capacity and each banks two units: Since the bank never goes negative, the real total cost is at most the total charged: 3n. Key takeaways An accounting proof charges cheap operations more than their immediate cost. Saved credit pays for later expensive operations. The credit must not go negative if the charges are to bound actual cost. Further reading Accounting method — Wikipedia) Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Use changes in a potential function to prove an amortised bound.
x: A potential function tracks stored credit for the whole structure rather than individual elements. This unit applies it to the doubling array. Method 3: the potential method Instead of credit on individual elements, define a single potential function Φ (the Greek capital letter phi) on the whole data structure, like stored energy. The amortised cost of an operation is its real cost plus the change in potential it causes: Summing over a sequence, the Φ terms form a telescoping sum: each intermediate Φ appears once with a plus and once with a minus, so they cancel: So if Φ starts at 0 and is never negative, the total actual cost is at most the total amortised cost. The art is choosing a Φ that rises during cheap operations and drops sharply when an expensive one happens. For the dynamic array, use Start with an empty array of capacity zero. After the first append, it is at least half full, so potential stays nonnegative: Append without resize: size rises by one while capacity stays fixed. Actual cost is one unit, potential rises by two, and their sum is three. Append with resize: the array is full, so its size equals its capacity. It doubles capacity, copies all existing elements and writes one new element: For capacity eight, actual cost is nine units; potential falls from eight to two, leaving amortised cost three, as the substitution below shows. Every append has amortised cost at most three; the very first append from zero to one capacity costs only two. Cheap appends build the potential that pays for copying. Key takeaways Amortised cost includes actual cost and the change in stored potential. Intermediate potential terms cancel when costs are summed. The starting and final potential determine whether the amortised total bounds the actual total. Further reading Potential method — Wikipedia Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Choose growth and shrink thresholds that avoid repeated full-array copying.
x: Here n is the number of stored elements or appends. Amortised bounds depend on the resizing policy as well as the data structure. Why the growth must be geometric Suppose instead the array grows by a fixed amount, say 10 slots each time. Resizes happen at sizes 10, 20, 30,..., and each copies the whole array: That is about 5 × 10^10 copies for a million appends, and the amortised cost per append is Θ(n), growing in proportion to n. Growing by a constant factor is what makes the series geometric and the amortised cost O(1). The factor doesn't have to be 2. Suppose each resize multiplies the capacity by a growth factor g, starting from capacity 1. Ignoring integer rounding: The bound in terms of an arbitrary append count needs the growth-factor multiplier because final capacity may exceed current size. Near a full final capacity, the smaller estimate applies. Doubling gives roughly one copy per stored element, while growth by one-half gives roughly two, as the card shows. Real implementations differ: Implementation Growth ------ CPython list ~1.125x + small constant OpenJDK ArrayList single-item growth preferred ~1.5x; implementation detail C++ libstdc++ vector single-item growth commonly ~2x; implementation detail Rust Vec amortised O(1) push; no particular growth factor guaranteed CPython's comment in listobject.c gives the capacities as 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76,... A smaller factor wastes less memory on empty slots but copies more often. Any factor above 1 keeps appends O(1) amortised. Shrinking without thrashing If the array also supports pop, you may want to free memory as it empties. The obvious rule, "halve the capacity when it becomes half full", has a nasty failure. Suppose the array is exactly full. Append doubles its capacity, copying the old contents. Pop makes it half full, triggering a shrink back to the original capacity and another full copy. Append again doubles it once more. Alternating push and pop at that boundary makes every operation cost Θ(n), where n is the element count, close to the original capacity. The fix is hysteresis: grow when full, but shrink only when the array is a quarter full, and then halve. After any resize the array is half full, so at least Θ(capacity) cheap operations must happen before the next resize. Both push and pop are then O(1) amortised. Key takeaways A fixed multiplicative growth factor preserves constant amortised append cost in the copy-on-resize model. Adding a fixed number of slots leads to a quadratic total copy cost. Separated growth and shrink thresholds prevent alternating operations from forcing a resize each time. Further reading Dynamic array — Wikipedia CPython listobject.c (list growth policy)

sum: Apply sequence reasoning to counters and queues while recognising latency spikes.
x: Here n counts operations or stored items, as stated in each example. Separate total work from the latency of one operation. More examples Binary counter. Incrementing a binary counter can flip many bits (0111 -> 1000), but over the sequence the lowest bit flips each time, the next about half as often, and the next about a quarter as often: So increment is O(1) amortised: a constant per operation, however large n is. Queue from two stacks. Push onto an inbox stack. To dequeue, pop from outbox; if it's empty, first move everything from inbox to outbox. A single dequeue can cost O(n), where n is the number of elements waiting, but each element is moved at most once, so every operation is O(1) amortised. Hash table resizing works just like the dynamic array: double the table when the load factor gets high, rehashing every key. Later modules meet more advanced cases: splay trees and union-find both have amortised bounds that worst-case analysis can't show. Pitfalls in production Amortised O(1) is not "every operation is fast". A Python list of 100 million pointers occupies about 800 MB; the append that triggers a resize may have to copy most of that, and the call pauses until it finishes. Amortisation bounds aggregate work, but allocation and copying still affect measured throughput. For latency-sensitive systems (trading, games, audio, real-time control), one slow append can blow a deadline. Ways to avoid spikes: Preallocate when you know the size: reserve() in C++, with_capacity() in Rust, [None] n in Python. Incremental resizing. Redis's hash tables rehash gradually: they keep the old and new tables side by side and move a few buckets on each operation (and in a background timer), so no single command pays for the whole rehash. Amortisation can break if expensive states can be replayed. The proofs assume each expensive operation is preceded by many cheap ones that build up credit. If a data structure is shared and old versions can be reused (some persistent or functional structures), an adversary can trigger the expensive operation on the same "full" version repeatedly. Okasaki's work on purely functional data structures handles this with lazy evaluation. Key takeaways Counters and two-stack queues reuse the same sequence-cost reasoning. A good amortised bound does not guarantee a fast individual operation. Preallocation and incremental resizing can help workloads with tight latency requirements. Further reading Amortized analysis — Wikipedia CPython listobject.c (list growth policy) Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Separate recursive subproblem costs from each call’s own work.
x: Loops can be analysed by counting. Recursive algorithms, especially divide and conquer (split the problem, solve the pieces recursively, combine), need a different tool. Their running time is naturally described by a recurrence: an equation that defines T(n), the running time on an input of size n, in terms of T on smaller inputs. This lesson is about writing those recurrences and solving them quickly. Throughout, n is the input size, O, Ω and Θ are the upper, lower and tight bounds from the asymptotic-notation lessons, and logarithms use base two unless another base is written. From code to recurrence Every recursive function's cost splits into the calls it makes and the work it does itself: Binary search makes one recursive call on half the range, plus a constant amount of work (O(1)). Merge sort calls itself on two halves and merges in linear time: Some common recurrence/solution pairs follow. Each pair uses T for its own cost function with a fixed positive base case: Pair Example Growth --------- 1 Binary search logarithmic 2 Halving then scanning linear 3 Tree traversal linear 4 Merge sort linear times log 5 Linear recursion linear 6 Selection sort quadratic 7 Towers of Hanoi exponential The following recurrence lessons derive these bounds. The base case costs a fixed amount when input is too small to split, so it is usually left implicit. Rounding fractional input sizes up or down does not change these asymptotic answers. Key takeaways A recurrence adds recursive subproblem costs to the work outside those calls. The number and size of recursive calls determine its shape. Base cases and rounding matter for exact counts even when they leave the eventual growth unchanged. Further reading Divide-and-conquer algorithm — Wikipedia Algorithms by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

sum: Sum level costs to identify whether roots, levels or leaves dominate.
x: Here n is the original input size. For the exact counts below, take n to be a power of two and use a base-case cost of one at size one. Any fixed positive base-case cost gives the same asymptotic bounds. A recursion tree makes the distribution of work across levels visible. The recursion tree The most intuitive method is to draw the tree of calls and add up the work at each level. For merge sort, two half-size calls are followed by a linear merge: Each level does n work in total, and the size halves at each level. Add the levels: For an input of 1,024 that is 11 levels of 1,024 work each, about 11,000 steps. Total: Θ(n log n). Now try three half-size calls plus linear outside work, the shape of Karatsuba multiplication. Level work changes as shown below: The second line exchanges the roles of logarithm base and exponent in the identity shown in the card. Here branching uses three children and splitting halves each input. A growing geometric series is dominated by its last term, so leaf growth determines the cost. Now take two half-size calls with quadratic outside work: The work shrinks by half per level. A shrinking geometric series is dominated by its first term, the root, giving Θ(n^2) work, where n is the original size. These three behaviours are the whole idea behind the Master Theorem. The three shapes - Work per level shrinks geometrically: the root dominates, so total work has the same tight growth as the root’s own work. - Work per level is equal: multiply one level’s work by the logarithmic number of levels. - Work per level grows geometrically: the leaves dominate, so total work has the same tight growth as the leaf count (with constant-cost leaves). Key takeaways Count the work on each level, then add the levels. Equal level costs accumulate over the tree depth. Geometrically shrinking costs favour the root; growing costs favour the leaves. Further reading Master theorem — Wikipedia) Algorithms by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

sum: Find the critical exponent and recognise leaf-dominated recurrences.
x: The Master Theorem The Master Theorem solves recurrences of this shape, where every recursive call gets the same fraction of the input: The key quantity is the critical exponent. It comes from counting the leaves of the recursion tree: The leaf-count term in the card gives the total bottom-level cost; the root costs the outside-work function. Comparing them says which end of the tree wins. Case 1 Case 1: outside work is polynomially smaller than leaf growth. The leaves dominate: Strassen and Karatsuba Here is the Strassen recurrence worked through in full: Two examples are famous. Strassen uses seven half-size matrix products instead of eight, beating cubic multiplication. Karatsuba uses three half-size integer products instead of four, beating quadratic multiplication. The card also gives Karatsuba’s recurrence. Reducing the number of subproblems lowers the critical exponent; with eight matrix products the exponent would be three, matching naive multiplication. Key takeaways The Master Theorem compares outside work with the recursion tree’s leaf count. When outside work is polynomially smaller, the leaves determine the tight bound. Reducing the number of subproblems can lower the exponent, as in Strassen and Karatsuba. Further reading Master theorem — Wikipedia) Strassen algorithm — Wikipedia Karatsuba algorithm — Wikipedia Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Handle matching costs and logarithmic factors with the second case.
x: The previous unit defined the critical exponent from the number of subproblems and their shrink factor. Here n is the input size. This unit covers the case where outside work matches that critical growth, possibly with logarithmic factors. Case 2 Case 2: outside work matches the critical growth. Every level does roughly equal work, so you multiply by the number of levels, which adds a log factor: (Levels are exactly equal only when the log-factor exponent is zero; for larger k, summing the slowly changing level costs still adds one log power.) Key takeaways Matching root and leaf costs adds a logarithmic factor across the levels. The stated logarithmic-factor extension adds one further log power. Apply the case’s conditions before reading off the result. Further reading Master theorem — Wikipedia) Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Check regularity and apply the complete three-case shortcut.
x: Here n is the input size. After the leaf-dominated and balanced cases, the final case considers a root whose own work outweighs its children. Case 3 Case 3: outside work is polynomially larger than leaf growth, and a regularity condition holds. Then the root dominates: Regularity means outside work really shrinks down the tree. It holds for ordinary polynomial outside work, such as the example below, where two children together do half the parent’s work. The condition rules out pathological, wildly oscillating functions. The simple version Most textbook recurrences have polynomial outside work. Compare its exponent with the critical exponent, as the three conditions below show: Outside-work exponent Result ------ Below critical exponent leaves dominate Equal to critical exponent add a logarithm Above critical exponent root dominates Equivalently, compare branching with the shrink factor raised to the outside-work exponent. Their ratio determines whether level costs grow, stay equal or shrink: Worked examples The following independent recurrence/solution pairs use the parameter values in the table beneath them. Exponents printed as decimals are rounded: Pair Children; shrink factor Critical exponent Outside work; case ------------ 1 1; 2 0 constant; 2 2 2; 2 1 linear; 2 3 3; 2 about 1.585 linear; 1 4 7; 2 about 2.807 quadratic; 1 5 4; 2 2 quadratic; 2 6 2; 2 1 quadratic; 3 7 1; 2 0 linear; 3 8 2; 2 1 linear times log; 2, log exponent one Key takeaways Polynomially larger outside work dominates only when the regularity condition also holds. For ordinary polynomial outside work, comparing exponents gives the familiar three-case shortcut. The worked table applies the same conditions to several common recurrences. Further reading Master theorem — Wikipedia) Erickson: Solving Recurrences

t: When the Master Theorem does not fit
sum: Recognise unsupported recurrences and prove a guessed bound by induction.
x: Here n is input size. Check the theorem’s assumptions first; otherwise use a recursion tree and induction. Where the Master Theorem doesn't apply Subtract-and-conquer. Subtracting from input size fails the required equal-fraction split. Unroll instead: Two calls one item smaller plus a constant outside step double work per level: For 10 discs that is 1,023 moves; for 64 discs, about 1.8 × 10^19. The gap between cases. With critical exponent one, outside work is smaller by a logarithm instead of a fixed positive power: So it falls between case 1 and case 2 of the standard statement. (The answer is Θ(n log log n), as the later Akra–Bazzi examples show. Some textbooks state an extended case 2 that allows negative k and covers this directly.) Uneven splits. Different-size children fail the equal-size assumption. Non-constant branching or shrink factors. Square-root-sized children with square-root branching need another technique. Rewriting input as a power of two halves its exponent: Substitution: guess and prove When no theorem fits, guess from a recursion tree and prove the bound by mathematical induction. For merge sort on powers of two, start at two items and choose a fixed multiplier covering that base case. Handle one item separately: its logarithm is zero: The second line assumes the bound for half-size input. The final subtraction cancels the added linear work because the fixed multiplier is at least one. The classic induction bug A linear growth class does not prove the same fixed multiplier works. The failed step increases the coefficient; hiding it inside Big-O incorrectly makes the induction appear to close. Key takeaways Subtracting from input size, uneven splits and some gap functions need other techniques. A substitution proof must preserve the same chosen constant through the induction. A loose asymptotic simplification inside the proof does not establish the required inequality. Further reading Master theorem — Wikipedia) Akra–Bazzi method — Wikipedia Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Balance unequal subproblems and account for work across their scales.
x: Akra–Bazzi: the general case The Akra–Bazzi method handles recurrences with several subproblem sizes under regularity assumptions: nonnegative g with suitable polynomial growth, bounded positive base cases, and sufficiently small perturbations of the subproblem sizes. The smooth polynomial/logarithmic examples here satisfy these conditions. The recurrence looks like this: Find the unique p that balances the subproblems' total weight: Then: The balancing exponent plays the same role as the critical exponent in the Master Theorem. It balances the total weight of the subproblems. Comparing outside work with the resulting leaf-growth term gives the correction, but the integral handles in-between cases smoothly. The theorem also tolerates small perturbations such as floors and ceilings. Example 1: uneven split. Split into one third and two thirds, with linear outside work: The recursion tree agrees: complete early levels each do linear work, and even the deepest chain has logarithmic depth. The card records the respective logarithm bases; rounding only changes these level counts by constants. Key takeaways Akra–Bazzi allows different subproblem fractions under its regularity assumptions. The balancing exponent describes the recursive structure. The integral adds the contribution of outside work across scales. Further reading Akra–Bazzi method — Wikipedia Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Apply the general method to linear selection and a gap between Master Theorem cases.
x: The previous unit introduced the balancing exponent and outside-work integral. Here n is the input size. These examples apply that method to selection and a recurrence whose outside work lies between the standard Master Theorem cases. Two applications Example 2: median of medians. Linear-time selection has one child a fifth of the size, another seven tenths, and linear outside work: Example 3: the gap case. Two half-size calls and linear work divided by a logarithm balance at exponent one. Use natural logarithms in the integral; changing base rescales outside work by a fixed factor: The integral starts at two rather than one because the logarithm at one is zero; the lower limit only changes constants. Key takeaways Subproblem fractions whose total is below one can lead to geometrically shrinking outside work. The integral distinguishes near-linear gap cases from the ordinary balanced case. A fixed lower integration limit avoids singularities without changing the growth class. Further reading Akra–Bazzi method — Wikipedia Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Use an explicitly assumed operation rate to screen algorithm choices.
x: Asymptotic analysis is a model. It is an excellent one, and for large enough inputs it predicts the winner. But it deliberately throws away information: constant factors, the memory hierarchy, the language runtime, and what your inputs actually look like. Experts know both the model and where it leaks. This lesson is about using complexity as an engineering tool rather than an exam answer. What fits in one second The most practical skill is estimating from the input size n which complexity you can afford. For the arithmetic exercise below, assume 10^8 counted operations per second and unit leading constants. This is a hypothetical model, not measured throughput or a guarantee for any language. The estimate is one division: In the table, factorial means the product of all positive integers up to n; exponential growth uses a fixed base of two. Here n is the input size and log is the base-2 logarithm. Largest n (about 1 s) Affordable complexity ------ 10 to 11 O(n!) 20 to 25 O(2^n) ~500 O(n^3) ~5,000 to 10,000 O(n^2) ~10^6 O(n log n) ~10^8 O(n) large n, subject to constants and storage O(log n), O(1) The table comes straight from the arithmetic: Read it backwards too. A 200,000-item quadratic problem needs 40 billion counted operations: 400 seconds at the assumed rate, far above a second. So seek O(n log n) or better, where n is the item count. At no more than 20 items, exponential subset search may instead be the simplest correct answer. Content gap: cross-language timings A reproducible benchmark for the claimed universal Python-to-compiled speed ratio is absent, so that ratio is omitted. Interpreter version, operation type, data and hardware matter. Native built-ins or vectorisation can reduce interpreter overhead; measure the actual workload. Key takeaways An operation budget is useful only with a stated rate and cost model. Large quadratic counts can rule out an approach before implementation. Small inputs can make exhaustive search a sensible starting point. Further reading Time complexity guide — USACO Guide

sum: Explain practical performance differences hidden by asymptotic labels.
x: Here n is the input size unless an example names another dimension. The asymptotic model leaves out factors that must be measured on the actual workload. Constant factors Big-O hides constants, but the computer doesn't. Two algorithms in the same class can differ by 10x, and an asymptotically worse one can win for all inputs you'll ever see. For sorting here, n is the item count. Insertion sort is Θ(n^2), but its inner loop is tiny, branch-predictable and works entirely in cache. For small n it beats merge sort and quicksort, so real libraries use hybrid sorts: Timsort-style natural merge sorts extend short runs with binary insertion sort, then merge them. Thresholds differ by implementation; modern CPython uses a Powersort merge policy, so a single threshold/policy should not be attributed to both Python and Java. Introsort (C++ std::sort in common implementations) runs quicksort, switches to heapsort if the recursion gets too deep (guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case), and leaves small partitions (16 elements in libstdc++) for a final insertion sort pass. The general lesson: the crossover point is found by measurement, not theory. The memory hierarchy The RAM model treats memory accesses uniformly, but real machines have caches, main memory and storage with different access costs. Content gap: hardware latency measurements The repository contains no reproducible measurement setup for the original latency table. Exact nanosecond and microsecond figures are omitted; consult the target hardware documentation and benchmark its access patterns. Cache-line size is hardware-specific (64 bytes is common on x86; ARM implementations vary). So access patterns matter enormously: Arrays vs linked lists. Summing an array and summing a linked list are both Θ(n). But the array is contiguous: a 64-byte cache line holds eight 8-byte values and the prefetcher streams the rest. A linked list's nodes can be scattered across memory, and each next pointer must be loaded before the following address is known, so ordinary demand loads form a dependency chain and are harder to overlap. The list is often several times slower, and much worse when nodes are scattered. Traversal order. C stores 2D arrays row by row. For an N by N array of 8-byte values, both loops below are Θ(N^2), touching every matrix element once: For large N (so the matrix doesn't fit in cache), the column-order loop touches a new cache line on almost every access and can be several times slower, sometimes by an order of magnitude. For search here, n is the key count. B-trees, with hundreds of keys per node, need fewer memory or disk accesses than binary search trees for the same Θ(log n) search. Cache-aware and cache-oblivious algorithms are designed around counting cache misses instead of instructions. Galactic algorithms Some algorithms have the best known asymptotic complexity but are never used, because their constants are astronomical. They're nicknamed galactic algorithms: they would only win on inputs larger than anything that fits on Earth. Matrix multiplication. For n by n matrices, the naive algorithm is Θ(n^3) and Strassen's is about Θ(n^2.807). Theoretical algorithms descending from Coppersmith–Winograd have pushed the exponent below 2.372, but they are useless in practice. Even Strassen is used only above a size threshold, if at all; optimised BLAS libraries mostly rely on carefully blocked Θ(n^3) code that uses the cache brilliantly. Integer multiplication. For n-digit numbers, Harvey and van der Hoeven's 2019 algorithm runs in O(n log n), believed optimal, but only beats existing methods for astronomically large numbers. Practical libraries such as GMP switch between schoolbook, Karatsuba, Toom–Cook variants and FFT-based multiplication at tuned size thresholds. The opposite trap also exists: assuming a fancy algorithm is needed when the simple one, with a good constant, is fast enough. Key takeaways Constant factors and memory access patterns can determine measured performance. Sequential array traversal has better locality than scattered dependent accesses. An asymptotically better algorithm may have constants that make it impractical. Further reading Locality of reference — Wikipedia Galactic algorithm — Wikipedia Introsort — Wikipedia Timsort — Wikipedia

sum: Recognise when an attacker can force expensive algorithm paths.
x: Here n counts input items or characters, as stated in each example. Hostile input makes worst-case behaviour an engineering concern. Worst case and adversaries Average-case performance is fine when inputs are benign. When an attacker controls the input, they will find your worst case. Hash flooding. Hash tables give O(1) average lookups, but if many keys collide, operations degrade to O(n) for a table of n keys, and inserting n colliding keys becomes Θ(n^2): roughly half the square of the key count in comparisons. In 2011, researchers showed that many web frameworks could be knocked over by a single POST request whose parameter names all collided. Languages responded by randomising their hash functions per process. Python has randomised str hashing by default since 3.3 and uses SipHash since 3.4. Regular expression backtracking. Many regex engines use backtracking, which is exponential on some patterns and inputs. In July 2019 a single badly behaved regular expression exhausted CPU across Cloudflare's network and caused a global outage. RE2 and Rust's regex provide bounded search complexity for supported patterns. Rust documents O(mn) for individual searches (pattern size m, haystack size n), while repeated-match iterators can reach O(mn²). A fixed-pattern single search is linear in n. Quicksort on sorted input. A first- or last-element pivot can turn sorted distinct input into Θ(n²). Randomisation gives an expected bound; introsort's heapsort fallback provides the worst-case bound. If an input could be hostile, choose algorithms with good worst-case bounds, or randomise. Key takeaways User-controlled input can expose an algorithm’s worst paths. Hash collisions, regex backtracking and bad pivots can amplify work. Choose a suitable worst-case guarantee or stated randomisation model for the workload. Further reading Introsort — Wikipedia

sum: Use doubling ratios and realistic constraints to choose a suitable implementation.
x: Here n is the input size. Measurement complements operation counting by exposing hidden costs and practical crossover points. Measuring: the doubling experiment You can estimate the exponent of an algorithm empirically. Time it at n, 2n, 4n and look at the ratios. These numbers are illustrative, not recorded measurements: n time ratio --------- 1,000 0.05 s 2,000 0.20 s 4.0 4,000 0.81 s 4.05 8,000 3.30 s 4.07 Why does the ratio reveal the exponent? If the running time is roughly a power of n, doubling n multiplies it by 2 to that power, and the constant cancels: A ratio of four suggests exponent two: quadratic. A ratio of 2 means linear; slightly above two suggests linear-times-log growth; 8 means cubic. The method assumes the time is close to a single power of n over the range measured; constant start-up costs or a change in cache behaviour between sizes can distort the ratios. This catches the "it's O(n) on paper but quadratic in practice" bugs from hidden costs (the code-analysis lessons). Measure carefully: warm up first (JIT compilers, caches), repeat runs and take the minimum or median, and use realistic data. In Python, the timeit module handles the repetition for you, and a profiler (such as cProfile) tells you where the time actually goes. Choosing between algorithms For these choices, n counts input items. A practical checklist: How big is n, really? Today and in a few years. If n will never exceed 1,000, an O(n^2) algorithm doing 1,000 × 1,000 = a million cheap steps is probably fine. Typical or worst case? Is the input adversarial or user-controlled? Do you have latency requirements (tail latency) or just throughput? Memory. Will the faster algorithm's extra space fit? (The space-complexity lessons.) Constants and hardware. Contiguous arrays and sequential access are fast; pointer chasing is slow. Simplicity. Simpler code has fewer bugs and is easier to change. Use the simplest algorithm that is fast enough for the largest n you expect. Use the library. Standard library sorts, hash maps and heaps are heavily tuned. Beating them is rarely worth the effort. Measure. Knuth's line, "premature optimization is the root of all evil", continues: "yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%". Profile to find that 3%. A realistic decision You need the top 10 scores from 50 million records. Sorting is O(n log n). A size-10 heap scan is O(n log 10), effectively O(n), and uses tiny memory. Quickselect is O(n) average. At that input size, the heap scan is simple, streaming (no need to hold all records) and fast, making it a suitable starting point to benchmark, even though sorting would also "work". Key takeaways Doubling experiments suggest growth only over the range and conditions measured. Profile realistic data to find which operations dominate. Choose the simplest approach that meets the input, memory and latency constraints. Further reading timeit — Python docs

t: Direct indexing with array address arithmetic
sum: Address arithmetic gives direct access to a fixed-width slot.
x: An array is the simplest data structure there is: a fixed number of same-sized slots laid out one after another in memory. Almost every other structure in this course is either built on arrays or defined by how it differs from one. Two properties make arrays special: Contiguous layout. Element at the next index sits immediately after its predecessor. There are no gaps and no pointers between them. Uniform element size. Every slot is the same number of bytes, so the machine can compute where any element lives. Everything good about arrays (instant indexing, cache-friendliness) and everything bad (expensive inserts, fixed size) follows from those two facts. Indexing is arithmetic Memory is a long row of numbered bytes; the number of a byte is its memory address. To read element i, the machine needs that element's address. Because the slots are contiguous and all the same size, it can work the address out directly from where the array starts: For the array drawn below, substitute its 4-byte slots and base address: The formula only works because every slot is the same size and there are no gaps; a structure without those two properties (a linked list, for example) has no such shortcut. That is one multiply and one add, whatever the array's length. This is why indexing is O(1), or constant time: the cost does not grow as the array gets longer. The CPU does not walk to element i, it calculates where it is. This also explains why most languages start indexing at 0: the index is an offset from the start. Element 0 is zero elements past base. O(1) access, O(n) search For an array of n elements: indexing by position is O(1). Finding a value in an unsorted array is still O(n) (linear time: the work grows in proportion to n), because you must look at each slot. If the array is sorted, binary search finds a value in O(log n), where log n means log₂ n, the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million elements). Key takeaways Address arithmetic gives direct access to a fixed-width slot. Position lookup and searching for an unsorted value are different operations. Further reading Array (data structure) — Wikipedia)

sum: Scan the contiguous dimension for sequential memory access.
x: The preceding unit derived an address from the array base, index and fixed slot size. Here n counts array elements, r and c are zero-based row and column indices, cols counts columns per row, and size is the number of bytes per element. Constant-time indexing is a data-structure model; memory locality explains why two linear scans can still differ in real elapsed time. Why contiguous memory is fast Both indexed access and a single pointer load are constant-time operations in the usual RAM model. Their measured latencies can differ because that model abstracts away the memory hierarchy. CPUs do not fetch single bytes from RAM. They transfer a cache line, whose size depends on the processor; this example assumes 64 bytes, and keep it in a small, fast cache. A cache hit can be much faster than a main-memory access; latency depends on hardware, contention and access pattern. Evidence gap Universal nanosecond latency figures are omitted because no measured hardware configuration or reproducible benchmark is provided. When you scan an array, one aligned 64-byte cache line contains sixteen 4-byte integers. A hardware prefetcher can recognise a sequential pattern and fetch later lines ahead of demand; effectiveness depends on the processor, stride and workload. This is spatial locality, and it is why a simple loop over an array is one of the fastest things a computer can do. A linked list (covered later in this module) scatters its nodes around the heap. Each step can be a cache miss. Scanning n elements is O(n) for both on paper; dependent pointer loads can make the list slower, but no speed ratio follows without measuring the workload. 2D arrays: row-major order A rectangular built-in C or C++ array is contiguous and row-major: row 0 first, then row 1. A newly created C-order NumPy array has this layout too; NumPy also supports other strides and orders. Java int[][] is an array of references to separate int[] rows, which may have different lengths. Fortran, MATLAB and R normally use column-major layout. To locate a row-and-column element, count complete earlier rows and then the earlier slots in its row: For the 3-by-4 grid of 4-byte integers starting at address 1000: In a column-major language the roles swap: you skip whole columns first. Loop order matters. Iterating row by row walks memory sequentially. Iterating column by column jumps a whole row's worth of bytes (the column count multiplied by the element size) every step, potentially touching a different cache line each time when that stride is large. Performance depends on dimensions, cache hierarchy and compiler transformations. Key takeaways Scan the contiguous dimension for sequential memory access. A cache-performance claim needs stated hardware and workload assumptions. Further reading Array (data structure) — Wikipedia) Row- and column-major order — Wikipedia

sum: Interior changes shift elements; position lookup does not.
x: An array gives direct indexed access, but its physical neighbours must move when you open or close an interior gap. In this unit n is the number of live elements and i is the zero-based position being changed. Operations and their cost In this table n is the number of elements in the array and i is the position being read or changed. Operation Cost Why --------- Read/write a[i] O(1) Address arithmetic Search (unsorted) O(n) Check every slot Insert/delete at end O(1) No shifting Insert/delete at i O(n − i + 1) without resizing Shift the tail; reallocation may add O(n) For a dynamic array, amortised; see below. Inserting at position i means shifting every later element one slot right to make room. Inserting at the front of a million-element array moves a million elements. Static vs dynamic arrays A fixed-size array has a size chosen when it is created; this is distinct from static storage duration. C's int a[100] and Java's new int[100] are fixed-size: you cannot append a 101st element. A dynamic array (resizable array) wraps a static array and tracks two numbers: length: how many elements are in use. capacity: how many slots the underlying array has. When the length equals the capacity and you append, it allocates a bigger array, copies everything across, and frees the old one. What the Python operations touch A CPython list’s contiguous slots hold references to objects. Indexing chooses one slot directly; membership scans values until a match or the end. An unsorted list does not get fast membership merely because its storage supports direct indexing. Equality comparisons can themselves be expensive; the linear scan bound counts comparisons, assuming each has fixed cost. An append usually writes into spare capacity. Occasionally it reallocates the backing storage, making that individual operation linear in the current length. “Amortised constant time” describes the total cost spread across a sequence, rather than promising identical latency for every append. The next unit proves why geometric growth gives that guarantee. Negative indices are translated relative to the stored length, so replacing the last item is still direct access. Removing the last item needs no shifting, while removing the first shifts the remaining references. CPython may also shrink its allocation on some pops; its end-pop bound is amortised. Key takeaways Interior changes shift elements; position lookup does not. Length counts live elements, while capacity includes spare slots. Further reading Dynamic array — Wikipedia Array (data structure) — Wikipedia)

sum: Multiply capacity by a constant factor greater than one to bound total copying.
x: A dynamic array distinguishes its live length from its backing capacity. When a full array grows, old elements may need copying. This unit counts that copying across a sequence of appends; allocation costs and allocator-specific in-place growth are outside the model. Why growth must be geometric Copying n elements is O(n) work, so you might expect appends to be slow. The trick is how much to grow. To compare growth policies, count the total number of element copies that resizing makes while you append n elements one at a time. If capacity doubles each time, starting from capacity 1, the resizes copy 1, then 2, then 4, and so on, each resize copying the whole old array: For example, 17 appends end at capacity 32 after copying 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 elements, fewer than 2 × 17 = 34. Spread over n appends, that is fewer than two copies per append: amortised O(1). Amortised means averaged over a long run of operations: an occasional append is expensive, but the total for n appends is still proportional to n. Growing by any constant factor greater than 1 works. Going backwards from the last resize, each earlier resize copied 1/r as many elements as the one after it, so the copies form a shrinking geometric series: The series is stated in terms of final capacity, not arbitrary stopping length.
