The formal upper error bound needs suitable independent universal rows and concerns one fixed query. Further reading Count–min sketch — Wikipedia Count-Min Sketch original paper

sum: HyperLogLog counts distinct hashes without keeping every item.
x: HyperLogLog counts distinct hashes without keeping every item. A rare leading-zero pattern suggests scale, while many registers reduce the noise of relying on a single maximum. HyperLogLog: counting distinct items Counting distinct items exactly needs a set of everything seen. HyperLogLog (Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet and Meunier, 2007) estimates it in a few kilobytes. The intuition Hash each item to a uniformly random-looking bit string. Look at how many leading zeros it has: Each bit of a good hash is 0 or 1 with equal chance, independently of the others, so long runs of zeros at the start are rare in a predictable way: So if the longest run of leading zeros you have ever seen is 20, you have probably seen around 2²⁰, about a million, distinct items. Duplicates hash identically, so they cannot change the maximum: only distinct items count. One maximum is a very noisy estimate (one lucky hash doubles it). HyperLogLog fixes this by stochastic averaging: Use the first few bits of the hash to pick one of the registers (small counters): 14 bits can pick any of 16,384 registers, since 2¹⁴ = 16,384. In that register, keep the maximum leading-zero count (plus one) of the remaining bits. Combine all the registers into one estimate, using the formula below. Practical variants add corrections for very small and very large counts. A harmonic mean (the reciprocal of the average of reciprocals) is used because it is barely moved by one register that got a lucky long run of zeros. The error of the estimate shrinks as you add registers: This is a typical (standard) error, not a maximum. Treating the error as roughly normally distributed, about 1 estimate in 20 is off by more than twice the standard error, and about 1 in 370 by more than three times. More registers, less error, and memory grows only with m, not with the count. Key takeaways Registers retain maximum leading-zero ranks after bucket selection. Harmonic aggregation reduces sensitivity to a lucky large rank. Standard error shrinks with the square root of register count and is not a maximum error. Further reading HyperLogLog — Wikipedia HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm (Flajolet et al., 2007) HyperLogLog — Redis docs HyperLogLog in Practice (Heule, Nunkesser and Hall, Google)

t: Merging HyperLogLogs and choosing a sketch
sum: Compatible sketches merge by register maxima, so duplicates across servers are counted once in the union estimate.
x: Compatible sketches merge by register maxima, so duplicates across servers are counted once in the union estimate. Subtracting approximate counts to estimate a tiny overlap is much less reliable. HyperLogLog in practice Redis's HyperLogLog (PFADD, PFCOUNT) uses sixteen thousand three hundred and eighty-four registers of 6 bits each: 12 KiB of dense register storage plus metadata per sketch, with a standard error of about 0.81%, using a sixty-four-bit hash space. Accuracy degrades near that hash-space limit because distinct inputs can share hashes; the usual error figure is not a guarantee across the entire range. Small sketches are stored sparsely and use far less. HyperLogLogs with matching hash/seed and register configuration are mergeable sketches: the union of two sketches is the register-by-register maximum. That makes them ideal for distributed counting, since each server keeps its own sketch and you merge them for the total, or for rollups, where 30 daily sketches merge into a monthly unique count without double-counting repeat visitors. Intersections are another matter. The usual trick is inclusion–exclusion: Each of the three estimates has a standard error of about 0.81%, roughly 8,000 to 16,000 here, which is larger than the 5,000 overlap itself. Inclusion–exclusion with HyperLogLog is unreliable when the overlap is small compared with the sets. Google's HyperLogLog++ improves the small-cardinality range with bias correction and a sparse representation; BigQuery's APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT is built on it. Choosing a structure Question Use Memory --------- Have I seen x? Bloom filter ~10 bits per item (1%) How often x? Count-Min rows times counters per row How many distinct? HyperLogLog ~12 KiB register payload, ~1% standard error None of them store the items themselves. If you need the items back, or exact answers, you need a real hash set or map. Key takeaways Compatible HyperLogLogs merge by register-wise maxima. A small intersection derived by subtracting approximate large counts can be unreliable. Membership, frequency and distinct-count sketches answer different questions and cannot enumerate items. Further reading HyperLogLog — Wikipedia HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm (Flajolet et al., 2007) HyperLogLog — Redis docs HyperLogLog in Practice (Heule, Nunkesser and Hall, Google)

sum: A rooted tree is connected and acyclic; only the root has no parent.
x: Arrays and linked lists are linear: every element has at most one successor. A tree lets an element have several successors, which is exactly the shape of a lot of real data: a file system, the HTML DOM, an organisation chart, a parsed expression, a JSON document. Trees also matter for speed. In this module, n is the number of items (keys or nodes) stored, and O(…) is Big O notation: it describes how the work grows as n grows. O(n) is a linear upper growth bound; O(log n) is a logarithmic upper growth bound using the base-2 logarithm of n, roughly the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million). O(1) means a fixed amount of work however large n is. A sorted array lets you search in O(log n) but inserts cost O(n), because every later item must shift along. A balanced binary search tree gives O(log n) search and insertion under constant-cost key comparisons: its height is logarithmic, and those operations follow a root-to-leaf path. An arbitrary well-shaped tree does not provide ordered search. What makes something a tree A tree is a set of nodes joined by edges, with one special node, the root node, such that: every node except the root has exactly one parent node; following parents from any node always leads back to the root; there are no cycles. Equivalently (in graph terms) a tree is a connected undirected graph with no cycles, with a root chosen for the rooted representation. Because every node except the root has exactly one edge up to its parent, you can count the edges of any tree without looking at its shape: So the tree below, with 8 nodes, has 7 edges, and a tree of a million nodes has 999,999, whatever its shape. The rule needs a single connected tree; a collection of separate trees (a forest) has fewer edges. Where trees appear File systems: a directory hierarchy is often modelled as a tree; empty directories are also leaves, and hard links or followed symbolic links need extra care. Compilers: source code is parsed into an abstract syntax tree; (2 + 3) 4 becomes a node with children + and 4. Databases: many indexes use B-trees, a many-children generalisation of search trees (covered in the System Design databases module). Ordered maps: Java's TreeMap uses a red-black tree; common std::map implementations do too, but the C++ interface does not require that representation (the balanced-tree units). Schedulers and priority queues: binary heaps (the binary heap units). Autocomplete and routing tables: tries (the trie units). Key takeaways A rooted tree is connected and acyclic; only the root has no parent. A nonempty tree has one fewer edge than nodes. Ordered search requires an ordering rule as well as a useful shape. Further reading Tree (data structure) — Wikipedia) Binary expression tree — Wikipedia

sum: Depth looks upwards to the root; height looks down to the deepest leaf.
x: Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes. Vocabulary Term Meaning (in the tree-structure unit’s A–H example) ------ Child / parent B is a child of A; A is B's parent Siblings B, C and D share a parent Leaf A node with no children: E, H, C, G Internal node Has at least one child: A, B, F, D Subtree A node plus all its descendants Ancestor A, B and F are ancestors of H Degree Number of children (A has 3) Depth versus height These two are easy to mix up because they both count edges, but they look in opposite directions. The node depth of a node is the number of edges from the root down to it. The root has depth 0; H has depth 3. The node height of a node is the number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf. Leaves have height 0; B has height 2; A has height 3. The height of the tree is the height of its root, which equals the maximum depth of any node. Conventions vary Some books count nodes rather than edges, so a single node has height 1 instead of 0. This module counts edges: a one-node tree has height 0 and an empty tree has height −1. Always check which convention a problem uses before you answer "what is the height?". Height has a neat recursive definition: the height of a node is one more than the taller of its children's heights, and an empty subtree has height −1 so that a leaf comes out as 0. That gives B height 2, matching the count by eye. For a finite acyclic binary tree with no shared children, this is the canonical recursive tree function. It visits each of the n nodes once, so it takes O(n) time, and it needs O(h + 1) recursive frames, where h is the tree's height (the exact maximum for a nonempty tree is its edge-counted height plus two: one frame per path node and a final temporary empty-child call). Deep trees can hit the runtime's recursion limit. The following binary Node stores each child reference explicitly. The sample builds a four-node tree; the height function below accepts this representation and returns two for that sample root. It does not implement general many-child height. Key takeaways Depth looks upwards to the root; height looks down to the deepest leaf. This module counts edges: leaves have height zero and empty trees height minus one. Recursive height combines children before their parent. Further reading Tree (data structure) — Wikipedia) Binary tree — Wikipedia

sum: Left and right child positions are distinct, even with only one child.
x: Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes. Binary trees A binary tree is a tree where every node has at most two children, called left and right. The order matters: a node with only a left child is a different tree from one with only a right child. Binary trees are the workhorse of this module. Binary search trees, AVL trees, red-black trees and binary heaps have binary shape. Other priority queue structures, such as d-ary heaps, allow higher arity, and expression trees can have unary or many-operand nodes. Use the Node representation from the depth-and-height unit; the four-node example there also illustrates these child-slot counts. Two useful counting facts. First, every node has two child slots, and every edge fills one of them, so the rest must be empty (None): In that earlier four-node tree, node 4 has two empty slots, node 3 has two and node 2 has one: 5 in total. This is why serialising a tree with a marker for every empty child writes one more marker than nodes (the common-problem units). Second, each level can hold at most twice as many nodes as the level above it, which caps how many nodes fit under a given height, and so how short a tree of n nodes can be: So height 3 fits at most 15 nodes, and a million nodes need height at least 19. That lower bound is why "O(log n)" keeps appearing: a well-shaped tree reaches any node in about log₂ n steps. Nothing stops a badly shaped tree being much taller: n nodes in a single chain have height one less than its node count. Key takeaways Left and right child positions are distinct, even with only one child. Count empty slots by subtracting occupied edges from child positions. Doubling each level gives the shortest possible height for a node count. Further reading Binary tree — Wikipedia

sum: Full describes child counts; complete describes filled positions.
x: Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes. Shapes: full, complete, perfect, balanced These four words get confused constantly, and interviewers love them. Full tree (or proper): every node has 0 or 2 children, never exactly one. A full binary tree always has one more leaf than internal node (see the formula below). Complete tree: every level is completely filled except possibly the last, and the last level is filled from left to right with no gaps. This is the shape a binary heap always has. Perfect tree: every internal node has two children and all leaves are at the same depth. Every level is full, so it holds exactly the maximum node count from the formula above: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31... nodes for heights 0 to 4. Height-balanced tree: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. More loosely, people say a tree is balanced when its height is O(log n), where n counts nodes. Two of these definitions are easier to apply as formulas. For a full tree, counting edges two ways gives the leaf count: The "Full" tree in the picture has two internal nodes and 3 leaves. A full tree with 3 internal nodes has 4 leaves and 7 nodes; every full tree has an odd number of nodes. The balance rule is a check you make at every node: The second line is a node whose left child has a child of its own but whose right side is empty: heights 1 and −1 differ by 2, so that node is unbalanced. Every perfect tree is both full and complete, but the other combinations are independent. In the picture, the "Full" tree is full but not complete: its last level is filled on the right with a gap on the left. The "Complete" tree is complete but not full: the right child of the root has only one child. Why shape matters Ordered searches and single-key updates in a balanced BST cost time proportional to the height; traversing all n nodes takes O(n). A complete tree with a million nodes has height 19; other balancing rules permit larger logarithmic heights. A degenerate one, where each node has a single child, has height 999,999 and is just a slow linked list. Key takeaways Full describes child counts; complete describes filled positions. Perfect requires every level to be full. Height balance must hold at every node, not just the root. Further reading Binary tree — Wikipedia

t: Linked nodes, arrays and parent pointers
sum: Arrays suit complete trees and calculate child positions without links.
x: Use the rooted-tree vocabulary from the earlier unit. The linked examples below assume a finite acyclic tree without shared child nodes. Count height and depth in edges, not nodes. A path ends at a leaf only when that node has no children. When an example uses n, it means the number of stored nodes. Representing trees in memory Linked nodes The usual choice: each node is an object with a value and pointers to its children (and sometimes its parent). It handles any shape. Relinking a known subtree can change only a few pointers, but locating it, maintaining metadata or balancing, and reclaiming removed nodes can require additional work. The cost is memory and cache behaviour. Object size depends on the interpreter version, build and class layout. Separately allocated nodes can reduce locality, but do not imply a cache miss on every visit. Evidence gap The previous universal 56-byte node size and one-cache-miss-per-node claim are omitted because no pinned interpreter measurement or hardware trace was supplied. Arrays (implicit trees) A complete binary tree can be stored in a plain array with no pointers at all. Put the nodes in level order (the root, then each level left to right), numbering slots from 0: Arithmetic on the index then replaces the pointers: So B at index 1 has its left child D at index 3, and F at index 5 has its parent C at index 2. A child index that falls past the end of the array means that child is missing. In Python the same arithmetic is 2i + 1, 2i + 2 and (i - 1) // 2, where // divides and rounds down. This is compact and cache-friendly, and it is exactly how binary heaps are implemented (the binary heap units). It wastes space badly for sparse, unbalanced trees, since a missing node still needs a slot. Follow a chain that only ever goes right: A chain of 4 nodes (height 3) sits at indices 0, 2, 6 and 14, so it needs 15 slots to store 4 values. Trees with many children For nodes with an unbounded number of children (a file system, the DOM), store a list of children per node. An older trick is left-child, right-sibling: each node keeps a pointer to its first child and one to its next sibling, which turns any tree into a binary tree. Parent pointers Adding a parent field makes it easy to walk upwards (to find an in-order successor, or the path to the root) at the cost of one more pointer per node and more bookkeeping on every change. Red-black trees in the Linux kernel and in common C++ standard-library implementations keep parent pointers for this reason. Key takeaways Arrays suit complete trees and calculate child positions without links. Sparse chains waste exponentially many slots in the implicit layout. Linked nodes and child lists accommodate irregular shapes. Further reading Tree (data structure) — Wikipedia) Binary tree — Wikipedia

sum: Pre-order handles parents first; post-order handles children first.
x: A list has one natural order: front to back. A tree does not. To visit every node you must decide, at each node, whether to handle the node itself before, between or after its children, and whether to go deep first or wide first. Those choices give the four traversals you will use constantly. Each emits every node once; with constant-cost node processing and suitable stack/queue operations, these implementations take O(n) time, where n is the number of nodes: the work grows in direct proportion to the size of the tree. Assume finite acyclic binary trees without shared subtrees or concurrent mutation. They differ in the order of visits and in how much extra memory they need. The running example Traversal Order Result --------- Pre-order node, left, right F B A D C E G I H In-order left, node, right A B C D E F G H I Post-order left, right, node A C E D B H I G F Level-order level by level F B G A D I C E H This tree happens to be a binary search tree, which is why in-order comes out alphabetical. That is not a coincidence (see below). Depth-first: pre, in and post-order The three depth-first traversals have identical structure; only the position of the "visit" line moves. A trick for doing them by hand: walk round the outline of the tree anticlockwise starting at the root, keeping the tree on your left. Pre-order records a node when you pass its left side, in-order when you pass underneath it, post-order when you pass its right side. What each order is for Pre-order sees a parent before its children. Use it to copy or serialise a tree, including null markers or other shape metadata when reconstruction is required; the root-first order supports top-down rebuilding, and to print indented outlines such as a directory listing. In-order on a binary search tree yields keys in sorted order. Use it to validate a BST, find the k-th smallest key or range-scan. Post-order sees children before their parent. Use it whenever a node's answer depends on its subtrees: computing node height or size, freeing memory (delete children before the parent), evaluating an expression tree (3 4 + is post-order for 3 + 4), or rm -r and du on a directory. Most tree problems are post-order "Compute something for every subtree and combine" (height, diameter, balanced check, max path sum) is post-order: recurse into both children, then combine their results at the node. The common-problem units is full of these. Space: the hidden cost Recursion is not free. Each pending call sits on the call stack, and the deepest the recursion goes is one call per level on the longest root-to-leaf path: The two example lines are a million-node complete tree (height 19, so 21 frames including an empty-child call) and a million-node chain (height one less than its node count, so 1,000,001 frames including an empty-child call). So depth-first traversal uses O(h + 1) working space, excluding the O(n) output: O(log n) for a balanced tree but O(n) for a degenerate one. CPython commonly starts with a recursion limit of 1,000; query sys.getrecursionlimit() for the actual process. A sufficiently deep chain raises RecursionError, accounting for existing call depth. Raising the limit can create resource risks; an iterative traversal avoids recursive call-depth limits but still needs memory. Key takeaways Pre-order handles parents first; post-order handles children first. In-order yields sorted values only when the tree has BST ordering. Recursive working memory grows with height; stored output grows with node count. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

sum: A LIFO stack reverses the order in which children are pushed.
x: Use the binary Node representation introduced earlier: each node has a value and optional left and right children. Assume finite acyclic trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Here n counts nodes and h is the root height in edges. Constant-cost processing at each visited node is assumed; returned output is separate from working memory. Iterative depth-first traversals Replace the call stack with an explicit list used as a stack. Pre-order Pop a node, visit it, then push its children. Push the right child first so that the left is popped first. In-order Slide down to the leftmost node, stacking each ancestor on the way. Pop, visit, then repeat the slide from the popped node's right child. This pattern is worth memorising: it is also how you build a BST iterator that yields the next key on demand. Over a full traversal of n nodes each advance costs O(1) amortised (constant on average, because each node is pushed and popped once in total), and the stack needs O(h + 1) memory for a tree of height h. Initialisation or an individual next call can cost O(h + 1). Post-order Post-order is the awkward one, because a node can only be visited after both children are done. The neat trick: do a pre-order that goes node, right, left, then reverse the output. Reversed, that is left, right, node. This uses O(n) memory for the output it reverses, for n nodes. If you need to act on nodes in post-order as you go (to free them, say), use the single-stack version that remembers the last node visited, so it can tell whether it is returning from the left or the right subtree. Key takeaways A LIFO stack reverses the order in which children are pushed. In-order keeps pending ancestors until their left side is finished. Reversing a right-first pre-order gives post-order output, with output storage. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

sum: A deque processes the shallowest pending nodes first.
x: Use the binary Node representation introduced earlier: each node has a value and optional left and right children. Assume finite acyclic trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Here n counts nodes and h is the root height in edges. Constant-cost processing at each visited node is assumed; returned output is separate from working memory. Breadth-first: level-order Level-order visits nodes by depth: the root, then all depth-1 nodes left to right, and so on. It uses a queue instead of a stack: first in, first out, so nodes are processed in the order they were discovered. Taking len(q) at the start of each round processes exactly one level per round. That is the hook for a whole family of problems: right-side view (last of each level), zigzag order, average per level, minimum depth. Use a deque, not a list list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element, so it is O(n) in the n items still in the list, and can make BFS quadratic (work growing with the square of the node count) on wide trees. deque.popleft() is O(1), a fixed cost. Space for BFS Here n counts tree nodes, h is height in edges, and w is the maximum number of nodes on any level. The queue can mix the unprocessed part of one level with discovered nodes of the next; its size grows with the tree's tree width (the most nodes on any one level), written O(width). A perfect tree is widest at its last level, which holds just over half of all its nodes: A perfect tree of 15 nodes has 8 leaves; one of 1,048,575 nodes has 524,288. So BFS uses O(n) memory on bushy trees, while DFS needs only O(log n) there. On a degenerate chain it is the other way round: the queue never holds more than one node, but recursive DFS needs O(n) frames. Iterative pre-order can keep only one pending node on a chain. For n nodes: Shape Recursive DFS stack BFS queue --------- Balanced O(log n) O(n) Chain O(n) O(1) BFS has one big advantage: it reaches shallow nodes first. To find the minimum depth of a tree, or the nearest node satisfying a condition, BFS can stop as soon as it finds one, while DFS might explore a huge deep subtree first. Key takeaways A deque processes the shallowest pending nodes first. Snapshot the queue length before processing a level. Breadth-first working space can be large on wide trees. Further reading Breadth-first search — Wikipedia collections.deque — Python docs

sum: Temporary predecessor links replace an explicit traversal stack.
x: Use the binary Node representation introduced earlier: each node has a value and optional left and right children. Assume finite acyclic trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Here n counts nodes and h is the root height in edges. Constant-cost processing at each visited node is assumed; returned output is separate from working memory. Advanced aside: Morris traversal Can you do an in-order traversal with O(1) extra space, no stack and no recursion? Yes, if you are allowed to modify the tree temporarily. Morris traversal (Joseph M. Morris, 1979) uses the empty right pointers of nodes as temporary threads back to their in-order successor: If the current node has no left child, visit it and go right. Otherwise, find its in-order predecessor (the rightmost node of its left subtree). If the predecessor's right pointer is empty, point it at the current node (a thread) and go left. If it already points at the current node, we have come back up via the thread: remove it, visit the current node and go right. Each edge is walked a constant number of times, so it is still O(n) time for n nodes. The catch is that the tree is temporarily rewired: it is unsafe if another thread is reading the tree concurrently, and if you stop early (say, on finding a key) you must still finish the walk or the threads stay in place. The O(1) bound excludes the output list: the shown function stores O(n) output. Exceptions or early exits also require cleanup of outstanding threads. Key takeaways Temporary predecessor links replace an explicit traversal stack. Remove each thread on the second encounter. Constant working space excludes output and requires safe cleanup. Further reading Threaded binary tree (Morris traversal) — Wikipedia

sum: Ordering constrains entire subtrees, not only immediate children.
x: Binary search on a sorted array of n keys finds a key in O(log n) steps (it halves the range each time, so about 20 steps for a million keys), but inserting a key means shifting everything after it: O(n), work in proportion to n. A binary search tree (BST) stores ordered partitions in linked nodes. A step need not halve the remaining keys; search follows a path, after which insertion or deletion relinks nodes. When the tree is reasonably balanced, search, insert and delete are all O(log n). When it is not, they degrade to O(n). Most of this lesson is about the operations; the later insertion-shape unit explains that failure mode, which the balanced-tree units address. The BST property For every node: every key in its left subtree is less than the node's key; every key in its right subtree is greater. The rule is about whole subtrees, not just immediate children. That distinction is where most BST bugs live (see the later successor-and-validation unit). An in-order traversal of this tree gives 20 30 35 40 45 50 60 65 70 80: a BST is a sorted sequence, stored as a tree. Duplicates need a policy. The common choices are to reject them (sets and maps), keep a count in the node, or consistently send equal keys to one side. The code below ignores duplicates and assumes mutually comparable keys with a consistent total order, constant-cost comparisons and no concurrent mutation. Recursive functions are limited by Python call depth. Maps generally update an existing key rather than reject its new value. Search Here h measures height in edges, and a successful path also includes the root node. Start at the root. If the key is smaller, go left; if larger, go right; stop when you find it or fall off the tree. Searching for 45: 50 (go left), 30 (go right), 40 (go right), 45. Four nodes visited; the Python code can perform both equality and ordering tests at a node. A search visits one node per level it passes through: So the cost is O(h + 1). The minimum is the leftmost node and the maximum is the rightmost, also O(h). Insert Search for the key; the place where the search falls off the tree is exactly where the new key belongs. A new key always becomes a leaf. The recursive style "return the (possibly new) subtree root and reassign it" is worth adopting. It avoids special-casing the empty tree and is the same shape you need for delete and for balanced trees. Insertion order determines shape The same set of keys can produce very different trees. The order above gives the height-3 tree in the diagram. Inserting the same ten keys in ascending order gives a chain of height 9. Key takeaways Ordering constrains entire subtrees, not only immediate children. Search follows a single root-to-key path. Insertion returns a possibly new subtree root and ignores duplicate keys here. Further reading Binary search tree — Wikipedia Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Deleting leaves and internal BST nodes
sum: Remove a leaf, splice a single child, or substitute a two-child node.
x: Earlier units established a strict BST ordering with distinct, mutually comparable keys: every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger. Use the Node with key, left and right fields introduced in the search unit. Here n counts keys and h measures tree height in edges. Comparisons have constant cost; recursive code remains limited by Python call depth. Delete: the three cases Deletion is the operation people get wrong, because removing a node can leave a hole that must be filled without breaking the ordering. Find the node, then: No children (a leaf). Just remove it. Deleting 20 sets 30's left pointer to None. One child. Splice the child into the node's place. Deleting 60 makes 65 the left child of 70. Everything in 60's subtree was already between 50 and 70, so order is preserved. Two children. You cannot splice two subtrees into one pointer. Instead, replace the node's key with its in-order successor (the smallest key in its right subtree), then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that second delete is always case 1 or 2. Deleting 30 (two children) from the example: its successor is 35, the leftmost node in its right subtree. Copy 35 into 30's node, then delete the old 35 leaf. Why does the successor work? It is larger than everything in the left subtree (it came from the right) and smaller than everything else in the right subtree (it was the minimum there). The in-order predecessor (maximum of the left subtree) works equally well. Copying keys is not always allowed Copying the successor's key into the node is fine for a textbook, but in real code other objects may hold references to nodes (iterators, handles). Production implementations such as the Linux rbtree and C++ std::map instead relink the successor node into the deleted node's position, so a node never changes key. Always using the successor (known as Hibbard deletion) is asymmetric: right subtrees keep losing their minimum, and after long random sequences of inserts and deletes the tree becomes visibly skewed to the left, and searches can degrade relative to the insertion-only random-tree model. Choosing between successor and predecessor does not establish a logarithmic-height guarantee. A self-balancing policy does. Key takeaways Remove a leaf, splice a single child, or substitute a two-child node. The successor is the smallest key in the right subtree. Reconnect each returned subtree root after a recursive deletion. Further reading Binary search tree — Wikipedia Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: A successor is the next key in sorted order, not necessarily a child.
x: Earlier units established a strict BST ordering with distinct, mutually comparable keys: every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger. Use the Node with key, left and right fields introduced in the search unit. Here n counts keys and h measures tree height in edges. Comparisons have constant cost; recursive code remains limited by Python call depth. In-order successor "What is the next key after k?" comes up in ordered maps (TreeMap.higherKey), range scans and iterators. Two cases: If the node has a right subtree, the successor is the leftmost node of that subtree. Successor of 30 is 35. Otherwise, it is the nearest ancestor whose left subtree contains the node. Successor of 45 is 50: walking up, 45 is in 40's right, 40 is in 30's right, but 30 is in 50's left. Without parent pointers you can find it top-down from the root: every time you go left, the current node is a candidate. This also works for keys that are not in the tree (successor of 47 is 50) and returns None for the maximum. It is O(h), where h is the tree's height: one step per level. Validating a BST A classic interview question with a classic wrong answer: check that each node's left child is smaller and its right child is larger. Every parent-child pair here looks fine, but 6 sits in the right subtree of 10, so this is not a BST. The damage is real: searching for 6 goes left at 10 because 6 is smaller, then right at 5, and falls off the tree. The key is present but unreachable. The fix is to pass down the range each node must fall within. This numeric example requires finite keys comparable with float infinities; it rejects NaN and infinite keys, and is not a validator for arbitrary string or custom-object keys: Going left tightens the upper bound; going right tightens the lower bound. An equivalent approach does an in-order traversal and checks each key is greater than the previous one. Both are O(n) for n nodes, since every node must be checked. Key takeaways A successor is the next key in sorted order, not necessarily a child. Ancestor bounds expose violations that local comparisons miss. Strict bounds match the distinct-key policy used here. Further reading Binary search tree — Wikipedia Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Sorted insertion creates a chain in an unbalanced BST.
x: Earlier units established a strict BST ordering with distinct, mutually comparable keys: every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger. Use the Node with key, left and right fields introduced in the search unit. Here n counts keys and h measures tree height in edges. Comparisons have constant cost; recursive code remains limited by Python call depth. Degenerate trees Search and single-key updates cost O(h + 1) for a tree of height h; full validation of n nodes costs O(n). With insertion only, order determines shape; deletions also change it. Input order Shape Height with 1,000 keys --------- Ascending Right chain 999 Uniformly random permutation Random shape Expected O(log n); no fixed height Median first, recursively Perfect-ish 9 Inserting sorted keys into a plain BST produces a linked list with extra pointers: every insert walks the whole chain built so far. The first insert visits no existing nodes, the second visits 1, and so on: The total has tight quadratic growth: Ten times as many keys costs about a hundred times as much: 1,000 sorted keys cost about half a million node visits, and a million keys about 5 × 10¹¹. Random insertion order is much kinder. For distinct keys inserted in a uniformly random permutation, the average depth of a stored key grows only logarithmically: For 1,000 random keys that is an average depth of about 14 by the leading term. Lower-order terms matter for finite sizes: the exact expected average is about 11, against an average depth of about 8 in the best (complete) shape, whose height is 9. Expected height is also O(log n); this is an expectation, not a bound on every insertion order. But real data is rarely random. Timestamps, auto-increment IDs and alphabetically sorted imports all arrive in order. For workloads requiring worst-case logarithmic access, use a self-balancing tree (AVL, red-black; the balanced-tree units), a B-tree (System Design, databases), a skip list, or a sorted sequence implementation. Python sortedcontainers uses a list of sorted lists; Redis can use a skip list plus dictionary or a compact encoding for sorted sets. Building a balanced BST from sorted data If you have all the keys up front and sorted, pick the middle key as the root and recurse on each half. For a nonempty sorted set of distinct keys, passing index ranges rather than copying slices builds the shortest possible tree (height 3 for the ten keys above, 9 for 1,000 keys) in O(n) time, assuming constant-time node creation. Key takeaways Sorted insertion creates a chain in an unbalanced BST. Random insertion gives expected logarithmic depth, rather than a worst-case guarantee. A sorted batch can be built from midpoint index ranges without copying slices. Further reading Binary Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne) Sorted Containers (Python) docs

t: Rotations and the AVL balance rule
sum: A rotation preserves in-order order while changing local parent links.
x: A plain BST is only as good as its insertion order. Feed it sorted keys and it becomes a linked list. AVL and red-black trees maintain balancing invariants after updates, using local rotations and metadata changes. Other balancing schemes can rebuild subtrees instead. The result is a hard guarantee: for n keys, the height stays O(log n) (growing only with the logarithm of n, a small multiple of about 20 for a million keys) no matter what order keys arrive in, so search, insert and delete are O(log n) worst case. The two classic designs are AVL trees (1962) and red-black trees (1972 as symmetric B-trees; the red/black formulation dates from 1978). They differ in how strict their invariant is. Rotations Here n is the stored key count; a rotation changes only a fixed number of links. A rotation changes the shape of a small part of the tree while preserving the in-order sequence, so the BST property still holds. Here A, B and C are whole subtrees. In both shapes the in-order sequence is A, x, B, y, C. A right rotation at y lifts x up one level and pushes y down; subtree B changes parent from x to y. A left rotation is the mirror image. A rotation updates a constant number of links and metadata fields and does no searching, so it is O(1): a fixed amount of work, however big the tree. AVL and red-black trees use rotations plus bookkeeping (heights for AVL, colours for red-black). AVL trees Named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis, the AVL tree was the first self-balancing BST. Invariant: at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. The difference is the node's balance factor: The third line is node 30 in the "insert 30, 10, 20" example in the later AVL insertion unit: its left child 10 has a child of its own and 30 has no right child, so the heights are 1 and −1 and the balance factor is 2, which breaks the invariant. The insertion unit's bf(n) computes exactly this. Key takeaways A rotation preserves in-order order while changing local parent links. The middle subtree changes parent during a rotation. AVL balance factors compare left and right subtree heights. Further reading AVL tree — Wikipedia AVL tree visualisation — USF

t: Minimum AVL nodes and the height bound
sum: The sparsest allowed children differ in height by one.
x: Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency. Why that guarantees O(log n) Here n counts stored keys and h is tree height in edges. The empty-tree base case is used only as a recurrence boundary. Ask: what is the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height h can have? The sparsest one has one subtree one edge shorter and the other two edges shorter (the most lopsided the invariant allows), each as sparse as possible, plus the root: Those counts are each one less than a Fibonacci number, so they grow exponentially with h, and turning that round gives the height limit: The last two lines check the Fibonacci form against the counts above. The logarithmic coefficient is a leading approximation for large node counts; exact finite heights require the recurrence. For a million keys: Key takeaways The sparsest allowed children differ in height by one. Minimum node counts obey a Fibonacci-related recurrence. Use exact counts when deciding a finite maximum height. Further reading AVL tree — Wikipedia AVL tree visualisation — USF

t: AVL insertion and single or double repair
sum: Repair LL and RR cases with a single rotation.
x: Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency. Insert and rebalance Insert as in a plain BST, then walk back up the path updating heights. At the first node whose balance factor becomes +2 or −2, one of four cases applies, named after the path from that node down to where the new key went. Case Shape Fix --------- LL left child left-heavy rotate right RR right child right-heavy rotate left LR left child right-heavy left at child, then right RL right child left-heavy right at child, then left The LR case is the one people miss. Insert 30, 10, 20: A single right rotation at 30 would just move the zig-zag to the other side; you have to straighten it first. The insertion function below uses rotate_right from the rotation unit; the Node, height helpers and rotate_left needed to run it are provided just after it. Together those definitions form the complete distinct-key insertion example. The following helpers complete the example. Keys are distinct comparable values; duplicate insertions leave the tree unchanged. Inserting 1 to 7 in order into this AVL tree gives the perfect tree with 4 at the root, where a plain BST would give a chain. After an insert that creates imbalance, one rebalancing step (one single or one double rotation) restores balance, because it returns the subtree to the height it had before the insert, so no ancestor needs fixing. Deletion is worse: a rotation can shrink a subtree's height, unbalancing its parent in turn, so a delete in a tree of n keys may need O(log n) rotations, up to one per level of the path. Key takeaways Repair LL and RR cases with a single rotation. Straighten a zig-zag before the second rotation in LR and RL cases. Insert and delete differ in whether height changes propagate. Further reading AVL tree — Wikipedia AVL tree visualisation — USF

sum: NIL child positions count as black for the path invariant.
x: Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency. Red-black trees A red-black tree relaxes the invariant. Instead of near-perfect balance, it only promises that root-to-NIL paths differ in length by at most a factor of two. In exchange, it does less restructuring. Every node is coloured red or black, and empty (NIL) children count as black leaves. The rules: The root is black. A red node has no red children (no two reds in a row). Every path from a node down to a NIL leaf passes through the same number of black nodes: its black-height. Every root-to-NIL path here has 3 black nodes, counting the root and the NIL itself (for example 13, 8, 1, 6, NIL passes 13, 1 and NIL), and no red node has a red child. Why the height is O(log n) For this proof, count a node's black-height without the node itself: the number of black nodes on a path below it down to NIL, including the NIL (so a NIL has black-height 0). This differs from the inclusive count used in the preceding diagram. Two facts combine: No two reds are adjacent, so at least half the nodes on any path below the root are black: the height is at most twice the root's black-height. A subtree whose root has black-height b holds a number of real (non-NIL) nodes that grows exponentially with its black-height (the first line below), which you can prove by mathematical induction: it holds for a NIL, and each child's black-height is at least the parent's black-height minus one. The third line comes from applying the first line at the root and substituting the second; solving it for h gives the fourth. For a million keys the bound is about 40; actual height depends on the implementation and update history. Java TreeMap uses this red-black structure. Its documented logarithmic get, put and remove guarantees hold for insertion orders such as ascending IDs; ordered arrivals do not turn it into the unbalanced chain studied earlier. Key takeaways NIL child positions count as black for the path invariant. No consecutive red nodes and equal black-height imply logarithmic height. Distinguish inclusive diagram counts from the proof’s exclusive black-height convention. Further reading Red–black tree — Wikipedia Balanced Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne) TreeMap (Java SE 25) — Oracle

sum: Repair insertion colours with uncle cases and rotations.
x: The preceding unit defined red-black invariants: a black root, no red parent with a red child, and equal black-height on every path to a NIL child. Start with strict BST ordering and distinct comparable keys. Here n counts stored keys. This is the conventional bottom-up repair outline, rather than an executable insertion implementation; left-leaning and other variants have different repair rules. Insertion and colour repair Insert as in a BST and colour the new node red (this preserves rule 3; rule 2 or the root-colour rule may need repair). If its parent is black, done. If its parent is red, look at the uncle (the parent's sibling): Uncle red: recolour parent and uncle black and the grandparent red, then repeat the check from the grandparent. No rotation; the problem moves up two levels. Uncle black: one or two rotations around the grandparent plus a recolour fix it for good. Colour the root black. For the conventional bottom-up red-black algorithms, insertion uses at most two rotations and deletion at most three. Recolouring and fix-up traversal can take O(log n) steps in one update of a tree of n keys, because the red-uncle case can repeat up the whole path. These rotation bounds do not apply automatically to every red-black variant. Red-black trees are 2-3-4 trees in disguise Glue each black node to its red children and you get a B-tree node with 2, 3 or 4 children. Rule 3 says all leaves of that B-tree are at the same depth. Sedgewick's left-leaning red-black tree (2008) restricts red links further and its 2-3 variant maps onto 2-3 trees, which makes the code much shorter. Key takeaways New nodes start red so existing black counts are unchanged. A red uncle allows recolouring and moves the conflict upward. A black uncle requires rotations and recolouring; restore the root to black. Further reading Red–black tree — Wikipedia Left-leaning Red-Black Trees — Robert Sedgewick (PDF) Red-black Trees (rbtree) in Linux — kernel docs

t: Choosing balanced trees for real workloads
sum: AVL has a tighter worst-case height bound, but speed needs measurement.
x: Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency. AVL versus red-black Side by side, the two height bounds for n keys are: (The exact AVL worst case for a million keys is 27, from the recurrence above.) AVL Red-black --------- Max height Approx. 1.44 times the base-2 logarithm Twice the base-2 log of one more key Lookup height bound Tighter Looser Rotations/insert At most one repair At most two Rotations/delete O(log n) At most three Extra data Height or balance factor 1 colour bit Search and single-key updates are O(log n) for n keys, with constant-cost comparisons; traversing all entries is O(n). Practical tradeoffs: AVL offers a tighter worst-case height bound; actual read performance needs measurement. Write-heavy or general-purpose libraries usually choose red-black: fewer rotations on delete, and a colour bit can be hidden in the low bit of an aligned pointer, as the Linux kernel does. Where they are used Java TreeMap and TreeSet: red-black trees, giving logarithmic get, put, floorKey and ceilingKey operations; full sorted iteration over n entries takes O(n). Java HashMap: since Java 8, when a single bucket grows past 8 colliding entries (in a table of at least 64 buckets), it is converted into a small red-black tree, Comparable keys can use ordering to obtain logarithmic bin searches. Equal-hash keys without usable comparison ordering can still require linear search within a tree bin. C++ std::map and std::set: red-black trees in the major standard libraries (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC). The standard requires logarithmic key lookup and key-based updates for n elements, with other operation-specific bounds; erasing through a known iterator is amortised constant time. Insertion preserves iterators, without requiring a specific representation. Linux kernel: a generic intrusive rbtree (lib/rbtree.c) used widely. The Completely Fair Scheduler kept runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by vruntime (virtual runtime) and ran the leftmost task, caching a pointer to it so picking the next task is O(1). Linux began transitioning fair scheduling toward EEVDF in version 6.6; its implementation uses an augmented red-black tree. epoll also stores its watched file descriptors in one. Why CFS wanted a tree, not a binary heap A binary heap gives the minimum just as fast. But the scheduler also removes arbitrary tasks (one blocks on I/O, one is killed) and re-inserts them with new keys. With an intrusive tree, each task embeds its own tree node, so removing a given task from n runnable tasks is O(log n) with no search. A binary heap would need an extra position index to find an arbitrary entry, and it cannot cheaply answer "which task comes next after this one?". Other balanced structures, briefly B-trees and B+ trees use the same idea with hundreds of keys per node, matching disk pages. Many relational database indexes use them; hash, bitmap and other index types also exist (covered in System Design: databases). Skip lists give expected O(log n) search over n keys with randomised towers of linked lists; Redis sorted sets can use a skip list plus dictionary or a compact encoding. Treaps and splay trees balance with randomness or by moving accessed nodes to the root. Python has no built-in balanced tree. sortedcontainers uses a list of sorted lists, which offers different locality and update tradeoffs from pointer-based trees. Evidence gap Universal AVL-versus-red-black lookup wins and sortedcontainers performance wins are omitted because no matching workload, implementation and reproducible benchmark were supplied. Key takeaways AVL has a tighter worst-case height bound, but speed needs measurement. Conventional red-black deletion uses a bounded number of rotations. Library and kernel uses must be distinguished from interface requirements. Further reading Left-leaning Red-Black Trees — Robert Sedgewick (PDF) Red-black Trees (rbtree) in Linux — kernel docs CFS Scheduler — Linux kernel docs TreeMap (Java SE 25) — Oracle HashMap implementation — OpenJDK Associative container requirements — C++ draft EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs

t: Heap order and implicit array layout
sum: A binary heap combines complete shape with parent-child priority order.
x: Many problems only ever need the smallest (or largest) item: the next job to run, the nearest unvisited city in Dijkstra's algorithm, the earliest timer to fire, the next event in a simulation. A BST can do that, but it keeps far more order than you need. A priority queue is the abstract data type for this job: push(item), pop_min() and peek(). The standard implementation is the binary heap. For a binary heap of n items it gives O(log n) push and pop (work growing with the logarithm of n, about 20 steps for a million items) and O(1) peek (a fixed cost), stored with implicit parent/child indices rather than tree-link pointers. Python lists still store references to their elements. Costs assume constant-time comparisons; dynamic-array resizing makes push/pop bounds amortized when allocation costs are included. The binary heap property A binary min-heap is a binary tree with two rules: Shape: it is a complete binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left). Order: every parent is less than or equal to its children. So the minimum is always at the root. A max-heap flips the order rule. Notice how much weaker this is than a BST. Siblings are unordered (3 is left of 2), and 4 sits deep on the left while 2 is near the top on the right. The binary heap only promises that every path from the root downward is sorted. That weaker promise is what makes it cheap to maintain. The array layout Because the tree is complete, it packs into an array in level order with no gaps (the tree-structure units): The parent and children of any slot are found by arithmetic on its index: So the 3 at index 1 has children at indices 3 and 4 (4 and 8), and the 9 at index 7 has its parent at index 3 (the 4). In the Python code below, the parent index is (i - 1) // 2, where // divides and rounds down. Avoiding explicit tree links saves their storage. The array of slots is contiguous, though referenced payload objects need not be; actual cache behaviour depends on layout and access patterns. The second half of the array is all leaves: In the 8-item example, indices 4 to 7 (values 8, 7, 6 and 9) are leaves: index 4's left child would be at 9, past the end. Key takeaways A binary heap combines complete shape with parent-child priority order. Array indices replace explicit links. Binary heap order does not sort siblings or the entire array. Further reading Binary heap — Wikipedia Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Sift up, sift down and priority removal
sum: Push appends and moves the new key toward the root.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. Sift up: push To push, append the new item at the end (the next free slot in the last level, which keeps the shape) and then sift up: while it is smaller than its parent, swap them. Pushing 0 into the binary heap above: it lands at index 8 (child of 4), swaps with 4, then 3, then 1, and becomes the new root. There is at most one swap per level, and a complete tree is short: Pushing 0 made exactly 3 swaps, the most possible. A million-item binary heap needs at most 19, so push is O(log n). Sift down: pop Here n counts entries before the pop; use the sift-up unit's complete-tree height bound. To pop the minimum, you cannot just remove the root: that would leave a hole at the top. Instead, move the last item into the root (keeping the shape), shrink the array, and sift down: swap it with its smaller child until it is no larger than both children. Swapping with the smaller child matters: that child becomes the parent of the other, so it must be the smaller of the two. Pop also makes at most one swap per level, the same height limit as push, so for n items it is also O(log n). Binary Heaps are not sorted Only a[0] is guaranteed to be the minimum. a[1] is not necessarily the second smallest (in the example it is 3, but 2 is smaller), and iterating over a binary heap list does not give sorted order. Popping repeatedly does. Key takeaways Push appends and moves the new key toward the root. Pop moves the final entry to the root and repairs downward. Choose the smaller child to preserve min-heap order. Further reading Binary heap — Wikipedia Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Build downward from the last internal node.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. Heapify in O(n) Given n unsorted items, you could push them one at a time. Each push can climb the full height, so in the worst case: That is O(n log n): n multiplied by log n. There is a faster way. Treat the array as a complete tree already, and sift down every non-leaf from the bottom up: Use the sift_down helper from the preceding unit to execute heapify. Both operate in place on a list of comparable values; heapify does not return a new sorted list. Trace on [9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 3] (8 items, so start at index 3): Why is that O(n)? The cost of sifting down a node is at most its node height, and most nodes have tiny heights. A rigorous bound counts nodes able to move down at least a given number of levels: at most half the nodes can move one level, a quarter two levels, an eighth three, and so on. Summing those possible levels gives: The trace above made 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 swaps, within the bound of 7. For the shown sift-down algorithm, this bounds swaps by n and key comparisons by twice the item count (at most two child comparisons per available downward level, including a level where no swap is needed); loop and index checks are additional constant work per step. Pushing one at a time is slower because new items arrive at the bottom, the level with the most nodes, and each may climb the full height. The intuition: sift-down costs are cheap where nodes are plentiful (the bottom) and expensive only where they are rare (the top). Sift-up is the reverse. Heapsort Heapify, then repeatedly swap the root with the last item and sift down over a shrinking prefix. That is heapsort: for n items, O(n log n) worst case (n pops, each sifting down at most the binary heap's height), O(1) extra memory, but not stable and with poor cache locality (child positions roughly double their parent position), which can affect practical performance. One use is the worst-case fallback inside introsort (the usual implementation of C++ std::sort), which switches to heapsort if quicksort recurses too deeply. Key takeaways Build downward from the last internal node. Most nodes can move only a few levels, making bottom-up heapify linear. Heapsort repeatedly repairs a shrinking binary heap and is not stable. Further reading Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Python priority queues and streaming top-k
sum: Use an insertion counter to break equal-priority payload ties.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. heapq in Python Python's heapq module implements a min-heap on a plain list. There is no binary heap class. Here n is the number of items in the binary heap (or in the input, for heapify and nlargest), and k is how many items you ask for. Function Cost ------ heappush(h, x) O(log n) heappop(h) O(log n) h[0] (peek) O(1) heapify(h) O(n), in place heapreplace(h, x) pop then push, O(log n) heappushpop(h, x) push then pop, O(log n) nlargest(k, it) O(n log(k + 1)) when k is between 1 and n; implementation may choose max or sorting Practical details: Max-heaps: before Python 3.14, negate the keys (heappush(h, -x)). Python 3.14 added heapify_max, heappush_max, heappop_max and friends. Priorities with payloads: push tuples (priority, item). If two priorities tie, Python compares the items, which fails for objects that don't support <. Add a counter: (priority, next(counter), item). This also makes ties first-in-first-out. Changing a priority ("decrease-key") is not supported. The usual trick is lazy deletion: push a new entry and mark the old one as removed, skipping stale entries when they are popped. Dijkstra's algorithm in Python is normally written this way. Pattern: top-k "Find the k largest of n items" (top 10 search results, the 100 busiest IPs in a log). Sorting is O(n log n). Better: keep a min-heap of size k holding the best k seen so far. Its root is the weakest of the current top k, so each new item only needs comparing with the root. Each item costs one comparison with the root, and at most one replace that sifts through a binary heap of only k items: So for a keeper count between one and the input size, cost is O(n log(k + 1)) time including final sorting, and O(k) memory. The + 1 keeps the logarithm above zero when there is one keeper. Larger k returns all n items; zero keepers returns immediately. With a billion log lines and 100 keepers, that is about 7 binary heap levels per item instead of the 30 a binary heap of all n items would need, and it works on a stream that never fits in memory. heapq.nlargest does this for you. Min-heap for the largest, max-heap for the smallest It feels backwards, but for the k largest you want quick access to the smallest of your keepers, because that is the one a newcomer must beat. If all n items are in memory and you only need the k-th element, quickselect finds it in expected O(n), but it does not stream and reorders the array. Key takeaways Use an insertion counter to break equal-priority payload ties. A min-heap retains the largest stream items by exposing its weakest keeper. Changing priorities requires an extra policy such as lazy deletion. Further reading heapq — Python docs

t: Heap merging and alternative priority queues
sum: Keep only one current head from each sorted input.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. Pattern: k-way merge Merge k sorted lists (sorted runs from an external sort, per-shard query results, SSTables in LSM-tree compaction). Put the head of each list in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push the next item from the same list. This function uses heapq; import it as in the previous unit before running the example. The sample call returns a list; the comment shows that returned list, rather than printed script output. The binary heap never holds more than k items, so each of the N output items costs one pop and at most one push through a small binary heap: So the binary heap merge costs O(k + N log(k + 1)), including scanning empty input lists, with O(k) binary heap space plus O(N) returned output. Merging the lists pairwise one after another would cost up to O(N·k), N times k. heapq.merge is a lazy version of this. Beyond binary heaps d-ary heaps (4-ary is common) are shallower, reducing possible upward levels but requiring more child comparisons per downward level. Cache and runtime effects depend on the implementation and workload. Fibonacci heaps support amortised O(1) decrease-key and O(log n) delete-min (for n queued items), giving O(E + V log V) for Dijkstra on a graph with V vertices and E edges, with suitable handles and nonnegative edge weights. Ordinary pairing heaps do not share this combined constant-amortized decrease-key guarantee; their analysis is different. Benchmark concrete implementations before choosing. Real uses: OS timer queues, Go's container/heap, Java's PriorityQueue (a binary heap), job schedulers, and the event queue in network simulators. Key takeaways Keep only one current head from each sorted input. After popping a head, advance only its input. Different priority queue structures trade off child comparisons and update costs. Further reading heapq — Python docs K-way merge algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Trie paths, exact lookup and prefixes
sum: Shared prefixes share a root-to-node path.
x: In this lesson L is the length of a key in characters and n is the number of keys stored. Hash-table lookup uses expected O(1) probes (a fixed number on average) under suitable hashing assumptions; hashing and equality on uncached strings can cost O(L), in proportion to the key's length. They cannot answer "which words start with inte?" without scanning every key. Balanced BSTs can, but each comparison is a string comparison: So a BST lookup costs O(L log n), and the trie below brings that down to O(L). Real string comparisons often stop at the first differing character, so the BST figure is a worst case. A trie (from retrieval, usually pronounced "try") is built for prefix questions. Instead of storing whole keys in nodes, it stores one character per edge. A key is a path from the root, and every key that shares a prefix shares the path for that prefix. The structure Here is a trie holding car, card, care, cat, do and dog. A marks a node where a word ends. Things to notice: The root represents the empty string. Each node represents the prefix spelled by the path to it. car and card share three nodes. Shared prefixes are stored once. do is a word and a prefix of dog, so an end-of-word flag is needed; you cannot rely on "is it a leaf?". Keys are never compared with each other. Lookup cost depends on the length of the key, not on how many keys are stored. Insert, search and prefix queries With the trie above: Call Result Why --------- search(root, "car") True path exists, flag set search(root, "ca") False path exists, no flag starts_with(root, "ca") True path exists search(root, "dot") False no t under do With constant-time child access, insertion, exact lookup and prefix-path lookup take O(L + 1) for a key or prefix of L characters: one step per character, plus the root (the + 1 covers the empty string, for zero characters). The dict-backed example uses expected constant-time child lookups. For an empty prefix, starts_with returns True even on an empty trie because the root exists; this tests path existence, not whether any word is stored. O(L) is not automatically faster than hashing Hashing a previously unhashed string inspects its characters; some runtimes cache string hashes, and equality costs also matter. Tries directly support prefix navigation and can stop early on a miss. Practical exact-match performance depends on representation and workload. Key takeaways Shared prefixes share a root-to-node path. An end flag distinguishes complete words from their prefixes. Lookup follows key characters with expected constant-cost dictionary access. Further reading Trie — Wikipedia Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Walk to the prefix node before enumerating descendants.
x: A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee. Autocomplete Autocomplete is "walk to the prefix node, then enumerate words below it". Run this function with the Node, insert and walk definitions from the lookup unit. Populate the trie with car, card, care, cat, do and dog to obtain the illustrative completion list below. Sorted child traversal produces Python string lexicographic order (code-point order, not locale-aware alphabetical collation). This simple implementation copies path strings and sorts child keys during recursion; enumeration costs include visited nodes, copied characters and output, and deep words can hit Python's recursion limit. An autocomplete design may rank by popularity. Enumerating and sorting every match can be expensive, so one option is to cache top-k word IDs at selected prefix nodes. Looking up such a cached list of k IDs for a prefix of L characters costs expected O(L + k) in this representation, excluding retrieval and transmission of the completion text. The trade-off is memory, and slower updates when popularity changes. Sizing an autocomplete trie In a hypothetical dataset, 10 million queries with mean length exactly 20 have 200 million characters in total, but shared prefixes typically cut the node count substantially. Storing the top 10 completions at every node as 4-byte IDs adds 40 bytes per node, before container overhead. A design can store these lists only at selected shallow nodes and compute other results on demand; the best policy depends on query traffic. Key takeaways Walk to the prefix node before enumerating descendants. Sorted child traversal gives code-point order, not locale-aware collation. Cached top completions exchange update and memory costs for query speed. Further reading Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Child arrays reserve every alphabet position even when unused.
x: A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee. The memory problem Tries are fast but notoriously memory-hungry, because every character of every unshared suffix gets its own node, and each node carries overhead. Common child representations differ in how much they reserve per node. An array of child pointers reserves one slot for every possible character, used or not: Children as Lookup Memory per node --------- Array of 26 (or 256) pointers O(1) index 208 B (or 2 KiB) with 8-byte pointers, mostly empty Hash map / dict O(1) expected Small, but high constant overhead Sorted list O(log σ) Compact O(log σ) is the cost of a binary search among at most σ sorted children. Dictionary and node object sizes vary by interpreter build. Evidence gap The claimed CPython dictionary sizes and 100,000-word, 65 MB benchmark are omitted because the pinned build, word list, measurement code and retained-object accounting were unavailable. No measured tenfold memory ratio is established. With long mostly unshared suffixes, many nonterminal trie nodes have exactly one child: the unshared tail of a single word like...ication. That observation drives the fix. Why uniform hashes share little structure SHA-256 values use 64 hexadecimal characters when encoded as hex. Imagine one million independent, approximately uniform hashes. Each additional character multiplies the possible prefixes by sixteen. At shallow depths many keys collide; farther down, almost every key owns its entire remaining suffix. Counting occupied prefixes at each depth estimates the non-root node count: This model estimates about 59.68 million nodes, not bytes. Allocation overhead remains representation-dependent. A radix tree compresses the long private suffixes; a hash set is usually the first structure to consider when the task needs only exact membership and no prefix queries. Real hashes are modelled as approximately uniform here, rather than assumed to make every finite sample perfectly balanced. Key takeaways Child arrays reserve every alphabet position even when unused. Dictionary and object overhead depends on the implementation. Mostly unshared suffixes make character tries poor exact-match indexes. Further reading Trie — Wikipedia Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Compressed paths, routing and trie variants
sum: Compress single-child chains only when no intermediate key ends there.
x: A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee. Compressed tries and radix trees A radix tree (also called a compressed trie, or a Patricia trie in its binary form) merges chains of single-child nodes that do not mark a key end into one edge labelled with a string rather than a character. Except possibly the root, every internal node now has at least two children (or marks a word end), so the node count is at most twice the number of stored keys, independent of key length (the count is below). Lookups compare chunks of characters along each edge, with the same O(L) total for a key of L characters. Inserting can split an edge: adding cab to the tree above splits nothing because ca already exists, but adding co would split ca into c with children a and o. The node bound comes from counting the only kinds of node compression leaves behind: The radix tree drawn above holds those 4 keys in 5 labelled nodes plus the root, within the bound of 8. A plain trie, by contrast, can need one node per character of every key. Radix trees are where tries meet production: IP routing: a router finds the longest prefix match of a destination address against a table of CIDR prefixes. Binary tries over address bits, compressed (Patricia, LC-tries), are a classic implementation; Linux's IPv4 routing table uses an LC-trie (fib_trie). HTTP routers: Go's httprouter and many others match URL paths with a radix tree. Redis Streams use a radix tree of listpacks; a radix-tree entry represents a packed group of stream entries rather than necessarily one node per message. Ethereum stores its world state in a Merkle Patricia trie. The Linux page cache historically used a "radix tree", now the XArray, to map file offsets to pages. Other variants, briefly Here P names the pattern string and P denotes its character count when quoting a Big O lookup bound. Ternary search trees store one character per node with less/equal/greater children, like a BST over characters. They use far less memory than array tries and still support prefix search. Suffix tries and suffix trees hold every suffix of a text, answering "does pattern P occur anywhere?" in time proportional to the length of P, written O(P), where P is the number of characters in the pattern. Suffix arrays are the space-efficient alternative. Aho–Corasick adds failure links to a trie of patterns, finding all occurrences of many patterns in one pass over a text (GNU grep uses it for multiple fixed patterns, and intrusion-detection systems can use it to match many signatures). Finite-state transducers can merge equivalent states and share suitable suffix structure as well as prefixes. Compression depends on the vocabulary and outputs. When to reach for a trie Use one when you need: prefix queries: autocomplete, "all keys under /api/v1/", routing; longest-prefix matching; many patterns matched at once (Aho–Corasick); sorted iteration over strings with shared prefixes. Avoid one when you only do exact-match lookups (use a hash set), when keys share few prefixes (random IDs, hashes: the trie degenerates into one long chain per key), or when memory is tight and a sorted array with binary search on prefixes will do. Key takeaways Compress single-child chains only when no intermediate key ends there. Insertion may split an edge at the first different character. Routing uses the longest matching prefix, while exact membership often suits hashing. Further reading Radix tree — Wikipedia Longest prefix match — Wikipedia Ternary search tree — Wikipedia Aho–Corasick algorithm — Wikipedia Fixed-pattern search performance — GNU grep manual

t: Lowest common ancestors in ordered and general trees
sum: A BST query follows the side containing both keys until they split.
x: Tree problems look endlessly varied, but nearly all of them use one of a few patterns. Learn the patterns and most "new" problems become variations. Post-order combine. Each call returns a summary of its subtree (height, sum, "found it?"), and the parent combines its children's summaries. Often a second value, the global best, is tracked on the side. Pre-order with state passed down. Each call receives information from above (a running sum, a valid range, a depth) and passes an updated version to its children. Level-order when the question mentions levels, widths or nearest anything. This lesson works through the classics. Assume finite acyclic binary trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation.
