Version 1: find any index of x (closed interval) Here a is the sorted array, n its length, x the value we are looking for, and lo and hi the indices bounding the part of the array still in play. Invariant: if x is in the array, it is in a[lo..hi] (inclusive). Every choice follows from the invariant. The range [lo, hi] is empty when lo > hi, so loop while lo <= hi. When a[mid] < x, mid itself is ruled out, so lo = mid + 1, not mid. Key takeaways Each probe shrinks the candidate range by roughly half. Closed intervals require an inclusive loop and updates strictly beyond a rejected midpoint. Further reading Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect

sum: The lower bound is the first not-less position and the upper bound the first greater position.
x: This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Version 2: lower_bound (half-open interval) Finding some match is often not enough. You want the first position where x could go: the binary-search lower bound (often called lower_bound), the index of the first element at least as large as the search value. This is what Python's bisect_left and C++'s std::lower_bound return. Invariant: all elements before lo are smaller than the search value, and all elements at or beyond hi are at least the search value. The candidate insertion indices include both endpoints, even though the remaining element range excludes hi. When the endpoints meet, every preceding key is smaller than the search value and every following key is at least that value. That is the answer by definition. Note hi = len(a), not len(a) - 1: the answer can be "after everything". Trace: find lower_bound of 8 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]. The binary-search upper bound (upper_bound: the first element > x, bisect_right) is identical except the test becomes a[mid] <= x. lower_bound and upper_bound together answer most real questions: does x exist (lo < n and a[lo] == x), how many copies, where to insert while keeping order, and range queries ("all orders between 10:00 and 11:00" is [lower_bound(10:00), lower_bound(11:00))). Java’s Arrays.binarySearch returns a match index if present. If absent, its negative result encodes the insertion point: negate the insertion point and subtract one. For [10, 20, 30, 40], searching for 25 has insertion point 2 and returns −3. For a nearest-value query, inspect the lower-bound position and the position immediately before it, when they exist. One is the first not-less value and the other the largest smaller value, so a closer candidate cannot hide farther away. Return the smaller absolute distance; decide how ties should be broken. A count over a value interval likewise comes from subtracting its two insertion-bound indices, rather than scanning every matching element. Key takeaways The lower bound is the first not-less position and the upper bound the first greater position. Their difference counts equal keys, and insertion positions may be after the entire array. Further reading Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect

sum: Avoid overflowing fixed-width midpoint arithmetic.
x: This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. The classic pitfalls 1. Midpoint overflow The following Java lines are alternative midpoint expressions, not three declarations to place in one scope. A 32-bit signed int can hold values only up to about 2.1 billion. Two large indices can add up to more than that: For nonnegative Java int indices, the addition lo + hi can wrap once the array has more than about a billion elements, producing a negative midpoint. Signed overflow in C and C++ is undefined behavior; other languages have their own checked, wrapping or unsigned rules. In 2006 Joshua Bloch revealed that this bug had sat in Java's Arrays.binarySearch for about nine years, and in the version in Programming Pearls for two decades. Python's integers do not overflow, but C, C++, Java, Go and Rust code must use the safe form. 2. Infinite loops If you ever write lo = mid, check what happens when hi = lo + 1. Then the rounded-down midpoint is lo itself, so lo = mid changes nothing and the loop spins forever: The fixes: make every branch move strictly past mid (lo = mid + 1), or round the midpoint up (mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2) when the branch is lo = mid, or loop while hi - lo > 1 (see the later integer-root unit). 3. Mixing interval conventions Most bugs come from mixing closed [lo, hi] and half-open [lo, hi) conventions: hi = len(a) with while lo <= hi reads past the end; hi = len(a) - 1 with hi = mid can never return n. Pick one convention per function and derive every line from it. 4. Unsorted or wrongly sorted input Binary search on data that is not sorted by the same ordering silently returns nonsense, not an error. Sorting by key=str.lower and then searching with raw strings is a classic mismatch. Test the edges Every binary search should be tested on: an empty array, one element, x smaller than everything, x larger than everything, x absent but in the middle, and many duplicates. Off-by-one bugs hide in exactly those cases. Key takeaways Avoid overflowing fixed-width midpoint arithmetic. Derive termination and updates from one interval convention and test empty, absent and duplicate cases. Further reading Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect

sum: With distinct keys, at least one midpoint half is sorted.
x: This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Searching a rotated sorted array A sorted array rotated at an unknown point, like [15, 18, 22, 3, 6, 9, 12], is not sorted, but at least one half around any mid is sorted. Check which half is sorted and whether x lies inside its range. This is still O(log n), but only for distinct keys. With duplicates, [2, 2, 2, 3, 2] makes it impossible to tell which half is sorted when a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi], and the worst case becomes O(n). The same idea finds the rotation point (the minimum): if a[mid] > a[hi], the drop is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left. Key takeaways With distinct keys, at least one midpoint half is sorted. Equal endpoints can hide the rotation and force linear worst-case work. Further reading Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect

sum: Feasibility must be monotone and cheap enough to evaluate.
x: This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Binary search on the answer The most powerful generalisation: you do not need an array at all. You need a monotone predicate: a yes/no test that is false up to some point and true from then on. Binary search finds the first true in about log₂ of the number of candidates evaluations of the predicate: Example. Packages with weights [1, 2,..., 10] must be shipped in order within 5 days. What is the minimum ship capacity that works? A ship capacity below 10 cannot carry the heaviest package; 55 (the total) does it in one day. So the answer is in [10, 55]. "Can we ship with capacity c?" is monotone: if c works, any larger c works. It is checked greedily in O(n). Five checks of O(n) each, instead of trying all 46 capacities. In general: The same pattern handles largest minimum separation of routers when feasibility is monotone and efficiently checkable. A job-scheduling decision can be monotone yet computationally hard. Content gap: learning-rate divergence is omitted as an example because general training dynamics do not supply a reliably monotone predicate. Key takeaways Feasibility must be monotone and cheap enough to evaluate. Shipping capacity uses a greedy ordered pass inside each binary-search check. Further reading Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect

t: Integer square roots and search applications
sum: A feasible lower endpoint and infeasible upper endpoint converge to the integer root.
x: This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Integer square root is another instance, using the hi - lo > 1 style: For real-valued answers, use a suitable tolerance and an iteration limit, and stop when the computed midpoint equals an endpoint. A fixed 100 halvings does not cover every possible binary64 interval, especially across large exponent ranges or near subnormal values. Binary search in the wild git bisect narrows commit ancestry using good/bad tests. On a linear, monotone history with no skipped commits, 1,000 candidates take about 10 tests; merge graphs, flaky tests and fixes/reintroductions complicate that model. B-tree pages in databases (PostgreSQL, InnoDB) binary search the sorted keys inside each page. Timsort's galloping (covered later in this module) is an exponential search: probe 1, 3, 7, 15... until overshooting, then binary search. That is the right tool when the answer is probably near the start or the range is unbounded. Standard libraries: Python's bisect, C++'s lower_bound, upper_bound and equal_range, Java's Arrays.binarySearch (returns -(insertion point) - 1 when absent), and Go's sort.Search, which is binary search on a predicate. Key takeaways A feasible lower endpoint and infeasible upper endpoint converge to the integer root. Library and real-valued searches require their own ordering, rounding and termination contracts. Further reading Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect Integer square-root contract — Python math

sum: Selection asks for ranks rather than an entirely sorted array.
x: Many questions that sound like sorting are really selection algorithm: find the median latency, the 99th percentile, the 10 highest-scoring posts, the k nearest points. You need one element (or k elements) in the right place, not the whole array ordered. Sorting answers all of these in O(n log n). But selection can be done in O(n), and top-k in O(n log(k + 1)). At a billion items, the base-two logarithm of the input size is about thirty; this compares asymptotic growth, not literal pass counts or measured runtime. Throughout, n is the number of elements, costs use Big O notation (how a cost grows with n, ignoring constant factors), and "k-th smallest" is 0-based: rank zero is the minimum, the last rank is the maximum, and the integer-divided halfway index is the upper middle value for even-length inputs. The numeric median of an even sample conventionally averages its two central values. The easy cases Minimum or maximum: one pass, one fewer comparison than the number of items. That is optimal: every element except the winner must lose at least one comparison. Min and max together: compare elements in pairs, then the smaller with the current min and the larger with the current max. That is about one and a half comparisons per element instead of two. Second smallest: a knockout tournament finds it in the following count: the runner-up must have lost directly to the winner, and the winner played only about a logarithmic number of matches. For 1,024 elements: 1,023 comparisons for the minimum, about 1,536 for min and max together instead of 2,046 separately, and 1,032 for the second smallest. The general k is where it gets interesting. Key takeaways Selection asks for ranks rather than an entirely sorted array. Tournament losers prove minimum and second-minimum comparison costs. Further reading Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq

sum: Only the side containing the requested rank survives.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Quickselect Hoare's quickselect (1961) is quicksort that only recurses into one side. Partition around a pivot. The pivot lands at its final index p. If p equals k, done. If k is smaller than p, the answer is on the left; otherwise it is on the right. Throw the other side away. (lomuto is the partition from the quicksort lesson.) This compact version has the expected linear guarantee for distinct keys. With duplicates, random pivots alone do not prevent quadratic time on all-equal input; use a three-way partition and discard the entire equal block for a duplicate-robust version. Because only one side survives, recursion becomes a loop. Trace with the last element as pivot (no randomisation, to keep it readable), finding k = 5 in [7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4]: Check: sorted, the array is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] and index 5 is 6. Why it is expected O(n) With a good pivot, each round discards a constant fraction. If every pivot split the array in half, the work would be a geometric series (each term a fixed fraction of the one before): So the total is linear. For distinct keys, with random pivots the splits are not exactly half, but the pivot lands in the middle 50% of the range with probability 1/2, and then at least a quarter is discarded. The expected cost is still a geometric series: O(n). A more careful analysis gives the expected comparisons for finding the median, and fewer for k near the ends: The worst case Bad pivots every round shrink the range by only one element, exactly like quicksort: With a first- or last-element pivot, a sorted input does this. Random pivots make it vanishingly unlikely, but not impossible, and an adversary who can predict your random number generator can still force it. Key takeaways Only the side containing the requested rank survives. Independent random pivots give expected linear work for distinct keys; poor splits still give a quadratic worst case. Further reading Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq Time bounds for selection — Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan Quickselect comparison analysis — Martínez and Roura

sum: Groups of five guarantee a fixed fraction on each side, allowing rounding corrections.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Median of medians: worst-case O(n) In 1973 Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan showed that selection can be done in O(n) guaranteed. The trick is to spend a little linear work finding a pivot that is provably not too far from the middle. Split the array into groups of 5. Find the median of each group (constant work per group). Recursively select the median of the group medians (one per five items, rounded up). Use it as the pivot. Partition and recurse into the side containing k. Why the pivot is good Picture the groups as columns, each sorted with its median in the middle row, and the columns ordered by their medians. M is the median of medians. Half of the medians are no larger than the chosen median M. Each of those medians has two more elements in its group below it. So at least 3 elements in each of about half the groups are no bigger than M, and by symmetry the same number are no smaller: For 1,000 elements the conservative finite bound excludes at least 294 and leaves at most 706 for the retained recursive side. The recurrence is: Ignoring constant rounding allowances for the asymptotic argument, the two recursive size fractions sum to nine tenths, which is less than one. The total work at each level of recursion shrinks geometrically, and the whole algorithm is O(n). Why groups of 5? With groups of 3, the guarantee is only about a third on each side, giving the recurrence below. This analysis establishes only O(n log n), not a matching lower bound. Five is the smallest odd group size giving linear time by this simple argument; other algorithms can use repeated grouping or different methods. Key takeaways Groups of five guarantee a fixed fraction on each side, allowing rounding corrections. Selecting the medians and the retained side together uses less than the whole input per asymptotic level. Further reading Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq Time bounds for selection — Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan

sum: Introselect needs a work budget and an appropriate fallback for its claimed worst-case bound.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Practical costs and hybrids The constant factor is large: sorting every group of 5, the extra recursive call and the partition add up to extra work compared with classical randomized selection; exact constants depend on the implementation, and the list-building version above also allocates heavily. So in practice median of medians is a fallback, not a default: Introselect (Musser, 1997) runs quickselect, and if it is not shrinking the range fast enough, switches to a fallback. A carefully budgeted linear-time fallback gives a linear worst-case bound; a heap fallback may give O(n log n). C++ requires only average linear complexity for ordinary std::nth_element and does not mandate an algorithm. NumPy documents O(n) worst-case introselect. Floyd–Rivest (1975) picks the pivot from a small random sample and achieves the expected comparison count below, close to the theoretical optimum. It is used for large in-memory selection. NumPy’s partition puts the requested rank in its sorted position. Values before it are no larger and values after it no smaller, but neither side is fully sorted. The function returns a partitioned copy; an ndarray’s in-place partition method has a different mutation contract. Key takeaways Introselect needs a work budget and an appropriate fallback for its claimed worst-case bound. The C++ and NumPy selection APIs promise different complexity contracts. Further reading Partition guarantees — NumPy documentation nth_element — C++ working draft Expected time bounds for selection — Floyd and Rivest

sum: For the smallest values, keep a max-heap whose root is the worst retained item.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. The k smallest with a heap Quickselect needs the whole array in memory and rearranges it. For top-k from a stream, or when k is much smaller than n, a heap is the better tool (heap operations are covered in the trees module). To keep the k smallest seen so far, keep a max-heap of size k. Its root is the largest of your current best k: the one to throw out when something smaller arrives. Trace for k = 3 over [9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3, 6, 4, 5]: The counter-intuitive part: to find the smallest k, use a max-heap; to find the largest k, use a min-heap. The root is the gatekeeper for "worst of the best". Time: O(n log(k + 1)). Each element costs at most one O(log k) heap operation, and once the heap holds good values, most elements are rejected by a single comparison with the root. The "+ 1" only keeps the bound sensible for one retained item, where its logarithm would otherwise be zero. Space: O(k), independent of n. It works on a stream you cannot store: the 100 smallest response-time records from a stream. Ranking query frequencies additionally needs counting or a frequency sketch. Python's heapq.nsmallest(k, it) and nlargest implement this. C++'s std::partial_sort puts the k smallest at the front in order. A heap is a common implementation; the standard specifies the result and comparison bound, not that algorithm. An alternative is to heapify the whole array in O(n) and pop k times: O(n + k log n). That is fast for small k, but it needs all the data in memory and rearranges it. Key takeaways For the smallest values, keep a max-heap whose root is the worst retained item. A fixed-size heap processes the stream in bounded memory and rejects worse newcomers cheaply. Further reading Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq

sum: Select a prefix and sort only that prefix when ordered top-k output is required.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Choosing a method Method Time Space Use when ------------ Sort O(n log n) O(n) / O(1) Need many ranks Quickselect O(n) exp. O(1) Array in memory Med. of medians O(n) worst O(n) in shown list version Guarantee needed Size-k heap O(n log(k + 1)) O(k) Streams, small k Practical notes: Many percentiles at once (p50, p90, p99, p99.9): one sort may be convenient; repeated or multi-rank selection can avoid sorting everything. Benchmark the implementation. Streaming monitoring can instead use bounded-memory summaries such as t-digest or configured HDR Histogram, with their own accuracy/range trade-offs. The k smallest, unordered in linear time: quickselect for the last retained rank leaves the k smallest in the first k array positions (in arbitrary order). Sort just those if you need them ordered: O(n + k log k). Running median of a stream: keep two heaps, a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalanced so their sizes differ by at most one. Each insert is O(log n) and the median is read from the roots in O(1). For a running median, keep every value in the lower heap no larger than every value in the upper heap. Maintain the lower heap at equal size or one larger. Insert into the appropriate side, then move a root if necessary. With an odd total, the lower root is the median; with an even total, the median convention may average the two roots. After the stream 5, 15, 1, 3, 8, the lower half is 1, 3, 5 and the upper half is 8, 15, giving median 5. Heap contents describe membership here, not their internal array order. Key takeaways Select a prefix and sort only that prefix when ordered top-k output is required. Two balanced heaps support a running median; several static ranks may justify sorting once. Further reading Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq

sum: Vertices identify entities; edges identify their connections.
x: A graph is a set of things and the connections between them. The things are vertices (also called nodes) and the connections are edges. Textbooks write a graph as a pair of two sets, and name the two sizes that every running time in this module is measured in: For example, a map can have four towns and five roads. Every cost in this module, such as O(n + m), is stated in terms of these two numbers. Graphs are everywhere once you look: road networks, social networks, package dependencies, web links, flight routes, the states of a Rubik's cube. A huge number of problems become easy once you notice "this is a graph" and reach for a standard algorithm. The vocabulary Directed or undirected In an undirected graph an edge {u, v} goes both ways: friendship on Facebook, a two-way street. In a directed graph (a digraph) an edge (u, v) goes from u to v only: following on X, a one-way street, "module A imports module B". In the undirected graph, every vertex can reach every other. In the directed one, A reaches B, D and C, and C reaches A, so here everything is mutually reachable too, but only because the arrows happen to form a loop. The vertex degree counts incident edge ends; a graph self-loop (an edge from a vertex back to itself) contributes two. In a digraph we split it into in-degree (arrows in) and out-degree (arrows out). Adding up every vertex's degree counts each edge twice, once from each end. This is the handshake lemma, and it lets you get the edge count from the degrees (or the other way round): The worked line is a five-vertex graph with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2: the sum is 12, so it has 6 edges. A consequence: the degree sum is always even, so no graph has degrees 3, 2, 2. In a directed graph the version is different: the in-degrees add up to m, and so do the out-degrees, because each arrow has one tail and one head. Key takeaways Vertices identify entities; edges identify their connections. Count edge ends to recover undirected edge counts. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Handshaking lemma — Wikipedia

sum: Distinguish walks, simple paths, cycles and connected trees.
x: A vertex is one entity; an edge joins two vertices. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Weighted edges attach a cost to a connection; the choice of cost determines which path is cheapest. Weighted or unweighted A weighted graph attaches a number to each edge: distance in km, latency in ms, cost in pounds, edge capacity in Mbit/s. Unweighted graphs treat every edge as cost 1. This distinction decides which shortest-path algorithm you can use (BFS for unweighted, Dijkstra and friends for weighted). Paths, cycles and connectivity A Walk (graph) follows a sequence of edges and may repeat vertices or edges. A simple path repeats no vertex; terminology for “path” varies, so this module specifies when repetitions matter. A cycle is a nonempty closed walk with no repeated vertices except its start/end and no repeated edges. In a simple undirected graph it has at least three edges: going along one edge and immediately back is not a cycle. A graph with no cycles is acyclic. A directed acyclic graph is a DAG, useful for prerequisite relations without circular dependencies. An undirected graph is connected if every vertex can reach every other. A connected acyclic undirected graph is a tree, and it always has exactly one edge fewer than it has vertices: a tree on 10 vertices has 9 edges. Dense or sparse How many edges can a graph have at most? In a simple graph (no graph self-loops, no two edges joining the same pair), each edge is a different pair of distinct vertices, so counting pairs gives the ceiling: The worked line is a five-vertex undirected graph: at most 10 edges (20 if directed). Both maxima grow like n², n multiplied by itself. A graph is dense if its edge count m is close to n² and sparse if m is closer to n. For a hypothetical simple undirected graph with one billion vertices and an average degree of 200, the handshake lemma gives the edge count, which is tiny next to the maximum: This is sparse. Content gap Population-wide claims about typical road or social graph degrees are omitted because no specified dataset and measurement support them here. Density, required operations, mutability and memory layout all affect the representation choice. Key takeaways Distinguish walks, simple paths, cycles and connected trees. Count possible edges only after specifying direction and whether the graph is simple. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Dense graph — Wikipedia

sum: Initialise isolates and sinks before adding edges.
x: Earlier units established direction, paths and density. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges; deg(u) is vertex u’s degree. Representation 1: adjacency list For each vertex, store a list of its neighbours. In Python, a dict of lists (or a list of lists when vertices are numbered 0..n−1). Pass every vertex explicitly, including isolates and directed sinks; each edge endpoint must belong to that set. Complexity assumes constant-size labels and expected O(1) dictionary/set operations. For a weighted graph, store pairs: adj[u].append((v, w)). The memory is one slot per vertex plus one list entry per edge end: The example has four vertices and four edges: four keys plus eight neighbour entries, twelve items in all. In the costs below, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges and deg(u) the degree of vertex u. O(…) is Big O notation: how the cost grows as the graph grows, ignoring constant factors. Space: O(n + m). Each undirected edge is stored twice, each directed edge once. Iterate neighbours of u: O(1 + deg(u)), which is exactly what BFS, DFS and Dijkstra need. Is there an edge u→v? O(1 + deg(u)) by scanning. Replace the inner lists with sets to make it O(1) on average. This is the default for almost every algorithm in this module. Representation 3: edge list Just a list of (u, v) or (u, v, w) tuples. Here m is the number of edges. Space: O(m) for edges, plus any separately stored vertex set. Requires a full scan for "who are u's neighbours?" (O(m) scan). Perfect when an algorithm processes edges as a whole: Kruskal's MST sorts the edges, and Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge each round. It is also how graphs usually arrive: a CSV of flights, a table of follower_id, followee_id rows. You read the edge list, then build whatever structure the algorithm needs. Comparison As before, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges and deg u the degree of vertex u. Operation List Matrix Edges ------------ Space O(n + m) O(n²) O(m) Edge u→v? O(1 + deg u) O(1) O(m) Neighbours O(1 + deg u) O(n) O(m) Add edge O(1) amortised O(1) O(1) amortised Traversing all vertices costs O(n + m) with adjacency lists and O(n²) with a matrix. A traversal from one source scans only reachable vertices; the displayed bounds are whole-graph upper bounds. These are growth rates, not measured elapsed times. Pitfalls Forgetting the reverse edge in an undirected graph: add both adj[u].append(v) and adj[v].append(u), or some intended paths may be lost. Isolated vertices vanish from an adjacency dict built only from edges. If vertex 7 has no edges, it never appears, and a "count components" loop will undercount. Initialise all n vertices first. Parallel edges and graph self-loops. Real data often contains duplicates. Decide whether they matter (they change degree counts and can break algorithms that assume a simple graph). Recursion limits. Python limits recursion depth (inspect sys.getrecursionlimit()); a sufficiently long path can raise RecursionError. Prefer iterative versions for large inputs. Key takeaways Initialise isolates and sinks before adding edges. Use lists to scan neighbours and an edge list to process edges globally. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Adjacency list — Wikipedia Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Adjacency matrices and compact CSR storage
sum: Matrices trade quadratic storage for constant-time edge lookup.
x: Adjacency lists store neighbours explicitly; an adjacency matrix instead allocates a cell for each ordered pair. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Representation 2: adjacency matrix For a simple unweighted graph, M[u][v] is 1 for an edge and 0 otherwise. For shortest-path weights, use infinity for absence so zero-weight edges remain distinguishable; initialise diagonal distances with the minimum of zero and any graph self-loop weight. A single cell cannot preserve multiple parallel-edge identities without additional data. An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix. The matrix has n rows and n columns, where n is the number of vertices: Space: O(n²), regardless of how many edges exist. Edge lookup: O(1), a single array index. Iterate neighbours of u: O(n), because you must scan the whole row, even if u has one neighbour. The n² trap A matrix for 1,000,000 vertices has 10¹² cells. Even at one bit per cell that is about 125 GB. A packed CSR representation of 5 million undirected edges using 32-bit neighbour IDs and offsets needs about 44 MB for those arrays. A Python dictionary of lists has substantial additional object overhead. Content gap: no measured Python-memory footprint or traversal timing is supplied; the packed-array calculation is not a benchmark. The two numbers in that warning come from these sums: The bit-packed matrix needs about 125 GB (gigabytes), nearly 3,000 times the CSR array figure. A decimal gigabyte is one billion bytes. The matrix cost does not fall at all if the graph has few edges, which is why it only pays off when the graph is small or dense. Matrices win for small or dense graphs, for algorithms built around them (Floyd–Warshall), and for linear algebra on graphs. Multiplying an unweighted adjacency matrix by itself counts walks: For instance, if 0→1→0 and 0→2→0 are the only two-step round trips from vertex 0, the row-zero, column-zero entry of the squared matrix is two. PageRank instead iterates a normalised random-surfer model with damping and handling for vertices without outgoing edges. Real-world representations Social and web graphs at scale use compressed adjacency lists. CSR (compressed sparse row) stores all neighbour lists in one flat array plus an offsets array: neighbours of u are nbrs[off[u]:off[u+1]]. It is compact and cache-friendly, and is used by graph libraries and sparse-matrix code alike. Graph databases such as Neo4j keep relationship adjacency with nodes so traversals can follow connections without a global relationship lookup at every hop ("index-free adjacency"). The physical representation depends on the store format: record formats and newer block formats organise relationships differently. Degree, caching, store format and the query still affect traversal cost. Routing engines for road maps preprocess the graph heavily (contraction hierarchies) because millions of queries hit the same static graph. Key takeaways Matrices trade quadratic storage for constant-time edge lookup. Packed CSR sizes describe arrays, not Python object memory or measured speed. Matrix powers count walks, not necessarily simple paths. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Adjacency matrix — Wikipedia Adjacency list — Wikipedia Neo4j store formats

sum: Generate predictable grid edges as needed.
x: Graph vertices need not be objects stored in a database. They can be cells or legal configurations, with a rule that generates the next possible states. Implicit graphs Often the graph is never stored at all. You have a rule that, given a vertex, generates its neighbours on demand. This is an implicit graph. Grids A maze or image is a grid where each cell is a vertex and neighbours are the adjacent cells. You can count a grid's size without building it. Each row has one link fewer than it has cells, and so does each column: The worked lines are the 3 × 3 grid above with its walls removed: 9 cells and 12 edges. Walls only remove vertices and edges, so a grid with walls has at most those counts. Large four-direction grids have about twice as many undirected edges as cells, so they are sparse. Generating neighbours avoids storing predictable edges; precomputing them can still help some repeated workloads. State spaces The vertices can be abstract states. In a sliding-tile puzzle, a state is a board arrangement and an edge is one legal move. In "word ladder" (turn COLD into WARM one letter at a time), a state is a word and an edge links words differing by one letter. In a lock with four dials, a state is a 4-digit code with 8 neighbours (each dial up or down). State spaces can be astronomically large: the 15-puzzle has about 10¹³ reachable states. Search often generates states as needed; even then exhaustive BFS can be infeasible. BFS, DFS and A can use a neighbours(state) function instead of stored adjacency. Spotting a graph problem Ask: "What are the states, and what moves take me from one to another?" If the answer is clear, you have a graph. BFS minimises the number of unit-cost moves when the reachable search space is manageable. Key takeaways Generate predictable grid edges as needed. A search vertex must encode a complete state, not just its visible position. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Implicit graph — Wikipedia

sum: BFS expands a FIFO queue in increasing edge-distance layers.
x: Almost every graph algorithm is a traversal in disguise. There are two basic ways to explore a graph from a starting vertex: Breadth-first search (BFS) spreads out like a ripple in a pond: first everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away, and so on. Depth-first search (DFS) behaves like someone in a maze with a ball of string: go as deep as possible down one corridor, and only back up when you hit a dead end. Both traversals touch each vertex and each edge a bounded number of times, so their running time grows with the size of the graph: For example, substituting one million junctions and 2.5 million roads gives a growth expression of 3.5 million; it is not an exact instruction count. This assumes adjacency lists and the usual constant-time access model; dictionary/set bounds here are expected bounds. All referenced vertices must have adjacency entries. What differs between BFS and DFS is the order, and that order is what makes each one useful. Throughout this lesson, n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges. We will use this graph throughout: Breadth-first search BFS uses a queue (first in, first out). Start by enqueuing the source. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex and enqueue any neighbours you have not seen yet. Here dist doubles as the visited set. Tracing from 0: Dequeue Enqueue Queue after --------- 0 1, 2 [1, 2] 1 3, 4 [2, 3, 4] 2 (none new) [3, 4] 3 (none) [4] 4 5 [5] 5 (none) [] Visit order: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Distances: 0→0, 1→1, 2→1, 3→2, 4→2, 5→3. Mark when you enqueue, not when you dequeue A classic bug If you mark a vertex visited only when it is dequeued, it can be enqueued many times by different neighbours before it is processed. On a dense graph the queue can grow to O(m) entries (in proportion to m, the number of edges), and some versions compute wrong distances. Mark (or set dist) at the moment you enqueue. BFS answers plain reachability and fewest unit-cost knight moves on an implicit chessboard graph. It does not minimise unequal road lengths or find a longest simple path in a general graph; the latter problem is NP-hard. Key takeaways BFS expands a FIFO queue in increasing edge-distance layers. Record discovery when enqueuing to prevent duplicate queue entries. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Breadth-first search — Wikipedia Breadth-first search — cp-algorithms Shortest path problem — Wikipedia

t: Recovering BFS paths and tracing DFS
sum: BFS parent pointers recover a shortest unweighted path.
x: The previous unit’s BFS returns a distance dictionary and parent pointers. In its running example the adjacency lists are 0:[1,2], 1:[0,3,4], 2:[0,4], 3:[1], 4:[1,2,5], 5:[4]. The source is vertex 0. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. BFS distances count edges. Why BFS finds shortest paths The key fact is an invariant (a rule that stays true at every step) about what the queue holds: In the trace above, after dequeuing 1 the queue is [2, 3, 4] with distances 1, 2, 2: never more than one apart. So BFS finishes every vertex at distance d before touching any at distance d + 1. The first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has reached it by the fewest possible edges. The invariant only holds because every edge counts as one step; with different edge costs it breaks. BFS always minimises edge count. This also minimises total cost when all edges have the same non-negative cost. For unequal non-negative weights use Dijkstra; negative weights require additional care (lesson 4). To recover the actual path, follow parent pointers back from the target and reverse: Depth-first search DFS uses a stack, either the call stack (recursion) or an explicit list. From 0 the recursive version visits 0, 1, 3, 4, 2, 5. It dives 0→1→3, hits a dead end, backs up to 1, goes to 4, then 2 (whose neighbours are all seen), backs up to 4, then 5. The iterative version avoids Python's configurable recursion-depth limit, which a long chain easily exceeds: This one visits 0, 2, 4, 5, 1, 3. It is still a valid DFS, but the order differs because the last neighbour pushed is popped first. Push neighbours in reverse if you need the recursive order. Note that here the seen check happens on pop, so a vertex may sit on the stack more than once; that is fine and still O(n + m) overall, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges. Key takeaways BFS parent pointers recover a shortest unweighted path. A stack changes the exploration order; neighbour order affects the trace. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Graph traversal — Wikipedia Depth-first search — cp-algorithms

sum: Linear-time traversal requires adjacency lists and bounded vertex processing.
x: The running six-vertex undirected example has six edges: 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 1–4, 2–4 and 4–5. Here n counts vertices, m counts edges, and deg(u) counts edges incident on vertex u. BFS uses a queue; DFS uses recursion or a stack. Complexity With an adjacency list, BFS enqueues each vertex once, and both shown traversals scan each processed adjacency list once. The iterative DFS can push duplicates, but at most O(n + m) entries overall. Adding up the work per vertex gives the total: The "each edge counted twice" step is the handshake lemma: every undirected edge u–v appears once in u's list and once in v's. In the example graph the degrees of vertices 0 to 5 are 2, 3, 2, 1, 3 and 1, which add up to 12: twice its 6 edges. In a directed graph each edge appears once, giving n + m. With an adjacency matrix, finding a vertex's neighbours means scanning its whole row of n cells, even if it has only one neighbour: BFS and recursive DFS use O(n) auxiliary space. The displayed mark-on-pop iterative DFS can retain O(m) duplicate stack entries, so its bound is O(n + m). An explicit stack of active neighbour iterators can reproduce recursive DFS with O(n) auxiliary space. The frontier shapes below refer to tree search without retaining a global visited set: BFS DFS --------- Structure Queue Stack Frontier memory Exponential in depth Linear in depth Shortest path Yes (unweighted) No Natural uses Distances, layers Cycles, ordering The frontier is the set of vertices discovered but not yet expanded. On a search tree where every vertex has the same number of children, the two traversals need very different amounts of frontier memory: With ten children per vertex and depth six, BFS holds about a million frontier vertices while DFS holds about sixty. The estimate assumes a full tree with no repeated states; on graphs with a visited set both still need memory for the set itself. That is why huge game-tree searches use DFS, or iterative deepening (DFS with depth limits 1, 2, 3,...), which finds a shallowest goal with linear-depth search memory on finitely branching trees, using appropriate depth-limit handling. Key takeaways Linear-time traversal requires adjacency lists and bounded vertex processing. Separate frontier memory from a global visited set. Iterative deepening repeats shallow levels to reduce search-tree memory. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Breadth-first search — cp-algorithms Iterative deepening depth-first search — Wikipedia

t: Components, flood fill and multiple sources
sum: Start traversals from every unvisited vertex to include all components.
x: These applications reuse BFS and DFS. The recursive dfs(adj, u, seen) routine from the earlier tracing unit marks u and explores unseen neighbours. Import deque from collections for the BFS fragment below. Every vertex, including isolates, must have an adjacency entry. Connected components A traversal from s finds everything reachable from s. To find every component of an undirected graph, loop over all vertices and start a new traversal from each unvisited one. Total work is still O(n + m), with n vertices and m edges: each vertex and edge is handled once across all traversals. (In a directed graph this gives "reachability trees", not strongly connected components; see lesson 3.) Flood fill Flood fill is a traversal on a grid: the paint-bucket tool, or "count the islands". Each land cell is a vertex; edges join adjacent land cells. That grid has 4 islands. The code is the components loop over cells, with a 4-direction neighbour function (lesson 1). Use an explicit stack or BFS: a recursive flood fill on a 1000 × 1000 image can recurse a million deep. Multi-source BFS Sometimes you want each vertex's distance to the nearest of several sources: the nearest exit, the nearest hospital, how many minutes until every orange in a crate rots. Running BFS from every source separately multiplies the work by the number of sources: With 500 hospitals on an unweighted road graph, that is the difference between 500 traversals and one; unequal travel times require a weighted shortest-path method. So put all sources in the queue at distance 0 and run one BFS. It works because it is equivalent to adding a virtual super-source joined to every real source by an edge, then doing ordinary BFS and subtracting one from every real vertex’s distance. The layers still expand in order. Pitfalls Forgetting the visited set on a graph with cycles: the traversal loops forever. Using DFS for "fewest steps". DFS finds a path, not the shortest. list.pop(0) as a queue is O(n) per pop in Python, where n is the current queue length, because every remaining item moves one place left. Use collections.deque. Missing disconnected parts. A single traversal only covers one component. Key takeaways Start traversals from every unvisited vertex to include all components. Seed every source at distance zero to find the nearest one in a single BFS. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Breadth-first search — Wikipedia Component (graph theory) — Wikipedia)

t: State-aware search and meeting in the middle
sum: Include keys, fuel or other move-dependent information in visited-state identity.
x: BFS finds fewest unit-cost moves. Its visited set records search states. A state must contain every fact needed to decide which next moves are legal. BFS over richer states If the rules depend on more than your position, put that extra information into the vertex. In a maze with keys and locked doors, being at cell (3, 4) holding key A is a different situation from being there empty-handed. So the state becomes (row, col, keys), where keys is a bitmask: one bit per key, set to 1 if you hold it. The number of possible states is the number of cells times the number of key sets: So a 50 × 50 grid with 6 keys has at most 160,000 cell/key-set states; walls and reachability may reduce this. With 20 keys it would be over 2.6 billion, so this trick only suits a handful of keys. Assess memory for the chosen implementation. The same trick handles "you may break at most k walls" (state includes walls broken so far) or "move with remaining fuel f". Where these show up Mark-and-sweep garbage collectors mark live objects by traversing the reference graph from the roots (a multi-source traversal), then sweep whatever was not reached. Web crawlers traverse link graphs; their scheduling may use breadth-first ideas, priorities and per-site limits. Degrees of separation can be found with BFS. Bidirectional BFS searches from both ends; in directed graphs the backward search follows reversed edges. In a roughly tree-like model, two half-depth searches are much smaller than one full-depth search: With 100 contacts each and six degrees of separation, that is about two million vertices instead of a trillion. Overlap between friend lists, degree variation and stopping rules affect actual work. Content gap No claim is made about LinkedIn’s current implementation: an authoritative implementation description was not verified. Build tools and package managers use DFS to walk dependency trees. Key takeaways Include keys, fuel or other move-dependent information in visited-state identity. Bidirectional search reverses edges on its backward side in a directed graph. Tree-like frontier estimates are modelling assumptions, not dataset benchmarks. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Breadth-first search — Wikipedia Implicit graph — Wikipedia

sum: Grey vertices remain on the active recursion path.
x: Lesson 2 used DFS just to visit things. Its real power is the structure it leaves behind: which vertices are still "open" on the stack, and the order in which vertices finish. That structure answers questions such as "is there a circular dependency?", "in what order should I build these modules?" and "which pages all link to each other?". Throughout this lesson, n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, and O(…) is Big O notation: how the running time grows with the graph's size, ignoring constant factors. Every algorithm here runs in O(n + m), the same as one traversal. The three colours Give every vertex a colour during DFS: White: not yet discovered. Grey: discovered, still on the recursion stack (we are somewhere inside its subtree). Black: finished; all its outgoing edges have been examined and all recursive calls it made have returned. When DFS at u looks at an edge u→v, the colour of v classifies the edge: v is Edge type Meaning --------- White Tree edge DFS goes to v Grey Back edge v is u or an ancestor of u Black Forward or cross Already done A back edge points from a vertex to one of its own ancestors, closing a loop. That gives the key theorem: a directed graph has a cycle if and only if a DFS covering all vertices finds a back edge. Cycle detection in directed graphs Why "visited" is not enough A plain visited set reports a cycle in this DAG, which has none: DFS goes 0→1→3, finishes, then 0→2 finds 3 already visited. But 3 is black (finished), not grey. It is a cross edge, not a loop. Grey, not visited Only grey means "on my current path". Checking v in visited instead of color[v] == GREY gives false positives on any DAG where two paths reconverge, such as the diamond above. Key takeaways Grey vertices remain on the active recursion path. A black reconvergence is not a directed cycle. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Depth-first search — Wikipedia

sum: Ignore the particular parent edge, not arbitrary edges to a parent.
x: Directed DFS colours were covered previously. Undirected adjacency lists store each edge at both endpoints, which creates an immediate reverse edge. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Cycle detection in undirected graphs In an undirected graph every edge appears in both directions, so from u you will always see your parent again. Ignore that one edge; any other already-visited neighbour closes a cycle. Two shortcuts. First, a connected undirected graph with no cycle is a tree, and a tree's edge count is fixed by its vertex count: So a connected graph with 10 vertices and 10 edges must contain a cycle. The test needs the graph to be connected: a triangle plus one separate, isolated vertex has 4 vertices and 3 edges, one fewer than the vertex count, yet it contains a cycle. Second, Union-Find (lesson 6) detects a cycle the moment an edge joins two vertices already in the same set. The code is presented for simple undirected graphs. In a recursive multigraph DFS, distinguish the particular parent edge by edge id: ignoring every edge to the parent can hide a genuine two-edge cycle. Pitfalls Directed cycle detection with a visited set: reports cycles in DAGs (the diamond). Undirected logic on a directed graph or vice versa: the parent trick is only for undirected graphs. Recursion depth: a sufficiently long chain can exceed Python’s configured recursion limit. Use iterative versions or sys.setrecursionlimit with care. Forgetting disconnected parts: every algorithm here needs the outer "for each unvisited vertex" loop. Key takeaways Ignore the particular parent edge, not arbitrary edges to a parent. The edge-count tree test requires connected input. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Cycle (graph theory) — Wikipedia)

t: Ordering dependencies with Kahn and DFS
sum: Orient prerequisite edges consistently.
x: A DAG is a directed graph with no cycle. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. DFS colour-based cycle detection is an earlier prerequisite; recursion-depth limits apply to the DFS implementation below. Topological sort A topological order of a DAG lists the vertices so that every edge u→v has u before v. For prerequisites, orient each edge from prerequisite to dependent: socks before shoes, shirt before tie. If edges instead point from a target to its dependencies, use reverse topological order. It exists if and only if the graph has no directed cycle, and there may be many valid orders. Example DAG (A→C, B→C, B→D, C→E, D→E): Kahn's algorithm (BFS-style) Repeatedly output a vertex with no remaining incoming edges, then delete its outgoing edges. On the example: in-degrees A0, B0, C2, D1, E2. The queue starts [A, B]. Output A (C→1), B (C→0, D→0), C (E→1), D (E→0), E. Order: A, B, C, D, E. If a cycle exists, its vertices never reach in-degree 0, so the output is short. That makes Kahn's a cycle detector for free. Replace the queue with a min-heap to get the lexicographically smallest order. DFS-based Run DFS and record each vertex when it finishes. A vertex finishes only after everything it points to has finished, so reversing the finish order puts every vertex before every vertex it has an edge to. On the example (starting from A): finish order E, C, A, D, B. Reversed: B, D, A, C, E. Different from Kahn's, and equally valid. (This version assumes a DAG; combine it with the grey check to detect cycles.) Both run in O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges. Kahn's DFS-based --------- Style Queue, in-degrees Recursion, finish order Cycle check Built in Needs grey check Parallelism Shows ready tasks No Recursion None Deep on long chains Where it is used GNU Make, Bazel and Gradle order build steps topologically. Package managers order installs. Acyclic spreadsheet formulas can be recalculated in dependency order; circular formulas need error handling or an explicitly supported iterative calculation mode. Python ships graphlib.TopologicalSorter, a Kahn-style sorter whose get_ready() returns every task that can currently run in parallel. Key takeaways Orient prerequisite edges consistently. Kahn detects a cycle when it cannot output every vertex. Reverse DFS finish order is valid only after establishing acyclicity. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Topological sorting — Wikipedia

t: Strong components with Kosaraju and Tarjan
sum: Strong connectivity requires reachability in both directions.
x: DFS discovery and finish order were established in earlier units. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. The recursive examples assume their depth fits Python’s configured recursion limit. Strongly connected components In a directed graph, u and v are strongly connected if each can reach the other. A strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of mutually reachable vertices. Edges: 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5, 5→3, 6→5, 6→7, 7→6. SCCs: {0, 1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}, {6, 7}. Collapse each SCC to a single vertex and discard internal edges; you get the condensation, which is always a DAG. That is why SCCs matter: they turn any directed graph into a DAG of "clusters" you can topologically sort. Kosaraju's algorithm DFS the whole graph, recording finish order. Reverse every edge. DFS the reversed graph, taking start vertices in decreasing finish time. Each tree found is one SCC. Why it works: the vertex that finishes last lies in a "source" SCC of the condensation. In the reversed graph that SCC becomes a sink, so a DFS from it cannot leak into other components. Two passes, each O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, and simple to get right. Tarjan's algorithm One DFS pass. Each vertex gets an index idx (discovery order) and a low value: the smallest index reachable from its subtree using tree edges plus at most one edge to a vertex still on the SCC stack. This separate stack can include vertices whose recursive calls have already returned; it is not the grey recursion stack. Vertices are pushed onto a separate stack as discovered. When a vertex finishes with low[u] == idx[u], it is the root of an SCC: pop the stack down to u. In symbols, the code updates low like this: If even that earliest reachable vertex is u itself (the equality tested in the code), nothing in u's subtree escapes to an older open vertex, so u and everything above it on the stack form one SCC. On the example it returns [5, 4, 3], then [2, 1, 0], then [7, 6]. Tarjan emits SCCs in reverse topological order of the condensation: sinks first. Also O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, one pass, no reversed graph, but the on_stack check is easy to get wrong. Uses of SCCs 2-SAT is solved by building an implication graph and checking that no variable sits in the same SCC as its negation. Compilers find mutually recursive functions. Garbage collectors and dependency analysers find reference cycles. Key takeaways Strong connectivity requires reachability in both directions. Condensation contracts mutually reachable groups into a DAG. Tarjan’s SCC stack differs from the recursion stack. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Strongly connected components — cp-algorithms Strongly connected component — Wikipedia Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: Colour every component, not just the one containing the first vertex.
x: BFS visits successive distance layers. Import deque from collections for the following function. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges; adjacency lists include every vertex and both directions of every undirected edge. Bipartite check An undirected graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two sides with every edge crossing between them: students and courses, jobs and machines. Equivalently, it can be 2-coloured so no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. Theorem: a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd-length cycle. A square (4-cycle) is bipartite; a triangle is not. BFS colours by layer parity (whether the layer number is even or odd): For example, a vertex 3 edges from the start gets colour 1. A clash means an edge inside one layer, or between two layers of equal parity, which closes an odd cycle. The check costs O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, and the outer loop handles disconnected graphs. Key takeaways Colour every component, not just the one containing the first vertex. A same-colour edge proves that the undirected graph is not bipartite. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Bipartite graph — Wikipedia

t: Relaxation and a lazy Dijkstra min-heap
sum: Relaxation improves a distance only when an edge yields a cheaper route.
x: BFS finds the path with the fewest edges. Once edges carry weights (kilometres, milliseconds, pounds), the fewest edges is no longer the cheapest. A motorway detour of 3 roads can beat a single slow lane. This lesson covers the single-source problem: the cheapest distance from one source s to every other vertex. Assume finite graphs, finite numeric weights and valid adjacency entries for every vertex. The Python min-heap examples require mutually orderable vertex labels to break distance ties. Arithmetic and expected dictionary access are treated as constant-time. Throughout, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges, w(u, v) the weight of the edge from u to v, and O(…) is Big O notation: how the running time grows with n and m, ignoring constant factors. Every algorithm here is built on one operation. Relaxation Keep a tentative distance dist[v] for every vertex, starting at infinity (0 for the source). The following fragment belongs inside a traversal with distances and parents already initialised. To relax an edge u→v of weight w is to ask "is going via u better than what I have?": In the worked line, v's best so far is 9, u is 3 away and the edge costs 4, so v improves to 7. In Python: Distances only ever decrease, and never drop below the true shortest distance. The algorithms differ only in which edges they relax, and in what order. Dijkstra's algorithm Intuition: grow a region of "settled" vertices outward from s, always settling the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance next. It is BFS where the queue is ordered by distance instead of arrival. Python's heapq has no "decrease key", so we push a new entry and skip outdated ones when they surface (lazy deletion). The min-heap holds O(m + 1) entries and can pop stale entries as well as live ones. Each push or pop costs time proportional to the logarithm of the min-heap size, and in a simple graph the min-heap size cannot outgrow n² by much: For a simple graph with one thousand vertices, a min-heap with up to a million entries has a base-two logarithmic factor of about twenty rather than ten: a constant factor, so the bound is unchanged. Arbitrary multigraphs (with repeated edges) can have m far above n², so the logarithmic factor for this lazy implementation depends on the edge count, with one added to keep the argument positive. Key takeaways Relaxation improves a distance only when an edge yields a cheaper route. Skip stale min-heap entries created by earlier tentative distances. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Dijkstra's algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Dijkstra traces, costs and negative edges
sum: Non-negative weights justify settling the closest unsettled vertex.
x: Earlier Dijkstra code uses heapq and tentative distances, re-pushing an improved vertex and skipping obsolete entries. Here n counts vertices, m counts edges, and edge weights have one common cost unit. The worked trace and correctness proof assume non-negative weights unless explicitly stated otherwise. A worked trace Edges: S→A 4, S→B 1, B→A 2, B→C 5, A→C 1, C→T 3. The table lists nonstale pops; obsolete A(4) and C(6) entries are skipped. Pop dist after relaxing ------ S (0) A 4, B 1 B (1) A 3, C 6 A (3) C 4 C (4) T 7 T (7) done The direct edge S→A (4) loses to S→B→A (3), and C improves twice. Final: S 0, B 1, A 3, C 4, T 7. Why it is correct When u is popped with the smallest tentative distance d, could a cheaper path to u exist? Any such path P must leave the settled region somewhere, through some unsettled vertex x: So d is final. The first inequality is exactly where non-negative weights are needed: a negative edge after x could make P cheaper than dist(x). Complexity Here n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges. An indexed binary min-heap extracts each reachable vertex once and uses decrease-key on improvements. The earlier lazy version can also pop stale entries, with at most one new push per successful edge relaxation. On simple graphs, both give this conventional growth bound: A road graph of a million junctions and four million road segments needs on the order of 10⁸ basic steps; that is a scale estimate, not a measured time. Priority queue Time ------ Binary min-heap O((n + m) log n) Fibonacci min-heap O(m + n log n) Unsorted array O(n²) For dense graphs, the O(n²) array bound avoids the binary min-heap bound’s logarithmic factor. Fibonacci min-heaps improve the asymptotic decrease-key bound. Actual speed depends on implementation, successful relaxations and workload; these bounds do not establish a universal winner. Why negative edges break it The correctness argument assumed that extending a path never makes it cheaper. A negative edge breaks exactly that. Pop A: tentative distances are four to B and five to C. Pop B at distance four and settle it: D becomes six. Pop C at distance five: its negative edge improves B to two. But B is already settled and its edge to D has already been used. Textbook settle-once Dijkstra reports six for D; the true A→C→B→D route costs four. "My lazy version handled it" The lazy-deletion code above does re-push B with distance 2 and fixes D, because it never marks vertices as final. That variant gives correct answers with negative edges (but no negative cycles), but a vertex can be re-processed many times, and the worst case becomes exponential. Use Bellman–Ford instead. You cannot fix negative edges by adding a constant to every weight either: a path with more edges gets penalised more, which changes which path is shortest. Key takeaways Non-negative weights justify settling the closest unsettled vertex. A lazy min-heap can pop stale entries; its simple-graph bound does not imply a measured winner. Constant edge shifts alter paths with different edge counts. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Dijkstra's algorithm — Wikipedia Dijkstra — cp-algorithms Johnson's algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: At most one fewer round than vertices suffices without a reachable negative cycle.
x: The previous unit’s negative-edge graph is A→B 4, A→C 5, C→B −3 and B→D 2. From A, correct distances are A:0, B:2, C:5 and D:4. Here n counts vertices and m counts directed edges; the edge list has numbered endpoints for the implementation below. Bellman–Ford Relax every edge for at most one fewer rounds than there are vertices. Why n − 1 rounds? A shortest path without cycles visits each vertex at most once, so it has at most one edge fewer than there are vertices: Each round extends correct paths by one more edge, so after round 3 on the four-vertex example every distance is final. On the negative-edge example above, Bellman–Ford correctly returns A 0, B 2, C 5, D 4. If an n-th round can still improve something, a negative cycle is reachable from the source. Distances are unbounded below for vertices reachable from that cycle; other vertices can still have finite distances. This implementation returns None for the entire result when it detects one. Bellman–Ford detects this; Dijkstra cannot. Time: up to n − 1 rounds, each relaxing all m edges: When there is at least one edge, this is conventionally written O(nm). The 10¹¹ figure counts edge-relaxation opportunities; it is not an elapsed-time prediction. Real uses: distance-vector routing protocols such as RIP are a distributed Bellman–Ford, each router relaxing the routes its neighbours advertise. Currency arbitrage detection turns exchange rates into weights with a logarithm, which turns multiplying rates into adding weights: For example, rates 0.9, 0.9 and 1.25 multiply to 1.0125, a 1.25% profit, so their weights sum to a negative number and Bellman–Ford flags the cycle. SPFA The "Shortest Path Faster Algorithm" only re-relaxes edges out of vertices whose distance just changed, using a queue. Its performance depends on edge order and graph structure; its worst-case bound remains O(nm) (vertices times edges) when m ≥ 1. Key takeaways At most one fewer round than vertices suffices without a reachable negative cycle. The extra relaxation test detects cycles reachable from the source. In-place relaxation can propagate through several edges in one round. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Bellman–Ford algorithm — Wikipedia

t: 0–1 BFS and choosing a shortest-path method
sum: A zero-weight improvement goes to the front of the deque.
x: Earlier units covered unweighted BFS, Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. INF in the snippet is float("inf"). A in the comparison table is introduced in the next two units; its heuristic is an estimate of remaining cost. 0-1 BFS If every weight is 0 or 1, you do not need a min-heap. Use a deque: push to the front for a 0-edge (same distance) and to the back for a 1-edge (one more). Queued distance labels occupy at most two consecutive values in nondecreasing order; obsolete entries are skipped. Thus, it behaves like Dijkstra's min-heap at O(1) per operation: O(n + m) total, for n vertices and m edges. Typical problems: the fewest walls to break in a maze (stepping into a wall costs 1, open floor 0), or a grid where following the printed arrow is free and changing direction costs 1. Choosing an algorithm In the table, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges, h the A heuristic, and log the logarithm. Graph Use Time --------- Unweighted BFS O(n + m) Weights 0/1 0-1 BFS O(n + m) Non-negative Dijkstra, simple graph O((n + m) log(n + 1)) One target + h A Depends on heuristic, ties and reopening Negative edges Bellman–Ford O(n + nm) DAG, any weights Topo order O(n + m) The last row: in a DAG, relax edges in topological order and each vertex is final when you reach it, even with negative weights. Key takeaways A zero-weight improvement goes to the front of the deque. Match edge-weight assumptions to the algorithm before comparing costs. Further reading Primary reference for this unit 0-1 BFS — cp-algorithms

t: A* priorities and a grid implementation
sum: A* orders by cost already paid plus estimated remaining cost.
x: Dijkstra’s min-heap ordering was covered earlier. This unit uses heapq and INF = float("inf"), as in that implementation. The grid has four-direction movement at unit cost; a # character is a wall. A search Dijkstra settles vertices by distance from the source; obstacles, weights and connectivity shape the explored region. If you want one specific target and can estimate how far you are from it, you can steer the search. A orders the min-heap by a priority that adds a guess of the remaining distance to the distance already travelled: A vertex six steps from the start and estimated four from the goal has priority ten, so it is expanded before one three steps from the start and estimated nine from the goal (priority twelve). On a grid the usual estimate is the Manhattan distance, the number of up/down/left/right steps ignoring walls: Key takeaways A orders by cost already paid plus estimated remaining cost. The grid implementation rejects blocked endpoints and ragged inputs. Manhattan distance fits four-way unit-cost movement. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Introduction to A — Red Blob Games

sum: Admissibility and consistency make different guarantees.
x: A ranks vertices using known cost plus a heuristic estimate; these quantities and edge weights share one cost unit. A heuristic’s guarantee depends on the graph and movement rules, not its name alone. Heuristic quality For finite graphs with non-negative edge costs, a zero heuristic at the reachable goal, and a heuristic expressed in the same cost units, two properties matter: For example, Manhattan distance on a 4-way grid with cost-1 moves is consistent: one move changes it by at most 1, the cost of the move. Admissible: h never overestimates the true remaining cost (the first line). A that reopens a vertex when a better g is found and stops when the goal is popped returns an optimal path. Merely discovering the goal is not a safe stopping condition. Consistent heuristic (monotone): the second line holds for every edge. With a zero heuristic at the goal this implies admissibility, and no settled vertex needs reopening. A zero heuristic gives Dijkstra’s ordering. A perfect-distance heuristic can still expand many vertices lying on different optimal paths; ties matter. Movement Admissible h ------ 4-way grid, cost 1 Manhattan 8-way grid, straight cost 1 and diagonal cost the square root of 2 Octile 8-way grid, all moves cost 1 Chebyshev Geometric edges costing at least their Euclidean length Euclidean Travel time with a valid global speed upper bound Straight-line distance ÷ that speed Trading optimality for speed Weighted A search inflates the heuristic to search more greedily towards the goal. It can reduce expansions, but a speedup is not guaranteed. The price is a bounded loss of optimality, shown below. On a finite graph with non-negative costs, an admissible heuristic that is zero at the goal, reopening on improved known cost, and stopping when the goal is popped, weighted A returns a cost within a known factor of the best: With an inflation factor of 1.5 and a true shortest cost of 100, the path found costs at most 150. Route-planning methods include contraction hierarchies and landmark heuristics (ALT). Content gap Product-specific implementations and millisecond/vertex-count performance claims are omitted: no identified dataset, implementation and reproducible measurement support them here. Key takeaways Admissibility and consistency make different guarantees. Stop on a popped goal, with the stated reopening policy. Weighted A trades an optimality bound for more goal-directed ordering. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Admissible heuristic — Wikipedia A search algorithm — Wikipedia Thayer and Ruml: Faster Than Weighted A

sum: The outer loop unlocks one possible intermediate vertex.
x: Sometimes one source is not enough. A delivery company wants the driving time between every pair of its 300 depots. A network tool wants every router's distance to every other to find the network's graph diameter (the longest shortest path). A game precomputes distances between all waypoints so that AI agents can look them up instantly. That is the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem: fill an n × n table where d[i][j] is the shortest distance from i to j. Just writing the answer down takes a lot of work: For 300 depots that is 90,000 distances. A compressed or query-only representation is a different task. Throughout, m is the number of edges and O(…) is Big O notation: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor. Assume finite weights and constant-time arithmetic in the complexity bounds below. Floyd–Warshall Floyd–Warshall is a short, elegant piece of dynamic programming. The idea Number the vertices 0 to n − 1. The DP table has one layer per number of "unlocked" vertices: The initial layer allows no intermediates: use minimum direct edge weights, also allowing the zero-length diagonal walk (so a negative graph self-loop can make the diagonal negative), and ∞ for absent connections. The final layer allows every vertex: it is the answer. For the finite shortest-distance recurrence, assume no negative cycles. Going from k to k + 1, we unlock vertex k. A shortest path using intermediates from {0..k} either avoids k (cost dₖ[i][j]) or passes through k exactly once (cost dₖ[i][k] + dₖ[k][j]). So: For the worked line, suppose there is an edge 2→0 costing five and an edge 0→1 costing three: before any vertex is unlocked, 2 cannot reach 1, but via vertex 0 it costs 5 + 3 = 8. The code drops the k subscript and updates one table in place. Key takeaways The outer loop unlocks one possible intermediate vertex. Initialise minimum parallel-edge weights and preserve negative self-loops. A negative diagonal reveals a negative cycle. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia Floyd–Warshall — cp-algorithms

t: Implementing Floyd–Warshall in the right order
sum: Keep the intermediate vertex loop outermost.
x: Earlier units defined the distance table by permitted intermediate vertices. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. The recurrence below assumes no negative cycles; affected pairs need the separate interpretation covered next. The worked graph used in this unit’s loop-order question has edges 0→1 3, 0→3 7, 1→0 8, 1→2 2, 2→0 5, 2→3 1 and 3→0 2. A wrong loop order can leave the 1→0 result at seven rather than the true five. The code A single matrix updated in place is safe: during round k, row k and column k do not change, because going through k to reach k adds nothing: So it does not matter whether you read old or new values. Time: O(m + n³), including edge initialisation, for n vertices and m edges; O(n³) for simple graphs. Skipping rows i that have no route to k can reduce actual iterations. Space: O(n²). Negative edges: fine. Negative cycles: afterwards some d[i][i] < 0. k must be the outermost loop The DP is over k. If you write for i: for j: for k:, then d[i][j] is finalised before the entries it depends on are ready. The code still runs and still looks plausible, but gives wrong answers on some graphs. Key takeaways Keep the intermediate vertex loop outermost. The diagonal identifies negative cycles after relaxation. In-place updates preserve the recurrence when shortest distances are finite. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia Floyd–Warshall — cp-algorithms

sum: A next-hop table reconstructs only valid unaffected shortest paths.
x: The previous unit’s floyd_warshall(n, edges) returns distance and next-hop matrices. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Each outer round permits one more intermediate vertex, and row/column indexing uses numbered vertices. A worked example k Key improvements ------ via 0 2→1: eight; 3→1: five; 1→3: fifteen via 1 0→2: five; 3→2: seven via 2 0→3: six; 1→0: seven; 1→3: three via 3 1→0: five; 2→0: three; 2→1: six Final matrix: Notice 1→0 improves twice: 8 directly, then 7 via 2, then 5 via 2 and 3 (1→2→3→0). Reconstructing paths Only reconstruct a pair after confirming no negative cycle lies on a route between its endpoints; affected pairs have no shortest path. For valid unaffected pairs, nxt stores the first hop. The guard below catches a cyclic or malformed table, but is not itself a complete negative-cycle test: This is a simplified shortest-path next-hop table. Real forwarding tables can aggregate destinations into network prefixes, use policy and offer multiple next hops. Why people like it Floyd–Warshall is four lines of logic, handles negative weights, has no min-heap, and array-based implementations can exploit contiguous rows and vectorised inner loops. The Python list implementation here does not itself guarantee those optimisations. For n up to a few hundred it is often the simplest correct choice. The three nested loops make the cost easy to count: Content gap CPython, C and NumPy runtime estimates are omitted because the project has no reproducible benchmark with specified hardware, data and implementation. Pitfalls Wrong loop order in Floyd–Warshall: k must be outermost. INF + INF overflow in C, Java or Go when INF is INT_MAX. Skip addition if either operand is the infinity sentinel, and establish bounds that keep every finite sum representable. A large infinity sentinel alone does not prevent overflow or spurious finite paths from adding a negative value to infinity. Memory. The table grows with the square of the vertex count: Negative cycles make some distances undefined (−∞). Check the diagonal and propagate: any pair whose path can touch a negative cycle is −∞. Key takeaways A next-hop table reconstructs only valid unaffected shortest paths. An explicit all-pairs table has quadratic storage. Infinity sentinel addition and negative cycles need handling beyond the basic recurrence. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Floyd–Warshall — cp-algorithms Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: Boolean closure tracks reachability rather than route cost.
x: Earlier Floyd–Warshall units established the intermediate-vertex recurrence. Here n counts vertices, m counts edges, and vertices are numbered from zero. The example graph has 2→0 of weight 5 and 0→1 of weight 3, so 2 can reach 1 through 0. Transitive closure Sometimes you only care whether j is reachable from i. Replace min/+ with OR/AND (Warshall's algorithm): In the example graph, 2 has no edge to 1, but 2 reaches 0 and 0 reaches 1, so unlocking vertex zero marks that pair reachable. Pack each row into a bitset, and a whole row updates in one operation: "if i reaches k, then i reaches everything k reaches". Python's arbitrary-size integers make this easy: This computes reflexive transitive closure: every vertex reaches itself via a zero-length walk. A row of n bits is stored in machine words of w bits each, so OR-ing two rows costs one operation per word: A row OR is therefore not constant time, but 157 word operations is far fewer than 10,000 single-bit ones. Python integers use implementation-specific internal digits (sys.int_info.bits_per_digit), not necessarily 64-bit payloads. Uses: "can this permission/role reach that resource?", "does module A transitively depend on B?", and query optimisers deriving implied joins. For sparse graphs, a BFS from every vertex costs O(n(n + m)), n traversals of O(n + m) each, which beats n³ when m is small.
