Two open subintervals can then be solved independently. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

sum: Matching ends enclose a smaller palindrome.
x: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. First require a unbroken range; the next unit will allow gaps between retained characters. Counting palindromic substrings P[i][j] records True if s[i..j] (characters i to j inclusive) is a palindrome, a string that reads the same backwards. It is exactly when the ends match and the inside is a palindrome (or there is no inside): "aaa" has 6 (three as, two aas, one aaa); "abc" has 3; "racecar" has 10. For a string of n characters this is O(n²) time and space. Note the loop order: i descending, j ascending, because P[i][j] reads P[i+1][j-1] (next row down). Looping by length works too. Expand around centre gets the same O(n²) time in O(1) space: a nonempty string has one centre per character and one per gap: For each one, grow outwards while the ends match. Manacher's algorithm computes a compact array of palindrome radii in O(n), reusing mirror information. That suffices to find a longest palindrome or count occurrences; explicitly listing all occurrences can require Θ(n²) output. Key takeaways Matching ends enclose a smaller palindrome. Single characters and matching pairs are base cases. Compact palindrome radii can be linear-sized even when occurrences are quadratic. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Longest palindromic substring

sum: Matching ends contribute two characters around the inner answer.
x: A palindromic subsequence may skip input characters. Keep an interval state, but compare dropping either end when they cannot both join the palindrome. Longest palindromic subsequence The characters need not be next to each other, so it's a classic interval DP: An empty range, whose left endpoint is past its right endpoint, counts as zero. For "bbbab" the answer is 4 ("bbbb"). Its length equals the LCS length of s and its reverse; an arbitrary reconstructed LCS need not itself be palindromic. For "acbac" and its reverse "cabca", the maximum common-subsequence length is three. Both "aba" and "abc" are longest common subsequences, but only the first is a palindrome. The equality of optimal lengths does not make every reconstructed sequence valid. Key takeaways Matching ends contribute two characters around the inner answer. A mismatch drops one end and keeps the better subproblem. Empty ranges and single positions need distinct base cases. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Longest palindromic substring

t: Choose non-adjacent nodes on a tree
sum: Include and exclude states separate the effect of choosing the parent.
x: DP on trees Once boundary information such as the parent’s selected status is represented in the state, the relevant child subtrees can be combined independently. That makes the tree itself the DP order: compute every child before its parent (a post-order traversal). Maximum independent set on a tree Choose as many nodes as possible so that no two chosen nodes are adjacent. (Or, weighted: maximise total weight. This is "house robber on a tree".) On general graphs this is NP-hard. On a tree with n nodes it's O(n). State: two values per node v: inc[v] records best in v's subtree if v is chosen. exc[v] records best in v's subtree if v is not chosen. Recurrence: If v is chosen, none of its children may be. If v isn't chosen, each child is free to be chosen or not. Bottom-up on the tree above: Answer 4: nodes {0, 3, 4, 5}. For the stated valid simple undirected tree (symmetric adjacency lists, integer vertices 0..n−1), each node is visited once and each edge twice: O(n) work. The routine assumes this tree structure; cycles or disconnected inputs require validation or a different traversal. Recursion depth on trees A tree can be a path of 100,000 nodes. A cold recursive Python DFS can exceed its configured call-depth limit; CPython usually starts with a limit of 1,000, but the actual threshold depends on existing call depth and implementation. For large inputs, compute an order with an explicit stack (or BFS), then process nodes in reverse order so children come before parents. Key takeaways Include and exclude states separate the effect of choosing the parent. Compute children before combining their answers. Use an explicit traversal order when recursion would be too deep. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

t: Tree covers, rerooting and interval applications
sum: Excluding a vertex forces every child into a vertex cover.
x: Other tree DPs with the same shape Tree diameter: for each node, the two longest downward paths through different children. Minimum vertex cover (the fewest nodes such that every edge touches at least one of them): the same two states, with min instead of max. Rerooting: for suitable constant-sized states and O(1)-per-edge combination/exclusion (often using prefix/suffix aggregates), a second top-down pass can compute every root’s answer in O(n). More expensive transitions change the bound. In the real world Parsing: CYK uses an interval DP for a grammar in Chomsky normal form, in O(n³ · G) time for a nonempty string of n words, where G is the size (number of rules) of the grammar; handle an allowed empty string separately. RNA secondary structure prediction in noncrossing base-pair models (such as Nussinov and Zuker formulations) uses interval DP; unrestricted pseudoknots need other treatment. Optimal binary search trees (given access frequencies) are interval DP; Knuth's observation that the optimal root index is monotone cuts it from O(n³) to O(n²) for n keys. Compilers use tree DP for instruction selection: tiling an expression tree with machine instructions at minimum cost. Key takeaways Excluding a vertex forces every child into a vertex cover. Rerooting is linear only with suitably cheap state combination. Parsing, RNA models, search trees and instruction selection use related DPs. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

t: Represent a small set with bits
sum: Each bit records whether one item is present.
x: Every DP so far has had states indexed by positions, lengths or weight limits. The following units cover three less obvious state spaces, then tie everything together with one idea: a finite, acyclic DP can be evaluated over a DAG of states. The module ends with a practical checklist for spotting DP in an interview. Bitmask DP When the state needs to know which items from a small set have been used, encode that set as the bits of an integer (a bitmask): bit j is 1 if item j is in the set. Each item is either in or out, so: With n items there are 2ⁿ subsets, so practical limits depend on the number of dimensions, transitions, representation and available resources; the following table shows growth, not a hardware guarantee. Items Subsets Endpoint slots Work proxy ------------ 10 1,024 ~10⁴ ~10⁵ 16 65,536 ~10⁶ ~1.7 × 10⁷ 20 ~10⁶ ~2 × 10⁷ ~4 × 10⁸ 25 ~3.4 × 10⁷ ~8 × 10⁸ ~2 × 10¹⁰ For example, start with cities zero, one and three included. Setting the bit for city two adds it; testing that bit before adding it reports absence. The following expression fragment assumes mask holds decimal 11, j is 2 and n is 5. It shows operations rather than printing their results. The bit operations you need: Key takeaways Each bit records whether one item is present. The number of subsets doubles with every extra item. State and transition dimensions determine feasibility. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

t: A visited-set state for travelling salesman
sum: Visited cities and current city determine the remaining tour choices.
x: Held–Karp: the travelling salesman Given distances between n cities, find the shortest tour that starts at city 0, visits every city exactly once, and returns. Brute force fixes city 0 as the start and tries every order of the rest: That is 120 quadrillion tours for just 20 cities. Hopeless. The key observation: once you've visited a set of cities and are standing at city j, the order you visited them in no longer matters for the rest of the tour. Only the set and the current city do. That's the state. State: dp[mask][j] records length of the shortest path that starts at 0, visits exactly the cities in mask, and ends at j. Recurrence: extend a path by one unvisited city k. Written "pulling" from the state before k was added: Base: dp[1][0] = 0 (only city 0 visited, standing at 0). The code below "pushes" forwards instead: from each finished state it tries every unvisited k and keeps the minimum, which computes the same values. Why does increasing mask order work? Adding a city sets a bit, so the new mask is numerically larger. Every state is final before anything reads it. For the four-city distance matrix it returns 80 (0 → 1 → 3 → 2 → 0: 10 + 25 + 30 + 15). Key takeaways Visited cities and current city determine the remaining tour choices. Adding a bit moves to a larger numeric mask. Close the full-set path by returning to city zero. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: Held–Karp reduces factorial enumeration to exponential DP.
x: The visited-set recurrence is exact for the stated cost matrix. Its resource requirements depend on the table representation and on which states are reachable. Let n be the number of cities. The allocated table has one slot per subset and endpoint, and each reachable state tries up to n next cities: So O(n² · 2ⁿ) time, O(n · 2ⁿ) space. Compare 4.2 × 10⁸ with the 1.2 × 10¹⁷ brute-force tours: about 300 million times fewer. It is a work-bound proxy, not this implementation’s exact transition count: many allocated states are unreachable. Content gap C++/Python running-time predictions and a universal city-count cutoff are omitted because no pinned implementation, machine and benchmark support them. Held–Karp remains exponential, but its bound is much smaller than factorial enumeration. NP-hardness does not prove that every exact TSP algorithm must take exponential time; even a proof that polynomial-time solving differs from polynomial-time verification would rule out polynomial time, not every subexponential possibility. Concorde uses branch-and-cut techniques and has solved particular large benchmark instances, which is not a worst-case guarantee. Content gap A claim that this is the current best exact worst-case TSP bound is omitted: that research frontier requires a separately scoped, up-to-date comparison of weight models and algorithm variants. Key takeaways Held–Karp reduces factorial enumeration to exponential DP. Allocated table states and executed transitions are different counts. Memory layout and available resources matter as much as the growth bound. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: A job mask can describe which assignments remain.
x: Bitmasks also represent assigned jobs or the occupied boundary of a grid. The mask must retain every fact needed by later choices, not merely count how much work is done. Other bitmask DPs Assignment problem: n workers, n jobs, cost matrix. dp[mask] records minimum cost to assign the first popcount(mask) workers (popcount is the number of 1 bits in the mask) to the jobs in mask. O(n · 2ⁿ). (The Hungarian algorithm does it in O(n³), but the bitmask DP generalises to constraints Hungarian can't handle.) Set cover / partition into groups: iterate submasks with sub = (sub - 1) & mask, stopping explicitly after zero (otherwise it wraps back to mask). Including the empty submask, the number of pairs is: By comparison, independently choosing two arbitrary masks gives: Transitions may still add work per pair. Profile DP (broken-profile, e.g. tiling a grid with dominoes): the mask records which cells of the current column boundary are already filled. When assignments interact The plain job mask is sufficient only when assignment costs depend on the current engineer and chosen project. If adjacent engineers’ project choices interact, also retain the previous engineer’s project. The engineer index is the mask’s set-bit count; the last-project flag supplies the missing boundary information. With n projects this gives O(n × 2ⁿ) allocated states and up to n next choices each, hence O(n² × 2ⁿ) transition work. A mask alone would incorrectly merge histories with different neighbouring costs. Key takeaways A job mask can describe which assignments remain. Extra interaction constraints may require additional boundary state. Stop a submask loop after zero to avoid wrapping around. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Count digit properties below a bound
sum: The tight flag records whether the prefix still matches the bound.
x: Digit DP How many integers in [0, N] have digits summing to k? (Or contain no "4", or have no two equal adjacent digits,...) N can be up to 10¹⁸. Enumerating every integer up to a bound of 10¹⁸ is impractical. Instead, build the number digit by digit from the left and count how many completions satisfy the property. State: (pos, acc, tight) pos: which digit we're placing. acc: whatever the property needs to remember (here, the digit sum so far). tight: whether every digit so far has equalled N's digit. If so, the next digit can be at most N's digit at this position; otherwise any digit 0–9 is allowed. count_digit_sum(100, 5) is 6 (5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50). count_digit_sum(2024, 10) is 120. Complexity: count the states: Many of those states are unreachable, and exceeding the target digit sum prunes more. Exact counts may require growing integers. Content gap The original microsecond running-time prediction is omitted because no reproducible benchmark supports it. Two standard moves: Ranges: count in [L, R] using the counts up to each end: Leading zeros: if the property cares about them (e.g. "no two adjacent equal digits", where 007 shouldn't count as having adjacent zeros), add a started flag to the state. The intuition Once you've placed a digit smaller than N's digit, you're "free": every remaining combination is below N. That's why the tight=False states are shared between many prefixes and get cached. tight=True is a single path that hugs N. Key takeaways The tight flag records whether the prefix still matches the bound. Cache repeated free suffix states instead of enumerating every integer. Subtract prefix counts for ranges and track leading-zero state when needed. Further reading Digit DP Python caching

t: Evaluate path recurrences on a DAG
sum: A topological order finalises every predecessor before its outgoing edges.
x: DP over DAGs: the unifying view Draw each state as a node and each "depends on" relation as an edge. For the finite recurrences here, dependencies are acyclic, so this graph is a DAG. More general cyclic Bellman equations may instead require iterative methods. Then: Bottom-up evaluation is processing nodes in topological order. Memoisation is DFS on that DAG with caching. Some optimisation DPs, such as sequence alignment, are shortest/longest path problems in that DAG. Some counting DPs count paths in the DAG. Others combine independent child choices by multiplication, so the dependency graph alone is not a path-counting recurrence. Edit distance, for example, is the shortest path through a grid DAG from the pair of empty prefixes to the pair of complete strings, with edges of weight 0 or 1. Knapsack is a longest path through a DAG of (item, weight limit) nodes. When the problem itself is a DAG, apply this directly: The inner line is the relaxation step: Given consecutively numbered vertices starting at zero, valid edges with integer weights and a complete topological order, this computes the best path starting anywhere, allowing a zero-edge path of value 0. For single-source shortest paths, initialise only the source to 0 and all other distances to +∞, use min-relaxation, and return the distance array rather than its maximum. Negative edge weights are valid in a DAG. Real uses: critical path method in project scheduling (longest path through task dependencies), scheduling lower bounds with unlimited parallel resources, and the Viterbi algorithm (most likely path through a layered DAG of hidden states over time). For shortest paths with nonnegative weights, the correctness proof of Dijkstra's algorithm gives a safe order for finalising distances even on cyclic graphs. This is not a topological order of all graph edges. Key takeaways A topological order finalises every predecessor before its outgoing edges. DAG longest and shortest paths support negative edges. Acyclic DP dependencies and safe shortest-path settling orders are different ideas. Further reading Topological sorting Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Choose a DP state from the problem
sum: Constraints suggest candidate state spaces, then you must estimate their work.
x: Recognising DP in an interview Wording signals "Count the number of ways..." → counting DP (often reported modulo 10⁹ + 7, the remainder after dividing by the prime 1,000,000,007, to keep numbers small). "Minimum cost / maximum value / longest / shortest..." with choices at each step → optimisation DP. "Is it possible to..." over subsets or partitions → feasibility DP. Greedy feels natural but you can construct a counterexample → DP. Constraint signals The input limits often tell you the intended complexity. Here n is the input size (number of items, string length and so on), N is a numeric bound on a value, and the O(...) entries are Big-O growth rates: Constraint Likely approach ------ Up to 20 items Bitmask, O(2ⁿ · n) Up to 500 items Interval, O(n³) Up to 5,000 items 2-D, O(n²) Up to 100,000 items 1-D, O(n log n) Values up to 10,000 Knapsack on values Decimal bound up to 10¹⁸ Digit DP These are prompts to estimate work and storage, not running-time guarantees. Transition costs, memory layout, hardware and language can change feasibility substantially. A process that works Brute force first: write the recursive "try every choice" solution. It defines the recurrence. Identify the state: which arguments does the recursion actually depend on? Small integer parameters suggest a manageable table, but you must still prove that they determine a subproblem and that dependencies and transitions are valid. Check for overlap: can two different paths of choices reach the same arguments? If yes, memoise. Count: states × transitions. Compare with the constraints. Convert to bottom-up only if you need the speed, the space optimisation, or to avoid recursion limits. When it's not DP The best choice is provably always the same local choice → greedy (interval scheduling by earliest finish, Huffman coding). The subproblems don't overlap → memoisation saves no repeated calls. Plain recursion or divide and conquer may suffice; tree DP can still combine disjoint subtrees. The state would have to include an unbounded history → look for a different formulation, or the problem may be NP-hard with no good DP (general longest path, general TSP for large n). Key takeaways Constraints suggest candidate state spaces, then you must estimate their work. Start with brute force, identify sufficient state, and check overlap. Greedy needs a proof; caching cannot rescue an enormous history state. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

t: Clarify the problem and work an example
sum: Clarify input domains, permitted mutations and the required return value before choosing an algorithm.
x: A routine can help you clarify the requested behavior, develop a correct approach, explain your reasoning and test boundary cases. Treat the following as practical advice, not a guarantee of interview success; interview formats and scoring vary. Content gap Population-wide claims about why most candidates fail are omitted because no reliable survey or causal evidence is provided. This module is a catalogue of patterns. These first units cover the routine you run before picking one. The five steps One possible allocation for a 45-minute practice session is: 5 minutes clarifying and on examples, 5–10 on the approach, 15–20 coding, 5–10 testing. Adjust this to the task and interviewer; a short or familiar problem may need less planning. Step 1: clarify Restate the problem in your own words, then ask about anything that would change the algorithm. Input size. "How large can n be?" Here, and throughout this module, n means the number of elements in the input (the length of the array or string) unless a problem says otherwise. Use the answer to compare growth against the resource budget (see the following input-growth unit). Value ranges. Negative numbers? Zeros? Can values cause integer overflow in 32 bits? Sortedness and duplicates. Is the array sorted? Can values repeat? Output shape. Indices or values? One answer or all? What if there is no answer: return -1, None, raise? Mutability. May I modify the input in place? Ties. If several answers are valid, does it matter which? Questions are signals "Is the array sorted?" is not small talk. A yes points straight at binary search or two pointers. "Can values be negative?" matters for monotone sum-window rules (the sliding-window units), though fixed-size windows and other window predicates can still handle negatives. Step 2: examples Write one ordinary example and work it by hand. Then list the edge cases you'll test at the end: empty input, a single element all values equal, all distinct already sorted, reverse sorted negatives, zeros, the largest allowed values the answer at the very start or very end Working an example by hand often reveals the algorithm. Watch what you do: if you keep scanning back over the same elements, that repeated scan is the thing to optimise. Key takeaways Clarify input domains, permitted mutations and the required return value before choosing an algorithm. Work a normal case by hand and record boundary cases for later tests. The five-step routine is practical advice; interview timing and scoring vary. t: From brute force to a lookup
sum: A brute-force solution supplies a correctness baseline and exposes repeated work.
x: The input has n elements. This unit turns a scan of all pairs into a lookup of earlier values, preserving original indices. Step 3: brute force State the obvious solution and its complexity out loud, even if it is slow. It proves you understand the problem, gives you a fallback, and is often the starting point for the optimisation. Classic example, two sum: given an unsorted array and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. The two loops look at every pair of positions once. The number of pairs tells you the cost: That is O(n²) time and O(1) extra space: the work grows with the square of n, while the memory used beyond the input stays fixed. You don't always need to code the brute force; saying it and its cost is usually enough. Step 4: optimise Look for wasted work. Three useful questions are: What is the bottleneck? In two sum, the inner loop: for each a[i], we search the rest of the array for target - a[i], the one value that would complete the pair: That single partner is what makes a lookup structure useful in the next question. Is there a data structure that answers that inner question faster? "Have I seen value v?" is a hash-set lookup: O(1) on average. Am I recomputing something? Running totals, window contents and "best so far" values can usually be carried forward instead of recomputed. Now it is expected O(n) time under constant-cost, well-distributed hashing and O(n) space. Numeric examples assume exact arithmetic; large Python integers add bit-length costs. We traded memory for time, which is the most common trade in this whole module. Why check before inserting? If x is exactly half the target (say target 6 and a current value of 3), inserting first would let x pair with itself. Checking first means a value can only pair with an earlier element. Reuse the lookup idea for duplicates To detect any duplicate, keep a hash set of values already scanned. Check membership before adding each value. A repeated value answers yes; exhausting the input answers no. Under expected constant-cost hashing, one pass takes expected O(n) time and up to O(n) set entries, where n is the input length. Sorting then comparing neighbouring values is another option with an O(n log n) comparison bound. It changes the data order, and Python’s in-place list sort can still need O(n) temporary references. Neither bound alone predicts the faster implementation for a particular input. If the optimal approach is unclear, stating a correct brute-force baseline exposes the bottleneck and gives a concrete direction to discuss. The routine does not require discovering the optimum before explaining any solution. Key takeaways A brute-force solution supplies a correctness baseline and exposes repeated work. Check the complement before inserting the current value so two sum uses distinct positions. Hash-based acceleration trades memory for expected speed under stated hashing and numeric-cost assumptions. Further reading Coding interview techniques — Tech Interview Handbook Coding interview cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook How to Solve It (Pólya) — Wikipedia Time complexity — Wikipedia

sum: Compare candidate growth expressions at the largest permitted input.
x: Input limits tell you which growth expressions deserve investigation. Here n is the number of input elements; constants, memory and the deadline still matter. Let the constraints choose the complexity Interview and contest problems specify limits on input size. For example, an array may contain between one and one hundred thousand elements: That is a heavy hint. Input size helps compare growth, but whether an approach is fast enough also depends on the algorithm’s constants, operation types, numeric sizes, memory, hardware and deadline. Content gap Generic C++/Python operations-per-second figures and universal pass/fail thresholds are omitted because no pinned benchmark or judge configuration establishes them. The table uses a few growth expressions you may not have met. Each one describes how the work grows with n: For zero items there is one empty ordering and one empty subset. The factorial product displayed above uses the usual continuation pattern for at least two items; its zero-input value is defined as one. The table also uses Big-O notation: O(f(n)) supplies an asymptotic upper bound, up to a constant factor, for a nonnegative cost function f(n). It need not be tight or count exact operations. A base-2 logarithm measures the exponent needed to produce its argument; for 100,000 it is about 16.6. The whole number of successive halvings needed to reach one or less is 17. The table lists growth expressions to investigate for illustrative input sizes, not guaranteed feasible limits. Example n Growth to investigate Candidate technique --------- ≤ 10 O(n!) Permutations ≤ 20 O(2ⁿ) Subsets, bitmasks ≤ 500 O(n³) Triple loop, DP ≤ 5,000 O(n²) Pairs, 2-D DP ≤ 10⁶ O(n log n) Sort, heap > 10⁶ O(n), O(log n) One pass, math Plugging the largest allowed n into two of these expressions shows the gap: These are work expressions, not exact operation counts inferred from big-O. Compare them with the actual resource budget before choosing. Key takeaways Compare candidate growth expressions at the largest permitted input. Factorial counts orderings; powers of two count subsets. Big-O expressions are not exact instruction counts or promises about runtime. t: Use problem cues to form a hypothesis
sum: A problem cue suggests a technique; its preconditions decide whether the technique is valid.
x: Before selecting a template, identify the input shape, the requested output and what information must be maintained. This short catalogue previews the concrete patterns that follow. Spotting the pattern Once you understand the problem, match its shape against the patterns in this module. Cue in the problem Try ------ Sorted array, pair/triple Two pointers Contiguous subarray/substring Sliding window Many range-sum queries Prefix sums Sum equals k, negatives allowed Prefix sum + hash map Next greater/smaller Monotonic stack Max of every window Monotonic deque Overlapping ranges, schedules Sort intervals k largest / k-th / stream Heap Merge k sorted inputs Heap (k-way) "Appears once", at most 20 items Bits, masks "Have I seen this?" Hash map/set Other modules cover the rest of the toolkit: binary search, BFS/DFS, backtracking and dynamic programming. Patterns are hypotheses A cue suggests a pattern; it doesn't prove it fits. "Longest subarray with sum at most k", where k is a limit the problem gives you, looks like a sliding window, but if values can be negative the window logic breaks. Check the pattern's preconditions before you commit. Key takeaways A problem cue suggests a technique; its preconditions decide whether the technique is valid. Signed sum problems often call for prefix values and an appropriate lookup structure. Other modules cover graph search, backtracking, binary search and dynamic programming. t: Test the code and audit hidden costs
sum: Trace representative and boundary inputs, then state an invariant or correctness argument.
x: Testing complements a correctness argument. Here n is the number of input elements; the earlier two-sum implementation checks a hash map before inserting the current element. Step 5: test Don't announce "done" and wait. Test like an engineer: Trace your normal example through the code line by line, tracking variables. This can reveal off-by-one errors; examples supplement an invariant or correctness argument rather than proving correctness for all inputs. Run the edge cases from step 2: empty input, one element, duplicates. Check the complexity you claimed against the code you wrote. A hidden in list check or slice inside a loop can turn O(n) into O(n²). For two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6): Note that 3 + 3 = 6 was correctly not returned, because there is only one 3. Talking through it Make your reasoning available for discussion. Useful ways to narrate include: Before coding: "Brute force is O(n²) by checking every pair. The inner loop is a lookup, so a hash map should get us to O(n) with O(n) space. Shall I go with that?" Getting a nod before coding avoids building the wrong thing. While coding: say what each block is for, not every keystroke. Use clear names (seen, lo, hi), not a1, tmp2. When stuck: say what you're trying. "Sorting would help, but we need original indices... we could sort pairs of (value, index)." Explaining the sticking point gives the interviewer something concrete to respond to. When you spot a bug: say so and fix it. Finding and explaining a bug makes the correction available for discussion. Hints are not failure. Take them, acknowledge them and build on them. Common pitfalls Solving the wrong problem. Returning values when indices were asked for; assuming sorted input when it wasn't. Premature optimisation. Spending 20 minutes hunting an O(n) trick and running out of time with nothing written. A correct O(n log n) beats an unfinished O(n). Skipping the complexity. Always state time and space, and justify them. Ignoring Python costs. x in some_list is O(n); s[1:] copies; list.pop(0) is O(n). Use sets, indices and collections.deque. Recap of the pattern family Run the same routine every time: clarify, examples, brute force, optimise, test. Ask about input size, value ranges, sortedness and duplicates; each changes the algorithm. Use constraints to compare growth and resource needs; an input of about 100,000 elements makes a quadratic scan a significant concern, not a universal impossibility. Optimise by finding the bottleneck, then asking which data structure answers it faster. Narrate your reasoning, get agreement before coding, and test by tracing, not by hoping. Key takeaways Trace representative and boundary inputs, then state an invariant or correctness argument. Python list membership, front removal and slices can add hidden linear work. Explain time and space costs alongside your reasoning. t: Discard impossible pairs in sorted input
sum: Sortedness proves which endpoint cannot participate in a remaining answer.
x: Many brute-force solutions look at every pair of positions (i, j) in an array of n elements: roughly half the square of the input length in pairs, which is O(n²) work (the work grows with the square of n). The two-pointer pattern keeps two indices and moves each one only forwards (or only backwards), so each pointer makes O(n) moves and together they make O(n) moves. Two same-direction pointers can together make nearly twice as many moves as there are elements. Costs below assume constant-time numeric operations and indexing. It works when there is a rule that tells you, after looking at the current pair, which pointer can safely move: that some whole set of pairs can be discarded without checking them. Usually that rule comes from the input being a sorted sequence, or from an invariant you maintain about the region each pointer has passed. There are three common flavours: Opposite ends: pair sum in a sorted array Problem. Given a sorted array and a target, find two elements that add up to the target. Start with the smallest and largest elements. Compare their sum with the target: Too small? Among the two allowed inward moves, moving lo right can increase the sum. a[lo] paired with any other remaining element gives a sum no larger, so a[lo] can't be in any answer: discard it. Too big? Symmetrically, a[hi] paired with any other remaining element is too big: move hi left. Trace with a = [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], target 10: Each step discards one element for good, so at most one fewer step than the array length: O(n) time, O(1) space. Compare the hash-map version of two sum (the earlier approach units), which is expected O(n) under constant-time, well-distributed hashing but needs O(n) extra memory and works on unsorted input. Three sum "Find all triples summing to 0" is: sort (O(n log n)), then for each i, run pair sum on the part after i with target -a[i]. That's O(n²) total for this algorithm, excluding integer bit costs. Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triples. Other safe opposite-end moves A palindrome scan compares the two outer values. If they differ, the sequence is not a palindrome; if they match, discard both and check the inner range. Each inward move is justified by an equality already checked. A merge of two sorted sequences instead keeps one forward index per input and takes the smaller current value. For the existing count_less question, if the two endpoint values sum below the target, the left endpoint pairs successfully with every remaining position up to the right endpoint. Count that whole block, then discard the left endpoint. Otherwise discard the right endpoint. This rule depends on sortedness just as pair-sum search does. Key takeaways Sortedness proves which endpoint cannot participate in a remaining answer. Use distinct positions: stop when the pointers meet. Sorting then fixing one element reduces three sum to repeated pair scans. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

sum: A container is limited by its shorter endpoint and the distance between endpoints.
x: Here n is the number of nonnegative heights. The input need not be sorted: the move rule follows from a bound on all pairs involving one endpoint. Opposite ends: container with most water Problem. h[i] is a nonnegative height of a vertical line at position i. Choose two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water. The water a pair of lines can hold is limited by the shorter line: The formula assumes the lines are thin and the water's surface is flat, so only the shorter line matters; it holds for any nonnegative heights. The array isn't sorted, so why do two pointers work? Start with the widest container (lo = 0, hi = n - 1). Suppose h[lo] < h[hi]. Any other container using lo with a partner inside the range: is narrower (the partner is closer), and has height at most h[lo] (the shorter line caps it). So it can never beat the current one. Every pair involving lo is discarded in one move: advance lo. Move the shorter line; if heights tie, either endpoint can be discarded. For fewer than two lines, the code returns 0. For [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7] the answer is 49, from the lines at positions 1 and 8: The proof is the pattern Two pointers are only correct when you can argue that the move discards nothing useful. If you can't say why a move is safe, you don't yet have a two-pointer solution; you have a guess. Key takeaways A container is limited by its shorter endpoint and the distance between endpoints. Discarding the shorter endpoint cannot remove an improvement inside the current range. Equal heights allow either endpoint to move; fewer than two lines give zero area. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Filter a sorted array with read and write indices
sum: The kept prefix contains the distinct values seen so far; the list itself is not resized.
x: Here n is the sorted array length. A read index scans the input and a write index marks the next kept position; constant extra space requires avoiding temporary slices. Same direction: remove duplicates in place Problem. Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in place so each value appears once, and return the length of the distinct prefix. The list is not resized; ignore the tail after that prefix. Extra space must be O(1). Use a read pointer r that scans every element and a write pointer w marking where the next kept element goes. The invariant: a[0:w] holds the distinct values seen so far, in order. The same read/write shape solves "move all zeros to the end", "remove all copies of value v" and "keep at most two of each value" (keep an item when w < 2 or it differs from a[w - 2]). Another same-direction variant is fast and slow pointers on a linked list: the slow pointer moves one step, the fast one two. Check equality after advancing: they eventually meet if there's a cycle (Floyd's algorithm). On an acyclic list, stop when fast cannot take another two-step advance; the chosen loop convention determines which middle node is returned for an even-length list. Key takeaways The kept prefix contains the distinct values seen so far; the list itself is not resized. Keep at most two copies by comparing with the value two kept positions back. Fast and slow linked-list pointers use a related movement pattern with a different invariant. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Partition the unknown region into three categories
sum: Dutch flag keeps known zero, one and two regions around an unknown region.
x: Here n is the input length. For the Dutch flag example every element must be 0, 1 or 2; the code sorts in place in one scan. Partitioning: the Dutch national flag Problem. An array contains only 0s, 1s and 2s. Sort it in one pass, in place. (Dijkstra posed it with the red, white and blue of the Dutch flag.) Keep three pointers and four regions: Look at a[mid], the first unknown element: 0: swap it into the 0s region (a[lo]), advance lo and mid. 1: already in place; advance mid. 2: swap it with a[hi], shrink hi. Don't advance mid: the element that just arrived from hi hasn't been examined yet. Why is it safe to advance mid after swapping with lo? If lo < mid, the swapped-in value comes from the known 1s region. If lo == mid, the swap is with itself and the current value has just been identified as 0. In either case advancing is safe. Each step either advances mid or shrinks hi, so the unknown region shrinks every iteration: O(n) time, O(1) space. Three-way partitioning is also how quicksort copes with many duplicate keys. Recognising the pattern Cue Flavour ------ Sorted array, find pair/triple Opposite ends Palindrome check Opposite ends Pick two ends to maximise Opposite ends In place, O(1) space, filter Read/write Linked list middle or cycle Fast/slow Gather by category in place Partition Merge two sorted arrays One pointer each Pitfalls Unsorted input. Pair sum's move rule depends on sortedness. If the input isn't sorted, either sort it (O(n log n), and you lose original indices unless you sort (value, index) pairs) or use a hash map. lo < hi vs lo <= hi. Pair problems need two distinct elements, so stop when they meet. Dutch flag uses mid <= hi because the element at hi is still unknown. Advancing after a swap from the right. In partitioning, the element swapped in from the right is unexamined; advancing past it is the classic bug. Duplicates in three sum. Without skipping equal values you'll report the same triple many times. Recap of the pattern family Two pointers replace an O(n²) scan of pairs with O(n) by proving each move discards only useless pairs. Opposite ends suits sorted arrays and "choose two ends" problems: move the pointer that can't be part of a better answer. Same direction (read/write, fast/slow) does in-place filtering and linked-list tricks in O(1) space. Partitioning keeps regions with invariants; the Dutch flag sorts three values in one pass. Always be able to state the invariant or the reason a move is safe. Key takeaways Dutch flag keeps known zero, one and two regions around an unknown region. A value swapped from the right is unexamined, so do not advance the middle index. State the invariant behind a pointer move rather than applying a template blindly. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Dijkstra on the Dutch National Flag

t: Maintain the sum of a fixed-size window
sum: A fixed window updates its sum by adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving value.
x: A sliding window is two pointers that bound a contiguous range a[lo..hi]. Instead of recomputing something about every subarray from scratch (an array of n elements has O(n²) subarrays, often with O(n) work each), you update the window's summary as the edges move: add the element entering on the right, remove the one leaving on the left. It is a candidate when a problem says subarray or substring (consecutive) and asks for the longest, shortest, maximum or count of windows satisfying some condition. The code uses random-access sequences. Arithmetic, equality and hashing costs are treated as constant; dictionary bounds are expected/amortised, not adversarial worst-case guarantees. Python string elements are Unicode code points, which need not be complete displayed characters. Fixed-size windows Problem. Find the maximum sum of any k consecutive elements. Brute force sums each window from scratch: about n windows of k elements each, so O(n × k) work, where n is the array length. But consecutive windows share all but one of their elements. Slide by adding the new element and subtracting the one that fell off: The worked line uses the example below: the window [2, 1, 5] sums to 8; sliding one step brings in a[3], whose value is 1, and drops a[0], whose value is 2. This only works because addition can be undone by subtraction; a window maximum can't be "un-added" like this (the monotonic stack and deque units handles that with a deque). For a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3: Each slide costs a constant amount of work, so the whole scan is O(n) time, O(1) space. The same idea handles "average of every window", "count anagrams of p in s" (a window of length len(p) with a character count) and rolling hashes (Rabin–Karp). Counts that update with the window For distinct values, keep a map from value to occurrence count. Increment the entrant, decrement the leaver and delete a key when its count becomes zero. The number of remaining keys is the current distinct count, read in constant time. For anagrams, compare counts against the pattern’s required counts. Maintain how many character counts currently disagree: when one count changes, update that mismatch count from its old and new equality status. This avoids scanning the whole alphabet on every slide. Build the target counts once and update a bounded number of keys per slide, assuming expected constant-time hashing. Account for both source and pattern lengths in the total cost. Key takeaways A fixed window updates its sum by adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving value. Maintain counts and a constant-time mismatch counter for anagram windows. A median needs order information; a running total alone does not suffice. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

sum: Longest-window validity must survive taking subwindows; shortest covering validity must survive expansion.
x: A variable window changes length to restore or preserve a predicate. Here n is the input length. A subarray or substring occupies a contiguous range; an arbitrary subsequence may skip positions. Variable-size windows Here the window grows and shrinks. The template: hi - lo + 1 is the window's length, because both ends are included: If the empty window is valid and add/remove/valid/record each cost O(1), both pointers only move forwards, so each element is added once and removed no more than once: O(n) total, even with the inner while. That amortised argument is the reason the pattern is fast. The precondition: monotonicity These variable-window templates need monotonic validity: every subwindow of a valid window stays valid for the longest/shrink-when-invalid template; every superwindow of a valid window stays valid for the shortest/shrink-while-valid template. Merely being able to make some invalid window valid by growing is insufficient. "Sum at most k", with non-negative numbers and a non-negative limit k, qualifies. With negative numbers, removing an element can increase the sum, so the window can't tell which way to move. Use prefix sums instead (the prefix-sum units). When to record a candidate For a longest valid window, shrink until validity is restored, then record its length. Typical downward-closed predicates are at most a specified number of distinct values, at most a specified number of zeros, or a sum at most a nonnegative limit when all values are nonnegative. For products of integers at least one and a limit greater than one, removing values cannot increase the product; the same longest/counting shape is valid. For a shortest window whose positive values sum to at least a positive target, expansion cannot destroy validity. Once valid, record a candidate inside the shrink loop, then remove from the left. Stop shrinking when the sum falls below target. Each endpoint still moves only forwards. For [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] with target 7, the final [4, 3] is the shortest qualifying range. A negative value can rescue an earlier sum that looked too large. For [3, -2, 1] with a limit of 2, removing the initial 3 immediately loses the valid whole-array answer. Use a prefix-based method that retains the needed starts instead. For counting under a downward-closed predicate, keep the smallest valid left edge. Every starting position from that edge through the current right edge then gives a valid ending subarray. Adding the number of such starts counts those subarrays once. Key takeaways Longest-window validity must survive taking subwindows; shortest covering validity must survive expansion. With constant-cost updates, forward-only endpoints give linear total work. Negative values can break monotone sum rules; consecutive positions alone does not prove a window solution. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

sum: Store each character’s last position to jump past a duplicate.
x: The earlier variable-window rule now tracks unique characters. Here n is the string length measured in Python code points; dictionary operations use the expected constant-cost hash model. Longest substring without repeating characters Problem. Return the length of the longest substring of s with all distinct characters. Window condition: no character appears twice. When s[hi] is already in the window, move lo just past its previous occurrence. Storing each character's last index lets lo jump instead of stepping. Trace for "abcabcbb": Answer 3. O(n) time; O(min(n, alphabet)) space, where n is the length of s, alphabet is the number of different characters that can occur, and min picks the smaller of the two: the map never holds more keys than either. Why >= lo matters For "abba": at the final a, last['a'] = 0, but lo is already 2 (moved by the second b). The old a is outside the window, so lo may never move backwards to 1. Without the >= lo check, the code returns 3 instead of 2. Key takeaways Store each character’s last position to jump past a duplicate. Ignore occurrences before the left edge so the edge never moves backwards. Python strings are scanned by code point, which can differ from displayed characters. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

t: Shrink a covering substring to its minimum
sum: A counter records missing occurrences, including repeated target characters.
x: Find the shortest contiguous substring covering every target occurrence. Hashing and character comparisons are assumed constant-cost, and each Python character is a code point. Minimum window substring Problem. Given s and t, find the shortest substring of s containing every character of t (with multiplicity). For s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC", the answer is "BANC". An empty target has answer ""; when no covering substring exists the answer is also "". This is a "shortest" problem: grow until the window is valid, then shrink while it stays valid, recording the best. Keep need[c]: how many more of c the window still needs (negative means surplus), and missing: the total number of required characters not yet covered. How it plays out on the example: Each character enters and leaves once. Writing s for the length of s and t for the length of t, that gives expected O(s + t) time, O(alphabet) auxiliary space plus the returned substring. The missing counter is what keeps the validity check O(1); comparing two full count maps each step would cost O(alphabet) per move. Key takeaways A counter records missing occurrences, including repeated target characters. Record a covering candidate before removing its leftmost character. An empty target or absence of a covering substring returns the empty string. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

sum: Every valid start between the left and right edges contributes one ending window.
x: Here n is the input length and k is an integer distinct-value budget. Values must be hashable; count-map operations have expected constant cost. Counting windows: the at-most trick "Count subarrays with exactly k distinct values" is awkward for a window: removing an element can keep the count at k or drop it, so there's no single clean shrink rule. But "at most k" is monotonic. For each hi, after shrinking, every window ending at hi and starting anywhere in [lo, hi] qualifies: that's hi - lo + 1 windows. These functions count nonempty subarrays; a negative distinct budget gives 0, and exactly(a, 0) gives 0. Values must be hashable. The subtraction works because every subarray with at most k distinct values has either exactly k or at most k − 1: For [1, 2, 1, 2, 3] with k = 2: twelve subarrays have at most two distinct values (all 15 except the three that end with 3 and also contain both 1 and 2), and five have at most one (the five single elements, since no two neighbours are equal). So exactly 7 subarrays have exactly two distinct values. Recognising the pattern Cue Kind of window ------ "every k consecutive" Fixed "longest... such that" Variable, shrink when invalid "shortest... containing" Variable, shrink while valid "count subarrays at most k" Variable, add hi-lo+1 "exactly k" Subtract two at-most counts Max/min of each window Monotonic deque (the monotonic stack and deque units) Sum equals k, negatives allowed Not a window: prefix sums Pitfalls Non-contiguous sequence problems. "Subsequence" means elements need not be adjacent; a contiguous window alone does not enumerate arbitrary subsequences. DP, greedy or other methods may apply. Negative numbers break sum-based windows, as above. Recording at the wrong time. For "longest", record after shrinking (window valid). For "shortest", record inside the shrink loop before removing. Expensive validity checks. Keep a counter (missing, len(count)) so each check is O(1). Stale map entries. Delete keys whose count hits 0, or len(count) overstates the distinct count. Recap of the pattern family A sliding window maintains a contiguous range's summary incrementally, turning O(n²) or O(n × k) into O(n), where n is the input length and k the window size. Each element enters and leaves the window no more than once, so the inner while doesn't make it quadratic. Variable windows need monotonic validity; negative numbers usually break sum conditions. "Longest" shrinks until valid then records; "shortest" records while shrinking a valid window. Count exactly a budget by subtracting the at-most-previous-budget count from the at-most-budget count. Key takeaways Every valid start between the left and right edges contributes one ending window. Subtract the at-most-lower-budget count from the at-most-budget count. Delete zero-count map keys; these examples count nonempty subarrays. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

t: Subtract prefixes to answer static range sums
sum: The padded prefix table starts with zero and totals elements before each position.
x: If you'll ask "what's the sum of a[l..r]?" many times, adding up the range each time costs O(n) per query. Here a[l..r] means the elements from index l to index r, both included, and n is the length of the array. A prefix sum array costs O(n) once and then answers every range query in O(1). The idea underpins far more than range queries: subarray-sum counting, difference arrays for batched updates, 2-D summed-area tables and cumulative frequency tables all reuse it. Examples use exact integer arithmetic. The O(1) arithmetic/hash model assumes values fit the chosen word size; Python arbitrary-precision costs grow with bit length. Floating-point prefix subtraction can lose accuracy through rounding and cancellation. The prefix array Build the prefix array one running total at a time: The prefix at an index totals that many earlier elements. The table has one more entry than the input because it includes the empty prefix. Any range sum is then one subtraction: The leading zero, P[0] = 0 in the implementation, is what makes ranges starting at index 0 work without a special case. This relies on subtraction undoing addition exactly, so it holds for integers but only approximately for floating-point numbers, and it does not work for operations like max that can't be undone. Off-by-one insurance Use the length-n + 1 array with P[0] = 0. Think of P[i] as the sum of the elements before index i. Then "sum of a[l..r]" is always "everything before r + 1 minus everything before l". Python provides these values as an iterator: itertools.accumulate(a, initial=0). Materialise it with list(...) for indexed range queries. Integer width and numeric limits Forgetting the leading zero: misses ranges that start at index 0. In frequency-counting variants, seed seen = {0: 1} for the same reason. Integer overflow in fixed-width languages: a prefix sum can be as large as the count times the largest value, which blows past a 32-bit integer: Key takeaways The padded prefix table starts with zero and totals elements before each position. Inclusive range queries subtract the prefix before the left edge from the prefix after the right edge. Use a suitable integer width and account for floating-point cancellation. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

sum: Count frequencies of earlier running totals, including one empty prefix.
x: Here n is the array length and k is a target sum. The preceding padded prefix convention represents the empty prefix with total zero. Subarray sum equals k Problem. Count the nonempty contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values may be negative. A sliding window fails because of the negatives (the sliding-window units). Prefix sums turn the question around: So as we scan, for each running total run, the number of subarrays ending here with sum k equals the number of earlier prefix values equal to run − k. Keep a hash map counting prefix values seen so far. Trace for a = [1, 2, 3], k = 3: The two subarrays are [1, 2] and [3]. Expected O(n) time with well-behaved constant-cost hashing, O(n) space. Why seen = {0: 1}? It represents the empty prefix P[0] = 0. Without it, subarrays that start at index 0 (like [1, 2] above, where the required earlier prefix is zero) are never counted. Key takeaways Count frequencies of earlier running totals, including one empty prefix. Query before inserting the current prefix so empty subarrays are excluded. Prefix-frequency counting handles signed values under expected constant-cost hashing. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

t: Use first indices and normalised remainders
sum: Store the first occurrence to maximise the length of a matching subarray.
x: Different prefix problems retain different information: counts for counting, earliest positions for longest ranges, or normalised remainders for divisibility. Here n is the number of elements. Prefix summaries for different questions The same "complement in a hash map" trick, borrowed from two sum, solves several variations: Problem Store in map ------ Count sum equals k prefix → count Longest sum equals k prefix → first index Sum divisible by positive k prefix % k → count Equal 0s and 1s map 0→−1, find sum 0 For "longest", seed first = {0: -1} and store the first ending index at which each running total appears (do not overwrite it). At ending index j, a match gives the length: Remainder and update caveats Negative modulo: in Python -1 % 5 == 4, which is what you want; in C, Java and JavaScript, -1 % 5 == -1, for positive k. In fixed-width code, the extra + k can itself overflow: compute r = x % k, then add k only if r is negative; ensure the preceding sum fits too. Java also provides Math.floorMod. Mutable data: prefix sums go stale after an update; rebuilding is O(n). Use a Fenwick tree if updates are frequent. Remainder frequencies For a positive modulus, reduce each running prefix sum to its canonical remainder between zero and one less than the modulus. Two prefixes in the same remainder class differ by a multiple of the modulus, so the subarray between them has divisible sum. Keep a frequency map, seeded with one empty prefix at remainder zero, and look up a remainder before inserting it. Python’s remainder has the positive divisor’s sign. Java’s remainder follows the dividend’s sign, so a negative running total can produce a negative key for the same class. With positive Java int modulus and int input values, widen the sum to long before Math.floorMod; merely normalising after an overflowing int addition does not repair that lost value. Key takeaways Store the first occurrence to maximise the length of a matching subarray. Equal normalised prefix remainders identify sums divisible by a positive modulus. Widen before Java addition and normalise remainders consistently. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

t: Record starts and stops for batched updates
sum: An inclusive update switches on at its first index and off just after its last index.
x: Here n is the array length and u is the number of updates. The batch starts with zeros; updates are applied before the final array is read. Difference arrays: batched range updates Prefix sums make range queries cheap. The inverse trick makes range updates cheap. Problem. Start with n zeros. Apply many updates "add v to every element in [l, r]", then report the final array. Doing each update directly is O(r − l + 1). Instead, record only where each update starts and stops: Each update touches two cells of the difference array: Each update is O(1); one prefix-sum pass at the end rebuilds the array. Total O(n + u) for u updates instead of O(n × u). Check index 2: covered by +2 and -1, so 1. Correct. Where you see this "Car pooling" (can a car with C seats take every trip?) and "flight bookings" are difference arrays over time or flight number. For positive-duration start-inclusive, end-exclusive bookings start,end), mark +1 at the start and −1 at the end, then sweep. Inclusive discrete ranges instead cancel just after the last included index. The interval units calls this a sweep line. The efficient batch use applies updates before rebuilding the values. Interleaved queries are possible but a plain difference array may need O(n) work per read. A Fenwick tree over differences supports range-add/point-query in O(log n); two Fenwick trees or an appropriately lazy segment tree support range-add/range-sum. Key takeaways An inclusive update switches on at its first index and off just after its last index. One final prefix pass reconstructs all batch-updated values. Efficient interleaved updates and queries need an appropriate tree rather than repeated rebuilding. Further reading [Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

sum: A zero row and column simplify rectangle boundaries.
x: The earlier prefix-subtraction idea extends to grids. The example uses exact integer arithmetic with constant-cost operations; returned and auxiliary storage must both be counted. 2-D prefix sums For a grid, let P[r][c] be the sum of the rectangle from (0, 0) up to but not including row r and column c. Build it with inclusion–exclusion: The query subtracts the strip above and the strip to the left, then adds back the corner that was subtracted twice: The drawing’s letters identify four regions. In the formula below, each letter denotes that region’s cell sum: For the grid the prefix table is and the rectangle rows 1–2, columns 1–2 (the cells 6, 3, 2, 0) comes from four lookups: This is the summed-area table from computer graphics, introduced for texture mapping in 1984. The Viola–Jones face detector used it (as the "integral image") to evaluate rectangular features in constant time, which helped make real-time face detection practical in the early 2000s. Recognising the pattern Many range-sum queries on a static array or grid. "Subarray sum equals / is divisible by k", especially with negatives. "Equal number of X and Y in a subarray" (map one to −1, look for sum 0). Many range updates followed by reads: difference array. Products work too (prefix products, or "product of array except self" with prefix and suffix passes), but watch out for zeros. Recap of the pattern family A padded prefix totals the elements before its index; an inclusive range subtracts the prefix before its start from the prefix just after its end. "Subarray sum equals k" becomes "count earlier prefixes equal to run − k", O(n) with a hash map and safe with negatives. Difference arrays make each range update O(1); one prefix pass recovers the final values. 2-D prefix sums answer any rectangle sum in O(1) with inclusion–exclusion. For interleaved updates and queries, move to a Fenwick or segment tree. Key takeaways A zero row and column simplify rectangle boundaries. Remove the upper and left strips, then restore their doubly removed corner. Static grid queries take constant arithmetic work after a table build. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

t: Fix endpoint semantics before merging ranges
sum: Closed intervals include both endpoints; positive-duration start-inclusive, end-exclusive meetings exclude the end.
x: Interval problems describe things that occupy a range: meetings, bookings, reservations, IP ranges, genome regions, time-series gaps. Each interval is a pair [start, end]. Throughout this lesson, n is the number of intervals. The questions are variations on "which ones overlap?", "how many at once?" and "how do I combine them?" Many interval algorithms begin with sorting. For merging, tracking the current merged block makes a linear scan sufficient. Individual intervals can overlap non-neighbours even after sorting (a long interval may contain many others). Other tasks need heaps, trees or even quadratic output when listing every overlapping pair. Overlap, precisely For valid closed intervals [a, b] and [c, d] (each start no later than its end), the overlap test is: That is, each starts before (or when) the other ends. The predicate uses two endpoint comparisons, whatever the interval lengths, and works for any ordered values: integers, times or real numbers. It's easier to remember the negation: they do not overlap if either interval ends strictly before the other starts. Closed or start-inclusive, end-exclusive? Do [1, 3] and [3, 5] overlap? Under the closed interval convention (both ends included), yes: they share the point 3. For meetings, usually no: a meeting ending at 3:00 frees the room for one starting at 3:00. That's a start-inclusive, end-exclusive interval [start, end), and for nonempty intervals the test becomes strict (see the formula below). The meeting and scheduling code below assumes positive duration and finite, consistently ordered numeric endpoints. Empty intervals require separate handling. Endpoint semantics affect overlap tests and event ties; merging adjacent half-open intervals is a separate policy, since their union can be consecutive even though they do not overlap. For half-open intervals the touching case no longer counts: Merging overlapping intervals Problem. Merge all overlapping intervals. [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]] becomes [[1,6], [8,10], [15,18]]. Sort by start. Walk through, keeping the last merged interval. If the next one starts no later than the last one ends, extend; otherwise start a new one. Why max when extending? For [[1, 10], [2, 3]], the second interval is entirely inside the first. Setting the end to 3 instead of max(10, 3) would shrink the merged interval: a classic bug. Why does sorting by start make one pass enough? After sorting, any interval that overlaps the current merged block must start before the block ends, and all such intervals come next in the order. Once you see a start beyond the block's end, no later interval (they all start even later) can touch it. Key takeaways Closed intervals include both endpoints; positive-duration start-inclusive, end-exclusive meetings exclude the end. Sorting by start permits a scan of the current merged block. Use the larger end when absorbing a contained interval. t: Insert a range in three ordered phases
sum: Copy intervals before the new range, absorb overlaps, then copy the remainder.
x: Here n is the number of valid closed intervals. The input is already sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, so one scan suffices. Inserting into a sorted list Problem. Given non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, insert a new one, merging as needed. A generic comparison sort gives an O(n log n) upper bound after appending. Python’s adaptive list sort can exploit the existing run and added interval to take O(n), but this explicit three-phase scan establishes O(n) without depending on sorting adaptivity: Inserting [4, 8] into [[1,2], [3,5], [6,7], [8,10], [12,16]]: The returned outer list is new, but unmerged intervals are shared with ivs; copy those pairs too if the caller needs independent mutable intervals. Output and slicing use O(n) space. Key takeaways Copy intervals before the new range, absorb overlaps, then copy the remainder. The linear scan relies on sorted, internally non-overlapping input. Unmerged interval pairs are shared unless explicitly copied. Further reading Interval cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Interval scheduling — Wikipedia Activity selection problem — Wikipedia Sweep line algorithm — Wikipedia heapq — Python docs

t: Count rooms with end times or events
sum: A room-count heap retains one last end time per allocated room.
x: Here n is the number of positive-duration, start-inclusive, end-exclusive meetings with finite consistently ordered endpoints. A room is reusable at exactly its previous end time. Meeting rooms I: any conflict? "Can one person attend all these meetings?" Sort by start; if any meeting starts before the previous one ends, there's a clash. O(n log n). Meeting rooms II: how many rooms? Problem. Given meetings [start, end), find the minimum number of rooms so that no two overlapping meetings share a room. For [[0,30], [5,10], [15,20]] the answer is 2. The answer equals the maximum number of meetings in progress at any instant. Two standard ways to find it. With a min-heap of end times Process meetings by start time. The heap holds the last scheduled end time of every room allocated so far, including rooms already free. Its minimum identifies a room whose availability time is earliest. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. The heap's size never shrinks, so at the end it equals the peak number of simultaneous meetings. To produce an allocation, extend the heap entries to (end_time, room_id) and record each assignment; this end-times-only version returns just the count. With a sweep line Turn each meeting into two events: +1 at its start and −1 at its end. Sort the events by time, sweep left to right, and track the running count. The peak is the answer. The tie-break is where the start-inclusive, end-exclusive semantics live. Sorting (time, delta) tuples puts (10, -1) before (10, 1), so a meeting ending at 10 frees its room before one starting at 10 claims it. For closed intervals you'd want starts first. The sweep line is a difference array (the prefix-sum units) over time, done with sorting instead of an array, so it works for huge or real-valued times. Geometric segment-intersection algorithms also sweep events, but they need additional ordering and intersection logic beyond this concurrency counter. A bounded integer timeline If every start and end is an integer minute in a known day, allocate one difference slot for each boundary. Add one at a start and subtract one at an end, then sweep the slots with a running sum. Aggregating all changes at the same boundary respects start-inclusive, end-exclusive semantics. The maximum running count is the room requirement. This takes O(n + T) work and O(T) slots, where T is the largest permitted integer boundary and n is the number of meetings. A 1,440-minute day needs 1,441 boundary slots when the final end is included in the sweep. Arbitrary real-valued times instead use sorted events or another ordered representation. Key takeaways A room-count heap retains one last end time per allocated room. Half-open event ties process ends before starts. A bounded integer timeline allows a difference-array scan without sorting. Further reading Interval cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Interval scheduling — Wikipedia Activity selection problem — Wikipedia Sweep line algorithm — Wikipedia heapq — Python docs

sum: Choose the compatible activity that finishes earliest.
x: Here n is the number of positive-duration half-open intervals. Touching endpoints are allowed; minimise removals by maximising the number retained. Non-overlapping intervals: the greedy choice Problem. Remove the fewest intervals so the rest don't overlap. Equivalently, keep as many as possible: the unweighted activity selection problem. Weighted scheduling generally requires a different method, such as dynamic programming. Sort by end time and greedily keep each interval that starts after the last kept one ends. Finishing earliest leaves the most room for everything else; an exchange argument shows no other choice can do better. Sorting by start instead fails: [[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]] would keep [1, 100] first and block the other two. Why replacing the first choice is safe Take an optimal compatible schedule and compare its first interval with the earliest-finishing interval. Replacing that first choice with the earliest-finishing one leaves no later finish time, so every later selected interval remains compatible. The replacement keeps the same number of intervals. Apply the argument again to the intervals that can start after that finish. This is a statement about unweighted counts and positive-duration half-open intervals. An early-finishing interval with a small reward need not belong to an optimal weighted interval schedule, whose objective is total reward rather than interval count. The algorithm sorts in O(n log n) time and scans in O(n), where n is the interval count. The scan uses constant extra state; Python’s in-place sort may still allocate linear temporary storage. Key takeaways Choose the compatible activity that finishes earliest. An exchange argument supports the greedy choice for unweighted activity counts. Weights change the objective and generally require a different method. Further reading Interval cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Interval scheduling — Wikipedia Activity selection problem — Wikipedia Sweep line algorithm — Wikipedia heapq — Python docs Princeton activity-selection exchange argument

sum: An intersection begins at the later start and ends at the earlier end.
x: Each input list contains valid closed intervals, sorted by start and internally non-overlapping. Here m and n are the two list lengths. Intersecting two sorted lists For two sorted lists of internally non-overlapping closed intervals, keep one current interval from each list. Their shared range begins at the later start and ends at the earlier end. Keep it when its start is no later than its end: a single-point overlap is valid for closed intervals. Advance whichever interval ends first. That interval cannot meet any later interval in the other list: later intervals start beyond the current one's end. If the two end times tie, advancing either is safe; advancing both is also safe under the strict internal non-overlap contract for closed intervals. For A = [[0, 2], [5, 10]] and B = [[1, 5], [8, 12]], the intersections are [[1, 2], [5, 5], [8, 10]]. First advance A past its end at 2, then B past its end at 5, then A past its end at 10. The pointer scan costs O(m + n) time, where m and n are the two list lengths, plus space for the returned intersections. This is an intersection, not a union: gaps in either input remain gaps in the result. With positive-duration half-open intervals, discard an equal-endpoint candidate because it contains no point. Recognising the pattern Cue Approach ------ Merge / union of ranges Sort by start, extend Insert in a sorted list Three-phase O(n) Any overlap at all? Sort, compare neighbours Max simultaneous / rooms Heap of ends or sweep Keep most / remove fewest Sort by end, greedy Intersect two sorted lists Two pointers Pitfalls Unsorted input. Most algorithms assume sorted by start; sort first unless the problem guarantees it. Inclusive vs exclusive ends. Decide early, then use < or <= consistently, including in sweep-line tie-breaks. Forgetting max on merge when one interval contains another. Mutating the caller's list. intervals.sort() sorts in place; use sorted() if the caller needs the original. Sorting by the wrong key in greedy selection: by end, not start or length. Recap of the pattern family Sort first: after sorting by start, overlaps involve only the current merged block, so one pass suffices. Merging extends the last block's end with max; insertion into a sorted list is O(n) in three phases. Minimum rooms equals peak concurrency: a min-heap of end times or a sweep over +1/−1 events. Keep the most non-overlapping intervals by sorting on end time and choosing greedily. Pin down closed vs half-open intervals; it decides every comparison and tie-break. Key takeaways An intersection begins at the later start and ends at the earlier end. Advance the interval ending first because it cannot intersect later intervals in the other list. Closed intervals can intersect at a single point; do not drop that endpoint.
