t: Skip-list pointer costs, caps and uses
sum: Promotion probability trades pointer memory against search constants.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Cost Read the search path backwards: from the found node, each step either goes up (if that node was promoted, which happens with the promotion probability) or left. Pugh's analysis turns that into an expected step count: O(log n) means the cost grows in proportion to the logarithm of n. Lower p means fewer, longer hops per level but fewer levels, so at a million keys both settings take about 40 steps. Pugh's full formula adds a small constant; the estimate ignores it. The memory cost is the number of forward pointers, one per level each node occupies (not counting the head): A million keys therefore cost about 2 million pointers with fair coins and about 1.33 million with a promotion probability of 1/4. Lower p saves pointers; search constants and variance also depend on the workload and implementation. The code caps levels at 32 for a bounded practical capacity. The number of nodes expected to reach the cap shows when that stops being enough: Well below that scale the capped top level has a small expected population. This is a probabilistic practical estimate, not a guarantee that the cap never affects a particular run. An asymptotic O(log n) guarantee for unbounded n requires a cap that grows with log n; a fixed cap eventually leaves too many nodes on its top level. Where skip lists are used Redis sorted sets (Redis 8.2 implementation) (ZADD, ZRANGE, leaderboards) pair a hash table with a skip list, using a promotion probability of 1/4 and a cap of 32 levels. Each forward pointer also stores a skip-list span, so rank queries (ZRANK) are O(log n) too, where n is the number of members in the set. Small sorted sets use a compact listpack instead. LevelDB uses a skip-list memtable. RocksDB uses a skip list by default and also offers other memtable representations. Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap is a sorted concurrent map. Its Java SE 21 API documents safe concurrent access and expected average logarithmic lookup and updates. That public contract does not promise lock-free progress; the hand-written example above is not a concurrent implementation. Key takeaways Promotion probability trades pointer memory against search constants. A fixed level cap is a practical capacity choice, not an unbounded logarithmic guarantee. Further reading Skip list — Wikipedia Treap — Wikipedia Treap (Cartesian tree) — cp-algorithms Reservoir sampling — Wikipedia Fisher–Yates shuffle — Wikipedia

t: Treaps, random priorities, split and merge
sum: A treap keeps BST order on keys and heap order on priorities.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Treaps A treap is a binary search tree where each node also has a random priority, and the tree is a heap on priorities: every parent's priority beats its children's. (The name is tree + heap.) For distinct keys and priorities, there is exactly one tree satisfying both rules. And it is the same tree you would get by inserting the keys in decreasing priority order into a plain BST. Since priorities are random, that is a random insertion order, and a BST built from random insertions has expected depth O(log n), where n is the number of keys: The average depth is about 14 for 5,000 keys (the leading term 2 ln(n) alone gives 17); the deepest node is somewhat deeper, but still logarithmic in expectation. So the treap's shape no longer depends on the order keys actually arrived. Inserting 5,000 sorted keys into a plain BST gives a chain of height 4,999 edges; a treap with independent random priorities has expected logarithmic height, though a linear-height outcome remains possible. Split and merge The cleanest treap implementations use two operations: split(t, key) returns two treaps: keys below key, and the rest. merge(a, b) joins two treaps when every key in a is smaller than every key in b. The root is whichever root has the higher priority. Assume distinct keys and independent priorities; insert below requires a key not already present. TNode generates a random priority, with a counter to break rare finite-precision ties. The ideal analysis assumes independent continuous priorities; this finite implementation approximates that model. The example uses import random, introduced with the skip-list implementation; run that import when using this excerpt separately. The recursive implementations can hit Python’s recursion limit on a sufficiently tall outcome; expected balance is not a hard stack bound. Each runs in expected time proportional to the tree’s depth, which is O(log n) for n keys. Delete is two splits (cutting out the key) and one merge. Split and merge are what make treaps popular in competitive programming. An implicit treap keys nodes by position (subtree sizes) instead of by value, giving a sequence that supports insert at index, delete range, moving a sequence fragment and reversing a range, with expected O(log n) tree work for a sequence of n items when properly augmented; reversal needs lazy tags. Inserting m fresh items costs at least O(m), and deleting nodes can add reclamation work. That is the same job a rope does, which the next lesson covers. Tree vs list Skip lists and treaps solve the same problem with the same expected bounds. Skip lists are simpler to make concurrent. Treaps are a real BST, so augmenting nodes (subtree sums, sizes) and split/merge come naturally. Key takeaways A treap keeps BST order on keys and heap order on priorities. Merge requires all left-treap keys to precede every right-treap key. Further reading Skip list — Wikipedia Treap — Wikipedia Treap (Cartesian tree) — cp-algorithms Reservoir sampling — Wikipedia Fisher–Yates shuffle — Wikipedia

sum: A later item enters a size-k reservoir with k divided by the number of items seen.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Reservoir sampling You are reading a log stream of unknown length and want a uniform random sample of k lines, using O(k) memory. You cannot store the stream, and you cannot know n in advance. Algorithm R keeps the first k items. Then, for each later item i (counting from 0), it draws j = randint(0, i); if j < k, the new item replaces sample[j]. Why it is uniform Assume independent uniform draws and a sample size no bigger than the stream. Follow one item: it must first enter the sample, then survive every later step, where it is evicted only if the draw picks exactly its slot. Multiplying those chances, most factors cancel (the product telescopes): The first k items start in with probability 1, and the same telescoping gives k/n: with 10 slots and 1,000 lines, every line has a 1 % chance. If the stream is shorter than k, the code returns everything it saw; a negative k is outside its contract. Equal inclusion probabilities alone do not prove uniform subsets. Algorithm R additionally gives every possible sample the same probability, by induction over each replacement step: Key takeaways A later item enters a size-k reservoir with k divided by the number of items seen. Uniform subsets need a replacement induction as well as equal item-inclusion probabilities. Further reading Skip list — Wikipedia Treap — Wikipedia Treap (Cartesian tree) — cp-algorithms Reservoir sampling — Wikipedia Fisher–Yates shuffle — Wikipedia Vitter’s reservoir-sampling paper

sum: Weighted sampling without replacement does not give simply proportional inclusion probabilities.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Reservoir variants Algorithm L computes how many items to skip before the next replacement, so it draws far fewer random numbers than one per item: For a 100-line sample from a billion lines, the displayed growth term is about 1,712. It illustrates scaling rather than predicting 1,712 actual draws: a common Algorithm L implementation uses three draws per selected replacement, as well as initialisation and termination work. Scanning a non-skippable input stream can still take linear time even when the random-draw count falls. Weighted sampling (Efraimidis–Spirakis): give each item a random key based on its weight and keep the k items with the largest keys, as below. This is sequential weighted sampling without replacement. It does not promise that each item's inclusion probability is k times its share of the total weight. Distributed: for a single-item sample, choose one shard's sample with probability proportional to its shard size. For larger reservoirs, simple repetition is insufficient: allocate shard counts with a hypergeometric distribution and subsample each local uniform reservoir without replacement. Each local reservoir must hold up to k items, or the whole shard if it is smaller. Key takeaways Weighted sampling without replacement does not give simply proportional inclusion probabilities. Shard samples must be combined with their shard sizes, not by a fair shard coin. Further reading Skip list — Wikipedia Treap — Wikipedia Treap (Cartesian tree) — cp-algorithms Reservoir sampling — Wikipedia Fisher–Yates shuffle — Wikipedia

sum: Draw from the remaining prefix, including the current position.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. The Fisher–Yates shuffle To shuffle an array uniformly, walk from the end. At each position i, swap a[i] with a[j] for j = randint(0, i), which can pick i itself. Think of it as drawing cards from a hat: the last position gets any of the items, the one before it any of the items left, and so on. Count the equally likely runs: For three items there are 6 runs and 6 orderings, each with probability 1/6. It takes O(n) time (proportional to n) and works in place. This is the version Durstenfeld published in 1964 and Knuth gives as Algorithm P; Python's random.shuffle uses it. Key takeaways Draw from the remaining prefix, including the current position. Each permutation corresponds to one equally likely sequence of draws. Further reading Skip list — Wikipedia Treap — Wikipedia Treap (Cartesian tree) — cp-algorithms Reservoir sampling — Wikipedia Fisher–Yates shuffle — Wikipedia

t: Shuffle bias, seed limits and adversaries
sum: Swapping with any array position creates unequal permutation counts.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. The classic bug A tempting variant swaps every position with any position: Count its runs against the possible orderings: Counting them: three permutations appear 5 times in 27 and three appear 4 times, so some come out with probability 5/27 ≈ 18.5 % instead of 1/6 ≈ 16.7 %. Unpredictability matters A fair permutation algorithm does not make a predictable generator secure. Use an operating-system-backed generator such as secrets.SystemRandom when choices must be unpredictable. Content gap: the specific historical poker incident is omitted because a reliable primary account establishing the exact loop and seed was not verified in this audit. Two more pitfalls: Sorting with a random comparator, such as JavaScript's arr.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5), gives biased, implementation-dependent results, because the sort assumes comparisons are consistent. Sorting by a random key drawn once per element is unbiased (ignoring ties), but O(n log n) for n elements. Too little randomness: a generator can only produce as many shuffles as it has possible seeds, as below. So a generator seeded with 32 bits can reach at most about 4 billion of the deck's orders, a vanishingly small fraction. Pitfalls Off-by-one ranges: randint(0, i) is inclusive in Python, randrange(i) is not. Drawing j with randrange(i) in Fisher–Yates, so position i can never keep its own item, is Sattolo's algorithm: it produces only single-cycle permutations, uniformly within that restricted class, rather than uniformly over all permutations. Ignoring the high-probability fine print: expected O(log n), for n keys, is extremely reliable at scale, but individual operations vary. Systems needing hard per-operation bounds use deterministic trees. Predictable seeds: if attackers can predict your priorities or independent random draws, they can build bad inputs for skip lists and treaps after all. Key takeaways Swapping with any array position creates unequal permutation counts. Unbiased algorithms still require enough unpredictable randomness for security-sensitive uses. t: Building sparse tables for static ranges
sum: Store every fitting power-of-two block summary.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. This index assumes a non-empty array and valid inclusive query endpoints. This unit builds a static range-minimum index from overlapping power-of-two blocks. Later units separately cover historical versions and editable text. Range minimum queries A range minimum query (RMQ) asks for the smallest value in a[l..r], the elements from index l to index r inclusive. The options so far, for an array of n elements (O(n²) means growing with n × n): Method Build Query Updates ------------ Scan none O(n) O(1) Every range O(n²) O(1) rebuild Segment tree O(n) O(log n) O(log n) Sparse table O(n log n) O(1) rebuild The sparse table is the right choice when the array never changes and there are many queries: for example, LCA queries on a fixed tree, or the LCP array of a suffix array. The sparse table Precompute the minimum of every block whose length is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …). Each row holds minima for one block length, twice the previous row’s length. Combine two adjacent half-size blocks from the preceding row to obtain each larger block: The worked lines use the example array below, a = [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6, 8]: the length-2 block starting at index 3 covers 7 and 1, so its minimum is 1. The recurrence only works for operations where combining two halves gives the answer for the whole, which holds for min. The code builds row after row (table is T, j is k and half is h): Each row fits as long as its block length is at most n, which fixes how many rows there are and bounds the size: The 8-element example below has 4 rows and 21 entries. A million elements need at most 20 million entries, about 80 MB as 4-byte integers (the exact count, about 18.95 million entries, is about 76 MB), and far more as Python objects. So the build is O(n log n) time and memory, and that memory is the main limit on how large an array a sparse table suits. For a = [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6, 8]: Key takeaways Store every fitting power-of-two block summary. Sparse-table preprocessing is worthwhile for many queries on unchanged data. Further reading Sparse Table — cp-algorithms Range minimum query — Wikipedia

sum: Two largest-fitting blocks cover any range.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. This index assumes a non-empty array and valid inclusive query endpoints. The O(1) query: overlap is fine Any range can be covered by two blocks of the same power-of-two length: the largest power of two that fits inside the range. One block starts at the left end and one ends at the right end. They may overlap in the middle. The worked lines are query(2, 6) on the example array: two length-4 blocks, a[2..5] and a[3..6], overlapping at indices 3 to 5: Overlap does not matter for min, because counting an element twice does not change a minimum. The overlap query needs an associative combine that is also an idempotent operation: combining a value with itself gives the value back. Min, max, gcd (greatest common divisor), bitwise AND and bitwise OR all qualify. Sums are not idempotent Overlapping blocks would double-count the middle for a sum. You can still answer range sums from a sparse table in O(log n), with n the array length, by decomposing the range into disjoint power-of-two blocks (like a Fenwick prefix), but a prefix-sum array does that job in O(1) with O(n) memory. A disjoint sparse table stores the table differently to give O(1) queries for any associative operation. In the Python, bit_length() - 1 computes k, the base-2 logarithm of the range length rounded down: 5 is 101 in binary, 3 bits long, so k is 2. C++ code often uses __builtin_clz or precomputes a log array. Key takeaways Two largest-fitting blocks cover any range. Overlap requires an associative idempotent combine; summation double-counts. sum: An Euler-tour depth minimum gives a lowest common ancestor.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Where it is used Lowest common ancestor: record an Euler tour of a tree (the nodes visited by a DFS, including returns) and their depths. The LCA of u and v is the shallowest node between their first appearances: an RMQ. For a tree of n nodes (the tour records the root once and one entry for each outward and return edge traversal), that is O(n log n) build and O(1) per LCA. Suffix arrays: the longest common prefix of two distinct suffixes is the minimum of the LCP array between their positions, so an RMQ structure answers it in O(1). Very large static data: specialised micro/macro RMQ constructions combine small in-block tables with summaries of block minima to obtain O(n) build and O(1) query, where n is the array length. Whether the more specialised implementation is worthwhile depends on memory limits and workload; compare those costs before choosing it. Pitfalls Sparse tables on changing data: a point update can affect O(n) blocks across all levels, where n is the array length. Use a segment tree instead. The count adds up like this: For a million elements, the top row is nineteen. The geometric bound allows up to 1,048,575 affected entries, about a million, against roughly twenty nodes in a segment tree. This is an upper bound, not the exact number affected at any chosen position. Using the overlap trick for sums: it double-counts. The combine must be associative and idempotent. Key takeaways An Euler-tour depth minimum gives a lowest common ancestor. A point change can affect linearly many sparse-table entries. sum: Copy the changed path and share untouched subtrees.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Persistent data structures Ordinary structures are ephemeral: an update destroys the old version. A persistent structure keeps old versions usable. A partially persistent structure lets you read every version but update only the newest; a fully persistent one lets you update them too, forming a tree of versions. This sounds expensive, but most of each version is shared with the previous one. Shared nodes must remain immutable: changing one in place corrupts every version that still references it. Path copying In a tree, an update only changes nodes on one root-to-leaf path. Copy just those nodes, and point the copies at the unchanged subtrees of the old version: Inserting 45 into the tree with keys 20, 30, 40, 50 and 70: v2 created four nodes (50', 30', 40' and 45); everything else is shared. Both roots remain valid. In a balanced tree, the copied root-to-leaf route is only as long as the tree is tall: So each update costs O(log n) time and memory: about 20 new nodes per insertion into a million-key tree, instead of copying a million. This only holds if the tree stays balanced; a badly unbalanced tree would copy a path as long as the whole chain. Other techniques: Fat nodes: each field stores a list of (version, value) pairs. Reads binary-search for the version. Good for partial persistence. Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator and Tarjan (1989) showed how to make linked structures with a constant number of fields per node and bounded in-degree persistent with O(1) amortised extra space per primitive field-update step. A whole operation may contain many such steps. Key takeaways Copy the changed path and share untouched subtrees. Logarithmic update overhead requires a balanced tree and immutable shared nodes. Further reading Sparse Table — cp-algorithms Range minimum query — Wikipedia Persistent data structure — Wikipedia Rope (data structure) — Wikipedia) Text Buffer Reimplementation — VS Code blog Making Data Structures Persistent

sum: Subtract two prefix versions’ counts to query one array slice.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. What persistence buys you Cheap undo and snapshots: retaining roots keeps historical nodes alive. Selecting a previous root is O(1), but storing history and reclaiming it have costs. Safe sharing between threads: immutable, safely published nodes need no mutation locks for readers. Publishing roots and keeping nodes alive still require the language's synchronisation and memory-reclamation rules. Queries on history: a persistent segment tree over value ranks, with one version per array prefix, answers "k-th smallest value in a[l..r]" in O(log n), with n the array length. It subtracts one version's counts from another's, node by node (shown below). In the worked lines, a = [5, 2, 4, 7] and v covers the values 1 to 4: the four elements a[0..3] contain two such values (2 and 4), a[0] contains none, so the slice a[1..3] has 2. Walking down, the query goes left when the left child's count is at least k and right otherwise. It needs a static array; changing an element would change every later version. Where you meet it Functional languages: Haskell, Clojure, Scala and Erlang default to immutable collections. Clojure’s vectors use a wide branching tree plus a tail buffer; hash maps use hash-array mapped tries with collision handling and specialised small forms. Path copying shares unchanged structure. For an idealised full 32-way tree, the height estimate is: In a model of full-width array nodes, copying six 32-slot nodes moves roughly 192 references. Actual Clojure copies depend on tails, occupied branches and hash collisions; this is not a universal copy count. Git: a commit points to a tree of blobs. Changing one file creates new blob and tree objects up the path to the root; unchanged subtrees are shared by hash. That is path copying. Databases and filesystems: LMDB and Btrfs use copy-on-write trees. Retaining old pages supports snapshots; publication, reader coordination and page reclamation still follow each system's synchronisation rules. Persistence vs MVCC PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps old row versions for concurrent transactions, which is persistence at the row level, but it is not path copying: it keeps old row versions in the table's own storage and cleans them up with VACUUM. LMDB's copy-on-write B-tree is the closer analogue. Key takeaways Subtract two prefix versions’ counts to query one array slice. Root publication and memory reclamation still need coordination even when nodes are immutable. sum: Rope leaves hold chunks; internal weights count left-subtree characters.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Ropes Inserting into a single flat text buffer can copy or shift a large part of a 100 MB document. The amount depends on the representation and edit position. A rope (Boehm, Atkinson and Plass, 1995) stores the text as a binary tree whose leaves hold short string chunks. Each internal node stores a rope weight: the total length of its left subtree. Indexing To find character i, compare it with the weight: go left if smaller, otherwise subtract the weight and go right. Tracing char_at(root, 10) on the rope above: Character 10 of Hello_my_name_is_Simon is indeed a. The cost is one step per level, so a balanced rope finds any character in O(log n) steps for n characters. Key takeaways Rope leaves hold chunks; internal weights count left-subtree characters. A right descent subtracts the skipped left-subtree length from the index. Further reading Sparse Table — cp-algorithms Range minimum query — Wikipedia Persistent data structure — Wikipedia Rope (data structure) — Wikipedia) Text Buffer Reimplementation — VS Code blog

t: Rope edits, balancing and practical trade-offs
sum: Split and concatenate around edits while maintaining balance.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Operations Here n is the length of the text in characters and m the number of characters inserted: Operation Flat string Balanced rope --------- Index O(1) O(log n) Concatenate O(n) O(log n) Insert m new characters O(n + m) O(log n + m) Delete a range O(n) Implementation-dependent Iterate all O(n) O(n) These bounds assume balanced trees and bounded leaf sizes, and constant-time character indexing in the flat representation. UTF-8 byte offsets and Unicode character positions need additional care. Inserting new text must read/copy its m characters; deletion can also incur work to reclaim removed nodes. Concatenation creates a new root over two ropes, then rebalances. Insert is split at the position, then two concatenations. Immutable rope nodes can share unchanged structure between versions, making undo history proportional to changed paths plus inserted text. Retaining roots keeps that shared storage alive. Real-world use Editors: the Xi editor and Zed use rope-like B-trees of text chunks. VS Code instead uses a piece table stored in a red–black tree (the "piece tree"), which records edits as references into the original file and an append-only buffer. Both avoid copying the document on each keystroke. Libraries: the SGI STL shipped rope, and Rust crates such as ropey provide them. Ropes are not always better. For short strings, pointer overhead and lost cache locality can outweigh the editing benefit. Chunking keeps substantial work on contiguous memory; chunk sizes are implementation and workload choices, rather than a universal recommendation. Shared-node and balancing pitfalls Mutating a "persistent" node: one in-place write corrupts every version sharing that node. Persistence relies on discipline or immutable types. Unbalanced ropes: repeated appends without rebalancing make a chain with O(n) indexing, where n is the number of leaves. Key takeaways Split and concatenate around edits while maintaining balance. Read or copy inserted characters and account for reclamation and pointer overhead. sum: Imperative code exposes state-changing steps.
x: A programming paradigm is a style of organising programs: what the basic building blocks are and how you combine them. It is not the same thing as a language. Most languages support several paradigms, and the same problem can be written in very different styles in one language. The most fundamental split is between imperative and declarative programming. Imperative: you give the computer a sequence of commands that change its state, step by step. You describe how. Declarative: you describe the result you want, and something else works out the steps. You describe what. Two ways to get a coffee Imperative: "Walk to the counter, take a cup, put it under the spout, press the button, wait 30 seconds, add 20 ml of milk." Declarative: "A flat white, please." The barista decides the steps, and may do them in a better order than you would. Imperative programming Imperative programming mirrors how the hardware works. The architectural view of a CPU exposes instructions operating on registers and memory. Modern processors can overlap and reorder execution internally while preserving the required observable behavior. The stored-program von Neumann model is a useful historical connection, rather than a complete description of every modern microarchitecture. Assembly language makes explicit instructions particularly visible. The core ingredients are: State: variables whose values change over time. Assignment: x = x + 1 is a command, not an equation. Sequence: statement two runs after statement one, and order matters. Control flow: if, loops and jumps decide which statement runs next. Procedural programming (C, Pascal, early Python scripts) is imperative code organised into procedures. Structured programming, pushed by Edsger Dijkstra's 1968 letter Go To Statement Considered Harmful, restricts control flow to sequence, selection (if) and iteration (loops). The Böhm–Jacopini theorem (1966) showed that flowchart computations can be represented with those control structures, allowing additional state variables. This is an expressiveness result, not a promise that every rewrite is equally clear or fast. Here is an imperative solution to a small task: sum the squares of the even numbers in a list. To understand it you mentally run it: total starts at 0, becomes 16, then 116. The program's meaning lives in the changing state. Key takeaways Imperative code exposes state-changing steps. Structured control flow can replace arbitrary jumps. Further reading Dijkstra: Go To Statement Considered Harmful Böhm and Jacopini: structured control flow

sum: A pipeline states transformations without a hand-managed accumulator.
x: A pipeline describes which values to keep, how to transform them and how to combine the results. Compare that description with the explicit accumulator from the previous unit. Declarative programming A declarative program states the relationship between input and output and leaves the execution strategy to a runtime, compiler or engine. The same task in a declarative style: There is no loop counter and no accumulator you update by hand. You say which numbers and what to do with them. Declarative languages are everywhere, often not recognised as programming languages at all: Language You declare Engine decides --------- SQL The rows you want Join order, indexes HTML/CSS Structure, style Layout, painting Regex A pattern Matching algorithm Make Targets, deps What to rebuild Terraform Infrastructure API calls to make Functional and logic programming are two important declarative families explored in the following units. The Python, Haskell and JavaScript examples assume nums contains the same finite integers used in the earlier imperative example; the SQL version assumes a table nums with a numeric column n. These are small values, so language-specific integer limits do not affect this example. Why declarative code can be faster Giving up control of how sounds like it would make code slower. Often the opposite is true, because the engine is free to choose a better strategy than you would. A SQL query does not say "loop over the orders table, then for each row look up the customer". The database's query planner looks at table sizes, indexes and statistics and picks a plan: perhaps a hash join, perhaps an index scan, perhaps a parallel scan across 8 workers. If you add an index tomorrow, the planner may use it to accelerate suitable queries without rewriting them; an index does not guarantee a faster plan. The same idea appears elsewhere: A Java parallel stream list.parallelStream().mapToInt(f).sum() can split work across cores because you never said "in this order, one at a time". A spreadsheet can use dependencies to avoid unnecessary recalculation; volatile formulas and full recalculation modes are exceptions. Haskell's compiler can fuse map f (map g xs) into a single pass with no intermediate list. The general principle: the less you over-specify, the more freedom the system has to optimise. Key takeaways A pipeline states transformations without a hand-managed accumulator. Planners and fusion can exploit freedom, subject to semantics. Further reading PostgreSQL: understanding execution plans GHC: rewrite rules and fusion

sum: Kubernetes reconciles continuously; Terraform normally acts during explicit runs.
x: A declarative description can specify a screen or infrastructure as well as a query result. The key question is when and how the system brings the observed state into line with that description. Declarative UI and desired state Two of the most influential modern systems are declarative at heart. React describes a user interface as a function of state. Instead of "find the button, change its text, hide the spinner" (the jQuery style), you write what the UI should look like for a given state: React compares the new description with the previous one and computes DOM updates needed by its reconciliation model. Components normally describe output rather than mutate React-managed DOM directly, although refs provide imperative escape hatches. Kubernetes continuously reconciles declared desired state, such as three Pod replicas, against observed state. When replicas disappear its controllers attempt to restore them, subject to capacity and scheduling constraints. Terraform also declares desired infrastructure, but normally refreshes and reconciles during explicit plan/apply runs; it is not a continuously running self-healing controller. Imperative scripts can also run repeatedly and inspect state if programmed to do so. Declarative surface, imperative engine Declarative systems are almost always built on imperative code. The SQL planner, React's reconciler and Kubernetes controllers are imperative programs. The paradigm describes the layer you work with, not what happens all the way down. A useful goal of desired-state operations is idempotence under stable inputs and provider behavior: applying the same declaration twice gives the same result as applying it once. Written as a formula, an operation is idempotent when: Running "ensure 3 replicas" ten times still leaves 3 replicas: from 0 running, the first run gives 3 and every later run finds 3 and does nothing. Running "start 3 containers" ten times leaves 30, because each run adds 3 more (0, then 3, then 6,...), so applying it twice does not give the same state as applying it once. The idea only holds while nothing else changes the system between runs. Key takeaways Kubernetes reconciles continuously; Terraform normally acts during explicit runs. Idempotence is a property of the operation under stable assumptions. Further reading React: describing the UI Kubernetes controllers Terraform state

sum: Inspect plans and effectful boundaries when an abstraction hides cost.
x: An engine can hide expensive work behind a short declaration. Inspect both the abstraction and its execution boundary when a readable program unexpectedly becomes slow. It's a spectrum "Imperative" and "declarative" are not two boxes; they are relative. A comprehension is more declarative than a for loop, but less declarative than SQL, because you still chose the data structure and evaluation order. A useful test: how much of the execution order and intermediate state is visible in your code? The more there is, the more imperative it is. Trade-offs and pitfalls Declarative code is usually shorter, has fewer places for bugs to hide (no off-by-one loop counter, no forgotten reset of an accumulator), and expresses intent directly. But the abstraction leaks. Performance cliffs. You do not control the plan, so when the engine picks badly, things get dramatically slower. For a hypothetical workload, a missing index or stale statistics could turn a 5-millisecond query into a 50-second scan while the SQL text stays identical. These illustrative timings are not measurements or a general cost ratio. The "how" sneaks back in. Real systems grow escape hatches: SQL index hints, React's useMemo, or explicit Terraform dependency declarations. You end up needing to know the engine's internals anyway. Debugging is indirect. Ordinary application breakpoints do not expose every step of the database execution engine. You read EXPLAIN output or a React profiler instead. Expressiveness limits. Pure SQL cannot easily express "loop until converged". SQL implementations offer procedural extensions; recursive CTEs also express iteration declaratively and can handle some convergence problems. Imperative is sometimes clearer. A complex algorithm with early exits, such as a state machine for parsing, is often easiest to read as explicit steps. An ORM's N+1 trap ORMs let you write for order in orders: print(order.customer.name), which looks like simple attribute access. Each.customer may fire a separate query, so 1,000 orders cause 1,001 round trips. The declarative-looking code hid an imperative cost. Eager loading with an appropriate join or batch query can avoid those per-object queries. The name "N+1" comes from counting the queries: one to load the list, then one more per item in it. At even 1 ms per round trip, 1,001 queries spend about a second just waiting on the database. For this simple relationship and one unbatched result set, an appropriate join or prefetch can reduce the count to one or two queries. Real pagination, batching, database parameter limits and additional relationships can require more queries. Key takeaways Inspect plans and effectful boundaries when an abstraction hides cost. An N+1 access pattern can issue one query per related object. Further reading PostgreSQL: understanding execution plans Django: database access optimisation

sum: Encapsulation protects an explicit object contract.
x: Object-oriented programming (OOP) organises a program around objects: bundles of state (fields) and the behaviour (methods) that operates on it. Instead of free-floating data passed to free-floating procedures, each piece of data comes with the operations allowed on it. The ideas came from Simula 67 (built for simulations, where "objects" were ships and customers) and Smalltalk (Alan Kay and colleagues at Xerox PARC in the 1970s). Kay has said the core idea was messaging: objects are like little computers that communicate only by sending each other messages. C++, Java, C#, Python and JavaScript all inherited some version of this. OOP is often combined with imperative code, but objects may be immutable and their methods may be pure. What it adds is a way to structure that state. Four ideas carry most of the weight: encapsulation, inheritance, composition and polymorphism. Encapsulation Encapsulation means an object hides its internal state and exposes only operations that keep that state valid. The rules that must always hold ("balance is never negative") are called invariants, and encapsulation is how you protect them. This educational account uses integer pence and rejects nonpositive amounts. Callers respecting the public API use these methods, so validation is centralized. Python’s underscore convention does not prevent direct mutation of _balance; this is not a concurrent or production banking implementation. How strictly languages enforce this varies: Language Mechanism Enforced? --------- Java, C# private, protected By compiler Python _name convention No Python __name mangling Weakly JavaScript #field By runtime In Python, self.__balance inside class Account is renamed to self._Account__balance. That avoids accidental clashes in subclasses but is not real privacy. Python's culture is "we are all consenting adults". Key takeaways Encapsulation protects an explicit object contract. Python privacy conventions differ from enforced access controls. Further reading Python: classes and private variables Simula: the birth of object orientation

sum: An inherited method can call an overridden method.
x: Calling an inherited method can run code in both a parent and a child class. Trace those calls before depending on inheritance for reuse. Inheritance Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another. A Dog is an Animal: it gets the parent's fields and methods and can override some of them. new Dog().greet() returns "I say Woof". The inherited greet calls speak, and because the object is a Dog, the overridden version runs. Inheritance does two separate jobs at once: Code reuse: the subclass gets the parent's implementation. Subtyping: a Dog can be used wherever an Animal is expected. Mixing these two jobs is where trouble starts. The fragile base class problem Because subclasses depend on how the parent is implemented, not just on what it promises, changes in the parent can break them. Joshua Bloch's Effective Java has the classic example: a set that counts attempted insertions, including duplicates. Calling addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c")) leaves added at 6, not 3. HashSet inherits addAll from AbstractCollection, which calls add once per element, and that call dispatches to the overridden add. Nothing in HashSet's public contract tells you this; you had to know its internals. Key takeaways An inherited method can call an overridden method. Subclass dependence on implementation details can double-count work. Further reading Java: AbstractCollection.addAll Java: inheritance and overriding

sum: Subtyping must preserve the promises callers rely on.
x: An inheritance relationship is useful only when callers can rely on its behavioral contract. Composition offers a separate way to reuse an implementation. Liskov substitution The Liskov substitution principle (Barbara Liskov, 1987) says a subtype must be usable anywhere its parent is, without surprising the caller. The famous violation is Square extends Rectangle. A rectangle lets you set width and height independently; a square cannot. Code that does r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(2) and expects area 10 breaks when handed a Square. In geometry a square is a rectangle, but in code a mutable square does not behave like a mutable rectangle. Composition Object composition builds objects out of other objects: a Car has an Engine. Instead of inheriting behaviour, an object holds a reference to a helper and passes calls on to it, which is called delegation. Now inner.addAll calls inner's own add, not ours, so the count is correct. The wrapper depends only on Set's public behaviour. You may substitute another Set implementation only if its contract suits callers: TreeSet requires an ordering and has different null and equality/ordering considerations. (In practice you would also implements Set<E> and forward the remaining methods, which is the decorator pattern.) The Design Patterns book (Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, 1994) summed it up as "favour object composition over class inheritance". The rule of thumb: Use inheritance for a genuine is-a relationship where the subtype honours the parent's contract, ideally when the parent was designed for extension. Use composition for has-a or uses-a relationships, and whenever you just want to reuse code. Many newer languages lean this way. The Go language has no class inheritance: it offers struct embedding (promoted fields and methods) and interfaces. Rust has traits but no inheritance between structs. Key takeaways Subtyping must preserve the promises callers rely on. Delegation can reuse behaviour without inheriting internals. Further reading Liskov and Wing: behavioral subtyping Go: embedding and interfaces

sum: Java overload selection uses static types; overriding uses the receiver at runtime.
x: One interface can have several implementations. Distinguish the language rule that selects an implementation from the runtime machinery that makes the call efficient. Polymorphism Polymorphism ("many forms") means one piece of code works with values of different types. There are three main kinds: Subtype polymorphism: code written for Animal works on any subclass. This is what OOP usually means. Ad hoc polymorphism: the same name has different implementations per type, such as overloading print(int) and print(String). Parametric polymorphism: type-parameterised definitions, like List<T>, that reuse a common implementation across element types. Actual language features can permit type-dependent behavior; Java generics are not a guarantee of mathematical parametricity (covered in the types module). Duck typing accepts objects according to the operations actually used, without requiring declared inheritance. It resembles structural interface compatibility, but a matching method name alone does not guarantee the right behavioral contract. Python does not care whether an object inherits from anything; if it has a.read() method, you can pass it where a file is expected. "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck..." How dispatch works Dispatch is how the language picks which method body runs for obj.speak(). Static vs dynamic dispatch With dynamic dispatch, the choice depends on the object's runtime class. A common implementation technique is a virtual method table (vtable). The diagram is a simplified model: actual Java, C# and C++ runtimes/ABIs differ in object layout, interface dispatch and optimization; language semantics do not mandate one table layout. In this simplified model, a.speak() loads the table and target before an indirect call; exact instruction and load counts vary, and JIT compilers like HotSpot often remove even that by inlining when they see only one class at a call site. Static dispatch picks the method at compile time from the declared type. In Java, overloading is resolved statically, while overriding is resolved dynamically. That catches people out: x holds a String at runtime, but its static type is Object, so the compiler picks f(Object). Single, double and multiple dispatch Ordinary Java and Python method selection uses single dispatch: the receiver (obj in obj.m(arg)) chooses the method. Languages such as Common Lisp (CLOS) and Julia use multiple dispatch, choosing on the runtime types of all arguments, which suits operations like collide(asteroid, ship). In single-dispatch languages the visitor pattern fakes double dispatch with two virtual calls. Key takeaways Java overload selection uses static types; overriding uses the receiver at runtime. Dispatch semantics and concrete vtable layouts are separate concerns. Further reading Java: method invocation Julia: methods and multiple dispatch

sum: Python super follows the MRO rather than a fixed parent.
x: Python and JavaScript both select methods at runtime, but they follow different lookup structures. Trace Python's class order first, then compare JavaScript's chain of prototypes. Python and JavaScript Python dispatch is a runtime lookup. With ordinary object.__getattribute__, lookup gives data descriptors found through the class MRO precedence over the instance dictionary, then considers non-data descriptors and other class attributes. Functions implement non-data descriptors, which bind ordinary methods. Custom attribute hooks can change lookup behavior. With multiple inheritance, the MRO is computed by C3 linearisation: In the "diamond", A comes after both B and C, so B and C get a chance to override A's methods. super() follows this MRO, not just "the parent". JavaScript is prototype-based: objects can inherit properties from other objects. To interpret the Python question, follow D, then B, then C, then A; cooperative super() calls continue along this full order. A property lookup walks the prototype chain. The class keyword (ES2015) is mostly syntax over that: class Dog extends Animal sets Dog.prototype's prototype to Animal.prototype. Pitfalls Deep hierarchies: five levels of inheritance means reading five files to know what a method does. God objects: one class that knows everything defeats encapsulation. Getters and setters for every field: if every field is exposed, you have a struct with ceremony and no invariants. Inheritance for reuse only: if you never use the subclass as the parent type, composition is almost certainly better. Key takeaways Python super follows the MRO rather than a fixed parent. JavaScript property lookup follows the prototype chain. Further reading Python: method resolution order ECMAScript language specification

sum: Purity requires explicit inputs and no observable external mutation.
x: Functional programming (FP) emphasises constructing programs from functions and their composition. Pure functional programming uses functions in the mathematical sense: for the same inputs, a terminating call returns the same value without observable side effects. Functional languages and functional style can also include explicit effects or mutation. Programs are made by combining small functions into bigger ones, rather than by sequencing commands that change state. Its roots are in Alonzo Church's lambda calculus (1930s), a model of computation with nothing but function definition and application. Lisp (1958) brought those ideas to real computers, followed by ML, Erlang, Haskell (1990), Scala, Clojure, F# and Elixir. FP ideas also appear in many mainstream languages: lambdas in Java 8, map/filter in JavaScript, comprehensions in Python, and React's push for immutable state. This lesson covers the basics. The functional programming module later goes deeper into laziness, monads and persistent data structures. Pure functions A function is a pure function if: Its result depends only on its arguments. It has no side effects: no mutating variables outside itself, no I/O, no exceptions that depend on hidden state, no reading the clock. In a value-oriented model with immutable inputs/results and no observable identity or timing effects, pure calls support referential transparency: any call can be replaced by its result without changing the program. If add(2, 3) appears anywhere, you can write 5 instead. You cannot do that with tick(), because the first call gives 1 and the second gives 2. Why that matters: Reasoning: you understand a pure function by reading it alone. No hidden state, no "it depends what ran before". Testing: no mocks or setup; call it and check the output. Caching: results can be memoised when keys represent all inputs and cached values are safe to share; Python functools.cache requires hashable arguments and returns the same cached result object. Concurrency: two threads calling pure functions can't race, because nothing is shared and mutated. Optimisation: compilers can sometimes reorder, merge or skip pure calls when the transformation also preserves termination, exceptions and other observable semantics. Real programs must do I/O, of course. The usual approach is functional core, imperative shell: keep the business logic pure and push side effects (database, network, clock) to a thin outer layer that calls into it. Key takeaways Purity requires explicit inputs and no observable external mutation. Cache keys and result sharing must preserve the intended value semantics. Further reading Python: functional programming Functional Core, Imperative Shell

sum: Binding protection and shallow freezing do not freeze nested objects.
x: Keeping old values unchanged makes updates easier to reason about. Check whether a language feature protects a binding, an object's immediate fields or the entire nested structure. Immutability In FP, data is immutable: instead of changing a value, you create a new one. Immutability removes a whole class of bugs: no function can change your data behind your back, and no other thread can observe a half-updated object. Languages give you different tools, and some are weaker than they look: Language Tool Catch --------- Python tuple, frozenset Tuples can contain mutable objects; set elements must be hashable JavaScript const Binding only JavaScript Object.freeze Shallow Java record, List.of Elements may be mutable Haskell Ordinary pure values Mutable references/arrays exist inside controlled IO/ST effects const is not immutability In JavaScript, const xs = [1, 2] stops you rebinding xs, but xs.push(3) works fine. const freezes the name, not the value. Likewise Object.freeze freezes only the top level of an object. Copying data on every change sounds expensive. Functional languages use persistent data structures that share most of their structure between versions. A map stored as a balanced tree only needs a fresh copy of the nodes on the path from the root to the changed key; every other node is shared with the old version. The path is short: For a balanced binary tree with one million entries, a root-to-leaf path is on the order of 20 nodes; exact path length and rebalancing copies vary. Here n denotes the number of entries: path copying uses O(log n) work rather than copying all O(n) entries. Clojure's persistent hash maps use a hash-array mapped trie with branching up to 32; hash width, sparse nodes and collisions affect the actual path and work. This is a structural model, not a measured allocation count. Key takeaways Binding protection and shallow freezing do not freeze nested objects. Balanced persistent structures reuse unchanged branches. Further reading Clojure: persistent data structures ECMAScript language specification

t: Functions as values and lazy iterators
sum: Higher-order functions accept or return functions.
x: Functions can be passed around just like other values. Each pipeline below assumes the finite integer input nums is [3, 4, 7, 10, 1]; the Java version uses a List<Integer>, and all four pipelines produce the numeric total 116. Functions as values In FP, functions are first-class functions: you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments and return them from other functions. A function that takes or returns a function is a higher-order function. The three workhorses replace most loops: map f xs: apply f to every element. filter p xs: keep elements where p is true. reduce / fold: combine all elements into one value. The same pipeline, sum the squares of the even numbers, in four languages: In Python, a comprehension (sum(n n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0)) is usually considered more idiomatic than map and filter with lambdas. Python's map is a one-shot iterator In Python 3, map and filter return lazy iterators. Once consumed, they are empty: sq = map(f, xs); sum(sq); sum(sq) gives the right total, then 0. Java streams also can't be reused; implementations may throw IllegalStateException when reuse is detected. Key takeaways Higher-order functions accept or return functions. Python map/filter iterators are consumed once. Further reading Python: functional programming Haskell: standard Prelude definitions

sum: A fold combines a seed with each element.
x: A fold records how an accumulated result combines with the next value. Its seed and grouping determine the answer when the operation is sensitive to order. Folds A fold walks a list, combining each element with an accumulator. It is the general pattern behind sum, max, len and even map itself. Each step applies the same rule to the accumulator: Haskell distinguishes the direction: foldl f z [a, b, c] = f (f (f z a) b) c: groups from the left. foldr f z [a, b, c] = f a (f b (f c z)): groups from the right. For a finite list, the two directions give the same mathematical result when the operation is associative and the seed is a two-sided identity element for it: Integer addition with seed 0 has both properties. Floating-point addition is not associative, because each step rounds. Subtraction is not associative either, so the direction matters: In Haskell those are foldl (-) 0 [1,2,3] and foldr (-) 0 [1,2,3]. Key takeaways A fold combines a seed with each element. Associativity and a two-sided identity allow left/right agreement on finite values. Further reading Haskell: standard Prelude definitions Python: functools.reduce

sum: A tail call has no remaining work after its result.
x: A recursive definition can follow the shape of a list directly. Its mathematical clarity does not by itself guarantee bounded stack use in the chosen runtime. Recursion instead of loops Pure functional code avoids mutable loop counters, so repetition is expressed by recursion, often with pattern matching on the shape of the data: Read it as two equations: the length of an empty list is 0; the length of a list with a head and a tail xs is one more than the length of xs. Deep recursion needs care. Each call normally uses a stack frame. Many functional-language implementations support tail-call optimisation (TCO): when the recursive call is the very last thing a function does, the frame is reused, so the tail-call stack can stay bounded. This does not guarantee constant total memory: lazy accumulators, retained data or allocation can still grow. Mainstream languages differ: CPython does not eliminate Python-function tail calls. A standard tested CPython interpreter reports a recursion limit of 1,000 via sys.getrecursionlimit(); this value is configurable and is not a Python-language guarantee. Recursing over a 10,000-element list raises RecursionError. JavaScript: ES2015 specified proper tail calls, but in practice JavaScriptCore (used by Safari) implements them; V8 (Chrome, Node) does not. Java: ordinary JVM bytecode provides no general proper-tail-call guarantee; Scala and Kotlin offer @tailrec / tailrec for self-recursion, compiled into loops. In practice, use map, filter and folds where you can; they express intent, but their space behavior still depends on language, implementation and strictness. Key takeaways A tail call has no remaining work after its result. Stack and total memory depend on the runtime and evaluation strategy. Further reading Guido van Rossum: tail recursion elimination WebKit: proper tail calls

sum: Currying represents several arguments as nested one-argument functions.
x: Functions can return specialised functions and can be combined into pipelines. Keep track of which argument is supplied now and which operation runs first. Currying, partial application and composition In Haskell, every function takes exactly one argument. A "two-argument" function is really a function that returns a function. This is currying, named after Haskell Curry. The type Int -> Int -> Int means Int -> (Int -> Int). Supplying only some arguments is partial application. Other languages do it explicitly: Function composition glues functions end to end. In maths it is written with a small circle: For a concrete example, let the outer function double its input and the inner function add one: Haskell writes the circle as a dot, (f. g) x = f (g x), so. also reads right to left: Writing functions purely as compositions, without naming the argument, is point-free style. Used sparingly it is elegant; overused it becomes cryptic. Trade-offs and pitfalls Performance: immutable updates allocate. Persistent structures and good garbage collectors make this cheap, but tight numeric loops are still often faster with mutation. Stack depth: naive recursion in Python or Java overflows on large inputs. Readability: long chains of map/filter/reduce with complex lambdas can be harder to follow than a plain loop. Name the intermediate functions. Hidden impurity: a "pure-looking" lambda that logs, mutates a captured list or reads a global breaks the guarantees silently. Mutating sorts: JavaScript's arr.sort() and Python's list.sort() mutate in place. Use toSorted() (ES2023) or sorted() for a new copy. Key takeaways Currying represents several arguments as nested one-argument functions. Composition applies the right-hand function first. Further reading Haskell: function expressions Python: partial application

sum: Facts and rules describe relations that queries can use in several modes.
x: Imperative, object-oriented and functional programming dominate everyday code, but two other paradigms quietly power a lot of software: logic programming, where you state facts and rules and ask questions, and dataflow programming, where a program is a graph through which values flow. You may never write Prolog for a living. You almost certainly use spreadsheets, build systems, reactive UI frameworks and static analysers, all of which borrow these ideas. Logic programming In logic programming, a program is a set of Prolog facts and Prolog rules in a form of logic. You run it by asking a query, and the system searches for values that make the query true. Prolog (Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel, Marseille, 1972) is the classic language. Here is a small family database: Read:- as "if" and, as "and". Variables start with a capital letter. The two rules say: X is an ancestor of Y if X is a parent of Y, or if X is a parent of some Z who is an ancestor of Y. There is no function called ancestor that you call with inputs. You ask questions: The same relation answers "is Tom an ancestor of Ann?", "who are Tom's descendants?" and, with ancestor(Who, pat), "who are Pat's ancestors?". The relation itself is not tied to one input/output direction. A particular predicate implementation can still require certain arguments to be bound to terminate or avoid errors; not every Prolog predicate runs safely in every direction. Unification Prolog matches queries against facts and rule heads by unification: finding values for variables that make two terms identical. Term 1 Term 2 Result --------- f(X, b) f(a, Y) X = a, Y = b f(X, X) f(a, b) Fails [H\T] [1, 2, 3] H = 1, T = [2, 3] The [HT] pattern splits a list into head and tail, much like pattern matching in Haskell, but unification works in both directions. That lets you run some predicates "backwards": append was written to join lists, yet here it enumerates every way to split one. Key takeaways Facts and rules describe relations that queries can use in several modes. Unification finds consistent bindings across whole terms. Further reading SWI-Prolog: a quick start SWI-Prolog: unification

sum: Ordinary untabled Prolog tries clauses and goals in a defined search order.
x: A set of logical rules also needs an execution strategy. Ordinary untabled Prolog's search order determines which answers appear and whether the search reaches them. Backtracking search Prolog answers a query by depth-first search with backtracking (using SLD resolution with this particular search strategy). It tries clauses top to bottom and goals left to right. When a goal fails, it backtracks to the most recent choice and tries the next alternative. This makes Prolog declarative in meaning but procedural in behaviour. Clause order and goal order matter: Left recursion loops Write the recursive rule as ancestor(X, Y):- ancestor(X, Z), parent(Z, Y). and put it first, and a query like ancestor(tom, W) calls ancestor(tom, Z), which calls ancestor(tom, Z2), forever, until the stack runs out. Logically it is the same rule. Operationally it never reaches a fact. Closed world and negation Prolog uses the closed-world assumption: a goal that finitely fails is treated as false for negation as failure. A search that loops has not established failure. Negation is negation as failure: \+ parent(ann, _) succeeds if Prolog fails to find any child of Ann. That is not the same as "Ann has no children" in classical logic; it means the goal finitely failed against the available facts and rules. Key takeaways Ordinary untabled Prolog tries clauses and goals in a defined search order. Negation as failure requires finite failure; looping is no proof of absence. Further reading SWI-Prolog: tabling SWI-Prolog: negation as failure/1)

sum: Finite positive function-free Datalog reaches a least fixed point.
x: A finite set of possible facts supports a different evaluation strategy: repeatedly derive facts until none are new. State the restrictions before relying on this process to terminate. Finite facts and practical logic languages For a small bottom-up trace, take the parent chain a → b → c → d and use the two ancestor rules from the earlier relations unit. Start with no ancestor facts, retaining the parent facts throughout. Each round uses only facts present at its start. Round one derives the three direct ancestor pairs. Round two adds the two pairs two edges apart. Round three adds a as an ancestor of d. A further round adds nothing, so the six ancestor pairs form the fixed point. This synchronous-round convention matters: an engine that immediately uses facts produced earlier in the same pass may require fewer passes, while deriving the same least fixed point. The finite-domain guarantee here assumes positive rules, no generated new constants and the ordinary set interpretation of facts. A safe rule binds its head variables through positive body relations; real Datalog dialects may offer additional constructs. Datalog is a restricted logic language: no compound data terms and (in its basic form) every rule must be safe. For basic positive, function-free Datalog over a finite domain, bottom-up fixed-point evaluation terminates because only finitely many facts can be derived. Bottom-up evaluation is common, not the only strategy. Extensions such as arithmetic that generates new values can lose the finite-domain termination guarantee. GitHub's CodeQL query language is a Datalog descendant used to find security bugs; Soufflé runs Datalog static analyses of Java programs; Datomic queries are Datalog. Policy engines: Open Policy Agent's Rego language was inspired by Datalog. SQL recursive CTEs compute the same transitive closure as ancestor. Constraint logic programming (for example CLP(FD) in SWI-Prolog) solves scheduling and puzzles by stating constraints instead of search code. Type checkers: Rust's trait solver and Haskell's type class resolution are logic-programming engines internally. Key takeaways Finite positive function-free Datalog reaches a least fixed point. Extensions must be checked before relying on that termination guarantee. Further reading Soufflé: Datalog tutorial CodeQL overview

sum: Dependency edges constrain a valid recalculation order.
x: A spreadsheet exposes data dependencies directly: each formula reads other cells. Those dependencies explain both recalculation order and circular-reference errors. Dataflow programming A dataflow program is a directed graph. Nodes are operations; edges carry values. A node runs when its inputs are available, and its outputs flow to downstream nodes. There is no program counter stepping through statements: order is determined by data dependencies alone. Because only dependencies constrain order, independent nodes can run in parallel automatically. Spreadsheets Spreadsheets are a familiar example of dataflow-style dependencies. Each formula cell is a node; references are edges. Cell Formula Value --------- A1 5 5 B1 =A13 15 C1 =A1+B1 20 In an automatic, nonvolatile acyclic calculation, changing A1 causes dependent cells to be recalculated in dependency order (B1 before C1, since C1 depends on B1). A formula that depends on itself, directly or indirectly, makes the graph cyclic, which Excel normally reports as a circular reference; optional iterative calculation can handle intentionally circular models subject to its convergence settings. A cyclic deps makes TopologicalSorter raise CycleError: the same check as a circular reference. Key takeaways Dependency edges constrain a valid recalculation order. Cycles require special semantics rather than ordinary topological evaluation. Further reading Excel recalculation Python: topological sorting

sum: Dataflow appears in pipes, builds, distributed processing and reactive UI.
x: The same dependency idea appears in build tools, stream processing and user interfaces. Reactive systems must avoid mixing a newly updated source with an old derived value. Other dataflow systems Unix pipes: cat log grep ERROR sort uniq -c is a linear dataflow graph; processes can run concurrently, but sort generally needs the complete input before producing globally sorted output. Build systems: Make and Bazel track dependencies to decide which targets need rebuilding. Missing outputs, changed commands or configuration, and explicitly always-run targets can also trigger work. Visual languages: LabVIEW (lab instruments) and Simulink (control systems) are programmed by wiring boxes together. Synchronous languages: Lustre and tools such as SCADE use clocked stream semantics for safety-critical embedded software. This is distinct from the fixed token-production/consumption model also called synchronous dataflow; both support static reasoning under their respective restrictions, but neither label alone proves every timing property. Data processing: Apache Beam, Apache Flink and Apache Spark build dataflow graphs of transformations and distribute them across a cluster. TensorFlow 1.x had you build a graph first, then run it. Reactive programming Reactive UI frameworks apply dataflow to user interfaces. In libraries based on reactive signals (SolidJS, Preact Signals, Angular signals, Vue's refs), a value declares what it is computed from, and the runtime tracks dependencies and updates only what's affected. A naive push-based implementation can suffer glitches. In the graph above, if a changes and c is recomputed before b, c briefly sees the new a with the old b: an inconsistent state that never "should" exist. Glitch-free systems either update in topological order or mark nodes dirty and recompute lazily on read. Trade-offs Paradigm Strength Weakness --------- Prolog Search, rules Hidden cost, loops Basic finite-domain Datalog Fixed-point termination Extensions may lose guarantee Dataflow Parallel, incremental Cycles, glitches Both paradigms shine when the problem is naturally a set of rules (permissions, type systems, code analysis) or a graph of dependent values (spreadsheets, builds, UIs), and are awkward for long sequential processes. Key takeaways Dataflow appears in pipes, builds, distributed processing and reactive UI. A glitch combines newly updated inputs with stale dependencies. Further reading Preact: how signals compute updates Verimag: Lustre and synchronous languages

sum: Most mainstream languages offer several ways to structure a program.
x: The earlier lessons treated paradigms as separate worlds. In practice, almost no popular language is "pure" anything. Python has classes, first-class functions, comprehensions and a match statement. Java added lambdas, records and pattern matching. Rust has no classes yet feels object-oriented and functional at once. A multi-paradigm language gives you several styles in one toolbox. That's powerful, but it moves the decision from the language designer to you. This lesson is about making that decision well. Why languages converged Paradigms began as rival camps. Smalltalk was objects all the way down; Haskell was pure functions; Prolog was logic. Over the last two decades, mainstream languages borrowed the best ideas from each: Language Base Borrowed --------- Java OOP Lambdas, streams (8), records (16), sealed types (17) C# OOP LINQ (3.0), pattern matching C++ Imperative/OOP Lambdas (C++11), ranges (C++20) Python Imperative/OOP Comprehensions, match (3.10) JavaScript Prototypes First-class functions from day one Newer languages were designed mixed from the start. Scala and Kotlin fuse OOP and FP on the JVM. Swift pairs classes with value-type structs and enums with payloads. F# and OCaml are functional-first but have objects and mutable state when you need them. Rust is a good example of how far the mix can go. It has: Structs and impl blocks with methods (object-like encapsulation) Traits for polymorphism, but no class inheritance Enums with data and exhaustive match (from the ML family) Iterator chains like map and filter that compile to tight loops Ordinary mutable variables and for loops The reason for the convergence is simple: each paradigm is good at different parts of a program, and real programs have all those parts. Key takeaways Most mainstream languages offer several ways to structure a program. Feature support and release versions are concrete language facts. Further reading Java 21 features Rust: object-oriented features

t: The expression problem and extension axes
sum: Class-based interfaces make adding implementations convenient.
x: A design can make adding data variants convenient or make adding operations convenient. Identify which axis changes most often before choosing how to organise the code. The expression problem The clearest way to see what each style is good at is the expression problem, a name Philip Wadler gave it in 1998. You have some types of data and some operations on them. Over time you'll add both. Which is easy depends on how you organised the code. Here is the object-oriented version. Each class carries its own operations: Adding a new type (Triangle) is easy: write one new class, without editing existing shape operations, assuming construction/registration is handled separately. Adding a new operation (perimeter) is hard: you edit every class. Here is the functional version, with plain data and functions that match on it: Now it flips. Adding perimeter is one new function. Adding Triangle means editing every function that matches on shapes. Neither is wrong. The question is which axis your code grows along: New types, fixed operations: GUI widgets, plugins, payment providers. Each new kind of thing implements a known interface. OOP fits. Fixed types, new operations: compilers and interpreters. The syntax tree has a stable set of node kinds, and you keep adding passes (type check, optimise, generate code). Pattern matching fits, which is why compilers are so often written in OCaml, Haskell, Rust or Scala. The visitor pattern OOP languages without pattern matching use the visitor pattern to get the functional trade-off: each node has an accept(visitor) method, and each operation is a visitor class with one method per node type. It uses double dispatch to make new operations cheap, at the cost of making new node types expensive. It's pattern matching written the long way. Closed variant sets support exhaustiveness checks where the language requires them, such as Rust match and Java 21 pattern-switch (Java sealed types themselves arrived in 17). Requirements vary by construct/language. Python’s interpreter does not check match exhaustiveness: no matching case continues after the statement, returning None only if the function then falls off its end. Key takeaways Class-based interfaces make adding implementations convenient. Pattern matching over closed variants makes adding operations convenient. Further reading Philip Wadler: the expression problem Python: pattern matching tutorial

t: A functional core with an imperative shell
sum: Supply external facts as parameters to pure decision functions.
x: A decision function is easier to test when the facts it needs arrive as arguments. Keep the work that obtains and stores those facts in an outer layer. Functional core, imperative shell A common way to mix paradigms in one program is the pattern Gary Bernhardt called functional core, imperative shell. Put the decisions in pure functions. Keep the side effects (network, database, clock, files) in a thin outer layer that calls them. The core is tested with plain values and no mocks: pass in an order and a date, check the number. The shell still needs integration tests for failures, retries, transactions and other relevant boundary behavior. Notice that today is a parameter, not a call to date.today() inside the core. Hiding the clock call inside would make the function impure and its tests depend on the day you run them. This scales up to architecture. Redux reducers and Elm's update function put a pure state-transition function at the centre. Event-sourced systems can use the same approach when replaying events; event sourcing itself specifies storing events, not a universal guarantee that every handler is pure. Key takeaways Supply external facts as parameters to pure decision functions. The effectful shell still needs integration tests and failure handling. Further reading Functional Core, Imperative Shell Elm architecture

t: Python style, copying and shallow freezing
sum: Python recursion and repeated list joining have practical limits.
x: Python supports functional techniques, but its recursion, containers and copying rules still apply. Trace allocation and mutation before choosing an apparently concise expression. Work with the language, not against it A multi-paradigm language still has a grain: styles it supports well and styles it only tolerates. Fighting the grain costs performance and readability. Python Python supports functional style but isn't built around it: No tail-call optimisation. Guido van Rossum rejected it deliberately, partly to keep full stack traces. A standard tested CPython configuration reports a limit of 1,000 (configurable), so a recursive sum over a 10,000-item list raises RecursionError. Use a loop or sum(). Lambdas are single expressions. Anything longer should be a named def. Immutability is shallow, and you must ask for it. A frozen=True dataclass blocks ordinary field assignment, but a list stored in a field can still be mutated. Use tuples and frozenset for the contents and ensure their nested contents are immutable too. Copying is not free. sum(list_of_lists, []) looks elegant but builds a new list at every step, which is quadratic for n single-element lists; more generally cost depends on both the number and lengths of the lists. itertools.chain.from_iterable is linear. Where the quadratic cost comes from: sum starts from [] and does acc = acc + item once per list. Each + builds a brand-new list and copies everything gathered so far, so with n lists of one item each, step k copies k items. For 10,000 lists that is 50,005,000 copies, about 50 million, against 10,000 for chain.from_iterable. Ten times more lists means about a hundred times more copying. This is what quadratic time means: cost growing with n squared, written O(n²). Linear time means cost growing in direct proportion to n, written O(n). Key takeaways Python recursion and repeated list joining have practical limits. A frozen dataclass can still contain mutable objects. Further reading Guido van Rossum: tail recursion elimination Python: frozen dataclasses

t: Choosing a language and a working style
sum: Language and style choices depend on the ecosystem, team and workload.
x: Compiler optimisation and runtime support influence which idioms work well. Use those constraints alongside the team, ecosystem and shape of the problem when choosing a language or style. JavaScript JavaScript has had first-class functions and closures since 1995, and map, filter and reduce on arrays since ES5 (2009). Its objects use prototypes, with class syntax added in ES2015 as a cleaner way to write the same thing. ES2015 also specified proper tail calls, but in practice JavaScriptCore (used by Safari) implements them, so deep recursion in Chrome or Node still overflows the stack. Rust and C++ Here the functional style is often free. A chain like v.iter().map(f).filter(g).sum() can compile, after suitable optimisation and inlining, to code comparable to a hand-written loop. The result depends on the functions, types, target and compiler options; the abstraction is not a universal performance guarantee. Rust's ownership rules also nudge you away from shared mutable state, the thing that makes OOP code hard to reason about. Java Streams are pleasant but have overhead: pipeline objects and boxing can add overhead, though JIT optimization can remove some allocations and boxed values may be cached or already exist.
