For hot loops over primitives, use IntStream or a plain for. Choosing a language The paradigm is rarely the deciding factor. In rough order of importance for most teams: Ecosystem and platform. Swift is a common native iOS choice, though Objective-C and cross-platform approaches also exist. The browser means JavaScript or TypeScript (or something that compiles to it or to WebAssembly). Python is widely used in data science, because that's where NumPy, pandas and PyTorch live. The team. A language five people know well beats a better one nobody knows. Hiring and onboarding count. Runtime needs. Latency, memory and startup time. A garbage collector may be fine for a web service and a problem for a game engine or an embedded device. Correctness needs. Strong static types and exhaustive matching catch whole classes of bug before production. That matters more for a payments ledger than a one-off script. Problem shape. Rules and queries suggest SQL or Datalog. Tree transformations suggest an ML-family language. Highly concurrent servers suggest Go, Erlang/Elixir or Rust. Most real systems use several languages: SQL for queries, a general-purpose language for services, a shell for glue, a configuration language for infrastructure. Choosing a language is often choosing which part of the system gets which one. Choosing a style within a language Inside one codebase, a few rules of thumb help: Data transformations: pipelines, comprehensions or iterator chains. Long-lived things with state and identity (a connection pool, a game entity): objects with encapsulated state. A closed set of variants (AST nodes, message types, results): sealed types or enums with pattern matching. An open set of implementations (storage back ends, payment providers): interfaces, traits or protocols. Effects: at the edges, so the middle stays pure and testable. Pitfalls Style soup. One module uses classes, the next uses closures and dictionaries, the next uses inheritance six levels deep. Pick conventions per layer and write them down. Clever over clear. A three-line loop is often more readable than a nested reduce with a lambda. Use the declarative form when it states the intent better, not to show off. Importing idioms that don't fit. Monad libraries in Python, or faking class inheritance in Rust by abusing Deref, usually fight the language. Choosing for the paradigm. Rewriting a working system in a "better paradigm" language rarely pays for itself. The ecosystem, team and runtime usually matter more. Key takeaways Language and style choices depend on the ecosystem, team and workload. Optimisation claims need the actual compiler and workload assumptions. Further reading Rust: loops versus iterators WebKit: proper tail calls

t: Binding times and lexical or dynamic scope
sum: Scope describes name resolution; lifetime describes existence during execution.
x: Every paradigm in this module rests on the same few questions. When you write x, which x do you mean? When a function is created inside another function, what happens to the variables it uses after the outer function returns? And when you call f(g()), does g() run before f, inside f, or maybe never? The answers are scope, binding, closures and evaluation strategy. Get them wrong and you get some of the most confusing bugs in programming: loops that capture the wrong value, defaults that remember old calls, and functions that mutate their caller's data "by accident". Binding and binding time A binding is an association between a name and something: a value, a memory location, a type, a function. Languages differ in when bindings are fixed: When Example ------ Language design + means addition Compile time A C declaration's type (storage placement can vary) Link/load time A call to printf resolved to an address Run time A Python name bound by x = 5 Earlier binding can enable optimisation and earlier diagnostics, but does not guarantee faster execution. Later binding can support more flexibility: Python can rebind any name, add methods to a class at run time, or swap a module during a test. The scope of a binding is the region of program text where the name refers to it. The lifetime is how long the thing exists. They aren't the same: a C static local has block scope but lives for the whole program, and a closure variable (below) outlives the function that created it. Lexical vs dynamic scope With lexical scope (also called static scope), a name refers to the binding in the nearest enclosing block in the source code. You can work it out by reading the program. Almost every modern language works this way: C, Java, Python, JavaScript, Rust, Haskell. With dynamic scope, a name refers to the most recent binding on the call stack at run time. Early Lisps worked this way, Emacs Lisp did by default for decades, and so does Bash: show has no x of its own. Under dynamic scope it sees whichever x its caller had. Under lexical scope it would always print global, because that's the x visible where show was written. Dynamic scope is occasionally handy (a "current output stream" every function picks up), but it makes code hard to reason about: a function's behaviour depends on who called it. Scheme (1975) showed lexical scope could work in Lisp, and the industry followed. Languages that want the dynamic behaviour now ask for it explicitly: Common Lisp's special variables and Perl's local. Python's contextvars explicitly propagates values through execution contexts, and React context through a component tree; neither changes those languages' lexical variable lookup. Key takeaways Scope describes name resolution; lifetime describes existence during execution. Dynamic scope follows active callers; lexical scope follows source nesting. Further reading Python: naming and binding Bash: shell functions

t: Python name resolution and local bindings
sum: A function binding normally makes the name local throughout that function.
x: Python usually resolves an ordinary name through local, enclosing-function, module and built-in namespaces. A binding anywhere in a function can change how every use of that name is classified. Python's scope rules Python resolves names in the LEGB order: Local, Enclosing function, Global (module), Built-in. The key subtlety: Python decides a name's scope at compile time, for the whole function. Unless a global or nonlocal declaration applies, binding a name anywhere in a function makes it local throughout that function: Because of x = 5, x is local to f. The print runs before that local has a value, so Python raises UnboundLocalError rather than reading the global. To assign to an outer name, declare it: global x rebinds the module-level x. nonlocal x rebinds x in the nearest enclosing function. Two more rules trip people up: Ordinary for and if suites do not create scopes. A variable assigned in a for or if is visible after it. After for k in range(3): pass, k is 2. The ordinary class namespace does not enclose methods. A method can't see class-level names directly; it must write self.y or ClassName.y. Comprehensions in a class body can't see them either, except in the outermost for... in expression. JavaScript had the block problem with var, which is function-scoped. ES2015's let and const are block-scoped, which is one reason style guides ban var. Key takeaways A function binding normally makes the name local throughout that function. Class namespace lookup differs from the enclosing-function rule. Further reading Python: naming and binding

sum: Each counter invocation creates a distinct captured binding.
x: Returning an inner function can keep an enclosing binding available after its creator returns. Separate that lifetime behavior from the time when each callback reads its binding. Closures A closure is a function together with the environment it was created in. It can use variables from enclosing scopes even after those scopes have returned: counter returned long ago, yet n lives on. Each call to counter() creates a fresh n, so two counters don't interfere. A closure is a little object with private state; the old saying goes "closures are a poor man's objects, and objects are a poor man's closures". Python closures capture bindings In Python and ordinary JavaScript closures, references to lexical bindings persist; other languages offer capture by value or reference. This distinction is the source of a famous bug: All three lambdas close over the same variable i. They don't look it up until they're called, by which time the loop has finished and i is 2. This is late binding. The usual fix is to bind the current value at creation time, using a default argument (defaults are evaluated when the function is defined): functools.partial does the same job more explicitly. JavaScript shows the same issue and a language-level fix: With let, the spec creates a new binding for each loop iteration, so each closure captures a different variable. Key takeaways Each counter invocation creates a distinct captured binding. Defaults or per-iteration bindings can preserve each loop value. Further reading Python: closures and cells ECMAScript language specification

sum: Escaping captures must remain valid beyond the creating call.
x: A captured value must remain valid whenever a closure uses it. Languages differ in how they retain bindings, copy values and reject references that would outlive their data. How closures are implemented A C function's automatic locals have block lifetime and are commonly stored in a call frame; static locals have a different lifetime and compilers can keep automatic values in registers or remove them entirely. A closure breaks that: an inner function may be returned and called later, after the outer frame is gone. This is the upward funarg problem, and it's why closures need captured variables to live somewhere longer-lived, usually heap storage. In the discussion below, c is the counter closure from the preceding unit, after three calls; its captured n binding holds the integer 3. CPython stores captured variables in cell objects. You can see them: c.__closure__[0].cell_contents is 3. Both the outer function and every closure share the same cell, which is how nonlocal writes are visible. Lua uses upvalues: they point into the stack while the outer function runs and are moved ("closed") to heap storage when it returns. C has no closures. Callbacks take a function pointer plus a void context argument, which is a closure built by hand. Rust and C++ make capture explicit. A C++ lambda says [x] (copy) or [&x] (reference); a reference that outlives x is undefined behaviour. Safe Rust rejects escaping borrows that outlive their referents. A move closure captures by value, moving or copying its captures; moving a borrowed reference does not extend the referent’s lifetime. Closures also keep their environment alive. In JavaScript, an event listener that closes over a large object keeps that object from being garbage collected while the listener and captured object remain reachable. Removing the listener helps only if no other live reference retains the closure or object. Key takeaways Escaping captures must remain valid beyond the creating call. Capture ownership and storage choices differ between languages. Further reading Lua: variable visibility and upvalues Rust: closure captures

t: Strict arguments, sharing and mutable defaults
sum: Mutating a shared object differs from rebinding a local parameter.
x: Evaluating an argument and passing its value does not imply copying the whole object. Separate a mutation of shared data from a reassignment of a local parameter. Evaluation strategies When you call f(expr), an evaluation strategy decides when expr is evaluated and what f receives. Strict: evaluate arguments first Most languages use strict evaluation (applicative order): argument expressions are evaluated to values before the call; this does not recursively force lazy objects or traverse referenced data. Within strict languages, the question is what gets passed: Call by value (C and Java, including Java reference values): the function gets a copy. Assigning to the parameter can't affect the caller. Call by reference (C++ int&, C# ref, Pascal var): the parameter is an alias for the caller's variable. Assigning to it changes the caller's variable. Call by sharing (a useful description of Python, JavaScript, Ruby and Java object-reference behavior): the function gets a copy of a reference to the object. The term comes from Barbara Liskov's CLU. Call by sharing confuses people because it behaves like reference for mutation and like value for assignment: rebind creates a new list and points the local name at it; the caller's L is untouched. extend looks like rebind, but += on a list calls __iadd__, which extends the list in place. On an immutable type like a tuple or int, += would rebind instead. Mutable default arguments Python evaluates default values once, when def runs. So def add(v, acc=[]) shares one list across every call: add(1) returns [1], then add(2) returns [1, 2]. Use acc=None and create the list inside the function. Key takeaways Mutating a shared object differs from rebinding a local parameter. Python evaluates default argument expressions when def executes. Further reading Python: calls and argument values Python: assignment statements

t: Call by name, call by need and short circuiting
sum: Call by name repeats demand; call by need shares an evaluated result.
x: Some languages defer an argument expression until its value is needed. The distinction between repeating a deferred computation and sharing its result affects both work and memory. Non-strict: evaluate arguments only when needed Call by name (Algol 60's default; Scala's x: => Int parameters): the argument expression is passed unevaluated and re-evaluated every time the parameter is used. Call by need (Haskell): like call by name, but the result is cached after the first evaluation. This is lazy evaluation. R's function arguments are also lazy "promises". The difference matters when an argument is expensive, has side effects, or never terminates. In this pseudocode, loop_forever() stands for a nonterminating expression; it is deliberately not supplied as a runnable function: Strategy Result ------ Call by value Hangs: b is evaluated first Call by name Returns 1: b never used Call by need Returns 1: b never used In the abstract strategies, if all three uses demand the argument value, call by name evaluates the expression on each demand, while call by need shares the result after the first evaluation. A real compiler may optimise pure expressions while preserving language semantics. With side effects, call by name can even give different values each time, which Algol programmers exploited in a trick called Jensen's device. Even strict languages have non-strict corners. and, or and the ternary a if c else b short-circuit: in x is not None and x.ok, the right side only runs if needed. Python generators and iterators are lazy too, as the functional basics lesson showed. Laziness has costs. Unevaluated expressions ("thunks") use memory, and it's hard to predict when work happens. Haskell programs sometimes leak memory by building long chains of thunks, which is why it offers strictness annotations and functions like foldl'. Pitfalls checklist Late-binding closures in loops: bind the value with a default argument, partial or let. UnboundLocalError: an assignment later in the function made the name local. Add global/nonlocal or rename. Mutable defaults: use None and create inside. Surprise mutation: under call by sharing, functions can mutate arguments. Copy defensively or use immutable types. Dangling captures in C++: capturing by reference in a lambda that outlives the scope. Leaky closures: long-lived callbacks can retain the captured objects they need; implementations may omit unused bindings. Key takeaways Call by name repeats demand; call by need shares an evaluated result. Laziness changes work and space behavior and does not force every nested value. Further reading Haskell: non-strict expression semantics ALGOL 60 revised report

sum: Static checking analyses a program before execution; dynamic typing checks operations on runtime values.
x: Every value in a running program is just bits. The bit pattern 0x41 could be the integer 65, the character A, or part of a pointer. A type is the extra knowledge that tells you which interpretation is meant, and therefore which operations make sense. Think of a type as a set of values plus the operations allowed on them. int is a set of whole numbers that you can add and compare. str is a set of character sequences that you can concatenate and slice. A type error is an attempt to apply an operation to a value outside its set: dividing a string, calling a number as if it were a function. A type system is the set of rules a language uses to detect (or prevent) those errors. Languages differ on two separate questions: When are types checked? Before the program runs (static) or while it runs (dynamic)? Which coercions are permitted? One informal use of strong/weak distinguishes fewer implicit conversions from more permissive conversions; these labels have no universal definition. People often blur these, saying "Python is weakly typed" when they mean "dynamically typed". The absence of annotations does not establish which conversions Python permits; keep the two questions separate. Static typing: check before running A statically typed language checks types by analysing the source code, usually at compile time. A checker assigns static types and reports violations of its rules before execution. Some tools still emit executable code despite errors, and runtime checks or escape hatches may remain. Java, C, C++, C#, Go, Rust, Haskell, OCaml, Kotlin, Swift and TypeScript are all statically typed. Static does not mean you must write the types. Haskell and OCaml infer almost everything, and Rust and modern Java infer local variable types: Writing types explicitly is called manifest typing. Working out types without explicit annotations uses type inference, covered in the following inference units. Dynamic typing: check while running In a dynamically typed language, the rules of an operation depend on the types of its runtime values, rather than requiring every operation to pass a static type checker. Rebinding rules are a separate language choice. Tagged values are a common implementation model, but optimizers can prove checks unnecessary or use other representations. The second call fails only when that line actually executes. Python's message is can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. A bug on a code path your tests never run will sit there silently until a user hits it. Python, JavaScript, Ruby, PHP, Lua, Erlang, Clojure and Lisp are dynamically typed. Dynamic does not mean untyped Python enforces operation rules at runtime. Lower-level untyped models lack comparable high-level guarantees; assembly instructions still have operand and representation requirements. Duck typing Dynamic languages usually care whether a value supports the operation, not what class it is. If it has a.read() method, you can read from it. This is duck typing: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck". It is flexible, and it is also why a typo in a method name can go unnoticed until run time. Key takeaways Static checking analyses a program before execution; dynamic typing checks operations on runtime values. Inference can make static code concise; runtime tags are an implementation technique, not the definition of dynamic typing. Further reading Luca Cardelli: Type systems Python built-in numeric types Java Language Specification: Conversions

sum: Strong and weak are informal labels; identify the exact conversion rules instead.
x: Static versus dynamic describes when checking happens. A different, informal discussion concerns which implicit conversions a language permits; it needs concrete operator examples rather than a single strength label. Strong and weak: how much coercion? The second axis is about implicit conversions (coercions). When you combine mismatched types, does the language refuse, or does it convert one of them for you? Unlike static/dynamic, "strong" and "weak" have no single formal definition. They describe a spectrum. JavaScript sits near the weak end: Under this informal coercion-based convention, Python sits near the strong end. "5" + 2 raises TypeError rather than guessing. Python still has a few deliberate coercions: 1 + 2.5 widens the int to a float, and 1 + True is 2 because bool is a subclass of int. Reading an operator before trusting it In the first JavaScript expression, addition first converts operands to primitive values. Because one primitive is a string, the other becomes text and concatenation produces two characters. Subtraction instead requests numeric operands, so the text digit becomes a number before subtraction. The result therefore depends on the operator as well as on the values. For equality, use the actual rule rather than the strong/weak label: JavaScript == can convert operands; === compares without that coercion. Strict equality still has its own rules, including that NaN is unequal to itself. Python’s refusal to concatenate a string and an integer does not imply it forbids every mixed numeric operation. Key takeaways Strong and weak are informal labels; identify the exact conversion rules instead. JavaScript addition and subtraction use different conversion rules; Python rejects string-plus-integer concatenation. Further reading ECMAScript specification: Expressions Python built-in numeric types C11 draft standard

sum: Rust requires an explicit integer widening conversion; Java permits selected widening and string conversions.
x: Python and JavaScript illustrated different mixed-type operations in the previous unit. Static languages also differ: inspect their numeric conversion rules and safety guarantees separately. Numeric conversions C is statically typed but weak in an important sense. It converts freely between numeric types (int x = 3.9; silently truncates to 3), and pointer casts can bypass useful static checks. A cast alone need not be erroneous, but invalid alignment or accessing an object through an incompatible type can cause undefined behaviour. Rust is at the strict end even for numbers. It will not widen an i32 to an i64 without being asked: Java, by contrast, widens int to long silently, and "a" + 1 is "a1" because + with a String converts the other side. The two axes together Strong-ish Weak-ish --------- Static Rust, Haskell, Java C, C++ Dynamic Python, Ruby JavaScript, PHP Treat this as a rough map, not a ranking. Every language makes some coercions and forbids others. A more precise discussion names the actual type safety property and its assumptions: the guarantee that a program which passes the checks can never perform an operation on a value of the wrong type in a way that corrupts memory or gets "stuck". Robin Milner summarised it in 1978 as "well-typed programs cannot go wrong". A checked Java cast can raise ClassCastException, and a Python operation can raise TypeError, rather than reinterpreting an object as arbitrary memory. These runtime protections differ from a proof that every statically accepted source program avoids unexpected type mismatches. C permits undefined behaviour in cases such as invalid typed memory access. Key takeaways Rust requires an explicit integer widening conversion; Java permits selected widening and string conversions. Static checking and memory safety are separate properties. Further reading Java Language Specification: Conversions The Rust Book: Generic types Luca Cardelli: Type systems C11 draft standard

sum: Checked casts, bounds and array-store checks can remain in statically typed languages.
x: Static checking can rule out classes of mistakes before execution while deliberately retaining some runtime checks. Its guarantee is relative to a language’s rules, implementation and explicit escape hatches. Static languages still check at run time Static checking cannot prove everything, so static languages keep some dynamic checks: Downcasts: in Java, (String) obj is checked at run time and may throw ClassCastException. Array bounds: Java, Rust and C# check indices at run time. Covariant array stores: Java checks that each value stored into a reference array fits the array's real element type (the JIT may eliminate checks it proves unnecessary) (the later variance units explain why). And dynamic languages can be checked statically: TypeScript adds static checking to JavaScript-compatible source, and mypy or Pyright check Python type hints. That hybrid is gradual typing (the later gradual-typing units). Static checkers are conservative A static checker must decide without running the program. Deciding exactly which programs will hit a type error is undecidable in general (it would solve the halting problem), so a checker has to approximate. Sound checkers err on the safe side and reject some programs that would actually run fine: The programmer knows o holds a String; the checker only knows its declared type is Object. You fix this with a cast or a better declared type. A checker’s accepted programs depend on its rules: an annotation, narrowing test or checked cast can communicate information its analysis does not otherwise retain. Trade-offs Static Dynamic --------- Type checks Static constraints before execution; runtime checks may remain Operation rules checked during execution Tooling Declared/inferred types can guide tooling Inference, annotations and runtime knowledge can guide tooling Speed Depends on representation and implementation Depends on representation and implementation Flexibility Must satisfy checked constraints Runtime operation rules still apply Quick experiments REPLs and incremental checkers are possible REPLs and compilation are possible What does this buy in practice? A 2017 study, To Type or Not to Type (Gao, Bird and Barr), examined a sample of fixed bugs in public JavaScript projects, added annotations, and found that TypeScript 2.0 and Flow 0.30 each detected about 15%. This historical sample does not estimate every project or current checker; undetected bugs were not all established to be inherently beyond type checking. A useful way to think about it A sound type system can prove specified properties about all executions within its model and assumptions. Practical checkers may intentionally be unsound. Tests are evidence about some executions, but can check anything. They complement each other. Common pitfalls Confusing the axes. Calling Python weak solely because it is dynamic confuses two questions. Calling C strong solely because it is static makes the same mistake; the strength labels are informal. Assuming static means safe. C and C++ are static but allow memory-unsafe casts and undefined behaviour. Assuming annotations are enforced. Python type hints can be checked by separate tools and remain available as annotation metadata (with deferred evaluation in Python 3.14); Python does not enforce them by itself. TypeScript type annotations are erased during compilation. def f(x: int) will happily accept a string at run time. Relying on coercion. JavaScript's == converts operands; use ===, which never coerces. Key takeaways Checked casts, bounds and array-store checks can remain in statically typed languages. Exact prediction of arbitrary runtime type errors is undecidable; sound analysis may reject safe executions. Historical bug-detection samples are evidence about that sample, not a universal forecast. Further reading Luca Cardelli: Type systems Java Language Specification: Conversions Java Language Specification: Arrays Gao et al.: To type or not to type

sum: Java infers a local binding from its initialiser; TypeScript also uses expected context.
x: Some statically typed APIs require repetitive annotations: ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();. The compiler already knew the right-hand side was an ArrayList<String>, so the annotation was pure ceremony. Type inference lets the compiler work types out from how values are used. You get the safety of static checking without most of the typing. How much a language can infer varies enormously, from "the type of this one variable" to "every type in the whole program". Local inference: from the right-hand side The simplest form looks at an initialiser and copies its type to the variable: C++ auto, C# var, Go's x:= 1 short declaration, Kotlin val and Swift let can similarly infer a local from its initialiser. This example does not describe each language’s full inference rules: contextual and bidirectional inference can also contribute. It has limits. In Java, var list = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<Object>, because the diamond operator <> has nothing to go on. Method parameters and fields must still be annotated. TypeScript: local plus contextual TypeScript infers variable and return types, and also flows types inwards from context (contextual typing): TypeScript does not infer parameter types from how a function body uses them. That last line is the key difference from Hindley–Milner. Rust: inference within a function Rust requires full signatures on functions but infers many local types inside the body, including from later uses: Sometimes nothing pins a type down, and you must help: Without the Vec<i32> annotation, neither parse nor collect knows what to produce, and the compiler reports that type annotations are needed (the diagnostic code depends on the unresolved constraint). Rust also accepts explicit type arguments at the call site:.collect::<Vec<i32>>() fixes both the collection and its element type. This::<...> notation is often called the turbofish. Writing only.parse::<i32>() fixes the parsed element but leaves collect ambiguous. Alternatively, Vec<_> on the binding fixes the collection while parse::<i32>() fixes its element; the underscore asks Rust to infer the remaining part. Python's mypy does something similar. x = [] followed by x.append(1) in the same scope infers list[int]; a bare x = [] with no later clue is an error: Need type annotation for "x". Key takeaways Java infers a local binding from its initialiser; TypeScript also uses expected context. Rust can use later local constraints; ambiguous parse and collect operations still need information. Further reading OpenJDK: Local variable inference TypeScript Handbook: Type inference Rust by Example: Inference mypy: Inference and annotations

sum: Hindley–Milner infers the core calculus using constraints, unification and let generalisation.
x: The previous unit used language-specific local inference. This unit studies the simpler Hindley–Milner core: ordinary functions, application and let bindings, before extensions such as overloading or subtyping. Global inference: Hindley–Milner ML, OCaml, Haskell, F# and Elm go much further. Their HM-style cores can infer principal types without annotations. Real languages add features and restrictions, so this is not a guarantee for every program in each language. The system behind this is Hindley–Milner (HM), discovered by Roger Hindley (1969) and independently by Robin Milner (1978). Milner's inference procedure is called Algorithm W; Luis Damas and Milner proved in 1982 that it always finds the most general type. HM works in three steps: Assign a fresh type variable to every unknown. Generate constraints from how things are used. Solve the constraints by unification, then generalise eligible variables not free in the typing environment at a let binding. Worked example: compose Type-theory papers use a compact notation for this, and the next three steps use it. A colon means "has type", and an arrow builds a function type. Steps 1 and 2: give each unknown a type variable, then read off one constraint per function call. g x applies g to x, so g must be a function from t3 to some new type t4. f (g x) then applies f to that t4, giving another new type t5: Step 3: substitute the solved t1 and t2 back into the type of compose, which takes f, then g, then x, and returns t5: Nothing constrains t3, t4 or t5, so they become universally quantified: the caller may choose any types for them. Renamed tidily (a for t3, b for t4, c for t5): In Haskell's own syntax,:: means "has type", -> is the arrow, and the "for all" is left implicit: That is exactly the type of Haskell's built-in (.). The compiler found it with zero annotations, and it is the principal type: every other valid type for compose, such as (Int -> Bool) -> (String -> Int) -> String -> Bool, is an instance of it. Key takeaways Hindley–Milner infers the core calculus using constraints, unification and let generalisation. A principal type contains every valid instance without adding unnecessary equalities. Further reading Milner: A theory of type polymorphism Damas and Milner: Principal type schemes Haskell 2010: Declarations and types

sum: Unification matches type constructors and solves variable substitutions.
x: The preceding composition example generated equality constraints between types. Unification now solves those constraints by matching structure and recording replacements for unknown type variables. Unification Unification asks: what substitution (a rule replacing each type variable with a type) makes two types identical? Take one function type with an unknown input and integer result, and another with Boolean input and unknown result. Matching argument with argument and result with result gives: Unification fails when two different concrete types meet, or when a variable would have to contain itself: Unify Result ------ Type variable with Int Replace the variable by Int a -> Int with Bool -> b Replace a by Bool and b by Int Int with Bool type error a with a -> b Infinite type; error Here is a small unifier in Python, not a complete Algorithm W implementation. It assumes finite, well-formed type terms and an acyclic substitution. Type variables are strings; other types are tuples like ("->", arg, result) or ("Int",). Unifying ("->", "a", ("Int",)) with ("->", ("Bool",), "b") returns {'a': ('Bool',), 'b': ('Int',)}. The occurs check What is the type of self_apply x = x x? Give x the type a. Applying x to an argument means a must be a function type, and the argument is x itself: The occurs check (does a appear inside the type we're binding it to?) catches this. Compilers reject this finite-type constraint; exact diagnostic wording varies. GHC 9.6.6 reports a mismatch between a type variable and a function type containing that variable. Key takeaways Unification matches type constructors and solves variable substitutions. The occurs check rejects a variable containing itself in a finite type. Further reading Damas and Milner: Principal type schemes Milner: A theory of type polymorphism GHC: Higher-rank polymorphism

sum: Each use of a generalised let-bound definition gets a fresh type instance.
x: Hindley–Milner generalisation makes a reusable identity function different from an unknown function parameter. The earlier composition and unification lessons supply the constraint-solving background. Let-polymorphism HM generalises at let bindings, but not at lambda parameters. This difference is subtle and important: In ok, ident is let-bound, so after inferring that its argument and result share a type, HM generalises that type variable. Each use then gets a fresh copy of t: one at a number type, one at Bool: In bad, f is a parameter. Its type is a single unknown t, with no "for all", shared across both uses: GHC reports this as No instance for (Num Bool). Allowing f to be polymorphic would need rank-2 types, which go beyond ordinary HM let-polymorphism. Rank-2 inference is decidable in the corresponding System F fragment; rank-3 and higher inference is undecidable. GHC requires annotations for higher-rank polymorphic arguments. Key takeaways Each use of a generalised let-bound definition gets a fresh type instance. Ordinary lambda parameters remain monomorphic; explicitly polymorphic arguments need richer types. Further reading Haskell 2010: Declarations and types Damas and Milner: Principal type schemes GHC: Higher-rank polymorphism Kfoury and Wells: Rank-2 type inference

sum: Worst-case ML typability is exponential-time complete; this does not predict routine application performance.
x: The previous lessons established principal types for the Hindley–Milner core. Real language extensions, diagnostics and compilation costs require additional assumptions. Cost and limits Speed. Small ordinary inference examples can be inexpensive, but there is no general near-linear bound. In theory, deciding ML typability is DEXPTIME-complete (Mairson; Kfoury, Tiuryn and Urzyczyn, 1990): nested lets can produce types that double in size at each level. This worst case is not a prediction of typical application performance. Extensions break completeness. Rich combinations of subtyping, higher-rank types, GADTs and type-level computation can lose principal types, require annotations or make inference undecidable; no such result follows merely from adding any one feature in any form. Consequently, a language with subtyping or overloading needs additional inference rules and design choices; ordinary HM is not a drop-in specification for its whole type system. Type classes add constraints. Haskell infers square x = x x as Num a => a -> a, read "for any type a that is a number type (Num a), a function from a to a". Sometimes a constraint can't be resolved: f = show. read fails with "ambiguous type variable", because nothing says which type to read. Error messages. The error is reported where unification fails, which can be far from the real mistake. A wrong argument on line 10 may be blamed on line 40. Annotate the boundaries Idiomatic Haskell and OCaml code still writes type signatures on top-level functions, even though they could be inferred. Signatures document intent, give better error locality, and stop a mistake in the body silently changing the inferred type that callers see. Rust requires function signatures; TypeScript can infer exported return types, so explicit exported signatures are a documentation policy rather than a universal compiler requirement. Comparison Language Infers Needs annotations on --------- Java, C# Locals from initialiser Ordinary method signatures and fields TypeScript Locals, returns, lambdas in context Parameters without contextual types Rust Many local types, including later constraints Function signatures, ambiguous locals Haskell, OCaml HM-style core expressions Higher-rank uses, restricted or ambiguous extensions Key takeaways Worst-case ML typability is exponential-time complete; this does not predict routine application performance. Annotations at module boundaries document intended types and localise errors. Further reading Mairson: Deciding ML typability GHC: Generalised algebraic data types Haskell 2010: Declarations and types OpenJDK: Local variable inference

sum: A type parameter links arguments and results without replacing them with an unchecked universal container.
x: You want a function that returns the first element of a list. Lists of ints, lists of strings, lists of users: the logic is identical. In a statically typed language without generics you have two bad options. Write it once per type: firstInt, firstString, firstUser. Duplicated code. Write it once for "anything", using Object or void, and cast the result back. The type checker loses track, and a wrong cast fails at run time (or, in C, silently). Java before version 5 (2004) used non-generic collections. This modern raw-list example illustrates that API style; the autoboxing of 42 itself requires Java 5 or later: Generics fix this. A type gets a type parameter, a placeholder filled in at each use, and the checker tracks it: Parametric polymorphism A function that works uniformly for every type shows parametric polymorphism. "Uniformly" is the important word: it runs the same code whatever the type, never inspecting it. In the Haskell line,:: reads "has type", [a] means "a list of a", and -> separates the argument type from the result type, so first takes a list of a and returns a Maybe a (either Nothing or Just one a). On an empty list these examples differ: Haskell returns Nothing, TypeScript returns undefined, and Python raises IndexError. The type variable (a, T) links the input to the output. Calling first on a list of numbers gives a number back, and the checker knows it. This is one of three kinds of polymorphism: Kind Idea Example --------- Parametric Same code for all types first<T> Ad hoc Different code per type Overloading, type classes Subtype Use a subclass where a superclass is expected Animal a = new Dog() Key takeaways A type parameter links arguments and results without replacing them with an unchecked universal container. Empty-input behaviour differs between Maybe, undefined and an exception. Further reading Java generics: Type erasure TypeScript Handbook: Generics PEP 695: Type parameter syntax Haskell 2010: Standard classes

sum: Bounds grant specific operations such as ordering or a length property.
x: Generic code can preserve an unknown type without knowing its operations. A bound makes the required capabilities explicit instead of assuming every value can be compared or inspected. Bounded generics Fully parametric code can't do much with a T: it can store it, return it and pass it along, but not compare or print it. To use operations, you bound the type parameter: "any T, as long as it supports X". In Python, a bound can be a Protocol, which checks structurally: These maximum examples require nonempty inputs and meaningful ordering; PartialOrd also admits incomparable values such as NaN, so the Rust loop is not a universal mathematical maximum. mypy accepts biggest([3, 9, 4]) (result int) and rejects biggest([object()]), because object has no usable __lt__. Beyond the basics Generic types, not just functions: struct Pair<A, B>, Map<K, V>, Result<T, E>. Higher-kinded types abstract over type constructors themselves. Haskell's Functor f works for any f such as Maybe or []: fmap:: (a -> b) -> f a -> f b. Java, TypeScript and Rust do not expose that same direct Haskell-style type-constructor parameter; encodings and other abstractions are separate possibilities. C++ templates check non-dependent constructs at definition and dependent constructs during instantiation. C++20 concepts express constraints checked when a specialization is considered. Avoid a parameter without a relationship Needless type parameters. The TypeScript handbook's rule: if a type parameter appears only once, you probably don't need it. function log<T>(x: T): void is no better than log(x: unknown). Key takeaways Bounds grant specific operations such as ordering or a length property. A partial ordering need not provide a mathematical maximum for incomparable values. Higher-kinded parameters abstract over constructors; templates have definition- and instantiation-time checks. Further reading Rust standard library: PartialOrd TypeScript Handbook: Functions PEP 695: Type parameter syntax C++ draft: Template name resolution Haskell 2010: Declarations and types

sum: Total parametric functions cannot inspect or invent values of an unknown element type.
x: A generic type signature relates inputs to outputs. Stronger reasoning requires genuinely uniform behaviour, with the totality and observation restrictions below. Parametricity: types as theorems Under total parametric semantics (excluding nontermination, exceptions, seq and unsafe inspection), because a parametric function cannot inspect its T, its type alone tells you a surprising amount about what it does. Philip Wadler called this theorems for free (1989). f:: a -> a. Under the stated total parametric assumptions, the only available result is the input itself, so f must be the identity. Nontermination is excluded by those assumptions. g:: [a] -> [a]. g cannot invent new a values or look at them. It can only drop, duplicate and reorder elements based on the list's shape. For finite lists, reverse and take 3 fit; cycle is a partial, potentially infinite example outside this total finite-list statement; sort does not (it needs Ord a). A consequence is the free theorem for g. Because g only moves elements by position, it doesn't matter whether you transform the elements before or after calling it: For example, with g = reverse and h adding 1: reversing [1, 2, 3] gives [3, 2, 1] and adding 1 gives [4, 3, 2]; adding 1 first gives [2, 3, 4] and reversing gives [4, 3, 2]. The theorem assumes total functions on finite, fully defined lists. This only holds if the language really is uniform. Java breaks it: a generic method can call instanceof, getClass() or hashCode() on a T. TypeScript can use typeof; Python can use type or isinstance. Haskell supports useful parametric reasoning subject to those caveats. Rust generics also permit observations such as size_of::<T>(), so merely avoiding Any is not a parametricity guarantee. Key takeaways Total parametric functions cannot inspect or invent values of an unknown element type. The list free theorem requires its totality and uniformity assumptions; mainstream generic syntax alone does not establish them. Further reading Wadler: Theorems for free Wadler: Parametricity papers

sum: Java erases generic arguments while preserving some signature metadata; Python annotations remain metadata.
x: Generic source code can preserve type relationships under several runtime strategies. Distinguish the checker’s guarantee from metadata, representation and generated machine code. How generics are implemented The type checker's job is the same everywhere; the run-time strategy differs a lot. Erasure: Java and TypeScript; Python metadata The compiler checks the types, then erases them. At run time, List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List, and the compiler inserts casts where values come out. Consequences in Java: No new T() or new T[10]: there's no T at run time to construct. You can't test at run time whether a list is a List<String>; only List<?>. Overloads f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>) clash: "same erasure". No primitives: List<int> is illegal, so ints are boxed into Integer objects, using object references; caching or existing objects can avoid a fresh allocation for each element. Java chose erasure in 2004 for migration compatibility: generic code had to run on existing JVMs and interoperate with old non-generic libraries. TypeScript erases all types when compiling to JavaScript, generics included. Python keeps annotations as metadata (list[int] is a real object you can inspect), but the interpreter never enforces them. Monomorphisation: Rust, C++ The compiler specializes generic code for concrete types used. Optimizers and linkers can inline, merge or eliminate instantiations, so the number of machine-code functions need not equal the number of types. largest::<i32> and largest::<f64> are distinct conceptual instantiations. Pro: concrete types permit direct specialised operations, inlining opportunities and unboxed value storage. This does not promise that every call is inlined or that every program has zero overhead. Con: code bloat and longer compile times. More instantiations can increase compilation work; their count is not a guaranteed count of emitted functions. Rust offers an alternative when you want one copy: &dyn Trait uses a vtable (dynamic dispatch) instead. Dictionary passing: Haskell In the usual dictionary-passing model, GHC compiles Ord a => [a] -> a to a function that takes an extra hidden argument: a type-class dictionary (record) of the Ord methods for that type. The unspecialised model shares code and selects methods through that dictionary; it need not emit an indirect call for every comparison after optimisation. The optimiser often specialises hot call sites to remove the overhead. Reification: C#/.NET.NET keeps generic type information at run time. typeof(T) works, new T() works with a where T: new() constraint, and List<int> stores raw ints with no boxing. The usual.NET JIT strategy shares generic code across reference-type instantiations and specializes value types. Details depend on the runtime and compilation mode. Strategy Languages Run-time types? Unboxed values? ------------ Erasure Java, TS Generic arguments not reified per object; Java signature metadata may remain Java collections use references Optional hints Python Annotation metadata retained Interpreter-dependent Monomorphise Rust, C++ n/a, compiled away Yes Dictionaries Haskell No Usually boxed Reified C#,.NET Yes Yes Pitfalls Raw types in Java. Using List without a parameter turns off checking and produces "unchecked" warnings. Don't ignore them. Boxing costs. A Java List<Integer> of a million elements holds a million references; these may share cached or pre-existing objects. Use int[] or a primitive collection library for hot paths. Monomorphisation bloat. In Rust, very generic code in a large codebase can noticeably inflate binary size and compile times. Key takeaways Java erases generic arguments while preserving some signature metadata; Python annotations remain metadata. Rust and C++ specialise concrete instantiations; optimisers can merge or eliminate emitted code. GHC passes type-class dictionaries;.NET retains generic types and commonly shares reference-type code. Further reading Java Language Specification: Types Java generics: Type erasure The Rust Book: Generic types Microsoft: Generics at runtime GHC: Type classes

sum: A subtype can stand in for its supertype under the relevant typing and behavioural contract.
x: If a function wants an Animal and you hand it a Dog, that should be fine: a dog can do everything an animal can. That is subtyping, written like this: The reverse direction is called a supertype: Animal is a supertype of Dog. The easy part is classes. The hard part, and the source of real bugs, is what happens to compound types. If Dog is a subtype of Animal, is a List<Dog> a List<Animal>? Is a function that takes a Dog usable where a function that takes an Animal is expected? The answers are "it depends" and "no", and the rules that decide them are called variance. The substitution principle The guiding rule is Barbara Liskov's substitution principle (1987, formalised with Jeannette Wing in 1994): a subtype should preserve the behaviour promised by its supertype’s contract. A type checker can enforce the shape part: a subtype must have every member the supertype has, with compatible types. It can't enforce the behaviour part. A Square subclass whose setWidth also changes the height type-checks fine as a Rectangle, and still breaks callers that assume width and height are independent. Nominal and structural subtyping Two important ways to establish subtype relationships are nominal declarations and structural compatibility. Real languages may combine them. Nominal: subtyping exists only where you declared it. Java, C# and Kotlin class hierarchies work this way. Rust trait conformance also requires declarations, but trait implementation is not class-style subtyping. Structural: a source type fits a target when it provides the target’s required members with compatible types, subject to the language’s additional rules. TypeScript, Go interfaces and Python Protocols work this way. Robot never mentions Named, but it has a name: string, so it fits. Structural typing is convenient for JSON-shaped data; nominal typing stops two types that merely look alike (UserId and OrderId, both strings) being mixed up. Many systems also have a top type for their relevant type domain (Object for Java reference types, excluding primitive types, unknown in TypeScript, object in Python, Any? in Kotlin) and many have a bottom type that is a subtype of everything in its domain and has no normally returned values (never in TypeScript, Nothing in Kotlin and Scala, Never/NoReturn in Python). Rust’s uninhabited! has a similar practical role, but the Rust Reference specifies coercion of never-typed expressions to other types rather than a universal subtype relation. Key takeaways A subtype can stand in for its supertype under the relevant typing and behavioural contract. Nominal declarations and structural member compatibility establish relationships differently. Top and bottom types have different roles; top types are defined relative to a type domain. Further reading Liskov and Wing: Behavioural subtyping TypeScript Handbook: Compatibility and soundness Java Language Specification: Types PEP 484: Type hints Rust Reference: Never type

sum: Covariance preserves a subtype direction; contravariance reverses it.
x: Use the earlier Dog subtype of Animal throughout. A generic constructor builds a compound type from its argument; variance describes whether changing that argument preserves, reverses or prevents a subtype relationship. Variance: the four cases Take a generic type F<T> (such as List<T>) and suppose Dog is a subtype of Animal. Variance says how F<Dog> relates to F<Animal>. The two directional cases, as rules: All four cases: Variance Rule ------ Covariant Dogs-to-animals direction preserved Contravariant Dogs-to-animals direction reversed Invariant neither Bivariant both (unsound in general) In the usual producer/consumer model, permitted operations on the type parameter guide safe variance: T only comes out (returned, read): covariant is safe. T only goes in (passed as an argument, written): contravariant is safe. T goes both in and out through freely aliased access: invariance is needed unless ownership restrictions or runtime checks provide another safeguard. Functions: contravariant in, covariant out Suppose code expects a callback of type (Dog) -> Animal. Which functions can safely be passed instead? The caller will only ever pass in a Dog. A function that accepts any Animal handles that fine. So a supertype in the parameter is safe: contravariant. The caller will treat the result as an Animal. A function that returns a Dog satisfies that. So a subtype in the return is safe: covariant. As a general rule for function types, with the Dog example substituted in the last two lines: In TypeScript with strictFunctionTypes: Key takeaways Covariance preserves a subtype direction; contravariance reverses it. A replacement function accepts at least the inputs promised and returns results compatible with its promise. Further reading Rustonomicon: Subtyping and variance TypeScript 2.6: Strict function types Microsoft: Generic variance

sum: Freely aliased mutable collections need invariance or another safety mechanism.
x: Assume Dog and Cat are different subclasses of Animal, and Dog alone supplies bark(). Aliases matter because two typed names can still refer to one mutable collection. Aliased mutable collections and invariance A read-only list of dogs can safely be read as a list of animals: everything you take out is an animal. But a mutable list lets values go in as well as out: Both names point to the same array. Through animals you put a cat in; through dogs you take it out as a dog. TypeScript accepts this code (arrays are covariant there, a deliberate unsoundness) and it crashes at run time with TypeError: dogs[1].bark is not a function. Java's arrays: covariant, checked at run time Java made reference arrays covariant before generics, allowing operations written for Object[] to accept arrays such as String[]. Primitive arrays are separate: int[] is an Object, but is not an Object[]. To stay safe, the JVM checks every store into a reference array: It is sound, but the error arrives at run time and runtime checks preserve compatibility, although the JIT may eliminate a check it proves redundant. C# copied this design, with ArrayTypeMismatchException. Java's generics: invariant, with wildcards Java generics learnt the lesson. List<Dog> is not a List<Animal>: Instead, each use of the type chooses its variance with a wildcard (use-site variance): An upper-bounded wildcard is not strictly read-only: clear, removals and add(null) can still be permitted. A lower-bounded list can still be read as Object. Joshua Bloch's mnemonic in Effective Java is PECS: producer extends, consumer super. The JDK's own signature follows it: Key takeaways Freely aliased mutable collections need invariance or another safety mechanism. Java arrays check stores at runtime; TypeScript can accept an alias that fails later. Producer extends and consumer super describe permitted reads and writes, not absolute immutability. Further reading Java Language Specification: Types Java Language Specification: Arrays Java generics: Wildcard guidelines TypeScript Handbook: Compatibility and soundness

sum: Kotlin and C# support declaration-site variance; Python checkers infer or declare it.
x: Variance rules become practical when an API declares which values it produces and consumes. The examples retain the earlier Animal supertype and Dog subtype; they illustrate each language’s static rules rather than one cross-language runtime model. Declaration-site variance Writing wildcards at every use is noisy. Kotlin, C# and Scala let the type's author declare variance once: The compiler checks the declaration: using an out T as a method parameter is an error. Kotlin's read-only List<out E> is covariant; MutableList<E> is invariant. C# marks IEnumerable<out T> and Action<in T> the same way, though only on interfaces and delegate types (C#'s named function types). TypeScript 4.7 added optional in/out annotations on type parameters, mainly to make variance explicit and checking faster. Python: invariant lists, covariant sequences Python's type checkers follow the same rules. list is mutable, so it's invariant; Sequence is read-only, so it's covariant: Callable[[Animal], None] is usable where Callable[[Dog], None] is expected (contravariant parameters). For your own generics, older code declares TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True); the Python 3.12 syntax class Box[T]: lets the checker infer variance from how T is used. Rust: lifetimes and higher-ranked types Rust has no class inheritance; traits use bounds rather than a Dog/Animal class-subtyping hierarchy. Its subtyping includes lifetime relationships and higher-ranked function/trait-object types. For references, a longer lifetime can be shortened: the longer reference can satisfy a shorter required lifetime, provided the referent type and other typing conditions also fit. A reference that lives longer can be used where a shorter one is needed. So &'static str can go wherever &'a str is expected. Variance still matters, and the compiler infers it from each type's fields: Type Variance in T ------ &'a T, Box<T>, Vec<T> Covariant &'a mut T Invariant Cell<T> Invariant fn(T) -> U Contra in T, co in U &mut T is invariant for exactly the mutable-list reason: if &mut &'static str could be treated as &mut &'a str, you could write a short-lived string through it and later read it back as 'static, a dangling reference. Variance trade-offs and runtime checks Language Hole Outcome --------- Java, C# Covariant arrays Run-time store check TypeScript Covariant arrays Silent, crashes later TypeScript Method params bivariant Silent Eiffel Covariant method params Catcall/type-validity concerns TypeScript's strictFunctionTypes (part of strict) applies to ordinary function types and function-typed properties. Parameters of methods and constructors declared with method syntax stay bivariant, so DOM-style event handler interfaces keep working: Pitfalls Expecting List<Dog> to be a List<Animal>. In Java, Python's list and Kotlin's MutableList it isn't. Accept List<? extends Animal>, Sequence[Animal] or List<Animal> (read-only) instead. Trusting TypeScript arrays. Passing Dog[] as Animal[] to a function that pushes into it compiles and corrupts the caller's array. Prefer readonly Animal[] parameters. Overriding with a narrower parameter. A subclass method that only accepts Dog where the parent accepted Animal breaks substitution. Java treats it as an overload, not an override. Confusing structural fits with intent. In TypeScript, two unrelated interfaces with the same shape are interchangeable. Use branded types when that matters. Key takeaways Kotlin and C# support declaration-site variance; Python checkers infer or declare it. Rust subtyping involves lifetimes and higher-ranked types; exclusive mutation explains key invariance rules. TypeScript method parameters remain bivariant under strictFunctionTypes. Further reading Kotlin: Generics and variance Python spec Rustonomicon: Subtyping and variance Rust Reference: Subtyping TypeScript 2.6: Strict function types TypeScript 4.7: Variance annotations

t: Building types from sums and products
sum: Products combine all fields and multiply finite value counts; tagged alternatives add them.
x: Most data is built from two ideas. An order has a customer and a list of items and a total. A payment is a card payment or a bank transfer or a voucher. Classes and structs handle "and" well. Many mainstream languages had no direct way to say "or", so programmers faked it with nullable fields, type codes and instanceof chains. Algebraic data types (ADTs) give you both as built-in tools. Combined with pattern matching, which takes them apart safely, they are one of the most useful ideas to have spread from ML and Haskell into Rust, Swift, Kotlin, TypeScript, Python and Java. Product types: "and" A product type holds several values at once: a tuple, struct or record. It's called a product because of how the number of possible values combines. A pair holds one value from each part, and every combination is allowed, so the counts multiply: Sum types: "or" A sum type (also called a tagged union, variant or discriminated union) holds exactly one of several alternatives, and records which one. Each alternative is a data constructor (or variant) and may carry its own data. A value is one alternative or another, never both, so the counts add: That is the "algebra": types built from sums and products. Type Values ------ () / unit 1 bool 2 (bool, bool) 2 × 2 = 4 Option<bool> 1 + 2 = 3 Result<bool, ()> 2 + 1 = 3 An empty type, such as Rust! 0 These counts concern fully defined finite values, excluding nontermination and partial values. Names like Java Void do not necessarily denote an uninhabited type. Counting is practical, not academic. If your domain has 3 valid states and your type has 4, one value of the type is a bug waiting to happen. Key takeaways Products combine all fields and multiply finite value counts; tagged alternatives add them. The counts concern defined finite values, not nontermination or arbitrary representation bytes. Further reading Haskell 2010: Declarations and types Rust standard library: Option representation The Rust Book: Generic types

sum: Match arms run in order, and guards further restrict an arm.
x: The preceding lesson introduced Shape as either Circle with a radius or Rect with width and height. The following pattern examples use those constructors; numeric lengths share one unit, and returned areas use its square. Pattern matching A pattern match checks which alternative a value is and binds its fields in one step: Patterns nest, so you can match deep structure, and they can carry pattern guards (an extra if condition on an arm): Arms are tried top to bottom, and the first match wins. Order matters: put specific cases before general ones. Exhaustiveness The big win is that the compiler knows every alternative, so it can check that you handled them all: Rust: a non-exhaustive match is a hard error (E0004), and it names the missing pattern. Haskell: GHC warns about incomplete patterns (with -Wall); at run time an unmatched value throws. Java 21: a switch over a sealed type must cover every permitted subtype. TypeScript, Python: possible with a never-typed trick, shown below. Add a Triangle variant, and an exhaustiveness check can flag matches lacking both that case and a catch-all arm. An ordinary open class hierarchy tested only with instanceof chains does not provide that same closed-set exhaustiveness check. Recursive types: trees and expressions Sum types can refer to themselves. An arithmetic expression is a number, or an operation on smaller expressions: eval (Add (Num 2) (Mul (Num 3) (Num 4))) is 2 + 12 = 14. Compilers use exactly this shape for their syntax trees, which is why ML-family languages are popular for writing compilers. In Rust a recursive variant needs indirection (Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>)), otherwise the type would have infinite size. Key takeaways Match arms run in order, and guards further restrict an arm. Exhaustiveness can expose a new unhandled variant; a catch-all can conceal it. Recursive expression trees evaluate by recursively visiting their constructors. Further reading The Rust Book: Pattern syntax Haskell 2010: Declarations and types GHC warning flags JEP 441: Pattern matching for switch

sum: Option and Result expose absence and failure to the checker; extracting a value still needs handling.
x: Absence and failure are separate domain alternatives. Use the sum-type model from the previous lessons to make those alternatives visible to callers before considering their memory representation. Option and Result: no more null Tony Hoare called the null reference his "billion-dollar mistake". The problem is that in Java, every reference type silently includes null, so the type String doesn't tell you whether a value can be missing. An ADT makes absence explicit: The Rust option type (Option<T>) has two variants, None and Some(T), and you can't use the T without matching (or calling a method that handles None). Errors work the same way with the Rust Result type, Result<T, E>, whose two variants are Ok(T) (success, holding a T) and Err(E) (failure, holding an error E): The? operator returns early on Err, giving exception-like brevity while keeping failure visible in the signature. Under the hood Rust Box is the owning pointer used for indirection here. The layout guarantee below concerns the documented payload types, with sized referents and the specified allocator where applicable. A common representation uses a tag and variant payload, but layout can be boxed or optimized. Rust guarantees that Option<&T> for sized T has the same size and alignment as the reference; the documented guarantee also includes Option<Box<T>> for sized T with the global allocator. Layout limit A universal byte count for Option<u32> is omitted because its layout is not guaranteed by the language. Measure a specified compiler and target if that size matters. Key takeaways Option and Result expose absence and failure to the checker; extracting a value still needs handling. Rust documents specific null-pointer optimisations, not one universal enum layout. Further reading Rust standard library: Option representation The Rust Book: Generic types Java Language Specification: Types

sum: TypeScript narrows discriminated unions; a never assignment detects missing cases.
x: A sum-type model needs a reliable way to inspect alternatives. These examples revisit the same circle-or-rectangle shape in three languages; radius, width and height are numeric field values, and each area function returns square units when the inputs use one consistent length unit. Sum types in other languages TypeScript: discriminated unions A union of object types that share a literal variant tag field: Checking s.kind narrows s in each branch. In default, every case has been removed, so s has type never. Add a "triangle" member and the assignment to never fails to compile: a hand-made exhaustiveness check. Python: dataclasses and match Python 3.10 added structural pattern matching. This version uses typing.assert_never, so the full example requires Python 3.11 or later: Python itself does not statically check exhaustiveness. Without a matching arm execution continues after the match; the shown catch-all arm instead calls assert_never, which raises at runtime. But mypy and Pyright narrow s in each case, and typing.assert_never (3.11+) makes a missing case a type error. A bare name in a Python case is a capture pattern, not a comparison with an existing variable. case RED: binds the matched value to a local name; use a dotted constant such as case Colour.RED: or a literal such as case "red": when comparing values. An unguarded capture that matches everything must be the last case; a guard can allow later cases to remain reachable. Java: sealed interfaces and records Java 17 added sealed types and Java 21 finalised pattern matching for switch and record patterns: No default is needed, because the compiler knows the permitted implementations. A null selector still throws NullPointerException unless a case null handles it. Key takeaways TypeScript narrows discriminated unions; a never assignment detects missing cases. Python capture patterns bind names; assert_never supports static exhaustiveness checks. Java 21 combines sealed types, records and switch patterns; null still needs deliberate handling. Further reading TypeScript Handbook: Narrowing PEP 636: Pattern matching tutorial Python typing documentation JEP 441: Pattern matching for switch JEP 440: Record patterns

sum: Explicit state alternatives tie required data to each valid state.
x: Sum types connect each state to exactly the data it needs. Their design value becomes clearer when compared with independent flags and optional fields. Make illegal states unrepresentable Yaron Minsky's slogan from Jane Street sums up the design use. Compare two models of a network connection: With the first, nothing stops connected: false with a sessionId, and every reader has to guess. With the second, narrowing to the live alternative guarantees a session id under the checked type. TypeScript structural typing can still admit additional properties; this is not runtime validation or a guarantee of exact object shape. Related advice: parse, don't validate. Turn raw input into a precise type once at the boundary, and the rest of the code can rely on it. The expression problem ADTs and classes make opposite things easy. Philip Wadler named this the expression problem (1998): Add a new operation Add a new variant --------- ADT + match Easy: one new function Edit every match Classes Edit every class Easy: one new class With an Expr ADT, adding prettyPrint is one function; adding Div touches eval, prettyPrint and every other match (and the compiler lists them). With an Expr class hierarchy it's the reverse. Choose ADTs when the set of cases is stable and operations grow, as in compilers and protocol messages. Pitfalls Wildcard catch-alls. A _ => arm silences exhaustiveness checking, so a new variant is silently handled by the default. Prefer listing cases. Order of arms. A general pattern above a specific one makes the specific one unreachable. Rust and GHC warn about this. Boolean blindness. process(true, false) says nothing. An enum like Mode::DryRun makes intent explicit. Unwrapping everywhere..unwrap() and Haskell's fromJust turn None back into a crash, undoing the point of Option. Python's match isn't switch. A bare name in a case binds a new variable rather than comparing against an existing one. case RED: matches anything; use case Color.RED:. Key takeaways Explicit state alternatives tie required data to each valid state. ADTs favour adding operations; class hierarchies favour adding variants in the simple expression-problem comparison. Catch-alls, blind booleans and unconditional unwrapping weaken the design benefits. Further reading Jane Street: Effective ML revisited Alexis King: Parse, don’t validate Wadler: The expression problem The Rust Book: Pattern syntax

sum: Progress and preservation establish soundness for a specified semantics and its assumptions.
x: You have 500,000 lines of JavaScript or Python. Rewriting them in a statically typed language is out of the question, but you'd like the checker to catch None being passed where a User was expected. Gradual typing lets you add types one file, one function, even one parameter at a time, with typed and untyped code living side by side. Examples of incremental static checking include TypeScript for JavaScript, mypy and Pyright for Python, Sorbet for Ruby, Hack for PHP. The strength of the guarantee depends on the tool, runtime checks and escape hatches; optional checking can sacrifice soundness. Understanding that trade is what this lesson is about. Soundness, precisely A type system is sound when accepted programs avoid the erroneous states ruled out by its formal model, under that model’s assumptions. A calculus may express this as the absence of unexpected runtime type errors; it does not mean every source-language failure or exception is impossible. Formally, soundness is usually proved as two theorems about a language's semantics, progress and preservation. Type-theory papers write them like this: Progress rules out getting stuck on something like "a" {}, where no rule says what to do next. Preservation means the guarantee lasts: after a million steps the program is still well-typed, so progress applies again. Together they mean a well-typed program never reaches a stuck state. This style of proof is due to Wright and Felleisen (1994). Soundness is about absence of false negatives for the errors excluded by the model. A sound checker may reject programs whose executions would avoid those errors, but never accepts one that reaches an excluded state under its assumptions. Controlled runtime failures explicitly allowed by that semantics, such as a bounds failure or checked downcast exception, do not contradict the theorem. "Sound" mainstream languages aren't perfect either Java: Amin and Tate (2016) showed that Java's and Scala's type systems are unsound, using null and wildcard bounds. Their exploit compiles and fails at run time with a ClassCastException. The JVM's own checks stop it becoming memory corruption. Rust: the language is designed to be sound in safe code, but the compiler has had long-standing soundness bugs, and incorrect unsafe code can violate safety guarantees; the keyword does not itself make correct code unsound. Haskell: unsafeCoerce and unsafePerformIO exist; their correct use requires additional reasoning beyond the ordinary safe fragment; the operations’ existence alone does not invalidate a theorem about that fragment. The useful question is not "is it sound?" but "where are the holes, and do I control them?" Key takeaways Progress and preservation establish soundness for a specified semantics and its assumptions. Language/runtime escape hatches and implementation bugs affect the guarantee available in practice. Further reading Wright and Felleisen: Type soundness Luca Cardelli: Type systems Amin and Tate: Java and Scala unsoundness The Rust Book: Unsafe Rust

sum: The dynamic type admits flows in both directions; a safe top type requires narrowing before type-specific operations.
x: Gradual typing permits statically checked and unchecked portions of one program to interact. The dynamic type records missing static information; it is distinct from a safe top type. The dynamic type The central idea, from Jeremy Siek and Walid Taha (2006), is a special type, written? in papers and any/Any in practice, meaning "not statically known". any is not just a top type like unknown or object. It works in both directions: unknown is a true top type: anything goes in, while type-specific operations require narrowing; operations such as equality checks remain available. any goes in and comes out as anything. The checker permits unsafe flows and operations. This is a useful intuition, not literal compatibility with every TypeScript type: for example, any is not assignable to never. Siek and Taha replace type equality with a consistency relation: the dynamic type is consistent with every type, and concrete base types are consistent only when they match; structured types compare their components recursively, so a structure containing dynamic components can be consistent with a more precise structure. Consistency is deliberately not transitive: If consistency were transitive, the second line would give number ~ string, and then every type would be compatible with every other. Keeping it non-transitive is what lets untyped and typed code meet without making everything compatible with everything. Gradual guarantee A well-designed gradual system also satisfies the gradual guarantee (Siek and others, 2015): making annotations less precise preserves static acceptance and successful computed behaviour under the formal system’s precision relation. More precise annotations may introduce a static rejection or a runtime cast error; the theorem constrains these changes rather than promising that adding types always succeeds. This is what makes migration incremental: a file with no annotations is still a valid program. Key takeaways The dynamic type admits flows in both directions; a safe top type requires narrowing before type-specific operations. Consistency is intentionally non-transitive; gradual guarantees constrain changes in precision. Further reading Siek: What is gradual typing? Siek et al.: Refined criteria for gradual typing TypeScript Handbook: Everyday types

sum: Type assertions and Python casts provide no runtime validation.
x: The previous unit distinguished dynamic types from safe top types. These TypeScript and Python examples show where optional static checking leaves runtime behaviour unchanged. TypeScript: unsound by design TypeScript's design goals list "apply a sound or provably correct type system" as an explicit non-goal. It prefers to accept common JavaScript idioms. The known holes: Hole Example ------ any const n: number = JSON.parse(s) Type assertions x as User, y! Covariant arrays Dog[] used as Animal[] Method bivariance Method parameters permit both directions Unchecked indexing xs[10] is T, not T \ undefined The indexing one surprises people: The checker typed xs[0] as number; at run time it's undefined. The noUncheckedIndexedAccess option makes index results T undefined, but it's not part of strict, and can require explicit handling of missing indexed values. And because TypeScript erases all types when emitting JavaScript, the emitted type annotations add no runtime enforcement. Ordinary JavaScript operations can still perform their normal runtime checks. A wrong as cast or an API returning an unexpected shape just flows on until something crashes, possibly far away. Python: hints, checked separately PEP 484 (Python 3.5, 2015) defined type hints, but the interpreter does not enforce them; it retains annotation metadata and may evaluate annotations when introspected. Checking is done by a separate tool: mypy, Pyright, Pyre or others. The same program can be fine under one and rejected by another. mypy accepts this, because Any is consistent with int. It prints 4242: the string "42" repeated twice. Python-specific holes and defaults to know: Unannotated functions are skipped. By default mypy doesn't type-check the body of a function with no annotations, and treats its parameters as Any. --check-untyped-defs (included in --strict) changes that. cast(T, x) does nothing at run time; it just tells the checker to trust you. # type: ignore silences a line. Missing stubs. Imports lacking usable type information can produce missing-stub diagnostics or Any, depending on checker configuration and whether implementation analysis is available. Because the hints are real objects at run time (typing.get_type_hints), libraries can enforce them where it matters. Pydantic validates data against annotated models when it's parsed; tools like beartype and typeguard check function calls.
