Key takeaways Type assertions and Python casts provide no runtime validation. Strict TypeScript still omits noUncheckedIndexedAccess; default mypy skips unannotated bodies. Further reading TypeScript Handbook: Compatibility and soundness TypeScript compiler options PEP 484: Type hints mypy: Command-line options Python typing documentation

sum: Higher-order contracts protect future calls and track blame, rather than checking a function only once.
x: Optional checkers do not enforce annotations at runtime. A sound gradual design must instead account for interactions between checked and unchecked code, including values that will be called or mutated later. Sound gradual typing: checks at the boundary There's another design. Keep the dynamic type, but insert run-time checks wherever a value crosses from untyped to typed code, so interactions preserve the specified soundness guarantee. Deep contracts and shallow checks protect different properties; a shallow list check, for example, does not establish every element’s type for all future uses. Approach How Example --------- Optional No type-enforcement checks inserted TypeScript, mypy Transient Cheap shape checks at uses Reticulated Python Guarded Wrappers/contracts on values Typed Racket Typed Racket wraps higher-order values (functions, mutable structures) in higher-order contracts that check every later use, and on failure assigns blame according to which side violates the contract. Typed Racket also offers shallow and optional modes with different guarantees and costs. Wadler and Findler's blame theorem is the slogan: "well-typed programs can't be blamed". The catch is cost. Takikawa and colleagues' 2016 paper Is Sound Gradual Typing Dead? studied combinations of typed and untyped modules in benchmark programs, and found that some partly typed configurations ran many times slower than either the fully typed or fully untyped versions, because of checks on busy boundaries. Later work (Typed Racket's "shallow" mode, transient checks, better compilers) has cut this, but the tension is real. Dart took the concrete route: Dart 2 made the type system sound, with run-time checks on casts and covariant generics, and Dart 3 enforces sound null safety. Its compilers use the guarantees for optimisation. Migrating a large codebase Dropbox's 2019 write-up describes checking over 4 million lines of Python with mypy, adopted gradually over several years. The common pattern in such migrations: Start permissive. Turn the checker on with loose settings so the build passes. Type the core first. Shared modules and data models give the most leverage; their types flow into callers. Ratchet. Per-module strictness flags (mypy per-module config, TypeScript project references). New files must be strict; old files can't get worse. Turn on the important flags. In TypeScript, strict (including noImplicitAny and strictNullChecks); in mypy, --strict or at least --check-untyped-defs and --disallow-untyped-defs. Validate at the edges. Types describe what should arrive. Validate network JSON with a correctly configured schema (such as Zod or Pydantic); this checks that schema, not every business invariant. Track the escape hatches. Count any, as, cast and type: ignore; lint against new ones. Pitfalls Treating any as "some type". It turns checking off, and spreads: a value derived from any is usually any too. Use unknown or object and narrow. Trusting annotations at boundaries. fetchUser(): Promise<User> is a claim, not a check. Validate external data. Assuming mypy checked a function. Without annotations, or with untyped imports, it may not have. as to silence errors. An assertion is a promise you make to the checker; it's the first place to look when a "typed" program crashes. Key takeaways Higher-order contracts protect future calls and track blame, rather than checking a function only once. Boundary-check overhead depends on mode and workload; benchmark results are not universal forecasts. Migrate incrementally, tighten checks, validate external inputs and track escape hatches. Further reading Typed Racket: Typed/untyped interaction Wadler and Findler: Well-typed programs cannot be blamed Takikawa et al.: Gradual typing benchmarks Dart: Type system Dart: Sound null safety Dropbox: Migrating four million Python lines mypy: Existing codebases

sum: A conventional call stack reclaims frames in last-in, first-out order; language storage durations and optimisations are more general
x: Programs need storage for materialised values, and finite storage eventually needs to be reused. Optimisation can remove a value entirely; long-lived storage can remain until process exit. Two common storage mechanisms are the call stack and heap memory, usually just called "the stack" and "the heap". Registers, static storage and optimizations also matter; this is an introductory model, not a complete classification. The difference is about object lifetime: how long a value stays valid. A conventional call frame is reclaimed on return, while block-scoped object lifetimes can end earlier. Heap allocations can outlive the allocating call; reclamation follows ownership, reachability or explicit deallocation rather than actual future need. The rest of this module is really about the heap, so it pays to understand why the stack is the easy case. Scope of this module The Operating Systems subject covers virtual memory, pages and how malloc carves up memory internally. Here we take the language-level view: who decides when a value dies, and how. The call stack In a conventional stack implementation, an active call has a stack frame for saved state and locals that need memory. Parameters and the return address may instead be held in registers, and optimisation can remove frames. Returning reclaims that frame; individual language-level object lifetimes can end earlier. A conventional fixed-size frame can have a fast path that moves the stack pointer register by a fixed amount, sometimes in one instruction. Freeing it is moving the pointer back. The simple LIFO fast path needs no free-list search. Function prologues, stack alignment, stack checks, page faults and runtime stack growth can add work; cache residency is not guaranteed. The catch is that the stack is strictly last in, first out. A conventional frame belongs to its active call. Many frames have a statically known size, though C variable-length arrays and other dynamic stack allocations are counterexamples. The heap The heap is a large pool of memory where blocks can be allocated and freed in any order. Heap storage is commonly useful when: A value must outlive the function that created it (returning a new object, storing it in a global or a long-lived data structure). The size is only known at run time (reading a file of unknown length, a list that grows). The value is large (a 50 MB image would blow the stack). The value is shared between threads or parts of the program with unrelated lifetimes. Heap allocation often costs more, although bump-pointer heap allocators also have cheap fast paths: the allocator must find a free block, record its size and later reclaim it. The really hard question is when to free it, because its lifetime need not coincide with the allocating call. That question is the subject of every other lesson in this module. Trade-offs at a glance Stack Heap --------- Allocate move a pointer allocator call Free automatic, at return manual or GC Lifetime active frame allocation contract Size bounded; often fixed allocator limits Performance-minded code in managed languages tries to avoid heap allocation in hot loops: reuse allocations, prefer values over pointers in Go, and let escape analysis keep short-lived objects off the heap. Every avoided allocation is also work the garbage collector never has to do. Key takeaways A conventional call stack reclaims frames in last-in, first-out order; language storage durations and optimisations are more general. Heap storage permits lifetimes independent of a call, but dynamic size, sharing and large size alone do not logically require it. Allocation fast paths are implementation choices; stack checks, allocator bookkeeping and reclamation add work. sum: A pointer to an expired C automatic object cannot safely be dereferenced, regardless of the output in a quick experiment
x: A returned pointer must still designate a live object. C makes the programmer obey storage-duration rules; Python names instead refer to managed objects. The same assignment spelling can therefore have very different consequences. The classic bug: returning a stack address C distinguishes storage durations; it does not require a physical stack. Automatic locals commonly use frames or registers, static locals use static storage, and malloc obtains allocated storage. bad returns a pointer to an automatic object whose lifetime has ended; a conventional stack frame is only the implementation model. Accessing the expired object is undefined behaviour regardless of whether later calls reuse that storage; no particular output or crash is guaranteed. Clang warns: address of stack memory associated with local variable 'x' returned. good returns NULL on allocation failure; on success the caller has a new duty: call free(p) once and only once. Python: names reference managed objects CPython represents values as objects with type and reference-management metadata. Most are dynamically allocated; some singleton/static objects and immortal objects are exceptions, and free-threaded builds have different counting details. Some objects, such as None and cached small integers, are shared rather than freshly allocated for each use; exact creation and caching details belong to the CPython implementation. A local variable is just a name in the frame that refers to an object. The list survives this call because a still refers to it. That is why "stack vs heap" rarely comes up in Python: you never place anything yourself, and the runtime manages reclamation; cycles and finalization complicate promptness. Value and reference semantics Placement is tied to what assignment means: Value semantics: assignment copies the data. C structs, Go structs and arrays, and Rust's Copy types behave this way. Reference semantics: assignment copies a pointer, so two names share one object. Python objects and Java objects behave this way. The list cannot be reclaimed while either name still strongly retains it. Other aliases can retain it too, so reclamation must account for every strong path, not only these two names. Key takeaways A pointer to an expired C automatic object cannot safely be dereferenced, regardless of the output in a quick experiment. CPython names refer to managed objects; retaining the returned list keeps that list alive. Assigning a Python list to another name shares the list rather than copying it. sum: HotSpot escape analysis can eliminate an object allocation through scalar replacement; it does not promise to put every non-escaping object on a stack
x: The language model describes observable behaviour; a compiler may use registers, inline fields or eliminate allocations while preserving it. This table is a starting model, not a physical-layout guarantee. How each language places values Language Stack Heap --------- C many automatic locals; placement optimized allocated storage from malloc CPython interpreter frames (details vary by version) most objects; some shared or static objects Java local slots conceptually; may be registers objects in JVM model; allocations may be eliminated Go non-escaping values escaping values Rust local values often inline or registers owned allocations through Box, Vec, String Java: frame values and semantic heap objects The JVM model gives methods local-variable slots and places class instances and arrays in the heap. Machine-code placement can differ: HotSpot can keep locals in registers or eliminate an allocation while preserving observable behaviour. The HotSpot JIT compiler performs escape analysis: if it can prove an object never leaves the method, it may eliminate the allocation entirely and keep the fields in registers ("scalar replacement"). You cannot request this; it is an optimisation. Go: the compiler decides with escape analysis Go makes escape analysis visible. You can return a pointer to a local variable, and it is perfectly safe: Analyzed as a non-inlined function returning an escaping pointer, p requires storage surviving the call and the standard compiler normally heap-allocates it. Inlining can change the result at a particular call site. Use go build -gcflags=-m to inspect decisions; nonescaping values can still need heap storage for implementation reasons such as size. Things that commonly force a value to escape in Go: returning its address, storing it in a global or a heap object, capturing it in a closure that outlives the call, or storing an interface value in an escaping location. Merely forming a pointer or interface does not universally force heap allocation. Key takeaways HotSpot escape analysis can eliminate an object allocation through scalar replacement; it does not promise to put every non-escaping object on a stack. Go can safely return a pointer to a local because its storage must survive the call; inlining changes particular allocation decisions. A pointer or interface value alone does not universally force Go heap allocation; inspect compiler diagnostics for the actual context. sum: Vec and String own heap buffers through local metadata; Box has a different representation, and zero-sized or empty allocations are special cases
x: Ownership and physical placement answer different questions. A small local handle can own a large allocation elsewhere; a stack budget must account for the storage actually materialised in frames. Rust: ownership and explicit allocations Rust values can live in locals, registers, static storage or inside another allocation. Box owns a heap allocation, while Vec and String usually own a heap buffer. A local Vec or String commonly has inline pointer/length/capacity metadata; a Box<T> for sized T has a pointer-sized representation, not those three fields, and its heap buffer is freed automatically when the owner goes out of scope. Stack limits and stack overflow Conventional OS threads have their own stacks; the standard Go runtime also manages separate goroutine stacks. Stack limits and growth policies differ from the available heap. Runtime Typical stack size ------ Linux main thread configured limit; inspect ulimit -s JVM platform thread platform/version-dependent; configure -Xss Go standard runtime goroutine small growable stack; implementation-dependent CPython interpreter recursion limit; inspect sys.getrecursionlimit() Deep recursion can exhaust a stack or encounter a runtime recursion guard. A C program has no language-guaranteed stack-overflow exception; a protected stack commonly faults. Java may throw StackOverflowError. The standard Go runtime reports a fatal stack-limit error; debug.SetMaxStack documents an initial maximum of 1,000,000,000 bytes on 64-bit systems. Python raises RecursionError at its interpreter recursion limit; excessive limits can still crash a process. Goroutine stacks are a neat trick. They start tiny and, when a function needs more room, the runtime allocates a bigger stack and copies the old one across, fixing up pointers into it. That is why a Go program can run hundreds of thousands of goroutines when the same number of 1 MB OS-thread stacks would not fit. Big arrays on the stack If double is 8 bytes and the array is materialized on the stack, double grid[2000][2000]; needs 32,000,000 bytes, exceeding an 8 MiB stack budget. Allocate it on the heap instead. To check whether a local array fits, multiply its element count by the size of one element and compare the result with the thread's stack budget: The same multiplication works for any fixed-size local: a 100-row, 100-column grid of eight-byte doubles needs 80,000 bytes and fits within the illustrative 8 MiB budget when that much space remains. The budget is not fixed: it depends on the operating system, ulimit -s and how the thread was created. Limits of this model A universal stack size or allocation latency is omitted: neither is guaranteed across runtimes, operating systems and compiler settings. Dynamic size and sharing alone do not require heap storage (C VLAs and safely scoped sharing are counterexamples). Key takeaways Vec and String own heap buffers through local metadata; Box has a different representation, and zero-sized or empty allocations are special cases. Thread and goroutine stack budgets depend on runtime, platform and configuration; recursion limits are not interchangeable with byte limits. Compare a materialised array's byte requirement with the whole available stack budget, including existing frames and other overhead. sum: An allocated C object remains valid until its lifetime ends through deallocation or successful reallocation
x: C allocated storage lasts from successful allocation until its lifetime ends through deallocation or replacement by a successful realloc. The language relies on the programmer to follow the contract; warnings, static analysis and run-time tools can detect some violations. That is wonderfully simple and fast, and it is the root of a large share of the world's security vulnerabilities. This lesson looks at the contract, the ways it breaks, and the techniques programmers use so that it breaks less often. The contract The rules are short: Release each owned allocation once when no longer needed, either with free or by a successful realloc that replaces its lifetime. Do not separately free the old pointer after successful realloc; on failure for a nonzero requested size, the original allocation remains valid. After free, the block is not yours: do not read it, write it or free it again. Only touch bytes inside the block you were given. malloc does not initialise memory; calloc zeroes it. C does not provide automatic enforcement of these rules. Losing an owned allocation can cause a memory leak; invalid accesses or deallocation can cause undefined behaviour, for which C requires no particular outcome. A leak alone need not be undefined behaviour. Who frees it? Ownership by convention The real difficulty is not calling free; it is knowing who should call it and when. A pointer in C says nothing about whether you own the memory. That information lives only in documentation and habit. Compare getenv, whose result you must not free, and strdup, whose result you must free. Both return char. Getting the convention wrong in either direction is a bug. Counting bytes for strings "Hello, " is 7 characters. A C string also needs a terminating NUL byte, so the allocation must be strlen(who) + 7 + 1. Forgetting the + 1 is one of the most common heap overflows. The allocation size for greet is the sum of its three parts: So greet("ann") allocates 11 bytes: Hello, ann is 10 visible characters plus the NUL. The code writes this as strlen(who) + 8, folding the 7 and the 1 together. Count encoded bytes, not visible letters: UTF-8 text can use several bytes per character. The added greeting is seven bytes on the assumed ASCII-compatible encoding. For arbitrary untrusted lengths, check that adding eight cannot overflow size_t before allocating. Key takeaways An allocated C object remains valid until its lifetime ends through deallocation or successful reallocation. Document who owns each returned pointer: getenv does not transfer ownership, while a successful strdup does. A C string allocation must include every payload byte and its terminating NUL, with checked size arithmetic for untrusted lengths. sum: Leaks retain allocations; use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds writes and uninitialised reads violate separate rules
x: Before choosing a tool or a repair, identify which allocation rule failed. These examples deliberately contain bugs; their invalid accesses have no guaranteed output. The five classic bugs 1. Memory leak Memory that is never freed, typically because the last pointer to it was lost. An ordinary process exit reclaims its address space, so a small bounded leak in a short-lived tool may have limited impact. In an illustrative server, leaking 4,000 bytes per request at 1,000 requests/s accumulates 345.6 GB per day (decimal). The time and mode of failure depend on memory limits, allocation behavior and the environment; an OOM kill within hours is not guaranteed. The daily figure is the leak rate multiplied by the number of seconds in a day: The model assumes a steady request rate and that nothing frees the leaked memory; real traffic varies through the day, so treat it as an order-of-magnitude warning, not a prediction. 2. Use-after-free Reading or writing a block after it has been freed. The pointer still holds the old address (a dangling pointer), and the allocator may already have given that memory to someone else. 3. Double free Calling free twice on the same block. This is undefined behavior. An allocator may detect and abort, or corruption and later exploitation may result; no specific allocator outcome is guaranteed. 4. Buffer overflow Writing past the end (or before the start) of a block, trampling the allocator's metadata or a neighbouring object. 5. Uninitialised read Using malloc'd memory before writing it. Its contents are indeterminate; stale bytes can cause information disclosure, and reading an uninitialized typed value can invoke undefined behavior. Fresh pages may happen to be zero-filled, but malloc does not promise initialization. Bug Symptom Danger --------- Leak memory grows outage Use-after-free random corruption exploit Double free allocator crash exploit Overflow corruption exploit Uninit read odd values info leak Key takeaways Leaks retain allocations; use-after-free, double free, out-of-bounds writes and uninitialised reads violate separate rules. A dangling pointer is not made safe by an allocator leaving familiar bytes behind. A steady leak-rate calculation is a sizing model, not a prediction of the exact time or mode of process failure. sum: Reusing a freed object's slot can turn a dangling function pointer into attacker-controlled execution, subject to allocator behaviour and defences
x: Memory corruption can cross a security boundary rather than merely crash. Tools help find exercised failures, while language and library contracts determine which operations are valid. Why these are security holes These bugs are not just crashes. Consider a use-after-free: The program frees an object that contains a function pointer, but keeps a dangling pointer to it. An attacker triggers an allocation of the same size with contents they control (say, a string from a network packet). The allocator reuses the freed slot. The program calls through its dangling pointer, reading the attacker's bytes as a function address. If the slot is reused as assumed and control-flow defenses do not stop the call through the corrupted pointer, this can enable arbitrary code execution. Overflows and double frees can be turned into similar primitives. Chromium’s published analysis reported roughly 70% of its high-severity security bugs as memory-safety issues, with use-after-free a major category. Treat this as the historical dataset described by the source, not a measured current rate across all products. A separate universal Microsoft annual percentage is omitted here because this review has not established its applicable period and dataset. This is why governments and large companies now push new code towards memory-safe languages: Java, Go, Python, C#, Swift and Rust. What "memory safe" means A memory-safe language guarantees you cannot read or write memory you do not own: no dangling pointers, no out-of-bounds access, no double free. GC languages achieve it by never freeing reachable memory and bounds-checking arrays. Rust combines static ownership checks with runtime checks such as bounds checks and library synchronization; unsafe code and native interfaces remain obligations in all these systems. Finding the bugs AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address in Clang and GCC) instruments relevant memory accesses in compiled code; uninstrumented code and other coverage limitations remain. It reports heap-use-after-free, buffer overflows and double frees with stack traces, with a typical slowdown of about 2x, so you can run your test suite under it. Valgrind Memcheck runs an unmodified binary on a simulated CPU. No recompilation, but programs run roughly 20 to 30 times slower. LeakSanitizer and Valgrind's --leak-check=yes report blocks still allocated at exit with no pointer to them. Fuzzers (libFuzzer, AFL) combined with sanitizers find the inputs that trigger these bugs. These find bugs in the code paths you exercise. They cannot prove their absence. Sound safe-language implementations instead enforce a class of validity rules for supported operations; unsafe code, native interfaces and implementation bugs remain obligations. Key takeaways Reusing a freed object's slot can turn a dangling function pointer into attacker-controlled execution, subject to allocator behaviour and defences. AddressSanitizer instruments compiled code; Memcheck can analyse a supported existing binary without rebuilding it. Passing sanitizer tests proves neither complete path coverage nor absence of all memory errors; quoted slowdown factors are documentation estimates. sum: A cleanup label can release every resource acquired before any failure, and free(NULL) needs no special case
x: Once ownership is explicit, arrange for release to follow one dependable lifetime boundary. C uses conventions and cleanup paths; arenas and C++ resource-owning objects reduce the number of individual decisions. Disciplines that help in C Single exit and cleanup Every path runs the same cleanup. The Linux kernel uses this goto pattern everywhere. Note that free(NULL) is defined to do nothing, which keeps this tidy. Arenas (region allocation) Instead of freeing objects one by one, allocate everything for one task (a request, a compiler pass, a game frame) from an arena allocator and free the whole arena at the end. Individual frees disappear, removing many per-object release mistakes. Pointers that outlive arena release still dangle, and oversized retention until arena teardown can waste memory. Compilers, game engines and web servers (nginx's per-request pools) use this heavily. C++: tie memory to object lifetime (RAII) C++ keeps manual memory but automates the free. RAII (resource acquisition is initialisation) means a resource is owned by an object, and the object's destructor releases it when the object goes out of scope, on normal scope exit and exception unwinding. Process abort, termination and deliberately leaked ownership do not promise destructor execution. std::unique_ptr<T>: exactly one owner; cannot be copied, only moved. Often pointer-sized with the default deleter; a stateful deleter or custom pointer type can change representation and cost. std::shared_ptr<T>: shared ownership via reference counting. Correctly designed resource-owning RAII types prevent many forgotten releases and duplicate releases. It does not stop use-after-free through raw pointers or references that outlive the owner. Rust's borrow checker is, in effect, RAII plus a compiler that proves those references cannot dangle. Key takeaways A cleanup label can release every resource acquired before any failure, and free(NULL) needs no special case. An arena is useful when many objects share one bounded task lifetime; references must not escape beyond arena release. RAII releases owned resources during normal scope exit and exception unwinding, while raw dangling references and termination paths remain separate concerns. sum: Reachable but obsolete cache entries cannot be identified as unnecessary by ordinary reachability collection
x: A collector answers whether an object is reachable, not whether retaining it still serves the application. Memory retention and resource release therefore remain design responsibilities even in a managed language. Garbage collection is not a cure for leaks GC languages free memory only when it becomes unreachable. If your program keeps a reference, the memory stays, even if you will never use it again. These are logical leaks: Common culprits in Python, Java and Go: unbounded caches and maps, listeners or callbacks that are registered and never removed, static collections, and (in Go) goroutines blocked forever on a channel, which pin everything they reference. GC also does not manage other resources. Files, sockets and locks must still be released deterministically: Language Mechanism ------ Python with open(...) as f: Java try-with-resources Go defer f.Close() C++ / Rust destructor / Drop Bound the retention policy For the report cache, specify an eviction or expiry rule as well as a lookup rule. A test can request many distinct user-and-day pairs and inspect whether obsolete entries leave the cache. A bounded cache may intentionally retain useful reports; indefinite retention without a useful policy is the logical leak. A blocked goroutine can also retain values needed by its suspended computation. Arrange cancellation or a channel protocol that lets it return, rather than assuming a collector will terminate the goroutine. Exact retained bytes depend on compiler liveness and runtime representation. Files and sockets use operating-system resources in addition to any small wrapper object. Closing them promptly avoids exhausting descriptors even when plenty of heap remains. Use the language's explicit cleanup construct and handle close errors where they matter, rather than relying on an unspecified finalizer schedule. Key takeaways Reachable but obsolete cache entries cannot be identified as unnecessary by ordinary reachability collection. Cancellation, listener removal and bounded cache policies control logical retention. Use with, try-with-resources, defer or documented destructor behaviour to release non-memory resources promptly. sum: The basic eager-counting model tracks strong owners and reclaims an acyclic, non-resurrecting value when its last owner releases it
x: The simplest automatic answer to "when can this object be freed?" is: when nobody refers to it any more. Keep a counter in every object of how many references point at it. When the counter drops to zero, free the object. That is reference counting. It runs inside CPython, Swift and Objective-C (as ARC), PHP, Perl, C++'s std::shared_ptr and Rust's Rc and Arc. It is easy to understand, it frees memory promptly, and it has one famous blind spot: cycles. The mechanism In the basic model each managed allocation has a strong-reference count (possibly in a separate control block). The runtime (or the compiler) adjusts it whenever a reference is created or destroyed: A reference is created (assignment, passing an argument, putting it in a list): increment. A reference is destroyed (a variable is reassigned or goes out of scope, an item is removed): decrement. The count reaches zero: free the object, and decrement everything it refers to. That last rule can create a cascading release. In an exclusively owned acyclic linked list, releasing the head can make each successor lose its last owner. Implementations can use worklists or other techniques rather than literal native-stack recursion. In the trace above, each rc= value is the object's reference count. Each update is a single addition or subtraction: Following the trace: Obj() starts at 1, b = a makes it 1 + 1 = 2, del a makes it 2 − 1 = 1, and b = None makes it 1 − 1 = 0, so the object is freed. The model assumes every reference is counted; weak references (below) deliberately are not. Watching it in CPython In ordinary GIL-enabled CPython, object headers include reference-count metadata. This simple non-resurrecting example illustrates prompt finalization; free-threaded/deferred counting, cycles and finalizers can alter timing: Output: del a only drops the count from 2 to 1, because b still refers to the object. del b drops it to 0, so the object is freed immediately, before the next line runs. Immortal objects Since Python 3.12, objects such as None, True and small integers are immortal objects (PEP 683): reference-count operations treat them specially and ordinary decrements do not deallocate them. The large reported count is not a reliable count of live references or a stable universal constant. Why people like it Promptness. Acyclic, non-resurrecting objects can be reclaimed promptly when their last strong owner releases them; allocator retention can still keep process memory high. Deterministic destruction. Simple eager counting has predictable release points. For files use with/open, RAII or explicit close; temporary-object destruction is not a portable resource-management guarantee, and cycles or deferred counting can delay it. Incremental by nature. The work is spread across the program, without requiring a separate whole-heap collection in the basic acyclic model; cascading release can still take substantial time. Locality. Basic count updates touch ownership metadata for the affected values rather than scanning an entire heap; releasing a final owner can touch further objects. Key takeaways The basic eager-counting model tracks strong owners and reclaims an acyclic, non-resurrecting value when its last owner releases it. Deleting one Python name does not destroy an object retained by another name. Cycles, deferred counting, immortal objects and finalizers qualify any claim of universally immediate destruction. sum: Count traffic, metadata, synchronisation and cascading release can each cost time or space
x: Reference counts replace a whole-heap tracing decision with ownership bookkeeping along execution paths. That work can be cheap in one setting and expensive in another; measure the actual implementation and sharing pattern. What it costs Reference counting is not free. Creating or releasing a strong ownership reference can require count traffic. Borrowed references, moves, immortal objects and optimization can avoid updates. Count updates everywhere. Passing, storing or returning strong references can touch counts, depending on borrowing conventions and optimization. In CPython this is a measurable share of interpreter time. Atomic operations under threads. Concurrent strong-count updates require synchronization, often atomic operations whose cost depends on hardware, contention and memory ordering. C++ shared_ptr and Rust Arc pay this; Rust's Rc does not, and the compiler refuses to let an Rc cross threads. CPython's GIL let it use plain increments; the free-threaded build (PEP 703) uses biased reference counting, where the owning thread updates a fast local count and other threads use an atomic shared one. Space. Counts and related metadata use storage; their size varies by implementation (in shared_ptr, usually a separate control block). Cascading frees. In the simple eager model, dropping the last owner of an exclusively owned acyclic 10-million-node tree can require releasing all 10 million nodes before returning. Shared owners, cycles or deferred destruction change that work; eager counting alone gives no short-pause bound. Copy-on-write damage. Some operations acquiring references write counts, which can dirty shared pages after fork. The cycle collector also changes bookkeeping. gc.freeze() (Python 3.7) avoids collector traversal of frozen objects; it does not suppress their ordinary reference-count updates. Avoiding count traffic C++ code passes const std::shared_ptr<T>&, or a plain T&, when the callee does not need to keep the object. Swift's optimiser removes retain/release pairs it can prove redundant. Rust makes clones of Rc explicit with Rc::clone(&x) so you can see each one. Choosing the ownership handle Use Rc when shared ownership stays within a thread; Arc synchronises its ownership counts for use across threads when the contained type satisfies the required thread-safety traits. Arc does not by itself synchronise accesses to the contained data. In C++, separate shared_ptr handles sharing a control block can be updated concurrently; simultaneous unsynchronised writes to the same handle are a different issue. After fork, reference-count writes and collector bookkeeping can dirty otherwise shared private pages. The resulting copies depend on the pages actually touched, not simply on the number of workers. CPython's freeze operation avoids later cycle-collector bookkeeping on frozen objects; ordinary counting writes can still occur. Keeping a dataset semantically read-only does not guarantee that its runtime metadata is never written. Key takeaways Count traffic, metadata, synchronisation and cascading release can each cost time or space. Borrowing, moving and compiler optimisation can avoid some reference-count updates. Rc and Arc express different thread-sharing contracts; neither a logical read-only dataset nor gc.freeze promises zero copy-on-write page copying. sum: An intact unreachable strong cycle keeps its own counts above zero under pure reference counting
x: A strong-reference count records incoming owners, not reachability from the running program. A group can therefore own itself after every outside reference disappears. The cycle problem In the diagram, A and B name the two objects, x and y are outside references, and rc labels each object's strong-reference count. It is a toy ownership graph with no additional references. Two objects that refer to each other each hold a count of at least 1, forever, even when nothing else can reach them. Cycles are everywhere in real programs: a parent node and its children with parent pointers, a doubly linked list, an object that adds itself as a callback, an exception that holds a traceback that holds the frame that holds the exception. Pure counting cannot reclaim an unreachable strong-reference cycle that remains intact. Weak edges, explicit link removal or a design that forbids strong cycles can avoid that situation. There are two fixes: make some references not count (weak references), or add a separate collector that finds cycles. Fix 1: weak references A weak reference points at an object without contributing to its count. When the object is freed, the weak reference becomes empty instead of dangling. The rule of thumb: owners hold strong references, back-pointers are weak. A parent owns its children; a child's pointer to its parent is weak. Language Strong Weak --------- Python normal ref weakref.ref Swift default strong weak (nil on release); unowned has a different lifetime contract C++ shared_ptr weak_ptr Rust Rc / Arc Weak Calling the weak reference returns the object, or None if it has been freed. C++'s weak_ptr::lock() and Rust's Weak::upgrade() work the same way: they give you a temporary strong reference or nothing. Swift adds unowned, a reference that does not keep its target strongly alive. You promise its target remains alive whenever it is accessed. Ordinary checked unowned traps on access after deallocation; unowned(unsafe) omits that protection. Swift closures are the classic cycle: a view controller stores a closure that captures self strongly. The fix is a capture list, { [weak self] in... }. Weak references only help where you can see the cycle coming. Ordinary Swift/Objective-C ARC and C++ shared_ptr have no general tracing cycle collector. Explicitly clearing links can also break a cycle; a retained cycle otherwise leaks. Xcode provides a memory graph debugger to investigate such ownership. Key takeaways An intact unreachable strong cycle keeps its own counts above zero under pure reference counting. Choose weak back-pointers where the domain's ownership relation permits them; acquiring a weak target can fail. Swift checked unowned references carry a lifetime obligation and trap after target deallocation; they are not interchangeable with optional weak references. sum: Subtract candidate-internal edges from scratch counts, preserve external roots and everything they reach, then reclaim the remaining unreachable group
x: CPython supplements strong-reference counting with a cycle collector. Its trial counts distinguish references coming from within a candidate group from references coming from the rest of the program. Fix 2: a cycle collector CPython takes the belt-and-braces route: reference counting for the common case, plus a cycle collector in the gc module for the rest. It only needs to consider container objects (lists, dicts, class instances), because ordinary built-in int and str instances do not contain references participating in cycles; subclasses and extension types can have different layouts. The algorithm is neat: For each container being examined, copy its reference count into a scratch field. For every reference between those containers, subtract one from the target's scratch count. Anything left with a scratch count above zero is referenced from outside the group, so it is alive. Everything reachable from it is alive too. Whatever remains is referenced only from inside the group: unreachable cycles. Free it. Steps 1 and 2 compute, for each container, how many of its references come from outside the group: In the two-node example below, after del x, y each node has a reference count of 1 and one reference from inside the group (the other node points at it), so its scratch count is 1 − 1 = 0: nothing outside holds them, and they are freed. An object with a scratch count above zero is alive, and step 3 keeps everything reachable from it alive too, even objects whose own scratch count is 0. Output (the two "freed" lines may come in either order): After del x, y, each node still has a count of 1 from the other, so nothing is freed. gc.collect() subtracts the internal references, finds both at zero, and frees them. Since Python 3.4 (PEP 442), a Python-level __del__ no longer by itself prevents collection of an unreachable cycle. Finalizers can still resurrect objects, and some extension types have different finalization constraints; gc.garbage is not universally empty. The collector is a generational collector: new containers are examined often, survivors less often, to exploit workload-dependent short object lifetimes. Scheduling depends on version/build: net allocation counts matter, and free-threaded CPython also considers process-memory growth. The thresholds are tunable with gc.set_threshold(). Disabling the cycle collector gc.disable() disables automatic cyclic collection. Reference counting still operates and explicit gc.collect() still works; unreachable intact strong cycles can accumulate until explicitly collected or broken. Some services do this deliberately for predictable latency and then must avoid creating cycles. Where reference counting sits Ref counting Tracing GC --------- When freed last strong release in the basic acyclic model during collection Cycles need extra help traced normally Cost paid on strong-reference updates and cascading release collection and barriers Destruction prompt in basic model runtime-specific timing Many systems blend the two. CPython is reference counting plus a tracing cycle collector. Research collectors use deferred reference counting, which skips count updates for stack variables and corrects the counts periodically, to get most of the promptness with much less overhead. Key takeaways Subtract candidate-internal edges from scratch counts, preserve external roots and everything they reach, then reclaim the remaining unreachable group. gc.disable stops automatic cyclic collection, while reference counting and explicit gc.collect continue to operate. CPython collection schedules depend on version and build; finalization and resurrection complicate the simple trial-count model. sum: Tracing follows strong paths from roots, so an unreachable cycle needs no special case
x: Reference counting asks each object "does anything point at you?". A tracing garbage collector asks a better question: "can the program still reach you?". It starts from the places the program can see directly, follows every pointer, and treats everything it did not reach as garbage. Cycles are not a special case: an unreachable cycle is simply never visited. Java, C#, Go, JavaScript, Haskell, OCaml and Ruby all use tracing collectors. Roots and reachability The GC roots are the references the running program can use without following any other pointer: local variables and temporaries in every thread's stack frames and CPU registers global and static variables runtime internals (for example JNI handles in the JVM, or the interpreter's own tables) A live object is one with a path to it from a root. Everything else is garbage, even if other garbage points at it. Note that "reachable" is an over-approximation of "will be used". A reachable object you will never touch again is a leak the collector cannot see. Mark-sweep McCarthy's 1960 Lisp paper describes the classic mark-and-reclaim approach. The basic mark-sweep model has two phases. Mark. Walk the object graph from the roots, setting a mark bit in each object reached. Sweep. Walk the whole heap. Unmarked objects go back on a free list; marked ones have their bit cleared ready for next time. The mark phase is just graph traversal. Here it is on a toy heap: Output: Collectors commonly use explicit worklists, bounded recursion or other traversal strategies so a long chain does not exhaust the native call stack. This toy algorithm assumes every referenced identifier names a heap object. Costs. In a simple model with bounded pointer fields per object, marking grows with roots and live data; sweeping examines the whole heap or its allocation metadata. Pointer density and implementation details affect actual work. Mark-sweep never moves objects, which makes it simple and friendly to C code holding raw pointers. The downside is heap fragmentation: after many cycles, free space is scattered in small holes, so allocation must search free lists and a large request can fail even though plenty of total memory is free. Mark-compact Mark-compact fixes fragmentation by sliding live objects together after marking, so all free space is one contiguous block at the end. Allocation becomes a bump pointer: hand out the next block of the requested size and advance the pointer, just like the stack: For example, with the pointer at address 1,000 a 48-byte request returns address 1,000 and leaves the pointer at 1,048. The price is extra passes over the heap: compute each object's new address, rewrite every pointer to it, then move it. HotSpot's Serial and Parallel collectors compact the old generation this way. Key takeaways Tracing follows strong paths from roots, so an unreachable cycle needs no special case. Plain mark-sweep reclaims unmarked objects without relocating survivors and can leave fragmented free space. Compaction packs movable live objects and updates references, enabling a bump-allocation fast path with capacity and alignment checks. sum: Cheney's scan and free pointers implement a breadth-first work queue within to-space, with forwarding records avoiding duplicate copies
x: A collector can reclaim a region by copying its reachable survivors elsewhere. The semispace model makes the trade-off clear: compact allocation and survivor-only copying in exchange for spare space and relocation work. Copying collection The simple semispace copying collector splits its managed region into two equal spaces. Other copying collectors use different region layouts. The program allocates in from-space with a bump pointer. When it fills: Copy each object reachable from the roots into to-space, packed tightly. Leave a forwarding pointer in the old copy, so later references to it can be redirected to the new address. Swap the roles of the two halves. Everything left in the old half is garbage and is discarded without being looked at. The usual object-graph presentation of Cheney's 1970 algorithm does this breadth-first with a scan pointer and a free pointer into to-space, without a separate traversal stack. The original paper describes list structures; this diagram uses general objects: Objects between scan and free are copied but not yet scanned; when scan catches free, the work is done. Why it is attractive. Apart from root scanning and fixed costs, copying and scanning work grows with live data and its reference fields. If 2% of the half-space is live, the collector touches that 2% and frees the other 98% for nothing. There is no fragmentation and allocation is a pointer bump. Why it is not used for everything. The simple semispace model reserves two equal spaces while using one for allocation; this is not a promise that total process memory doubles. Repeatedly copying large, long-lived objects adds work. It also moves objects, so references to moved objects must be found and updated safely, or handled through a suitable indirection or pinning protocol. Precise vs conservative A precise collector knows the exact location of every pointer, from type information and compiler-generated stack maps. A conservative collector, such as the Boehm GC used with C and C++, treats any word that looks like a heap address as a possible pointer. It cannot safely relocate objects retained by ambiguous words by rewriting those words (they might be integers); hybrid mostly-copying designs can still move other objects, and it may keep garbage alive by mistake, but it works without compiler help. Comparing the three Cost grows with Moves? Fragments? ------------ Mark-sweep live + heap no yes Mark-compact live + heap yes no Copying live yes no Key takeaways Cheney's scan and free pointers implement a breadth-first work queue within to-space, with forwarding records avoiding duplicate copies. A simple semispace collector reserves two spaces while allocating into one; its total work also includes roots and pointer fields. Ambiguous machine words cannot safely be rewritten as pointers; mostly-copying designs pin ambiguously referenced objects while moving others. sum: Generational collection relies on workload-dependent survival patterns; promotion and collection terminology vary across runtimes
x: Two different observations can reduce tracing overhead: young allocations may have low survival, and a larger allocation allowance can buy more time between collections. Keep empirical survival patterns separate from the assumptions of a cost model. The generational hypothesis Many workloads have the useful empirical pattern that most allocations become unreachable quickly, but survival rates and lifetimes are workload-dependent. Temporary strings, iterators, boxed numbers and request-scoped objects are common examples. A minority, such as caches and configuration, live for the whole run. Generational collectors exploit this by splitting the heap by age: New objects are bump-allocated in the young generation (classic HotSpot generational collectors use eden and survivor spaces; G1 uses regions). When it fills, a minor collection copies its few survivors out. Because the young generation is small and mostly dead, this is fast, with a pause depending on live bytes, root scanning and the implementation. Objects that survive several minor collections are moved to the old generation; this is called object promotion or tenuring. The old generation is usually examined less often. Terminology varies: an old-generation or major cycle need not be a full-heap stop-the-world collection. Rough numbers In a simplified fill-and-collect model, a service allocates 500 MB/s into 250 MB of available young allocation space. Ignoring pause time and survivor-space overhead, it fills in 0.5 s. If 2% of those bytes survive, each collection copies about 5 MB. The other 245 MB is reclaimed without being touched. The two numbers in that example come from one division and one multiplication: Double the allocation rate and collections come twice as often; double the survival fraction and each one copies twice as much. Real collectors also scan roots and dirty cards, so a minor collection has a cost even when almost nothing survives. The space-time trade-off In a steady model with fixed live size, allocation rate and dominant marking cost, each collection costs roughly the live data and yields about the spare room. Ignoring sweep, root and fixed overhead: Here the total heap doubles, but headroom grows from 0.5 GB to 2 GB: fourfold, so this model predicts four times less work per allocated byte. That is why GC languages often run with heaps two or more times their live data, and why Go exposes the trade-off directly as GOGC. Tracing GC buys safety and throughput with memory. Key takeaways Generational collection relies on workload-dependent survival patterns; promotion and collection terminology vary across runtimes. In the simplified nursery model, divide allocation space by allocation rate for the fill time and multiply by survival fraction for copied bytes. With fixed live size and dominant tracing cost, more headroom reduces work per allocated byte; roots, sweeping and pacing limit the model. sum: A write barrier records relevant stores so a partial collection cannot miss objects reached through older regions
x: Collecting only part of a heap is safe only if references entering it are accounted for. A collector must also inspect threads and relocate objects using a protocol compatible with their changing state. The catch: old-to-young pointers A minor collection only traces the young generation. But an old object can point at a young one: If that Entry is reachable only through cache, a minor GC that ignored the old generation would free it while still in use. Scanning the whole old generation every time would defeat the point. The answer is a write barrier: code associated with relevant reference stores, with redundant barriers sometimes eliminated. When the program writes a pointer into an old object, the barrier records it. A common HotSpot configuration divides memory into 512-byte cards; collector/version settings can change the granularity. A card-based collector records relevant reference stores in a card table. At a minor GC, only dirty cards are scanned as extra roots. A remembered set records relevant incoming locations, at slot or coarser region/card granularity depending on the collector. This is the real cost of generational GC: relevant pointer writes may pay a small tax (some barriers are elided or use different mechanisms), in exchange for cheap minor collections. Stop-the-world and safepoints Collectors move objects and read the stacks, so the classic approach is to stop the world: pause every application thread, collect, then resume. In a conventional precise stop-the-world design, threads are brought to safepoints, places where the compiler has recorded exactly where every pointer is (for example, at method calls and loop back-edges). Pause length grows with the work: a minor GC pause tracks the survivors, while a full mark-compact of a 30 GB old generation can pause for seconds. The modern-collector units cover how modern collectors do most of that work concurrently. Diagnose the scanned work A large old cache can point into many young objects without being collected itself. A young collection still needs to find those incoming references. Dirty-card scanning or remembered-set processing can therefore grow even if the young allocation area is unchanged. The live survivors, roots and scan workload matter more than the nursery size alone. Safepoints make particular runtime state understandable to a precise collector; they are not a universal claim that every collector stops every thread for an entire collection. Modern collectors use barriers and additional protocols to do substantial marking or relocation concurrently. Here the stop-the-world design provides the simpler baseline. Key takeaways A write barrier records relevant stores so a partial collection cannot miss objects reached through older regions. Cards record coarse regions, while remembered sets may record slots or regions; implementations and granularity vary. Safepoints provide inspectable execution state for a conventional precise collector; actual pause time depends on the work performed. sum: Parallel describes several GC workers; concurrent describes overlap with application execution
x: A stop-the-world collector can be simple, but pause duration depends on live data, roots, heap work and hardware. Large full collections can take seconds; heap size alone does not determine a pause. For a trading system, a game or a web service with a 100 ms latency budget, that is unacceptable. Modern collectors attack the pause by doing most of their work while the program keeps running. This unit introduces the marking abstraction. The following units explain barriers and how G1, ZGC and Go implement concurrent collection. Three things you can't all maximise Every collector balances: Latency: how long the program is paused (worst case and p99). GC throughput: what fraction of CPU time goes to the application rather than to GC. Memory footprint: how much extra memory the heap needs beyond the live data. GC throughput is usually quoted as a percentage of time: Note that a collector can have high GC throughput and still a bad latency: 5% of CPU spent in one 5-second pause every 100 seconds is 95% GC throughput, but any request that arrives during that pause waits up to 5 seconds. Collector Optimises for ------ Parallel (JVM) GC throughput G1 (common HotSpot default) balance, pause goal ZGC (JVM) latency, big heaps Go latency, simplicity Concurrent collectors buy low latency with GC throughput (barriers cost the application CPU) and footprint (garbage piles up while the collector is still running). Terminology Parallel collection means several GC threads work at once. That work may be stop-the-world or concurrent; the JVM collector named Parallel GC is stop-the-world. Concurrent collection means GC threads run at the same time as the application. A collector can be both. The tri-colour abstraction To mark concurrently, think of every object as one of three colours: White object: not yet seen. At the end of marking, white means garbage. Grey object: seen, but its fields haven't been scanned yet. Black object: seen, and all its fields scanned. Marking starts with the roots grey, then repeatedly picks a grey object, greys its white children and turns it black. When no grey objects remain, every white object is unreachable. Key takeaways Parallel describes several GC workers; concurrent describes overlap with application execution. GC throughput, pause latency and memory footprint are different measurements and must be assessed separately. White, grey and black describe unvisited, pending-scan and completed-scan states in the basic marking abstraction. sum: Creating a black-to-white edge and destroying every remaining tracing path can hide a live object without a suitable barrier
x: Concurrent marking must preserve a route to every object that remains live while application threads change references. The lost-object example motivates barriers; G1 combines such a barrier with region-level pause planning. The lost-object problem Now let the program (the mutator, in GC jargon) run during marking. Suppose: Black object A is already scanned. The mutator stores a pointer to white object C into A. The mutator then deletes the only other path to C, from grey object B. The collector will never rescan A (it's black) and can no longer reach C through B. C stays white and is freed while live. That is a memory-safety bug, not a performance problem. The object is lost only if both things happen: a black-to-white pointer is created, and every grey path to the white object is removed. A barrier prevents one or the other: Barrier On pointer write... ------ Insertion (Dijkstra) shade the new target grey Deletion / SATB (Yuasa) shade the old target grey Snapshot-at-the-beginning (SATB), used by G1 and Shenandoah, treats everything reachable when marking began as live. It's conservative: objects that die during marking can remain as floating garbage until a later eligible collection (floating garbage). Go uses a hybrid write barrier that combines both, introduced in Go 1.8, which removed a stop-the-world stack rescan. The Go team reported substantially shorter pauses for its evaluated workloads; no fixed pause bound follows for an arbitrary program. G1: regions and a pause-time goal G1 ("Garbage-First") became HotSpot's default for server-class configurations in JDK 9 and remains the default on most current configurations; Serial GC is still selected on some configurations. Instead of a few large contiguous generations, it divides the heap into many equal heap regions (ergonomically often 1–32 MB; JDK 25 also permits explicitly configured larger sizes). Regions have roles such as eden, survivor, old or free, with special handling for humongous allocations. Young collections are stop-the-world but parallel. They evacuate (copy) live objects out of eden and survivor regions. Concurrent marking runs alongside the application once the heap reaches an occupancy threshold, using SATB barriers, and works out how much live data each old region holds. Mixed collections then evacuate the young regions plus selected old regions predicted to reclaim space efficiently: hence "garbage first". Garbage amount and predicted collection cost both influence selection. Fewer live bytes to copy means more space freed per millisecond of pause. You give G1 a pause-time goal (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, default 200 ms) and it sizes the young generation and the number of old regions per mixed collection to try to meet it. It's a soft goal, not a guarantee. Objects of half a region or more are humongous objects and get their own contiguous regions, which can cause trouble if you allocate many of them. Key takeaways Creating a black-to-white edge and destroying every remaining tracing path can hide a live object without a suitable barrier. Insertion and deletion barriers protect different marking invariants; SATB can retain floating garbage. G1 marks concurrently and evacuates selected regions in pauses; its configured pause goal is a planning target, not a bound. sum: Generational ZGC uses load barriers for relocated references and store barriers for additional generational and marking work
x: Low pauses do not imply identical collector architecture. ZGC relocates heap objects concurrently; the standard Go runtime keeps heap objects in place and concentrates on concurrent marking and sweeping. ZGC: concurrent compaction Concurrent marking alone isn't enough: someone still has to move objects to defragment, and moving objects while threads use them is the hard part. G1 does its moving in pauses. ZGC does it concurrently. Its key mechanisms: Coloured pointers. ZGC stores a few metadata bits inside each 64-bit object reference, recording which GC phase the pointer is "good" for. Load barriers. Conceptually, relevant heap-reference loads check those bits; the compiler can eliminate redundant barriers. If the pointer is stale (say its object has been relocated), a slow path fixes it, finding or completing the move, and writes the corrected pointer back. Later loads can then take the fast path in that phase; future phases can require more work: the barrier is a self-healing barrier. ZGC is designed for very short pauses that do not scale with heap size; this is a design goal, not a latency guarantee for your service. Generational ZGC arrived in JDK 21, became the default ZGC mode in JDK 23, and the non-generational mode was removed in JDK 24. Generational ZGC uses store barriers as well as load barriers; the simplified load-barrier description above explains concurrent relocation, not its entire barrier design. The costs include reference-load/store barriers (some checks can be optimized), extra CPU for the concurrent GC threads, and the need for headroom. If the application allocates faster than ZGC can reclaim, threads hit an allocation stall and wait, which is a pause by another name. Shenandoah is another concurrent-compaction design; actual pause comparisons require workload measurements. Go: concurrent, non-moving, with heap and memory goals Go's collector is deliberately different. It is a concurrent tri-colour mark-sweep collector that is non-moving and, non-generational, unlike the generational HotSpot collectors discussed here. Go's escape analysis keeps many short-lived values on the stack, which weakens the case for a young generation, and fixed heap-object addresses simplify some runtime interactions. cgo still has strict pointer-passing and pinning rules; a non-moving heap does not make arbitrary Go pointers safe to retain in C. A Go GC cycle: A brief stop-the-world to turn on the write barrier. Concurrent marking, using about 25% of GOMAXPROCS worth of CPU in background workers. Mark assists: a goroutine that allocates heavily during marking is made to do some marking itself, so allocation can't outrun the collector. A brief stop-the-world to finish marking. Concurrent sweeping, done bit by bit as memory is reallocated. The 25% background share in step 2 translates into whole CPUs like this: Mark assists come on top of this when the application allocates faster than the background workers can mark. Go targets short pauses, but no per-workload pause bound is guaranteed; measure pause distributions and assist time. Key takeaways Generational ZGC uses load barriers for relocated references and store barriers for additional generational and marking work. Concurrent work still costs CPU and needs headroom; insufficient reclaimed space can stall an allocating application thread. The standard Go collector is concurrent, non-moving and non-generational; its heap policy does not prevent goroutine stacks from moving. t: Go heap goals and soft memory limits
sum: GOGC controls an allocation allowance based on live heap plus roots; examples that omit roots are simplified sizing models
x: The standard Go runtime's pacer aims to finish marking by a heap goal. This goal is distinct from the earlier point where concurrent marking starts, and from a hard operating-system or container memory limit. GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT You tune Go's GC mostly with GOGC (default 100). Ignoring roots for a moment, GOGC sets a heap-size goal based on growth since the last live-heap measurement. The GC pacer starts collection before reaching that goal so concurrent marking has time to finish: With the same 400 MB live heap and the same simplified assumptions, GOGC=50 gives a 600 MB goal, and GOGC=200 gives a 1,200 MB goal. Since Go 1.18 the roots count too: The 400 MB examples above neglect roots. In the guide’s steady model (constant live heap and allocation rate), changing GOGC adjusts the allocation allowance and the dominant GC frequency/cost. Roots, memory limits, changing liveness and fixed costs can alter the simple inverse relationship. GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19) adds a soft memory limit: as Go-runtime-managed memory approaches it, the GC runs more often regardless of GOGC. In containers, leave measured headroom below the container limit for memory outside the runtime; a fixed percentage cannot suit every application, and this soft limit cannot guarantee avoidance of an OOM kill. Setting GOGC=off disables automatic growth-triggered collection but leaves memory-limit-driven collection enabled; explicit runtime.GC() can still request a collection. Beware: if live data really approaches the limit, the GC runs almost continuously (a death spiral), so the runtime applies a soft GC CPU limiter targeted at about 50% over its accounting window; it can then exceed the memory limit to keep making application progress. Key takeaways GOGC controls an allocation allowance based on live heap plus roots; examples that omit roots are simplified sizing models. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft limit for Go-runtime-managed memory, with exclusions and possible overshoot. When live data approaches a limit, repeated collection can cost CPU without freeing much; measure external memory and leave suitable headroom. sum: Under uniform arrivals and the stated no-queueing assumptions, only requests arriving during a pause receive its residual waiting time
x: A low average does not describe how the slowest requests feel. Explicit pause and fan-out models make their assumptions visible, while measurements tell you whether the model resembles your service. Pauses and tail latency Averages hide GC pauses; percentiles expose them. A pause in the p99 Assume requests otherwise take a fixed 5 ms, arrivals are uniform, a 150 ms pause starts every 5 s, and ignore requests already in progress and post-pause queueing. Then 3% arrive during the pause and wait 0–150 ms extra. In this simplified model p99 is 105 ms: the upper 1% corresponds to waits above 100 ms. Real queueing can add delay. The p99 (99th percentile) is a latency boundary at or below which 99% of requests fall; ties and finite-sample conventions matter. Here is how the 105 ms comes out: The model only works when the fraction hitting a pause is above 1% (otherwise the p99 never sees the pause at all, though p99.9 might). The median is still 5 ms, so a median or average alone can obscure the tail effect even though a pause can change the mean. A fan-out that waits for all 100 backends sees the slowest response. If each independently has a 1% chance of a slow response, the chance that at least one is slow is: So a 1-in-100 event on each backend becomes the common case for the whole request. Correlation, hedging and partial-result policies change this. This is why low-latency collectors matter so much for microservices. Choosing and tuning Measure first. Turn on GC logs (-Xlog:gc in Java, GODEBUG=gctrace=1 in Go) and find out whether pauses or CPU are the problem. Reduce allocation. The cheapest GC work is the work you don't create: reuse scratch memory, avoid autoboxing, use sync.Pool in Go for hot temporary objects. Give it headroom. Insufficient headroom is one cause of GC pressure; logs may instead reveal root scanning, allocation churn or scheduling problems. Test collector candidates by goal. Parallel GC is a throughput candidate for batch work; G1 is a general-service baseline; ZGC or Shenandoah are latency candidates for large heaps. Measure the full application before choosing. Don't over-tune. Modern collectors are adaptive; dozens of flags copied from an old blog post often make things worse. Key takeaways Under uniform arrivals and the stated no-queueing assumptions, only requests arriving during a pause receive its residual waiting time. Independent slow-backend probabilities compound in all-results fan-out; correlation and early-result policies change the model. Choose and tune collectors from measured pause, CPU, allocation and memory data rather than assuming a universal best collector. sum: A Rust move transfers a non-Copy value and leaves the moved place uninitialised until valid reinitialisation
x: Every approach so far has a price. Manual allocation offers explicit control but relies on correct lifetime management. Reference counting and tracing can automate reclamation within sound implementations, while adding run-time work, metadata, headroom or pauses. None is universally fastest. Rust takes a fourth route. Normal drops follow the language’s scope and ownership rules, with code emitted by the compiler, as C++'s RAII does, and the compiler also proves that no reference outlives what it points to. Ordinary Rust ownership requires neither a tracing garbage collector nor reference counting; library types can add counting, and safe code is designed to avoid use-after-free, double free and data races through static restrictions and safe runtime abstractions, assuming sound compiler/library implementations. The price is paid at compile time, in rules you have to learn. The three ownership rules From The Rust Programming Language: Each value has a memory owner: a variable, a field, or an element of a collection. There can be only one owner at a time. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory and resources are released). For this example the compiler emits destruction at scope exit. Rust does not guarantee every destructor runs: intentional leaks, cycles, abort and process exit are exceptions. Moves Assigning or passing an owned non-Copy value by value moves it. A borrow does not, and the moved place can be used again after valid reinitialisation; partial moves have more precise field rules. Why forbid it? Both s1 and s2 would point at the same heap buffer, and both would free it at the end of scope: a double free. Rust's answer is that after the move, only s2 owns it, so exactly one free happens. For String a move transfers its pointer/length/capacity representation without cloning its heap buffer. Physical copies may be optimized away, and non-Copy values need not be on the stack or own heap memory. Passing to a function moves too: Two escape routes: Copy types (integers, f64, bool, char, and tuples or arrays of them) permit implicit duplication, so the original remains usable. Copy describes semantics, not location: a Copy value can be stored in a heap object, and shared references to heap data are Copy too..clone() invokes type-specific cloning. String clones its heap buffer, but Rc/Arc clones share an allocation; Clone is not a universal deep-copy guarantee. Compare C++ std::move is a cast enabling move overloads; it does not itself move or modify the source. Standard-library moved-from objects generally remain valid with type-specific guarantees (a moved unique_ptr is empty). Rust rejects reading an uninitialized moved value, but permits reinitialization and valid uses of unmoved fields after partial moves. Key takeaways A Rust move transfers a non-Copy value and leaves the moved place uninitialised until valid reinitialisation. Copy permits implicit duplication, while Clone runs type-specific code and need not make a deep copy. Normal ownership-driven drops differ from guaranteed destruction in every execution; safe intentional leaks and termination remain possible. sum: Local bindings normally drop in reverse declaration order; fields drop in declaration order
x: Owners provide normal release points; borrows let code use an owned value without transferring it. Review both the lifetime of the owner and the period during which a reference is actually used. Drop order Initialized local bindings are normally dropped at scope exit in reverse declaration order. Struct fields instead drop in declaration order: Output: For a newly created temporary such as Guard::new(), let _ =... does not retain it beyond the statement; let _guard =... does. Applying a wildcard to an existing place does not necessarily move/drop it. Current rustc denies let _ = mutex.lock() by default via let_underscore_lock, because otherwise the temporary guard would immediately unlock. Because drop is deterministic, Drop releases far more than memory: a File closes, a MutexGuard unlocks, a transaction wrapper may roll back according to that library’s documented Drop contract. Borrowing Moving everything around would be painful, so Rust lets you take a Rust borrow: take a reference without taking ownership. &T is a shared borrow: ordinary mutation is restricted, but interior-mutability types can provide controlled mutation, and you can have any number at once. &mut T is a mutable borrow: read-write, and it must be the only borrow while it's in use. The rule is aliasing XOR mutation: at any moment you can have many readers or one writer, never both. That single rule rules out a surprising number of bugs. Iterator invalidation, caught at compile time This isn't pedantry. push may reallocate the vector's heap buffer to a bigger one and free the old one, leaving first pointing into freed memory. In C++ comparable code can compile and becomes a dangling-reference access if reallocation actually invalidates that reference. In Rust it can't be written in safe code. Non-lexical lifetimes A Rust borrow can end after its last use, before the block ends; control flow and destructor requirements also constrain its lifetime. Delete the println! above and the code compiles: first is never used after the push, so the borrows don't overlap. This refinement, non-lexical lifetimes, arrived in the 2018 edition and removed many spurious errors. Data races The same rule prevents data races. A data race involves conflicting concurrent accesses, at least one a write, without the required synchronization; atomic/synchronized access is different. Exclusive &mut makes that impossible within safe code, and the Send and Sync traits extend the check across threads (the concurrency module covers these). Key takeaways Local bindings normally drop in reverse declaration order; fields drop in declaration order. Many shared borrows or one exclusive mutable borrow may be in use; interior-mutability abstractions supply controlled exceptions to ordinary shared mutation restrictions. Non-lexical lifetimes can end a borrow after its last use, preventing a live reference from overlapping a potentially reallocating push.
