t: Reuse workers and estimate waiting-job waves
sum: A pool reuses a bounded number of workers rather than creating an unbounded thread per request.
x: Thread pools Creating a thread involves allocation and runtime/OS work; no reproducible creation-time benchmark is supplied here. More importantly, a server that creates one thread per request without admission or concurrency limits has no application-level bound: a traffic spike can create thousands of threads until resource limits or failures intervene. A bounded thread pool reuses workers and caps active jobs; its submission queue still needs an overload policy. A fixed set of worker threads pulls jobs from a shared queue: Threads are created once and reused, and the pool size caps concurrency. Examples include Java's ExecutorService, the worker pools in web servers, database connection handlers, and Python's concurrent.futures. The values are [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]; the elapsed-time suffix is machine-dependent and should be near or above the ideal one-second schedule. When every job takes the same time, a pool works through them in "waves": each wave runs one job on every worker at once. So twenty half-second jobs on ten workers take about 1 second instead of 20 × 0.5 = 10 seconds serially. This assumes the jobs mostly wait (here they sleep), so the workers do not compete for CPU; Pure-Python CPU-bound jobs in one GIL-enabled interpreter cannot run bytecode simultaneously. The later GIL unit covers native extensions and other interpreter builds. map returns results in input order, regardless of which finished first. Key takeaways A pool reuses a bounded number of workers rather than creating an unbounded thread per request. Equal-duration waiting jobs finish in whole waves; map preserves input order. Elapsed time depends on scheduling and overhead; the wave calculation is an ideal approximation. t: Size pools and avoid nested-job deadlock
sum: Start pool sizing from available compute capacity and measured waiting time.
x: How big should the pool be? It depends on what the jobs spend their time doing: CPU-bound jobs (compression, image processing): start near the effective logical CPU capacity or quota, then measure. SMT, memory bandwidth, blocking, the GIL and job size can change the best size. I/O-bound jobs (waiting on network or disk): more threads than cores, so that something is computing while others wait. Where does the I/O-bound number come from? A thread that waits 90 ms for every 10 ms it computes keeps a core busy only a tenth of the time, so you need about ten such threads per core to keep the core busy. In general, each thread keeps a core busy for its compute time divided by its total (wait plus compute) time, and the number of threads needed per core is that fraction turned upside down. A common rule of thumb follows: So 8 cores and jobs that wait 90 ms on a database for every 10 ms of CPU give 80 threads. Treat it as a starting point and measure: it assumes whatever the threads wait on (the database here) can serve 80 requests at once, and it ignores memory per thread and, in Python, the GIL. Python's own default is simpler. Since Python 3.13, ThreadPoolExecutor sizes itself like this when you don't pass max_workers: In Python code that is min(32, (os.process_cpu_count() or 1) + 4), which replaced the earlier formula based on os.cpu_count(). Pool-induced deadlock If jobs in a pool submit child jobs to the same pool and wait for them, they can deadlock. With 2 workers, two parent jobs each wait for a child; both children sit in the queue with no free worker to run them. Use a separate pool for child jobs, or avoid blocking waits inside jobs. Also watch the queue. An unbounded queue hides overload: under a sustained spike it grows until you run out of memory, and every queued request is already late. Bounded queues that reject or apply backpressure fail more honestly. Key takeaways Start pool sizing from available compute capacity and measured waiting time. The waiting-to-compute ratio is a starting estimate, subject to downstream capacity and memory limits. Workers waiting for queued children in the same exhausted pool can deadlock; bound queues to expose overload. t: Python’s GIL, races and parallel alternatives
sum: GIL-enabled CPython executes bytecode in one thread at a time per interpreter.
x: Python's GIL A GIL-enabled CPython interpreter has a Global Interpreter Lock: a single lock that a thread must hold to execute Python bytecode. Python threads are real OS threads (1:1), but only one at a time runs Python code. Why it exists CPython manages memory with reference counts on every object. Incrementing and decrementing those counts from several threads at once would need a lock or atomic operation on every object access. One big lock was simpler and made single-threaded code fast. What it means for CPU-bound code On a standard build the two lines print roughly the same time. The threads take turns holding the GIL (a waiting thread asks the holder to drop it after the switch interval, 5 ms by default, see sys.getswitchinterval()), so there is no parallel speed-up. What it does not hurt The GIL is released during blocking I/O (socket.recv, file reads, time.sleep) and by many C extensions during long computations (NumPy array operations, hashlib on large inputs, zlib). So threads work well for I/O-bound Python, as in the pool example above, and for code that spends its time in GIL-releasing libraries. What it does not prevent: races A common myth is that the GIL makes Python code thread-safe. It only guarantees that the interpreter's own internals stay consistent. Thread-switch points depend on the CPython version, and bytecodes may invoke user code or extensions. Do not assume a shared read-modify-write sequence is atomic: This is a race demonstration, not a reproducible output guarantee. Depending on build, scheduling and implementation, it may lose updates or print the expected count; a passing run does not establish correctness. One possible interleaving is that a thread reads counter, switches before completing the call and store, and later writes back a stale value. Exact switch opportunities depend on the interpreter version; loss is possible, not guaranteed by a particular source line. A plain counter += 1 in the loop often happens to give the right answer on recent CPython versions, because of where the interpreter checks for thread switches. That is an implementation detail, not a guarantee, and it is not a safe shared-counter protocol on free-threaded builds. Protect shared state with a threading.Lock (the next module covers locks properly). Some simple built-in operations have useful implementation-level locking or atomicity, but callbacks, custom key methods and free-threaded builds complicate the rules. Use documented guarantees and explicit synchronisation for shared invariants; check-then-insert is not automatically atomic. Getting real parallelism in Python Processes: multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor. Each process has its own interpreter and GIL. The cost is pickling data between processes. C extensions that release the GIL (NumPy and friends). Free-threaded CPython (PEP 703): a build with no GIL, experimental in 3.13 and officially supported (but not the default) from 3.14. It's installed as a separate interpreter, e.g. python3.14t. Single-threaded code runs somewhat slower, and C extensions must be marked compatible or the GIL is turned back on. Subinterpreters: Python 3.14 added concurrent.interpreters and InterpreterPoolExecutor, where each interpreter has its own GIL. Content gap: runtime measurements No reproducible record supports exact thread-creation timing, a particular racy counter output, false-sharing slowdown or ideal pool speed-up. Examples show mechanisms; timing and capacity must be measured for the chosen runtime and workload. Key takeaways GIL-enabled CPython executes bytecode in one thread at a time per interpreter. Blocking I/O and compatible native extensions can release the GIL; multi-step shared invariants still need synchronisation. Processes, GIL-releasing native work, free-threaded builds and isolated interpreters offer different routes to parallel computation. sum: Response measures arrival to first service; turnaround measures arrival to completion.
x: A machine can have more runnable threads than available logical CPUs; at other times many or all threads are asleep. The scheduler is the part of the kernel that decides which runnable thread gets each core next, and for how long. Every scheduling algorithm is an answer to one question: when the CPU becomes free, who goes next? The answers differ because they optimise for different goals. What are we optimising? Metric Meaning Want --------- CPU utilisation Fraction of time the CPU is busy High Throughput Jobs finished per unit time High Turnaround time Arrival to completion Low Waiting time Time spent ready but not running Low Response time Arrival to first run Low Fairness Similar jobs get similar shares Even The three times in the table are all worked out from moments on one clock that starts at 0 when we begin watching. Each is a subtraction. These identities hold for a job that never blocks, so it needs the CPU for one stretch (one CPU burst, defined in the next unit) and is either running or waiting in the queue: For example, a job that arrives at 2 ms, first runs at 5 ms, needs 4 ms of CPU in total and finishes at 12 ms has a turnaround time of 12 − 2 = 10 ms, a waiting time of 10 − 4 = 6 ms and a response time of 5 − 2 = 3 ms. If a job also blocks for I/O, the time it spends blocked is neither running nor waiting in the ready queue, so you would subtract that too before calling the remainder "waiting". These goals conflict. A batch system crunching overnight jobs wants throughput and doesn't care about response time. An interactive desktop or a web server wants low latency: a keypress should be handled within milliseconds even if a compile is running. Fairness can cost throughput, because switching between jobs wastes time and cache. Key takeaways Response measures arrival to first service; turnaround measures arrival to completion. Subtract CPU service and any blocked time to distinguish ready-queue waiting from time in the system. Choose metrics for the workload; fairness, overhead and throughput can conflict. sum: CPU-bound tasks compute for long bursts; I/O-bound tasks frequently block.
x: CPU bursts and I/O bursts Programs alternate between using the CPU (a CPU burst) and waiting for something (an I/O burst: disk, network, keyboard, a lock). CPU-bound threads (video encoding, compiling, number crunching) have long bursts and rarely block. I/O-bound threads (a shell, an editor, a web server waiting on clients) have short bursts and block often. Burst distributions depend on workload; interactive tasks often have short bursts between waits. A good scheduler lets I/O-bound threads run promptly when they wake. They need the CPU only briefly, then go back to waiting, which keeps both the CPU and the I/O devices busy. Preemptive versus cooperative The scheduler can make a decision when a thread: blocks (for example on I/O) or yields; finishes; becomes ready (an I/O completes, a new thread is created); is interrupted by the timer. A cooperative (non-preemptive) scheduler only acts on 1 and 2: a thread keeps the CPU until it gives it up. Windows 3.1 and classic Mac OS worked this way, and one misbehaving program could freeze the whole machine. Today, cooperative scheduling survives inside programs: Python asyncio tasks yield when an await actually suspends, while event loops also move on when callbacks or coroutines return; so a coroutine stuck in a CPU loop stalls everything else in that loop. A preemptive scheduler can also act on 3 and 4. A periodic timer interrupt returns control to the kernel, which can take the CPU away from a thread that has run long enough. Every mainstream OS (Linux, Windows, macOS) preempts user threads. Each switch costs something: saving and restoring registers, running the scheduler, and, less visibly, cold caches and TLB for the incoming thread. There is no platform-independent switch-time constant; both direct and cache costs need measurement. Key takeaways CPU-bound tasks compute for long bursts; I/O-bound tasks frequently block. Cooperative execution depends on returning or suspending; a CPU loop can stall an event loop. Preemption lets the kernel regain control, at a workload-dependent direct and cache cost. Further reading Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia) Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia Shortest job next — Wikipedia Convoy effect — Wikipedia

t: Trace FCFS and the convoy effect
sum: FCFS serves arrival order without preempting a running job.
x: First-come, first-served (FCFS) Run jobs in arrival order, each to completion. It's a simple FIFO queue and is non-preemptive. Three jobs arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3, with CPU bursts of 24, 3 and 3 ms: Job Burst Waiting Turnaround ------------ P1 24 0 24 P2 3 24 27 P3 3 27 30 To compare schedules with one number, take the average waiting time: add every job's waiting time and divide by the number of jobs. The average waiting time is 17 ms. If the short jobs had arrived first (P2, P3, P1), the waits would be 0, 3 and 6 ms: an average of (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = 3 ms. Same work, nearly six times better. This is the convoy effect: short jobs stuck behind a long one, like cars behind a lorry on a single-lane road. With a mix of one CPU-bound and several I/O-bound threads, the I/O-bound ones queue behind the hog while the disks sit idle, then all finish their I/O together while the CPU sits idle. Key takeaways FCFS serves arrival order without preempting a running job. Short jobs behind a long CPU burst suffer the convoy effect. Compute waiting times from the stated arrivals and schedule before averaging them. Further reading Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia) Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia Shortest job next — Wikipedia Convoy effect — Wikipedia

t: Trace SJF and shortest remaining time
sum: Non-preemptive SJF selects the shortest available burst and then lets it finish.
x: Shortest job first (SJF) Always run the job with the shortest next CPU burst. When all jobs are available at once, SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time: moving a short job ahead of a long one reduces the short job's wait by more than it increases the long one's. Now use staggered arrivals: Job Arrival Burst --------- P1 0 8 P2 1 4 P3 2 9 P4 3 5 Non-preemptive SJF. At time 0 only P1 is there, so it runs to completion. At 8, P2 (4), P3 (9) and P4 (5) are waiting; the shortest is P2, then P4, then P3. Each job runs in one piece, so its waiting time is simply its start time minus its arrival time: The average waiting time is 7.75 ms. Shortest remaining time first (SRTF) The preemptive version: whenever a job arrives, compare its burst with the remaining time of the running job, and switch if it's shorter. At 0 ms: P1 starts (remaining 8). At 1 ms: P2 arrives needing 4, less than P1's remaining 7. Preempt; P2 runs. At 2 ms and 3 ms: P3 (9) and P4 (5) arrive; neither beats P2's remaining 3 or 2. At 5 ms: P2 done. Remaining: P1 7, P3 9, P4 5. P4 runs. At 10 ms: P4 done. P1 (7) runs, then P3. A preempted job can wait in several pieces (P1 waits from 1 to 10 ms), so "start minus arrival" no longer works. Instead take the job's whole time in the system and subtract the time it actually ran: The average is 6.5 ms, better than non-preemptive SJF. Key takeaways Non-preemptive SJF selects the shortest available burst and then lets it finish. SRTF can preempt when a newly arrived burst is shorter than the running job’s remaining work. For a job that never blocks, waiting is turnaround minus total CPU service, even after preemptions. Further reading Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia) Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia Shortest job next — Wikipedia Convoy effect — Wikipedia

t: Predict bursts and understand SJF’s limits
sum: Exponential averaging blends the measured burst with the previous prediction.
x: The catch: you don't know the future The OS can't know how long a burst will be. It can predict from history. Threads tend to behave like they did recently, so a common textbook method is an exponential average: after each burst, blend the burst that just happened with the previous prediction. It is called exponential because each update multiplies older contributions by the complement of the latest-burst weight. With the weight set to one half, the burst before last counts a quarter, the one before that an eighth, and so on. For a fixed weight strictly between zero and one, old contributions approach zero without reaching it in exact arithmetic. At a weight of one, only the latest burst counts; at zero, the prediction never updates. The method works only as well as the past predicts the future; a thread that suddenly changes behaviour is mispredicted for a few bursts. SJF also risks starvation: if short jobs keep arriving, a long job may never run. The next lesson covers how real schedulers avoid that. Key takeaways Exponential averaging blends the measured burst with the previous prediction. The newest burst’s weight controls how quickly the estimate adapts. Known-burst SJF results depend on the arrival and cost model; repeated short arrivals can starve a long job. Further reading Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia) Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia Shortest job next — Wikipedia Convoy effect — Wikipedia

t: Round robin: response versus switching cost
sum: Round robin rotates runnable jobs after a quantum and lets short bursts finish early.
x: Round robin (RR) Give each job a fixed time quantum (time slice), then preempt it and put it at the back of the ready queue. RR is FCFS plus a timer, and it is the basis of most interactive scheduling. Back to P1 = 24, P2 = 3 and P3 = 3, all at time 0, with a quantum of 4 ms: P2 and P3 finish within their first quantum and leave early. P1 then runs alone, quantum after quantum. Job Waiting Turnaround Response ------------ P1 6 30 0 P2 4 7 4 P3 7 10 7 Averaging the columns: Average waiting is about 5.67 ms and average response time about 3.67 ms, against 17 ms and 17 ms for FCFS in the original order (under FCFS a job's first run is also its only run, so its response time equals its waiting time). A tie-breaking convention When a job's quantum expires at the same moment a new job arrives, most textbooks put the new arrival in the queue first, then the preempted job. State your convention when you work these by hand; it can change the answer. Choosing the quantum Too large, and RR degenerates into FCFS: interactive jobs wait behind CPU hogs. Too small, and the CPU spends its time switching. To see how much is wasted, assume every job uses its full quantum, so each quantum of useful work is followed by one context switch. The wasted fraction is the switch time divided by the whole cycle: With a 0.1 ms switch cost, a 10 ms quantum wastes about 1% and a 1 ms quantum about 9%, before counting cache effects. Choose the quantum from measured burst lengths, latency goals and overhead. No workload trace or platform-specific measurement is supplied to justify a universal percentile target or slice range here. RR has good response time and is fair, but its average turnaround can be poor when jobs are of similar length: with three 10 ms jobs and a 1 ms quantum, all three finish near 30 ms, whereas FCFS finishes them at 10, 20 and 30. Comparison Algorithm Preemptive Strength Weakness ------------ FCFS No Simple, no starvation Convoy effect SJF No Optimal avg wait Needs burst length; starvation SRTF Yes Even better avg wait Same, plus more switches RR Yes Response time, fairness Turnaround; quantum tuning No real general-purpose OS uses any of these alone. Linux, Windows and macOS combine their ideas: priorities, time slices, and rewarding threads that block a lot. The following lessons build up to what Linux actually does. Key takeaways Round robin rotates runnable jobs after a quantum and lets short bursts finish early. State how arrivals and expired quanta are ordered when their timestamps tie. Small quanta improve first response but increase switching overhead; similar jobs can finish later overall. Further reading Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia) Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia Shortest job next — Wikipedia Convoy effect — Wikipedia

sum: Strict priority can starve lower-priority work; Linux nice values instead express fair weights.
x: FCFS, SJF and round robin treat all jobs as equals. Real systems don't: an audio thread that misses a 5 ms deadline produces a click, while a backup job can wait. Priority scheduling lets the system express that. It also introduces two classic failure modes, starvation and priority inversion, and the multilevel feedback queue adapts scheduling to observed behaviour. Priority inheritance addresses lock-related priority inversion separately. Priority scheduling In a strict-priority model, the scheduler chooses the highest-priority ready thread. Linux nice values instead set relative fair-scheduling weights; they are not strict priorities. Threads of equal priority usually share the CPU round robin. With preemption, a higher-priority thread that becomes ready takes the CPU immediately. Conventions vary, so always check which way the numbers run: System Range Higher priority is --------- Linux nice −20 to 19 Lower number Linux real-time 1 to 99 Higher number Windows 0 to 31 Higher number There are static priorities (set once by the user or administrator) and dynamic priorities (adjusted by the OS based on behaviour). SJF is in fact a priority scheduler whose priority is the predicted burst length. Starvation and aging Strict priority has an obvious hole: if high-priority work keeps arriving, low-priority work never runs. That is starvation. Content gap: unverified historical anecdote A commonly repeated story about a job waiting for years on an early time-sharing system has been omitted because this audit could not establish a reliable primary record. The starvation mechanism does not depend on that story. The standard cure is aging: increase a thread's priority the longer it waits, so that eventually it beats the steady stream of newcomers. How long does aging take? Suppose priority numbers run from 0 (highest) to 127 (lowest), and a waiting thread improves by one level every second. A thread at 127 competes with a constant load at priority 20. The wait is the number of levels it must climb times the time each level takes: So it reaches equal priority after 107 seconds. Actual first service also depends on tie-breaking and queue length, and a chosen policy may reset the priority after the thread has run. Key takeaways Strict priority can starve lower-priority work; Linux nice values instead express fair weights. Check whether a larger numeric priority means more or less importance. Aging can raise waiting work to a competing priority; first service still depends on ties and queued work. Further reading Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue — OSTEP Glenn Reeves: what happened on Pathfinder — firsthand correction in RISKS Priority inversion — Wikipedia Priority inheritance — Wikipedia RT-mutex subsystem with PI support — Linux kernel docs Multilevel feedback queue — Wikipedia

t: Learn job behaviour with feedback queues
sum: New jobs start at the top so genuinely short jobs can finish promptly.
x: The multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) The deeper problem is that the OS doesn't know which jobs are short or interactive. SJF needs that knowledge; round robin ignores it. The multilevel feedback queue, first described by Corbató's CTSS in 1962 (part of the work that earned him the Turing Award), learns it by watching how jobs behave. MLFQ keeps several ready queues, one per priority level. The textbook rules (as in OSTEP) are: If job A has a higher priority than job B, A runs. If A and B have the same priority, they share the CPU round robin. A new job enters at the highest priority. Once a job uses up its time allotment at a level, however many times it gave up the CPU along the way, it moves down one level. After a fixed period (the boost period), move every job back to the top queue (the priority boost). Lower queues usually get longer quanta: short slices at the top for responsiveness, long slices at the bottom where CPU-bound jobs live and switching overhead matters more. Why it approximates SJF Rule 3 assumes every new job might be short. If it is, it finishes (or blocks) while still at the top, getting SJF-like treatment. If it isn't, Rule 4 pushes it down level by level until it sits with the other long jobs. The scheduler has learned the job is CPU-bound without being told. A worked trace Three levels as above, with an allotment of one quantum per level. A CPU-bound job A arrives at 0. An interactive job B arrives at 50 and repeatedly runs for 2 ms, then waits 8 ms for I/O. 0–10: A uses its full 10 ms at Q2 and is demoted. 10–30: A uses 20 ms at Q1 and is demoted to Q0. 30–50: A runs at Q0. 50: B arrives at Q2 and preempts A immediately (Rule 1). B runs 2 ms and blocks; A carries on until B's I/O completes at 60, when B preempts it again. In the idealised zero-overhead trace, B runs immediately when ready; no measured wake-up latency is implied. A uses all the leftover time. That's the behaviour we want from a desktop. Key takeaways New jobs start at the top so genuinely short jobs can finish promptly. CPU-heavy jobs sink through queues with longer slices. Higher-priority arrivals preempt lower queues in the stated idealised policy. Further reading Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue — OSTEP Glenn Reeves: what happened on Pathfinder — firsthand correction in RISKS Priority inversion — Wikipedia Priority inheritance — Wikipedia RT-mutex subsystem with PI support — Linux kernel docs Multilevel feedback queue — Wikipedia

t: Prevent gaming and starvation in MLFQ
sum: Count cumulative CPU consumption at a level, not just the latest uninterrupted burst.
x: Rule 4 and gaming the scheduler Early MLFQ designs had a gentler rule: a job that gives up the CPU before its quantum expires keeps its priority. That rewards interactive jobs, but it can be gamed. A job that runs for 9.9 ms of a 10 ms quantum, then issues a trivial I/O, stays at the top forever and gets nearly all the CPU. Rule 4 closes the hole with better accounting: the scheduler tracks total CPU used at a level, not per burst. In the preceding feedback-trace unit, B uses 2 ms per burst. Dividing its allotment by the CPU it uses per burst gives the number of bursts before it is demoted: So after five bursts B drops to Q1. That is the cost of being game-proof: even a genuinely interactive job slowly sinks. Rule 5 lifts it back. Rule 5: the priority boost Without boosts, two things go wrong: Starvation: many interactive jobs at the top can use all the CPU, and jobs in Q0 never run. Changing behaviour: a job that was CPU-bound (say, a program loading data) and then becomes interactive is stuck at the bottom. Boosting everything to the top once every boost period fixes both. The length of that period is one of Ousterhout's "voodoo constants": too long and long jobs starve; too short and interactive jobs lose their advantage. Real systems tune it, or replace the boost with aging or decay of usage history. MLFQ in real systems The cited historical Solaris documentation describes 60 time-sharing priorities and default quanta from 40 ms at priority 59 to 200 ms at priority 0; these are version/configuration-specific values. Windows uses 32 priority levels with dynamic boosts for threads that finish waiting on I/O or own the foreground window. FreeBSD's ULE scheduler computes an "interactivity score" from sleep and run times. Linux took a different route: since 2.6.23 (2007) its normal scheduler has been built on fairness rather than feedback queues, as the next lesson explains. Key takeaways Count cumulative CPU consumption at a level, not just the latest uninterrupted burst. Periodic boosts let long-waiting jobs run and let changed workloads regain priority. Queue counts, quanta and boost intervals are policy choices; historical system examples have version-specific values. t: Priority inversion and inherited lock priority
sum: A medium-priority task can delay a high-priority waiter by preempting its low-priority lock holder.
x: Priority inversion Priorities interact badly with locks. Take three threads on one CPU, sharing a mutex m: H: high priority, needs m briefly; M: medium priority, CPU-heavy, never touches m; L: low priority, takes m now and then. L takes m. H wakes, preempts L and tries to lock m. It blocks. M wakes. It outranks L, so it preempts L. L can't run, so it can't release m, so H can't run. H is now waiting for M, a lower-priority thread that has nothing to do with m. The priorities have been inverted. Worse, the delay isn't bounded by L's short critical section; it lasts as long as M (and any other medium-priority work) keeps running. This is unbounded priority inversion. Mars Pathfinder, 1997 Glenn Reeves, who led Pathfinder's software team, describes a priority inversion involving a semaphore inside VxWorks select/pipe handling. The low-priority ASI/MET task held the resource; intermediate work delayed it while the higher-priority bc_dist task waited. A deadline check by bc_sched triggered a reset. Engineers reproduced the failure with tracing, enabled priority inheritance through a configuration change, tested the wider effects and deployed it using their validated spacecraft patch mechanism. Reeves explicitly says they did not use the VxWorks shell for the update. He also says the pre-landing occurrence was investigated and remained unresolved, rather than being dismissed as a hardware glitch. This firsthand correction matters: retain the inversion lesson without repeating the inaccurate interpreter-fix and ignored-warning story. Priority inheritance The fix is priority inheritance: while a thread holds a lock that a higher-priority thread is waiting for, it temporarily runs at the waiter's priority. H blocks on m, held by L. L is boosted to H's priority. M wakes but can't preempt L, which now outranks it. L finishes its critical section and releases m, dropping back to low priority. H takes m and runs. In this isolated three-thread example, H waits for L's remaining critical section plus scheduling overhead. General bounds must include nesting, higher-priority interference and any blocking by the holder. Inheritance must be transitive: if L is itself blocked on a lock held by another thread, that thread is boosted too. An alternative is an immediate priority ceiling protocol: each mutex gets a ceiling based on the highest priority of any thread that may lock it. With POSIX PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT, a holder immediately runs at the higher of its own priority and the highest ceiling of its owned protected mutexes, even when nobody is waiting. Ceilings must be assigned in advance. Acquiring or releasing a protected mutex can still change effective priority; this is precomputed boosting, rather than a guarantee of fewer priority changes. POSIX exposes both as mutex attributes. This configuration fragment assumes m is a declared mutex; production code must check the return values and destroy the attribute object when finished: On Linux, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT mutexes are built on PI futexes and the kernel's rt_mutex, which handles chains of boosts. The PREEMPT_RT real-time kernel goes further and converts most kernel spinlocks into priority-inheriting sleeping locks for the same reason. Priority inversion matters most for real-time threads with strict priorities. Ordinary Linux threads under the fair scheduler suffer milder versions: a low-weight thread holding a lock still runs, just slowly. The next module covers locks in depth. Key takeaways A medium-priority task can delay a high-priority waiter by preempting its low-priority lock holder. Priority inheritance boosts holders along blocking chains; priority ceilings use precomputed mutex ceilings. Pathfinder’s firsthand account describes enabling inheritance through a tested patch, without using a VxWorks shell. t: Linux scheduler history and class ordering
sum: Classic scheduler names describe different selection policies across kernel versions.
x: The earlier MLFQ units describe a policy that guesses which jobs are interactive and rewards them. Linux took a different route in 2007: stop guessing, and divide the CPU fairly, in proportion to a weight. That idea, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), entered mainline in Linux 2.6.23. Linux 6.6, released in 2023, changed fair-class selection to EEVDF, which keeps weighted fairness and adds an explicit notion of latency. Deployed distributions can retain older kernels or backport changes. Real-time work sits above all of this, in strict-priority classes that the fair scheduler never overrides. A short history The O(...) labels are Big O notation, where n is the number of runnable tasks: O(n) means picking the next task took time proportional to n, and O(1) means it took the same time however many tasks there were. Kernel Scheduler ------ 2.4 O(n): scan runnable tasks 2.6.0 (2003) O(1): priority arrays plus interactivity heuristics 2.6.23 (2007) CFS 6.6 (2023) EEVDF replaces CFS's pick logic 6.12 (2024) sched_ext: schedulers in BPF The O(1) scheduler was fast but relied on heuristics to guess which tasks were interactive, much like MLFQ. Those heuristics could be fooled, and desktop latency suffered under load. Con Kolivas's fairness-based RSDL patches showed a simpler approach worked, and Ingo Molnar wrote CFS in response. Scheduling classes The kernel doesn't have one scheduler; it has a stack of scheduling classes, checked in strict order. Ordinary selection considers higher classes first, subject to bandwidth limits. A deadline-class fair server can also dispatch fair work to prevent starvation. Ignoring throttling and fair-server service, an eligible SCHED_FIFO thread outranks normal threads regardless of nice. Ordinary applications usually use SCHED_NORMAL (SCHED_OTHER in the userspace API). A loaded sched_ext scheduler can take over normal, batch and idle-policy tasks; in partial mode it handles only SCHED_EXT tasks. Key takeaways Classic scheduler names describe different selection policies across kernel versions. Real-time and deadline classes normally outrank fair work, subject to bandwidth controls and fair-server service. sched_ext can replace normal scheduling according to its configured mode. sum: Classic CFS selects the task with the smallest virtual runtime.
x: CFS: an ideal CPU, simulated CFS’s design starts from an imaginary ideal multi-tasking CPU. For equal-weight runnable tasks sharing one CPU, each receives an equal fraction of its service: Different weights produce unequal shares, covered in the next unit. Real hardware can run only one task per CPU at a time, so CFS tracks how far each task has fallen behind that ideal. The tool is virtual runtime (vruntime), in nanoseconds. Every task has a scheduling weight (set by its nice value, below); a normal nice 0 task has weight 1024. When a task runs, its vruntime is advanced by the real time it ran, scaled by how its weight compares with 1024: In the example, a nice 0 task with vruntime 50 ms runs for 4 ms and ends up at 54 ms. The formula is the whole of CFS's fairness: it holds for tasks in the fair class competing on one run queue. The rule for picking is then trivial: run the task with the smallest vruntime, the one that has had least. To find it fast, CFS keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by vruntime, caching the leftmost node. Here n is the number of tasks represented in the tree. Picking is O(1); inserting a task after it runs or wakes is O(log n), time that grows with the logarithm of n: roughly one more step each time the number of runnable tasks doubles. As C runs, its vruntime rises. The current task is normally kept outside the queued-task tree, then reinserted at its new ordering position when descheduled. Classic CFS compares its service with queued competitors and applies slice/granularity and wake-up checks to decide when to reschedule; the picture shows key ordering rather than a node continuously moving through the tree. Key takeaways Classic CFS selects the task with the smallest virtual runtime. Virtual runtime grows faster for lighter tasks and slower for heavier tasks. A cached leftmost tree node makes selection constant-time; maintaining the ordered tree costs logarithmic time. t: Turn nice weights into CPU shares
sum: Nice changes a task’s fair scheduling weight, not its scheduling class.
x: Weights and nice Nice values map to weights through a fixed table in the kernel. Nice 0 is 1024, and each step is a factor of about 1.25, so the table is close to this formula: The exact kernel values: Nice Weight ------ −20 88761 −5 3121 0 1024 1 820 5 335 19 15 Weights turn into CPU time like this: when several tasks in one fair group all want the CPU, each gets its weight divided by the total weight of the competitors. So for two otherwise equal competitors in one fair group, moving one from nice 0 to nice 1 changes the split from 50/50 to about 55.5/44.5. The share change depends on the competitors. A higher weight makes vruntime grow more slowly, so it needs more real CPU service to reach the same virtual-clock advance. This explains the larger fair share under classic CFS and EEVDF; EEVDF additionally compares eligibility and virtual deadlines. Worked example: who gets what? Three CPU-bound tasks in the same fair group share one CPU: A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5. Check with vruntime: after 10 ms of real time each, A and B gain 10 ms of vruntime, but C gains about 30.6 ms. C’s virtual runtime advances about three times as fast per unit of real execution, so its long-run CPU service is about a third of either nice 0 competitor’s. This is a service-time ratio, not a guarantee about how often dispatches occur. Note what nice is not: it's not a strict priority. A nice 19 task alongside a nice 0 task still gets 15 / 1039, about 1.4%. That proportional share assumes competition within the same fair group, available CPU bandwidth and no overriding higher-class work. Key takeaways Nice changes a task’s fair scheduling weight, not its scheduling class. A task’s long-run share is its weight divided by the competitors’ total in the same fair group. The approximate geometric mapping explains the trend; the kernel uses an exact rounded weight table. t: Classic CFS sleeper placement and slices
sum: Classic CFS bounds a returning sleeper’s credit rather than replaying all missed service.
x: Sleepers and new tasks A task that sleeps for a minute would wake with a tiny vruntime and monopolise the CPU while it "caught up". CFS prevents this with min_vruntime, a monotonic floor tracking the smallest vruntime in the queue. A waking task's vruntime is raised to roughly min_vruntime minus a small bonus (half a latency period), so interactive tasks get a modest head start, not a minute's worth: This was classic CFS behaviour, in kernels before 6.6, with its default GENTLE_FAIR_SLEEPERS setting, which halves the bonus (without it the bonus was a whole target latency). EEVDF, from 6.6, handles sleepers through lag instead. New tasks start near min_vruntime too. Latency and slices CFS had no fixed quantum. It aimed to run every runnable task once within a target latency, with a minimum slice so that hundreds of tasks wouldn't each get microseconds. Both defaults grow a little on machines with more CPUs, because more CPUs share the load: On a 4-CPU machine, for example, the factor is 3, giving 18 ms and 2.25 ms. That worked, but latency was a side effect of fairness. There was no way to say "this task wants short, frequent slices", so CFS grew wake-up heuristics to keep desktops snappy, and these were hard to reason about. Key takeaways Classic CFS bounds a returning sleeper’s credit rather than replaying all missed service. Target latency and minimum granularity were scaled CFS tunables, not universal application latency guarantees. The historical CFS sleeper rule differs from EEVDF lag handling. sum: Eligibility excludes tasks already ahead of their fair service.
x: EEVDF: fairness plus deadlines Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First comes from a 1995 paper by Ion Stoica and Hussein Abdel-Wahab. Peter Zijlstra's implementation became the fair-class scheduler in Linux 6.6. Weights, nice and the red-black tree stay; the picking rule changes. The following equations explain an idealised single-run-queue model. Actual kernels also apply feature settings, clamping, preemption protection and hierarchical group accounting. Two ideas: Lag. Compare the service a task should have received on the ideal CPU with what it actually got. Positive lag means it is owed CPU; negative means it has had more than its share. In practice the kernel computes the weighted average vruntime of the queue, and a task is eligible if its vruntime is no more than that average (lag of zero or more): Virtual deadline. Each task requests a slice (by default the base slice). Its deadline is its vruntime plus that slice scaled by weight: The rule: among eligible tasks, run the one with the earliest virtual deadline. Eligibility keeps it fair: nobody who is ahead of their share gets picked. Deadlines add latency control: a task asking for a shorter slice gets an earlier deadline, so it runs sooner, though in smaller pieces. Over time it gets the same total share. Worked example: short slice, same weight. A and B are both nice 0 (weight 1024) with vruntime 0. A uses a 3 ms slice; B asks for 1 ms. Both are eligible, because both vruntimes equal the average, 0. B now waits for A to catch up before it is eligible again, so neither gets more than its half. B simply gets its half in smaller, more frequent pieces. In the checked Linux 6.12 source the unscaled base slice is 0.75 ms; the default logarithmic scaling gives 3 ms at eight or more CPUs. Tunables and later kernels can differ. Since Linux 6.12 a normal task can request its own slice, between 0.1 ms and 100 ms, through the sched_runtime field of sched_setattr(). Lag also needs care for sleepers. A task that sleeps with negative lag shouldn't wipe out its debt by sleeping briefly. Linux 6.12 introduced deferred dequeue: an over-served sleeping task can remain represented on the run queue in a "deferred dequeue" state so its lag decays, rather than simply resetting it. Is CFS gone? The name lingers: the fair class still lives in kernel/sched/fair.c, and many docs and tools still say CFS. Weights, nice, vruntime, group scheduling and CFS bandwidth control all carried over. What changed is how the next task is chosen and how preemption is decided. Key takeaways Eligibility excludes tasks already ahead of their fair service. Among eligible tasks, the earliest virtual deadline wins; a shorter requested slice changes service timing. Virtual deadlines are fairness coordinates, not application wall-clock deadlines; weight still controls long-run share. t: Fairness between groups and scheduler inspection
sum: Thread-level nice acts within a scheduling group; group weights control competition between groups.
x: Fairness between whom? Linux schedules threads, not processes. Within one fair group, equal-weight runnable threads compete individually: sixteen such threads collectively receive sixteen shares against one for a single-threaded competitor, when CPU capacity is contested. Two mechanisms rebalance this: Group scheduling: with cgroups, the fair scheduler first divides CPU between groups (by cpu.weight in cgroup v2, default 100), then between tasks within a group. systemd commonly organises services and user sessions into cgroups; the actual hierarchy and enabled controllers determine the competing groups. Autogroup (since 2.6.38): on kernels with it enabled, each terminal session gets its own group, so a make -j32 in one terminal doesn't swamp your desktop. One surprise follows: under group scheduling, a thread's nice value only matters relative to other threads in the same group. When two autogroups compete and a task is alone in its group, renicing that task changes no relative competitor inside that group. Different cgroup layouts or other tasks within the groups can change the outcome. The other fair policies SCHED_BATCH: fair share, but treated as CPU-bound and preempts others less; good for batch jobs that want cache-friendly long runs. SCHED_IDLE: extremely low-weight background work in the fair class. It is not the per-CPU idle task and does not promise zero service whenever normal work is runnable. Seeing it on a real system The following ps listing is illustrative; policies, identifiers and commands on your host will differ. TS is the fair class, FF is FIFO, RR is round robin, DLN is deadline. In top, the PR column shows 20 plus the nice value for normal tasks; real-time tasks show negative numbers (minus 1 minus their real-time priority), and rt for real-time priority 99. /proc/<pid>/sched shows a task's vruntime, slice and switch counts, and perf sched records scheduling latency. Several fair-scheduler debugging tunables moved from /proc/sys/kernel to /sys/kernel/debug/sched/ in Linux 5.13. Other settings, including RT bandwidth and RR timeslice controls, remain sysctls; availability also depends on configuration and privileges. Pitfalls Expecting nice to be a priority. It's a weight. Nice 19 gets a small fair share; SCHED_IDLE gives background work an even smaller weight, not a strict idle-only guarantee. Renicing across groups. With autogroup or cgroups, nice only competes within the group. Use cpu.weight between groups. Making things real-time "to be safe". An RT thread that spins starves everything below it, including kernel threads that it may depend on. Use RT for short, bounded work. RT with ordinary locks. RT threads sharing locks with normal threads invite priority inversion; use PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT mutexes. Key takeaways Thread-level nice acts within a scheduling group; group weights control competition between groups. SCHED_IDLE remains a low-weight fair policy, separate from the per-CPU idle task. Inspect per-thread policies and queue behaviour before changing tunables or selecting real-time policies. sum: FIFO has no quantum; RR rotates tasks only within equal RT priorities.
x: Real-time classes For audio, industrial control and low-latency trading, fairness is the wrong goal. The rt class gives strict priorities from 1 to 99 (higher wins): SCHED_FIFO: runs until it blocks, yields or is preempted by a higher RT priority. No time slice at all. SCHED_RR: the same, but threads at equal priority rotate with a time slice (100 ms by default, sched_rr_timeslice_ms). From the shell: chrt -f 50./audio-engine, and chrt -p <pid> to inspect. A runaway FIFO thread A SCHED_FIFO thread stuck in a busy loop never yields, so nothing below it runs on that CPU: not your shell, not kill. Linux guards against this. RT throttling commonly limits RT work to 950 ms per 1 s (sched_rt_runtime_us / sched_rt_period_us). Linux 6.12 also introduced a deadline-class fair server that can supply CPU to fair tasks. These are distinct mechanisms; behaviour depends on kernel version, configuration and tunables. SCHED_DEADLINE Since Linux 3.14, the top policy is SCHED_DEADLINE. Instead of a priority, a task declares three numbers: Runtime parameter: CPU time budget for the reservation per period; Deadline parameter: by when the job should finish, relative to its release; Period parameter: the reservation’s nominal repeating interval. That says "5 ms of CPU every 16.7 ms frame, finished within 10 ms". The kernel schedules deadline tasks by Earliest Deadline First, and uses the Constant Bandwidth Server to stop any task exceeding its runtime. It also performs admission control. Each task's utilisation is the fraction of one CPU it reserves, and the kernel refuses a new task if the total would go over the permitted limit: If the new task does not fit, sched_setattr() fails with EBUSY. From Linux 6.12 the fair server described above is itself a deadline reservation (by default 50 ms in every 1 s, 5 % of each CPU) counted in the same total, so in the checked 6.12 source ordinary deadline tasks can reserve only about 90 % of each CPU unless the fair server is reconfigured. Admission checks reserve bandwidth; acceptance alone is not a universal proof that application deadlines will be met. Worst-case execution time, blocking, deadline versus period, CPU topology and scheduling assumptions still matter. The kernel documentation distinguishes schedulability tests from the simpler utilization admission test. Key takeaways FIFO has no quantum; RR rotates tasks only within equal RT priorities. Deadline scheduling reserves runtime, deadline and period parameters and rejects excess bandwidth reservations. Admission alone is not a proof of all application deadlines; blocking, execution bounds and topology still matter. t: Hardware topology, cache affinity and run queues
sum: Logical CPUs can share core resources and caches, so thread count is not physical-core capacity.
x: Everything so far assumed one CPU. Servers may expose many logical CPUs, arranged in hardware-dependent hierarchies of SMT threads, cores, caches and memory nodes. The scheduler now answers two questions: which thread runs next, and where. Getting "where" wrong costs cache misses, remote memory accesses, and, inside containers, whole periods of enforced idleness. The hardware the scheduler sees SMT siblings (hyper-threads) share one core's execution units and L1/L2 caches. Resource contention can make two busy siblings slower than using separate physical cores; the effect depends on the workloads. Cores in one CPU socket may form several cache-sharing groups, especially across chiplets. Many designs share an L3 within a group; the exact layout is hardware-specific. NUMA nodes each have their own memory. Reaching another node's memory goes over an interconnect and is slower. A thread that has been running on a CPU has a warm cache there: its working set is in L1, L2 and L3. Move it, and it pays to reload that state. This is cache affinity, and it is the central tension of multicore scheduling: keep threads where their data is, but don't leave CPUs idle while work waits elsewhere. One queue or many? OSTEP frames the two basic designs: Design Pros Cons --------- Single shared queue Simple, balanced by construction Lock contention, poor affinity Per-CPU queues Scalable, natural affinity Load imbalance In a simple global-queue design, scheduling decisions contend for one lock and may move tasks between CPUs. The scaling limit and cache cost depend on implementation and workload; a global queue can also incorporate affinity heuristics. With per-CPU run queues, each CPU normally uses its own queue lock rather than one lock shared by every CPU, and threads tend to stay put. The cost is load imbalance: CPU 0 might have four runnable threads while CPU 1 is idle. The fix is task migration, moving threads between queues, typically by work stealing: an idle or lightly loaded CPU pulls work from a busier one. Linux has used per-CPU run queues since the O(1) scheduler in 2.6.0. Go's runtime, Java's ForkJoinPool and Tokio use the same per-worker-queue-plus-stealing idea in user space. Key takeaways Logical CPUs can share core resources and caches, so thread count is not physical-core capacity. Per-CPU queues reduce shared contention and preserve locality but can become imbalanced. Migration balances work at the cost of moving away from warm data. t: Balance load or constrain placement with affinity
sum: Scheduling domains represent hardware locality and guide balancing.
x: How Linux balances load Linux describes the topology as nested scheduling domains, built at boot: Balancing happens at each level, more often and more eagerly at the bottom, where moving a thread is cheap (siblings share caches), and less often at the top, where it is expensive (crossing NUMA nodes loses cache and memory locality). Three triggers drive it: Periodic balancing: from the scheduler tick, each CPU checks whether its domain is imbalanced and pulls tasks if so. Intervals grow with domain level. Idle balancing: a CPU that is about to go idle first tries to pull a task from a busier CPU ("newidle" balancing). Wake-up placement: when a thread wakes, the kernel chooses a CPU for it. It prefers the previous CPU (warm cache), or an idle CPU sharing the same last-level cache, and considers placing a wakee near its waker. The balancer also avoids moving a task that ran very recently, treating it as cache-hot (the default threshold, sched_migration_cost, is 0.5 ms). Balancing considers several signals, including runnable task counts and PELT averages. PELT tracks load, runnable time and running utilization separately; weighted load and CPU utilization are not interchangeable. SMT is treated specially Two busy threads on sibling hyper-threads of one core, while another core sits idle, is a bad placement. Linux's balancer prefers spreading busy work across physical cores first, and only then doubling up on siblings. CPU affinity: pinning threads Sometimes you know better than the balancer. Affinity restricts which CPUs a thread may run on. The following output is illustrative for an eight-CPU Linux environment where CPUs 2 and 3 are allowed; identifiers and masks differ on other hosts. From the shell: taskset -c 2,3./server, or taskset -cp <pid> to inspect. In C, sched_setaffinity() or pthread_setaffinity_np() per thread. Affinity is inherited across fork(). Layers of control, from soft to hard: Default (soft affinity): the scheduler prefers the last CPU but migrates freely. sched_setaffinity / taskset: a hard mask per thread. cpuset cgroups (cpuset.cpus, cpuset.mems): a mask for a whole group, which processes inside cannot widen. Kubernetes's static CPU manager can give eligible Guaranteed containers with integer CPU requests exclusive logical CPUs. Whole-core allocation additionally depends on policy options such as full-pcpus-only. isolcpus= / nohz_full= boot options: selected isolcpus modes can exclude CPUs from general domain balancing; nohz_full can suppress periodic ticks when its conditions are met. Neither option alone removes every interrupt, kernel task or housekeeping activity. Used for packet processing, HFT and real-time control. When pinning helps: Latency-critical threads that must never share a core (with the rest of the system kept off those CPUs). Keeping a thread on the same NUMA node as its memory or NIC interrupts. Benchmarks, where migrations add noise. When it hurts: Pinning everything to the same few CPUs while others idle; the balancer can't fix a mask you set. Pinning two hot threads to SMT siblings, so they compete for one core. Hard-coded CPU numbers that are wrong on the next machine, or inside a container that was given different CPUs. Key takeaways Scheduling domains represent hardware locality and guide balancing. The scheduler balances periodically, before idling and when placing waking tasks. Hard affinity and cpusets limit the balancer’s choices; validate CPU numbers and measure the result. t: Place memory near the threads that use it
sum: New private anonymous pages commonly follow the first write under local policy, subject to allocation and migration rules.
x: NUMA: memory has an address and a location On a multi-socket server, each node's memory is local to its cores. Remote memory access cost and interconnect bandwidth depend on the machine and workload. Content gap No reproducible machine-specific NUMA measurements accompany this lesson, so no universal remote/local latency multiplier is provided. numactl --hardware shows the nodes and a distance table (10 means local; remote nodes are larger, commonly around 20). Linux normally prefers local allocation. For new private anonymous memory, the first write fault commonly allocates a page near the executing CPU. Explicit policies, cpusets, fallback under memory pressure, huge pages and later migration can change placement. That causes a classic bug: The single-threaded initialiser A program allocates and zeroes a 64 GiB array in its main thread on node 0, then starts 32 worker threads spread across both nodes. Assume the main thread stays on node 0, local memory is sufficient, writes fault in new pages and no policy or migration changes placement. The pages then start on node 0. Half the workers make every access remotely, and node 0's memory bandwidth is shared by everyone. Fix: initialise each slice from the thread that will use it, or interleave. Tools and policies: numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0./db runs a process on node 0's CPUs with node 0's memory. numactl --interleave=all spreads pages round robin across nodes: distributed allocation rather than guaranteed per-thread locality. It can reduce concentration on one node, but does not guarantee removal of all hot spots. Often a good choice for large shared caches, such as a database buffer pool. Automatic NUMA balancing (since Linux 3.8, kernel.numa_balancing): the kernel periodically unmaps pages to sample which node touches them through "hinting faults", then migrates pages towards their users, or tasks towards their memory. It helps long-running, well-partitioned workloads, at the cost of some overhead. numastat -p <pid> shows where a process's memory actually lives. The scheduler is NUMA-aware: its top-level scheduling domain balances reluctantly across nodes, because moving a thread can turn accesses to its existing memory into remote accesses; cache hits and pages already elsewhere are exceptions. Key takeaways New private anonymous pages commonly follow the first write under local policy, subject to allocation and migration rules. Initialising each worker’s slice can preserve locality; interleaving distributes allocation instead. Remote/local cost depends on hardware and workload; use NUMA tools rather than a universal multiplier. t: Separate CPU shares from CPU quota
sum: Weight sets relative shares only when groups compete.
x: Containers: shares versus quotas Containers use cgroups to control CPU in two very different ways. Control cgroup v2 file Behaviour --------- Weight cpu.weight Share under contention Quota cpu.max Hard cap, even when idle CPUs exist Weight (default 100) is proportional sharing between groups, just like nice between threads. If the machine is otherwise idle, a low-weight container can still use every CPU. It's work-conserving. A CPU quota is set through CFS bandwidth control. cpu.max holds two numbers, "quota period", in microseconds. Dividing one by the other tells you how many CPUs' worth of time the group may use: So 200000 100000 means 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, 2 CPUs' worth. Fair-class CPU time is charged across the group. Exhausted local bandwidth allocations cause throttling even with idle CPUs. Ancestor quotas, per-CPU runtime accounting and configured burst credit also affect the exact timeline. In Kubernetes, a pod's CPU request becomes its cgroup weight, and its CPU limit becomes its cpu.max quota (with the default 100 ms period). Key takeaways Weight sets relative shares only when groups compete. Quota limits aggregate CPU time per period, even when unused host CPUs exist. The quota-to-period ratio expresses a capacity ceiling; ancestor limits and accounting details also apply. t: Trace throttling and its effect on request latency
sum: Several runnable threads can consume an aggregate CPU budget before the period ends.
x: How throttling wrecks tail latency Worked example: two CPUs of quota, eight busy threads. A container has cpu.max = 200000 100000 and a server with 8 worker threads, on a 32-core host. In an idealised model, all 8 run simultaneously from the period boundary, with no other contention, overhead, burst credit or carried local runtime. Eight threads on eight CPUs burn 8 ms of CPU time for every millisecond of wall-clock time, so: So for the remaining 75 ms of each period nothing in the container runs, and a request arriving 26 ms into the period has a latency of at least 79 ms; queueing behind existing work can add more. Average usage is "2 CPUs, within limit", so dashboards look fine. The symptom is p99 latency far above p50 while CPU usage looks modest. Check cpu.stat: The fraction of periods that ended in throttling is one counter divided by the other: Here a quarter of periods were throttled. Ways out: Size thread pools to the quota, not the host. Eight threads chewing through two CPUs' quota in a quarter of the period is worse than two threads using it smoothly. Remove CPU limits for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests (weights) for fairness. The trade-off is weaker isolation from competing workloads; inherited parent quotas can still throttle the group. Allow bursting: cpu.max.burst (Linux 5.14+) lets a group bank unused quota for short spikes. Use exclusive CPUs (eligible Guaranteed containers under Kubernetes static CPU management; whole cores require appropriate policy options) when you need both isolation and predictability. Key takeaways Several runnable threads can consume an aggregate CPU budget before the period ends. Requests arriving during throttling wait for service to resume and may also queue behind other work. Compare throttled periods with enforcement periods and test concurrency, quotas and isolation changes. t: Count usable CPU capacity inside containers
sum: Visible host CPU count, affinity and cgroup quota describe different limits.
x: Runtimes that count the wrong CPUs Many runtimes size their worker pools from the CPU count, and the CPU count visible inside a container is usually the host's: Python's os.cpu_count() returns the host's logical CPUs. os.process_cpu_count() (3.13+) respects the affinity mask, but not a cpu.max quota. Go 1.25 introduced container-aware defaults: logical CPUs, affinity and cgroup CPU bandwidth all participate. Fractional quotas are rounded up, and the default generally stays at least 2 unless CPU count or affinity is lower. Explicit settings and compatibility controls can override this. The JVM has been container-aware since JDK 10 (backported to 8u191). For example, 64 visible logical CPUs, no narrower affinity and no Python CPU-count override can yield a default maximum of 64 processes despite a two-CPU quota. Workers start as jobs are submitted, with behavior depending on Python version and start method. A simple cgroup-v2 quota reader is: This helper reads one visible cgroup only. It does not discover the process's cgroup or ancestor limits, handle cgroup v1, or combine quota with affinity. An unlimited leaf can still have a constrained ancestor. Pitfalls Treating CPU limits as harmless. A quota caps every period, not the average. Bursty, multi-threaded services get throttled while looking underused. Ignoring SMT. "16 CPUs" may be 8 cores. Two hot threads on siblings don't double throughput. Over-pinning. A hard affinity mask disables the balancer's ability to help; it's only better when you've measured. NUMA-blind initialisation. First touch puts memory where it's first written, not where it's used. Trusting cpu_count() inside containers. Key takeaways Visible host CPU count, affinity and cgroup quota describe different limits. Runtime defaults depend on versions and configuration; verify what the deployed interpreter uses. A single cpu.max reader is illustrative and does not discover ancestor limits or combine all constraints. sum: Trace the load, add and store behind a shared counter update.
x: Threads in the same process share memory. That is what makes them fast to communicate, and it is also what makes them dangerous. When two threads touch the same data and at least one of them writes, the result can depend on exactly how the scheduler happened to interleave their instructions. A bug whose outcome depends on timing is called a race condition. Races are notorious because they are non-deterministic: the program passes a thousand test runs, then corrupts data in production on a busy Tuesday. The simplest broken program Two threads each add one to a shared counter a million times. You would expect 2,000,000. This deliberately broken C program has a data race and undefined behavior, so no output is guaranteed at any optimization level. A lost-update trace below illustrates a simplified machine model, not all behavior permitted for this C program. Content gap No reproducible record supports the original exact sample counts, so they are omitted. A run that prints 2,000,000 does not establish correctness. Why counter++ is not one step counter++ looks like a single operation. A simplified x86-style expansion separates three actions: Each thread has its own registers. A thread can be interrupted, or simply run in parallel on another core, between any two of those instructions. Even when the compiler emits a single inc [counter] instruction, it is still a read-modify-write that is not atomic across cores unless it carries the lock prefix. "One line of C" or "one instruction" is never a proof of atomicity. Tracing a lost update Start with counter = 5. Each thread has a private register (rA, rB). Two increments ran; the counter went up by one. Thread B's store overwrote Thread A's, because B's value was computed from a stale read. This is a lost update. Not every interleaving is bad. If A finishes all three steps before B starts its load, the answer is 7. The bug only appears when the windows overlap, which is why it is intermittent. Key takeaways A plain C increment shared without synchronisation has undefined behaviour; no observed output makes it correct. A load/add/store trace explains one lost-update symptom, rather than bounding C behaviour. Neither one source line nor one ordinary x86 instruction proves cross-core atomicity. Further reading OSTEP: Concurrency, an introduction C11 draft: memory model and atomics Python threading ThreadSanitizer documentation

sum: Construct the smallest and largest counter values in a precisely stated interleaving model.
x: A simplified model lets us reason about schedules without pretending that undefined C behaviour has a finite outcome set. Each increment loads the shared counter, adds one privately, then stores the private value. How bad can it get? Take a simplified, sequentially consistent model: every load and store happens whole, one at a time, in some interleaved order. Two threads start with the counter at 0 and each run the same number of load/add/store increments, at least two each. The range of possible final values is: For example, if each thread performs one million increments, this model permits final values from 2 to 2,000,000. This is a modelled result, not a bound on the broken C program. The top value needs no overlapping read/modify/write windows. The bottom value, 2, needs a pathological schedule: A loads 0 and stalls. B runs all but one of its increments. A stores 1, wiping out all of B's work. B loads 1 and stalls. A runs all of its remaining increments. B stores 2, wiping out all of A's work. Unlikely, but the scheduler is allowed to do it. The bound needs at least two increments per thread: with just one each, the final value can be 1 (both load 0, both store 1). This is an interleaving exercise, not a guarantee for a data-racing C program, whose behaviour is undefined. Key takeaways The model assumes indivisible loads/stores and preserved per-thread order; it is not data-racing C. For at least two increments per thread, a delayed stale store can leave only two counted increments. One increment per thread has different possible results: one or two. Further reading OSTEP: Concurrency, an introduction C11 draft: memory model and atomics Python threading ThreadSanitizer documentation

sum: Distinguish a successful Python test run from a documented atomicity guarantee.
x: Python also shares mutable objects between threads. A conventional CPython GIL can mask a race in a particular workload, so the reason for correctness must come from the synchronisation protocol. The same bug in Python The global interpreter lock (GIL) serialises Python execution in a conventional CPython build, but it is not a language-level guarantee that every bytecode is atomic: operations can invoke user code or release the GIL. counter += 1 also spans several bytecodes: That illustrative listing uses CPython 3.14 instruction names; names and switching points vary between versions. If execution can interleave a load and a later store, an update can be lost. The existence of several bytecodes does not itself prove that a particular CPython build switches between them. On modern CPython with a GIL this often prints the right answer, because the interpreter only considers switching threads at certain points. That is luck, not correctness. Free-threaded builds and changes that introduce additional switching points can expose lost updates; neither failure nor a particular count is guaranteed. Key takeaways A GIL is an interpreter mechanism, not a portable contract for compound operations. An exact output or a failure is not promised for the unsynchronised counter example. Use a documented lock around the complete shared update. Further reading Python 3.14 disassembler Python threading Python free-threading guidance

sum: Separate undefined C data races from higher-level races in individually locked operations.
x: Data races versus race conditions These two terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things. A data race is a precise, language-level definition. In C and C++ it is two accesses to the same memory location, from different threads, where the accesses conflict (for example, at least one writes), at least one is non-atomic, and neither happens before the other (no lock, no other synchronisation). In C and C++ a data race is undefined behaviour: the compiler may assume it never happens. A race condition is a broader, semantic bug: the program's correctness depends on the relative timing of events. Data race No data race --------- Race condition counter++ unlocked check-then-act No race condition rare, still UB in C correct code The interesting cell is "race condition without a data race". Every individual access can be protected and the program can still be wrong: Two threads can both see a balance of 150, both pass the check, and both withdraw. Each method is thread-safe; the combination is not. This pattern is called check-then-act (or time-of-check to time-of-use, TOCTOU), and it is also a classic security bug with files: checking permissions on a path, then opening it after an attacker has replaced it with a symlink. The fix is to make the check and the action a single atomic unit: hold one lock across both, or offer an operation like withdraw_if_at_least(100). Where races hide in real systems Lazy initialisation: two threads both see cache is None and both build it, or worse, one sees a half-built object. Statistics counters shared by worker threads. Collections: appending to a C++ std::vector or a Java HashMap from several threads can corrupt the structure itself, not just lose a value. Files and databases: two processes read-modify-write the same row or file. The same lost-update anomaly appears in databases, where it is handled by transactions and isolation levels. Tools help find them. ThreadSanitizer (-fsanitize=thread in GCC and Clang) detects data races at run time; Helgrind (Valgrind) does similar. Neither finds check-then-act bugs where every access is locked. Key takeaways A C/C++ data race involves conflicting accesses not ordered by happens-before, with at least one non-atomic access. Individually locked methods can still form an incorrect check-then-act sequence. Race detectors inspect executed memory accesses; they do not prove application invariants. Further reading OSTEP: Concurrency, an introduction C11 draft: memory model and atomics Python threading ThreadSanitizer documentation

sum: Check mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting before trusting a locking protocol.
x: A critical section protects a shared invariant across several operations. Protecting only one read or write is insufficient when another thread could invalidate the decision between them. Critical sections A critical section is a piece of code that accesses shared state and must never be executed by more than one thread at a time. In the counter example, the load-add-store is the critical section. The general shape of a solution: Any correct solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three requirements: Mutual exclusion. At most one thread is in the critical section at any time. Critical-section progress. If no thread is in the critical section and some want to enter, one of them must be allowed in, and the decision cannot be postponed forever. Only threads trying to enter take part in deciding. Bounded waiting. Once a thread has asked to enter, there is a limit on how many times other threads can enter ahead of it. No thread waits forever (no starvation). In practice we also care about performance: the overhead when there is no contention, and how well the lock behaves when many threads want it. Mutual exclusion alone is easy A "solution" that never lets anyone in satisfies mutual exclusion perfectly. That is why progress and bounded waiting matter: they rule out deadlock and starvation. Deadlock gets a module of its own next. Early software attempts Can we build mutual exclusion from plain loads and stores? A naive flag fails: The check and the set are separate steps, so this has exactly the same race it was meant to prevent. Peterson's algorithm (1981) solves it for two threads using only loads and stores. Each thread raises a flag saying "I want in" and then politely gives the other thread the turn: Under sequentially consistent atomic reads/writes and suitable progress assumptions, the algorithm satisfies these requirements. The plain C version is broken as written because it has data races and undefined behavior; hardware store buffering is an additional way a literal load/store implementation can fail. Both threads can then read the other's flag as 0 and enter together. The later memory-ordering units explain why; for now, the lesson is to use a documented lock or atomic protocol rather than copy these plain C flags. Key takeaways Mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting answer different correctness questions. Checking a plain flag and setting it later is not one atomic action. Peterson’s algorithm needs a valid atomic model and progress assumptions; the plain C sketch is deliberately broken. Further reading OSTEP: Concurrency, an introduction C11 draft: memory model and atomics Python threading ThreadSanitizer documentation

sum: Use a mutex for a shared update and understand the limits of masking local interrupts.
x: A lock (or mutex, for mutual exclusion) turns a critical section into something only one thread can run at a time. You call lock() before touching shared data and unlock() afterwards. If another thread holds the lock, you wait. Python's with releases the lock even if the body raises, which is the main reason to prefer it over calling acquire() and release() by hand. The interesting question is how lock() itself avoids the race it is meant to prevent. Option 1: turn off interrupts On a single CPU, disabling maskable interrupts can protect a short kernel section against relevant interrupt handlers, provided it cannot block, yield or otherwise schedule and the kernel's preemption rules are respected. It does not exclude every context, such as non-maskable interrupts. This is genuinely used inside kernels for very short sections, but it fails as a general lock: It is a privileged operation; user programs cannot do it (and you would not trust them to). It does nothing on a multiprocessor: other cores keep running. Interrupt handling is delayed. Many interrupt sources remain pending, but excessive latency or finite device buffering can still lose events or data. Ownership A mutex has an owner: only the thread that locked it should unlock it. Unlocking a mutex you do not hold is undefined for a default pthread mutex (error-checking mutexes report it). Python's threading.Lock has no owner and can be released by any thread; threading.RLock has an owner and can be re-acquired by the same thread (re-entrant). Key takeaways Hold a lock across the entire shared invariant, and release it on every exit path. Disabling local maskable interrupts does not stop other CPUs or all execution contexts. Python Lock is non-recursive and has no owner; RLock tracks ownership and nesting. Further reading OSTEP: Locks Futexes Are Tricky — Ulrich Drepper Linux futex manual Linux lock types and PREEMPT_RT PEP 703

t: Build a spinlock from atomic operations
sum: Understand test-and-set and the expected-value update performed by C compare-exchange.
x: The lock’s own admission step must be atomic. An ordinary read followed by an ordinary write would simply move the original race into the lock implementation. Option 2: atomic hardware instructions Mainstream multiprocessors provide atomic read-modify-write facilities for supported memory types and operand sizes. Two are fundamental. Test-and-set test_and_set(addr) writes 1 to addr and returns the old value, atomically. On x86 this is xchg. If the old value was 0, you have just taken the lock; if it was 1, someone else already had it. This is a spinlock: a waiting thread loops ("spins") until the lock is free. It is correct because two threads can never both see the old value 0; the hardware serialises the two exchanges. Compare-and-swap CAS(addr, expected, new) says: "if addr still equals expected, set it to new; tell me whether it worked". On x86 it is lock cmpxchg. Note the C11 quirk: on failure, atomic_compare_exchange_ stores the value it actually found into expected, so the loop must reset it. The _weak form may fail spuriously (on ARM's load-linked/store-conditional instructions), which is fine inside a retry loop. For arbitrary thread counts, CAS has a stronger consensus power than test-and-set. It can implement a single-object read-modify-write update ("read the current value, compute the new value from it, CAS it in, retry if someone beat you"), which is the foundation of the later lock-free units, under their atomic-progress and memory-lifetime assumptions. Primitive x86 ARMv8 --------- test-and-set xchg swp / LL-SC compare-and-swap lock cmpxchg cas / LL-SC fetch-and-add lock xadd ldadd / LL-SC (ARMv8.0 builds these from ldxr/stxr pairs; ARMv8.1 added single-instruction atomics such as cas and ldadd.) Key takeaways An atomic test-and-set lets exactly one contender observe an unlocked flag. A failed C compare-exchange updates the expected argument, which a lock retry must reset. Weak compare-exchange may fail spuriously; the retry protocol must tolerate it. Further reading OSTEP: Locks Futexes Are Tricky — Ulrich Drepper Linux futex manual Linux lock types and PREEMPT_RT PEP 703

t: Ticket order and the cost of spinning
sum: Follow ticket admission and decide when busy waiting is appropriate.
x: A lock can be correct yet waste most of the machine’s time. Fair admission and efficient waiting are separate design choices.
