Fairness: the ticket lock A plain spinlock is unfair: when it is released, whichever core wins the race takes it, and an unlucky thread can starve. A ticket lock fixes this with fetch-and-add, like the numbered tickets at a deli counter: Tickets order admission by ticket allocation, assuming holders and waiters keep progressing and counter wraparound does not alias outstanding tickets. Linux queued spinlocks use queue-based waiting, but their implementation and fairness properties are not the same as this simple ticket model. What spinning costs Spinning burns CPU doing nothing useful. Worse, every test_and_set is a write, so each spinning core demands exclusive ownership of the lock's cache line. The line ping-pongs between cores, slowing down the holder too. Two improvements: Test-and-test-and-set: spin on a plain atomic load (which all waiters can share in their caches) and only attempt the expensive exchange when the lock looks free. Back off: pause between attempts (x86's pause instruction, or an exponential delay). The deeper problem is preemption. If the thread holding a spinlock is descheduled, every waiter spins for its whole time slice, achieving nothing. With 4 threads on 1 core and a 10 ms quantum, a waiting thread can burn the full 10 ms each time it is scheduled. So spinlocks suit one niche: very short critical sections on multicore machines, where the holder will not be preempted. On non-PREEMPT_RT Linux, spinlock_t disables preemption while held; irqsave variants also mask local interrupts. Under PREEMPT_RT, spinlock_t instead has sleeping-lock semantics, while raw_spinlock_t remains a strict spinning lock. Key takeaways Tickets order admission by allocation, subject to progress and safe counter-wrap assumptions. Spinning on a held lock consumes CPU and can increase cache-line contention. Pure spinning requires a suitable execution context; Linux PREEMPT_RT changes spinlock_t semantics. Further reading OSTEP: Locks Futexes Are Tricky — Ulrich Drepper Linux futex manual Linux lock types and PREEMPT_RT PEP 703

sum: Explain the userspace fast path and the atomic compare-and-block that avoids a lost wakeup.
x: When a lock holder may be descheduled, putting waiters to sleep usually avoids wasting their time slices. The difficult part is closing the gap between checking the lock and actually sleeping. Sleeping locks and the futex For user programs the right answer to "lock is busy" is usually: stop running and let the OS wake you when it is free. That needs the kernel, because only the kernel can put a thread to sleep. Avoiding a kernel transition can reduce uncontended fast-path overhead; actual costs and contention rates are workload- and platform-dependent. You do not want a syscall when nobody else is waiting. Linux solves this with the futex ("fast userspace mutex"). It has two halves: A plain integer in user memory, manipulated with atomic instructions. A syscall, futex(), with two key operations: FUTEX_WAIT(addr, val): "if addr still equals val, put me to sleep". The check and the sleep are atomic with respect to wakers, which prevents a lost wakeup. FUTEX_WAKE(addr, n): "wake up to n threads sleeping on addr". A mutex built on a futex uses three states: 0 = unlocked, 1 = locked with no waiters, 2 = locked and someone may be waiting. This is the design in Ulrich Drepper's paper Futexes Are Tricky: (futex_wait and futex_wake are illustrative wrappers. A real Linux implementation needs a correctly aligned 32-bit futex word compatible with its atomic representation, the appropriate private/shared operation and handling for interruptions, spurious wakes and errors.) The fast paths are the point. An uncontended lock is one CAS; an uncontended unlock is one atomic decrement. This teaching algorithm illustrates the fast-path principle. Ordinary glibc mutexes also use user-space atomic state plus futex slow paths, but exact instructions and control flow differ with mutex type, glibc version and optimizations. Windows (SRWLOCK, WaitOnAddress) and macOS (os_unfair_lock) also provide blocking synchronisation facilities; their APIs and implementation details differ from Linux futexes. Many mutexes are also adaptive: on contention they spin briefly first, betting the holder is running on another core and will release soon, and only then sleep. The Linux kernel's own mutex does this "optimistic spinning" while the owner is running. Key takeaways A futex mutex can acquire and release an uncontended ordinary lock without a syscall. FUTEX_WAIT compares the word and queues the waiter atomically with respect to relevant futex operations. The three-state teaching mutex records possible waiters so unlock knows when to wake. Further reading OSTEP: Locks Futexes Are Tricky — Ulrich Drepper Linux futex manual Linux lock types and PREEMPT_RT PEP 703

sum: Apply Amdahl’s idealised model to a serial critical section.
x: Before dividing a lock, estimate how much work it serialises. Amdahl’s law describes a fixed-work idealisation, rather than a hardware benchmark. Contention and granularity A correctly implemented lock still needs a correct application protocol: all relevant accesses must participate, lifetimes must be valid and lock ordering must avoid deadlock. Performance then depends partly on contention. No reproducible uncontended-lock timing is supplied here. When it is heavily contended, threads queue, sleep and wake, and the critical section becomes a serial bottleneck. Amdahl's law puts a number on that bottleneck. It answers "how much faster can more cores make this program?" when part of the work must run one thread at a time, as everything under a single lock does: For example, if ten percent of the single-core work is serial and there are sixteen cores: The law assumes the parallel part splits perfectly and ignores the extra cost of contention itself (cache-line transfers, sleeping and waking). For lock-bound programs, treat its figure as an optimistic upper estimate: real ones usually do worse. Key takeaways The serial fraction does not shrink when more cores share a fixed amount of work. With ten percent serial work, sixteen ideal cores give a speed-up of 6.4. Contention and scheduling overhead can make actual performance worse than the model. Further reading OSTEP: Locks Futexes Are Tricky — Ulrich Drepper Linux futex manual Linux lock types and PREEMPT_RT PEP 703

sum: Trade simpler invariants against contention, ordering risk and false sharing.
x: One global lock is easy to understand, but unrelated operations can queue behind it. Splitting it helps only when the application can maintain its invariants under the new protocol. The main lever is granularity, meaning how much data each lock protects. Coarse-grained Fine-grained --------- Example one lock per table one lock per bucket Simplicity easy to get right many locks to order Parallelism low high Overhead one lock op more lock ops Real systems have moved from coarse to fine over time: Linux's Big Kernel Lock let only one CPU run most kernel code at a time when SMP support was first added. It was gradually replaced by fine-grained locks and finally removed in 2.6.39 (2011). CPython's GIL is a coarse interpreter lock in conventional builds, limiting parallel execution of Python bytecode within an interpreter. Extensions can release it. PEP 703 specifies a free-threaded build using mechanisms including per-object locking; performance depends on the build and workload. Java's ConcurrentHashMap originally used lock striping (16 segments by default, each with its own lock). The JDK 8 implementation uses CAS for an empty bin and bin-level locking for several occupied-bin updates, with additional tree-bin and resizing protocols. These are version-specific internals, rather than a description of every operation. Fine-grained locking has costs. More locks mean more chances to take them in inconsistent orders, which leads to deadlock (the subject of the next module), and operations spanning several items (resizing the whole table) become harder. Practical rules: Keep critical sections short. Avoid blocking I/O, logging or network calls under a hot lock where the required ordering and lifetime rules permit moving them out. Measure before splitting. Profilers and perf lock or mutex contention counters tell you which lock is actually hot. Avoid sharing instead of locking it. Per-thread counters combined at the end can reduce contention when delayed aggregation preserves the required semantics. Watch for false sharing. Independent writes sharing a cache line can cause coherence traffic even under separate locks. Cache-line size is architecture-dependent; 64 bytes is one common example. Priority inversion A low-priority thread holds a lock, a high-priority thread waits for it, and a medium-priority thread preempts the low one. The high-priority thread is now effectively blocked by the medium one. This famously reset the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997. The fix is priority inheritance: the holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT). Content gap No reproducible lock or syscall benchmark accompanies this lesson, so exact nanosecond costs and universal speed-up claims are omitted. The futex code is a teaching sketch, not a portable production mutex. Key takeaways Fine-grained locks can expose parallelism but complicate multi-object operations and lock ordering. Measure hold times and contention before changing the protocol. Per-thread aggregation, false-sharing fixes and shorter sections must preserve the required semantics. Further reading OSTEP: Locks Futexes Are Tricky — Ulrich Drepper Linux futex manual Linux lock types and PREEMPT_RT PEP 703

sum: Use semaphore initial values for exclusion, resource pools and non-blocking acquisition.
x: A lock answers one question: "may I enter?" Threads often need to wait for something else entirely: "is there an item in the queue?", "has the worker finished?", "is a connection free?". Spinning on a flag wastes CPU and, as the earlier race-condition units showed, is a data race unless done with atomics. This lesson covers the two classic tools for waiting on a condition: semaphores, and condition variables used with a mutex. Semaphores A semaphore, introduced by Edsger Dijkstra in the 1960s, is an integer counter with two atomic operations: wait (also called P, down, acquire, sem_wait): decrement the counter. If the result would be negative, block until it can proceed. signal (also called V, up, release, sem_post): increment the counter, waking one blocked waiter if there is one. P and V are historical names for the wait and signal operations. The counter represents a number of available permits. Each completed wait takes one permit and each signal gives one back, so at a quiescent point when none of these operations is in flight: For example, start with three permits, complete three waits and one post, and leave no operation in flight: one permit remains. With no competing operation or further post, the next successful wait consumes it and a following blocking wait cannot proceed yet. What you use a semaphore for depends on the initial value. Initial value Use ------ 1 mutual exclusion, with balanced waits/posts pool size a pool of identical resources 0 "wait until X happens" As a lock Initialised to 1, the first wait takes it to 0 and enters; the next wait blocks until a signal. As a resource pool Initialised to the size of a pool, say 10, up to 10 threads proceed at once and the 11th waits. A web server might allow at most 10 concurrent database queries: BoundedSemaphore raises ValueError if a release would raise its current count above the initial value. This detects over-release, but does not track which thread acquired each permit. Key takeaways A completed successful wait consumes a permit; a post supplies one. A pool semaphore limits concurrency only when acquisitions and releases are balanced. BoundedSemaphore detects a release that would exceed its initial count. Further reading OSTEP: Condition variables OSTEP: Semaphores POSIX condition wait Python threading Java Object monitor methods

sum: Coordinate a child and parent without losing a signal sent before the wait.
x: A completion signal must survive a scheduling gap: the worker may finish before the parent reaches its wait. A semaphore records that completion in its permit count. As an ordering tool Initialised to 0, a wait blocks until some other thread signals. This makes "B must happen after A" trivial: Assuming initialization and calls succeed, it works whichever thread runs first. POSIX sem_wait can fail with EINTR; real code must retry that case and handle other errors rather than enter a protected section without a permit. The snippets omit this error handling. If the child posts before the parent waits, the counter is 1 and the parent thread's wait returns immediately. The semaphore remembers the signal. That memory is the key difference from a condition variable. Semaphore versus mutex A binary semaphore looks like a mutex, but: A semaphore has no owner. Any thread can post, which is what makes the ordering pattern work, but also means nobody catches a stray release. A POSIX mutex has an owner, enabling ownership-based error checks and optional recursive or priority inheritance protocols. A counting semaphore supplies no single designated owner to boost; do not infer mutex-style priority inheritance from it. Python’s primitive Lock is a documented ownership exception, as discussed earlier. Use a mutex for mutual exclusion and a semaphore for counting or signalling. Key takeaways An initial count of zero makes a semaphore suitable for a completion event. A post before a wait leaves a permit, so the ordering works in either execution order. A semaphore has no owner; POSIX wait errors must be handled before assuming a permit was acquired. Further reading OSTEP: Condition variables OSTEP: Semaphores POSIX condition wait Python threading Java Object monitor methods

sum: Combine a condition variable, shared state, mutex and while loop to avoid missed work.
x: A condition variable supports richer questions than a permit count, such as whether a queue contains work. Correctness comes from a predicate and mutex protocol, rather than from the notification alone. Condition variables A condition variable (CV) is a queue of threads waiting for some condition on shared state to become true. It has no counter and no memory. Use it with the mutex that protects the shared predicate; the APIs shown here require that mutex during wait. The operations (POSIX names): pthread_cond_wait(&cv, &m): the caller must hold m. It atomically releases m and puts the thread to sleep. When woken, it re-acquires m before returning. pthread_cond_signal(&cv): wake at least one waiting thread, if any. pthread_cond_broadcast(&cv): wake all waiting threads. If nobody is waiting, signal does nothing. It is not remembered. The canonical pattern, waiting for a child thread to finish: Three parts are essential, and each one fixes a real bug. 1. The state variable Without done, if the child signals before the parent waits, the signal is lost and the parent sleeps forever. The CV is just a waiting room; the truth lives in shared state (done, a queue length, a counter). 2. The mutex Suppose the parent checks done == 0 without the lock. Between that check and the call to wait, the child can set done = 1 and signal. The parent then sleeps, having missed the only wakeup. This is a lost wakeup. Holding the mutex across the check, and having wait release it atomically as it sleeps, closes that window. (It is the same reason FUTEX_WAIT checks the value inside the kernel.) 3. The while loop Always re-check the condition after waking: There are two reasons. Mesa semantics. When thread A signals, the woken thread B does not run immediately. It merely becomes runnable and must re-acquire the mutex. In the meantime another thread C can grab the mutex and change the state. By the time B runs, the condition may be false again. A signal is only a hint that the state has changed. Spurious wakeups. POSIX explicitly allows pthread_cond_wait to return even though nobody signalled. Allowing this makes CVs easier to implement efficiently, particularly on multiprocessors and when signals interrupt the wait. The if bug, traced One item slot, two consumers C1 and C2, one producer P. C1 waits (queue empty). P adds an item and signals; C1 becomes runnable but has not run yet. C2 arrives, takes the mutex, sees an item and consumes it. Now C1 runs, returns from wait, and (with if) assumes there is an item. It pops from an empty queue. With while, C1 re-checks, sees it is empty and waits again. The alternative, Hoare semantics, hands the mutex directly to the woken thread so the condition is guaranteed to hold. This gives a stronger handoff contract. POSIX, Java and Python instead require callers to tolerate delayed reacquisition and recheck their predicates; the performance trade-off depends on implementation. Key takeaways The predicate is the remembered truth; a condition-variable notification is not remembered. Wait atomically releases the mutex and begins waiting, then reacquires before returning. A while loop handles both delayed reacquisition and spurious wakeups. Further reading OSTEP: Condition variables OSTEP: Semaphores POSIX condition wait Python threading Java Object monitor methods

t: Monitors and choosing who to wake
sum: Use separate predicates, appropriate notification and structured monitor APIs.
x: A signalled waiter still has to reacquire the mutex and recheck its predicate. The choice of notification affects progress and overhead even when every waiter uses a correct while loop. signal or broadcast? POSIX signal unblocks at least one waiter, if any; callers must tolerate extra or spurious wakeups. Use it when any waiter can make progress and only one should. broadcast wakes all of them. Use it when waiters wait for different conditions on the same CV, or when a change could let several proceed (for example, freeing a large block that several allocation requests are waiting for). With correctly protected predicates and a sound protocol, broadcast preserves the safety of the wait loop but can cause a thundering herd: 100 threads wake, contend for the mutex, 99 find nothing to do and sleep again. A common, cleaner design is one CV per condition (not_empty, not_full), so signal always wakes a thread that cares. Monitors A monitor packages the pattern into a language construct: an object whose methods run under one implicit lock, plus condition variables for waiting inside those methods. The idea comes from Per Brinch Hansen and Tony Hoare in the early 1970s. Java is the best-known example. Every object has an intrinsic lock and one implicit condition: Because there is only one condition per object, producers and consumers share it, which is why notifyAll is the safe default there. java.util.concurrent.locks offers explicit locks with several Conditions. Python's threading.Condition combines a lock and a CV, and its wait_for method writes the while loop for you: Here, without a timeout, wait_for(predicate) checks the predicate under the associated lock, waits and rechecks until it returns a true value. With a timeout it may instead return a false value when time expires. Semaphores or condition variables? They are equally powerful: each can be built from the other plus a mutex. In practice: Semaphore Mutex + CV --------- Remembers signals yes (count) no Condition count above 0 any predicate Ownership none mutex has owner Typical use pools, signalling general waiting Semaphores are compact when the problem is really about counting. Condition variables are clearer for arbitrary conditions ("queue not empty and not shutting down"), because the condition is written explicitly in the while loop rather than encoded in a count. Many style guides prefer CVs for that reason. Common mistakes Waiting with if instead of while. Breaks under Mesa semantics and spurious wakeups. Signalling without changing state. The waiter re-checks, finds nothing changed, and sleeps again. Changing state without holding the mutex. Creates a lost-wakeup window even if the signal happens later. Calling wait without holding the mutex. Undefined in POSIX; Python raises RuntimeError. Doing long work while holding the mutex after waking. Take what you need, unlock, then work. For POSIX condition variables, signalling with or without the mutex held is permitted, but predicate changes and object lifetime must remain correctly coordinated. Python notify/notify_all and Java notify/notifyAll require holding their associated lock or monitor; the POSIX rule must never be copied into those APIs. Key takeaways Signal is appropriate when any awakened waiter can make progress; broadcast is useful for multiple predicates or several eligible waiters. Separate condition variables can keep producers from waking other producers. Python and Java notification require the associated lock; POSIX permits signalling without it under a sound predicate/lifetime protocol. Further reading OSTEP: Condition variables OSTEP: Semaphores POSIX condition wait Python threading Java Object monitor methods

sum: Coordinate free slots, filled slots and protected circular-buffer updates.
x: A handful of synchronisation puzzles have been studied since the 1960s and 70s. They survive because each one isolates a pattern you meet constantly in real systems: a queue between stages, a cache that is read far more than written, threads that need several resources at once, a server with a waiting room. Work through them once with semaphores and condition variables and you will recognise them everywhere. 1. Producer–consumer (bounded buffer) Producers create items and put them in a buffer with a fixed number of slots; consumers take them out. A producer must wait when the buffer is full, a consumer when it is empty, and the buffer itself must never be corrupted by concurrent access. This is every queue between pipeline stages: a web server's accept queue, a logging thread, Kafka consumers, the pipe in cat log grep error. With semaphores Three semaphores, named after what they count, with these starting values: The buffer is used as a circular buffer. The indices in (next slot to write) and out (next slot to read) move forward one slot at a time and wrap from the last slot back to the first, which is what % N does in C: The two counting semaphores always add up to the capacity when nobody is part-way through an operation: For example, with five slots and two stored items, at a quiescent point full is 2 and empty is 3. That invariant holds only when no operation holds an outstanding permit. During in-flight operations, reserved permits are not yet reflected in the opposite semaphore; that interval can be arbitrarily long if a thread is delayed. These C sketches assume successful initialization/calls; production code must handle EINTR and other semaphore errors. Order of the waits matters Exchange the first two lines of the producer so it takes mutex before empty. When the buffer is full, the producer holds the mutex and sleeps on empty. The consumer that would free a slot blocks on mutex. Neither can proceed: a deadlock. Always wait for the resource, then take the lock. (The next module covers deadlock in depth.) Key takeaways The slot semaphores and the buffer mutex protect different invariants. Acquire a resource permit before the mutex, so a sleeping producer does not block the consumer that could free space. The free-plus-full invariant describes quiescent points without outstanding reservations. Further reading The Little Book of Semaphores — Allen B. Downey OSTEP: Semaphores Python queue glibc read-write lock preference

sum: Use condition-variable predicates and a library queue to stop producers outrunning consumers.
x: A bounded buffer can also be expressed with a mutex, a count and condition variables. The queue’s capacity limits accumulated work, while the consumer’s service rate still limits sustained throughput. With condition variables get is the mirror image: wait while count == 0, take an item, signal not_full. Two CVs ensure producers only wake consumers and vice versa. In Python you would almost never write this yourself. queue.Queue(maxsize=N) is exactly a bounded buffer built from one lock and condition variables, and put and get block appropriately: The bound matters. An unbounded queue between a fast producer and a slow consumer grows until memory runs out. A bounded one applies back-pressure: the producer is forced to slow to the consumer's pace. Key takeaways Use separate not-full and not-empty predicates, both protected by the buffer mutex. queue.Queue provides a bounded blocking queue without reimplementing the protocol. A bounded queue eventually blocks a faster producer; an unbounded queue can grow without limit. Further reading The Little Book of Semaphores — Allen B. Downey OSTEP: Semaphores Python queue glibc read-write lock preference

sum: Trace first-reader and last-reader coordination and choose a fairness policy.
x: Concurrent readers are safe only when they do not change the protected structure. A writer must exclude both other writers and all current readers. 2. Readers–writers Many threads read a shared structure; a few write it. Readers do not interfere with each other, so any number may read at once. A writer needs exclusive access: no other writers and no readers. Real examples: a routing table, a configuration object, an in-memory cache, a database page. Readers-preference solution The first reader in locks writers out on behalf of the whole group; the last reader out lets them back in. The flaw is writer starvation. If readers keep arriving so that readers never drops to 0, a waiting writer never gets rw. For a cache read thousands of times per second, the update might be delayed indefinitely. Fixing starvation Writers-preference: once a writer is waiting, new readers block. This flips the problem: a steady stream of writers starves readers. Fair (turnstile): add a turnstile with an explicit fair policy for letting readers and writers in. Plain POSIX/Python semaphore APIs do not by themselves promise FIFO wake order. A waiting writer holds the turnstile, so readers arriving after it queue behind it. Real read-write locks expose this choice. glibc's pthread_rwlock_t prefers readers by default (its nonrecursive writer-preference mode requires promising that read locks will not be acquired recursively; the similarly named recursive writer-preference setting is ignored by glibc); Java's ReentrantReadWriteLock offers a fair mode. The later read-write-lock unit discusses when reader parallelism actually helps. Concurrency and immutable alternatives A high read rate is not a guarantee of starvation, but the amount of overlapping read work helps explain why reader preference deserves scrutiny. For a stable stream, Little’s law relates mean arrival rate and mean residence time to mean work in flight: A writer-preference or explicitly fair admission policy can limit new readers bypassing a waiting writer, under its scheduling and progress assumptions. Another option is immutable replacement: construct a new configuration privately, publish its pointer with a valid ordering protocol, and let readers retain the old unchanged object. Publication can then avoid waiting for every existing reader, but old storage must remain alive until a reclamation protocol proves no reader can use it. Atomic pointer replacement alone does not supply those ordering and lifetime guarantees. Key takeaways The first reader acquires exclusion on behalf of a group; the last releases it. Reader preference can starve a writer, and writer preference can reverse that problem. A fair admission protocol must supply its own fairness assumptions; a semaphore alone does not promise FIFO order. Further reading The Little Book of Semaphores — Allen B. Downey OSTEP: Semaphores Python queue glibc read-write lock preference Little: A proof for the queuing formula (1961)

sum: Trace circular waiting when each participant holds one resource and needs another.
x: The dining-philosophers puzzle isolates multi-resource acquisition. The same circular wait can occur when two bank transfers lock their source and destination accounts in opposite orders. 3. Dining philosophers Five philosophers sit at a round table with one chopstick between each pair (five chopsticks). To eat, a philosopher needs both the left and right chopsticks. They alternate between thinking and eating. The problem is due to Dijkstra (1965), with the dining story popularised by Tony Hoare. The naive solution: Each philosopher's left chopstick has the philosopher's own number, and the right chopstick is the next one round the table. The % 5 in the code is what makes the numbering wrap round: In the code, each chopstick is one semaphore in an array, indexed by the chopstick's number. If all five pick up their left chopstick at the same moment, each waits forever for a right chopstick held by a neighbour. That circular wait is deadlock; here we only look at the standard ways out. Key takeaways Each philosopher needs two neighbouring chopsticks and holds the first while waiting for the second. Symmetric left-then-right acquisition can make a complete cycle. Resource numbers and the drawing must describe the same neighbouring pairs. Further reading The Little Book of Semaphores — Allen B. Downey OSTEP: Semaphores Python queue glibc read-write lock preference

sum: Compare resource ordering, an admission limit and an arbitrator without assuming starvation freedom.
x: Five philosophers share five chopsticks in a ring, and each needs its own chopstick and the next one clockwise. Several remedies prevent the cycle; their fairness properties need separate reasoning. Break the symmetry (resource ordering). Number the chopsticks and always pick up the lower-numbered one first. Philosopher 4 needs chopsticks 4 and 0, so picks up 0 first. Now a full cycle of waiting is impossible. This is the most common real-world fix: a global lock order. Limit the diners. A semaphore initialised to 4 lets at most four philosophers try to eat at once. By the pigeonhole principle, at least one of them can get both chopsticks (worked through below). A waiter (arbitrator). A single mutex or monitor hands out both chopsticks at once, or neither. Simple, but it serialises chopstick allocation through one point. Chandy–Misra. A distributed protocol marks chopsticks "dirty" or "clean" and transfers them under specified request and ownership rules. Its starvation-freedom argument also needs the protocol’s acyclic initial precedence and progress/message-delivery assumptions. Why limiting the diners works: suppose the worst case, where every philosopher at the table holds exactly one chopstick and waits for another. Then: To see who eats, follow the chain of waiting. A diner holding one chopstick waits for the chopstick on their other side. If a neighbour holds that chopstick, the neighbour is waiting for the chopstick on their other side, and so on round the table in one direction. With at most four diners the chain cannot reach all the way round, so it ends at a chopstick nobody holds, and the diner at the end of the chain picks it up and eats. With all five at the table, the same sum gives 5 − 5 = 0 free chopsticks, and the circular wait is possible again. Avoiding deadlock is not the same as avoiding starvation. With some solutions, two fast neighbours can alternate eating so that the philosopher between them almost never gets both chopsticks. A monitor-based solution where a hungry philosopher eats only when neither neighbour is eating is deadlock-free but can still starve someone unless you add ordering or ageing. The real-world version: a bank transfer that locks account A then account B, running concurrently with a transfer from B to A. Lock ordering by account ID fixes it. Key takeaways A global resource order removes circular wait. Admitting at most four diners breaks this five-resource cycle under the stated acquisition pattern. Deadlock freedom alone does not promise that each hungry participant will eventually be served. Further reading The Little Book of Semaphores — Allen B. Downey OSTEP: Semaphores Python queue glibc read-write lock preference

sum: Follow permit handshakes for a sleeping worker, waiting clients and rejected arrivals.
x: A bounded server can reject work instead of blocking the producer. The sleeping-barber model combines that admission decision with a worker that sleeps while no work is available. 4. The sleeping barber A barbershop has one barber, one barber's chair and a fixed number of waiting chairs (3 in the code below). If there are no customers, the barber sleeps. A customer arriving at a sleeping barber wakes him. A customer arriving while the barber is busy sits in a free waiting chair, or leaves if none are free. It models any server with a bounded waiting queue that sheds load when full: a thread pool with a fixed-size queue that rejects work, or a call centre with a maximum hold queue. The difficulty is avoiding races between the barber checking for customers and customers checking whether the barber is asleep. How it works: customer_ready counts customers waiting. The barber sleeps on it when it is 0, which is the "sleeping" part. barber_ready calls one customer. The seated, done and left handshakes coordinate chair arrival, haircut completion and departure before the next customer is called. These snippets assume no cancellation or failure during the handshake. free_seats is protected by seats, so two customers cannot both take the last chair. Because semaphores remember posts, it does not matter whether a customer arrives just before or just after the barber goes to sleep. That is the race that breaks naive solutions using flags. This version does not guarantee customers are served in arrival order, since whichever waiting customer's acquire returns first gets the chair. Adding a FIFO queue of per-customer semaphores fixes that. Comparing them Problem Pattern Real system --------- Bounded buffer queue + back-pressure pipes, Kafka Readers–writers shared vs exclusive rwlocks, caches Philosophers many resources lock ordering Sleeping barber bounded wait, shed thread pools Key takeaways The seats lock protects the waiting-chair count; semaphores coordinate arrival and service phases. The protocol assumes no cancellation or failure partway through its handshakes. It sheds arrivals when the waiting room is full and does not promise arrival-order service. Further reading The Little Book of Semaphores — Allen B. Downey OSTEP: Semaphores Python queue glibc read-write lock preference

sum: Distinguish atomic updates from volatile accesses and a data-racing polling loop.
x: So far, locks have hidden a question you can no longer ignore: when one thread writes memory, when, and in what order, do other threads see those writes? You might assume each thread's operations happen in program order and every core sees one shared, up-to-date memory. That model is called sequential consistency (Lamport, 1979). Uncoordinated accesses do not generally provide that model; language rules and hardware ordering permit optimizations. The performance effect of stronger ordering depends on the target and workload. This lesson explains what they do instead, and how to get back the guarantees you need. Atomic operations An atomic operation is indivisible: no other thread can observe it half done. C11 provides them in <stdatomic.h>: For supported scalar atomic types, compilers commonly use lock xadd or lock add on x86 and an LL/SC loop or LSE ldadd on AArch64. Unlike hits++ on a plain int, it never loses an update and is not a data race. For some atomic types, an implementation may use internal locks; the atomic API does not universally promise lock-free machine instructions. Atomicity solves indivisible access to the atomic object. It does not, on its own, say anything about the order in which other memory operations become visible. That is memory ordering. Who reorders, and why The compiler Within one thread, the compiler may reorder, merge or delete memory accesses as long as the single-threaded result is unchanged. It assumes there are no data races, because a data race is undefined behaviour. In an invalid program that concurrently writes this plain flag without synchronisation, the behaviour is undefined. Hoisting its load is one illustrative compiler transformation; the resulting behaviour is not restricted to that symptom. C/C++ volatile constrains access to volatile objects according to the implementation’s documented rules, but supplies no inter-thread atomicity or synchronisation for these plain accesses. It is meant for memory-mapped hardware, not threads. (Java's volatile is different and does provide ordering.) Key takeaways Atomic read-modify-write avoids lost counter updates, subject to representing the result. C volatile does not supply the atomicity or synchronisation needed for shared-thread state. A data-racing plain polling loop has undefined behaviour; a particular assembly symptom is only illustrative. Further reading C11 draft: memory model and atomics Linux memory barriers The Double-Checked Locking declaration Java memory model specification Python free-threading guidance The Go memory model

sum: Compare a sequentially consistent store-buffering trace with hardware-permitted outcomes.
x: CPU memory ordering and the C language memory model answer different questions. A literal assembly litmus test can demonstrate a hardware-permitted result without making a racing C translation valid. The CPU Modern cores execute out of order, and each core has a store buffer: writes are queued there and drained to cache later, so the core does not stall on every store. Loads can complete before earlier stores have left the buffer. This simplified table concerns ordinary accesses to coherent normal cacheable memory, not every memory type, special instruction or dependency rule: Reordering x86-64 ARMv8 --------- load → load no yes load → store no yes store → store no yes store → load yes yes x86's model is called TSO (total store order): the only visible reordering is a later load passing an earlier store to a different address. ARM and POWER are weakly ordered, allowing more independent-access reorderings under their specified memory types, dependencies and barriers. Code that "works on my laptop" (x86) can break on ARM servers or phones. Two litmus tests Store buffering Under sequential consistency at least one thread sees the other's write, so r1 == 0 && r2 == 0 is impossible. On real x86 it happens: both stores sit in store buffers while both loads read 0 from cache. This can break a literal load/store implementation of Peterson’s algorithm; the earlier plain C version already has data races. In the machine-code model, a full fence between the store and load in each thread forbids that result (for example mfence on x86). In C, first use valid atomic accesses; a hardware fence does not legalize races on plain objects. Key takeaways The hardware table assumes ordinary coherent normal cacheable memory and independent accesses. Store buffering can permit both loads to see zero on x86 as well as weaker targets. Language-level C data races remain undefined even when a hardware trace looks plausible. Further reading C11 draft: memory model and atomics Linux memory barriers The Double-Checked Locking declaration Java memory model specification Python free-threading guidance The Go memory model

t: Publish data with release and acquire
sum: Use an observing acquire load to order access to a plain payload.
x: To publish an object, atomic access to its flag is only part of the protocol. The reader also needs the ordering edge that makes the earlier payload writes safe to read. The message-passing test Assume one producer and one consumer, initialised globals and no other accesses. The plain data accesses lack a happens-before edge and therefore race: the C program has undefined behavior, not merely a choice between 0 and 42. Weakly ordered machine traces explain one possible stale-read symptom but do not bound C behavior. Acquire and release With one producer and one consumer, initialised globals and no other accesses, the fix uses an observing acquire. If the consumer reaches the print, the payload is 42: The following movement rules are a useful reasoning model for observable ordering, not a ban on every compiler transformation that preserves the language contract. A release store orders earlier writes before accesses after a matching observing acquire. Think of those earlier accesses as staying before publication. An acquire load orders its later accesses after the release it observes. Think of those later accesses as staying after observation. If an acquire load reads the value written by a release store, the two establish a synchronises-with edge: everything before the release is visible to everything after the acquire. The names come from locks. Taking a lock is an acquire (the critical section cannot leak upwards out of it); releasing it is a release (the critical section cannot leak downwards). Correct standard mutex use supplies the synchronization needed for protected accesses. Applications must still coordinate object lifetime, initialization and every piece of code that touches the data; having a lock somewhere is not enough. For ordinary supported scalar atomics on coherent normal memory, x86 compilers commonly use plain mov for acquire loads and release stores. AArch64 commonly uses ldar and stlr; exact code generation depends on type, target and compiler. Key takeaways A relaxed flag alone does not order plain payload accesses. An acquire that observes the release publication links earlier writes to later reads. Assuming successful one-time publication and no competing accesses, the consumer prints 42 if it reaches the print. Further reading C11 draft: memory model and atomics Linux memory barriers The Double-Checked Locking declaration Java memory model specification Python free-threading guidance The Go memory model

sum: Choose counter ordering and trace synchronisation edges across threads.
x: Memory order is part of the algorithm’s correctness argument. The store-buffering test starts two atomic variables at zero; each thread stores one to its own variable and then loads the other. The C11 orderings Order Guarantee Use --------- relaxed atomic only counters acquire later ops stay later lock, read flag release earlier ops stay earlier unlock, publish acq_rel both, for RMW CAS in a lock seq_cst one global order default C11 also defines memory_order_consume. Mainstream compiler implementations have generally strengthened it to acquire; avoid relying on a cheaper dependency-only mapping without checking the compiler and language version. Sequentially consistent (seq_cst) is the default for every atomic operation without _explicit. All seq_cst operations appear in a single total order agreed by every thread. Using seq_cst for all four operations in this litmus test forbids both loads seeing zero. Other correctly constructed synchronization protocols or fence placements can also forbid it. For ordinary scalar atomics, x86 compilers commonly implement a sequentially consistent store using xchg or a suitable fenced sequence. Costs depend on hardware, contention and surrounding code; no universal timing ratio is asserted. Relaxed is fine when you need the value to be correct but nothing else to be ordered with it, such as a statistics counter read after all threads are joined. Default to seq_cst Use the default orderings until a profiler proves the fence matters. Weaker orderings are an optimisation with a high cost in reasoning, and bugs in them often appear only on one architecture under load. Fences A fence (memory barrier) orders memory operations without being attached to a particular variable: atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_seq_cst) in C11. Hardware equivalents include x86 mfence and ARM dmb ish. The Linux kernel has its own family (smp_mb(), smp_wmb(), smp_rmb(), smp_store_release(), smp_load_acquire()), documented at length in memory-barriers.txt. There is also a compiler-only barrier, such as asm volatile(""::: "memory") in GCC, which stops the compiler moving accesses across it but emits no instruction. Happens-before The formal model ties this together. The happens-before relation is built from: Sequenced-before: within one thread, program order. Synchronises-with: a release store and an acquire load that reads its value; an unlock and a later lock of the same mutex; pthread_create and the start of the new thread; a thread's end and pthread_join returning. Transitivity: happens-before chains, as the formula below shows. Writing an arrow for "happens-before": The earlier message-passing unit supplies one such chain. The write data = 42 is sequenced-before the release store; the release store synchronises-with the acquire load that reads 1; the acquire load is sequenced-before the read of data. Chaining the three edges gives "the write of 42 happens-before the read", so if the consumer reaches the print, it prints 42. The rule that matters: if a write happens-before a read of the same location (and no other write intervenes), the read sees that write. If two conflicting accesses are not ordered by happens-before and are not both atomic, you have a data race, and in C, C++ and Rust that is undefined behaviour. Java and Go define similar happens-before rules; Java gives racy programs weaker but defined semantics rather than UB. Key takeaways Relaxed counters need no payload-publication edge when the final read follows thread joins. Using sequentially consistent operations throughout the store-buffering test excludes the both-zero result. Happens-before chains through sequenced-before and synchronises-with; elapsed time alone supplies no edge. Further reading C11 draft: memory model and atomics Linux memory barriers The Double-Checked Locking declaration Java memory model specification Python free-threading guidance The Go memory model

sum: Repair double-checked locking and use documented initialisation mechanisms.
x: Lazy initialisation must guarantee both that construction is coordinated and that a reader sees a fully initialised object. Checking a pointer twice does not itself provide either ordering guarantee. The double-checked locking bug Lazy initialisation of a shared singleton is a classic. To avoid locking an already-initialized fast path, programmers wrote: The idea: check without the lock (fast path); if it looks uninitialised, take the lock and check again. It is broken: the unlocked plain pointer read races with publication in C. One illustrative failure is incomplete publication. Line 3 performs two kinds of write: the writes inside make() that fill in the object's fields, and the write of the pointer into instance. Nothing stops the pointer store becoming visible to another thread before the field stores (the compiler can reorder them, and so can a weakly ordered CPU). A second thread then passes check 1, sees a non-null pointer, skips the lock entirely, and reads uninitialised fields. The famous "Double-Checked Locking is Broken" declaration, signed by Bill Pugh and a group of Java and concurrency researchers, documented why the ordinary fast path was unsound under the old Java memory model. Prefer a documented initialisation protocol; the following choices supply the required construction and visibility guarantees: C11: make instance an _Atomic(Singleton ), load it with memory_order_acquire, store it with memory_order_release. Java 5+: declare the field volatile (JSR-133 gave volatile acquire/release semantics). C++11: just use a function-local static; its initialisation is guaranteed thread-safe ("magic statics"). POSIX: pthread_once. Python: initialise at module import, or use a lock; functools.cache alone does not promise the function runs only once under concurrency. The inner load can be relaxed because the mutex already orders it after any previous initialiser’s unlock. Assume initialisation before thread creation, a successful make(), and an object that remains alive and unchanged for these readers; failure and shutdown need their own policy. What this means for Python Python has no memory_order. A conventional CPython GIL serialises Python execution while held, but this implementation mechanism does not specify a complete language-level ordering contract for arbitrary compound operations. Free-threaded CPython currently uses internal locking for many built-ins, but that is not a blanket language-level atomicity contract. In both cases use documented threading and queue protocols for shared invariants. Python does not specify the complete C11 memory model described above. Key takeaways An unlocked plain singleton pointer races with publication in C. The repaired example uses acquire/release publication and a mutex around construction. Prefer language/library initialisation protocols, and do not infer an entire memory model from the Python GIL. Further reading C11 draft: memory model and atomics Linux memory barriers The Double-Checked Locking declaration Java memory model specification Python free-threading guidance The Go memory model

sum: Separate blocking, obstruction-free, lock-free and wait-free progress and trace a maximum update.
x: Locks are simple and correct, but they have one structural weakness: if the thread holding a lock stops, everyone waiting for it stops too. The holder might be preempted, page-faulting, running a signal handler, or simply slow. Under heavy load that one stalled thread sets the pace for all the others. Lock-free techniques avoid holding anything that others must wait for. Instead of "acquire, modify, release", threads prepare a change privately and publish it with a single atomic instruction, retrying if someone else got there first. This lesson covers how that works, why it is much harder than it looks, and the more practical read-mostly tools (read-write locks, seqlocks and RCU) that real kernels and servers rely on. Progress guarantees "Lock-free" has a precise meaning. It describes what happens when threads are delayed, not whether the code contains the word lock. Guarantee Promise ------ Blocking a stalled thread can stop all Obstruction-free a thread alone finishes Lock-free some thread always progresses Wait-free every thread finishes, bounded Blocking algorithm: any algorithm using a mutex. If the holder is descheduled, nobody else in that critical section progresses. Obstruction-free: a thread finishes in a bounded number of steps if all others pause. Contending threads may keep undoing each other's work. Lock-free: continued execution guarantees system-wide operation progress under the algorithm's primitive and scheduling assumptions. An individual operation can starve; this is not a fixed wall-clock completion deadline. Wait-free: every thread completes in a bounded number of its own steps, however others behave. The strongest guarantee and the hardest to build. A spinlock built from CAS is not lock-free: if the holder is preempted, every spinner makes zero progress. Using atomic instructions does not by itself make an algorithm lock-free. Maurice Herlihy showed in 1991 that primitives differ in power. Plain loads and stores, or test-and-set, cannot build wait-free versions of every data structure for arbitrary numbers of threads; compare-and-swap (and LL/SC) can. That is why CAS is the foundation of everything in this lesson. The CAS retry loop The example keeps a maximum with an initial floor of zero: values below zero do not lower that floor. The basic lock-free pattern is: read the current value, compute a new one privately, and CAS it in. On comparison failure, another update changed the expected value; a weak CAS may also fail spuriously. Reload/recompute as the algorithm requires. On failure, C11's CAS writes the value it found into cur, so the loop re-tests with fresh data. Assuming lock-free atomic primitives and their required forward progress, the loop has system-wide non-blocking progress. A comparison mismatch shows interference; a weak CAS can also fail spuriously, so not every failed call proves another operation succeeded. CAS retry loops generally do not give each thread a fixed retry bound. By contrast, a fetch-add implemented as one native instruction has a bounded number of algorithmic steps, assuming that primitive completes. This is not a bound on wall-clock latency: scheduling, faults and hardware contention still matter. Key takeaways A spinlock remains blocking even when it uses compare-and-swap. Lock-free gives system-wide progress, while wait-free bounds each operation’s own steps under its assumptions. Non-spurious comparison failure indicates interference; weak CAS may also fail spuriously. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading

t: Treiber stack and the ABA trap
sum: Trace pointer publication and an old next pointer that survives a changed-then-restored top.
x: A Treiber stack is a useful algorithm sketch, but the bare C fragments below omit a complete memory-reclamation protocol. Retain node lifetimes and prevent node reuse when experimenting with its pointer-update logic. A lock-free stack The Treiber stack (R. Kent Treiber, IBM, 1986) is the "hello world" of lock-free structures. The Treiber stack is a linked list, and top is an atomic pointer. Push links the new node to the current top, then tries to swing top to it. If another thread pushed or popped in between, top no longer equals old, the CAS fails, old is refreshed and we relink. Garbage collection helps with lifetime reclamation, but atomic publication and node-reinsertion rules still matter. In bare C the marked dereference can access freed memory. Separately, a later CAS can install a stale next pointer after an ABA cycle. The ABA problem CAS asks "is top still equal to old?". It cannot tell whether top changed and then changed back. That is the ABA problem. Start with the Treiber stack A → B → C. T1's CAS succeeds because top is A again, but the A it sees is a different moment of A, and the next it computed (B) is stale. The Treiber stack now points at memory that was already freed, and C is no longer reachable from top through a valid chain. A memory allocator recycling a freed node's address causes exactly the same thing, so you do not need to push the "same" node deliberately. The fixes: Tagged pointers. Pair the pointer with a version counter and CAS both together. Every successful update increments the counter, so "A, version 7" no longer matches "A, version 9". x86-64 offers a 16-byte CAS (cmpxchg16b) for pointer-plus-counter pairs; packing a small counter into pointer bits is platform-specific and requires validating address representation and atomic support. A tag with a fixed number of bits eventually wraps around to a value it has held before: So a 16-bit tag repeats after 65,536 updates, and a thread stalled across exactly 65,536 updates (or any multiple of it) would see a matching tag and could still be fooled. Any finite tag needs an argument that wraparound cannot alias an outstanding observation. LL/SC. A genuine load-linked/store-conditional protocol validates an exclusive reservation rather than only comparing values, so an intervening write can invalidate it even if the value returns. Reservations may fail for other reasons too. C11 compare-exchange still exposes value comparison, even when implemented with LL/SC; it does not acquire an automatic ABA guarantee. Do not reuse memory while anyone might hold a reference. This is the real fix, and it leads to the next problem. Key takeaways A Treiber push or pop publishes its change through compare-exchange. Value equality cannot reveal an intervening change and return to the same pointer value. Version tags require safe wraparound assumptions and do not by themselves make dereferences safe. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading

sum: Separate address-reuse ABA from the earlier dereference that may already access freed memory.
x: In a Treiber pop, a thread first loads the atomic top pointer, then reads the node’s next field, then attempts CAS. Another thread must not free or recycle that node between the first two steps. Safe memory reclamation The second bug on the (!) line is a use-after-free. Between T1 loading old and reading old->next, T2 may have popped that node and freed it. T1 then reads memory that was already freed, which may crash or return garbage, even if the CAS later fails. With a sound shared-lock and lifetime protocol, removal/freeing and every relevant dereference are coordinated. A lock protects nothing if some accesses or frees ignore it. Without one, you need a way to know when no thread can still be looking at a node. The main schemes are: Scheme Idea ------ Garbage collection freed only when unreachable Hazard pointers threads announce what they read Epoch-based free after all threads move on RCU free after an RCU grace period Garbage collection prevents freeing a node or recycling its address while a live reference remains. It does not prevent logical ABA if the program explicitly removes and reinserts the same node, so node-reuse rules still matter. This removes one reclamation burden in managed runtimes, while logical reuse still needs an algorithmic argument. java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue is based on the Michael–Scott queue (1996), which uses CAS on both the head and the tail. Hazard pointers (Maged Michael, 2004): before dereferencing a node, a thread publishes its address in a per-thread "hazard" slot and re-checks it is still reachable. A thread that wants to free a node first scans everyone's hazard slots and defers the free if it finds a match. Epoch-based reclamation (used by Rust's crossbeam-epoch): threads mark themselves as active in a global epoch; retired nodes are freed once every active thread has moved past the epoch in which they were retired. This can reduce per-access announcement work compared with hazard pointers, but the cost depends on the implementation and workload; one stalled pinned thread can prevent epoch advancement and delay reclamation. WG21 adopted P2530R3 (hazard pointers) and P2545R4 (RCU) into the C++ working paper at the June 2023 Varna meeting. The proposed hazard_pointer and rcu headers still require an appropriate language/library implementation; check its actual interface and availability before relying on them. Key takeaways Reading a removed node before CAS can already be a use-after-free. Hazard pointers and epoch schemes delay reuse while a reference could remain live. A reclamation scheme also needs valid publication and node-reinsertion rules; finite tags alone are insufficient. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading WG21 editor report: June 2023 adopted motions

sum: Compare concurrent read work with shared reader-metadata overhead.
x: Read-mostly is a useful workload description, rather than a sufficient proof that a read-write lock will be faster. The length of each protected read and the lock implementation also matter. Read-write locks Many shared structures are read far more often than written: routing tables, configuration, caches, DNS zones. A read-write lock lets any number of readers in at once and gives writers exclusive access. It seems like an obvious win, but it often disappoints: Readers still write. Many implementations update shared reader metadata on entry and exit. With 32 cores doing short lookups, that one cache line bounces between cores just as a mutex's would. For read sections that are short enough, this overhead can outweigh reader parallelism; there is no universal duration threshold. Starvation. As in the readers–writers problem, a reader-preferring lock (glibc's default) can starve writers; a writer-preferring one can starve readers. Upgrade deadlock. Two readers that each try to upgrade to a write lock wait for each other to stop reading. Most libraries do not support upgrading for this reason. Longer read sections and rare writes can make reader parallelism worthwhile, but the crossover must be measured on the actual implementation and hardware. For short, very hot reads you want readers that write nothing shared at all. Key takeaways Read-write locks allow parallel readers but can still contend on shared metadata. Preference policies and attempted upgrades can introduce starvation or deadlock. Choose a documented library protocol and measure the actual workload before replacing a mutex. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading

sum: Use an even unchanged sequence value to decide whether a retry-safe copy is usable.
x: A short update to several plain values can overlap a reader’s copy. A sequence counter lets a reader detect that overlap and discard the speculative copy under a memory model that permits the protocol. Seqlocks A seqlock lets readers proceed without writing anything. The writer increments a sequence counter before and after each update, so the counter is odd while a write is in progress. Readers read the counter, read the data, then read the counter again, and retry if it was odd or has changed. The acceptance rule can be expressed precisely. This model assumes the counter cannot wrap back to the same value during one read attempt: This is algorithm pseudocode. Portable C requires a race-free representation (for example atomic fields) plus a proven ordering protocol; retrying does not undo undefined behavior. Linux seqlock APIs follow the Linux kernel memory model and do not magically make arbitrary plain C fields portable atomic objects. Writers must also meet the API's serialization and non-preemption requirements. These readers do not take the writer lock or update a shared reader count, reducing contention. They do not scale perfectly: cache traffic and repeated retries still cost time. The cost: a reader may read torn, inconsistent data and must throw it away and retry, so it must never follow pointers inside that data (they might point to memory that was already freed). Seqlocks suit small, plain values updated often and read constantly. Linux timekeeping uses sequence-counter protocols for consistent snapshots. Clock-specific fast paths, tickless operation and clocksource handling differ; not every clock query or time update follows one universal path. Key takeaways Accept a copy only when the sequence value was even and is unchanged. Readers may need retries and must not dereference pointers that an update could invalidate. Portable C and kernel seqlock implementations need their own proven race-free/order protocols. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading

sum: Publish a replacement object and wait for pre-existing readers before reclamation.
x: An RCU reader may keep using an old object after another thread publishes a replacement. Safe reclamation therefore depends on reader lifetimes as well as pointer visibility. RCU: read-copy-update RCU supports efficient read-side access to linked, pointer-based data; its exact read-side cost depends on flavour and configuration. It has been used throughout the Linux kernel since 2002 (Paul McKenney and others), for routing tables, the directory-entry cache, module lists and much more. The idea is in the name. In this immutable-configuration example, a writer does not modify a published object. Instead it: Reads the current version. Copies it and modifies the copy. Updates the shared pointer using the RCU publication API, providing the ordering required for readers of the new object. Waits for an RCU grace period: until every reader that might still be using the old version has finished. Frees the old version. This is RCU-style pseudocode: a real kernel implementation uses kernel allocation and protected pointer-access APIs; a liburcu application needs its selected flavor's headers, registration, start-up and shutdown rules. Assume cur initially refers to a valid object and writers hold the same mutex. For this publication pattern, rcu_assign_pointer supplies release-style ordering and rcu_dereference supplies the required pointer-dependency/compiler ordering. It is not a blanket claim that every RCU dereference is a C11 acquire load. That is the double-checked-locking lesson again. synchronize_rcu waits for read-side sections that pre-exist its invocation, not necessarily every later reader. In the simplified diagram publication and the start of the grace-period wait are adjacent; R1/R2 may retain the old object. R3 is drawn as observing the replacement, which is one possible execution, not an immediate-visibility guarantee from its wall-clock start time. The RCU implementation must also supply the ordering that prevents a reader from using reclaimed old storage after the grace period. Actual grace-period completion need not coincide with the last illustrated unlock. How can the kernel identify completion? In non-preemptible RCU, a context switch is one kind of quiescent state showing that a CPU is no longer executing a pre-existing read-side section; idle and user-mode transitions can also supply quiescent states. Preemptible RCU additionally tracks preempted readers. Readers must obey their flavour’s blocking and lifetime rules; read-side overhead varies with configuration. Costs and grace-period duration depend on RCU flavor, configuration and workload; no fixed timing is supplied here. call_rcu() lets a writer register a callback to free the old data later instead of blocking. The trade-offs: Readers that retained an old version can see stale data. RCU supplies no fixed maximum age: whether that is acceptable depends on the application’s consistency and lifetime requirements. This copy-update example serialises writers with a mutex. Other RCU algorithms can use different update protocols; update/reclamation cost is workload-dependent. Old versions stay in memory until their RCU grace period ends, so a rapid run of updates can raise memory use. In user space, liburcu provides RCU for applications. Key takeaways RCU publication orders construction before readers use the newly observed pointer. A grace-period wait covers pre-existing read-side sections; later readers need not delay it. Reader cost, grace-period duration and permitted operations depend on the RCU flavour and configuration. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading

sum: Use a brief lock for publication and keep previously returned versions unchanged.
x: The useful RCU idea here is an unchanged published version. A managed runtime helps preserve object lifetime, while a documented lock supplies the publication protocol in this Python example. The same idea in Python Managed runtimes help keep referenced objects alive, but do not supply publication ordering or application immutability automatically. This example uses a brief shared lock to obtain or publish a snapshot, then allows use of that immutable snapshot outside the lock. Readers briefly take the publication lock, then retain a reference to an unchanged dictionary. Reclamation timing is runtime-dependent. Callers must never mutate the returned dictionary or mutable objects reachable from it. Java’s CopyOnWriteArrayList similarly provides snapshot iteration using replacement arrays for mutative operations; frequent copying can make it unsuitable for write-heavy workloads. The rule that makes this safe: never mutate a published object. _config["timeout"] = 30 could break the guarantee that a published dictionary never changes; do not equate Python multi-step-operation races with the precise C data-race definition. Content gap No hardware-specific lock, cache-transfer or RCU timing benchmark is available. The Treiber stack example deliberately omits safe reclamation, and the seqlock/RCU fragments are protocol illustrations, not complete production implementations. Choosing a tool Situation Reach for ------ Shared counter atomic fetch-add Small, hot, plain data seqlock Read-mostly linked data RCU or copy-on-write updates Long reads, some writes read-write lock Queue between threads library queue Anything else a mutex Lock-free is not automatically faster Under heavy contention on one word, CAS loops fail and retry repeatedly, and the cache line still bounces between cores. A well-implemented mutex that puts waiters to sleep can beat a naive lock-free structure. Lock-free code is also very hard to get right and test. Use proven libraries (java.util.concurrent, Rust's crossbeam, Folly, Boost.Lockfree, liburcu) and benchmark before replacing a lock. Key takeaways Build a private replacement and publish it under the shared lock. A retained reference keeps an old dictionary alive, but the application must also keep it unchanged. This lock-assisted snapshot example is not a lock-free Python RCU implementation. Further reading Herlihy: Wait-free synchronization Michael–Scott queue paper Linux RCU documentation Linux sequence counters and seqlocks Userspace RCU Python threading

sum: A deadlocked set has a circular dependency that its members cannot resolve alone.
x: In the previous module you learnt to protect shared data with locks, semaphores and condition variables. Those tools fix races, but they introduce a new way to fail: threads that wait for each other forever. A set of threads is deadlocked when every thread in the set is waiting for something that only another thread in the same set can provide. Nobody can move, so nobody ever will. The affected operations stop making progress. Sleeping lock waits can consume little CPU, while deadlocked spinlocks can burn CPU; detectors, timeouts or recovery logic may report errors. The intuition: a four-way junction Picture four cars arriving at a junction with no traffic lights, each wanting to go straight on. Each car edges forward into the middle and now blocks the car on its left. Every driver is waiting for the car in front to move, and that car is waiting for the next. Nobody is doing anything wrong locally, yet the whole junction is frozen. Two things are worth noticing: Each car holds some road while waiting for more. The waiting forms a circle. If any one car could reverse, the jam would clear. That is deadlock in miniature. The classic bug: two locks in opposite order Here is a common deadlock pattern. Two threads transfer money between the same two accounts, in opposite directions. Some schedules finish; this interleaving deadlocks: Thread 1 holds A and wants B. Thread 2 holds B and wants A. Neither with block can finish, so neither lock is ever released. Deadlocks hide in testing The bad interleaving needs a context switch in a narrow window. A test suite may run it a million times without failing, then production hits it under load on a Friday night. "It passed the tests" tells you very little about deadlock. The four Coffman conditions For the classical reusable-resource model, Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani's 1971 treatment identifies four necessary conditions for resource deadlock: Mutual exclusion. At least one resource can be held by only one thread at a time. (A mutex, a printer, a row lock held for writing.) Hold and wait. A thread holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire another. No preemption. A resource cannot be forcibly taken away; the holder must release it voluntarily. Circular wait. There is a cycle of waiting threads: each waits for a resource held by the next, and the last waits for the first. Check them against the transfer bug: Condition In the transfer bug ------ Mutual exclusion Only one acquisition succeeds at a time Hold and wait Holds src, wants dst No preemption No participant forcibly releases the other lock Circular wait T1 → T2 → T1 The resource model and acquisition policy determine which conditions are possible; actual hold-and-wait and circular-wait relationships describe a particular state. The conditions are necessary: break any one of them and deadlock is impossible. That fact is the basis of every prevention technique in the next lesson. Necessary, and with single instances, sufficient When every resource has exactly one instance (as with ordinary mutexes), a cycle of waiting threads is a deadlock. When resources have several identical instances (say, 3 database connections), a cycle is necessary but not always sufficient, as we will see below. Key takeaways A deadlocked set has a circular dependency that its members cannot resolve alone. All four classical Coffman conditions are necessary; breaking one prevents resource deadlock. Opposite lock orders permit a deadlocking schedule even if many test runs finish. Further reading OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems Python: primitive and re-entrant locks

sum: Request edges point from a process to a resource; assignment edges point back to a holder.
x: Resource-allocation graphs A resource-allocation graph (RAG) makes the conditions visible. It has two kinds of node and two kinds of edge: Circles are threads (or processes): T1, T2. Boxes are resources: [A], [B]. Dots inside a box show how many instances it has. A request edge T → R means T is waiting for R. An assignment edge R → T means R is held by T. The transfer deadlock looks like this: Follow the arrows: A → T1 → B → T2 → A. A cycle. When a cycle isn't a deadlock Suppose resource R has two instances (two identical database connections, say) and resource S has one: There is a cycle T1 → S → T2 → R → T1. But T4 also holds an instance of R and is not waiting for anything. When T4 finishes and releases its instance, T2 gets it, finishes, releases S, and T1 proceeds. The cycle dissolves. So the rules are: No cycle: no deadlock, guaranteed. Cycle, single-instance resources: deadlock, guaranteed. Cycle, multi-instance resources: deadlock possible; you need a more careful check (the detection algorithm in the detection and recovery lessons). Key takeaways Request edges point from a process to a resource; assignment edges point back to a holder. A cycle proves deadlock for exclusive single-instance resources. With interchangeable multiple instances, a holder outside the cycle may release a unit and unblock it. Further reading OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems

sum: Joins, bounded queues, nested pool submissions and pipes can form dependency cycles.
x: Deadlock beyond mutexes Anything a thread can wait on can be part of a deadlock cycle, not just mutexes. Self-deadlock. A thread takes a non-reentrant lock it already holds. A second blocking acquisition of a held threading.Lock waits; if no other thread releases it, this is self-deadlock. threading.RLock supports same-thread re-entry. Joining. Thread A calls b.join() while holding a lock that B needs before it can exit. Bounded queues. Producer P blocks on a full queue Q1 while consumer C blocks putting a reply onto full queue Q2 that P is supposed to drain. Thread pools. A task running on a pool of size 4 submits a sub-task to the same pool and waits for its result. If all 4 workers do this at once, no worker is free to run any sub-task. This is a classic in Java ExecutorService and Python concurrent.futures code. Processes and pipes. A parent writes a large input to a child's stdin and only then reads its stdout. The child fills its stdout pipe buffer (capacity depends on page size, limits and configuration) and blocks writing; the parent blocks writing because the child stopped reading. Python's subprocess docs warn about exactly this and recommend communicate(). Key takeaways Joins, bounded queues, nested pool submissions and pipes can form dependency cycles. A pool task waiting for work queued to the same exhausted pool cannot progress. Drain child output while supplying input; communicate() handles the pipe interaction. Further reading Python: executor deadlock examples Python: subprocess pipe interactions Python: primitive and re-entrant locks

sum: Database recovery aborts a victim; applications must handle the failed transaction.
x: Database deadlocks Database writes can acquire row, page or table locks, with duration depending on engine, isolation level and lock type. PostgreSQL row locks from these updates normally last until transaction end (commit or rollback). That makes them a rich source of deadlocks, often in code with no explicit locking at all. This is the transfer bug again, written in SQL. The difference is that databases expect it. PostgreSQL, after a session has waited for deadlock_timeout (default 1 second), runs a deadlock check, finds the cycle and aborts one transaction with ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01). The other transaction then proceeds. SQL Server returns error 1205 and MySQL's InnoDB returns error 1213 in the same situation. So a database turns a permanent hang into a failed transaction that your application must be ready to retry. The detection and recovery lessons looks at how they do it. Deadlock, or just slow? When a service "hangs", it is worth separating three situations, because they have different fixes: Symptom Likely cause ------ 0% CPU, threads blocked on locks Deadlock 100% CPU, no progress Livelock or busy loop Progress, but some requests never finish Starvation Sleeping deadlock victims may wait on futexes or conditions, while spin deadlocks can consume CPU. Low CPU and blocked stacks are clues rather than proof of a cycle. A thread dump (the debugging lessons) will show each stuck thread's stack and, often, which lock it is waiting for. Four strategies for dealing with deadlock The rest of this module follows the classic taxonomy: Prevention: design the system so that one Coffman condition can never hold (the prevention lessons). Avoidance: let the system check each request and refuse those that could lead to deadlock (the avoidance lessons). Detection and recovery: let deadlocks happen, notice them, and break them by killing or rolling back a victim (the detection and recovery lessons). Ignore it: the "ostrich algorithm". General-purpose OS kernels largely do this for user-space locks: if your program deadlocks its own threads, Linux will not intervene. It is your bug. Applications can prevent cycles through lock ordering; databases can combine ordering, detection and other concurrency controls. Avoidance illustrates explicit reasoning about safe resource states. Key takeaways Database recovery aborts a victim; applications must handle the failed transaction. CPU use and blocked stacks are clues; confirm the dependency cycle. Prevention, avoidance, detection/recovery and leaving recovery to the application are different strategies. Further reading PostgreSQL: explicit locking and deadlocks OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems

t: Removing exclusive resources and nested waits
sum: Immutable data, ownership and copies can remove some shared locks.
x: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.
