This is the basis of musical pitch arithmetic. Exponentials and logarithms, briefly Two identities do almost all the work. The first says that adding in an exponent (the small raised number, "the power") multiplies the result: The second undoes the first. The base-2 logarithm answers "how many doublings make x?": Most languages offer log2; otherwise use the last line, which works because any logarithm divided by the same logarithm of 2 gives the base-2 version. Logarithms are defined only for positive numbers, which is fine here: frequencies and their ratios are always positive. The practical rule follows: do pitch arithmetic in note space, then convert to hertz once at the end. In note space, transposing, bending and modulating are simple additions. In hertz they're multiplications, and mixing the two up is a classic bug. Semitones and equal temperament Western chromatic music commonly divides the octave into 12 semitones. In twelve-tone equal temperament (12-TET), every semitone has the same frequency ratio. Twelve of them must make an octave (×2), so each one is the number that gives 2 when 12 copies of it are multiplied together: For example, the note one semitone above A4 (440 Hz) is A♯4, at 440 × 1.059463 ≈ 466.16 Hz. That irrational ratio is the price of a tuning where every key is equally in tune. Simple whole-number ratios such as 3:2 (the pure ratio of a perfect fifth) don't land exactly on a 12-TET note: Interval Just ratio 12-TET ratio Difference ------------ Octave 2.000 2.000 0 cents Fifth 1.500 1.4983 12-TET 1.96 cents flat Major third 1.250 1.2599 12-TET 13.69 cents sharp The difference column uses cents: hundredths of a semitone, explored in the tuning unit. 12-TET is a common default tuning; alternative tunings are a later feature. Pitfalls Adding hertz for musical intervals. "Up a fifth" is ×1.4983, not +220 Hz. Key takeaways An octave doubles frequency; musical intervals use ratios rather than fixed hertz differences. Exponentials turn octave offsets into ratios, and base-2 logarithms count doublings. In 12-TET, twelve identical semitone ratios multiply to two. Just intervals differ slightly. Further reading Equal temperament — Wikipedia Cent (music) — Wikipedia)

sum: Turn note numbers into hertz, invert the conversion and avoid integer-division and octave-label bugs.
x: MIDI note numbers MIDI identifies notes with a number from 0 to 127. Note 60 is middle C, and 69 is the A above it, which is tuned to 440 Hz by convention. Each step of 1 is one semitone. Your synth needs to turn a note number into a frequency, and the standard conversion (the Wikipedia article on the MIDI Tuning Standard gives it) is: Going the other way, a tuner or a pitch detector turns a frequency back into a (usually fractional) note number: Both formulas assume 12-TET and A4 = 440 Hz; another tuning system or reference pitch changes the constants. Notes 21 to 108 are the 88 keys of a piano (A0 to C8). Note 0, at about 8.2 Hz, is below hearing; you'd hear it only through its harmonics. Octave labels vary, numbers don't In scientific pitch notation middle C is C4, so note 60 = C4 and 69 = A4. Some software and instruments label note 60 as C3 instead: Ableton Live’s manual gives its full MIDI range as C−2 to G8, which places note 60 at C3. The number on the wire is always 60, so think in note numbers and check how each piece of gear displays them. Keep the 440 as a parameter (a4 above). A "master tune" control is just a different reference. Pitfalls Integer division. In C-family languages, (n − 69) / 12 with integers truncates to whole octaves. Use floating point. Assuming octave labels. Use note numbers between systems. Key takeaways The conventional 12-TET reference is note 69 at 440 Hz, with one semitone per note-number step. Use floating-point division in the exponent and keep the reference pitch configurable. Note 60 is middle C; displayed octave names vary between products. Further reading MIDI Tuning Standard — Wikipedia MIDI 1.0 core specifications — MIDI Association Piano key frequencies — Wikipedia Sampler key range — Ableton Live 12 manual Tuning reference and note mapping — MIDI Association

sum: Express tuning errors in cents and predict the beat rate of two close tones.
x: Cents A cent is 1/100 of a 12-TET semitone, so there are 1200 cents per octave. To measure how far apart two frequencies are in pitch, count the octaves between them and multiply by 1200: To shift a frequency by a number of cents, undo the logarithm: How small is a cent? It is often smaller than a pitch change a listener can reliably distinguish between separate tones. The just-noticeable difference depends on frequency, duration, level, timbre, training and the listener. Secondary summaries sometimes quote 3 Hz below 500 Hz or 0.6% above 1 kHz; these are rough examples, not universal thresholds. For scale, 3 Hz at 440 Hz is about 12 cents, while a 0.6% change is about 10 cents. Research finds substantial variation with test conditions, so use measured results for the particular listening task. Two tones played together are another matter: even a cent or two of mistuning can be heard as slow beating. Cents are the natural unit for detune. Here's a function that finds the nearest note and how far off it is: The n // 12 − 1 gives the octave number in scientific pitch notation, because note 0 is C−1. Detuning and beats Play two oscillators at nearly the same frequency and you hear the level wobble. That's beating: the two sines drift in and out of phase, reinforcing then cancelling. The wobble happens once for every cycle one oscillator gains on the other, so its rate is the difference in frequency. Detune one 440 Hz oscillator by +10 cents: The difference formula describes the interference envelope. A difference of a few hertz sounds like a slow level wobble. As the difference grows into tens of hertz, listeners may hear rapid beats, roughness or two distinct tones rather than a countable wobble. The perceptual boundaries depend on the tones and listener. Because the detune is in cents, the beat rate grows with pitch: the same 10 cents at 880 Hz beats at about 5.1 Hz. This is why a fixed-cents detune sounds "wider" in the high register, and some synths offer a fixed-Hz detune as an alternative. Key takeaways A semitone contains 100 cents, and an octave contains 1200. Use a logarithm to measure an interval and an exponential to apply detune. Two close tones beat at their frequency difference; fixed-cents detune beats faster on higher notes. Further reading Cent (music) — Wikipedia) Frequency-discrimination study — Micheyl, Xiao & Oxenham Beats and their perception — UNSW Physclips Beat (acoustics) — Wikipedia)

sum: Compare fixed-hertz and fixed-cents vibrato and combine bend, detune and modulation before conversion.
x: Linear vs exponential modulation Suppose an LFO adds vibrato. Two ways to do it: Linear (in Hz): add a fixed number of hertz. Exponential (in pitch): multiply by a fixed ratio, set in cents. With D of 10 Hz, a 440 Hz note swings about ±39 cents. At 110 Hz the same ±10 Hz swings about +151 and −165 cents, a much wider wobble. With exponential vibrato, d sets the depth in cents, and it sounds equally deep on every note. Option 2 is what players expect for vibrato and pitch bend. MIDI pitch bend, for example, is normally interpreted as a number of semitones (the bend range), added in note space. Analogue synths face the same problem in hardware. The common 1 volt per octave standard, used by Moog instruments, makes control voltage linear in pitch: each extra volt doubles the oscillator frequency, using an exponential converter inside the oscillator. Real oscillators only follow this law over a limited range, which is why analogue synths need calibrating. Pitfalls Converting too early. Keep pitch as a float note number (including bend, detune and modulation in semitones), then convert to hertz, then to a phase increment. Key takeaways Fixed-hertz modulation changes its musical depth across the keyboard. Fixed-cents modulation applies the same interval on every note. Add bend, detune and modulation in note space, then convert to frequency and phase increment. Further reading MIDI Tuning Standard — Wikipedia CV/gate — Wikipedia

sum: Separate pitch from harmonic content and explain beating between equal-tempered notes and harmonics.
x: Pitch vs timbre Play a sine and a sawtooth at 220 Hz. They have the same pitch but sound completely different. The difference is timbre, often loosely called "tone colour". A sawtooth at 220 Hz contains sine components at 220, 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on: the harmonic series, every whole-number multiple of the fundamental. In an ideal sawtooth their amplitudes fall off steadily: A sine has only the 220 Hz component. Because all the extra components are exact multiples, the waveform still repeats every 1/220 s, and the ear still hears 220 Hz. The harmonic series is also where just ratios come from: harmonics 2, 3, 4, 5 give an octave, a fifth above that, another octave, and a major third. The 5th harmonic of 110 Hz is 550 Hz, about 14 cents below the 12-TET C♯5 (554.37 Hz). Timbre also depends on how the sound changes over time: the attack, how harmonics fade, noise. Subtractive synthesis works by starting with a harmonically rich wave and filtering harmonics away, changing timbre while leaving pitch alone. That's the next module. The missing fundamental Pitch perception isn't just "find the lowest component". If you remove the 220 Hz component from a sawtooth and keep 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on, most listeners still hear a pitch of 220 Hz, because the harmonics are spaced 220 Hz apart. This is why small speakers can suggest bass notes they can't reproduce. Key takeaways A periodic waveform’s harmonics lie at whole-number multiples of its fundamental. Harmonic amplitudes and changes over time shape timbre. Listeners can hear a missing fundamental from the spacing of the remaining harmonics. Further reading Equal temperament — Wikipedia Beat (acoustics) — Wikipedia) Timbre — Wikipedia

t: Sample timing, block deadlines and memory
sum: Interpret sample instants and budget processing time, buffer memory and audio data rate.
x: A digital synth never handles a continuous wave. It handles a stream of numbers, one every 1/48,000 of a second or so, and a converter turns them into a voltage. This lesson is about what those numbers are, how precise they need to be, and what goes wrong at the edges. Two separate settings decide the quality of a digital signal. Sample rate sets how often you measure. Bit depth sets how finely each measurement is recorded. Neither of them is the playback volume, which is decided by the numbers' size relative to full scale and by whatever amplifier follows the converter. Discrete-time signals Sampling a signal means measuring a continuous signal at evenly spaced instants. The spacing between instants is the sample period, and sample number n is simply the signal's value at n sample periods: Picture each sample as a lollipop: a value at an instant, with nothing defined in between. A sample is not a little rectangle of constant value. The DAC's job (explained in the reconstruction unit) is to rebuild a smooth signal that passes through every lollipop. Common sample rates: Rate Typical use ------ 44.1 kHz CD audio 48 kHz Video, most pro audio and audio hardware 96 kHz High-resolution recording; some synth internals The sample rate fixes the highest frequency you can represent: half the sample rate, as the Nyquist-limit unit explains. 48 kHz covers up to 24 kHz, above the roughly 20 kHz limit of hearing. Higher rates mostly buy room for processing that creates high frequencies (distortion, sharp waveforms), not extra audible treble. It also sets your time budget. Synths process audio in blocks (a fixed number of samples handled in one go), and the hardware plays a block in a fixed time: All the work for a block must finish in less time than that, every time. If it doesn't, the hardware runs out of samples and you hear a click or dropout. How much data is that? The numbers add up quickly, which matters on a microcontroller: One second of mono float32 at 48 kHz is 192,000 bytes, about 192 kB (kilobytes). Stereo 24-bit audio data at 48 kHz is 2.304 Mbit/s (megabits per second). On an I²S bus, 24-bit samples often travel in 32-bit slots, so the bit clock runs at 48,000 × 32 × 2 = 3.072 MHz. A delay effect with a two-second buffer needs 48,000 × 2 × 4 = 384,000 bytes (384 kB) per channel in float32. Check this against your board's RAM before designing features. Pitfalls Confusing the three settings. Sample rate (how often), bit depth (how finely), level (how big relative to full scale). Turning a synth down in software doesn't change its bit depth, but very quiet integer signals do use fewer effective bits. Key takeaways Sample rate determines the spacing of sample instants and the duration of each processing block. Finish each block before the hardware consumes it or audio can drop out. Buffer memory scales with duration, sample rate, bytes per sample and channel count. Further reading Sampling (signal processing) — Wikipedia)

sum: Count sample levels and calculate quantisation steps while distinguishing rounding from clipping.
x: Bit depth and quantisation Each sample must be stored with finite precision. Every extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so with N bits a signed integer sample has this many possible values: Bits Levels Integer range --------- 8 256 −128 to 127 16 65,536 −32,768 to 32,767 24 16,777,216 −8,388,608 to 8,388,607 Rounding the true value to the nearest level is quantisation. The levels are evenly spaced, so the step size is the width of the range divided by the number of levels, and rounding to the nearest level is wrong by at most half a step either way: This assumes the signal stays inside full scale; a value beyond the top or bottom level is clipped, and its error can be much larger. Pitfalls Truncating instead of rounding. Truncation toward zero gives sign-dependent error approaching a full step; it need not add DC to a symmetric signal. Rounding downward instead has a negative bias, averaging about half a step under the uniform-error model. Nearest rounding limits error to half a step away from overload. Key takeaways Each extra bit doubles the number of distinct integer sample values. Nearest rounding stays within half a step away from overload. Signed integer endpoints are asymmetric; overload and truncation require separate care. Further reading Quantization (signal processing) — Wikipedia) Audio bit depth — Wikipedia Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001

sum: Derive the full-scale-sine SQNR rule and see where coarse quantisation breaks its assumptions.
x: Quantisation noise and the six-decibel rule For a busy signal much larger than one step, the error behaves like a small random noise added to the signal: quantisation noise. How far that noise sits below the signal is the SQNR, the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio, measured in decibels (dB, a logarithmic scale for ratios explained in the decibel-gain unit). The standard result, for a full-scale sine wave, is: Each extra bit adds about 6 dB, because it halves the step size and halving an amplitude is −6.02 dB. 16 bits gives about 98 dB; 24 bits about 146 dB. Where do the two numbers come from? The rounding error is spread evenly across one step, which gives it a predictable RMS (root-mean-square, a kind of average size; the peak-and-RMS unit). A full-scale sine spans all the steps, so its peak is half of that span, and a sine's RMS is its peak divided by about 1.414. Putting those together: The derivation shows the assumptions: a sine that fills full scale without overloading, and an error that is evenly spread and unrelated to the signal. A quieter signal gets proportionally less SQNR, and very coarse quantisation breaks the second assumption. You can check this in a few lines: At 12 and 16 bits the formula agrees closely. At 4 bits this example also overloads the positive endpoint: its largest code is 7/8, below the sine's 0.999 peak. That clipping contributes substantial error. In addition, the uniform, signal-independent error model is only an approximation; low-resolution periodic quantisation can produce distortion rather than a gentle hiss. Why 997 Hz? Test tones are often slightly "odd" frequencies like 997 Hz rather than 1000 Hz. With 1000 Hz at 48 kHz, each cycle is exactly 48 samples, so the same few quantisation errors repeat every cycle and pile up at harmonic frequencies. An odd frequency spreads them out. Key takeaways The uniform-error model predicts about 6.02 dB per bit plus 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine. Lower signal level reduces SQNR even when the file’s bit depth stays fixed. Coarse quantisation and endpoint overload can produce distortion and disagree with the noise model. Further reading Quantization (signal processing) — Wikipedia) Audio bit depth — Wikipedia Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001

sum: Explain why reducing bit depth needs dither and why a converter’s word length exceeds its effective resolution.
x: Dither and real converter noise The same problem returns for very quiet signals, even at 16 bits. A sine whose amplitude is under half a step rounds to zero every time and vanishes completely. A fade-out turns gritty in its last few bits. Dither addresses this by adding a tiny amount of random noise before quantising. Common triangular (TPDF) dither spans two quantisation steps peak-to-peak. With suitable dither and no overload, the output error’s mean and noise power no longer vary with the signal: you trade extra hiss for removal of systematic quantisation distortion, and quiet details survive statistically inside the noise. This does not mean every property of the total error is independent of the signal. Dither matters whenever you reduce bit depth, such as when exporting 16-bit files. Inside a 32-bit float synth it's rarely needed. Real converters A "24-bit" converter outputs 24-bit words, but its analogue noise floor is far above the theoretical 146 dB. Examples from TI’s datasheets are 99 dB typical for the PCM1808 ADC and 112 dB typical for the PCM5102A DAC. These are A-weighted figures under the stated test conditions. The higher-performance PCM1792A specifies 127 dB with a 2 V RMS stereo test output and 132 dB in its mono test configuration. These are different configurations, not a guaranteed range for any board. Board circuitry and power supplies affect the result, so check the datasheet and measure. 24 bits gives a comfortable margin so that converter noise, not quantisation, sets the floor. A noise-only estimate of effective resolution can be obtained by rearranging the full-scale-sine SQNR rule from the preceding unit. Formal ENOB measurements normally use SINAD, which includes distortion as well as noise; substituting an A-weighted dynamic-range figure gives only an estimate. Key takeaways Dither adds noise before quantisation to decorrelate error from quiet signals. Use dither when reducing bit depth; continuous float processing usually does not need it. A 24-bit converter’s analogue noise floor is higher than ideal 24-bit quantisation noise. Check and measure the hardware. Further reading Dither — Wikipedia Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001 PCM5102A audio DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments PCM1808 ADC datasheet — Texas Instruments PCM1792A DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments SINAD, SNR and ENOB — Analog Devices MT-003

sum: Keep internal float headroom and convert safely at fixed-format boundaries.
x: The −1..1 convention and floating point Inside most audio software, samples are floating-point numbers where ±1.0 means full scale. The converter's maximum output corresponds to 1.0. This convention lets the same code work whatever bit depth the hardware uses. Why floats internally? Headroom. A float can hold 3.7 or −12.0 without trouble. Mixing several voices can exceed 1.0 mid-chain and be scaled down later without clipping; normal floating-point rounding still applies. Integers would overflow or clip. Resolution where it matters. A 32-bit float has a 24-bit significand plus an exponent. Quiet signals in the normal range keep their relative precision, because the exponent scales with the value; subnormal values lose significant bits. Simple maths. Gain is a multiply; mixing is an add. Integer and fixed-point arithmetic formats still matter at the edges: WAV files, converter interfaces, and microcontrollers without a floating-point unit. The conversion at the boundary is where bugs live: Three things to notice: 1.7 was clipped to 32767. Over-range floats must be clipped at conversion, never cast directly. In C and C++, converting a float to an integer type that can't hold its value is undefined behaviour. In practice you may get a wrapped value or, on x86, the "integer indefinite" value −2,147,483,648: either way, a loud crack. NumPy is no safer: in testing, np.array([1.7 32767]).astype(np.int16) gave −9833, silently. Asymmetry. Integers run from −32768 to +32767, so full scale isn't symmetric. Libraries choose 32767 or 32768 as the scale factor. Inconsistent scale factors. Here the code multiplied by 32767 but divided by 32768, so a round trip shrinks the signal very slightly. Pick one convention and use it both ways. Pitfalls Casting instead of clipping at float-to-integer conversion. Denormals. Float values extremely close to zero (subnormals, or denormals) are much slower to process on some processors: some x86 instructions on some processors need a slow assist, costing tens or hundreds of cycles. The penalty depends on the processor, instruction and floating-point mode; benchmark the target rather than assuming a fixed cost. Decaying filters and reverbs can produce them. The usual fixes are to switch on the CPU's flush-to-zero (and denormals-are-zero) mode for the audio thread, as many audio frameworks do, or to add a tiny offset or noise so the values never get that small. Key takeaways With floats, ±1 is nominal full scale and intermediate results can exceed it. Clamp over-range values before integer conversion and use consistent scale factors. Float precision follows the signal’s scale, but subnormal values can have processor-specific performance costs. Further reading Single-precision floating-point format — Wikipedia Subnormal number — Wikipedia Subnormal numbers — Intel documentation Floating-to-integer conversion — C++ standard draft

t: The Nyquist limit and ambiguous samples
sum: Explain why sufficiently band-limited signals reconstruct exactly and why frequencies beyond Nyquist become ambiguous.
x: Sampling has a hard limit. Above a certain frequency, a sampled signal stops meaning what you think it means: a 30 kHz tone and an 18 kHz tone can produce exactly the same samples. This is digital aliasing, usually just called aliasing, and it's the most important limitation in digital synthesis. For a synth builder it's not an abstract worry. The classic analogue waveforms (sawtooth, square, pulse) have harmonics that go on for ever. Generate them naively in software and some of those harmonics fold back into the audible range as clangy, out-of-tune tones. This lesson explains why, and how to predict exactly where they'll land. The sampling theorem The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem says: A signal containing no frequencies at or above B can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples if the sample rate fs is greater than 2B. As a condition, and turned around into the highest frequency a given sample rate can carry: That limit, fs/2, is the Nyquist frequency: Sample rate Nyquist frequency ------ 44.1 kHz 22.05 kHz 48 kHz 24 kHz 96 kHz 48 kHz "Perfectly reconstructed" is a strong claim and it's true. Below Nyquist, samples aren't a rough approximation of the wave: they contain all its information. A 10 kHz sine at 48 kHz has only 4.8 samples per cycle and looks like a jagged mess on a plot, yet ideal reconstruction rebuilds a pure 10 kHz sine from those samples. Real DACs approximate the ideal with finite filters, finite precision and analogue noise. The condition is strict: below fs/2, not at it. A sine at exactly fs/2 gets sampled twice per cycle. Depending on its phase, the samples might be +1, −1, +1, −1 or 0, 0, 0, 0. They can't tell you the amplitude. What aliasing is Take a sine at 30 kHz and sample it at 48 kHz. Each sample advances 30/48 = 0.625 of a cycle. Since the samples only see the phase modulo whole cycles, that's indistinguishable from moving back 0.375 of a cycle, which is what an 18 kHz sine does (18/48 = 0.375), only played in reverse: The 30 kHz samples equal the 18 kHz samples with the sign flipped (a phase inversion). Once sampled, nothing can tell them apart. A DAC will output 18 kHz. The 30 kHz tone has taken on an alias frequency, or alias. Key takeaways The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate; the reconstruction condition is strictly below it. A band-limited wave’s samples retain its information even when a plot looks jagged. Above-Nyquist tones can produce the same samples as lower tones, so their original frequency is lost. Further reading Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem — Wikipedia Aliasing — Wikipedia

sum: Wrap a component by the sample rate, reflect it below Nyquist and trace rising-frequency sweeps.
x: Calculating the alias frequency Picture the frequency axis folded back and forth like a paper fan, with creases at every multiple of the Nyquist frequency (fs/2 in the drawing, where fs is the sample rate): Any frequency maps to the point directly below it on the first segment, from 0 up to the Nyquist frequency. As a procedure: Divide the frequency by the sample rate and keep the remainder (this is "modulo"), giving a value from 0 up to the sample rate. If the result is above the Nyquist frequency, subtract it from the sample rate. As a formula: The formula holds for any frequency, sine by sine. A complex sound is a sum of sines, so apply it to each component separately. Worked through: 30 kHz: 30k mod 48k = 30k, above 24k, so 48k − 30k = 18 kHz. It folded back off the Nyquist "wall". 47 kHz: just under fs. Folds to 48k − 47k = 1 kHz: an ultrasonic tone has become a low, obvious one. 50 kHz: 50k mod 48k = 2 kHz. Just above fs it appears as a low frequency, without folding. 97 kHz: 97k mod 48k = 1k. Two cycles round the fan. Notice the behaviour as an input sweeps upwards: the alias rises to 24 kHz, then falls to 0 at 48 kHz, then rises again. A rising pitch whose alias falls is the unmistakable sound of aliasing. Key takeaways Take the frequency’s remainder after division by the sample rate. Reflect remainders above half the sample rate back into the lower half. Compute complex sounds component by component; aliases reverse direction at fold points. Further reading Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Aliasing — Wikipedia

t: Why naive sawtooths and squares alias
sum: Predict the frequencies and levels of harmonics that fold from sharp digital waveforms.
x: Why sharp waveforms alias A sine has one frequency. A sawtooth has harmonics at every whole-number multiple of its frequency, and their amplitudes fall slowly: A square has only the odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …), whose amplitudes also fall as one over the harmonic number. That fall-off is slow, so a lot of energy sits in very high harmonics. The cause is the waveform's sharp edge. A discontinuity (an instant jump) needs infinitely many harmonics to describe, and a waveform with a jump has harmonics that fall off at 1/k (6 dB per octave). A triangle wave has corners but no jumps, and its harmonics fall as 1/k² (12 dB per octave), so it aliases far less. A naive sawtooth is generated directly from the phase accumulator (the phase-accumulator unit) by rescaling the phase: That jump makes it a sample of the ideal infinite-bandwidth sawtooth. Every harmonic above Nyquist folds back. Take a high note, 1760 Hz (A6), at 48 kHz: Harmonics up to k = 13 (22,880 Hz) are below 24 kHz and fine. Harmonics 14 and up fold back, and they aren't at multiples of 1760 Hz. Which aliases land low, where they are most audible? Harmonic 27 lands at 480 Hz, below the note's own fundamental, only about 29 dB down. None of these are harmonics of 1760 Hz, so they sound like an inharmonic, metallic ring. As the note bends, they slide in the wrong directions. Low notes are less affected (their high harmonics are much weaker by the time they reach Nyquist), which is why naive oscillators can sound fine in the bass and terrible at the top. You can't filter it out afterwards Once an alias is at 480 Hz, it's indistinguishable from a real 480 Hz component. A low-pass filter after the oscillator can't remove it without removing real content too. Aliasing has to be prevented where the high frequencies are created. Key takeaways Sawtooth and square jumps need slowly decaying harmonics, so high pitches alias strongly. A folded harmonic can fall below the fundamental and become an inharmonic tone. After folding, an alias cannot be distinguished from wanted content at the same frequency. Further reading Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms — Stilson & Smith (CCRMA) Aliasing — Wikipedia Sawtooth wave — Wikipedia

sum: Choose input filtering, band-limited oscillators and oversampling where new high frequencies are created.
x: Preventing aliasing in a synth There are two situations. 1. Sampling a real analogue signal (an ADC). Here an anti-aliasing filter removes content above Nyquist before it can fold. Every audio interface input has one. In a modern delta-sigma ADC, the converter samples many times faster than the final sample rate, so a simple analogue low-pass in front is enough, and a steep digital filter does the rest before the rate is reduced to the final rate. 2. Generating a signal digitally (an oscillator). There's no analogue signal to filter: the samples are computed directly. So the oscillator itself must only generate content below Nyquist. Established techniques, at a conceptual level: Additive synthesis: sum sines for each harmonic, stopping below Nyquist. Exact, but costly for low notes with hundreds of harmonics. Band-limited wavetables: precompute a single cycle with only the harmonics that fit, keeping several tables for different pitch ranges and picking one per note. BLIT: construct a band-limited impulse train and integrate it to obtain the desired waveform, taking care with DC and numerical drift. BLEP methods: replace each naive discontinuity with a band-limited step, often by adding a precomputed correction. PolyBLEP uses a cheap polynomial approximation to the step correction. Oversampling: run the oscillator at, say, 4× the output rate, low-pass filter digitally, then discard samples. Aliases still occur, but further up where harmonics are weaker, and the filter removes content outside the output passband before downsampling. Aliases already folded into that passband remain. The roadmap suggests comparing a naive waveform with a library's band-limited version rather than inventing a technique. Stilson and Smith's paper in the further reading is the classic overview. Nonlinear processing aliases too. Clipping, distortion and waveshaping create new harmonics. FM creates sidebands, which need not be harmonics. A hard clipper applied to a 5 kHz sine creates harmonics at 15, 25, 35 kHz and so on, and those above Nyquist fold back. Oversampling around the nonlinear stage is the standard remedy. Key takeaways ADC input filtering removes unwanted high frequencies before sampling or decimation. Digital oscillators need band-limited generation or a suitable correction technique. Nonlinear processing also generates above-Nyquist content. Oversampling helps, but it does not make naive waveforms alias-free. Further reading Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms — Stilson & Smith (CCRMA) Oversampling — Wikipedia Hard Sync Without Aliasing — Eli Brandt

sum: Distinguish out-of-band DAC images from in-band aliases and trace the conversion chain.
x: Reconstruction: the DAC side A DAC is given one number per sample period. A crude converter holds each value until the next (a zero-order hold), producing a staircase. That staircase contains the wanted signal plus image frequencies: copies of the spectrum mirrored around every multiple of the sample rate. Images are not aliases. An alias is a wrong frequency inside the audio band, created when sampling; images sit above Nyquist, created when converting back to analogue, and a filter can remove them. A reconstruction filter (anti-imaging filter) removes the images, leaving the smooth wave the theorem promises. Most modern audio converters are delta-sigma designs that internally oversample and do much of this filtering digitally, so their external analogue filtering can be simple. Follow the converter or codec datasheet's recommended output circuit. Key takeaways Holding samples creates image frequencies around multiples of the sample rate. Reconstruction filtering removes images; it cannot undo aliases already in the samples. Modern converters combine internal digital filtering with their specified analogue circuits. Further reading Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Reconstruction filter — Wikipedia PCM5102A audio DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments

sum: Choose amplitude or power decibels and convert a chain of gains to a sample multiplier.
x: A synth that's too quiet is annoying. One that clips is broken: harsh, aliasing distortion every time a chord gets loud. Managing level is a constant job, from the first oscillator to the final converter, and decibels are the language for it. Why decibels Level ratios in audio span an enormous range. The loudest signal a 24-bit converter handles is millions of times larger in amplitude than its quietest. Ratios like that are unreadable as plain numbers, and our perception of loudness is roughly logarithmic anyway, so audio uses a logarithmic unit: the decibel (dB). A decibel is always a ratio to something. There are two formulas, and mixing them up is the most common mistake. For quantities that measure power or energy: For amplitudes (sample values, voltages, sound pressures): Why the different factors? Power is proportional to amplitude squared, and the logarithm of a square is twice the logarithm: Both formulas give the same dB value for the same change; you just use the one matching the quantity you have. Samples, voltages and pressures are amplitudes, so in synth code you'll nearly always use 20·log10. Going back from decibels to a multiplier undoes the logarithm: The same two conversions in Python: Memorise a few: doubling an amplitude adds about 6 dB, ×10 adds 20 dB, and ×1.414 (the square root of 2) adds about 3 dB. In power terms, doubling power is +3 dB. Gains in dB add where the ratios multiply: Key takeaways Use twenty times the log for amplitude ratios and ten times the log for power ratios. Doubling amplitude adds about 6 dB; doubling power adds about 3 dB. Serial gains add in decibels and multiply as linear factors. Further reading Decibel — Wikipedia

sum: Measure digital level, compare crest factors and recognise different RMS meter conventions.
x: dBFS: decibels relative to full scale dBFS measures a digital level relative to a defined full-scale reference. In a fixed PCM output format, that reference corresponds to the largest permitted sample level; floats can also hold values above it. With floats in ±1.0, full scale is 1.0, so the reference amplitude in the decibel formula is 1: 0 dBFS is the nominal sample-peak maximum at a fixed-format output. Smaller peaks read negative: a peak of 0.5 is −6 dBFS, a peak of 0.1 is −20 dBFS. A value of 2.0 would be +6 dBFS: fine inside a float pipeline, but it will clip at the converter. RMS and dBFS conventions differ For peak levels, dBFS is unambiguous. For RMS levels, conventions differ. AES17 (and related IEC and ITU standards) defines the RMS of a full-scale sine as 0 dBFS, so a full-scale square wave reads +3 dBFS. Other meters use the plain maths, where a full-scale sine reads −3 dBFS RMS. When comparing figures, check which convention a meter or datasheet uses. This lesson uses the plain maths. Peak, RMS and crest factor Two measurements describe a signal's level: Peak level: the largest absolute sample value. It decides whether the digital samples exceed the fixed-format limit. Reconstructed analogue peaks can be higher between samples, which needs a separate true-peak check. RMS (root mean square): the square root of the average of the squared samples. It tracks the signal's power, and relates more closely to perceived loudness than peak does. The name describes the recipe, read from right to left: square every sample, take the mean, then the square root. For a sine, the result is always its peak divided by about 1.414 (the square root of 2): The ratio of peak to RMS is the crest factor, often given in dB: Waveform Crest factor In dB --------- Square 1 0 Sine 1.414 (square root of 2) 3.01 Saw, triangle 1.732 (square root of 3) 4.77 Music (varies widely) often much higher 12–20 is an example A square wave and a sine with the same peak don't sound equally loud: the square has 3 dB more RMS. Switching from sine to square at the same peak increases RMS by 3 dB and often sounds louder, but perceived loudness also depends on spectrum and listening level. Synths may compensate per waveform. Key takeaways Peak level tells you whether nominal full scale is exceeded; RMS measures average squared signal size. Crest factor is peak divided by RMS: a sine has about 3 dB, a square has 0 dB. RMS dBFS references differ between meters. Check conventions before comparing figures. Further reading dBFS — Wikipedia Crest factor — Wikipedia

sum: Predict in-phase and unrelated sums and compare safe voice scaling with average-level scaling.
x: Summing signals Mixing digital signals is just addition, sample by sample. What happens to the level depends on how the signals relate: Identical, in phase: amplitudes add. Two equal signals give +6.02 dB. Identical, 180° out of phase: they cancel. Unrelated (different frequencies, noise): powers add. Two equal signals give about +3 dB of RMS. For N equal signals: But peaks are what clip, and unrelated signals still line up their peaks now and then. Here's an A major triad, each voice a sine at 0.8 (−1.9 dBFS): The RMS rose by the expected amount for three unrelated signals: But the peaks hit the worst case, 3 × 0.8 = 2.4. Converted to a fixed format, almost a third of the samples would clip. Headroom is the gap between your normal peak level and 0 dBFS. For an N-voice synth there are two common ways to scale the voices before summing: Dividing each voice by N guarantees no overflow, but makes single notes quiet. Dividing by the square root of N keeps average loudness steadier but can still peak over. Many designs do this and add a soft clipper or limiter at the end to catch the rare peaks. Key takeaways Identical in-phase signals add amplitudes; unrelated signals add power on average. Unrelated signals can still align their peaks and exceed full scale. Dividing by voice count protects against the worst case; square-root scaling needs protection for overshoots. Further reading Decibel — Wikipedia dBFS — Wikipedia Gain stage — Wikipedia

sum: Compare clipping curves and measure the new harmonics that require alias control.
x: Clipping: hard and soft When a signal exceeds what a stage can represent, it clips. Hard clipping flattens anything beyond the limit: Explicit saturating conversion does this. A raw integer cast is not a clipper: out-of-range conversion can wrap or be undefined, so clamp before converting to the DAC format. It creates a sharp corner where the wave meets the ceiling, and sharp corners mean strong high harmonics. A symmetric clip of a sine, or another input with half-wave symmetry, creates only odd harmonics before sampling. Symmetry of the clipper alone does not remove even harmonics already in an arbitrary input. Soft clipping bends the wave gradually towards the limit. A common choice is the hyperbolic tangent: Small signals pass almost unchanged; big ones are squashed smoothly. It still distorts, but its high harmonics fall away much faster. Compare both on a 1 kHz sine driven 6 dB over full scale (amplitude 2.0). The levels are relative to the fundamental: (The FFT reading is explained in the FFT measurement units. This experiment runs at a very high sample rate to greatly reduce alias contamination of the harmonics measured here. A finite sample rate cannot eliminate every alias from ideal hard clipping.) By the 9th harmonic, soft clipping is about 20 dB cleaner. Inside a synth running at 48 kHz, both clippers' harmonics above 24 kHz will alias, which is why distortion stages are often oversampled. Clipping as a sound Deliberate saturation is a classic synth effect. Accidental clipping at the output is a fault. The difference is whether you chose where it happens and controlled its aliasing. Key takeaways Hard clipping flattens over-range samples; a raw integer cast is not a safe clipper. Soft clipping bends smoothly and usually produces weaker high harmonics for comparable drive. Both introduce nonlinear harmonics; control aliasing around intentional distortion stages. Further reading Clipping (audio) — Wikipedia)

t: Stage gain and protect the output
sum: Place headroom and protection in a float synth and measure worst-case patches.
x: Gain staging inside a digital synth Gain staging means setting the level at each stage so that no stage clips and none is needlessly quiet. In a floating-point synth, intermediate stages almost never clip, so the concerns are different from analogue gear: Practical rules: Know where the hard limit is. In a float pipeline it's the final conversion. Everything before can exceed 1.0 temporarily. Budget headroom where levels can grow: summing voices, resonant filters (which can boost signals near the cutoff well above the input level) and feedback effects. Protect the output. A soft clipper or limiter just before conversion turns rare overshoots into mild saturation instead of harsh clipping. Measure. Log peak and RMS in an offline render of your worst case: all voices, full resonance, maximum velocity. Change gain smoothly. Jumping a gain value between samples causes clicks; stepping it in coarse increments when a knob turns causes "zipper noise". Smoothing is covered in the synthesis module. Key takeaways Budget headroom for mixing, resonance and feedback effects. Intermediate float signals can exceed nominal full scale; protect the final fixed-format conversion. Measure worst-case peak and RMS, and smooth control changes to avoid clicks and zipper noise. Further reading dBFS — Wikipedia Gain stage — Wikipedia

t: From digital full scale to line voltage
sum: Convert dBu and dBV to RMS volts and match the synth output to its destination safely.
x: From dBFS to volts The DAC turns 0 dBFS into some maximum output voltage. That voltage is set by the codec and the output circuit, so it's on the board's datasheet, not a universal number. What your audio interface expects is in its manual. Two common nominal line levels use different references: Level Reference RMS voltage --------- +4 dBu (pro) 0 dBu = 0.7746 V ≈ 1.228 V −10 dBV (consumer) 0 dBV = 1 V ≈ 0.316 V Converting either unit to an RMS voltage is the decibel formula run backwards, with that unit's reference voltage: These are nominal levels; real signals peak well above them, and equipment has headroom for that. Check both the synth's maximum output and the interface input's maximum level in their manuals, and set the synth's output level so that its loudest patch doesn't overload the input. Keep to line-level connections Line, instrument, microphone, headphone and speaker connections are not interchangeable. Never connect a power amplifier's speaker output to a line input or to a development board. Work only with low-voltage, battery or USB-powered circuits and the board's documented audio outputs, and add any output protection the board's documentation recommends. Key takeaways dBu and dBV use different RMS voltage references; digital dBFS depends on the actual converter and circuit. Nominal line level leaves headroom for signal peaks. Check both devices’ maximum levels. Use documented line-level outputs and low-voltage circuits; speaker outputs must not feed line inputs. Further reading Line level — Wikipedia

t: Check and plot an offline test signal
sum: Build a reproducible Python workbench and check signal length, level, DC and zero-crossing frequency.
x: Ears are good at telling you something is wrong and bad at telling you what. Is that buzz aliasing or clipping? Is the note 3 cents flat, or is it a filter making it sound duller? The roadmap's readiness test for this stage is to "explain each sample's meaning, verify frequency and level from the data". This lesson builds a small offline toolkit for doing exactly that. The tools are standard: numpy for arrays and the FFT, matplotlib for plots, soundfile for WAV files. You're using an FFT, not writing one; FFT implementation is deliberately deferred. Set up Use a virtual environment so the experiments are reproducible from a clean checkout: Commit requirements.txt with your experiments. The outputs below were produced with numpy 2.5, matplotlib 3.11 and soundfile 0.14; numbers in the last decimal place may differ slightly on other versions. Protect your ears and speakers A full-scale sine is very loud and fatiguing. Generate test files at −12 dBFS or lower, turn the monitor level down before playing anything new, and raise it gradually. Never play untested generated audio on headphones at volume. Generate a test signal and check it numerically Start with a known signal and check that the numbers match the theory: Each check has a reason: Length: 1 s at 48 kHz must be 48,000 samples. Off-by-one-block errors show up here. Peak 0.5 is −6.02 dBFS, as requested. RMS 0.3536 is the peak divided by 1.414 (the square root of 2), the sine's crest factor (the peak-and-RMS unit). DC offset (the mean) should be essentially zero for this whole-cycle capture. Partial cycles can have a non-zero mean even when the underlying wave is centred correctly. A non-zero mean means the waveform is shifted off centre, which wastes headroom and can thump when audio starts and stops. Other cheap sanity checks are worth wrapping in a function: np.isfinite(x).all() (NaN or infinity anywhere means a bug, often a filter blowing up), and the number of samples at or beyond ±1.0. Plot the waveform A plot shows what summary numbers hide: discontinuities, glitches at block boundaries, asymmetry. Plot short windows (a few cycles) to see the shape, and mark the samples as dots, because they're the real data. The lines joining them are just a drawing aid; recall from the reconstruction unit that the true reconstructed signal is smooth, not straight-sided. Fixing the y-axis at ±1 makes levels comparable between plots. Measure frequency in the time domain For a clean, single-frequency signal, count upward zero crossings: places where a sample is negative and the next one isn't. Average the spacing between them: The frequency is one over the average period, where each period is measured in samples and converted to seconds: This counts whole samples, so it's only accurate to a fraction of a sample per period (here 0.01 Hz after averaging many periods). It's fooled by noise and by waveforms with several crossings per cycle. For anything richer than a sine, use the spectrum. Key takeaways Check sample count, peak, RMS, DC offset and finiteness before listening at a safe level. Plot short windows with sample dots; joining lines are a visual aid. Upward zero crossings estimate a clean sine’s period but are unreliable on noisy or complex waveforms. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation python-soundfile documentation

sum: Calculate FFT bin frequencies and choose a capture long enough for the spacing you need.
x: Read a spectrum with numpy's FFT The FFT (fast Fourier transform) takes N samples and returns how much of each frequency they contain, at evenly spaced frequencies called FFT bins. For real input (ordinary audio), numpy's rfft returns the bins from 0 Hz up to the Nyquist frequency: Three facts you need to read it correctly: Bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the number of samples. One second at 48 kHz gives 1 Hz bins; 0.1 s gives 10 Hz bins. Longer captures give finer frequency resolution. Scaling: numpy's raw output grows with N. For ordinary positive-frequency bins, multiply by 2 and divide by the sum of the window (in the next unit). DC and the even-length Nyquist bin have no negative-frequency partner and are not doubled. Windowing: multiply the capture by a smooth window (Hann is a good default) that tapers its ends to zero. Without it, a frequency that doesn't fit a whole number of cycles in the capture smears energy across the spectrum. That smearing is called spectral leakage. Zero-padding a capture gives more displayed frequency points by interpolating the same transform. It adds no measured information and cannot replace a longer capture when separating nearby tones. Key takeaways For even-length real input, rfft returns half the sample count plus one bins. Bin spacing is sample rate divided by capture length in samples. Longer captures give finer bin spacing; windowing and correct scaling are also needed to read a spectrum. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation numpy.fft.rfftfreq — NumPy documentation Zero padding and spectral interpolation — Julius O. Smith

sum: Use a Hann window and the window sum to recover a bin-centred sine’s amplitude.
x: Analyse a real sample array with NumPy's rfft. In this unit, the capture length is the number of input samples and bins are indexed from zero. A bin-centred sine completes a whole number of cycles in the capture. Window and scale an FFT The Hann window numpy uses is a single raised cosine, zero at both ends and 1 (or, for an even number of samples, just under 1) in the middle: And the scaling that turns a bin's raw magnitude into a sine's amplitude: The 0 Hz bin and (for even N) the Nyquist bin have no mirror, so they are not doubled; the spectrum function below halves them back. Both the frequency and the level match what we generated: the round trip from theory to data and back works. Key takeaways A Hann window tapers the capture endpoints to reduce abrupt boundaries. Divide FFT magnitude by the window sum and double ordinary positive-frequency bins. DC and the even-length Nyquist bin are not doubled; accurate bin-level readings assume a bin-centred tone. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation numpy.fft.rfftfreq — NumPy documentation Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA) numpy.hanning — NumPy documentation

sum: Compare rectangular and Hann captures and explain why between-bin peak readings understate amplitude.
x: FFT bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the capture length in samples. The preceding FFT units explain the amplitude scaling; here we compare what happens when a tone falls between bins. Leakage between FFT bins What if the frequency falls between bins? With a 0.1 s capture (10 Hz bins), compare 1000 Hz (exactly on a bin) with 1005 Hz (halfway between two bins), with and without a window: (−120 here means "at or below −120 dB"; the floor hides meaningless rounding noise.) On a bin, both are perfect. Between bins, the unwindowed ("rect") capture loses 3.9 dB at the peak and leaks energy to −52 dB as far as 500 Hz away, which would mask real low-level components such as aliases. The Hann window loses only 1.4 dB at the peak and keeps the far leakage near −118 dB. A between-bin amplitude shortfall is called scalloping loss. For accurate amplitudes, use coherent sampling (whole cycles), a flat-top window (which widens the main peak), or a peak-interpolation method with an amplitude correction matched to the chosen window. Practical consequences: window when leakage is a concern; a rectangular window is suitable for a coherent capture containing whole cycles. Read levels from a capture long enough that the bins are fine; and when you need an exact level, generate test frequencies that land on bins (an integer number of cycles in the capture). Key takeaways An unwindowed, between-bin tone leaks energy into distant bins and can hide faint components. A Hann window reduces distant leakage, but a between-bin peak still underreads amplitude. For an exact level check, capture a whole number of cycles and use the correct scaling. Further reading Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA) Window function — Wikipedia Spectral leakage — Wikipedia Flat-top amplitude measurement — SciPy documentation

sum: Compare a naive sawtooth’s spectrum with predicted folded harmonics and recognise aliases hidden on harmonic bins.
x: Verify an aliasing prediction The sharp-waveform unit predicted where a naive 1,760 Hz sawtooth's harmonics fold at 48 kHz. Now measure it. A 1 s capture makes each bin exactly 1 Hz, so bin index equals frequency: The predictions were −28.6, −28.9, −28.3 and −29.2 dB for the four aliases (each harmonic's amplitude is one over its harmonic number, here 27, 28, 26 and 29), and −6.0 dB for the 2nd harmonic. The measurements agree to about 0.1 dB, and the small differences come from other, much weaker harmonics folding onto the same bins. This is the "compare a deliberately aliased signal with its predicted apparent frequency" exercise from the roadmap. Later, run the same script against a band-limited oscillator from a library and watch those aliases drop. If the sample rate is an exact multiple of a waveform’s fundamental, aliases can land on existing harmonic bins. They then change harmonic levels rather than appear as extra inharmonic lines. Test awkward frequencies as well as neat ones. Key takeaways Predict alias frequencies and relative levels before measuring the spectrum. Several higher harmonics can fold onto the same bin, changing its observed level. A neat ratio of note frequency to sample rate can hide aliases on existing harmonics; also test awkward frequencies. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA)

t: Write WAV files and check the round trip
sum: Export with explicit clipping and fades, then verify rate, subtype, length and quantisation error.
x: Write a WAV file with a library Writing a WAV encoder isn't a learning goal; a library handles the format. soundfile (a wrapper for libsndfile) takes float arrays and converts them to the requested subtype: Reading the file back and comparing is the important habit. The sample rate, format and length are as intended, and the error is at most one 24-bit step (2⁻²³ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁷). That's quantisation, not a bug. It's a full step rather than the half step that rounding would give because, in the libsndfile version bundled here (1.2.2), the clipping conversion rounds down: every error lies between 0 and −1 step. At 24 bits that's harmless, but it's exactly the kind of detail a read-back check reveals. Notes: sf.read returns float64 in ±1.0 by default. Pass an integer type, as in sf.read(path, dtype="int16") (or "int32"), to get integers instead. These are scaled to fill the integer type, not the file's raw values: a 16-bit file read as int16 gives its stored samples, but a 24-bit file read as int32 comes back multiplied by 256. Use sf.write(path, x, fs, subtype="FLOAT") to keep a 32-bit float file with headroom above 1.0 for analysis. Use PCM_16 or PCM_24 for files to share or import into a DAW. soundfile switches on libsndfile's clipping option whenever it opens a file, so in testing it clipped 1.7 to full scale when writing PCM rather than wrapping it. Clip explicitly anyway, so your output never depends on a library setting. The fades matter: a file that starts or ends mid-wave clicks, which is easy to mistake for a synth bug. A measurement checklist Before trusting any experiment's audio, check: Check How ------ Length and rate len(x), sf.info Finite values np.isfinite(x).all() Peak level np.max(np.abs(x)), then dBFS RMS and DC np.sqrt(np.mean(x2)), np.mean(x) Full-scale warnings np.sum(np.abs(x) >= 1) Frequency windowed FFT peak Unwanted content FFT, compare with prediction Then listen at a safe level. Measurement tells you what's there; listening tells you whether it matters. Key takeaways Use the library’s subtype to choose PCM or float storage and clip explicitly before PCM output. Short fades prevent start and stop discontinuities. Read each file back to check metadata and sample error; library versions can affect conversion details. Further reading python-soundfile documentation

sum: The main ways synths make sound (subtractive, additive, FM/PM, wavetable, sample-based, physical modelling), the classic subtractive voice, and how monophonic and polyphonic synths allocate voices.
x: A synthesiser is a program (or circuit) that turns control information, such as "play note 60, fairly hard", into a stream of audio samples. Every design answers the same two questions: Where does the raw sound come from? A waveform, a recording, a mathematical model. How is it shaped over time? Filters, envelopes and modulation. The different "kinds" of synthesis are mostly different answers to the first question. Before choosing one for your instrument, it helps to know what each costs and what it is good at. The main approaches Approach Raw material Shaped by --------- Subtractive Bright waves (saw, square) Filters remove harmonics Additive Many sine waves Per-partial levels FM / PM Sines modulating sines Modulation index Wavetable Stored single cycles Scanning through tables Sample-based Recordings Pitch shift, envelopes Physical modelling Model of a vibrating object Model parameters Subtractive Start with a waveform rich in harmonics and remove what you don't want with a filter. A sawtooth through a low-pass filter whose cutoff falls over time gives the classic "pluck" or brass sound. This is the architecture of the Minimoog and most analogue synths, and it is the one you'll build first in this module because each block is simple and audible. Additive Any periodic sound can be described as a sum of sine waves (the next-but-one lesson shows why). Additive synthesis builds the sound directly from those sines, each with its own frequency and level, often with its own envelope. It gives total control, but a low note can need hundreds of sines per voice, and controlling that many parameters musically is hard. FM and PM In frequency modulation one oscillator (the modulator) varies the frequency of another (the carrier) at audio rate. This creates new frequency components, called sidebands, at the carrier frequency plus and minus multiples of the modulator frequency, so two sine oscillators can produce a complex spectrum. The formula below tells you where those sidebands land: For example, a 400 Hz carrier modulated by a 100 Hz modulator gives sidebands at 300 and 500 Hz (k = 1), 200 and 600 Hz (k = 2), and so on, so the result sounds like a 100 Hz harmonic tone. An unrelated ratio such as 400 Hz and 141 Hz gives sidebands that are not multiples of one fundamental, which is where FM's bell and metallic sounds come from. How strong each pair is depends on the modulation index (how hard the modulator pushes); a low index gives only the first pair or two, a high index spreads energy over many. (A sideband that would land below 0 Hz reflects back to a positive frequency.) John Chowning developed FM synthesis at Stanford from 1967 and Yamaha licensed it; the DX7 (1983) made it famous. Yamaha's commercial "FM" (the DX7 included) is actually implemented as phase modulation (adding the modulator to the carrier's phase rather than its frequency). The two are mathematically closely related: phase-modulating with a signal is the same as frequency-modulating with its derivative. A practical advantage of PM is that a modulator with a DC offset only shifts the carrier's phase, whereas in true FM it shifts the carrier's pitch. FM is cheap in CPU but notoriously hard to programme by ear. Wavetable Store a set of single-cycle waveforms (a wavetable) and play one back with a phase accumulator, optionally sweeping or crossfading through the set to make the timbre evolve. Wolfgang Palm of PPG developed his multi-wavetable version in the late 1970s (Hal Chamberlin had described table-lookup wavetables in 1977, and Michael McNabb developed a similar idea independently); Waldorf instruments continue Palm's approach. Each table is cheap to play, but high notes alias unless you keep band-limited versions of each table (lesson 4). Sample-based Play back recordings of real sounds, re-pitched by reading them faster or slower, then shape them with envelopes and filters. Realism is excellent; memory use is large, and expressive range is limited to what was recorded. Your Digitakt is a sample-based instrument. Physical modelling Simulate the physics of a string, tube or membrane. The classic small example is Karplus–Strong: fill a short delay line with noise and feed it back through a gentle low-pass filter. The loop's length sets the pitch, and the filter makes high harmonics die first, like a plucked string. One trip round the loop is one period of the note, so the length you need is: So a 220 Hz string at 48 kHz needs a loop of about 218 samples, and a note an octave up (440 Hz) needs about 109. Julius O. Smith's Physical Audio Signal Processing covers this family in depth. A reasonable first instrument Subtractive is the usual first build because each block (oscillator, filter, amplifier, envelope, LFO) can be built and tested on its own. The project brief suggests a monophonic digital subtractive synth as an option; this module teaches every block it would need without committing you to it. The classic subtractive voice A voice is everything needed to play one note. The textbook subtractive voice looks like this: Oscillator (VCO/DCO): generates a periodic waveform at the note's pitch. Filter (VCF): usually a resonant low-pass; its cutoff sets brightness. Amplifier (VCA): multiplies the signal by a gain, so the note can start and stop. Envelopes: time-varying control signals started by the key (the gate). One drives the amplifier, another typically sweeps the filter cutoff. LFO: a slow oscillator (below about 20 Hz) that wobbles pitch (vibrato), level (tremolo) or cutoff. The "V" names come from analogue gear where each block was voltage controlled. In software the same structure holds: audio flows left to right, and control signals arrive from below. Notice there are two kinds of signal. Audio signals run at the sample rate and you hear them. Control signals (envelopes, LFOs, knob positions, MIDI) change more slowly and steer the audio blocks. Keeping these separate is central to real-time design, as later lessons show. Monophonic and polyphonic A monophonic synth has one voice: it plays one note at a time. A polyphonic synth has several voices and can play chords. Paraphonic designs sit between: several oscillators at different pitches share one filter and amplifier. Monophonic: note priority When you hold two keys on a mono synth, which one sounds? That rule is note priority: Last-note priority: the most recently pressed key wins. Releasing it falls back to a key still held. Low-note or high-note priority: the lowest or highest held key wins. Last-note priority needs a stack of held notes, otherwise releasing the newest note while an older one is held leaves silence or a stuck note: When note_off returns a note, the voice glides or jumps back to it; None means start the release. Polyphonic: voice allocation A poly synth has a fixed pool of voices (say 4 or 8). The voice allocator decides which voice plays each new note: If a voice is free, use it. If all are busy, steal one. Common choices: the oldest note, the quietest voice, or a voice already in its release phase. This sketch marks a voice free as soon as its key is released, so a voice still sounding its release tail can be reused abruptly. Real voice allocators track the envelope state, prefer voices that have finished, and fade a stolen voice out over a few milliseconds to avoid a click (lesson 5). Stuck notes Every note-on must eventually be matched by a note-off for the same note, or a voice sounds forever. Handle the MIDI convention that a note-on with velocity 0 means note-off, and give yourself an "all notes off" escape. The project brief lists "no stuck notes" as a success criterion. Cost and choice Polyphony multiplies everything: 8 voices means 8 oscillators, 8 filters and 16 envelopes per sample. On a microcontroller this decides your CPU budget. A mono synth is the smallest complete instrument, and a well-structured monophonic voice becomes one voice of a poly synth later. Key takeaways Synthesis methods differ mainly in where the raw sound comes from: filtered rich waves, summed sines, modulated sines, stored cycles, recordings or physical models. The subtractive voice is oscillator → filter → amplifier, steered by envelopes and LFOs. Audio signals run at the sample rate; control signals steer them more slowly. Mono synths need a note-priority rule and a held-note stack; poly synths need a voice allocator and a stealing policy. Polyphony multiplies CPU cost per voice. Further reading Subtractive synthesis — Wikipedia Frequency modulation synthesis — Wikipedia Wavetable synthesis — Wikipedia Karplus–Strong string synthesis — Wikipedia Physical Audio Signal Processing — Julius O. Smith, CCRMA Polyphony and monophony in instruments — Wikipedia

sum: How a digital oscillator keeps track of phase across audio blocks, turns frequency into a phase increment, shapes sine, saw, square, triangle and pulse waves, wraps phase correctly and avoids precision drift.
x: An oscillator's job sounds trivial: output a repeating waveform at a chosen frequency. The interesting part is state. Audio arrives in blocks (say 32 or 48 samples at a time), the frequency may change between or within blocks, and the oscillator must continue exactly where it left off. Get the state wrong and you hear clicks, buzzes and detuning. Nearly every digital oscillator is built on one idea: the phase accumulator. Phase as a fraction of a cycle Represent phase as a number in [0, 1): how far through the current cycle you are. 0 is the start of a cycle, 0.5 is halfway, and 1.0 wraps back to 0. Each sample, advance the phase by the phase increment: the fraction of a cycle that passes during one sample. In one second the oscillator must complete as many cycles as its frequency, while the system produces as many samples as the sample rate, so each sample covers the frequency divided by the sample rate of a cycle: With an increment of 0.0091667, it takes about 109 samples (48,000 / 440) for the phase to go round once, so the output repeats 440 times per second. Double the frequency and the increment doubles, so each cycle takes half as many samples. A waveform is then just a function of phase. Written as maths, with the phase p running from 0 up to 1: For example, a quarter of the way through the cycle (p = 0.25) the sine is at its peak of +1, the saw is at −0.5 and the triangle is at 0. The square and pulse waves are simpler still: +1 while the phase is below a threshold (0.5 for a square, the chosen width for a pulse), otherwise −1. In code: Separating "where am I in the cycle?" from "what value is there?" is what makes the design flexible: the same accumulator drives a sine, a wavetable lookup or an LFO. Pulse width A pulse wave is high for a fraction width of each cycle. At 0.5 it is a square wave. Narrower widths sound thinner and more nasal; pulse-width modulation (sweeping the width with an LFO) gives a chorus-like movement. Avoid widths of exactly 0 or 1: the wave becomes a constant (DC) and goes silent. State carried across blocks Here is a minimal oscillator that processes a block at a time. The phase lives in the object, not in the function: Output: You can check the printed phase by hand. After n samples the phase has advanced n increments: The last sample of block A and the first of block B are consecutive points on the same sine. The block-boundary bug If phase were a local variable reset to 0 in each process call, every block would restart the waveform. At a 64-sample block size that is a discontinuity 750 times a second (48,000 / 64), heard as a buzz at 750 Hz on top of the tone. The roadmap's first oscillator exercise exists to make you get this right. Frequency control Musical pitch is exponential: each octave doubles the frequency. MIDI note numbers convert to hertz with the twelve-tone equal temperament formula (from module 1): So note 60 (middle C) is 261.63 Hz, and note 81 (an octave above note 69) is 880 Hz. Pitch modulation, pitch bend and detune are added in semitones or cents before this conversion, then the increment is recomputed. Because the increment is just the frequency divided by the sample rate, it can change every sample without any glitch: the phase simply advances faster or slower from wherever it is. Wrapping the phase correctly When the phase passes 1.0, subtract 1. Don't reset it to 0. Setting it to 0 discards the fraction that overshot, so each cycle becomes a whole number of samples long. That quietly detunes the oscillator: You can predict this error without running anything. With reset-to-zero, each cycle lasts the ideal number of samples rounded up to a whole number: So resetting makes every 1100 Hz cycle exactly 44 samples, giving 1090.9 Hz: about 14 cents flat, an audible error. The error is worst for high notes, where one extra sample is a large part of a short cycle. Subtracting 1 keeps the fraction, so cycle lengths vary between 43 and 44 samples and average out to exactly the right pitch. Two more wrapping cases matter: Increment of 1 or more (a very high frequency or extreme modulation): a single subtraction is not enough. Use p = p - floor(p). Negative increments (through-zero FM, reversed playback): the phase can go below 0, so wrap upwards too. p - floor(p) handles both directions. Beware that some languages' remainder operators (such as C's fmod) return negative results for negative inputs. Here is why p - floor(p) works in both directions: Integer phase accumulators Hardware and many embedded libraries use an unsigned 32-bit integer for phase, where the full range 0 to 2³² − 1 represents one cycle. Integer overflow then is the wrap, for free and with no drift: For 1000 Hz at 48 kHz the increment is 1000 × 4,294,967,296 / 48,000 ≈ 89,478,485 counts per sample. In C, using the shift operator >> to keep the top bits: The frequency resolution is the frequency that one count of increment represents: This is the numerically controlled oscillator at the heart of direct digital synthesis (DDS) chips, and the PJRC Teensy Audio Library's waveform object uses a uint32_t phase accumulator in the same way (source checked 2026-10-04). Floating-point precision drift Single-precision float has a 24-bit significand, about 7 significant decimal digits. That matters in two ways. Wrapped phase in float is fine. Running a float32 accumulator at 440 Hz for a simulated minute gave 439.99972 Hz on average, an error of about 0.001 cents. The phase stays below 1, where floats are precise. Unwrapped phase in float is a bug. If you never wrap, or compute each sample directly from a growing sample counter like this: then the number grows, and floats get coarser as they grow. The increment gets rounded to the coarse spacing: Time running Effective pitch ------ 1 s 439.5 Hz 10 s 445.3 Hz 60 s 468.8 Hz 300 s 375.0 Hz The note goes audibly out of tune within seconds and wildly wrong after a few minutes. The reason is the gap between neighbouring float32 values, which doubles every time the number doubles. After 60 s at about 440 Hz the unwrapped phase is roughly 60 × 440 = 26,400 cycles: That matches the measured 468.8 Hz. As the phase keeps growing the gap keeps doubling, which is why the error gets worse (it does not always err upwards: after 300 s the simulated phase is about 118,000 cycles, where the gap between neighbouring float32 values has grown to about 0.0078 cycles, so the increment of 0.0092 rounds down to a single gap, 0.0078 × 48,000 = 375 Hz). A drone or a held pad would expose this on stage. Always keep phase wrapped to one cycle (or use the integer form). From oscillator to instrument A practical oscillator also needs: Band-limiting for saw, square and pulse, or high notes alias badly (lesson 4). Smoothed or per-sample frequency so pitch changes don't step audibly (lesson 5). A reset policy: resetting phase on each note-on gives a consistent attack; free-running sounds more like analogue oscillators. Both are valid choices. Libraries such as DaisySP (Oscillator) and the Teensy Audio Library (AudioSynthWaveform) provide band-limited waveforms and a way to set or reset phase. Neither smooths frequency changes for you (both simply recompute the increment when you set a new frequency, as checked in their source on 2026-10-04), so smoothing remains your job. The roadmap suggests writing your own sine oscillator first, then comparing with a library's. Key takeaways Store phase as a fraction of a cycle and advance it by the frequency divided by the sample rate each sample. Phase is state: keep it in the oscillator object so blocks join seamlessly. Wrap by subtracting 1 (or p - floor(p)), never by resetting to 0, which detunes. Waveforms are functions of phase; pulse width sets the high fraction of the cycle. Unbounded float phase loses precision and drifts badly; wrapped float or 32-bit integer accumulators are stable. Further reading Numerically controlled oscillator — Wikipedia Direct digital synthesis — Wikipedia Single-precision floating-point format — Wikipedia DaisySP Oscillator header (GitHub) Teensy Audio Library — PJRC Pulse wave — Wikipedia

sum: Why a sawtooth sounds different from a square or triangle at the same pitch, the 1/n and 1/n² harmonic patterns that define them, and how to check them yourself with numpy's FFT.
x: Play a sine, a triangle, a square and a sawtooth at the same pitch and loudness. Each sounds clearly different: the sine pure, the triangle soft, the square hollow, the saw buzzy and bright. Pitch and loudness are equal, so the difference is timbre, and for steady periodic tones timbre is largely set by the spectrum: which frequencies are present, and how strong each one is. This lesson gives you the spectra of the standard waveforms and a way to verify them. Every later block (band-limiting, filters) is easier to reason about in these terms. Fourier series: any periodic wave is a sum of sines A waveform that repeats at a fixed interval (its period) has a fundamental frequency of one divided by that period, and it can be written as a sum of sine waves at whole-number multiples of that frequency: For example, a wave repeating every 10 ms (T = 0.01 s) has f_0 = 100 Hz, so its components can only be at 100, 200, 300 Hz and so on. DC is the mean value (zero for the centred waveforms here). n = 1 is the fundamental; perceived pitch need not equal the strongest component. n = 2, 3, 4... are the harmonics (or overtones) at 2, 3, 4... times f_0. A_n is each harmonic's amplitude, and φ_n its phase. This is the Fourier series. Intuitively: a sine is the only waveform with a single frequency, so anything more complicated must be several sines added together. The sharper the features of a waveform (corners, jumps), the more high harmonics it needs to build them. The magnitudes A_n plotted against frequency form the magnitude spectrum: a row of spikes at multiples of f0, each with a height. The standard waveforms Wave Harmonics present Amplitude of n --------- Sine 1 only — Saw all (1, 2, 3...) 1/n Square odd (1, 3, 5...) 1/n Triangle odd (1, 3, 5...) 1/n² For waves swinging between −1 and +1, the standard series are: The factors in front (2/π ≈ 0.637, 4/π ≈ 1.273 and 8/π^2 ≈ 0.811) are the amplitudes of each wave's fundamental. The alternating signs are phases; they shape the waveform but not the magnitude spectrum. The sign of the saw series depends on whether it ramps up or down; this one ramps up. To compare harmonics by ear it helps to convert their relative amplitudes into decibels: What this means for the sound: Saw has every harmonic, falling at 6 dB per octave of harmonic number (each doubling of the harmonic number halves the amplitude). This is the brightest standard wave and the usual starting point for subtractive brass, strings and basses. Square has only odd harmonics at the same 1/n rate. Missing even harmonics give its hollow, woody, clarinet-like character. Triangle also has only odd harmonics, but they fall at 1/n², i.e. 12 dB per octave. The 3rd harmonic is 1/9 of the fundamental (−19 dB), so it sounds close to a sine. Pulse waves A pulse wave's harmonics depend on its width (the fraction of each cycle it spends high): Wherever n × w is a whole number, sin(π × n × w) is zero and that harmonic vanishes. At w = 0.5 all even harmonics vanish (a square). At w = 0.25 every 4th harmonic vanishes: for n = 4, n × w = 1. This is why sweeping pulse width changes the timbre so audibly. Check it with numpy The roadmap asks you to compare spectra with an existing analysis tool rather than writing an FFT. numpy's rfft computes the discrete Fourier transform of a real signal. The FFT reports the signal's content in a row of evenly spaced frequency slots called bins. Their spacing, and which bin holds a given frequency, follow from the sample rate and the number of samples analysed: A useful trick follows: analyse exactly one second at an integer frequency. Then the FFT bins are exactly 1 Hz apart and every harmonic lands exactly on a bin, so there is no spectral leakage (energy smearing into neighbouring bins) to worry about. Half a second (24,000 samples) would give 2 Hz bins, so 300 Hz would be in bin 150. Output (harmonics 1 to 7, relative to the fundamental): (Spacing tidied to fit; values unchanged.) The 1/n, odd-only and 1/n² patterns appear exactly. The absolute fundamental amplitudes come out as 0.6366, 1.2732 and 0.8106, matching the leading factors of the three series above. Note the scaling: rfft returns sums, not amplitudes, so the code multiplies by 2 / N: So one second of a 0.5-amplitude sine gives a raw magnitude of 12,000, and 2 × 12,000 / 48,000 brings it back to 0.5. For non-integer frequencies or real recordings, apply a window (e.g. np.hanning) before the FFT and expect peaks to spread across neighbouring bins. Phase changes shape, not (much) timbre Two waves can have identical magnitude spectra but different shapes. Build a 39-harmonic saw-like tone twice: once with all harmonics in sine phase, once all in cosine phase. Same harmonic amplitudes, but the cosine-phase version has a peak 2.3 times higher, because all its harmonics reach their crests together at the start of each cycle.
