Successful timely refreshes hide expiry for hot keys; slow or failed refreshes can still lead to a miss. Keys nobody reads near expiry are left to expire, so cold data is not refreshed for nothing. If the predictions are poor, you pay for reloads that nobody uses. Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite is an example. The later early-refresh unit shows a probabilistic version that reduces stampede risk. Key takeaways The refresh factor sets the entry age at which a read starts background work. Earlier refreshes provide more time to finish but can perform work nobody uses. Only timely successful refreshes hide expiry; cold keys and failed refreshes can still miss. Further reading Refresh — Caffeine documentation Caching best practices — AWS

sum: Implement constant-time LRU operations and explain why one-off scans pollute a recency-based cache.
x: A cache is smaller than the data behind it, so eventually it fills up. When a new item arrives and there is no room, the cache must choose an eviction victim to throw out. The rule it uses is the eviction policy (or replacement policy). The goal is to evict the item least likely to be needed again soon. Nobody knows the future, so every policy is a guess based on the past. The best guess depends on the access pattern. Eviction (removing items because memory is full) is different from expiry (removing items because their time is up). Most caches do both. FIFO: first in, first out Evict the item that was inserted earliest, regardless of how often it has been used. Trivial to implement: a queue. Ignores popularity. A key read 10,000 times a second is evicted just as readily as one read once. Variants such as CLOCK and SIEVE build on cheap queues and reference bits without maintaining exact recency order. LRU: least recently used Evict the item that has gone longest without being accessed. The bet is temporal locality: what was used recently will be used again. The classic implementation combines a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. Both get and put have expected/amortized O(1) cost with ordinary hash-table assumptions. O(1), read "order one" or constant time, means the work per operation does not grow with n, the number of keys in the cache: a cache of a million keys does a get as cheaply as a cache of ten. This is an executable cache class; it prints nothing by itself. The later questions trace the keys it retains. Where LRU breaks: scans LRU has a famous weakness. A one-off scan (a batch job reading a million keys once) pushes every key to the front, flushing the genuinely hot items out. After the scan, the cache is full of data nobody will ask for again. This is called cache pollution. LRU and a scan Capacity 3, contents [A, B, C] with A and B read constantly. A report reads X, Y, Z once each. LRU now holds [X, Y, Z], and the next reads of A and B both miss. Defences include segmented LRU (new items must prove themselves before entering the protected segment), LRU-K, 2Q and ARC, all of which consider more than one access. Key takeaways FIFO evicts the oldest insertion; LRU evicts the least recent access and assumes temporal locality. A hash map plus a doubly linked list gives expected or amortised constant-time LRU operations. A scan can replace useful hot keys with one-off reads; policies that consider reuse can protect the hot set. Further reading OrderedDict — Python documentation Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia Adaptive replacement cache — Wikipedia

t: Separate frequency eviction from TTL expiry
sum: Compare LFU popularity with TTL freshness, including decaying counts and active expiry.
x: Eviction makes room under memory pressure; expiry stops reuse after a lifetime. Frequency-based eviction needs to adapt when yesterday’s popular item stops being useful. LFU: least frequently used Evict the item with the fewest accesses. This protects consistently popular keys from scans, since a key read once never outranks a key read a thousand times. LFU has its own problems: Stale popularity. A key that was hugely popular last week keeps a high count and squats in the cache. Real LFU implementations decay counts over time. New items struggle. A brand-new key starts at count 1 and is the first candidate for eviction, even if it is about to become hot. Cost. Exact LFU needs a counter per key and a structure ordered by count. O(1) designs exist, but they are fiddlier than LRU. TTL: time to live A TTL says how long an entry may be served before it is considered expired, regardless of memory pressure. It is a freshness rule, not a capacity rule, but it frees memory too. Short TTLs limit residence of an individual copy, at the cost of misses; delayed or lagging-source fills can still supply older data. Long TTLs (hours) give high hit ratios but serve stale data longer. Add TTL jitter (randomise each TTL by up to ±10%) so that keys loaded together do not all expire together (see the later avalanche unit). How does Redis actually remove expired keys? Two ways: Lazily: when a client touches an expired key, Redis deletes it and reports a miss. Actively: A background active-expiry cycle samples TTL-bearing keys under a CPU budget. Sampling and timing vary by Redis version, hz/dynamic-hz and active-expire-effort; inspect that version rather than relying on universal batch sizes or thresholds. So an expired key can still occupy memory for a short time after its TTL; it will never be returned, though. Comparison Policy Evicts Good at Weak at ------------ FIFO Oldest insert Simplicity Ignores use LRU Least recent Recency Scans LFU Least frequent Stable hot set Shifting trends TTL Expired Freshness Not capacity-aware To diagnose missing hot keys, compare expired_keys with evicted_keys in Redis INFO stats. Many expiries, few evictions and spare memory point to TTL policy rather than capacity pressure. Key takeaways LFU protects frequently used items but needs decay and a way for new items to become established. TTL limits an entry’s residence, rather than guaranteeing the age of data supplied by a delayed or lagging fill. Redis removes expired entries on access and through a budgeted active-expiry cycle; expiry and capacity pressure need different diagnosis. Further reading EXPIRE — Redis documentation Key eviction — Redis docs

sum: Explain sampled eviction, memory overhead and the scope of allkeys and volatile policies.
x: Exact recency tracking consumes memory and updates metadata on reads. Redis approximates eviction and lets you select which keys may be victims when its accounted memory exceeds the limit. What real systems do Exact LRU needs a linked list with two pointers per key and list updates on hits; shared concurrent implementations also need synchronisation. The pointers alone cost: At millions of keys and millions of reads per second, systems use approximations. Redis: sampled LRU and LFU Redis does not keep a linked list. Each key stores a 24-bit field in its object header. In LRU mode it holds a coarse last-access clock. In LFU mode it holds an 8-bit frequency counter plus a 16-bit timestamp of the last decay. When memory exceeds maxmemory, Redis: Samples maxmemory-samples random keys (default 5). Adds the best candidates to a small eviction pool (16 entries) kept across rounds. Evicts the best candidate in the pool. Redis's documented comparison found five samples close to true LRU and ten closer, at extra CPU cost. Accuracy still depends on the access pattern; measure your workload. Redis eviction policies, set via maxmemory-policy: Policy Candidates Rule --------- noeviction none Reject writes allkeys-lru all keys Approx. LRU allkeys-lfu all keys Approx. LFU volatile-lru keys with TTL Approx. LRU volatile-lfu keys with TTL Approx. LFU volatile-ttl keys with TTL Soonest expiry -random all / TTL Random Redis 8.6 added allkeys-lrm and volatile-lrm (least recently modified), which only update the timestamp on writes, so keys that are read a lot but never updated can still be evicted. The default is noeviction Out of the box, Redis does not evict. When its accounted memory is above the limit, memory-growing commands can fail with OOM while existing-key reads continue; maxmemory is not a strict RSS ceiling. For a pure cache you almost always want allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu. The volatile- policies evict nothing if no keys have a TTL. Choosing a policy Start with LRU (allkeys-lru). It is a good default for most web workloads. Switch to LFU if scans or one-off reads are polluting the cache, or if there is a stable set of popular keys. Always set TTLs on data that can go stale, independent of the eviction policy. Measure: watch evicted_keys and the hit ratio in Redis INFO stats. Many evictions with a falling hit ratio can indicate insufficient working-set capacity or a poor eviction policy. Key takeaways Redis samples candidates and retains an eviction pool instead of maintaining an exact recency list. The default noeviction policy rejects memory-growing commands; reads continue and maxmemory is not a strict RSS ceiling. Allkeys policies consider all keys; volatile policies need TTL-bearing keys. Separate persistent and disposable workloads when practical. Further reading Key eviction — Redis docs Redis 8.6 features — Redis documentation

t: Calculate Redis LFU increments and decay
sum: Use Redis’s sampled logarithmic counters to estimate popularity without interpreting them as exact hit counts.
x: Redis’s LFU mode keeps an 8-bit counter and a 16-bit decay timestamp in the 24-bit access field introduced in the preceding unit. It samples eviction candidates rather than ordering every key by exact frequency. The LFU mode (since Redis 4.0) uses a probabilistic logarithmic counter in 8 bits. Each access increments it with a probability that falls as the counter grows, so 255 can represent around a million hits (tuned by lfu-log-factor, default 10). Elapsed decay is applied lazily when an object is accessed or considered for eviction (one per lfu-decay-time minute by default), rather than actively decrementing every idle key. New keys start at 5 rather than 0, giving them a chance to establish popularity; they can still be evicted immediately. To get a feel for the log counter, the Redis config file gives these figures for the default factor of 10: Hits Counter ------ 100 ~10 1,000 ~18 100,000 ~142 1,000,000 255 The rule behind these figures comes from the Redis source. Below saturation, each access increments the counter only with this probability: For example, with the default factor of 10: So the counter climbs quickly at first and then ever more slowly, which is how 8 bits (0 to 255) can stand for about a million hits. It is a rough popularity score, not an exact count. A counter of 255 stays at 255. Decay works the other way. For a positive decay-time setting, Redis computes a lower score for elapsed idle periods when considering a key. Ordinary accesses store the decayed-and-incremented score and a new timestamp; eviction sampling computes the score without updating that stored timestamp: For example, a key with counter 200 left idle for 3 hours (180 minutes) decays to 200 − 180 = 20. Setting lfu-decay-time to 0 turns decay off and is outside the division formula. The 16-bit minute clock wraps after about 45.5 days, so the simple idle-time model must not be extrapolated to arbitrarily long gaps. Key takeaways The probability of a counter increment falls as the counter rises, allowing eight bits to summarise many accesses. New keys start at five; the counter saturates at 255 and is an approximate popularity score. Idle time reduces the score when Redis examines it, allowing an old favourite to lose to a currently popular key. Further reading Key eviction — Redis docs Redis eviction implementation (8.6)

t: Protect hot data with segments and admission
sum: Explain Memcached slab pressure and compare segmented LRU with Caffeine’s frequency-based admission.
x: A cache can choose where an item fits and whether it deserves protected capacity at all. Segments and admission decisions help avoid replacing a hot set with a stream of one-off reads. Memcached: segmented LRU per slab class Memcached 1.6.39 defaults to 1 MiB (1,048,576-byte) pages, and assigns each page to a slab class that cuts it into fixed-size chunks (for example 96 B, 120 B, 152 B and so on, each class 1.25× the last by default). The chunk sizes grow geometrically: An item (key, value and a build-dependent header, roughly 50 bytes in this illustrative sizing) goes into the smallest chunk that fits it, so part of each chunk is usually wasted. A smaller growth factor wastes less space per item but needs more classes. Each class has its own LRU, split into HOT, WARM and COLD segments. New items enter HOT and flow down into COLD. Items that are hit again (while in HOT or COLD) move to WARM, where they are relatively protected. Items never hit again pass through COLD and out of the bottom, so a scan mostly churns COLD. A background "LRU crawler" also reclaims expired items. A consequence: eviction is per slab class. If most of your memory was assigned to 1 KB chunks and your values shrink to 100 B, the small class can be evicting heavily while plenty of memory sits in the large class (Memcached has a slab rebalancer to help). Caffeine and W-TinyLFU The Java library Caffeine uses Window TinyLFU. An adaptive LRU window admits new items. The main-cache admission decision compares the candidate’s estimated frequency with the victim’s. In Caffeine 3.2.3 a higher frequency is accepted; warmer candidates can also be accepted with a small random probability to resist hash-collision attacks. Frequencies are kept in a compact Count-Min Sketch (few-bit counters in shared hashed buckets) that is periodically halved. This is an admission policy: it decides not just what to evict but whether a new item is worth caching at all. Its authors report strong hit ratios across their benchmark traces; results depend on workload and implementation. Key takeaways Memcached allocates items into size classes, so one class can be under eviction pressure while another has spare capacity. HOT, WARM and COLD segments give reused items more protection than new or one-off items. Caffeine’s W-TinyLFU compares estimated frequency before admitting a candidate to the main cache. Further reading Memcached modern LRU Memcached wiki TinyLFU: A Highly Efficient Cache Admission Policy Caffeine 3.2.3 admission implementation Memcached 1.6.39 slab implementation Caffeine efficiency (W-TinyLFU)

sum: Follow a CLOCK hand through reference bits and distinguish the textbook algorithm from Linux reclaim.
x: An operating-system page cache also needs victims. CLOCK approximates recency using one reference bit per page, avoiding a list update on every access. Operating systems: CLOCK A traditional Linux reclaim design uses active/inactive LRU lists and referenced-bit information; calling it CLOCK is only an analogy, not its exact implementation. The textbook CLOCK algorithm works as follows. CLOCK arranges pages in a ring with a "referenced" bit. The hand sweeps round: a page with the bit set gets a second chance (bit cleared); a page with the bit clear is evicted. It approximates LRU with no list reordering on each access. Current Linux kernels also offer MGLRU (multi-generational LRU), which sorts pages into several age generations instead of two lists. Whether it is enabled depends on kernel configuration and runtime settings. Key takeaways A referenced page gets a second chance: clear its bit and continue sweeping. The first page encountered with a clear reference bit is evicted. CLOCK is a teaching model; Linux reclaim uses its configured LRU or multi-generational LRU implementation. Further reading Multi-gen LRU — Linux kernel documentation Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia

t: Prefer deletion when concurrent writers race
sum: Trace stale reads and out-of-order cache updates, then explain why delete-on-write is the safer default.
x: There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things. — Phil Karlton A cache holds a copy. The moment the original changes, the copy is wrong. Cache invalidation is how you bring the copy back in line, and it is hard because the cache and the database are two separate systems with no shared transaction. Any sequence of operations across them can be interleaved with other requests, or fail halfway. These invalidation units concern the cache-aside world (app, Redis, database), which is where most of these bugs live. The options for keeping a cache fresh Expire it (TTL). Bound the lifetime of a cached copy after insertion. Data can be older than one TTL if a delayed read or lagging replica refills the cache. Delete it on write. The writer removes the key; the next read reloads. Update it on write. The writer sets the new value in the cache. Let the database tell you. Stream the database's change log and invalidate from that. Nearly every production design is TTL plus one of the others. TTL limits the residence of one copy; repeated stale refills can extend the age of data served. Stale reads are the normal case Even a perfect design has a short window where the cache is stale: Between t1 and t3 readers see the old value. The window depends on request timing, failures and invalidation delivery; whether it is tolerable is a product requirement. The real problems are races that leave stale data in the cache for a whole freshly started TTL, or longer if later refills are also stale. Race 1: update-on-write with concurrent writers Two requests update the same user at almost the same time, and each writes the DB then sets the cache. The database says Bea, the cache says Ann, and it stays wrong until the TTL. Network delays make A's cache write arrive after B's even though A's database write came first. This is why deleting is preferred over updating. Deletes are idempotent and commutative: two deletes in either order leave the same result (an empty key), and the next reader loads the true value. Delete vs update: summary Delete on write Update on write --------- Concurrent writers Deletes commute Can leave old value Next read Miss Hit Expensive values Recompute on read Recompute on write Hot keys Herd risk on miss No miss Delete is the safe default. Update (with versioning) is worth it for hot keys where a miss would cause a stampede. Key takeaways Database and cache operations can interleave or fail separately, leaving a stale copy. Two deletes commute; two independent cache updates can finish in the wrong order. Keep a TTL alongside explicit invalidation, while remembering stale refills can carry older source data. Further reading Cache-aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF TwoHardThings — Martin Fowler

sum: Explain the cache-aside reader/writer race and the timing limit of delayed double delete.
x: Deleting after a database commit avoids racing cache updates, but a reader may already have fetched an old row. Its later refill can resurrect that row after the delete. Race 2: the cache-aside read/write race Delete-on-write still has a race, involving a slow reader. R read the old row before W committed, but its SET lands after W's DEL. The cache now holds the old value with a fresh TTL, and nobody will delete it again. This interleaving is possible even without an exceptional pause; its frequency depends on the workload. Pauses and network delays widen the opportunity. Facebook's memcache paper calls a write like R's a stale set: a value put into the cache that no longer reflects the latest data. Mitigations Short TTLs bound how long the bad value survives. Delayed double delete: delete, then delete again after a delay longer than nearly all miss-path reads take (say 500 ms). It narrows the window but is a heuristic, not a guarantee. Leases (covered in the following units) reject fills whose token was revoked by an invalidation, when the cache enforces that protocol. Versioned writes (covered in the following units) make stale sets lose. For the delayed double delete, the second delete only helps if it lands after the slow reader's SET. So the delay has to be longer than the slowest read you want to cover: For example, if 99.9% of miss-path reads finish within 400 ms, a 500 ms delay catches them. A reader stalled for 2 s (a long garbage-collection pause, say) still lands after both deletes, which is why this is only a heuristic. Key takeaways A miss-path reader can load old data, pause, and set it after a writer commits and invalidates. A second delete catches only refills that land before it; a delay based on a percentile remains a heuristic. Leases tied to invalidation and version checks with retained metadata can reject stale refills. Further reading Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Cache-aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center

t: Reject older cache writes with version guards
sum: Use an atomic version comparison, then explain why deletion needs retained metadata or tombstones.
x: An incoming cached value can carry the database revision it represents. Compare that revision atomically so delayed writers cannot replace a newer cached revision. Versioning Store a version with each cached value (a database-ordered row version or other strictly increasing per-record revision). Only allow a cache write if it is newer than what is there: In the earlier concurrent-writer race, suppose B's write carries version 8 and A's late-arriving write carries version 7. When A's arrives, 7 is not greater than 8, so it is rejected. The check has to run atomically inside Redis, which is why it is a Lua script rather than a read followed by a write from the application: The Python assignment defines a Lua script for an application adapter to execute in Redis; it prints nothing by itself. The Lua return values report whether the cache changed. The Lua example assumes non-negative integer versions no greater than 9,007,199,254,740,991 (two to the power 53, minus one: up to this limit a standard 64-bit floating-point number, which is what tonumber returns, holds every whole number exactly; above it, some whole numbers are skipped), so they compare exactly, and retained version metadata. With these assumptions, Race 1 is fixed: A's late write of version 7 is rejected because B already wrote version 8. Versioning alone does not fix Race 2 after a delete, because the key is empty and any version is "newer" than nothing. A tombstone can retain the new version floor, but its comparison metadata must survive until older fills are impossible or rejected by another authority. Expiry/eviction loses that protection. A tombstone-aware script must permit equal-version data to replace that tombstone; the simple strict-greater script shown above does not do so. A different form of versioning is versioned keys: include a version in the key name, such as user:42:v8. The writer bumps the version (stored somewhere cheap); readers build the key from the current version, and old keys simply age out via TTL. Fingerprinted asset URLs are the HTTP version of this. Key takeaways An atomic strictly-newer comparison fixes out-of-order updates when database-ordered revisions and comparison metadata survive. An empty key has no revision floor: expiry, eviction or deletion removes the protection. A tombstone must retain the revision floor and permit equal-version data to replace it; the simple script shown needs that extension. Further reading Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Redis Lua scripting Client-side caching and invalidation — Redis

t: Use invalidation-aware leases for stale fills
sum: Follow a lease token from miss to refill and explain how leases also reduce concurrent database loads.
x: A lease grants permission to fill a missing key, then invalidation can revoke that permission. This closes the stale-set race when the lease protocol is enforced by the cache. Leases (Facebook memcache) Facebook's 2013 paper Scaling Memcache at Facebook introduced leases to fix both stale sets and thundering herds. On a miss, memcached gives the client a lease token for that key. The client reads the database and calls set with the token. If the key was deleted in the meantime, the token is invalidated and the set is rejected. The stale set in Race 2 simply fails. The paper compares this to load-link/store-conditional on a CPU: the write only succeeds if nothing touched the key in between. Leases also tame thundering herds. By default Facebook's servers handed out at most one token per key every 10 seconds. Other clients that missed were told to wait briefly and retry; the token holder usually set the value within a few milliseconds, so the retry tended to hit. Over a week of measurements on keys particularly prone to herds, the paper reports peak database query rates falling from 17K/s (17,000 queries per second) without leases to 1.3K/s with them, roughly a 13-fold cut. A refinement lets readers accept stale values: a deleted item is kept briefly in a side structure, and a miss can return it marked as stale. Applications that can tolerate slightly old data carry on without waiting. Leases were Facebook's own extension, but modern memcached (1.6+) offers similar ideas through its meta commands, which can tell one client it has "won" the right to recache a key while others are served a stale value. Key takeaways A token-bearing refill fails if a delete invalidated the token after the reader’s miss. Limiting tokens per key also reduces the number of concurrent database rebuilds. Eligible stale values can keep readers moving while the winner refreshes; Facebook’s lease extension and modern meta commands are implementation-specific. Further reading Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Meta text protocol — Memcached

t: Invalidate from committed changes and preserve own writes
sum: Compare CDC-driven invalidation with targeted read-your-writes safeguards across clusters and regions.
x: Writers outside the main application can bypass its invalidation code. A change-log pipeline broadens coverage, while users who just wrote may still need a faster, version-aware read path. Change data capture (CDC) Instead of every writer remembering to invalidate, let the database's commit log drive invalidation. Facebook's version works slightly differently. SQL statements that modify data are amended to carry the memcache keys to invalidate. A daemon called mcsqueal on each database reads the committed statements from the commit log, extracts those deletes, and broadcasts them in batches to every frontend cluster in the region (via mcrouter). Because the keys travel with the transaction, lost or misrouted invalidations can simply be replayed from the log. Today you might use Debezium reading the Postgres WAL or MySQL binlog, publishing to Kafka, with a consumer that maps changed rows to keys and deletes them. Benefits: invalidation can cover committed changes from all configured logged tables regardless of client. Preserve relevant per-key order, include every dependent key and account for filters, publication scope, retention and failed delivery; a pipeline does not automatically provide global commit-order consumption. Consumers can retry failed deletes. Costs: added latency that depends on capture, batching, processing and delivery, more infrastructure, and you must map rows to the cache keys that depend on them, which is hard for cached aggregates or joins. Read-your-writes Users notice staleness most when it's their own change. Even if global staleness of a few seconds is fine, the person who just clicked "Save" expects to see it. Options: Version-aware write-through with ordering/failure safeguards, or carry the committed version and require reads to return at least that version. Invalidate synchronously in the writer's own cluster as well as through the slower CDC pipeline. Facebook's web servers did exactly this for read-after-write within a request's cluster. Remember "user 42 wrote at time t" and bypass the cache for that user; a fixed-duration window is a heuristic unless replica lag and stale fills are bounded. A required-version check is stronger. Facebook used remote markers across regions: before a write from a non-primary region, the client sets a marker that redirects subsequent misses to the primary until replication delivers its removal. The paper notes that concurrent updates can remove a marker too early and eviction can lose it, so this reduces stale-read probability rather than guaranteeing read-your-writes. A layered recipe TTLs on disposable cached values (with TTL jitter) + delete after commit + invalidation-aware leases or retained version metadata + CDC for writes that bypass the app. These address different failure modes under their stated assumptions. Key takeaways CDC covers configured committed changes only when capture scope, key mapping, ordering, delivery and retention are correct. Capture and processing introduce lag; invalidate synchronously or require a committed version for a user’s immediate reread. Remote markers redirect misses to the primary while present; concurrent removal and eviction remain consistency risks. Further reading Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF PostgreSQL connector — Debezium

t: Decide whether an HTTP response is still fresh
sum: Interpret Cache-Control storage directives, current age and the requirement to validate stale responses.
x: HTTP has caching built into the protocol. Browsers, corporate proxies, reverse proxies and CDNs all follow the same rules, defined in RFC 9111. If you set the headers correctly, a compliant cache may reuse eligible responses; actual cache enablement and optional feature support depend on the browser/provider. If you set them wrongly, you get stale pages, or worse, one user's private data served to another. There are two separate questions a cache asks: Freshness: may I serve my stored copy without asking the origin? Validation: once it's stale, can I cheaply check whether it's still correct? Freshness: Cache-Control The origin tells caches how to behave with the Cache-Control response header. Directive Meaning ------ max-age=N Fresh for N seconds s-maxage=N Like max-age, shared caches only public Any cache may store it private Only private caches (the browser) no-cache Store, but revalidate every use must-revalidate Once stale, never reuse unvalidated no-store Forbid intentional HTTP-cache storage immutable Won't change while fresh Most directives are defined in RFC 9111; immutable comes from RFC 8246, and the stale- directives from RFC 5861 (covered in the later stale-serving unit). Two common points of confusion: no-cache does not mean "don't cache". It means "you may store it, but you must check with me before each use". Use no-store to prohibit intentional HTTP-cache storage. It is not a guarantee that data never reaches disk, browser history or a compromised cache, nor a complete privacy mechanism. private matters for shared caches. A response containing a user's name or basket must be private (or no-store), otherwise a CDN might hand it to the next visitor. A response's age is the time since the origin generated or last validated it; shared caches pass it on in an Age header. A stored response is fresh while its age is less than its freshness lifetime, which comes from s-maxage (shared caches only), then max-age, then the older Expires header. RFC 9111 states the test like this: For example, a browser that receives max-age=300 from a CDN with Age: 250 may treat it as fresh for only 300 − 250 = 50 more seconds, not 300. A response whose age reaches its lifetime is stale: the cache must revalidate it before reuse, unless a directive such as stale-while-revalidate allows otherwise. Why must-revalidate? HTTP normally lets a cache serve a stale response in some situations, such as when it is disconnected from the origin. must-revalidate forbids that: once stale, the cache must revalidate successfully or return an error (typically 504 Gateway Timeout). Use it when serving stale data would be worse than serving an error. Key takeaways A response is fresh only while its current age is less than its freshness lifetime; time upstream has already consumed part of it. No-cache allows storage but requires validation; no-store prohibits intentional HTTP-cache storage and is not a complete privacy mechanism. Must-revalidate prevents reuse of a stale response without successful validation; private keeps a response out of shared caches. Further reading RFC 9111: HTTP Caching Cache-Control — MDN RFC 8246: HTTP Immutable Responses

t: Set explicit lifetimes for HTML and versioned assets
sum: Avoid heuristic freshness surprises and pair fingerprinted assets with HTML validation.
x: A missing freshness policy does not necessarily make a response uncacheable. Set explicit lifetimes so an unchanged-looking page does not remain silently fresh after you publish a new version. If there is no explicit lifetime, caches may apply a heuristic to responses that are cacheable by default (such as a 200 to a GET). RFC 9111 encourages a lifetime of no more than some fraction of the time since Last-Modified, and says a typical setting of that fraction might be 10%: So a file last changed 10 days ago may be treated as fresh for a day, with no request to the origin. This surprises people, so always set Cache-Control explicitly. Typical policies HTML is set to no-cache so the browser always checks for a new page, which in turn references the latest fingerprinted assets. The number 31536000 is simply one year in seconds: Key takeaways Heuristic freshness is provider-dependent; the RFC’s ten-percent example is guidance, not a universal rule. Fingerprinted asset names allow long fresh lifetimes because a new version has a new URL. HTML with no-cache checks for a new document, which can then reference the latest assets. Further reading RFC 9111: HTTP Caching HTTP caching — MDN RFC 8246: HTTP Immutable Responses

t: Validate a retained response without its body
sum: Trace ETag and Last-Modified conditional requests and keep validators stable across origin servers.
x: Once freshness ends, a retained response can still save bandwidth. A conditional request asks whether its validator still identifies the current representation. Validation: ETag and Last-Modified When a cached response goes stale, the cache doesn't have to download it again. It can send a conditional request asking "has this changed?". ETag / If-None-Match The origin labels each version of a resource with an ETag, an opaque identifier, often a hash of the content. A 304 Not Modified has no body, so it saves bandwidth and the cache updates the stored response headers and recomputes its age and freshness under RFC 9111. A 304 does not unconditionally grant a new fixed lifetime. If the resource has changed, the origin replies 200 with the new body and a new ETag. ETags can be strong ("a1b2c3", byte-for-byte identical) or weak (W/"a1b2c3", semantically equivalent, for example the same article with a different timestamp in the footer). Some servers, including the Nginx 1.26.3 gzip filter, turn a strong ETag into a weak one when they compress a response on the fly, because the bytes are no longer the ones the ETag described. Weak ETags are fine for If-None-Match but not for byte-range requests. Last-Modified / If-Modified-Since The older mechanism uses timestamps: Its weakness is one-second resolution, and it relies on reliable modification times. When both are present, If-None-Match takes precedence. A 304 still costs a round trip Validation saves bytes, not latency. For a 2 KB JSON response the round trip dominates, so a max-age that avoids the request entirely is worth far more than an ETag. ETags and multiple servers If each server generates ETags from local details (Apache once used inode numbers), the same file has different ETags on different servers, and switching servers can cause unnecessary full responses even when the file is unchanged. Generate ETags from the content (a hash) or from a version number in the database. Key takeaways A matching conditional request gets a body-free 304; changed content gets a new body and validator. Validation still pays a network round trip, so freshness and validation save different costs. Use content or database revisions for consistent validators across servers; If-None-Match takes precedence over a modification-time condition. Further reading RFC 9111: HTTP Caching RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

t: Control HTTP variants and shared-cache privacy
sum: Use Vary and s-maxage without fragmenting a public cache or leaking personalised responses.
x: A shared cache may answer many users from one stored response. Its cache key and storage policy must describe when those users are entitled to the same representation. Vary: one URL, several responses A cache keys stored responses by method and URL. But the same URL may return different content depending on request headers, such as compression or language. The Vary header tells caches which request headers must also match. Reuse must match the nominated Accept-Encoding request header, allowing the cache to distinguish encoding variants. Header normalisation and the encodings a client accepts determine which variant is eligible. Use Vary carefully: Vary: Accept-Encoding is common and usually necessary when encoding changes the representation; it still adds variants. Vary: User-Agent is almost always a mistake. There are thousands of distinct user-agent strings, so the cache fragments into thousands of copies and the hit ratio collapses. Vary: Cookie keys variants by the cookie header; user-specific cookies can fragment a shared cache, but identical cookie values can still hit. Often better: strip cookies at the CDN for anonymous pages, or mark personalised responses private. CDNs often normalise headers before using them as a key (for example collapsing Accept-Encoding to br, gzip or none) to stop this fragmentation. Shared caches and purging A CDN or reverse proxy is a shared cache. Use s-maxage to give it a different lifetime from browsers. A common pattern: Browsers always revalidate; the CDN keeps it for 5 minutes. When content changes, you purge the CDN through its API, whereas browser clearing requires a later response such as supported Clear-Site-Data and is not a universal immediate remote purge. Many CDNs support tag-based purging (Surrogate-Key / Cache-Tag headers), so "purge everything tagged product-9" clears every page that shows that product. Caching authenticated responses Shared caches won't store a response to a request with an Authorization header unless the response explicitly allows it with public, s-maxage or must-revalidate. Note that cookies get no such protection: a response to a request carrying a session cookie can be stored by a shared cache unless you mark it private. Adding public to an API that returns per-user data is a classic data leak. Key takeaways Vary includes selected request headers in variant matching; user-agent and cookie values can create many distinct copies. S-maxage gives a shared cache its own lifetime, and provider purge APIs remove shared responses after publication. Cookie-bearing requests have no automatic protection equivalent to Authorization; mark personalised responses private or no-store. Further reading RFC 9111: HTTP Caching Vary — MDN

t: Bound stale serving during refreshes and outages
sum: Calculate stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error windows and check optional provider support.
x: When slightly old content is acceptable, optional HTTP extensions can return it while refreshing or while the origin fails. Their windows begin when the ordinary freshness lifetime ends. stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error Defined in RFC 5861, these let a cache serve stale content in controlled ways. For the first 60 s: fresh, served directly. From 60 s to 360 s: serve the stale copy immediately, and refresh it in the background. If the origin is unreachable or returns 500, 502, 503 or 504: serve the stale copy for up to a day (86,400 s) after it went stale. The window boundaries are sums of the directives: stale-while-revalidate hides origin latency from users: a supporting cache may serve stale within the window and refresh asynchronously. Coalescing can reduce background requests, but the directive does not itself guarantee exactly one refresh. stale-if-error turns your cache into an availability tool: a crashed origin shows slightly old pages rather than an error. Support varies These directives are optional for caches: a cache that doesn't understand them simply ignores them. Browser versions and CDN products differ in which directives and failure cases they support. Use your deployed cache’s documentation and an integration check. Check your provider before relying on either. Key takeaways Add a stale window to the freshness lifetime to calculate the permitted response age. Stale-while-revalidate can hide refresh waits; stale-if-error can preserve availability during eligible origin failures. These extensions depend on cache support and do not themselves guarantee exactly one background refresh. Further reading RFC 5861: stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error Keeping things fresh with stale-while-revalidate — web.dev

sum: Compare Redis, Valkey and Memcached by operations, threading, replication and restart behaviour.
x: One cache server eventually runs out of memory, network bandwidth or CPU. Capacity depends on instance size, payload, commands and workload. A universal per-node capacity figure is absent because no representative benchmark is established here. If one instance cannot meet measured requirements, a cluster can partition the key space. Distributing a cache raises three questions: Partitioning: which node holds which key? Replication: what happens when a node dies? Persistence: does the data survive a restart? Redis vs Memcached Both are in-memory key-value stores whose latency depends on payload, network, commands and load. They make different trade-offs. Memcached Redis --------- Data model Opaque strings Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams Threads Multi-threaded Mostly single-threaded commands Persistence Optional graceful warm restart; not crash-safe durability RDB snapshots, AOF Replication None built in Primary–replica Clustering Client-side Redis Cluster String/item size 1 MiB default item 512 MiB default string limit Memcached is deliberately simple. It is a pure cache: if a node dies, its data is gone and the clients rehash to the remaining nodes. Its multi-threaded design scales well across cores on a single large machine. Facebook ran thousands of Memcached servers. Redis is a data structure server. Atomic operations like INCR, ZADD (leaderboards), LPUSH (queues), Lua scripts, pub/sub and streams make it useful far beyond caching. Command execution is single-threaded per instance (network I/O can be threaded since Redis 6), so you scale out by running more instances or shards, not by adding cores. Valkey In 2024 Redis moved from the BSD licence to source-available licences, and the Linux Foundation forked Redis 7.2 as Valkey, which AWS ElastiCache, Google Cloud Memorystore and others now offer. Redis 8 (2025) added the open-source AGPLv3 as a licence option. The two projects are starting to diverge in features, but shared ancestry does not guarantee identical versioned features, threading, durability or managed-service behaviour. Check the chosen engine and service version. Rule of thumb: choose Memcached for a simple, large, multi-threaded look-aside cache of blobs. Choose Redis when you need data structures, atomic operations, replication or persistence. Key takeaways Measure node limits from your payload, commands and workload before deciding to partition. Memcached serves simple blobs with multiple threads; Redis adds atomic data structures, replication and persistence. Engine features and licences evolve; choose from required operations and deployed versions rather than universal performance figures. Further reading Choosing between Redis/Valkey and Memcached — ElastiCache Redis licences Valkey Warm restart — Memcached

t: Compare modulo routing with consistent hashing
sum: Calculate key movement when adding a node and explain how virtual nodes spread ownership and failures.
x: A partitioning rule maps each key to a cache server. Changes to that rule can turn a routine capacity increase into a sudden wave of misses. Partitioning The naive approach: hash mod N The simplest way to pick a node is to turn the key into a number and take the remainder after dividing by the number of nodes: In code this is hash(key) % N. For example, a key whose hash is 1,000,003 goes to node 1,000,003 mod 4 = 3 in a four-node cluster. This spreads keys evenly, but it falls apart when N changes. Going from 4 to 5 nodes, a key stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder when divided by 4 as when divided by 5. The pair of remainders repeats every 20 numbers (20 is the smallest number divisible by both 4 and 5), and they match only for hashes that leave a remainder of 0, 1, 2 or 3 when divided by 20: 4 cases in 20. In general, growing from N to N + 1 nodes: So about 1 in 5 keys stay, and 80% of keys suddenly live on a different node, all of them missing at once. For a cache, that is a self-inflicted stampede on the database. Consistent hashing Map both nodes and keys onto a ring (for example, a 32-bit hash space with 4,294,967,296 possible positions). A key belongs to the first node clockwise from its position. k1 → N2, k2 → N3, k3 → N1. Add a node N4 between N3 and N1: only the keys between N3 and N4 move. Remove N2: only N2's keys move, to the next node clockwise. When the points are evenly spread, the new node ends up with an equal share of the ring, and that share is all that moves: Going from 4 to 5 nodes moves about 20% of keys, against 80% for hash mod N. Removing a node moves only that node's share, about 1 / N of the keys. The problem with one point per node is uneven arcs: one node may own 40% of the ring. The fix is virtual nodes: each physical node is placed at many ring positions, perhaps 150 in an illustrative design; choose and measure the count for the implementation. Arc sizes average out, and when a node fails its load is spread across many survivors rather than dumped on one neighbour. Memcached clients and proxies can use the ketama consistent hashing algorithm; check the client’s configured distribution policy. Amazon's Dynamo and Cassandra use the same idea for databases. Key takeaways Changing hash-modulo node counts remaps most keys; adjacent counts preserve only a small fraction. Consistent hashing moves the new node’s share when ownership is balanced. Many virtual positions per physical node smooth ring ownership and distribute a failed node’s keys across survivors. Further reading Consistent hashing — Wikipedia Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store

t: Route and migrate Redis Cluster hash slots
sum: Use hash tags for multi-key commands and distinguish permanent MOVED redirects from temporary ASK redirects.
x: Redis Cluster keeps a fixed slot space and assigns slots to primaries. Clients track ownership while keys migrate, rather than changing the key-to-slot formula when nodes are added. Redis Cluster: hash slots Redis Cluster uses a fixed set of 16,384 hash slots: Each primary owns a set of slots. Adding a node means migrating some slots to it, key by key, while the cluster keeps serving. Clients cache the slot map and send each command straight to the right node. If a client uses an out-of-date map, the node replies MOVED <slot> <host:port>: the slot now lives elsewhere permanently, so the client updates its map. While a slot is mid-migration, a key that has already moved gets an ASK redirect: the client retries that one command on the target node (preceded by ASKING) but does not update its map, because the migration hasn't finished. A fixed slot count is what makes this cheap. Moving a node's share means reassigning a few thousand slot numbers, not recomputing a ring for every key. Multi-key operations (MGET, transactions, Lua) only work if all keys are in the same slot. Hash tags force that: only the part inside {} is hashed, so {user:42}:profile and {user:42}:cart share a slot. Hash tags create hot slots Putting too much under one tag ({global}:...) piles all of it on a single node, recreating the bottleneck you sharded to escape. Key takeaways Redis Cluster hashes keys into 16,384 slots; ownership changes by migrating slots and their keys. MOVED updates a client’s ownership map; ASK redirects one command during migration and requires ASKING. Hash tags place related keys together for multi-key operations, but a large tag can concentrate load on one shard. Further reading Redis Cluster specification

t: Plan cache failover without assuming durable writes
sum: Explain asynchronous replication loss and compare replica failover with Facebook’s spare gutter pool.
x: Replication can keep a cache available when a node fails. It does not remove stale-read and lost-write risks, so a cache failover plan still needs freshness and backend-load safeguards. Replication Redis supports a primary with one or more replicas. Replication is asynchronous: the primary acknowledges a write to the client, then streams it to replicas. Failover is handled by Redis Sentinel (for non-clustered setups) or by Redis Cluster itself: if a primary is unreachable for long enough, a replica is promoted. Consequences of asynchronous replication: Acknowledged writes can be lost. If the primary dies after acking but before the replica receives the write, the promoted replica never had it. Replica reads can be stale. Reading from replicas spreads load but may return slightly old values. Split brain: during a network partition, a client still talking to the old primary may write data that is discarded when the partition heals. min-replicas-to-write with min-replicas-max-lag refuses writes when too few connected replicas meet the lag threshold; it still cannot prove receipt of each write. WAIT returns the number of replicas that acknowledged this connection’s preceding writes before the requested count or timeout; check that returned count. Receipt is not necessarily disk persistence. Acknowledgements reduce loss risk but do not make Redis strongly consistent or eliminate acknowledged-write loss during failover. For a pure cache, losing a new insertion causes a miss, but losing an update or invalidation can leave an old value on the promoted replica. Keep freshness safeguards even when cache entries are disposable. Replication's real value for caches is availability, avoiding the "cache gone, database flooded" scenario from lesson 1. Memcached has no replication. Facebook handled failures with a small pool of spare servers called gutter, about 1% of the memcached servers in a cluster. When a client gets no response from a server, it retries against gutter; on a gutter miss it reads the database and stores the result in gutter, where entries expire quickly. Facebook chose this over rehashing a failed server's keys across the survivors, because a single key can account for a large share of one server's traffic (the paper cites up to 20%), and moving it could overload its new home and cascade. The paper reports that gutter cut client-visible failures by 99% and converted 10–25% of failures into hits each day. When a server failed completely, gutter's hit rate typically passed 35% within four minutes. Key takeaways An asynchronous replica can miss an acknowledged write, and reads from it can be stale. WAIT acknowledgements reduce risk only when their returned count is checked; they do not guarantee disk persistence or strong consistency. Facebook’s short-lived gutter pool absorbed failed-server traffic without spreading a hot key into an overload cascade. Further reading Redis replication WAIT — Redis documentation Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF

t: Budget persistence and warm restart memory
sum: Compare RDB and AOF loss windows and estimate copy-on-write memory during a snapshot.
x: A disposable cache can still benefit from saved state: restarting warm avoids refilling every key from the database. Persistence has its own latency, loss-window and memory costs. Persistence Memcached is ordinarily a volatile cache; optional warm restart preserves data over supported graceful restarts, not arbitrary crashes. Redis offers two persistence mechanisms: Mode How Loss on crash --------- RDB Periodic snapshot via fork() Since last snapshot AOF everysec Log every write, fsync 1/s About 1 s AOF always fsync each write Minimal; slow None Memory only Everything RDB snapshots are compact and fast to load, but the fork() uses copy-on-write: under heavy writes, memory usage can nearly double while the snapshot runs. Every memory page the parent changes during the snapshot gets copied, so: This first-order estimate excludes non-dataset allocations, buffers, allocator fragmentation, page-size effects and other process overhead. A 26 GB dataset on a 32 GB machine may fit normally, but with 30% of pages rewritten during the snapshot it needs about 33.8 GB and can be killed for running out of memory. Leave headroom (do not run Redis at 95% of RAM with RDB enabled). AOF (append-only file) logs every write command, and is periodically rewritten to stay compact. Many deployments use both: AOF for durability, RDB for backups and fast restarts. Why would a cache want persistence? Warm restarts. A 200 GB cache that restarts empty can take hours to refill and floods the database while doing so. Loading a saved state can reduce refill pressure, but restart and refill durations require measurement. Key takeaways RDB restores snapshots; AOF logs writes with a durability/latency trade-off selected by its fsync policy. Forked snapshots copy pages changed during the snapshot and can require substantial memory headroom. Copy-on-write arithmetic is a first-order model; measure buffers, fragmentation and restart times for the actual deployment. Further reading Redis persistence Warm restart — Memcached

t: Reduce cache connections with a proxy tier
sum: Choose a cache topology and calculate the per-node connection count before and after adding proxies.
x: A large application fleet can create thousands of connections to every cache node. Proxies hide the fleet topology and concentrate backend connection pools into fewer clients. Topology choices Option Good for ------ Single node + replica Workload fits one node Client-side sharding Memcached fleets Redis Cluster Large, self-managing Proxy (mcrouter, Envoy) Many clients, simple config A proxy layer hides the topology from clients and pools connections, which matters when thousands of app instances would otherwise each open connections to every node. Each node holds one pool per client that connects to it: Facebook's mcrouter is a proxy of this kind for Memcached; it also routes invalidations and can replicate writes to pools of servers. Twemproxy (from Twitter) and Envoy's Redis proxy play the same role, and modern Memcached ships its own built-in proxy. Key takeaways A single node with a replica suits a measured workload that fits one primary; partitioning and proxies address different scaling pressures. Per-node connections are direct clients multiplied by each client’s pool size. A proxy tier simplifies routing and reduces backend connections but introduces another service to operate. Further reading mcrouter — Meta Built-in proxy — Memcached Redis Cluster specification

t: Bound duplicate rebuilds when a hot key expires
sum: Calculate a stampede and use bounded request coalescing with ownership-safe distributed locks.
x: A cache that works well becomes load-bearing. The database is sized for the miss rate, not the full traffic. So when the cache misbehaves, the failure is rarely gentle. The database's load scales with the miss ratio, so a change in hit ratio multiplies its load by: So a 99% hit ratio dropping to 0% means 100× the database load, instantly. The following failure-mode units cover these five ways it goes wrong and what large systems do about each. Failure Trigger ------ Stampede One hot key expires Hot key One key gets huge traffic Penetration Requests for keys that don't exist Avalanche Many keys expire at once, or cache dies Cold start Empty cache after deploy/restart 1. Cache stampede (thundering herd) A popular key, say the homepage feed, gets 5,000 requests a second and takes 200 ms to rebuild. It expires. How many requests pile in before the first rebuild finishes? Every request that arrives during the rebuild misses: About 1,000 requests all run the same expensive query at once. The database slows down, so each rebuild takes longer, so more requests pile up. This feedback loop is what turns a stampede into an outage. Fix A: request coalescing (single flight) Make sure only one request rebuilds a given key; the rest wait for its result. In-process, Go's singleflight or a per-key future/promise does this per server. With one coalescing group per server and no explicit forgetting, 50 servers allow at most 50 simultaneous rebuilds for the key; later calls can start new flights. Across servers, use a short lock in the cache: This is adapter-based pseudocode. publish_if_owner must atomically check the lock token and publish only while ownership is current; release must atomically compare-and-delete. A Redis Cluster implementation must colocate lock and data keys in one hash slot. The atomic lock-token comparison rejects publication after lease expiry on that Redis state. An asynchronously replicated lock can be lost during failover, allowing overlapping owners; this is duplicate-work mitigation, not a fault-tolerant mutual-exclusion proof. It also does not by itself order concurrent database invalidations. The lock TTL stops a crashed rebuilder holding it forever. This illustrative function returns its computed value to the caller even if its publication is rejected after lease expiry; a requirement for the latest value needs an additional version-aware read policy. Two details matter in practice: Release only your own lock. If a rebuild takes longer than 10 s, the lock expires and another caller may take it. A plain DELETE would then remove their lock. Store a random token and release with a small Lua script that deletes the key only if it still holds your token. Bound the retries. Waiters should give up after a limit and serve an acceptable stale value or fail with controlled load shedding; unbounded fallback rebuilds recreate the stampede, rather than spinning forever if the lock holder dies. Facebook's leases (the earlier invalidation units) are the same idea built into the cache. Key takeaways Duplicate rebuilds grow with request rate and rebuild time, creating a feedback loop under overload. Single-flight combines requests per process; an ownership-safe cache lock can coordinate across servers. Publish and release only under current ownership, bound waiting, and avoid falling back to unbounded concurrent rebuilds. Further reading singleflight package — Go Distributed locks — Redis Thundering herd problem — Wikipedia Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF

t: Refresh stale values or expire them probabilistically
sum: Compare soft/hard expiry with XFetch’s random head start and calculate the early-refresh probability.
x: Readers need not all wait for a popular value to be rebuilt. A retained stale value can hide background work, and probabilistic refresh can begin that work before the nominal expiry. Fix B: serve stale while refreshing Store the value with a soft expiry inside it and a longer hard TTL on the key. After the soft expiry, one request refreshes in the background while everyone else keeps getting the slightly stale value. This is stale-while-revalidate applied to your application cache, so readers with a retained eligible stale value can avoid waiting; after hard expiry, eviction or loss they still miss. Fix C: probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) Instead of everyone noticing expiry at the same instant, each request independently decides to refresh a little early, with a probability that rises as expiry approaches. From Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein (VLDB 2015), each request refreshes when: Because −ln(U) follows an exponential distribution with mean 1, the chance that a single request refreshes early, with some time Δ still left before expiry, works out as: So with a 0.5 s rebuild, each request 2 s before expiry has about a 1.8% chance of refreshing. In code (using 1 − random() so the logarithm never sees zero): With 5,000 requests a second, one of them almost certainly refreshes shortly before expiry, making expiry less likely under load; refresh failure or unlucky sampling can still let it expire. Rarely-read keys almost never refresh early, so you don't waste work on them. beta > 1 refreshes earlier; beta < 1 later. The refresh decision needs no lock or coordination, but overlapping refreshes are still possible; it does not guarantee exactly one rebuilder. Key takeaways Soft expiry permits stale reuse during refresh; hard expiry, eviction or cache loss still produces a miss. XFetch increases refresh probability as expiry approaches and as measured rebuild time grows. Probabilistic decisions reduce stampede risk without guaranteeing one refresh or preventing every eventual expiry. Further reading Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention (VLDB 2015) RFC 5861: stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error Cache stampede — Wikipedia

t: Relieve a single overloaded cache key
sum: Estimate local-cache fills and compare copied keys, read replicas and hot-key detection.
x: Adding ordinary shards spreads different keys, but leaves one exceptionally popular key on one owner. To relieve it, distribute reads for that value while meeting its staleness requirement. 2. Hot keys Sometimes a single key gets an enormous share of traffic: a celebrity's profile, a flash-sale product, a live match score. Partitioning doesn't help, because one key lives on one node. If that node handles 100k ops/s and the key gets 300k ops/s, it saturates regardless of cluster size. Fixes: Local (in-process) cache in front of Redis with a 1–5 s TTL. With 100 app servers, with per-server coalescing and no early eviction, Redis sees roughly 100 fills per TTL period for that key, rather than 300,000 a second: Key replication / splitting: store copies as score:match9#0 to score:match9#9 and have readers pick a random suffix. Load spreads over up to 10 nodes; writers update all copies. If the 10 copies really do land on 10 different nodes, each gets about a tenth of the reads: 300,000 reads a second becomes about 30,000 a second per node. Read replicas for the shard holding the hot key. Detect them: Redis has redis-cli --hotkeys (with LFU policy) and per-key monitoring in managed services. You can't fix what you can't see. Hot keys at Twitter-scale As an illustrative workload, suppose a celebrity with 100 million followers posts. Every timeline render that includes the tweet reads the same tweet object. Process-local caches can absorb repeated reads of the object when the allowed staleness fits; this is a design illustration, not a measured description of Twitter’s deployed system. Key takeaways One hot key can saturate one shard even when the rest of the cluster is idle. Per-process caches reduce Redis fills to roughly one per server per TTL when coalescing and retention assumptions hold. Copied keys or read replicas can spread reads, but copies need coordinated updates and suitable freshness guarantees. Further reading Redis anti-patterns Redis CLI hot-key detection

t: Cache missing records without hiding new records
sum: Use short-lived negative entries for repeated misses and invalidate them when a missing record is created.
x: A normal cache stores successful lookups. Repeated requests for absent records still reach the database unless the absence itself is represented in the cache. 3. Cache penetration Requests for keys that don't exist in the database are never cached (there is nothing to cache), so every one goes straight to the database. This can be accidental (a bug requesting user:undefined) or an attack: someone requests product:<random> 50,000 times a second. Fix A: negative caching Cache the absence: This adapter-based Python fragment illustrates storing a miss marker; it requires a database, cache and marker definition and has no console output. Use a short TTL, because the item may be created soon. Negative caching works well for repeated misses on the same keys. It does not stop an attacker using fresh random keys every time, since each is a new miss, and it fills the cache with markers. When the record is created, invalidate its negative entry as part of the write path. Otherwise readers can continue seeing the cached absence until that entry expires. A delayed negative fill can still race with creation and deletion; strict immediate visibility needs the same leases or retained version safeguards as positive values. Key takeaways Negative caching answers repeated lookups for the same absent key without returning to the database. Use a short TTL and invalidate a negative entry when creating that record so new users are not hidden. Fresh random keys defeat reuse of negative entries; validation, rate limits and set-membership filtering address different parts of penetration. Further reading Cache-aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center Negative cache — Wikipedia

t: Size and maintain a Bloom filter for valid keys
sum: Calculate memory from a false-positive target and preserve complete coverage before rejecting absent IDs.
x: A stream of random invalid IDs has no repeated key for a negative cache to absorb. A compact membership filter can reject most of them before the cache or database lookup. Fix B: Bloom filter A Bloom filter is a compact bit array that answers "is this key possibly in the set?" with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate. Put every valid id into it; check it before touching the cache or database. Sizing comes from the standard Bloom filter analysis. With the best number of hash functions, the bits needed per stored id depend only on the false-positive rate you accept: So 9.6 bits per element for a 1% false-positive rate, and the whole filter is: A random invalid id is rejected 99% of the time without any database work. The formula assumes a well-chosen number of hash functions (about 7 for 1%) and that every valid id has been added. Caveats: standard Bloom filters can't delete entries (use a counting filter or Cuckoo filter, or rebuild periodically), and new ids must be included before they become visible, or a negative result must fall back to the source while coverage is uncertain. A stale filter can otherwise reject a valid new id. Also: validate input (reject malformed ids at the edge) and rate-limit clients that generate many misses. Key takeaways A correctly populated Bloom filter rejects definite absence and permits some false positives. About 9.6 bits per valid ID gives an approximate one-percent false-positive rate with an appropriate hash count. Keep new IDs covered before relying on negative results; ordinary Bloom filters need a variant or rebuild strategy for deletion. Further reading Bloom filter — Wikipedia Network applications of Bloom filters: a survey

t: Spread mass expiry and protect the database
sum: Use TTL jitter for synchronised misses and layer capacity limits when the whole cache tier fails.
x: An avalanche affects many keys at once. Jitter addresses synchronised expiry; a cache outage also needs enough remaining capacity, controlled misses or degraded responses. 4. Cache avalanche An avalanche is a mass miss: many keys at once, rather than one hot key. Cause 1: synchronised expiry. A job warms 1 million keys at 09:00 with ex=3600. At 10:00 they all expire together. Fix: TTL jitter. This Python fragment requires random and base_ttl from its caller. It produces a random TTL and has no console output: With a one-hour base TTL the TTL jitter is up to 360 s, so the expiries spread over six minutes. A 10% spread over an hour turns one cliff into a gentle slope. One million keys expiring over 360 s is about 1,000,000 / 360 ≈ 2,800 expiries a second instead of a million at once, and only keys that are read again cause a reload. Cause 2: the cache tier fails. A Redis cluster goes down, or a network partition cuts it off. All traffic falls to the database. Fixes: High availability: replicas and automatic failover, spread across availability zones. Circuit breakers and load shedding: when the database is struggling, fail fast or serve degraded responses rather than queueing every request. Rate-limit misses: cap concurrent database rebuilds per key or per service. Multi-level caching: an in-process cache can carry the hottest keys for a while. A gutter pool (the earlier replication and gutter unit): Facebook sent traffic for failed memcached servers to a small pool of spare servers with short TTLs, so a few failed nodes did not become a database flood. Key takeaways Random TTL jitter spreads a batch’s expiry times; only keys requested again cause reloads. Replica availability, local caches and spare cache pools can absorb part of a tier failure. Compute residual database traffic and shed or cap misses when it exceeds sustainable capacity. Further reading Using load shedding to avoid overload — AWS Builders’ Library Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Key eviction — Redis docs

t: Bring a cold cache online within backend capacity
sum: Calculate a safe traffic ramp and compare pre-warming, peer fills, persistence and shadow traffic.
x: An empty cache behaves like a failed cache until useful keys are filled. Treat a restart, new region or key-format migration as a backend-load event and choose the traffic share from measured misses. 5. Cold starts and warming A new cache cluster, a restart without persistence, or a new region all start empty. With a database sized for a 1% miss rate, sending full production traffic to a cold cache is a self-inflicted avalanche. Warming strategies: Gradual traffic shift: route 1%, then 5%, 25%, 100% of traffic to the new cache over minutes, so it fills while the database copes. Pre-warm from data: load the most-requested keys, say the top 100,000 (from access logs or the old cluster's --hotkeys) before taking traffic. Warm from a peer: Facebook's cold cluster warm-up let a new cluster's clients read misses from a warm cluster's cache instead of the database, bringing cold clusters to full capacity in a few hours instead of a few days. To avoid copying a value that had just been invalidated, deletes in the cold cluster carried a two-second hold-off that made later adds fail; a failed add told the client to read the database instead. The paper records that an invalidation delayed beyond the two-second hold-off can still cause inconsistency; this timing safeguard was an operational trade-off, not a consistency guarantee. Persistence: Redis RDB/AOF restores a node warm after restart. Shadow traffic: mirror reads to the new cache before it serves users. How big can each traffic step be? At each step, the new cache sends the database its share of the traffic times its current miss ratio (traffic not yet moved is still served as before): If spare database capacity is 2% of full traffic, the new cluster alone uses that allowance at 5% traffic and a 60% hit ratio. Include the old cluster’s misses, warming work and other queries when comparing total load with capacity. In practice, leave headroom rather than stepping exactly at capacity. Deploys can flush caches Changing the cache key format (say, adding a field to the serialised object and bumping v2 to v3 in every key) makes every existing entry unreachable. That is a full flush on deploy. Roll it out gradually or run both versions side by side. Putting it together Each layer defends against a different failure. You won't need all of them for every service, but you should know which one you are relying on. Key takeaways Ramp traffic as the hit ratio rises, accounting for both the new cluster’s misses and traffic still served elsewhere. Pre-warming, peer fills, saved state and mirrored reads can reduce cold-start load, with correctness safeguards for copied values. A key-prefix change makes old entries unreachable; stage the transition or serve both key versions. Further reading Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Redis persistence Cache warming — AWS

sum: Use typed tables and ordinary constraints to reject invalid rows, and choose exact representations for money.
x: Relational databases are a common choice for transactional data: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, or a cloud variant such as Amazon Aurora. Before reaching for anything more exotic, you need to know what the relational model gives you for free. The relational model A relational database stores data in database tables (relations). Each table has a fixed set of typed database columns, and each database row is one record. A primary key uniquely identifies each row (users.id). A foreign key is one or more columns referring to an eligible unique or primary key, possibly in the same table (orders.user_id → users.id). The database can enforce that the referenced row exists. Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK) push data rules into the database so that every application that writes to it obeys them. The schema is the set of table definitions. Relational databases are schema-on-write: data that doesn't fit the schema is rejected when you write it. Document stores often permit flexible document shapes, but many also enforce declared validation rules; readers must handle permitted historical shapes. Store money as integers total_p stores pence. Floating-point types can't represent 0.10 exactly, so sums drift. Use integer minor units or numeric. What ordinary constraints can express A foreign key alone permits NULL, so add NOT NULL when every order must name a user. A CHECK can test the row being written, such as a nonnegative total; PostgreSQL does not support a CHECK that continuously validates other table rows. A rule such as "invoice total equals the sum of its lines" needs a suitable redesign or another enforcement mechanism. Key takeaways A primary key identifies a row; foreign keys and NOT NULL work together to require a valid reference. UNIQUE and CHECK enforce declared rules, with limits on what a row constraint can express. Store currency in integer minor units or exact numeric values. Further reading PostgreSQL: Constraints

sum: Read a query plan, choose a join shape, and avoid LEFT JOIN filtering errors and N+1 round trips.
x: SQL separates the result you ask for from the access path that produces it. Use that separation to fetch related data in one deliberate query rather than many network trips. SQL is declarative You describe what you want; the query planner decides how to get it: which index to use, which join algorithm, which order to join tables in. This is a big deal. The same query can go from a full scan to an index lookup after you add an index, with no application change. The SQL fragments assume the tables and suitable rows already exist; results depend on those rows. The query above returns at most ten users, ranked by paid spend in pence. Run EXPLAIN in front of a query to see the plan the database chose, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to also run it and report how long each step actually took. Because ANALYZE really executes the statement, wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in a transaction you roll back. Joins A join combines rows from two tables on a condition. Join Returns ------ INNER Only rows matching on both sides LEFT All left rows, NULLs if no match FULL All rows from both sides CROSS Every combination (rarely wanted) Under the hood the planner picks one of three algorithms: Nested loop: for each outer row, look up matches in the inner table. Great when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index. Hash join: build a hash table on the smaller input, then stream the larger one past it. Good for large, unsorted inputs with equality conditions. Merge join: sort both sides on the join key (or read them in index order) and walk them together. A WHERE clause can undo a LEFT JOIN users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE o.status = 'paid' silently drops users with no orders: their o.status is NULL, and the WHERE filters NULL out. To keep them, put the condition in the join: ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid'. The N+1 query problem An ORM loop that loads 100 orders and then runs one query per order to fetch its user makes 101 round trips. At 1 ms each that is 101 ms of round-trip latency before execution. A join can make one trip; fetching orders then users in bulk usually makes two. The name comes from the count: one query for the list, plus one more for each of the N rows in it. Because every query waits for a full network round trip, the time grows with the length of the list even when each query is fast: For the 100 orders above at 1 ms per round trip: A join replaces the N extra queries with none, so Q falls to 1. The formula assumes the queries run one after another; an ORM that batches or runs them in parallel changes the count, which is why you should check what your ORM actually sends. Key takeaways The planner chooses indexes and join algorithms from the query and data. Move a right-side filter into ON when a LEFT JOIN must retain unmatched left rows. N+1 loading makes one list query plus one query per row; joins or batching reduce round trips. Further reading PostgreSQL: Joins Between Tables PostgreSQL: Using EXPLAIN

sum: Trace a two-account transfer and separate database guarantees from application invariants and external effects.
x: A transfer changes two balances but represents one business event. Transactions let the database commit those row changes together; the application must still define which business rules make the transfer valid. ACID A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit. ACID describes what the database promises about it. Atomicity: all of the transaction's writes happen, or none do. If the server crashes halfway through, the partial work is rolled back. "Abortability" would be a better name. ACID consistency: the transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, according to your invariants (constraints, foreign keys). This is mostly the application's responsibility; the database only enforces the constraints you declared. Transaction isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. How strong this is depends on the isolation level, which is a whole lesson later in this module. Durability: with a durable commit configuration and functioning storage, an acknowledged commit survives the failures covered by that configuration. In practice this means it has been flushed to a write-ahead log on disk (and possibly to replicas). The SQL assumes an accounts(id, balance) table with both rows present and a business decision that permits the transfer. Neither UPDATE by itself proves those prerequisites. If the process dies after the first UPDATE, atomicity guarantees that the debit is undone. No money vanishes. The C in ACID isn't the C in CAP ACID consistency means "invariants hold". CAP consistency means linearizability across replicas. Same word, unrelated ideas. Consistency models get their own module.
