Replica counting directly commits only current-term entries; earlier entries commit with a later current-term entry. Further reading The Raft consensus algorithm (visualisations, implementations) In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper)

t: Raft majority size and commit latency
sum: Calculate failure tolerance and choose the follower acknowledgement that sets commit latency.
x: Raft commits a current-term log entry after durable replication to a majority. That requirement determines both the failures the cluster tolerates and the network acknowledgements on its critical path. Cluster size A majority is more than half the nodes, and the cluster keeps working as long as a majority is alive: Because M + M is always more than N, any two majorities share at least one node. That shared node is what carries committed entries from one leader to the next. Nodes Majority Tolerates --------- 3 2 1 failure 4 3 1 failure 5 3 2 failures 7 4 3 failures Even sizes add cost without extra tolerance. Each write needs a majority; more replicas add work, but commit latency depends on placement and acknowledgement speeds, not node count alone. Three or five nodes are the usual production choices; balanced placement over three availability zones survives one zone loss when no zone holds more than the tolerated number of failures. Commit latency is set by the majority's slowest member, not the cluster's. The leader counts itself, so in a five-node cluster it waits for the second-fastest follower acknowledgement (including its fsync). With a fast leader and two fast followers, even two slow followers can be bypassed; three slow followers force the leader to wait for at least one slow acknowledgement. Worked example: a five-node cluster needs a majority of 3, so its leader needs 2 follower acknowledgements. Its leader is in London and its followers are 1 ms, 15 ms, 15 ms and 75 ms away. Sorted, the second-fastest follower is 15 ms away, so commits take about 15 ms. The 75 ms follower never slows a commit while the others are healthy. If both 15 ms followers fail, the second-fastest becomes the 75 ms one and commits slow to about 75 ms. Key takeaways A Raft group makes progress with a reachable majority; adding an even-numbered node gives no additional crash tolerance. The leader counts itself, so a five-node group needs acknowledgements from two followers. Ignoring disks, commit latency follows the slowest member of the fastest available majority, not the slowest node. Further reading The Raft consensus algorithm (visualisations, implementations) In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper)

t: Raft partitions, reads and rejoining nodes
sum: Handle stale minority leaders, confirm read authority and prevent disruptive term inflation.
x: A network partition can leave an old leader running while a majority elects a new one. The write quorum preserves log safety, but read authority and recovery behaviour still need explicit protocols. Partitions in Raft The old leader n1 can still accept client writes but can't commit them (no majority). n3–n5 time out, elect a new leader in term 4 and continue. When the partition heals, n1 sees term 4, steps down, and any conflicting uncommitted suffix is overwritten. An entry that matches the new leader's log may remain. Reads need care too. A leader that was partitioned may not know it's been deposed, so serving reads from local state can return stale data. Raft offers ReadIndex (confirm leadership with a heartbeat round before reading) or leader leases (rely on bounded clock drift). etcd uses ReadIndex for linearizable reads. Disruptive rejoiners: Pre-Vote and CheckQuorum Partitions cause a second, nastier problem. An isolated follower keeps timing out and incrementing its term: 5, 6, 7... 40. When it reconnects, its high term forces the healthy leader to step down, and the cluster holds a needless election (which the rejoiner can't even win, since its log is behind). Two common extensions fix this, and etcd implements both: Pre-Vote: before incrementing its term, a candidate asks "would you vote for me?". Peers say no if the candidate's log is behind or (in etcd, with CheckQuorum on) if they've heard from a live leader recently. Only a candidate that could actually win goes on to increment its term, so an isolated node never inflates it. CheckQuorum: a leader that hasn't heard from a majority within an election timeout steps down by itself, so a stale minority leader doesn't keep accepting writes indefinitely. Membership changes and snapshots Adding or removing nodes is done one at a time (or via joint consensus) so that old and new majorities can't both decide independently. Logs are compacted into snapshots; a far-behind follower receives InstallSnapshot instead of every entry. A safe read protocol also needs a committed entry from the leader’s current term and a state machine applied through the required commit index. A quorum heartbeat then confirms the leader has not been superseded; the current-term commit establishes the committed prefix for that term. Key takeaways A minority leader can accept proposals but cannot commit them; it steps down after learning the majority’s higher term. Local leader state alone does not prove authority for a linearizable read; use a safe ReadIndex or bounded lease protocol. Pre-Vote reduces rejoin disruption, CheckQuorum makes isolated leaders step down, and membership changes preserve quorum overlap. Further reading The Raft consensus algorithm (visualisations, implementations) In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper) etcd API guarantees etcd's Raft library (Pre-Vote, CheckQuorum, ReadIndex)

sum: Follow Paxos value preservation and compare the coordination primitives offered by etcd and ZooKeeper.
x: Raft is one way to package consensus into a replicated log. Paxos preserves chosen values through numbered proposals, and coordination services expose these protocols through safer application primitives. Paxos at a high level Lamport's Paxos (1989, published 1998) predates Raft and is the basis of Chubby, Spanner and many others. Single-decree Paxos agrees on one value in two phases: The key rule: if any acceptor reports a previously accepted value, the proposer must propose that value (the highest-numbered one) rather than its own. That's how a chosen value survives. Multi-Paxos elects a stable leader that skips phase 1 for subsequent slots, which looks a lot like Raft. The differences are mostly in what's specified: Raft prescribes how logs, leaders and membership work; Paxos leaves much of that to implementers, which is why it's known as hard to get right. Raft Multi-Paxos --------- Leader Required, strong Optimisation Log gaps Not allowed Allowed Spec Complete system Core protocol etcd and ZooKeeper etcd is a Raft-based key-value store, used as Kubernetes' brain. It offers linearizable reads and writes, watches, leases (keys that expire unless refreshed) and transactions (compare-and-swap). Every key has a revision number that only increases, useful as a fencing token. ZooKeeper uses Zab, a Paxos-like atomic broadcast protocol. It offers a hierarchical namespace of znodes, ephemeral znodes (deleted when the client session dies) and sequential znodes (with an auto-incrementing suffix). Writes are linearizable; reads can be stale. A preceding sync improves freshness but does not strictly guarantee it under every failure, because sync is not a quorum operation. Classic recipes: leader election (lowest sequential ephemeral node wins), locks and group membership. In the election recipe, each waiting worker watches its next-lower predecessor and rechecks the ordering when that znode disappears. Watching a predecessor avoids waking every waiting worker on each change. Kafka used it for metadata until replacing it with its own Raft-based KRaft; Kafka 4.0 (2025) removed ZooKeeper support entirely. Don't build it yourself Consensus is notoriously easy to get subtly wrong. Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul for coordination, or a library like etcd's raft package, rather than writing your own. Key takeaways Paxos prepare discovers previously accepted proposals; the proposer preserves the highest-numbered reported value. A stable Multi-Paxos leader can reuse its preparation for later slots. etcd packages Raft with revisions and leases; ZooKeeper packages Zab with ephemeral and sequential znodes, while reads can be stale. Further reading Paxos Made Simple (Lamport) etcd API guarantees ZooKeeper leader election and lock recipes ZooKeeper overview etcd's Raft library (Pre-Vote, CheckQuorum, ReadIndex)

t: Lease expiry and the paused holder
sum: Time a lease conservatively while recognising why client-side checks cannot ensure exclusive action.
x: Many systems need exactly one actor doing something at a time: one scheduler running cron jobs, one primary database, one worker processing a given file. On a single machine you'd take a mutex. Across machines, it's much harder, because the holder can crash, pause or be cut off while holding it. Locks are really leases A distributed lock that never expires is useless: if the holder crashes, nobody can ever take it. Lease-based services use an expiry or session timeout to recover ownership automatically after failure; some systems instead require explicit recovery of persistent locks. A lock with a timeout is a lease: "you own this for the next 10 seconds, renew it if you want to keep it." The holder renews well before expiry (often at a third of the lease). If it crashes, renewals stop and the lease expires, letting someone else take over. Why use a lease for leader election? Leader election is a lock on the role "leader". Kubernetes controllers use a Lease object (in the coordination.k8s.io API, stored in etcd behind the API server); HDFS and HBase use ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes; AWS describes the same pattern with DynamoDB conditional writes in its Builders' Library. Choosing the lease duration is a trade-off: Lease Pro Con --------- Short (2 s) Fast failover False expiry on GC/network blips Long (60 s) Few false failovers Long outage if holder dies The fundamental problem: the holder doesn't know it lost A lease expiry is decided by the lock service's clock. The holder only believes it holds the lease, based on its own sense of time. Process pauses break that belief: Checking "do I still hold the lease?" right before writing doesn't help: the pause can happen between the check and the write. Network delays do the same: A's write can sit in a TCP buffer and arrive after B's. You can't fix this on the client Any client-side check is a check-then-act race. The only safe place to reject a stale holder is the resource being protected. Holder-side hygiene still matters Client checks can't make a lease safe, but they make trouble rarer, and getting them wrong makes it common: Start the clock before you ask. Record the monotonic time just before sending the acquire request, and count the lease from then. The service starts its countdown when it grants, which is later, so the holder's view expires first. Use the monotonic clock, never the time-of-day clock, so an NTP step can't extend the lease. Leave a margin for clock rate drift. Two machines don't need synchronised clocks for leases, but clock-rate error must stay within the protocol's assumed bound. Stop acting a little before your local expiry. Put together, the holder works out its own deadline like this: Worked example: the request takes 300 ms to arrive, so the service grants at 0.3 s and its lease runs to 10.3 s. The reply takes another 300 ms. Counting from the reply would let the holder act until 10.6 s, after the service has already given the lease away. Counting from the send, with the margin, the holder stops at 9.5 s, safely first. This assumes the two clocks run at nearly the same rate; it does nothing about a pause that strikes between checking the deadline and acting. Key takeaways A lease expires unless renewed, trading failover speed against false expiry during pauses and delays. A holder can pause between checking its lease and acting, so a client check cannot make the resource safe. Count from before acquisition on a monotonic clock and leave a drift margin; that hygiene does not eliminate check-then-act races. Further reading How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann) Leader election in distributed systems (AWS Builders' Library) ZooKeeper recipes: locks and leader election Leases (Kubernetes docs)

t: Fencing stale holders at the resource
sum: Reject old lock epochs with monotonically increasing tokens and a consistent resource-side check.
x: A lease holder cannot reliably prove it is still current after a pause. Fencing moves that decision to the resource, which can compare the holder’s epoch with epochs already accepted. Fencing tokens The fix, described in the Chubby paper and popularised by Martin Kleppmann: every time the lock service grants the lock, it also returns a fencing token, a number that strictly increases with each grant. The client sends the token with every request to the protected resource. The resource remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any request with a lower one. The resource's rule fits on one line: Once the resource has accepted a higher token, it rejects lower-token writes. Acquisition alone does not notify the resource: register the new epoch before reading or acting on state when the protocol requires that boundary. Where tokens come from System Natural fencing token ------ etcd Lock key's create_revision or mod_revision ZooKeeper Lock-node creation zxid Raft/Paxos Term/ballot for leader epochs Database A version column updated with each grant ZooKeeper sequence numbers and parent cversion counters are only ordered within the same surviving parent and before integer wraparound. Recreating the parent or wrapping the counter can reuse or decrease a token; use the lock node's creation zxid, or a durable namespace epoch, when those risks apply. Durable token history must also survive service restore: recreating or restoring a token namespace must not restart it below epochs the resource already accepted. A Raft term orders leader epochs, but several application-lock grants in one term need a separate committed grant counter or log index. Raft's term is itself a fencing token for leaders: followers reject AppendEntries from a leader with a lower term. That's why stale Raft leaders can't corrupt the log. The catch The resource has to cooperate. A database can do it with a conditional update: This SQL fragment assumes a jobs table with id, owner and token columns, a non-null stored token and no trigger that suppresses matching updates. It changes no row when that row has already accepted a higher token. The <= lets the current holder write repeatedly with the same token, while any lower (stale) token matches no rows. Check the affected row count: zero means no row matched. If the job exists and its token is non-null, a higher stored token means you've been fenced off. The check must also happen in one consistent place. If the "resource" is three asynchronously replicated copies that each track their own highest token, a stale write can still succeed on a copy that hasn't yet seen the newer token. A single leader or a linearizable conditional write does the job; independent replicas don't. An arbitrary payment or email API may not accept your fencing token. Some storage APIs offer conditional writes, which must be integrated into the resource protocol. For those, you need idempotency (so a duplicate is harmless) or you must accept the risk. Key takeaways Each lock grant gets a strictly increasing fencing token, attached to every protected operation. The resource rejects tokens below the highest one it has accepted; acquisition alone does not notify it of a new epoch. Token checks need one consistent authority, and external APIs without fencing support need another protection such as idempotency. Further reading UPDATE and affected-row results (PostgreSQL) How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann) Leader election in distributed systems (AWS Builders' Library) ZooKeeper recipes: locks and leader election

sum: Choose an efficiency or correctness lock and avoid deleting a successor’s lease.
x: The required lock strength depends on the consequence of two actors working at once. Even when duplication only wastes CPU, a stale actor must not erase its successor’s lock. Efficiency locks versus correctness locks Kleppmann distinguishes two purposes: Efficiency: avoid doing the same work twice (e.g. two workers both regenerating a report). An occasional double run wastes money but is harmless. Correctness: two holders would corrupt data, double-charge or lose updates. For efficiency, a simple single-node Redis lock (SET key token NX PX 10000) is perfectly fine. For correctness, you need a consensus-backed lock service and fencing at the resource. Even an efficiency lock needs a careful release. A plain DEL key is wrong: if your lease expired during a pause and someone else acquired the lock, you'd delete their lock. Release only if the value is still your random token, atomically, with a small Lua script: The lock key is KEYS[1]; this worker’s random ownership token is ARGV[1]. Execute the fragment as one Redis Lua script, so no other command can replace the key between the check and deletion. A return of 1 means this script deleted the key; 0 means it did not. Partitioning work by key, as Kafka consumer groups do, can reduce the need for per-key distributed locks. Keep each account’s ledger operations ordered, and enforce sequencing or fencing at external storage so a stale consumer cannot reorder writes during a rebalance. Idempotency suppresses repeated operations but does not order different operations. Key takeaways An efficiency lock avoids duplicated work; a correctness lock protects an invariant that concurrent holders would break. Release only when the stored random ownership token still matches, checking and deleting atomically. Partitioning work by key can reduce distributed locking, but external writes still need ordering or fencing through rebalances. Further reading How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann) Distributed locks with Redis (Redis docs)

t: Redlock validity and the fencing debate
sum: Calculate Redlock’s remaining validity and assess its timing assumptions for correctness-sensitive work.
x: Redlock extends an expiring Redis lock across independent servers. Its validity calculation is useful to understand, but the preceding distinction between ownership tokens and fencing tokens remains central. Redlock and why it's controversial Redlock is an algorithm proposed by Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), Redis's creator, for a lock that survives a Redis node failing. It uses N independent Redis masters (typically 5), with no replication between them: Read the current time (call it T1). Try SET resource token NX PX ttl on all 5 instances, with a short per-node timeout. Here ttl is the lock's time to live: how long each instance keeps the key before deleting it. Read the time again (T2). The lock is held only if a majority of instances (at least 3 of 5) succeeded and acquiring took less than the ttl. The client may use the lock only for the remaining validity time, worked out below. On failure, release on all instances. The safety of this calculation rests on clocks: if an instance's clock runs fast or jumps, its copy of the key expires earlier than V assumes. That is the heart of the critique below. Kleppmann's critique (2016) No fencing tokens. Redlock returns a random value, not a monotonically increasing number, so a resource can't tell an old holder from a new one. Process pauses still cause two holders, as in the diagram above. It depends on timing assumptions. Safety relies on bounded network delay, bounded pauses and clocks that don't jump. If a Redis node's clock jumps forward (NTP step, admin change), its key expires early: A node crashing and restarting without persisted keys (or with fsync every second) has the same effect. His conclusion: Redlock is too heavy for efficiency locks (one Redis is fine) and not safe enough for correctness locks (use ZooKeeper or etcd with fencing). Antirez's response Antirez argued that: the random token can be used for compare-and-set at the resource in some cases; Redlock's step 3 detects long delays during acquisition; clock jumps can be avoided operationally by slewing rather than stepping, so the timing assumptions are reasonable; every lock with auto-release has the GC pause problem, including ZooKeeper's. The last point is true, and it's exactly why fencing tokens are the real answer: they make safety independent of timing. Redlock's problem is that it doesn't produce one. Practical guidance For efficiency only, a single Redis SET NX PX is fine. For correctness, use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul, plus fencing tokens at the resource, plus idempotency where the resource can't check tokens. Or partition work by key, as Kafka consumer groups do, and enforce sequencing or fencing at external storage so a stale consumer cannot reorder writes during a rebalance. Key takeaways Redlock requires a majority of independent Redis instances and subtracts acquisition time and drift allowance from the TTL. Clock jumps, restarts and pauses can undermine the timing assumptions; a random ownership token does not order grants. The debate distinguishes acquisition checks from resource fencing: stale work must be rejected where it acts. Further reading How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann) Is Redlock safe? (antirez's reply) Distributed locks with Redis (Redis docs)

sum: Identify the participant and coordinator promises that make a distributed commit atomic.
x: A transaction on one database is atomic: all of its writes happen or none do. Once a business operation spans several databases or services (charge a card, reserve stock, book a courier), you need a way to keep them consistent. There are two broad answers: atomic commit protocols that make many participants behave like one transaction, and sagas that give up atomicity in favour of compensation. The atomic commit problem Every participant must reach the same decision, commit or abort, and commit is only allowed if every participant voted yes. That differs from consensus, where a majority suffices: here a single "no" (constraint violation, out of stock) must abort everything. Two-phase commit (2PC) 2PC uses a coordinator (often the application's transaction manager) and participants (databases, queues). Phase 1: prepare The coordinator asks each participant "can you commit?". A participant that says yes must first persist enough transaction state or redo information and a prepare record to complete after recovery, and hold its locks. From then on it has given up the right to abort: it must commit if told to, even after a crash and restart. Phase 2: commit or abort If every participant voted yes, the coordinator writes COMMIT to its own log (this is the commit point) and tells everyone. If any voted no or timed out, it writes ABORT. The coordinator retries the phase 2 message until every participant acknowledges, forever if necessary. There are two points of no return: the participant's yes vote and the coordinator's decision log record. Recovery: presumed abort What if the coordinator crashes and, on restart, finds no decision record for a transaction? Then it never reached the commit point, so no participant can have been told to commit. It is safe to abort, and the coordinator does so. This convention, presumed abort, means the coordinator only needs to force-write COMMIT records; aborts can be logged lazily or not at all. Participants that crash recover the same way from their own log: no prepare record means they never voted yes and can abort; a prepare record with no outcome means they are in doubt and must ask the coordinator. Key takeaways Atomic commit requires every participant’s yes vote; a majority vote cannot override a business-level no. A participant prepares durably before voting yes and then loses the right to abort independently. The coordinator’s durable decision is the commit point; recovery without a decision uses the presumed-abort convention. Further reading Two-phase commit protocol (Wikipedia) PREPARE TRANSACTION (PostgreSQL docs)

sum: Diagnose in-doubt transactions and understand which failures consensus replication and 3PC can address.
x: The preceding unit established what a prepared participant has promised. If the coordinator disappears before that participant learns the decision, preserving the promise can prevent all progress. The blocking problem Suppose a participant has voted yes and the coordinator then crashes before sending the decision. P1 can't commit (maybe P2 voted no). It can't abort (maybe the coordinator logged COMMIT and P2 already committed). Asking P2 doesn't help if P2 is also in doubt. Both must wait for the coordinator to recover, holding row locks the whole time. Other transactions touching those rows block too. This is why 2PC is called a blocking protocol: a single coordinator failure can stall participants indefinitely. In practice, operators sometimes resolve in-doubt transactions by hand (Postgres COMMIT PREPARED / ROLLBACK PREPARED), which risks inconsistency if they guess differently from the coordinator. Postgres disables prepared transactions by default (max_prepared_transactions = 0) partly because forgotten ones hold locks and block vacuum. Other costs At least two round trips and several forced disk writes (fsync) per transaction. Locks held across a network round trip, which hurts throughput under contention. The slowest participant sets the latency. XA (the cross-vendor 2PC standard) acts as a lowest common denominator; failure handling across heterogeneous systems is notoriously fragile. 2PC on top of consensus Spanner and CockroachDB still use 2PC across shards, but each participant and the coordinator are Raft or Paxos groups, not single machines. A coordinator "crash" just means its group elects a new leader, which reads the decision from the replicated log. This permits recovery from an individual coordinator failure while its group retains a quorum; losing that quorum or an essential participant can still block progress. CockroachDB's parallel commits go further, overlapping the two phases so that a typical distributed transaction commits after a single round of consensus writes. Three-phase commit (3PC) 3PC (Skeen, 1981) inserts a pre-commit phase so that no participant is ever uncertain while another might have committed: After coordinator failure, survivors run a termination protocol that exchanges their states and coordinates a common outcome. A participant that voted yes must not simply abort on its own because its local preCommit message has not arrived; another survivor may already be prepared. The catch: this reasoning assumes a synchronous network with bounded delay and perfect failure detection. Under a partition, a recovery coordinator may be unable to exchange states with all required participants. Treating local timeout alone as authority to commit or abort can produce conflicting decisions; the termination protocol's synchrony and failure assumptions are essential. Because real networks are partially synchronous, 3PC is rarely used. The practical answer is 2PC with a replicated, consensus-backed coordinator. Key takeaways Prepared participants retain locks while an unknown decision prevents safe commit or abort. Replicating coordinators and participants reduces blocking after individual node failures while reachable quorums remain. Three-phase commit needs its termination protocol and strong timing assumptions; local timeout decisions are unsafe under partitions. Further reading Two-phase commit protocol (Wikipedia) Three-phase commit protocol (Wikipedia) PREPARE TRANSACTION (PostgreSQL docs) Parallel commits in CockroachDB (Cockroach Labs)

t: Saga steps, compensation and late work
sum: Order compensatable and irreversible steps, and prevent delayed forward work from undoing cancellation.
x: Long service workflows often cannot hold database locks until the whole business operation finishes. Sagas trade global atomicity for local commits and explicit compensation. Sagas Microservices usually can't (or shouldn't) hold locks across services for the duration of a business process. A saga (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) breaks a long transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each committed immediately in its own service. If a later step fails, previously completed steps are undone by compensating transactions. Compensating actions A compensation is a semantic undo, not a rollback. A refund is not the same as never having charged: the customer may see two lines on their statement. Some actions can't be compensated at all (an email sent, a parcel shipped), so order steps carefully: Compensatable steps first (create order in PENDING, reserve stock). The pivot step: the point of no return (charge the card). Retriable steps after the pivot, which must eventually succeed (send confirmation email, notify warehouse). Compensations must themselves be idempotent and retried until they succeed; if a refund call times out, you retry it. Timeouts make it harder A step that times out has an unknown outcome, exactly as in the earlier timeout unit. If the orchestrator gives up on "charge card" and starts compensating, the charge might still happen later: the request could be sitting in a queue. So: A compensation must be safe to run even if the forward step never happened (refunding an unknown charge is a no-op). The service should record the compensation, so a forward request that arrives after it is rejected rather than applied. Use a shared saga or step identifier for correlation, with distinct idempotency keys for the forward action and compensation; a durable step state machine must reject late forward work after cancellation. Where possible, ask the service for the step's status (by idempotency key) before deciding to compensate. Key takeaways A saga commits local steps and later compensates completed work after failure; semantic undo is visible to users. Put compensatable work before the pivot, then steps that can be retried to eventual success. A timeout leaves an unknown outcome; cancellation needs durable correlated state and distinct idempotency keys to reject late forward work. Further reading Sagas (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) Saga pattern (microservices.io) Saga distributed transactions (Azure Architecture Center) Compensating Transaction pattern (Azure)

t: Saga control, isolation and the outbox
sum: Choose a durable workflow style and publish events reliably without pretending intermediate state is isolated.
x: The preceding unit explained saga compensation and the danger of late requests. A real saga also needs durable control, a plan for intermediate state and reliable event publication. Orchestration versus choreography Orchestration Choreography --------- Control Central orchestrator Services react to events Visibility Saga state in one place Spread across services Coupling Orchestrator knows all Services know events Best for Complex, many steps Short, simple flows Orchestration: an orchestrator (a state machine, often built on Temporal, AWS Step Functions or Camunda) tells each service what to do and handles failures. The orchestrator's own state must be durable, so a crash mid-saga resumes where it left off; durable-execution engines like Temporal exist largely to provide that. Choreography: each service publishes events and others subscribe. OrderCreated triggers Payments; PaymentFailed triggers Inventory to release stock and Orders to cancel. There's no central coordinator, but the flow is implicit and harder to trace or change, and cyclic dependencies creep in. Isolation: the saga's weakness Sagas preserve local transaction guarantees but do not provide global ACID atomicity or isolation; compensation is a later business action, not an invisible rollback. Other transactions see intermediate states: a product shows "reserved" stock for an order that's about to be cancelled, or a balance briefly includes a charge that will be refunded. Anomalies include lost updates and dirty reads across steps. Countermeasures: Semantic locks: mark records as PENDING so others treat them carefully. Commutative updates: design steps so order doesn't matter (increment/decrement). Re-reading values before acting, or versioning records. Reliable messaging Every step needs "update my database and publish an event" atomically, otherwise a crash between them stalls the saga. The standard fix is the transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction, and have a relay (or CDC tool like Debezium) publish it. Consumers must deduplicate, because delivery is at least once. Choosing Situation Use ------ Shards of one database 2PC over consensus groups Few systems, short, need atomicity 2PC/XA (carefully) Microservices, long-running flow Saga Can redesign boundaries Avoid it: one service owns the data Key takeaways Orchestration centralises durable saga state; choreography spreads control across event reactions. Sagas expose intermediate state, so semantic locks, commutative updates and version checks help manage anomalies. The transactional outbox commits data and event intent together; its relay may repeat delivery, so consumers deduplicate. Further reading Sagas (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) Saga pattern (microservices.io) Saga distributed transactions (Azure Architecture Center) Compensating Transaction pattern (Azure)

sum: Detect concurrent versions and understand when timestamp resolution loses useful updates.
x: Systems that accept writes on several replicas at once (multi-leader, leaderless, offline-first apps, multi-region active-active) will see concurrent writes to the same data. They must merge them so that every replica ends up with the same value. The following units cover conflict resolution, then how clusters learn about each other through gossip. Detecting conflicts: version vectors Before you resolve a conflict you need to know one exists. A version vector (a vector clock keyed by replica rather than by client) records, for each replica, how many updates from it this version has seen. Compare {A:1, B:1} with {A:2}: each is ahead in one entry, so they're concurrent. A store like Riak keeps both as siblings and returns both to the next reader, who merges them and writes back with a vector that dominates both, {A:2, B:1} plus an increment of the coordinating replica’s own entry. If one vector dominates (at least as large in every entry), the dominated version is simply obsolete and can be discarded. Last-write-wins (LWW) The simplest resolution: attach a timestamp to every write and keep the highest (ties broken by something deterministic, such as replica id). Cassandra does this per column; DynamoDB global tables do it per item in their default, eventually consistent mode. It's simple and converges, but it silently loses data: Two concurrent writes: one is discarded, even though both clients got "success". With clock skew, a write that happened later can lose to an earlier one with a faster clock. LWW is fine when writes are naturally immutable (each key written once, e.g. keyed by UUID) or when losing a concurrent update is acceptable (a user's "last seen" time). For anything like a shopping cart, you need a merge. Dynamo's shopping cart The Dynamo paper's cart merged siblings by taking the union of items. That never loses an add, but a removed item could reappear if a concurrent sibling still contained it. That's exactly the problem the OR-Set solves. Key takeaways A version vector records replica progress; incomparable vectors identify concurrent siblings to merge. A merged version must dominate its inputs and include the new coordinator update. Last-write-wins converges by a deterministic winner but can discard concurrent adds or later writes with slower clocks. Further reading Version vector (Wikipedia) Conflict-free replicated data type (Wikipedia)

t: CRDT merge laws and growing state
sum: Check both merge algebra and inflationary updates before claiming convergence without coordination.
x: A conflict-free replicated data type supplies a merge policy in advance, instead of asking a reader to resolve siblings by hand. Its convergence guarantee has requirements on both merge and update behaviour. CRDTs A Conflict-free Replicated Data Type is a data structure designed so that replicas can be updated independently and always merge to the same result, with no coordination and no conflicts to resolve by hand. State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs) define a merge function that is: Property Meaning ------ Commutative Order of the two inputs doesn't matter Associative Grouping doesn't matter Idempotent Merging something with itself changes nothing Written as equations: For example, if merge is "take the larger number", merging 3 with 5 gives 5 either way round, merging three states in any grouping gives the largest of the three, and merging 5 with 5 gives 5. Those three properties mean replicas can exchange state in any order, any number of times, via any path (gossip), and still converge. That's strong eventual consistency: replicas that have received the same updates are in the same state. There's a fourth condition that's easy to miss: local updates may only move the state "upwards", so that the updated state, merged with the old one, gives the updated state. Formally, states form a join-semilattice, merge is the least upper bound, and updates are inflationary. That's why a G-Counter may only increase entries and why a set "remove" is recorded as a tombstone rather than by deleting the element: a deletion would be undone by the next merge with a replica that still has it. Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs) instead broadcast operations. Concurrent operations must commute, and the delivery layer usually has to deliver each operation exactly once and in causal order. They send less data but need more from the network. Delta-state CRDTs sit in between: they ship only the recently changed part of the state, merged with the same join. A grow-only set is another simple example: adds grow the state, and union is a commutative, associative and idempotent merge. Key takeaways State-based merges are commutative, associative and idempotent, making exchange order and repeats harmless. Local updates must grow in the state’s partial order; merge is the join, not any arbitrary function with three algebraic properties. Operation-based and delta-state CRDTs trade data volume against delivery assumptions; strong eventual consistency concerns replicas that received the same updates. Further reading Conflict-free replicated data type (Wikipedia) A comprehensive study of CRDTs (Shapiro et al.) crdt.tech: resources and implementations

sum: Merge replicated counts without double-counting and distinguish convergence from stock invariants.
x: The merge laws become concrete in counters. Each replica owns a part of the history, and repeated exchange must preserve that history without counting it twice. G-Counter (grow-only counter) Each replica keeps a vector of counts, one per replica, and only increments its own entry. Why max and not sum? Because merging the same state twice must not double count (idempotence). Each entry is only ever increased by its owner, so the max retains the largest owner count present in the states being merged. An update not yet delivered is still missing. PN-Counter (increment and decrement) A G-Counter can't decrement: lowering an entry would be undone by max. So use two G-Counters: P for increments and N for decrements. merge merges P and N separately, each by element-wise max. The numbers in the block come from this example: Used for like-counts, stock levels where brief overselling is tolerable, and Redis Enterprise's active-active counters. Note that a PN-Counter can't enforce "never below zero": that's a global invariant needing coordination. A middle ground is an escrow (or bounded) counter: split the available stock between replicas up front (say 60 units to EU, 40 to US). Each replica can decrement its own share without coordination and only needs to talk to others to borrow more. The invariant holds, and coordination happens only near the limit. Key takeaways A G-Counter lets each replica grow its own entry and merges by entry-wise maximum, avoiding double-counting repeated state. A PN-Counter subtracts a grow-only decrement vector from a grow-only increment vector. A convergent PN-Counter can oversell; preallocating escrow rights preserves a bound while permitting local use of those rights. Further reading Conflict-free replicated data type (Wikipedia) A comprehensive study of CRDTs (Shapiro et al.) Escrow rights and numeric invariants (Balegas et al.) crdt.tech: resources and implementations

sum: Trace tagged adds and removes, then identify what an offline replica means for metadata collection.
x: Counters can preserve an update history by growing vectors. Sets need a way to record removals without letting an old replica’s add silently undo them. G-Set and 2P-Set A G-Set only grows; merge is union. A 2P-Set adds a "tombstone" set of removed elements; an element is present if it's in the add-set and not the remove-set. Its flaw: once removed, an element can never be re-added. OR-Set (observed-remove set) The OR-Set fixes that. Every add(x) attaches a unique tag (e.g. replica id + counter). remove(x) removes only the tags the remover has observed. Concurrent add and remove resolves to add wins, which is usually what users expect (re-adding milk to the shopping list shouldn't be cancelled by someone else's earlier removal). Riak's sets and maps, Redis CRDB sets and Automerge's internals use this idea. Beyond sets LWW-Register / MV-Register: a single value, resolved by timestamp or kept as multiple values. Maps of CRDTs, recursively. Sequence CRDTs (RGA, Logoot, Yjs, Automerge) for collaborative text editing, as in many live collaborative editors. Costs: metadata grows (tags and tombstones accumulate and need garbage collection). Arbitrary independent updates cannot preserve every invariant; bounded counters can enforce non-negative stock using preallocated rights, as described above. Garbage-collecting tombstones is the hard part. A tombstone can only be dropped once every replica has seen it; otherwise a replica that was offline still holds the old add, and the next merge brings the element back. Knowing that every replica has caught up is itself a coordination problem, the same one behind Cassandra's gc_grace_seconds in the earlier background-repair unit. (Optimised OR-Sets such as Riak's ORSWOT avoid most tombstones by using version vectors, but pay in vector size instead.) Choosing Use a CRDT when its merge semantics and permitted updates preserve your application's requirements. Invariants incompatible with independent updates need coordination or a design such as preallocated escrow rights. Key takeaways Grow-only sets merge by union; a two-phase set cannot re-add an element after removal. An OR-Set removes only observed add tags, so an unobserved concurrent add survives. Discarding removal metadata before every relevant replica has caught up can resurrect data; richer CRDTs also pay metadata costs. Further reading Conflict-free replicated data type (Wikipedia) A comprehensive study of CRDTs (Shapiro et al.) crdt.tech: resources and implementations CRDTs: the hard parts (Martin Kleppmann)

t: Gossip rounds and the slow tail
sum: Explain random-peer dissemination and why reaching the last nodes takes longer than ideal doubling.
x: Replicas need to exchange CRDT state and membership information. Gossip spreads that information through local random contacts rather than one all-cluster broadcast coordinator. Gossip protocols Large clusters (Cassandra, Consul, Riak, ScyllaDB) need every node to learn membership, liveness and metadata without a central server. Gossip (epidemic) protocols do this: Every interval (e.g. 1 s), each node picks a random peer (or a few). They exchange state digests and the newer entries (push, pull or push-pull). Information spreads like an infection. The doubling picture is the optimistic phase. Because peers are picked at random, more and more messages land on nodes that already know, and the last few uninformed nodes take a while to be hit. For ideal synchronous push gossip on a complete graph, starting from one informed node with independent uniform peer choices, reliable delivery and fanout 1 (each informed node tells one peer per round), the leading terms of the asymptotic expected round count are: With one round per second, the leading-term estimate for a 1,000-node cluster is about 17 seconds, before the asymptotic constant and implementation effects. This is an estimate, not a completion deadline. Push-pull (where uninformed nodes also ask random peers) finishes the tail much faster. Either way the number of rounds grows with the logarithm of the cluster size, written O(log N): doubling the cluster adds only about one or two rounds. At fixed fanout, each informed node initiates a constant number of contacts per round. Incoming contacts fluctuate, and bytes transferred depend on the metadata and state size; constant fanout is not constant bandwidth. Gossip tolerates node and message loss naturally. CRDT merges pair well with gossip because they're idempotent and order-insensitive. Key takeaways Gossip periodically exchanges state with random peers, avoiding a central dissemination server. Early spread resembles doubling; repeated contacts with informed peers create a slower tail. The push fanout-one round estimate is asymptotic, and CRDTs tolerate repeated, reordered state exchange. Further reading Rumour-spreading models and bounds (Doerr, Friedrich and Sauerwald) Gossip protocol (Wikipedia) HashiCorp memberlist (SWIM implementation)

sum: Interpret model-based heartbeat silence and use indirect probing before declaring membership failure.
x: Gossip can spread membership information, but a node must first decide how suspicious another node’s silence is. Failure detectors supply evidence and thresholds rather than certainty. Failure detection Heartbeats with a fixed timeout The simplest detector: if no heartbeat for T seconds, mark dead. Pick T too short and you get false positives under load; too long and real failures go unnoticed. One threshold can't suit every network condition. Phi accrual failure detector Hayashibara et al. (2004), used by Cassandra and Akka, output a suspicion level φ instead of a yes/no. Each node records recent heartbeat inter-arrival times and models them as a distribution (the original paper uses a normal distribution with the observed mean and variance; Cassandra uses a simpler exponential model). From that model it works out how unlikely the current silence is, and turns that into φ: In Cassandra's exponential model, the probability of a heartbeat being later than t falls off exponentially with t, and φ reduces to a straight line: With a 1-second mean interval, this model reaches Cassandra's default threshold of 8 after 8 / 0.434 ≈ 18 seconds of silence. A peer with a longer average interval takes proportionally longer to convict. φ Modelled heartbeat tail probability ------ 1 10% 3 0.1% 8 0.000001% The application chooses a threshold (Cassandra's phi_convict_threshold defaults to 8). The adaptation depends on the model: Cassandra's exponential detector uses the observed mean interval, so extra variance alone at the same mean does not guarantee later conviction. The tail probability is not a measured false-positive rate. SWIM SWIM (Das, Gupta and Motivala, 2002) is a scalable membership protocol, used in HashiCorp's memberlist (Consul, Nomad, Serf). Each period, A pings one random member B. No ack? A asks a few other members (k of them; HashiCorp's memberlist LAN and WAN configurations use 3 by default) to ping-req B on its behalf (indirect probing), which can reveal a problem with A's direct path if a helper succeeds; failed helpers still do not prove B is dead. Still nothing: B is suspected, not dead. Suspicion is gossiped; B can refute it by gossiping an incremented incarnation number. After a suspicion timeout, B is declared dead. Membership updates piggyback on ping and ack messages, so there's no separate broadcast traffic. In the paper's model, expected probe-message load per member and expected time until some healthy member first detects a failure do not grow with group size. Dissemination to the whole group and implementation suspicion timeouts are separate costs. HashiCorp's Lifeguard extensions further reduce false positives from slow, overloaded nodes. Key takeaways A fixed heartbeat timeout trades recovery speed against false positives; phi reports suspicion under a model of observed heartbeat intervals. Cassandra’s exponential model depends on the mean interval, so greater variance alone does not guarantee later conviction. SWIM uses indirect probes, a suspicion period and incarnation numbers; a failed direct path is not proof that the node failed. Further reading SWIM paper (Das, Gupta, Motivala) HashiCorp memberlist (SWIM implementation)

t: Synchronous dependencies: availability and tail latency
sum: Calculate the reliability and latency costs of waiting for several required services.
x: When one service needs another to do something, it has two basic choices. It can ask and wait (synchronous), or it can leave a note and move on (asynchronous). Almost every messaging system you will meet in this module exists to make the second option reliable. Synchronous: request and wait In a synchronous call, the caller sends a request (usually HTTP or gRPC) and logically waits for a response or timeout; a nonblocking client need not block an operating-system thread. This is simple and gives you an immediate answer, which is exactly what you want when the user is waiting for that answer: "was my card accepted?" But synchronous chains have three structural weaknesses: Availability multiplies. If Checkout requires three services that are each 99.9% available and their failures are independent, all three must be up at once, so together they are only about 99.7% available (worked out below). Correlated failures change this calculation, and Checkout has its own failure modes. That is about 26 hours of downtime a year instead of 8.8. Latency adds up. Sequential dependent calls add their durations; parallel fan-out waits for the required critical path, and tail latency (p99) gets worse as you add hops, because the slowest dependency dominates. If a request touches 5 services with independent delays and each is slow 1% of the time, the request hits at least one slow call about 4.9% of the time (worked out below): tail slowness becomes more frequent at the request level; exact quantiles depend on the full latency distributions. Load is coupled. A spike at the front door hits every downstream service at the same instant. If Fraud can only handle 500 requests a second, Checkout can only handle 500 requests a second. Both numbers come from one rule of probability: when events are independent, the chance that all of them happen is the product of their separate chances. For availability, a request that needs every dependency succeeds only when all of them are up: To turn an availability into downtime, multiply the fraction of time it is not up by the 8,760 hours in a 365-day year: For tail latency, it is easier to work out the chance that every call is fast and subtract that from 1: Both formulas assume independence. Shared causes (one database, one network link, one bad deploy) make failures and slow calls happen together, so real systems can be better or worse than these numbers, and you should measure. Key takeaways A synchronous request waits logically for a result; it need not block an operating-system thread. Independent required dependencies multiply availability, while parallel fan-out exposes the slowest required call. Shared failures break the independence assumption, so measure the actual critical path. Further reading Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center) Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging

sum: Separate temporal, rate, location and fan-out decoupling without losing sight of the message contract.
x: Asynchronous messaging separates accepting work from finishing it. A queue carries a command to its intended handler; a topic can announce a fact to several independent subscribers. For example, publishing one OrderPlaced event lets email, loyalty and warehouse services subscribe independently. Sending a separate command to every team instead makes the producer maintain that list of handlers. Pub/sub is explored later in the module. Asynchronous: send and carry on In asynchronous communication, the producer hands a message to an intermediary (a broker) and can continue after the required broker acknowledgement without waiting for processing. A consumer picks the message up later, maybe milliseconds later, maybe hours. With durable queues, suitable publish acknowledgement and retention settings, the broker retains the message, so the producer and consumer do not need to be running at the same time. This is the key idea: the queue decouples the two sides in time. Message vs event vs command A command message asks for something to happen ("SendReceiptEmail"). An event message states that something happened ("OrderPlaced"). Both travel as messages. Commands usually have one intended handler; events can have many. You will see why this matters in the pub/sub and event-driven lessons. The kinds of decoupling "Decoupling" gets used loosely. It helps to separate it into distinct properties: Kind What it means ------ Temporal Consumer can be down when producer sends Rate Each side runs at its own speed Location Producer doesn't know consumer's address Fan-out Add consumers without changing producer A direct HTTP request does not by itself buffer work during consumer outages or fan it out; service discovery, proxies and other infrastructure can hide physical consumer addresses. A queue gives you the first three. A publish/subscribe topic adds the fourth. What a queue does not decouple is the message format. If the producer changes the shape of the payload, consumers still break. Contracts and schema evolution (for example, Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry) remain your problem. Brokers you will meet Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus: message queues. A message is handed to one consumer and deleted once acknowledged. Amazon SNS, Google Pub/Sub: publish/subscribe. One message is copied to many subscribers. Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Redpanda: distributed logs. Messages are appended and retained; consumers track their own position and can replay. The next lessons take each family in turn. Key takeaways Durability, publish acknowledgement and retention let a consumer process work after the producer has moved on. Queues decouple time, rate and consumer addresses; pub/sub also lets new subscribers join without changing the producer. The payload remains a contract: asynchronous transport does not make incompatible schemas safe. Further reading What is a message queue? (AWS) Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging

t: Absorb a burst and calculate the drain time
sum: Work out backlog growth, spare drain capacity and the longest FIFO wait.
x: A durable queue can hold a temporary traffic spike while a smaller worker fleet catches up. The useful question is how long users must wait, and whether the fleet can ever catch up. Load levelling The most common practical reason to add a queue is to protect a slow or fragile component from bursts. This is the queue-based load levelling pattern. Imagine an image-thumbnail service. Uploads arrive in bursts: 2,000 per second for 30 seconds after a marketing email, then 50 per second for the rest of the hour. Each worker can process 100 images per second. Without a queue, you need 20 workers (2,000 ÷ 100) sitting mostly idle to survive the peak. With a queue and 2 workers (200 per second capacity), the backlog grows while arrivals exceed capacity: After the burst, arrivals drop to 50 per second, so the workers eat into the backlog with whatever capacity is left over: The message at the back of the burst waits roughly as long as it takes the workers to get through everything in front of it: So you trade latency (the longest wait is about 270 seconds, while the queue returns to empty after 6 minutes) for cost and stability (10× fewer workers in this idealised fixed-rate model; consumer admission and downstream capacity still need protection). That trade is acceptable when the product permits the resulting delay, including an explicit pending-job experience. A queue is not infinite capacity Load levelling only works if the average arrival rate is below the processing rate. If arrivals average 250 per second and you can do 200, the backlog grows forever. A queue hides overload; it does not fix it. Always alarm on queue depth and on the age of the oldest message. Key takeaways During overload, the backlog grows by the difference between arrivals and processing capacity. After a burst, new arrivals consume capacity too; only spare capacity drains the backlog. Average arrivals must remain below processing capacity: a queue cannot cure sustained overload. Further reading Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center) Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library)

t: Convert average queue depth into waiting time
sum: Use Little's Law with a stable queue and a consistent system boundary.
x: Queue depth is a count, but users experience a delay. Little's Law connects the two. Decide what you count before using it: messages still waiting correspond to queue wait, while waiting plus in-flight messages correspond to total time in that system. Little's Law: a useful sanity check Little's Law says that, in a stable system (one where, over time, items leave as fast as they arrive), the average number of items in it equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends in it. Rearranged, it tells you the average wait from two numbers a dashboard already shows: So a queue that receives 400 messages per second and holds a steady 12,000 makes each message wait about 30 seconds on average. This turns "queue depth" (which dashboards show) into "delay" (which users feel). It holds for long-run averages in a stable system; while a queue is growing during a burst, the momentary numbers need not match it. Key takeaways In a stable system, average depth divided by average arrival rate gives average time spent inside the measured boundary. Waiting-only depth measures time before processing; including active work measures the whole residence time. Use long-run averages; a snapshot taken during burst growth need not obey the steady-state estimate. Further reading Little's law (Wikipedia) Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library)

t: Choose async work and keep the user informed
sum: Place work according to the response users need, then handle pending results, failures and tracing.
x: An asynchronous design changes the promise the product makes. Accepting a job means it will be attempted later; it does not mean its database write or external side effect has already succeeded. When to choose which Situation Better fit ------ User needs the answer now Sync Work can finish later Async Downstream is slow or flaky Async Strong read-after-write needed Sync Many systems react to one fact Async (pub/sub) A common shape is sync at the edge, async inside. The checkout API synchronously authorises the payment (the user needs to know), writes the order, then reliably publishes OrderPlaced, for example via an outbox committed with the order. Email, analytics, loyalty points and warehouse picking all happen asynchronously. The costs of going async Asynchrony is not free. It moves complexity rather than removing it: Eventual consistency. The user may see "order placed" before the loyalty points appear. The UI and product need to tolerate that. No direct error path. If the email worker fails, it cannot return an HTTP 500 error to the user. You need retries, dead-letter queues and alerts instead. Duplicate and out-of-order delivery. Most brokers deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent. Later lessons cover this in depth. Harder debugging. A request's story is split across processes and time. You need correlation IDs and distributed tracing (for example, propagating a W3C traceparent header in message attributes). One more system to run. The broker itself must be highly available, monitored and capacity-planned. Async request-reply Sometimes you need a result but the work is slow (video transcoding, report generation). Return 202 Accepted with a job ID, process via a queue, and let the client poll a status endpoint or receive a webhook. Webhooks and WebSockets are covered in the API design module. Key takeaways Keep work required for the immediate success response on that response path. Slow jobs can return a job ID with 202 Accepted, then expose status or notify the client. Asynchronous writes require an explicit pending-state experience; message trace context connects the request to later work. Further reading Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern (Azure Architecture Center) Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library) Enterprise Integration Patterns: Messaging

sum: Trace receive, process and acknowledgement to see why a worker crash can cause loss or duplication.
x: A message queue is the simplest broker: producers put messages in, consumers take them out, and each delivery is assigned to one competing consumer, rather than broadcast to every consumer. This is called point-to-point messaging. It is the workhorse behind background jobs, email sending, image processing and most "do this later" tasks. Competing consumers You scale a queue by running several consumers against it. They compete for messages: whichever is free takes the next one. This gives you three properties almost for free: Horizontal scaling. More workers can increase throughput until queue partitions, broker resources, contention or downstream capacity limit it. Resilience. If worker B crashes, A and C keep going. Natural load balancing. A fast worker simply asks for more often. The catch is ordering. With several competing consumers, m2 may finish before m1. If ordering matters, you need FIFO queues with group IDs (covered later in this module) or partitioned processing on a log like Kafka; application concurrency must also preserve the required order. The core problem: when is a message "done"? A consumer can crash halfway through processing. If the broker deleted the message the moment it was handed out, that work would be lost. So brokers separate delivery from completion using acknowledgements. If step 3 never happens, the broker assumes the worker died and redelivers the message to someone else. This is what makes queues reliable, and it is also why messages can be delivered more than once: a worker might finish step 2, then crash before step 3. Ack after, not before Acknowledging before processing (auto-ack) gives you at-most-once delivery: a crash mid-processing loses the message. Acknowledging after processing gives you at-least-once: a crash after processing but before the ack means a duplicate. Most systems choose at-least-once and make consumers idempotent. Key takeaways Consumers share work rather than each receiving a broadcast copy. Completion acknowledgements let the broker redeliver unfinished work after a consumer disappears. A crash after an effect but before acknowledgement can repeat the effect; consumers must tolerate duplicates. Further reading RabbitMQ tutorial: work queues, acks and fair dispatch Competing Consumers pattern (Azure Architecture Center)

t: SQS visibility timeouts and processing leases
sum: Tune visibility for job duration and understand why receipt handles and timeouts do not guarantee exclusive work.
x: SQS treats a received message as temporarily leased work. A worker must finish and delete it before that lease expires, or extend the lease while it continues. How SQS does it: visibility timeouts Amazon SQS has no persistent connection between broker and consumer, so it cannot notice that a consumer died. Instead it uses a visibility timeout. A consumer calls ReceiveMessage. SQS returns the message plus a receipt handle, and normally hides it from other consumers. Standard queues can still deliver duplicates during the visibility window, so visibility is not an exclusive-processing lock. The message stays invisible for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours). The consumer uses the most recent receipt handle with DeleteMessage after processing. Standard queues can occasionally redeliver even after deletion, and an obsolete receipt handle does not guarantee deletion. If not, the message becomes visible again and another consumer can receive it. (Times are seconds after the first receive.) The key tuning rule: set the visibility timeout comfortably longer than your worst-case processing time. When SQS triggers AWS Lambda, AWS gives a recommended minimum, because Lambda may need to retry a throttled batch before the messages reappear: If jobs genuinely vary (a 10-second job sometimes takes 10 minutes), the worker can call ChangeMessageVisibility periodically as a heartbeat to extend its lease. Key takeaways Visibility temporarily hides a delivery; SQS standard queues can still deliver a duplicate. Delete with the latest receipt handle after successful processing, and extend visibility when long jobs need it. For SQS-triggered Lambda, AWS recommends at least six times the function timeout plus the batching window. Further reading Amazon SQS visibility timeout (AWS docs) SQS event source configuration (AWS Lambda)

t: SQS polling, payloads and FIFO throughput
sum: Reduce empty receives, keep large payloads outside the queue and size FIFO traffic by message groups.
x: Once acknowledgement timing is correct, the remaining SQS design choices are how to fetch efficiently, what belongs in the payload, and how ordered traffic is distributed. SQS limits, polling and FIFO throughput Other SQS details worth knowing: Setting Value ------ Max message size 1 MiB (256 KB before 2025) Retention 1 min–14 days (default 4) Long poll wait up to 20 s Batch receive up to 10 messages For anything bigger than the limit (images, large documents), use the claim check pattern: store the payload in S3 and send a small message holding its key. AWS's extended client libraries do this for you. Use long polling (WaitTimeSeconds=20). Short polling returns immediately even when the queue is empty, which wastes requests (and money, since SQS bills per request) and can miss messages because it samples only a subset of servers. Standard SQS queues offer nearly unlimited throughput but only best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery. SQS FIFO queues guarantee order within a message group and deduplicate within a 5-minute window, at lower throughput. Without high-throughput mode, a FIFO queue handles 300 API calls per second per action (SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage). Each call can carry a batch of up to 10 messages, which sets the ceiling: High-throughput mode spreads groups across internal partitions and raises this to thousands or tens of thousands of calls per second, depending on the region, provided you use many distinct message group IDs. Key takeaways Long polling reduces empty receive traffic; batches move up to ten messages per SQS API call. Use a claim check for large files: store the object and send its reference. FIFO orders each message group; high throughput also requires enough distinct groups to distribute load. Further reading Amazon SQS message quotas (AWS docs)

t: RabbitMQ prefetch and replicated quorum queues
sum: Control unacknowledged deliveries and calculate how many replica failures a quorum queue survives.
x: RabbitMQ pushes deliveries over an existing connection. The consumer controls its exposure with prefetch, while replicated quorum queues protect the broker-side record of the work. How RabbitMQ does it: channels, acks and prefetch RabbitMQ consumers hold a long-lived TCP connection. The broker pushes messages to them, and it knows a consumer has died when the connection or its AMQP channel closes. Consumers send basic.ack when done, or basic.nack / basic.reject to give up (optionally with requeue=true). Unacknowledged messages on a closed channel are requeued automatically. Consumer prefetch (basic.qos) limits how many unacknowledged messages a consumer may hold at once. The prefetch limit is a crucial knob. With an unlimited classic-queue prefetch, a consumer can buffer a large backlog before others connect. Broker defaults and quorum-queue limits can impose bounds. A prefetch of 1 prevents a consumer holding multiple unacknowledged deliveries, but is not a perfect fairness guarantee and can reduce throughput. Values between roughly 10 and 300 usually balance throughput and fairness; the right number depends on processing time. Producers publish to a RabbitMQ exchange, which routes each message into queues. There are four exchange types: direct exchange, topic exchange, fanout exchange and headers exchange. For durability use quorum queues, which replicate each queue across nodes using the Raft consensus algorithm. A write is confirmed once a majority of replicas have it, and the queue keeps working only while a majority is still up. That fixes how many failures it survives: A 4-replica queue still survives only one failure (⌊3 / 2⌋ = 1), which is why replica counts are usually odd. Lose the majority and the queue stops accepting work rather than risk losing confirmed messages. Quorum queues are always durable and cannot be exclusive or transient. The older alternative, classic mirrored queues, was deprecated for years and removed in RabbitMQ 4.0 (2024). Anything still relying on mirroring must move to quorum queues (or streams) before upgrading. Key takeaways RabbitMQ requeues unacknowledged deliveries when their channel closes. Prefetch limits in-flight work and can prevent an early consumer taking a large backlog; benchmark the setting. Quorum queues need a surviving majority, and classic mirroring was removed in RabbitMQ 4.0. Further reading RabbitMQ tutorial: work queues, acks and fair dispatch Quorum queues (RabbitMQ docs)

t: Poison messages, receive counts and dead letters
sum: Classify failures, set aside broken messages and keep recoverable outages from exhausting the retry budget.
x: After processing fails, decide whether another attempt can help. A durable queue gives you time to recover, but repeated receives alone do not repair malformed input or an unavailable dependency. Poison messages and dead-letter queues Some messages will never succeed: malformed JSON, a reference to a deleted customer, a bug triggered by one specific input. Without protection, such a poison message is retried forever, wasting capacity and, in FIFO queues, blocking later work in its message group when processing preserves order. The fix is a dead-letter queue (DLQ): after a set number of failed attempts (say 5), move the message aside. SQS: set a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount (say 5). SQS tracks ApproximateReceiveCount; when it exceeds the limit, the message moves to the DLQ. You can later redrive messages back to the source queue once the bug is fixed. RabbitMQ: configure a dead-letter exchange. Messages are dead-lettered when rejected without requeue, when their TTL expires, or when the queue exceeds its length limit. Quorum queues also enforce a delivery-limit, which defaults to 20 since RabbitMQ 4.0: a message redelivered more often than that is dead-lettered if a dead-letter exchange is configured, and dropped if not. Exactly which kinds of return count towards the limit has changed between 4.x releases, so check the docs for your version. A DLQ nobody watches is a black hole Always alarm when DLQ depth is above zero, keep DLQ retention longer than the source queue's (otherwise messages can expire before anyone looks), and record why a message failed (an error attribute or a log line with the message ID). Choosing a receive count Too low a maxReceiveCount (1 or 2) dead-letters messages that hit a transient error, such as a database failover lasting 20 seconds. Too high (100) lets a poison message burn capacity for ages. Three to ten is an illustrative starting range to test against expected outage duration and retry cost, combined with backoff between attempts so that transient faults have time to clear. SQS standard queues have no native per-message backoff, but you can approximate it by calling ChangeMessageVisibility on failure with an increasing delay (for example, 30 s, 2 min, 10 min based on the receive count). Queue vs log, in one table Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) Log (Kafka) --------- After ack Deleted Retained Unit of scaling Message Partition Replay No Yes Per-message retry Easy Awkward Queues shine for task distribution: independent jobs where each should be done once and individual failures should be retried or set aside. Logs, covered later, shine for event streams that many consumers read and replay. Key takeaways A poison message needs a bounded retry path and an inspected DLQ, rather than endless redelivery. Receive limits and visibility delays must accommodate the outages you expect to recover from. RabbitMQ quorum delivery limits can drop messages without a dead-letter exchange; SQS FIFO poison work can block its group. Queues suit individually retried tasks; retained logs suit replayable streams. Further reading Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS (AWS docs) Quorum queues (RabbitMQ docs) Dead Letter Channel (Enterprise Integration Patterns)

t: Independent subscriptions with SNS and SQS
sum: Give every reacting service its own durable queue and understand partial subscriber completion.
x: A queue hands each message to one consumer. But many real messages are facts that several systems care about. When an order is placed, billing, shipping, analytics and email all want to know. Publish/subscribe (pub/sub) solves this: a publisher sends a message to a pub/sub topic, and the broker delivers to each matching subscription according to its delivery guarantees. Topics and subscriptions The message publisher knows only the topic name. It has no idea who is listening. Each subscription is an independent stream of copies with its own delivery state. Adding a new consumer means adding a subscription. The publisher does not change or redeploy. This is the fan-out decoupling from the first lesson: the producer is decoupled from the number and identity of consumers. Subscription vs consumer In most systems a subscription can itself have several consumers competing for its messages. Google Pub/Sub, Azure Service Bus topics and Kafka consumer groups all work this way: pub/sub between subscriptions, competing consumers within one. The SNS + SQS fan-out pattern On AWS, SNS is the topic and SQS queues are the subscriptions. This combination is so common that it has a name: fan-out. Why not have each service subscribe to SNS directly over HTTP? Because the queue in between gives each consumer: Durability while it is down. SNS retries HTTP endpoints for a while, but an SQS queue holds messages for up to 14 days. Its own pace. Shipping can lag by an hour without affecting billing. Its own retries and DLQ. A poison message for email does not affect shipping. Independent scaling. Each queue has its own worker fleet. Two configuration details trip people up: The SQS queue's access policy must allow the SNS topic to send to it. Enable raw message delivery if you want the SQS body to be your original payload. Otherwise SNS wraps it in a JSON envelope (Type, MessageId, TopicArn, Message...), and your consumer must unwrap it. SNS FIFO topics can fan out to SQS FIFO queues when ordering within a message group matters. Delivery to each subscription is independent. Billing may not have created an invoice when Email starts handling the same OrderPlaced event. If Email requires an invoice, trigger it from InvoiceIssued or use another explicit readiness protocol rather than assuming Billing runs first. Key takeaways Pub/sub copies a fact to each matching subscription; workers within one queue compete for its copy. SNS-to-SQS fan-out isolates each service’s backlog, retry path and worker capacity. Configure the queue access policy and either unwrap the SNS envelope or enable raw delivery. Independent subscribers do not complete together: publish or check explicit prerequisites. Further reading Fanout Amazon SNS notifications to Amazon SQS queues (AWS docs) Publish–subscribe pattern (Wikipedia)

sum: Apply SNS filter policies and RabbitMQ topic bindings to deliver only matching events.
x: A subscription need not receive every published event. Filtering selects the subset before a worker spends time receiving and discarding it. In the policy below, all three listed fields must match; the array for a field lists its accepted alternatives. Filtering Often a subscriber cares about only some messages. Shipping does not need OrderCancelled events for digital goods. Rather than receiving everything and discarding most of it, the subscriber can set a filter policy. The example accepts physical OrderPlaced messages whose numeric amount is at least 100; it does not transform the payload. SNS evaluates filter policies against message attributes by default, or against the message body if you set the filter policy scope to MessageBody. Messages that do not match are simply not delivered to that subscription. Filtering saves consumer compute and queue costs, but it moves routing logic into infrastructure configuration. Keep filter policies in version control alongside the consumer's code. RabbitMQ achieves similar routing with topic exchanges: queues bind with patterns such as order..physical or order.#, where matches one word and # matches zero or more. Key takeaways SNS filters use message attributes by default, with an optional message-body scope. RabbitMQ topic bindings use a one-word wildcard and a zero-or-more-word wildcard. Keep routing configuration versioned with the subscriber so filtering changes can be reviewed. Further reading Amazon SNS message filtering (AWS docs) AMQP 0-9-1 model explained (RabbitMQ)

sum: Choose how messages reach a consumer and how overload signals reach the broker.
x: The delivery protocol determines who decides when more work arrives. Judge it against processing cost, endpoint reachability and the consumer’s ability to report excess demand. Push vs pull consumers For HTTP push versus polling pull, how does a message reach the consumer? A broker may also push over a connection the consumer originally opened, as RabbitMQ does. Push Pull --------- Who starts Broker calls you You ask broker Flow control Broker guesses Consumer decides Endpoint Must be reachable Can be private Examples SNS→HTTP, Pub/Sub push SQS, Kafka Push delivery (SNS to an HTTPS endpoint, Google Pub/Sub push subscriptions, webhooks) is convenient for serverless handlers: you just expose an endpoint. But the broker controls the rate. If your endpoint slows down, the broker must infer overload from errors or latency and back off.
