sum: The sum and product rules, permutations and combinations, repetition and stars and bars, the binomial theorem, and the pigeonhole principle behind hash collisions and impossible compressors.
x: Counting sounds like primary school, but it is how you estimate brute-force search spaces, password strength, the number of test cases, the probability of a collision and the size of the output of an algorithm. Most errors come from one of two mistakes: counting the same thing twice, or not being clear whether order matters. The good news is that nearly every problem reduces to a handful of rules, applied carefully. The two basic rules Product rule. If a task is a sequence of steps, and the number of choices at each step doesn't depend on what you chose earlier, multiply the counts. Sum rule. If a task can be done in one of several disjoint ways (no outcome belongs to two of them), add the counts. Three everyday examples: a 4-digit PIN, a PIN with no repeated digit, and a lower-case password of length 1 to 3. How big is a brute-force search? An 8-character password over 62 symbols (a–z, A–Z, 0–9) has 62⁸ ≈ 2.18 × 10¹⁴ possibilities. At an assumed 10¹⁰ guesses per second, exhausting the space takes about 6 hours; this is arithmetic, not a measured hardware benchmark. Add 4 characters and it becomes 62¹² ≈ 3.2 × 10²¹, around 10,000 years. For independently and uniformly chosen symbols, adding length multiplies the search space exponentially. Human-chosen passwords need a different model. Permutations: order matters A permutation is an ordering. To put n distinct items in order there are n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the second, and so on down to 1. That product has its own name and symbol, the factorial: Often you only fill k places from n items (no item used twice). You stop the product after k factors, which is the same as dividing n! by the (n − k)! orderings of the items you didn't use: Factorials grow very fast. 10! is about 3.6 million and 20! is about 2.4 × 10¹⁸. However large a fixed base you pick, the factorial eventually overtakes its powers: That is why brute-forcing the travelling salesman problem (trying every ordering of cities) quickly becomes impractical as the number of cities grows (the cutoff depends on the implementation and hardware). It is also where the lower bound for comparison sorting comes from. A sort that only compares items must be able to tell all n! orderings of its input apart, and each yes/no comparison at best halves the possibilities, so it needs about log₂(n!) comparisons in the worst case: Combinations: order doesn't matter A combination is a subset: a choice of items where order is irrelevant. The number of k-element subsets of an n-element set is the binomial coefficient. Count the ordered selections, then divide out the overcounting: each unordered group of k items appears k! times among the ordered ones. This "count ordered, then divide out the overcounting" move is one of the most useful in counting. Three facts about binomial coefficients, each with a one-line counting argument: Symmetry. Choosing who's in is the same as choosing who's out. Pascal's rule. Pick one particular item: either it is in the subset or it isn't, and those two cases are disjoint. Sum of a row. Adding the counts for every possible subset size gives the total number of subsets, and each item is independently in or out. Pascal's rule is exactly how each number in Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it: The binomial theorem Binomial coefficients get their name from expanding a power of a two-term sum such as x + y. Expanding (x + y)ⁿ means picking either x or y from each of the n brackets and multiplying; the number of ways to pick x exactly k times is C(n, k). Substituting 1 for both x and y makes the left side 2ⁿ and the right side the sum of the row, which recovers the row-sum fact above. Lattice paths How many shortest paths are there on a grid from (0, 0) to (4, 3), moving only right (R) or up (U)? Every path is a string of 4 Rs and 3 Us, and choosing which 3 of the 7 positions are Us fixes it: Many dynamic-programming problems ("unique paths") are this binomial coefficient in disguise. Repetition allowed In this table, n is the number of distinct items (or kinds of item) available, at least 1, and k is how many you pick, 0 or more. nᵏ means k copies of n multiplied together. Order? Repeats? Count --------- Yes No P(n, k) Yes Yes nᵏ No No C(n, k) No Yes C(n+k−1, k) The no-repeat formulas assume you pick no more than n items; otherwise the count is zero. The last row, multisets (collections where an item may appear more than once), is counted with stars and bars. Distributing k identical items into n distinct bins is the same as arranging k stars and n − 1 bars in a line, where the bars separate the bins: Every such line is fixed by choosing which positions hold bars: If every worker must get at least one job, hand one to each first, then distribute the remaining 6 freely: 6 stars and 3 bars, so C(9, 3) = 84 ways. Arrangements with repeated letters The number of distinct arrangements of a word with repeated letters is the multinomial coefficient: arrange all the letters as if they were distinct, then divide by the orderings of each group of identical letters, which don't change the word. Check by brute force When in doubt, write the dumbest possible enumeration for a small case. Python's itertools and math make this one line each: Brute force for small n, then the formula for large n, is the standard workflow for avoiding off-by-one and overcounting mistakes. The pigeonhole principle If there are more pigeons than holes, some hole has at least two pigeons. More generally, if you spread items over boxes, some box must hold at least the average, rounded up: The bound is the best possible: spreading the items as evenly as you can gives a fullest box of exactly ⌈N/k⌉. It sounds trivial, but it proves things that are otherwise surprising: Among 13 people, two share a birth month. Hash 1,000,000 keys into 4,096 buckets and some bucket receives at least 245 keys (the example in the formula), however good the hash function. In a group of at least two people with mutual friendships and no self-friendships, two have the same number of friends within the group. In a group of 10, the possible friend counts are 0 to 9, but 0 and 9 can't both occur (someone with 9 friends is friends with everyone), so 10 people share at most 9 different counts. No compressor shrinks every file A lossless compressor must be injective (different inputs give different outputs), or decompression would be ambiguous. Count the files of exactly n bits against all the strictly shorter ones: So no injective compressor can map all 2ⁿ inputs to shorter outputs. A compressor defined on all finite bit strings that shrinks some inputs must expand others (an identity encoding need not expand anything); format framing and block overhead are concrete reasons gzip or zstd output may grow. The counting argument proves that some growth is unavoidable for such a total shrinking compressor; it does not require a particular header design. The birthday problem Pigeonhole is also the root of the birthday problem, which asks the harder question of when a collision becomes likely rather than certain. In the model of independent, uniformly distributed birthdays over 365 possible days, certainty needs 366 people, but 23 already give a better than 50% chance. For hashes, the same model gives: That probability calculation is covered in the probability module. Common traps Order or not? "Choose a committee" is a combination; "choose a president, secretary and treasurer" is a permutation. A committee of 3 with a chair can be counted two ways (first block below), and both must agree. Overcounting symmetric arrangements. Seating people round a table where rotations count as the same: each seating appears once per seat it could be rotated to (second block below). "At least one". Count the complement: all possibilities minus those with none (third block below). Trying to count "exactly one digit, plus exactly two, plus …" directly is slower and error-prone, and "pick a position for the digit, then fill the rest" overcounts. Disjointness in the sum rule. If the cases overlap you need inclusion–exclusion, which is the next lesson. Key takeaways Product rule for sequences of choices, sum rule for disjoint cases; nearly everything builds on these two. Permutations count ordered selections; combinations count unordered ones, which is the ordered count divided by the number of orderings of each selection. Stars and bars counts identical items into distinct bins; multinomial coefficients handle words with repeated letters. Pigeonhole: items spread over boxes force some box to hold at least the average rounded up, which is why hash collisions and incompressible files must exist. Count the complement for "at least one", and always check a small case by brute force. sum: Counting overlapping cases with inclusion–exclusion, derangements and surjections, setting up and solving recurrences, and using generating functions to turn counting into polynomial multiplication.
x: The basic counting rules break down in two common situations. When cases overlap, the sum rule double-counts. When a problem is easiest to describe in terms of smaller versions of itself, a direct formula is hard to see. Inclusion–exclusion fixes the first; recurrences fix the second. Generating functions are a power tool that packages a whole sequence into one object, so that counting problems become algebra. These are also the tools you need to analyse algorithms: recurrences describe the running time of recursive code, and the same "count the ways" reasoning is what dynamic programming computes. Inclusion–exclusion When two groups overlap, adding their sizes counts everyone in the overlap twice, so subtract the overlap once: Two sets In a team of 30 engineers, 18 know Python, 15 know Java and 8 know both. Those who know at least one: 18 + 15 − 8 = 25. So 30 − 25 = 5 know neither. For three sets, subtracting the pairwise overlaps removes the triple overlap one time too many, so add it back: The general pattern alternates: add singles, subtract pairs, add triples, subtract quadruples, and so on. To see why it works, follow one element that lies in exactly m of the sets. It is counted once for every single set it is in, minus once for every pair, plus once for every triple, and so on: Worked example: divisibility How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by 2, 3 or 5? The multiples of d up to 1000 number ⌊1000 / d⌋. The multiples of both 2 and 3 are the multiples of 6, and so on, because 2, 3 and 5 share no factors. So 734 are divisible by at least one, and 1000 − 734 = 266 by none. Each term is one integer division (constant time in a fixed-width arithmetic model), so inclusion–exclusion counts without iterating. The same idea computes Euler's totient function (written with the Greek letter phi), which you'll meet in the number theory lesson. Derangements A derangement is a permutation where nothing stays in its original place: every guest leaves with someone else's coat, or every reviewer gets someone else's pull request. Let Aᵢ be the permutations that fix item i (leave it in its original position). Fixing any particular k items leaves (n − k)! permutations of the rest, and there are C(n, k) ways to choose which k. Inclusion–exclusion over "at least one fixed point" gives: The bracket is the start of the series for e⁻¹ (1 divided by Euler's number e ≈ 2.718), which gives a shortcut: The values run 0, 1, 2, 9, 44, 265, … for 1 to 6 items. The limit is approached quickly, but small cases differ substantially: for 1 item the probability is 0, and for 2 items it is 1/2. Counting onto functions How many ways can you assign 5 distinct jobs to 3 servers so every server gets at least one? There are 3⁵ assignments in all. Subtract those missing a given server, add back those missing two: The same pattern counts onto functions from an m-element set to an n-element set: add or subtract, for each number j of excluded targets, C(n, j) × (n − j)ᵐ, with the sign + for even j and − for odd j. Inclusion–exclusion is the go-to method whenever the condition is "every X is covered" or "no X is bad": count the complement events, which are often easier, and alternate. Recurrences A recurrence defines each term of a sequence from earlier terms, plus base cases. Setting one up is often easier than finding a formula directly, because it mirrors how you'd build the objects. Setting up a recurrence Binary strings with no two adjacent 1s Count the binary strings of a given length that never contain "11". Look at the first character. If it's 0, the rest is any valid string one character shorter. If it's 1, the next must be 0, and then any valid string two characters shorter follows. The two cases don't overlap, so the count is the sum of the two shorter counts. The skill is finding the right first decision that splits the objects into disjoint cases, each a smaller instance of the same problem. It is exactly the step you take when designing a dynamic-programming solution. The Tower of Hanoi is the classic: to move n discs, move n − 1 out of the way, move the biggest, then move the n − 1 back on top. Guessing a formula from small values and proving it by induction is a perfectly good method. For 10 discs it gives 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1,023 moves. Solving linear recurrences A linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients makes each term a fixed weighted sum of the previous terms, with nothing else added. For the second-order case, guess a solution of the form rⁿ. Substituting and dividing by rⁿ⁻² gives the characteristic equation: A full example, with a(0) = 2 and a(1) = 5: Fibonacci, where each number is the sum of the two before it, works the same way: This is why naive recursive Fibonacci, whose call count obeys a Fibonacci-like recurrence, takes exponential time, and why memoisation reduces it to O(n) additions, where n is the index of the Fibonacci number. Exact Fibonacci values grow to about 0.69 × n bits, so this is not a linear bit-complexity bound. Divide-and-conquer recurrences Recursive algorithms that split the input into equal parts give recurrences of a standard shape. Merge sort splits into two halves and merges in linear time. Unrolling its recursion tree shows the same work on every level: The master theorem packages this. Compare the outside work f(n) with the work at the leaves of the tree: So binary search (constant outside work, which matches its single leaf) is O(log n); merge sort (linear outside work, matching its n leaves) is O(n log n); Karatsuba multiplication (linear outside work, less than its n^1.585 leaves) is O(n^1.585), where O(…) means "grows at most proportionally to" and n is the input size. The DSA subject covers it in depth. Generating functions A generating function stores a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … as the coefficients of a power series: For the formal counting manipulations here we do not need to evaluate x; it is just a clothes line to hang the numbers on. The magic is that multiplying two generating functions convolves the sequences: the coefficient of xⁿ in the product adds up every way to split n into a part from the first factor and a part from the second. That is exactly how "split n into a part from here and a part from there" counts combine. The building block is the geometric series: Example: making change How many ways can you make n pence from 1p, 2p and 5p coins (order doesn't matter)? Any number of 1p coins is allowed, with one way to use each number, which is the geometric series. 2p coins can only make even amounts, and 5p coins multiples of 5. Each term in the product picks one power from each factor, so the coefficient of xⁿ counts the combinations: Multiplying the polynomials (truncated at degree n) is precisely the classic coin-change dynamic programme. In this code, n is a non-negative integer and coins contains distinct positive integer denominations: The inner loop multiplies the series in w by one coin's factor. Because w[v − c] has already been updated when w[v] uses it, the loop computes: Generating functions give a way to derive DP algorithms and prove them correct, and with more algebra they give closed forms. For Fibonacci: Catalan numbers The Catalan numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, … count balanced bracket strings (by the number of bracket pairs), ordered rooted binary-tree shapes (by the number of nodes, left/right distinguished) and, from size 1 upwards, triangulations of a convex polygon with two more vertices than the size. They satisfy a convolution recurrence, and the generating function solves to a closed form (both below). There are 14 balanced strings of 4 bracket pairs. Pitfalls Forgetting the intersections. Adding counts of overlapping cases is the most common counting bug. If cases can overlap, you need inclusion–exclusion or a disjoint reformulation. Wrong base cases. The recurrence "each term is the sum of the two before" gives Fibonacci numbers, Lucas numbers or something else entirely, depending on the first two values. Check the recurrence against brute force for lengths 1, 2 and 3. Non-disjoint cases in a recurrence. If your first-step cases overlap, you overcount, just as with the sum rule. Repeated roots. For a genuine second-order recurrence whose characteristic equation has a nonzero double root, the solution needs an extra factor of n (below). Key takeaways Inclusion–exclusion corrects overlapping counts: add singles, subtract pairs, add triples, and so on. It counts derangements (about n!/e of the n! orderings of n items) and onto functions, and anything phrased as "none bad" or "every one covered". Recurrences come from a first decision that splits the objects into smaller instances, which is the same step as designing a DP. Linear recurrences are solved with the characteristic equation; divide-and-conquer ones by unrolling or the master theorem. Generating functions turn sequences into power series, so combining choices becomes polynomial multiplication; the coin-change DP is that multiplication. Further reading Inclusion–exclusion principle — Wikipedia Derangement — Wikipedia Recurrence relation — Wikipedia Generating function — Wikipedia Master theorem — Wikipedia) Catalan number — Wikipedia

sum: Degrees and the handshaking lemma, trees, Euler and Hamilton paths, bipartite graphs and colouring, and planarity with Euler's formula, plus where each shows up in real systems.
x: A graph is a set of things and the connections between them. Road networks, the web, social networks, package dependencies, chip layouts, the call graph of a program and the interference between variables in a compiler are all graphs. The DSA subject covers graph algorithms (BFS, Dijkstra, and so on). This lesson is about the theory: the facts that tell you what is possible before you write any code, and which problems have efficient general algorithms and which have no known polynomial-time solution. Vocabulary A graph is made of vertices (the things, also called nodes) and edges (the connections). In an undirected graph an edge just joins two vertices, with no direction; in a directed graph it points from one vertex to another. A simple graph has no self-loops (an edge from a vertex to itself) and no repeated edges. Unless stated otherwise, "graph" here means simple and undirected. Textbooks write all this in a compact notation that the rest of the lesson uses: For example, a triangle on vertices a, b and c has V = {a, b, c} and E = {{a, b}, {b, c}, {a, c}}, so n = 3 and m = 3. The degree of a vertex v, written deg(v), is the number of edges touching it. In the triangle every vertex has degree 2. A walk is a sequence of vertices joined by edges. A simple path repeats no vertex; a cycle closes a path by returning to its start, with no other repeated vertices. An Euler trail may revisit vertices but never edges. A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. The complete graph Kₙ has an edge between every pair of its n vertices. The number of edges in a complete graph is the number of ways to pick an unordered pair of vertices: This grows with the square of n: a full mesh of 100 servers needs 100 × 99 / 2 = 4,950 links. The handshaking lemma Every edge has two ends, so if you add up the degrees of all the vertices, each edge is counted exactly twice. This holds for every undirected graph: Consequences you can use immediately: The degree sum is even, so the number of vertices with odd degree is always even. There is no graph on 7 vertices where every vertex has degree 3: the degree sum would be 7 × 3 = 21, which is odd, and the edge count would be 21 / 2 = 10.5. Dividing both sides by the number of vertices links edges to the average degree: The handshaking lemma is about undirected edges. In a directed graph the same counting gives: the in-degrees add up to m, and so do the out-degrees. Representations Adjacency list Adjacency matrix --------- Space O(n + m) O(n²) Is u–v an edge? O(deg u) O(1) List neighbours O(deg u) O(n) Good for Sparse graphs Dense graphs In the table, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges and deg u the degree of vertex u. For sparse graphs (far fewer edges than the roughly n²/2 a complete graph would have), adjacency lists save space. The table assumes unsorted neighbor lists; hash-set or sorted representations change membership costs. Trees A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Its edge count is fixed by its vertex count, and the same idea extends to a forest (a graph with no cycles that need not be connected, so it is a collection of separate trees): Why: start with n isolated vertices, which is n separate pieces. Adding an edge between two different pieces (which never creates a cycle) merges them, so the count drops by exactly one per edge. A 10-vertex tree therefore has 9 edges, and a 10-vertex forest with 7 edges has 3 components. This only holds when there are no cycles: an edge added inside a piece makes a cycle and does not reduce the count. For a nonempty finite simple undirected graph with n vertices, these are equivalent: It is connected and acyclic. It is connected and has exactly n − 1 edges. It is acyclic and has exactly n − 1 edges. There is exactly one simple path between every pair of distinct vertices. These equivalences are surprisingly handy. Adding an edge between previously nonadjacent vertices of a tree creates exactly one cycle; removing any edge disconnects it. The forest count is what Kruskal's algorithm and union-find exploit: each edge that joins two different components reduces the count by one. A spanning tree of a connected graph is a tree that uses all its vertices. Network protocols (the Spanning Tree Protocol in Ethernet switching) build one to avoid broadcast loops. How many different trees can be built on a fixed set of labelled vertices is given by Cayley's formula: The 16 for n = 4 splits into 4 stars (pick the centre) and 12 paths (the 24 orderings of the 4 vertices, halved because a path read backwards is the same tree). The count grows very fast: 10 vertices already allow 10⁸ trees. It counts labelled trees; if you ignore labels, 4 vertices only make 2 shapes (the star and the path). Euler paths: every edge once The founding problem of graph theory: in 18th-century Königsberg, could you walk across each of the seven bridges once and only once? Euler modelled land masses as vertices and bridges as edges (a multigraph) and noticed that every time a walk passes through a vertex it uses two edges, one in and one out. Euler's theorem on circuits A connected graph has an Euler circuit (a closed walk using every edge once and only once) if and only if every vertex has even degree. It has an Euler path (not necessarily closed) if and only if exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. With 2, the path must start at one odd vertex and end at the other. Königsberg's four land masses had degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3: four odd vertices, so no such walk exists. (As a check, 5 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 14, twice the 7 bridges, as the handshaking lemma requires.) Checking the condition takes O(n + m), and Hierholzer's algorithm finds the Euler circuit in O(m). For a directed Euler circuit with at least one edge, each vertex must have equal in-degree and out-degree, and all non-isolated vertices must belong to one connected component when directions are ignored. Balance alone is insufficient. Euler paths are used in DNA sequence assembly (de Bruijn graphs of overlapping fragments), in route planning for snowploughs and postal delivery (the Chinese postman problem), and in generating de Bruijn sequences. Those give minimal universal strings for a sliding-window code tester; a keypad that requires Enter, resets after failure or locks out attempts needs a different model. Hamilton paths: every vertex once A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once and only once and returns home. It looks like a small change from Euler, but it's a completely different world: There is no known efficient test. Deciding whether a Hamiltonian cycle exists is NP-complete, as is the decision version of travelling salesman (is there a tour whose total cost is at most a given budget?). Finding a cheapest tour is an NP-hard optimization problem. There are useful sufficient conditions: if they hold, a Hamiltonian cycle is guaranteed, but a graph can have one without meeting them. The best known is Dirac's theorem: For example, K₃,₃ (two groups of 3, every vertex joined to all 3 in the other group) has n = 6 and every degree 3, which is 6 / 2, so Dirac guarantees a Hamiltonian cycle; one is a1, b1, a2, b2, a3, b3, back to a1. The condition is not necessary: a plain cycle on 10 vertices has every degree 2, far below 10 / 2 = 5, and is itself a Hamiltonian cycle. Euler and Hamilton are independent. Two triangles sharing one vertex (a "bowtie") has all degrees even, so it has an Euler circuit, but any cycle through all 5 vertices would have to pass through the shared vertex twice, so there is no Hamiltonian cycle. Spot the trap "Visit every edge once" is linear-time. "Visit every vertex once" is NP-complete. When a problem lands on your desk, figure out which one it really is before reaching for an algorithm. Bipartite graphs and colouring A proper colouring assigns a colour to each vertex so that adjacent vertices differ. The chromatic number is the fewest colours needed. Two bounds pin it down for many graphs: For example, K₄ needs 4 colours, and a cycle on 5 vertices has maximum degree 2, so it needs at most 3 colours (it needs exactly 3, as the list below explains). The second bound is often loose: a star with 100 leaves has maximum degree 100 but needs only 2 colours. A graph is 2-colourable (bipartite) if and only if it has no odd cycle. Even cycles need 2 colours; odd cycles need 3. BFS checks bipartiteness in O(n + m), where m is the number of edges: colour by distance parity and look for an edge between two vertices of the same parity. Deciding 3-colourability is NP-complete. Greedy colouring (go through vertices, give each the smallest colour not used by its neighbours) uses at most Δ + 1 colours, which is where the bound above comes from: when a vertex is coloured, at most Δ neighbours already hold a colour, so one of Δ + 1 colours is always free. It can be far from optimal depending on the order. Colouring shows up wherever conflicting things must be kept apart: Register allocation. Compilers build an interference graph with a vertex per variable and an edge between variables that are live at the same time. Colours are CPU registers. If the fixed graph needs more colours than there are registers, it cannot be allocated as-is. An allocator can spill values to memory or transform live ranges, for example by splitting or rematerializing values. Chaitin and colleagues described an implemented graph-colouring allocator in their 1981 paper Register allocation via coloring. Scheduling. Exams that share a student can't be at the same time: colours are time slots. Frequency assignment. Nearby transmitters need different frequencies. The four colour theorem says every finite simple planar graph can be properly vertex-coloured with at most 4 colours. For maps, this corresponds to connected regions sharing a boundary segment; meeting at one point does not require different colours. Its 1976 proof by Appel and Haken was among the first major proofs to rely on a computer check. Planarity A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane with no edges crossing. For a connected planar drawing, Euler's formula relates vertices, edges and the faces of a drawing (regions, including the outside one): Note that this lesson switches here from n and m to V and E for the counts (earlier, V and E named the sets themselves), because that is how Euler's formula is always written. The formula needs the drawing to be connected; for a drawing in several separate pieces, the 2 becomes 1 plus the number of pieces. Euler's formula also limits how many edges a planar graph can have. For a connected simple plane graph with at least 3 vertices, each face boundary walk has length at least 3. Counting edge sides with multiplicity (a bridge is traversed twice on the same face) gives total boundary length 2E, hence 3F ≤ 2E. Substitute F = 2 − V + E from Euler's formula: If the graph has no triangles (no cycle of length 3), every face boundary has length at least 4. The same steps give a tighter bound: These inequalities give quick proofs of non-planarity. K₅ is the complete graph on 5 vertices; K₃,₃ (the "three houses, three utilities" puzzle) joins each of 3 vertices to each of 3 others and is bipartite, so it has no triangles: Kuratowski's theorem says these two are the only obstacles: a graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K₅ or K₃,₃. Planarity can be tested in linear time (the Hopcroft–Tarjan planarity test, 1974). It matters in chip and PCB layout, where crossing wires need extra layers, and in graph drawing tools. The inequalities only work one way: satisfying E ≤ 3V − 6 does not prove a graph is planar. K₃,₃ has 9 edges, within the general limit 3 × 6 − 6 = 12, yet it is not planar; only the triangle-free bound catches it. Key takeaways The degrees add up to twice the number of edges, so the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. A tree has one fewer edge than vertices and a unique path between any two vertices; a forest's number of components is its vertex count minus its edge count. When all edge-bearing vertices are connected, an undirected Euler circuit exists exactly when all degrees are even; an Euler trail needs 0 or 2 odd vertices. Construction is linear; deciding Hamiltonian-cycle existence is NP-complete. A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd cycle; general colouring is NP-hard but models register allocation and scheduling. In a connected crossing-free drawing, vertices − edges + faces = 2 (Euler's formula). A simple planar graph with at least 3 vertices has at most 3 × vertices − 6 edges; the triangle-free limit of 2 × vertices − 4 is what rules out K₃,₃. sum: Modular arithmetic, Euclid's algorithm and its extended form, modular inverses, primes and primality testing, fast exponentiation, Fermat and Euler, and how they combine into RSA.
x: Number theory underpins public-key systems such as RSA and finite-field or elliptic-curve key exchange. HTTPS can use different TLS authentication and key-exchange modes; RSA is not required for every connection. Even outside cryptography it is everywhere: hash functions, ring buffers, random number generators, checksums and consistent hashing all live in modular arithmetic. This lesson builds up the handful of results that RSA needs, with an algorithm for each, so that by the end you can do RSA by hand on small numbers and understand why it works. Division and remainders Everything starts with whole-number division with a remainder, the kind you learned before decimals. Dividing any integer by a positive integer gives exactly one quotient and one remainder, as long as the remainder is required to lie between 0 and the divisor: For example, 17 = 3 × 5 + 2, so 17 mod 5 = 2. For a negative number the quotient rounds down, not towards zero: −7 = (−3) × 3 + 2, so −7 mod 3 = 2, because the remainder can never be negative. In Python, divmod(a, n) returns the pair (q, r). Negative numbers differ by language Python's % follows the rule above, so -7 % 3 is 2 (and -7 // 3 is -3). Modern C/C++, Java and Go integer division truncates towards zero. JavaScript Number division is floating-point, but its remainder also gives -7 % 3 == -1 (BigInt division truncates). A negative remainder may be an invalid index. For a positive modulus use Java Math.floorMod, or compute r = a % n and add n only when r < 0. Unconditionally adding n in ((a % n) + n) % n can overflow a fixed-width signed integer. Modular arithmetic Two numbers are congruent modulo n when they leave the same remainder after dividing by n. A 12-hour clock is the everyday example: 17:00 and 5 o'clock show the same hand position. This is the equivalence relation from the relations lesson, and its classes are the n residues 0, 1, …, n − 1: every integer is congruent to exactly one of them. Congruence plays nicely with addition and multiplication. If you swap a number for anything congruent to it, sums and products stay congruent: For example, the last digit of 17 × 23 is the last digit of 7 × 3 = 21, which is 1; indeed 17 × 23 = 391. So you can reduce at every step. This is how you compute huge expressions without huge numbers, and how fixed-width hardware arithmetic works: unsigned 64-bit arithmetic in C/C++ wraps modulo 2⁶⁴. Other languages may use checked arithmetic or wider integers; signed C/C++ overflow is not defined as modular wraparound. Here is the trick on the last digit of 7¹⁰⁰ (the last digit is the remainder mod 10). Reduce after each multiplication until the powers repeat: Division is the exception. You can't just cancel a common factor from both sides: "Dividing by a" means multiplying by an inverse of a, which only sometimes exists (see below). Greatest common divisor and Euclid's algorithm For two integers, not both zero, the greatest common divisor (gcd) is the largest positive whole number that divides both. Euclid's algorithm (about 300 BC, and still the one we use) rests on one fact: replacing the larger number by its remainder after dividing by the smaller one doesn't change the gcd. Why it works: a mod b is a − q × b for the quotient q, so any number that divides both a and b also divides the remainder, and vice versa; the two pairs have exactly the same common divisors. We use the programming convention gcd(0, 0) = 0. For positive inputs, Euclid's algorithm uses O(1 + log min(a, b)) remainder steps; one operand zero is an immediate case. This counts arithmetic operations, not their growing bit cost. The worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers, as Lamé showed in 1844. For 2048-bit numbers that is a few thousand iterations at most. Bézout and the extended algorithm Bézout's identity says the gcd can always be built from the two numbers by multiplying each by some integer (possibly negative) and adding: The extended Euclidean algorithm finds x and y by tracking how each remainder is built from a and b. This recursive teaching version accepts non-negative integers; large worst-case inputs can exceed Python's recursion limit, so use an iterative implementation for those cases: Modular inverses The modular inverse of a modulo n is the number that multiplies a to give 1, in remainder arithmetic. It plays the role that 1/a plays for ordinary fractions: Worked example: the inverse of 7 modulo 40. If the gcd is bigger than 1 there is no inverse: 6 has none modulo 10, because every multiple of 6 is even and so leaves an even remainder, never 1. Python 3.8+ does this for you: pow(7, -1, 40) returns 23, and raises ValueError if no inverse exists. When the modulus is a prime, every nonzero residue has an inverse. That makes the residues modulo a prime a field: addition, subtraction and multiplication are defined, and division by nonzero residues is possible. Elliptic curves and Shamir secret sharing can use prime fields; binary extension fields are another option. Reed–Solomon codes work over finite fields, with GF(2⁸) a common byte-oriented choice. GF(2⁸) is not ordinary integer arithmetic modulo 256. Primes A prime number has exactly two positive divisors, 1 and itself. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says every integer above 1 factors into primes in exactly one way (up to order). There are infinitely many primes (Euclid again), and the prime number theorem says how common they are: So a random 1024-bit odd number is prime with probability roughly 1 in 355. That is why generating RSA primes by "pick random, test, repeat" is quick: a few hundred tries on average. Finding and testing primes Trial division: try every divisor up to the square root of the number (a factor above the square root would need a partner below it). Fine for small numbers, hopeless for 300-digit numbers. Sieve of Eratosthenes: list all primes up to a limit N in O(N log log N) time by crossing out multiples of each prime. Miller–Rabin: a probabilistic test. For a fixed odd composite number, each round with an independently, uniformly chosen base wrongly reports "probably prime" with probability at most 1/4. OpenSSL documents trial division followed by Miller–Rabin rounds; its round policy is version-dependent. The rounds are independent, so their failure chances multiply: This is a conditional false-pass bound for one given composite, not the probability that a number which passed is composite (that also depends on how candidates are chosen). Testing primality is easy; factoring a product of two large primes is believed to be hard. Factoring an RSA modulus breaks its private-key protection, but hardness of factoring alone is not a proof that every RSA-based scheme is secure. Fast modular exponentiation Computing a power modulo n by multiplying the base by itself once per unit of the exponent is impossible when the exponent has 600 digits. Square-and-multiply uses the binary digits of the exponent instead: square repeatedly to get the base to the powers 1, 2, 4, 8, …, and multiply together the ones whose bit is 1, reducing mod n after each step. Each bit of the exponent costs one squaring, plus one extra multiplication if the bit is 1, so the work grows with the number of bits, not the size of the exponent: So square-and-multiply needs O(log e) multiplications, where e is the exponent. Tracing modpow(3, 13, 7): the bits of 13 are read from the lowest, a is the current square of the base mod 7, and result is the running product: Python's built-in pow(a, e, n) performs efficient modular exponentiation and also supports invertible negative exponents. The teaching routine above is for a non-negative exponent and a positive modulus and is not constant-time cryptographic code. Fermat and Euler Fermat's little theorem tells you what happens when you raise a number to the power one less than a prime: So exponents can be reduced modulo p − 1: every block of p − 1 in the exponent contributes a factor of 1. For example, the remainder of 3²⁰⁰ divided by 13: (Here 3³ = 27 already leaves remainder 1 when divided by 13, which gives the same answer faster: 200 = 66 × 3 + 2, and 3² = 9.) Euler's totient counts how many of the numbers from 1 to n share no common factor greater than 1 with n. Euler's theorem generalises Fermat to any modulus: For example, the numbers from 1 to 10 coprime to 10 are 1, 3, 7 and 9, so the totient of 10 is 4, matching (2 − 1) × (5 − 1) = 4. And 3⁴ = 81, which leaves remainder 1 when divided by 10, as Euler's theorem predicts. For a prime modulus the totient is p − 1, so Euler's theorem becomes Fermat's. Fermat's test can be fooled The converse of Fermat's theorem is false: passing the test does not prove a number prime. 561 is a Carmichael number: composite, yet it passes Fermat's test for every base that shares no factor with it (see below). Miller–Rabin adds stronger checks; base 2 rejects 561, but a single round is not guaranteed to reject every Carmichael number. RSA Now everything fits together. Key generation For this mathematical two-prime construction, pick two distinct odd primes. Production key sizes and generation requirements must follow the chosen library and current deployment policy. Multiply them to get the public modulus, and compute its totient (formula below). Choose a public exponent of at least 3, below the modulus, that shares no factor with the totient. The conventional choice is 65537 when it satisfies these requirements; the small example below uses 17. Compute the private exponent: the inverse of the public exponent modulo the totient, with the extended Euclidean algorithm. Public key: the modulus and the public exponent. Private key: the private exponent (and the two primes, kept secret). In symbols, with a message encoded as a number smaller than the modulus: Why it works: d was chosen so that e × d is one more than a multiple of the totient. Euler's theorem then collapses all those multiples to 1: (The case where the message shares a factor with the modulus also works, via the Chinese remainder theorem.) A complete example with tiny primes: Security connection: knowing the RSA primes p and q lets an attacker compute a private exponent. However, inverting the RSA function has not been proved equivalent to factoring, and attacks can target weak encoding, key generation, side channels or protocols without factoring n. Secure RSA schemes require their own assumptions and implementation protections. Shor's algorithm would factor n on a sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computer. Evidence gap No universal RSA latency or hardware attack-time estimate is supplied: this lesson has no reproducible benchmark or deployment threat model for one. Textbook RSA is not secure RSA The bare formula above is deterministic (the same message always encrypts the same way) and malleable (multiplying ciphertexts multiplies plaintexts). Real systems use padding such as OAEP for encryption and PSS for signatures, and generate keys with a cryptographically secure RNG (secrets, not random). Never implement RSA yourself for production use. Implementations use the Chinese remainder theorem to decrypt: compute modulo each prime separately (with half-size numbers) and combine, which reduces operand sizes and can accelerate decryption; the speedup depends on arithmetic, hardware and implementation. Finite-field Diffie–Hellman uses modular exponentiation. Recovering its shared secret from public group elements is the computational Diffie–Hellman problem; solving discrete logarithms would solve it, but the two hardness assumptions are not known to be equivalent. Authentication and the full protocol introduce additional requirements. Key takeaways Modular arithmetic lets you reduce after every addition and multiplication; unsigned 64-bit C/C++ arithmetic wraps modulo 2⁶⁴; other language/type rules differ. Watch out for negative % in C-family languages. Euclid's algorithm computes the gcd in a number of steps proportional to the number of digits of the smaller input; the extended version gives Bézout coefficients. A number has an inverse modulo the modulus exactly when they share no common factor (gcd 1); Python's pow(a, -1, n) finds it. Square-and-multiply computes a modular power in a number of multiplications proportional to the exponent's bit length; Fermat and Euler let you reduce exponents. RSA: the modulus is the product of two secret primes, and the private exponent is the inverse of the public exponent modulo the totient; factoring the modulus breaks the key, but secure use also depends on the scheme assumptions, encoding, randomness and implementation. sum: Sample spaces, events, the axioms, complements, independence and conditional probability, with the counting tricks and reliability sums engineers use every day.
x: Probability is the maths of uncertainty. In computer science it turns up everywhere: hash collisions, randomised algorithms, network packet loss, cache hit ratios, the chance that three replicas fail at once, and every A/B test your product team runs. This lesson builds the vocabulary from first principles. Everything later in the module (Bayes, expectation, distributions) rests on the ideas here, especially conditional probability. Sample spaces and events A random experiment is anything with an uncertain outcome: rolling a die, sending a packet, picking a random pivot. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes; formulas write it as the Greek capital letter omega. For one die, the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. A random event (usually just called an event) is a subset of the sample space. "Roll an even number" is the event {2, 4, 6}. A probability P assigns each event a number between 0 and 1. In a finite nonempty sample space, when every outcome is equally likely (a fair die, a uniformly random key), probability is just counting: the number of outcomes you are interested in, divided by the number of outcomes there are. Rolling two independent fair six-sided dice gives 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Six of them sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). This only works when the outcomes really are equally likely. If they are not (a loaded die, a skewed traffic mix), you must weight each outcome by its own probability instead of counting. Order matters when counting (1,6) and (6,1) are different outcomes. A classic mistake is to treat the 21 unordered pairs as equally likely: that gives the mixed pair {1,6} probability 1/21 instead of 2/36, or gives sum 7 probability 3/21 instead of 6/36. They are not: a double like (3,3) can happen one way, a mixed pair two ways. The axioms and the rules that follow In general probability spaces, events belong to a specified collection of measurable subsets. For finite examples here, every subset can be an event. Kolmogorov's axioms are three rules every probability must obey: no probability is negative, something always happens, and for events that cannot happen together (disjoint events) probabilities add. The third rule holds for any countable collection of pairwise disjoint events; for two events it reads as the last line below. From these three come the everyday rules. The complement of A is the event "A does not happen"; the addition rule (union rule) handles "A or B" when the two can overlap; the union bound is a cruder but always-safe version of it. The addition rule (inclusion–exclusion) subtracts the overlap, which would otherwise be counted twice. Of the numbers 1 to 100, 50 are divisible by 2, 33 by 3, and 16 by both (the multiples of 6). The union bound drops the subtraction. It is crude but always safe, and it is the workhorse of algorithm analysis: if each of several bad events is individually unlikely, the chance that any of them happens is at most the total. For example, 100 hash lookups that each fail with probability at most 0.0001 fail one or more times with probability at most 100 × 0.0001 = 0.01. The bound becomes useless once n × p exceeds 1, because every probability is at most 1 anyway. The complement trick "At least one" questions are almost always easier through the complement. What is the chance of at least one six in four independent rolls of a fair six-sided die? Counting directly means handling one six, two sixes and so on. Instead, work out the chance of no six at all (each roll avoids a six with probability 5/6, and independent rolls multiply), then subtract from 1. This is the same calculation as "what is the chance at least one of my 4 requests hits a slow server?" It relies on the rolls (or requests) being independent; correlated failures break the multiplication. Conditional probability Often you learn something that shrinks the sample space. When P(B) > 0, the conditional probability of A given B is: The formula fails when P(B) = 0: you cannot condition on something that never happens, and the division would be by zero. Two dice, sum is 8 Given that two independent fair six-sided dice sum to 8, what is the chance the first die shows 3? The outcomes summing to 8 are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2). That is 5 outcomes, and one has a first die of 3. Rearranging gives the multiplication rule, which is how you compute probabilities of sequences (the conditional on the right requires P(A) > 0): Draw two cards from a uniformly shuffled standard 52-card deck without replacement. The chance both are aces is: The second fraction is conditional because the first draw changed the deck. The law of total probability If B₁, B₂,... form a countable partition of the sample space into disjoint pieces (every outcome lies in exactly one piece), you can find P(A) by working out A's chance inside each piece and weighting by how likely each piece is. Pieces with zero probability are left out. Suppose 70% of your traffic hits region X with a 1% error rate and 30% hits region Y with a 4% error rate. This rule is the denominator of Bayes' theorem in the next lesson. Independence A and B are independent events if knowing one tells you nothing about the other: Independence is a property of the numbers, not of physical separation, and it can be surprising. With two independent fair six-sided dice, "first die is even" and "sum is 7" are independent, but "first die is even" and "sum is 8" are not: The intuition: whatever the first die shows, exactly one second-die value makes 7, but a first die of 1 can never make 8. Disjoint is not independent If A and B are disjoint and both have positive probability, they are dependent: knowing A happened tells you B certainly did not. Reliability: the engineer's favourite use Independence makes system reliability easy to estimate. System availability is the fraction of time a component is up and serving. In a series system (components in series: every component must work), multiply the availabilities. A request that passes through three services, each independently up 99.9% of the time, in a model with no other causes of failure: So the chain is down about 0.3% of the time, roughly three times worse than any single service. Long chains of dependencies erode availability. With parallel redundancy (components in parallel: any one working replica is sufficient, with ideal routing and failover), multiply the failure probabilities. Three replicas, each down 1% of the time independently: Real failures are correlated The six-nines figure assumes the replicas fail independently. Put them in the same rack, region, power feed or software version and a single event takes them all down. Separating replicas across failure domains can reduce shared infrastructure risks, while a bad deployment across all replicas can still defeat redundancy. When an estimate looks too good, the independence assumption is usually the culprit. Checking your answers by simulation When you are unsure of a calculation, simulate it. For independent trials from the specified model, the sample frequency converges to the model probability as the number of trials grows. This checks arithmetic against a simulation; it does not establish that the model describes the real system. For small sample spaces you can be exact instead, by enumerating every outcome: How close should the simulated fraction be? Each simulated run is a Bernoulli trial (a yes/no experiment), and the typical size of the error in the estimated fraction is its standard error: This is not a guarantee of three correct decimal places: the estimate can stray a few standard errors. Rare events (tiny p) can require far more trials for small relative error; exact enumeration is preferable when feasible. Common pitfalls Assuming equal likelihood. Counting outcomes only works if each is equally likely. "Either it rains or it doesn't" is not 50/50. Confusing "A given B" with "B given A". The chance a test is positive given disease is not the chance of disease given a positive test. The next lesson is entirely about this. Assuming independence by default. Retries to the same overloaded server, disks from the same batch, and users in the same household can be correlated. The gambler's fallacy. Independent events have no memory. After five heads, a fair coin is still 50/50. Key takeaways In a finite nonempty sample space with equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes; count ordered outcomes carefully. Use the complement for "at least one": one minus the chance of none. The conditional probability of A given B is the chance of both divided by the chance of B. It requires B to have positive probability and restricts the sample space to B; the multiplication rule chains conditionals. Independence means the chance of both equals the product of the chances. Disjoint events with positive probability are dependent. Series availability multiplies uptimes; parallel availability multiplies failure probabilities, but only if failures are truly independent. Simulate or enumerate to check any answer you are unsure of. Further reading Probability axioms — Wikipedia Conditional probability — Wikipedia Independence (probability theory) — Wikipedia) Mathematics for Computer Science (MIT OCW 6.042J) Introduction to Probability — Grinstead and Snell (free PDF) Evidence gap The previous precise attribution of the four-roll example to a particular 1654 exchange is omitted because that historical detail was not independently established in this review. The calculation is unchanged.

t: Bayes' theorem and the base-rate fallacy
sum: How to turn the chance of the evidence given a cause into the chance of the cause given the evidence, how rare events and false-positive rates affect the meaning of an alert, and how naive Bayes spam filters work.
x: In a hypothetical example, your fraud model detects 98% of fraud and only flags 1% of honest payments. A payment is flagged. How likely is it to be fraud? The 98% detection rate is not the answer. Under this model, if 1 in 1,000 payments is fraudulent, the answer is about 9%. More than nine out of ten alerts are false alarms. Ignoring the base rate when interpreting that detection rate is the base-rate fallacy, and Bayes' theorem is the tool that fixes it. It matters for monitoring, intrusion detection, spam filtering, medical tests, ML classifiers and debugging alike. The theorem Bayes' theorem answers one question: you know how likely the evidence is if a cause is true, and you want how likely the cause is now that you have seen the evidence. It comes straight from the multiplication rule of the previous lesson, which writes the chance of "A and B" in two ways. Both events need positive probability for the conditionals to make sense. Renamed for real use, with H a hypothesis (a possible cause) and E the evidence you observed, each part has a name: The denominator comes from the law of total probability: the evidence can arise when H is true or when it is false. That second term, the false positives from the huge "not H" population, is what intuition forgets. The classic test example In a hypothetical probability model, a condition affects 1% of people and a test has: Sensitivity (true positive rate) 99%: an ill person tests positive 99% of the time. False positive rate 5%: a healthy person tests positive 5% of the time (so the specificity, the chance a healthy person tests negative, is 95%). You test positive. What is the chance you are ill? Only about 1 in 6 positives is genuinely ill, despite 99% sensitivity. Sensitivity and overall accuracy are different quantities. Natural frequencies make it obvious Use expected counts in a hypothetical group of 10,000 people: The positives are 99 + 495 = 594 people, and 99 of them are ill: The 495 false positives swamp the 99 true positives because the healthy group is 99 times larger. The table of counts makes the numerator and denominator explicit; its entries are expected counts, not guaranteed outcomes in every sample. Evidence gap The previous broad claim about how much better people reason with counts is omitted here because its study populations, tasks and effect sizes were not established in this review. No population-wide claim is needed for the arithmetic. The base-rate fallacy in engineering The same arithmetic applies to anything that detects rare events. Fraud alerts 1,000,000 payments, 0.1% fraudulent, the model catches 98% of fraud and flags 1% of legitimate ones. - Fraud: 1,000, of which 980 flagged. - Legitimate: 999,000, of which 9,990 flagged. Under these fixed rates, a randomly selected alert has fraud probability about 8.9%; a finite queue need not match that fraction exactly. The same shape shows up in: Intrusion detection. When attacks are rare enough relative to the false positive rate, benign connections can generate most alerts. The operational effect depends on traffic volume and triage capacity. Pager alerts. A noisy alert that fires on harmless blips teaches on-call engineers to dismiss it. The Google SRE book's advice to alert on symptoms that matter to users is partly a base-rate argument. Flaky tests. Suppose 1 in 500 builds contains a bug, the test detects every such bug, and it also fails on 2% of bug-free builds. Then only about 9% of failures mean a real bug (worked below). This is a hypothetical model, not a judgement about a particular failed build. ML classifiers on imbalanced data. A model that says "never fraud" is 99.9% accurate and useless. Report precision and recall, not accuracy. Precision is the posterior In machine learning (ML) terms, the chance a case is actually positive given that it was predicted positive is precision (also called positive predictive value), and the chance it is predicted positive given that it is actually positive is recall (sensitivity, the true positive rate). Holding sensitivity and false positive rate fixed, changing the base rate changes precision. Recall is a conditional rate; it can also change if the population shift changes the mix of positive cases. What actually improves an alert? Take the hypothetical test (1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity, 5% false positive rate, posterior 16.7%) and vary one thing at a time, keeping the other conditional rates fixed: Change Chance ill if positive ------ Baseline 16.7% Sensitivity 99% to 100% 16.8% False positives 5% to 1% 50% Test only a group with 10% prevalence 68.8% In this example, false positives dominate and sensitivity is already near 100%, so that small sensitivity increase barely helps. Reducing the false positive rate or testing a higher-prevalence population raises precision if other rates stay fixed. A real filtering step can also change sensitivity and false positive rate; re-estimate them on the selected population. Low prevalence alone does not imply mostly false alerts: a detector with zero false positives is a counterexample. The odds form: Bayes in your head Odds compare the chance something happens with the chance it does not. A probability of 1% is odds of 1: 99 ("1 to 99"). In odds form Bayes becomes a single multiplication by the likelihood ratio (LR), how many times more likely the evidence is when H is true than when it is false. This needs the false positive rate to be above 0. For the test, prior odds are 1: 99: Same answer as before, with no denominators to work out. Likelihood ratios multiply when the evidence pieces are conditionally independent both given H and given not H. Under that assumption, a second positive test multiplies the odds by 19.8 again: Yesterday's posterior is today's prior. This sequential updating is the heart of Bayesian reasoning. Naive Bayes classifiers A spam filter wants the chance an email is spam given the words in it. Bayes flips this round to the chance of those words given spam, which is easy to estimate by counting words in labelled email. Ham is the usual name for legitimate, non-spam email. The naive assumption is that words are independent given the class. Then each word contributes its own factor, and the denominator (the same for both classes) can be dropped when you only want to know which class wins: Compute the score for spam and for ham, and pick whichever is larger. Real words can remain correlated even within a class (for example, words in fixed phrases), so the naive assumption is an approximation and posterior scores may be poorly calibrated. Paul Graham’s 2002 "A Plan for Spam" describes a related Bayesian filter with token-selection and scoring choices beyond the simple model here. Two practical details matter: Work in logs. Multiplying hundreds of small probabilities underflows to 0.0 in floating point. Summing finite logs avoids that product underflow and preserves the mathematical ranking; floating-point rounding can still affect close scores. Smooth the counts. If "invoice" never appeared in your spam training set, its estimated chance in spam is 0, and one word vetoes everything else. Laplace (add-one) smoothing adds 1 to each token count in a fixed vocabulary and normalises by the total count plus vocabulary size. Every token in that vocabulary then has positive probability in every class; out-of-vocabulary tokens need a separate policy. The log step and the smoothing step, written out: For example, if "invoice" appears 0 times in 50,000 spam words with a 10,000-token vocabulary, the smoothed estimate is (0 + 1) / (50,000 + 10,000) ≈ 0.0000167 instead of 0. A small number, but no longer a veto. Pitfalls Confusing the inverse. The chance of the evidence given the hypothesis and the chance of the hypothesis given the evidence are not equal in general. In court this is the prosecutor's fallacy: "the chance of a DNA match if innocent is 1 in a million, so the chance he is innocent is 1 in a million." In a hypothetical population of 10 million innocent people each with that marginal match probability, the expected number of matches is 10; the actual count and posterior need further assumptions. Ignoring the prior. "The test is 99% accurate" says nothing about the chance a positive person is ill until you know prevalence. Assuming tests are independent. Rerunning the same test on the same sample often repeats the same error. Using unchanged per-test likelihood ratios requires conditional independence both with and without the condition. Otherwise use the likelihood of the new evidence conditional on what was already observed. Priors of exactly 0 or 1. Within a fixed model, conditioning on positive-probability evidence preserves probability-zero and probability-one events. Evidence the model assigns probability zero makes the elementary update undefined; revise the model rather than dividing by zero. Key takeaways Bayes: the posterior equals the likelihood times the prior, divided by the overall chance of the evidence, which comes from the law of total probability. With rare events, even a small false positive rate can make most alerts false; calculate the posterior from all three rates. Natural frequencies (counts out of 10,000) make Bayesian reasoning easy to explain. Reducing false positives or raising prevalence improves precision when the other rates stay fixed; the size of a sensitivity improvement matters too. Odds form: posterior odds are prior odds times the likelihood ratio; likelihood ratios multiply under the appropriate conditional-independence assumptions. Naive Bayes multiplies per-feature likelihoods; compute in logs and smooth zero counts. sum: Random variables, expected value and variance, and linearity of expectation with indicator variables, the trick behind most average-case analyses in algorithms.
x: Average-case analysis asks questions like: how many comparisons does randomised quicksort make on average? How many swaps does insertion sort do on a random input? How many servers sit idle if jobs are assigned at random? Each answer is an expected value, and nearly all of them are found with one remarkably powerful tool: linearity of expectation. This lesson builds up to it. Random variables A random variable is a function that assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. Despite the name, it is neither random nor a variable: it is a rule. Roll two dice; X = their sum. X maps (3, 5) to 8. Hash n keys into a table; Y = the number of collisions. Run quicksort on a random permutation; C = the number of comparisons. The probability distribution (or probability mass function, PMF) of a discrete random variable lists, for each value it can take, the probability that it takes that value. For the sum of two fair dice, the PMF at 8 is 5/36, because 5 of the 36 ordered pairs sum to 8. Expected value The expectation (expected value, or mean) of a random variable is the probability-weighted average of its values: each value counts in proportion to how likely it is. For a discrete variable it is a sum over every value; we need the sum of the absolute values to be finite, so the answer does not depend on the order of adding. For one fair die, each face has probability 1/6: The expected value need not be a possible outcome: you never roll 3.5. For independent, identically distributed repetitions with finite absolute expectation, sample averages converge to it by the law of large numbers. Some distributions have no finite expectation. Waiting for success: the geometric case A request succeeds with the same probability p (more than 0, at most 1) on each independent attempt. How many attempts does it take on average? The number of attempts T has a geometric distribution, and: A neat derivation: with probability p you finish after 1 attempt; otherwise you have used 1 attempt and are back where you started, because independent attempts have no memory. Variance For a variable with a finite second moment (finite expected square), the mean says where values centre; variance says how spread out they are. It is the average squared distance from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root, which is back in the original units. For one fair die: Two systems with the same mean latency can feel completely different if one has much higher variance. Engineers care about the spread as much as the centre (lesson 6 returns to this with percentiles). Linearity of expectation For random variables X and Y with finite absolute expectations, and constants a and b: The crucial point: this holds even when X and Y are dependent. No independence assumption is needed. That is what makes it so powerful: you can break a complicated count into simple pieces, find each piece's expectation separately, and add, without ever working out how the pieces interact. For example, the sum of two dice has expectation 3.5 + 3.5 = 7, and twice one die plus 1 has expectation 2 × 3.5 + 1 = 8. What does NOT hold in general Products, sums of variances and non-linear functions do not behave like linearity. The three rules below are the true versions. More generally, the expectation of a non-linear function of X need not equal that function of the expectation, though it can in particular cases. The pitfall section at the end shows the cost. Indicator variables An indicator variable for an event A is 1 if A happens and 0 otherwise. Its expectation is just a probability: The recipe for "expected number of things that happen" is: Write the count as a sum of indicators, one per thing. Find each indicator's probability. Add them up, by linearity. Example: fixed points of a random permutation At least one person (n of them) checks their hat; the hats are handed back in a uniformly random order. How many people expect to get their own hat? A person who gets their own hat back is a fixed point of the shuffle. Each person's hat is equally likely to be any of the n hats, so each person gets their own with probability 1/n. The answer is 1 for every positive n, whether 3 people or 3 million. With two or more people the indicators are dependent (if all but one have their own hats, the last must too), but linearity does not care. Example: idle servers A load balancer assigns n jobs to n servers (at least one of each), each job independently to a uniformly random server. How many servers get no job? Each job misses a given server with probability 1 − 1/n, and the n jobs choose independently, so the server is idle with probability (1 − 1/n)^n. Add one indicator per server: With 100 jobs and 100 servers, the expected number of idle servers is about 36.6; other servers may receive one or several jobs. Random assignment is far from balanced, which motivates the power of two choices technique: in the sequential model with n unit jobs, n initially empty servers, independent uniform candidate choices and current load information, picking the less loaded of two candidates dramatically reduces the maximum load with high probability as n grows. Real scheduling systems need their own workload and measurement assumptions. Example: inversions and insertion sort An inversion (array inversion) in an array is a pair of positions where the earlier element is bigger than the later one. The adjacent-swap version of insertion sort performs exactly one swap per inversion; the usual shifting version instead performs one rightward shift per inversion. For a uniformly random permutation of distinct values, each pair is equally likely to be in either order, so each is inverted with probability 1/2. For n = 100 that is 2,475 swaps on average. Using Θ (big-Theta, "grows exactly as fast as, up to constant factors") with n the array length, that is Θ(n²) even in the average case, only half the worst case. Example: how often does the running maximum change? For a uniformly random permutation of distinct finite numbers, the i-th element is the largest of the first i with probability 1/i (each of the first i is equally likely to be the biggest). Adding one indicator per position: The harmonic number H_n turns up all over algorithm analysis, because it grows like the logarithm of n. Example: coupon collector You independently choose a shard uniformly from n shards (at least one) on each request, with replacement, until every shard has been hit one or more times. When you have seen k shards, a new one turns up with probability (n − k)/n, so the wait for it is geometric with mean n/(n − k). By linearity, add the waits: This also tells you how long random testing takes to cover every case, or how many random probes find every node. (The shortcut n ln(n) leaves out about 0.577 × n requests, so it undercounts noticeably for modest n: 50 × ln(50) ≈ 196, about 13% below the exact 225.) Checking by simulation Markov's inequality: a free tail bound Expectation alone gives a crude but guaranteed bound on the tail probability, the chance of a large value. If mean request latency is 20 ms, at most 20% of requests can take 100 ms or more. The true tail can be smaller or attain this bound. For a useful finite bound, Markov needs a nonnegative variable and a known finite mean. It is used to turn expected running time into a "with probability at least 1/2" statement. Chebyshev's inequality bounds deviations in both directions using the variance: It need not improve every Markov bound at every threshold. Pitfall: the mean of a ratio The fact that the expectation of a function need not equal the function of the expectation matters in practice. Each download independently selects a speed of 10 MB/s or 90 MB/s with equal probability and keeps that speed for the entire transfer. The average speed is 50 MB/s, so you might predict a 100 MB download takes 2 s. But the expected time is: The slower transfers contribute more to the mean duration. This model differs from a single transfer whose speed fluctuates rapidly with equal time spent at each rate. When you average rates, decide whether you mean per unit time or per unit of work. Key takeaways A random variable assigns a number to each outcome; its expected value is the probability-weighted average of its values, and iid sample averages converge to it. Variance (mean of the square minus the square of the mean) measures spread; finite variances add over pairwise uncorrelated variables; independence is sufficient. Linearity (the expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations) holds even for dependent variables. Count with indicators: the expected number of events that happen is the sum of their probabilities. Classic results: expected fixed points 1; idle bins about n/e; inversions n(n − 1)/4; record updates the harmonic number; coupon collector n times the harmonic number; geometric wait 1/p. Markov's inequality gives a tail bound from the mean alone; never assume the expectation of a non-linear function equals the function of the expectation.
