sum: RP, coRP, ZPP and BPP, error amplification, Freivalds and polynomial identity testing, the conjecture that P = BPP, and BQP with what Shor and Grover do and don't show, keeping proven results apart from beliefs.
x: Some of the most useful algorithms flip coins. Miller–Rabin is widely used in probable-prime generation, randomised quicksort illustrates efficient expected-time sorting, and hashing with random seeds defends against adversarial inputs. Randomness also gives us algorithms for problems where no deterministic polynomial algorithm is known at all. Quantum computers go further: they manipulate amplitudes that can interfere. This lesson looks at both through complexity classes, and keeps a careful line between what is proven and what is believed. Two kinds of randomised algorithm Las Vegas: always correct, running time is random. Randomised quicksort with distinct keys and uniform random pivots: always sorts, in an expected O(n log n) comparisons, where n is the number of keys. Monte Carlo: a bounded running-time guarantee, but some chance of a wrong answer. Actual running time can still vary. Miller–Rabin: may call a composite "probably prime". The error probability is over the algorithm's own coin flips, for every input. No assumption about the input being random is needed. The classes RP, coRP and BPP use a worst-case polynomial time bound; ZPP uses expected polynomial time. Class If answer is yes If answer is no --------- RP accept w.p. ≥ 1/2 always reject coRP always accept reject w.p. ≥ 1/2 BPP accept w.p. ≥ 2/3 reject w.p. ≥ 2/3 ZPP never wrong expected poly time The same definitions in symbols, where Pr[...] is the probability over the algorithm's own coin flips: coRP swaps the roles (never wrongly rejects a yes-instance; rejects each no-instance with probability at least 1/2). ZPP sits exactly where the one-sided classes overlap: The constants 1/2 and 2/3 don't matter, thanks to amplification. Amplification One-sided error (RP). Run the algorithm several times and accept if any run accepts. A no-instance is never accepted; a yes-instance is missed only if every run misses: Two-sided error (BPP). Run the algorithm an odd number of times and take the majority answer. The majority is wrong only when at least half of the runs are wrong: The code below evaluates the same sum, starting from error 1/3: So BPP with error 2 to the power −100 is the same class as BPP with error 1/3. The mathematical error bound assumes independent random choices and correct execution; it is not a hardware-reliability estimate. Randomness in action Freivalds: checking a matrix product Multiplying two n × n matrices naively costs about n³ multiplications; subcubic algorithms also exist. The comparison below is with naive multiplication, not a claim about the current best exponent. Checking a claimed product is cheaper: using exact integer or field arithmetic, pick a random vector of 0s and 1s and multiply it through both sides. If C is wrong, a single trial exposes it with probability at least 1/2, so the chance that t independent trials all miss is at most 2 to the power −t (about one in a million for t = 20). For bad, the only wrong entry is at row 1, column 1 (0-indexed), so a trial catches it exactly when the random vector's entry r[1] is 1, with probability exactly 1/2. Content gap: empirical measurement The previous measured detection-rate claim has been omitted because no reproducible run record was available to verify it. The probability calculation above follows directly from the two equally likely values of r[1]. With 20 trials, bad slips through with probability 2 to the power −20, about one in a million. Polynomial identity testing Given an arithmetic circuit (a network of additions and multiplications) computing a polynomial in many variables, is that polynomial identically zero, meaning every coefficient cancels? Expanding it can produce exponentially many terms. The Schwartz–Zippel lemma says a random evaluation almost never lands on a root of a nonzero polynomial: So evaluate at one random point: if the result is nonzero, the polynomial is certainly nonzero. Repeating with independent points multiplies the bounds. The lemma needs S chosen from a coefficient field (or an integral domain) and the degree known in advance. So polynomial identity testing is in coRP, and no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is known. Kabanets and Impagliazzo (2004) showed that derandomising it would imply circuit lower bounds that nobody can currently prove. Primality: a derandomisation story Miller–Rabin declares a composite "probably prime" with probability at most 1/4 per random base, and independent bases multiply: This put PRIMES in coRP (composites are detected with one-sided error) decades ago. In 2002 the AKS algorithm put PRIMES in P. Practice still uses Miller–Rabin: it's much faster. How BPP relates to the rest The proven containments: Why each holds: The chain and RP inside NP. A zero-error algorithm can be cut off and made one-sided; one-sided error is a special case of two-sided. For RP, an accepting coin sequence is a certificate, since no coin sequence makes it accept a no-instance. BPP inside PSPACE. Try every coin sequence one after another, count acceptances and reuse the space. BPP inside Σ₂ ∩ Π₂ (Sipser, Gács and Lautemann, 1983). So if P equals NP, the whole polynomial hierarchy collapses to P and P equals BPP. BPP inside P/poly, counted below. Adleman (1978) proved it for one-sided error (RP); Bennett and Gill (1981) extended it to BPP, and the result is often called Adleman's theorem. The coin string it finds is non-uniform advice, not a known efficient way to find it. Adleman's argument first amplifies the error below 2 to the power −n for inputs of n bits, then applies a union bound (the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances): Open, and surprising: whether BPP is contained in NP. Nobody has proved that randomised algorithms can be simulated by short certificates. Conjectured: P equals BPP. Impagliazzo and Wigderson (1997) proved a conditional version: The hypothesis is an unproven circuit lower bound, so the result is conditional. Under widely believed hardness assumptions, randomness gives at most a polynomial speed-up for decision problems. The primality story fits that pattern. What "P = BPP" would and wouldn't mean It wouldn't make randomness useless: randomised algorithms are often simpler or faster by a polynomial factor, and randomness is essential in cryptography, distributed protocols and sampling. It would mean randomness can't turn exponential into polynomial for decision problems. Quantum: BQP A quantum computer on a register of qubits has a state described by complex amplitudes, one per possible bit string. Quantum gates update all of them at once, and measurement returns a single outcome: The power isn't "trying everything in parallel"; measurement gives you one outcome. It is interference: arranging for amplitudes of wrong answers to cancel and right answers to reinforce. BQP is the set of decision problems solvable by a polynomial-time-uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits with error at most 1/3 (amplifiable, as for BPP). What's proven: BQP inside PSPACE (Bernstein and Vazirani, 1993): sum the amplitudes path by path, reusing space. BQP inside PP (Adleman, DeMarrais and Huang, 1997). That last containment is why a classical-versus-quantum separation is so hard to prove: So proving BQP and BPP different would prove P and PSPACE different, which is far beyond current techniques. This rules out claiming a proven separation of BQP from BPP. It does not rule out proven query-complexity advantages or smaller speed-ups within polynomial time. Shor and Grover Shor (1994) factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time on a quantum computer. The associated factoring decision problem is in BQP; Shor also recovers the factors. It is not known to be outside BPP; the best known classical algorithm (the number field sieve) is sub-exponential. This breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography once large fault-tolerant machines exist, which is why NIST standardised post-quantum schemes such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203) in 2024. Published resource estimates for RSA-2048 have fallen over time (Gidney's 2025 estimate is under a million noisy qubits running for under a week). This is a dated resource estimate under stated hardware assumptions, not a measurement of currently available machines. Grover (1996) searches unstructured items with about the square root of the number of queries a classical search needs (below). This is proven optimal for black-box search (Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani, 1997). For brute-force SAT it is a quadratic speed-up, still exponential. Quantum computers are not believed to solve NP-complete problems efficiently Factoring is in both NP and coNP and not believed NP-complete. Grover's bound shows that any quantum algorithm treating SAT as a black box needs about the square root of the 2-to-the-n brute-force steps (n variables). Whether NP is contained in BQP is open, but it is widely believed false. Evidence about BQP Oracle separations: Raz and Tal (2018) found an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained in the polynomial hierarchy. This is evidence, not proof, about the real world (recall relativisation from lesson 1). Quantum advantage experiments: Google's 2019 random-circuit sampling claim targeted a sampling task believed hard classically under complexity assumptions. Improved classical simulations later narrowed the claimed gap. Such experiments test conjectures; they don't prove separations. The map, with confidence levels Relationship Status ------ P inside BPP inside BQP inside PSPACE Proven BPP inside Σ₂ and Π₂ Proven P equals BPP Conjectured BPP inside NP Open Factoring in BQP Proven (Shor) Factoring not in BPP Believed, unproven NP inside BQP Believed false Key takeaways RP and coRP have one-sided error (each extra run halves the error); BPP has two-sided error (majority vote, error falls exponentially); ZPP, the overlap of RP and coRP, is zero-error, expected polynomial time. Freivalds checks a claimed matrix product with three matrix–vector products per trial; Schwartz–Zippel puts polynomial identity testing in coRP, with no deterministic polynomial algorithm known. Proven: P inside BPP, BPP inside Σ₂ ∩ Π₂ and inside P/poly. Conjectured: P equals BPP (implied by plausible circuit lower bounds). Open: whether BPP is inside NP. Proven: BPP inside BQP inside PP inside PSPACE; separating BQP from BPP would separate P from PSPACE. Query-model advantages such as Grover's do not require that class separation. Shor puts factoring in BQP; Grover gives a proven-optimal quadratic speed-up for black-box search. NP inside BQP is believed false.
